items.stem: What does the adage “Don't count your chickens before they hatch” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: An adage is a well-known saying that gives advice. This one warns against planning on uncertain results.
explanation.tip: Ask: what advice would this saying give a person?

options.label: A
options.text: Farmers should hatch more eggs.
options.rationale: This is too literal.

options.label: B
options.text: Chickens are hard to count.
options.rationale: This misses the lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: Don't depend on something before it actually happens.

options.label: D
options.text: Always count your chickens carefully.
options.rationale: The adage is not about real chickens.

items.stem: Which sentence contains a simile?

explanation.whyCorrect: Similes compare two things using like or as: “as soft as a feather.”
explanation.tip: Spot the word like or as connecting two unlike things.

options.label: A
options.text: She spoke softly to the baby.
options.rationale: This is literal.

options.label: B
options.text: Her voice was a gentle breeze.
options.rationale: This is a metaphor; it has no like or as.

options.label: C
options.text: The feather floated down.
options.rationale: No comparison is made.

options.label: D
options.text: Her voice was as soft as a feather.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for enormous?

explanation.whyCorrect: Synonyms have almost the same meaning: enormous and huge both mean very big.
explanation.tip: Synonym = same meaning. Antonym = opposite meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: huge

options.label: B
options.text: tiny
options.rationale: Tiny is an antonym (opposite).

options.label: C
options.text: ancient
options.rationale: Ancient means very old.

options.label: D
options.text: noisy
options.rationale: Noisy is about sound, not size.

items.stem: Which word is an antonym for generous?

explanation.whyCorrect: A generous person shares; a selfish person does not. They are opposites.
explanation.tip: Test an antonym by putting “not” in front: not generous = selfish.

options.label: A
options.text: giving
options.rationale: Giving is a synonym.

options.label: B
options.text: selfish

options.label: C
options.text: helpful
options.rationale: Helpful is similar, not opposite.

options.label: D
options.text: kind
options.rationale: Kind is close in meaning to generous.

items.stem: Choose the relative pronoun that best completes: “The girl ____ won the race is my cousin.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Who refers to people and connects the clause “won the race” to “the girl.”
explanation.tip: who/whom → people, which → things, that → both.

options.label: A
options.text: which
options.rationale: Use which for things, not people.

options.label: B
options.text: where
options.rationale: Where is a relative adverb for places.

options.label: C
options.text: who

options.label: D
options.text: whose
options.rationale: Whose shows ownership.

items.stem: This is the park ____ we had our picnic.

explanation.whyCorrect: Where is a relative adverb that refers to a place (the park).
explanation.tip: where → place, when → time, why → reason.

options.label: A
options.text: when
options.rationale: When refers to a time, not a place.

options.label: B
options.text: who
options.rationale: Who refers to a person.

options.label: C
options.text: why
options.rationale: Why gives a reason.

options.label: D
options.text: where

items.stem: Which sentence uses the PAST progressive tense?

explanation.whyCorrect: Past progressive = was/were + -ing verb. It shows an action that was ongoing in the past.
explanation.tip: Progressive tenses use a form of be + a verb ending in -ing.

options.label: A
options.text: We were walking to school when it started to rain.

options.label: B
options.text: We walk to school every day.
options.rationale: This is the simple present.

options.label: C
options.text: We are walking to school now.
options.rationale: This is the present progressive.

options.label: D
options.text: We will be walking to school tomorrow.
options.rationale: This is the future progressive.

items.stem: Tomorrow at noon, I ____ my grandmother.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tomorrow at noon” points to an ongoing action in the future: will be + visiting.
explanation.tip: Time clue words (yesterday, now, tomorrow) tell you which tense to use.

options.label: A
options.text: visited
options.rationale: Visited is simple past.

options.label: B
options.text: will be visiting

options.label: C
options.text: am visiting
options.rationale: Am visiting is present.

options.label: D
options.text: was visiting
options.rationale: Was shows past time, but “tomorrow” is future.

items.stem: Which modal verb shows that something is REQUIRED? “Visitors ____ wear a helmet in the factory.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Must expresses a rule or requirement.
explanation.tip: Modals: can (ability), may/might (possibility), must (necessity).

options.label: A
options.text: can
options.rationale: Can shows ability or permission.

options.label: B
options.text: may
options.rationale: May shows permission or possibility.

options.label: C
options.text: must

options.label: D
options.text: might
options.rationale: Might shows something is possible, not required.

items.stem: Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct order?

explanation.whyCorrect: Order: opinion → size → age → shape → color → origin → material → purpose.
explanation.tip: Say it aloud: the correct order usually “sounds right” in English.

options.label: A
options.text: She wore a blue long beautiful dress.
options.rationale: Color should come after opinion and size.

options.label: B
options.text: She wore a beautiful blue long dress.
options.rationale: Size (long) comes before color (blue).

options.label: C
options.text: She wore a long beautiful blue dress.
options.rationale: Opinion (beautiful) comes before size (long).

options.label: D
options.text: She wore a beautiful long blue dress.

items.stem: What is the prepositional phrase in this sentence? “The cat slept under the warm blanket.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition (under) and ends with a noun (blanket).
explanation.tip: Common prepositions: in, on, under, over, near, after, between.

options.label: A
options.text: under the warm blanket

options.label: B
options.text: warm blanket
options.rationale: This leaves out the preposition under.

options.label: C
options.text: slept under
options.rationale: A prepositional phrase starts with the preposition and ends with its object.

options.label: D
options.text: The cat slept
options.rationale: This is the subject and verb.

items.stem: Which of these is a complete sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: A complete sentence has a subject (My brother) and a predicate (plays soccer) and expresses a complete thought.
explanation.tip: Ask: Who or what? Does what? If either is missing, it's a fragment.

options.label: A
options.text: Because it was raining.
options.rationale: This is a dependent clause that cannot stand alone.

options.label: B
options.text: My brother plays soccer on Fridays.

options.label: C
options.text: Running across the big field.
options.rationale: There is no subject—who is running?

options.label: D
options.text: The tall boy with the red hat.
options.rationale: There is no verb telling what the boy does.

items.stem: Which is the best way to fix this run-on? “I finished my homework I went outside to play.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Joining the two sentences with a comma and a conjunction (and) fixes the run-on.
explanation.tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma + and/but/so.

options.label: A
options.text: I finished my homework I went, outside to play.
options.rationale: A comma in the wrong place does not fix the run-on.

options.label: B
options.text: I finished my homework I went outside, to play.
options.rationale: Two sentences are still joined with nothing between them.

options.label: C
options.text: I finished my homework, and then I went outside to play.

options.label: D
options.text: I finished. My homework I went outside to play.
options.rationale: This creates a fragment and an awkward sentence.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “____ going to the museum on Saturday.”

explanation.whyCorrect: They're is a contraction of they are: They are going to the museum.
explanation.tip: Test it: replace with “they are.” If it works, use they're.

options.label: A
options.text: Their
options.rationale: Their shows ownership (their bags).

options.label: B
options.text: Theyre
options.rationale: This is missing the apostrophe.

options.label: C
options.text: There
options.rationale: There tells about a place.

options.label: D
options.text: They're

items.stem: Which sentence uses its or it's correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Its (no apostrophe) shows ownership; it's means it is.
explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes: his, hers, its, ours, theirs.

options.label: A
options.text: The dog wagged its tail.

options.label: B
options.text: The dog lost it's bone.
options.rationale: It's means it is; ownership is its.

options.label: C
options.text: It's tail was wagging.
options.rationale: It's means it is.

options.label: D
options.text: Its raining outside.
options.rationale: It is raining needs it's.

items.stem: I would like ____ cookies, please.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two is the number 2.
explanation.tip: to = direction, too = also/very, two = 2.

options.label: A
options.text: two

options.label: B
options.text: to
options.rationale: To shows direction or is part of a verb (to go).

options.label: C
options.text: too
options.rationale: Too means also or very.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a pronoun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Remove “Ali and” to test: “Mom gave the tickets to me.” That sounds correct.
explanation.tip: Cover the other person's name, then choose the pronoun that sounds right.

options.label: A
options.text: Ali and me went to the show.
options.rationale: Subjects need subject pronouns: Ali and I.

options.label: B
options.text: Mom gave the tickets to Ali and me.

options.label: C
options.text: Me and Ali got the tickets.
options.rationale: Me cannot be the subject; use Ali and I.

options.label: D
options.text: Mom gave the tickets to Ali and I.
options.rationale: After a preposition (to), use the object pronoun me.

items.stem: Choose the verb that agrees with the subject: “The students in my class ____ to recess at noon.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The subject is students (plural), not class. Plural subjects take go.
explanation.tip: Ignore the prepositional phrase (in my class) to find the real subject.

options.label: A
options.text: is going
options.rationale: Is goes with a singular subject.

options.label: B
options.text: goes
options.rationale: The subject students is plural, so the verb has no -s.

options.label: C
options.text: go

options.label: D
options.text: has gone
options.rationale: Has goes with a singular subject.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Sheep is an irregular plural—it stays the same: one sheep, two sheep.
explanation.tip: Irregular plurals don't add -s: child → children, mouse → mice, sheep → sheep.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Swim is irregular: swim → swam → swum.
explanation.tip: Irregular verbs change their spelling in the past tense instead of adding -ed.

items.stem: Which sentence compares correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Compare TWO things with -er (or more); compare THREE or more with -est (or most).
explanation.tip: Never use more AND -er together.

options.label: A
options.text: This puzzle is more harder than the last one.
options.rationale: Do not use more with -er.

options.label: B
options.text: This puzzle is hardest than the last one.
options.rationale: Use -est for three or more things, and never with than.

options.label: C
options.text: This puzzle is most hard than the last one.
options.rationale: Most is for three or more things.

options.label: D
options.text: This puzzle is harder than the last one.

items.stem: Which sentence avoids a double negative?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use only one negative word in a sentence: don't + any.
explanation.tip: Negative words: no, not, never, nobody, nothing, none.

options.label: A
options.text: I don't have any homework tonight.

options.label: B
options.text: I haven't got no homework tonight.
options.rationale: Haven't and no are two negatives.

options.label: C
options.text: I don't never have homework.
options.rationale: Don't and never are two negatives.

options.label: D
options.text: I don't have no homework tonight.
options.rationale: Don't and no are two negatives.

items.stem: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, months, and names of places.
explanation.tip: Proper nouns (specific names) need capitals.

options.label: A
options.text: Last July, my Family visited Riyadh.
options.rationale: Family is a common noun here.

options.label: B
options.text: Last July, my family visited Riyadh.

options.label: C
options.text: last July, My family visited Riyadh.
options.rationale: Capitalize the first word; don't capitalize my in the middle.

options.label: D
options.text: Last july, my family visited riyadh.
options.rationale: Months and city names are proper nouns.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Put quotation marks around the exact words spoken, with the question mark inside.
explanation.tip: Punctuation of the spoken words stays inside the quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.text: “Can we go to the park,” asked Huda?
options.rationale: The question mark belongs inside the quotation marks.

options.label: B
options.text: Can we go to the park? “asked Huda.”
options.rationale: Only the spoken words go inside quotation marks.

options.label: C
options.text: “Can we go to the park?” asked Huda.

options.label: D
options.text: “Can we go to the park”? asked Huda.
options.rationale: End punctuation goes inside the closing quotation mark.

items.stem: Where does the comma belong? “I wanted to play outside but it was raining.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so) that joins two complete sentences.
explanation.tip: Remember FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

options.label: A
options.text: after but
options.rationale: The comma comes before but, not after.

options.label: B
options.text: No comma is needed.
options.rationale: Two complete sentences joined by but need a comma.

options.label: C
options.text: after wanted
options.rationale: The comma goes before the conjunction that joins two sentences.

options.label: D
options.text: after outside: “I wanted to play outside, but it was raining.”

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Beauty + ful: change y to i and add -ful = beautiful.
explanation.tip: When a word ends in consonant + y, change y to i before adding most suffixes.

options.label: A
options.text: beautiful

options.label: B
options.text: beatiful
options.rationale: Missing the u after the e-a.

options.label: C
options.text: beautyful
options.rationale: When adding -ful, change y to i.

options.label: D
options.text: beutiful
options.rationale: Missing the a.

items.stem: Add -ing to the word hop: I am ____ on one foot.

explanation.whyCorrect: Hop has one short vowel and ends in one consonant, so double the p: hopping.
explanation.tip: Short vowel + one consonant → double it before -ing or -ed.

items.stem: Which word is the most precise replacement for went in: “The rabbit went across the yard when it heard the dog”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Darted shows a quick, sudden movement—exactly what a frightened rabbit does.
explanation.tip: Replace vague verbs (went, got, said) with words that show HOW.

options.label: A
options.text: moved
options.rationale: Moved is just as vague as went.

options.label: B
options.text: darted

options.label: C
options.text: walked
options.rationale: Walked doesn't show the rabbit's fear or speed.

options.label: D
options.text: was
options.rationale: Was is not an action.

items.stem: Which sentence would be best in a formal report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Formal language is clear and serious, without slang or casual words.
explanation.tip: Ask: would this sound right in a science textbook?

options.label: A
options.text: Guess what? Sun = tall plants.
options.rationale: Formal writing uses full sentences, not shortcuts.

options.label: B
options.text: So, like, the sunny plants won.
options.rationale: Like and won are casual words.

options.label: C
options.text: The experiment showed that plants grew taller in sunlight.

options.label: D
options.text: The plants totally grew way taller in the sun!
options.rationale: Totally and way are informal.

items.stem: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about why owls are good night hunters?

explanation.whyCorrect: A topic sentence tells the main idea the whole paragraph will explain.
explanation.tip: A good topic sentence is broad enough to cover all the details.

options.label: A
options.text: Owls are birds.
options.rationale: Too general—it doesn't introduce the topic of night hunting.

options.label: B
options.text: I saw an owl once at my uncle's farm.
options.rationale: This is a personal story, not a topic sentence for this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: Their feathers are soft.
options.rationale: This is a detail, not the main point.

options.label: D
options.text: Owls have special features that make them excellent hunters at night.

items.stem: Choose the best linking word: “Bats sleep during the day. ____, they hunt for insects at night.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences contrast day and night, so a contrast transition fits.
explanation.tip: Transitions show how ideas connect: adding, contrasting, giving examples, or showing time.

options.label: A
options.text: Instead

options.label: B
options.text: Because
options.rationale: Because cannot start this kind of contrast.

options.label: C
options.text: Also
options.rationale: Also adds a similar idea; this idea contrasts.

options.label: D
options.text: For example
options.rationale: The second sentence is not an example of the first.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to make a clear story.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences follow time order: waking, getting ready, a problem, and the solution.
explanation.tip: Use time words (first, when, later) to help readers follow events.

sequence: Sami woke up early on the first day of school.
He packed his bag and ate breakfast quickly.
When he reached the gate, he realized he had forgotten his lunch.
Luckily, his father arrived a minute later holding the lunch box.

items.stem: Which detail BEST supports the opinion “Students should have longer lunch breaks”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A strong reason connects directly to the opinion and can be supported with facts.
explanation.tip: Ask: does this detail prove WHY the opinion is right?

options.label: A
options.text: Lunch is my favorite part of the day.
options.rationale: This is a personal feeling, not a reason others can check.

options.label: B
options.text: Many students do not have time to finish their food in 20 minutes.

options.label: C
options.text: Pizza is served on Thursdays.
options.rationale: This fact doesn't support longer breaks.

options.label: D
options.text: Some schools start at 7:30.
options.rationale: School start time is not about lunch length.

items.stem: From whose point of view is “The Second Try” told?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator says “I” and describes their own shaking hands and burning face.
explanation.tip: First-person narrators use I, me, and my and are part of the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Dana, the narrator's best friend
options.rationale: Dana is a character the narrator talks about.

options.label: B
options.text: an outside narrator who knows everyone's thoughts
options.rationale: The story uses “I” and only shares one person's thoughts.

options.label: C
options.text: the student giving the speech, in first person

options.label: D
options.text: Mr. Farouk, the teacher
options.rationale: Mr. Farouk is described from the outside.

items.stem: How does the first-person point of view affect how the first speech is described?

explanation.whyCorrect: Because the narrator tells their own experience, we get feelings and sensations, not just events.
explanation.tip: Ask: what can THIS narrator know and feel? How does that shape what we learn?

options.label: A
options.text: Readers learn exactly what every classmate was thinking.
options.rationale: A first-person narrator cannot know others' thoughts.

options.label: B
options.text: Readers see the speech mainly through Dana's eyes.
options.rationale: Dana does not narrate.

options.label: C
options.text: Readers get a calm, factual report of the speech.
options.rationale: The description is emotional, not factual.

options.label: D
options.text: Readers feel the narrator's panic from the inside, like the words “slipped away like sand.”

items.stem: Which sentence best states the theme of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last line—“Being knocked back … isn't the same as being beaten”—expresses the theme.
explanation.tip: Theme often appears in what a character realizes at the end.

options.label: A
options.text: A setback is not a failure if you keep trying.

options.label: B
options.text: Sea turtles have a hard life in the ocean.
options.rationale: This is a topic of the speech, not the story's lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers should give students second chances.
options.rationale: This focuses on the teacher, not the narrator's growth.

options.label: D
options.text: Note cards make speeches harder.
options.rationale: The narrator leaves the cards behind, but that is a detail, not the theme.

items.stem: How does the memory of the baby turtles help the narrator?

explanation.whyCorrect: The turtles keep crawling despite waves, and the narrator applies that lesson to their own situation.
explanation.tip: When a character remembers something, ask how it changes their next action.

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the narrator decide to skip the speech.
options.rationale: The narrator decides to try again.

options.label: B
options.text: It gives the narrator courage to try the speech again.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes the narrator want a new speech topic.
options.rationale: The narrator keeps the same topic.

options.label: D
options.text: It reminds the narrator to study more facts.
options.rationale: The narrator already knows the facts well.

items.stem: “Every word I had memorized slipped away like sand through my fingers.” What does this simile show?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sand runs out of your hand even when you grip it—just as the words escaped the nervous narrator.
explanation.tip: Figure out what quality the two things share.

options.label: A
options.text: The narrator enjoyed the speech.
options.rationale: The rest of the paragraph shows fear.

options.label: B
options.text: The words were written in the sand.
options.rationale: The comparison is about memory, not writing.

options.label: C
options.text: The narrator could not hold on to the words, no matter how hard they tried.

options.label: D
options.text: The narrator was standing on a beach.
options.rationale: The speech is in a classroom; the sand is figurative.

items.stem: Compare the narrator at the first speech with the narrator at the second speech.

explanation.whyCorrect: The change from shaking and mumbling to smiling and answering questions shows growth.
explanation.tip: Compare the same character at two points in a story to see how they change.

options.label: A
options.text: The narrator reads more cards the second time.
options.rationale: The cards stay in the desk the second time.

options.label: B
options.text: The narrator is nervous both times and never improves.
options.rationale: By the end, the narrator is smiling and answering questions.

options.label: C
options.text: The narrator is confident both times.
options.rationale: The narrator's hands shook the first time.

options.label: D
options.text: First the narrator relies on note cards and freezes; second the narrator speaks freely and engages the class.

items.stem: Which TWO quotations show that the second speech went well?

explanation.whyCorrect: The class reacting with interest and asking questions shows success.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that directly proves the answer, not details that point the other way.

options.label: A
options.text: “Heads lifted. Someone gasped.”

options.label: B
options.text: “I almost said no.”
options.rationale: This happens before the second speech.

options.label: C
options.text: “the class was asking questions I could actually answer.”

options.label: D
options.text: “My voice wobbled at first.”
options.rationale: This shows some nervousness.

items.stem: True or false: The narrator starts the second speech with a surprising fact to grab the audience's attention.

explanation.whyCorrect: Starting with “Did you know…?” and a surprising statistic makes heads lift—an attention-grabbing hook.
explanation.tip: Infer the purpose of a choice by looking at its effect on others.

items.stem: How do the three stanzas of “City Morning” fit together?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first two stanzas build noise and activity; the last stanza contrasts it with a quiet golden sky.
explanation.tip: Look for a turn: a word like “but” or a change in mood between stanzas.

options.label: A
options.text: Stanzas 1–2 show the city waking up loudly; stanza 3 turns to the speaker's quiet moment.

options.label: B
options.text: The stanzas tell events from evening to midnight.
options.rationale: The poem takes place in the morning.

options.label: C
options.text: Every stanza repeats the same idea in the same way.
options.rationale: The last stanza shifts to a new idea.

options.label: D
options.text: Each stanza describes a different city.
options.rationale: All three describe the same morning.

items.stem: “The city yawns and stretches wide.” What kind of figurative language is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: The city is given human actions (yawning and stretching), so this is personification.
explanation.tip: Personification = giving human qualities to something that isn't human.

options.label: A
options.text: onomatopoeia
options.rationale: Yawn is not a sound word here.

options.label: B
options.text: personification

options.label: C
options.text: rhyme
options.rationale: Rhyme is about sounds, not giving human actions.

options.label: D
options.text: simile
options.rationale: There is no like or as.

items.stem: “The busy, bustling, buzzing throng.” Which sound device is used?

explanation.whyCorrect: Repeating the starting sound b in nearby words is alliteration. It makes the line sound fast and noisy.
explanation.tip: Alliteration = same first consonant sound in a row of words.

options.label: A
options.text: onomatopoeia — every word is a sound
options.rationale: Busy and bustling are not sound words.

options.label: B
options.text: repetition of a whole line
options.rationale: No full line repeats.

options.label: C
options.text: alliteration — repeated b sounds

options.label: D
options.text: rhyme — the words end with the same sound
options.rationale: The words share beginning sounds, not ending sounds.

items.stem: How does the speaker reflect on the morning in the last stanza?

explanation.whyCorrect: “That minute, friend, is mine” shows the speaker treasures the calm moment.
explanation.tip: In poems, the speaker's final lines often reveal their feelings about the topic.

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker wishes the city were louder.
options.rationale: The speaker prefers the quiet minute.

options.label: B
options.text: The speaker complains about the baker's singing.
options.rationale: The baker is part of the description, not a complaint.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker plans to leave the city forever.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests leaving.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker values a short, quiet moment before the busy day begins.

items.stem: What problem does “Catching Water in the Desert” describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paragraph 1 explains that rare rain rushes over dry ground and disappears.
explanation.tip: Problem-and-solution texts usually state the problem first.

options.label: A
options.text: Rainwater rushes away before people can use it.

options.label: B
options.text: Solar pumps are expensive.
options.rationale: Cost is not discussed.

options.label: C
options.text: Deserts have too many farmers.
options.rationale: The text never says this.

options.label: D
options.text: Cisterns are too old to work.
options.rationale: Old cisterns are evidence that the idea works.

items.stem: Which solutions does the article describe? Choose all that apply.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains two solutions: cisterns and check dams.
explanation.tip: Look for signal words: One solution…, Another solution….

options.label: A
options.text: cloud seeding to make rain
options.rationale: This is not mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: underground cisterns

options.label: C
options.text: moving villages to rivers
options.rationale: This is not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: check dams across valleys

items.stem: Why does water in a cistern evaporate slowly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Because the tank is underground and covered, the water stays cool and does not evaporate quickly.”
explanation.tip: Because introduces a cause.

options.label: A
options.text: Check dams protect the cisterns.
options.rationale: Check dams are a separate solution.

options.label: B
options.text: The tank is underground and covered, so it stays cool.

options.label: C
options.text: Gutters cool the water.
options.rationale: Gutters only guide water into pipes.

options.label: D
options.text: Plastic liners stop water from moving.
options.rationale: Liners are a modern material; the article links slow evaporation to being underground and covered.

items.stem: Which TWO main ideas does the article develop?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains the problem and then shows old and new ways to store water.
explanation.tip: Grade 5 texts may have more than one main idea. Check each section.

options.label: A
options.text: Deserts are hot, and rain is dangerous.
options.rationale: Rain is helpful when it can be saved.

options.label: B
options.text: Farmers dislike storms, and walls stop floods.
options.rationale: The walls help water soak in; they don't just stop floods.

options.label: C
options.text: Desert communities face a water problem, and both ancient and modern methods help solve it.

options.label: D
options.text: Archaeologists study old tanks, and engineers build pumps.
options.rationale: These are supporting details.

items.stem: “The water stays cool and does not evaporate quickly in the heat.” What does evaporate mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Heat causes water to disappear into the air—a cause/effect clue to the meaning.
explanation.tip: L.5.4: cause-and-effect relationships can reveal meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: flow downhill
options.rationale: Flowing is not caused by heat.

options.label: B
options.text: become dirty
options.rationale: Nothing suggests dirt.

options.label: C
options.text: freeze into ice
options.rationale: Freezing happens in cold, not heat.

options.label: D
options.text: turn into vapor and disappear into the air

items.stem: Why does the author mention that some cisterns are more than two thousand years old?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence before says “These methods are not new.” The ancient cisterns are evidence for that point.
explanation.tip: Find which point a detail supports by reading the sentence just before it.

options.label: A
options.text: to support the point that these water-saving methods are not new

options.label: B
options.text: to show that cisterns break easily
options.rationale: Surviving 2,000 years suggests the opposite.

options.label: C
options.text: to explain how solar pumps work
options.rationale: Pumps are mentioned later as modern.

options.label: D
options.text: to prove deserts used to have more rain
options.rationale: The detail is about the method, not the climate.

items.stem: How are the two accounts of the storm different?

explanation.whyCorrect: A firsthand account tells personal experience; a secondhand account reports facts.
explanation.tip: Ask: Who wrote it? Were they there? What do they focus on?

options.label: A
options.text: They describe two different storms.
options.rationale: Both describe the same March 12 storm.

options.label: B
options.text: Rania's journal describes feelings and experiences; the news report gives facts and numbers.

options.label: C
options.text: The news report describes being scared at night.
options.rationale: Feelings appear only in the journal.

options.label: D
options.text: Both accounts give exact wind speeds.
options.rationale: Only the news report gives wind speed.

items.stem: Which information appears ONLY in the news report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Only the reporter gives details about crews and power being restored.
explanation.tip: Compare point of view: what can each writer know?

options.label: A
options.text: The storm happened during the night.
options.rationale: Both accounts show it happened early in the morning.

options.label: B
options.text: There was flooding on the streets.
options.rationale: Both mention flooding.

options.label: C
options.text: Electricity was restored to most homes by noon.

options.label: D
options.text: The wind was very strong.
options.rationale: Both describe strong wind.

items.stem: In Rania's journal, the wind “howled … like an angry animal.” This is an example of —

explanation.whyCorrect: The wind is compared to an animal using like, so it is a simile.
explanation.tip: Simile = like/as.

options.label: A
options.text: an idiom
options.rationale: It is a new comparison, not a common saying.

options.label: B
options.text: a fact
options.rationale: It is a figurative description.

options.label: C
options.text: a metaphor
options.rationale: The comparison uses like.

options.label: D
options.text: a simile

items.stem: About one week after a new moon, what phase do we see?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article says about one week after the new moon we see the first quarter.
explanation.tip: In sequence texts, notice time words: a few days later, about one week, after two weeks.

options.label: A
options.text: first quarter

options.label: B
options.text: new moon
options.rationale: That is the starting point.

options.label: C
options.text: full moon
options.rationale: A full moon appears after about two weeks.

options.label: D
options.text: crescent
options.rationale: A crescent appears just a few days after the new moon.

items.stem: Put the Moon's phases in order, starting with the new moon.

explanation.whyCorrect: The lit part we can see grows from nothing, to a sliver, to half, to the whole face.
explanation.tip: Use the time clues in the text to order events.

sequence: new moon
crescent
first quarter
full moon

items.stem: Why do we see almost nothing during a new moon?

explanation.whyCorrect: The Moon is between Earth and the Sun, so its lit half faces away from us.
explanation.tip: Read carefully for the scientific reason, not a guess from everyday experience.

options.label: A
options.text: The Moon stops reflecting light.
options.rationale: The Sun always lights half the Moon.

options.label: B
options.text: The lit side of the Moon is facing away from Earth.

options.label: C
options.text: Earth's shadow covers the whole Moon.
options.rationale: The text explains phases by viewing angle, not Earth's shadow.

options.label: D
options.text: Clouds always cover the Moon at that time.
options.rationale: Weather is not mentioned.

items.stem: True or false: According to the article, the amount of the Moon that the Sun lights up changes every night.

explanation.whyCorrect: The Sun always lights half the Moon. What changes is how much of that lit half WE can see.
explanation.tip: Watch for statements that sound right but change one key detail.

items.stem: “People have used this dependable pattern for thousands of years.” What does dependable mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: A pattern used for calendars must be reliable; depend + -able = able to be depended on.
explanation.tip: Combine context with word parts to check your answer.

options.label: A
options.text: hard to understand
options.rationale: People could use it for calendars, so it must be easy to predict.

options.label: B
options.text: brand new
options.rationale: It has been used for thousands of years.

options.label: C
options.text: able to be trusted to happen the same way

options.label: D
options.text: very bright
options.rationale: Brightness is not related to the word.

items.stem: The Greek root tele means far, and scope means look. What is a telescope?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tele (far) + scope (look) = a tool to look at far objects.
explanation.tip: Learn common roots: tele, scope, graph, phon, auto, bio.

options.label: A
options.text: a small, close object
options.rationale: Tele means far, not close.

options.label: B
options.text: a tool for writing
options.rationale: Graph means write.

options.label: C
options.text: a tool for hearing far away
options.rationale: Phone means sound; scope means look.

options.label: D
options.text: a tool for looking at things far away

items.stem: Match each root to its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Audience (hear), visible (see), transport (carry), construct (build).
explanation.tip: Think of a word you know with the root to remember its meaning.

items.stem: The Latin root dict means say or speak. Which word means “to say what will happen in the future”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pre (before) + dict (say) = to say beforehand.
explanation.tip: Combine the prefix and the root meanings.

options.label: A
options.text: predict

options.label: B
options.text: dictionary
options.rationale: A dictionary contains words but doesn't describe the future.

options.label: C
options.text: dictate
options.rationale: Dictate means to say aloud for someone to write.

options.label: D
options.text: contradict
options.rationale: Contra (against) + dict = to say the opposite.

items.stem: In which sentence does wind mean to turn or twist?

explanation.whyCorrect: Wind (rhymes with find) is a verb meaning to turn. Wind (rhymes with pinned) is moving air.
explanation.tip: Homographs are spelled the same but have different meanings and sometimes different pronunciations.

options.label: A
options.text: The wind felt cold this morning.
options.rationale: This is moving air.

options.label: B
options.text: Please wind the string around the spool.

options.label: C
options.text: The wind blew the leaves away.
options.rationale: Here wind is moving air.

options.label: D
options.text: A strong wind knocked the sign over.
options.rationale: This is moving air.

items.stem: “The doctor wound a bandage around the wound.” What do the two words mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Wound (rhymes with sound) is the past of wind; wound (rhymes with moon) is an injury.
explanation.tip: Use each word's job in the sentence (action or thing) to choose its meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: first: an injury; second: wrapped
options.rationale: The order is reversed.

options.label: B
options.text: both mean wrapped
options.rationale: The second wound is a thing that is wrapped.

options.label: C
options.text: first: wrapped; second: an injury

options.label: D
options.text: both mean an injury
options.rationale: The first wound is an action.

items.stem: What does the proverb “Actions speak louder than words” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: This proverb teaches that behavior proves what a person really means.
explanation.tip: Proverbs give advice or a truth about life.

options.label: A
options.text: Quiet people are better.
options.rationale: The proverb is not about quiet people.

options.label: B
options.text: People should speak more loudly.
options.rationale: This is too literal.

options.label: C
options.text: Words are more important than actions.
options.rationale: It means the opposite.

options.label: D
options.text: What people do shows more than what they say.

items.stem: “We're in the same boat,” said Lina when both of them forgot their homework. What does she mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “In the same boat” means facing the same problem.
explanation.tip: Idioms can't be understood word by word.

options.label: A
options.text: They are in the same situation.

options.label: B
options.text: They are going sailing.
options.rationale: There is no real boat.

options.label: C
options.text: They both like boats.
options.rationale: This is the literal meaning.

options.label: D
options.text: They need to row together.
options.rationale: The idiom is about sharing a situation, not rowing.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a metaphor?

explanation.whyCorrect: The metaphor says the classroom IS a beehive to show how busy it was.
explanation.tip: Metaphors compare without like or as.

options.label: A
options.text: The classroom was very busy.
options.rationale: This is literal.

options.label: B
options.text: The classroom was a beehive of activity.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees live in hives.
options.rationale: This is a literal fact.

options.label: D
options.text: The classroom was as busy as a beehive.
options.rationale: This uses as … as, so it is a simile.

items.stem: Which pair of words are antonyms?

explanation.whyCorrect: Ancient means very old; modern means new—opposites.
explanation.tip: Antonyms are opposites.

options.label: A
options.text: ancient / old
options.rationale: These are synonyms.

options.label: B
options.text: ancient / historic
options.rationale: These are similar.

options.label: C
options.text: ancient / modern

options.label: D
options.text: modern / new
options.rationale: These are synonyms.

items.stem: Compared to the noisy cafeteria, the library felt serene. What does serene mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comparison with noisy shows that serene means quiet and calm.
explanation.tip: L.5.4.a: comparisons in a sentence are clues to meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: crowded
options.rationale: The comparison with noisy suggests the opposite.

options.label: B
options.text: dark
options.rationale: Nothing mentions light.

options.label: C
options.text: boring
options.rationale: Serene describes a peaceful feeling, not interest.

options.label: D
options.text: calm and peaceful

items.stem: Which resource would BEST help you find a synonym for happy?

explanation.whyCorrect: A thesaurus lists synonyms and antonyms.
explanation.tip: Dictionary → meaning and pronunciation; thesaurus → synonyms.

options.label: A
options.text: a thesaurus

options.label: B
options.text: a calendar
options.rationale: A calendar shows dates.

options.label: C
options.text: an encyclopedia
options.rationale: An encyclopedia gives facts about topics.

options.label: D
options.text: an atlas
options.rationale: An atlas contains maps.

items.stem: Which word is a conjunction in this sentence? “I wanted pizza, but my sister wanted pasta.”

explanation.whyCorrect: But joins two ideas, so it is a conjunction.
explanation.tip: Coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

options.label: A
options.text: pasta
options.rationale: Pasta is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: but

options.label: C
options.text: my
options.rationale: My is a possessive pronoun.

options.label: D
options.text: wanted
options.rationale: Wanted is a verb.

items.stem: Which word is an interjection? “Wow, that roller coaster was fast!”

explanation.whyCorrect: An interjection is a word that shows strong feeling, often followed by a comma or exclamation point.
explanation.tip: Interjections: wow, oh, ouch, hooray.

options.label: A
options.text: was
options.rationale: Was is a verb.

options.label: B
options.text: that
options.rationale: That is a demonstrative.

options.label: C
options.text: Wow

options.label: D
options.text: fast
options.rationale: Fast is an adjective.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the present perfect tense?

explanation.whyCorrect: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
explanation.tip: Perfect tenses use has, have, had, or will have.

options.label: A
options.text: She had finished before dinner.
options.rationale: This is past perfect.

options.label: B
options.text: She will have finished by Friday.
options.rationale: This is future perfect.

options.label: C
options.text: She finished her science project.
options.rationale: This is simple past.

options.label: D
options.text: She has finished her science project.

items.stem: By the time we arrived, the movie ____ already started.

explanation.whyCorrect: Past perfect (had + participle) shows an action finished before another past action.
explanation.tip: Two past actions? The earlier one often uses had.

options.label: A
options.text: had

options.label: B
options.text: have
options.rationale: Have does not match the singular movie or past time.

options.label: C
options.text: has
options.rationale: Has is present perfect; the sentence is about the past.

options.label: D
options.text: will have
options.rationale: Will have is future.

items.stem: Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in verb tense?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yesterday shows past time, so walk should be walked to match bought.
explanation.tip: Keep verb tenses consistent unless the time actually changes.

options.label: A
options.text: Every day we walk to the store and buy milk.
options.rationale: Both verbs are in the present.

options.label: B
options.text: Yesterday we walk to the store and bought milk.

options.label: C
options.text: Tomorrow we will walk to the store and buy milk.
options.rationale: Both verbs refer to the future.

options.label: D
options.text: Yesterday we walked to the store and bought milk.
options.rationale: Both verbs are in the past.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Last summer” and “stayed” show past time, so the verb must be traveled.
explanation.tip: Find the time clue, then check every verb against it.

items.stem: Which pair of correlative conjunctions completes the sentence? “You can ____ walk ____ ride your bike.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Correlative conjunctions come in pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also.
explanation.tip: Memorize the four pairs.

options.label: A
options.text: both … or
options.rationale: Both pairs with and.

options.label: B
options.text: not only … or
options.rationale: Not only pairs with but also.

options.label: C
options.text: either … or

options.label: D
options.text: neither … or
options.rationale: Neither pairs with nor.

items.stem: Neither my brother ____ my sister likes spinach.

explanation.whyCorrect: Neither always pairs with nor.
explanation.tip: N goes with N: Neither → Nor.

options.label: A
options.text: but
options.rationale: But is not part of this pair.

options.label: B
options.text: or
options.rationale: Or pairs with either.

options.label: C
options.text: and
options.rationale: And pairs with both.

options.label: D
options.text: nor

items.stem: Which sentence has correct pronoun-antecedent agreement?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each is singular, so the pronoun and noun that follow must be singular.
explanation.tip: Words like each, every, and everyone are singular.

options.label: A
options.text: Each student brought his or her own lunch.

options.label: B
options.text: Each student brought their own lunches.
options.rationale: Each is singular, so lunches should be lunch.

options.label: C
options.text: Each student brought our own lunch.
options.rationale: Our does not refer to student.

options.label: D
options.text: Each student brought its own lunch.
options.rationale: Its is for things, not people.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a relative adverb correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: When refers to a time (day).
explanation.tip: where → place, when → time, why → reason.

options.label: A
options.text: This is the reason when I'm late.
options.rationale: Reason needs why.

options.label: B
options.text: I remember the day when we moved here.

options.label: C
options.text: That's the house why I grew up.
options.rationale: House is a place, so use where.

options.label: D
options.text: I remember the day where we moved here.
options.rationale: Day is a time, so use when.

items.stem: Which sentence is complex (has an independent clause and a dependent clause)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Although it was late” cannot stand alone, so the sentence is complex.
explanation.tip: Dependent clauses often begin with although, because, when, if, since.

options.label: A
options.text: Finishing the game late.
options.rationale: This is a fragment.

options.label: B
options.text: We finished the game.
options.rationale: This is one independent clause.

options.label: C
options.text: Although it was late, we finished the game.

options.label: D
options.text: It was late, and we finished the game.
options.rationale: This is compound: two independent clauses.

items.stem: Which word correctly completes: “This is the ____ book I have ever read.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing with all books ever read needs the superlative best.
explanation.tip: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

options.label: A
options.text: goodest
options.rationale: Good is irregular; goodest is not a word.

options.label: B
options.text: more good
options.rationale: Use best, not more good.

options.label: C
options.text: better
options.rationale: Better compares two things.

options.label: D
options.text: best

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a series?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use commas to separate three or more items in a series.
explanation.tip: Put a comma after each item except the last.

options.label: A
options.text: We packed sandwiches, apples, and juice.

options.label: B
options.text: We packed, sandwiches, apples, and juice.
options.rationale: No comma after the verb.

options.label: C
options.text: We packed sandwiches apples, and juice.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after sandwiches.

options.label: D
options.text: We packed sandwiches, apples, and, juice.
options.rationale: No comma after and.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma after an introductory element?

explanation.whyCorrect: Put a comma after an introductory phrase or clause.
explanation.tip: Read it aloud; the comma goes where you naturally pause after the opener.

options.label: A
options.text: After the bell rang the students, lined up.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: B
options.text: After the bell rang, the students lined up.

options.label: C
options.text: After, the bell rang the students lined up.
options.rationale: After is part of the introductory phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: After the bell, rang the students lined up.
options.rationale: The comma splits the clause.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a comma for direct address?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma to set off the name of the person you are speaking to.
explanation.tip: Direct address = talking TO someone by name.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya please close the door.
options.rationale: A comma is needed after the name.

options.label: B
options.text: Maya please close, the door.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: C
options.text: Maya, please close the door.

options.label: D
options.text: Maya please, close the door.
options.rationale: The comma should come right after the name.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a tag question?

explanation.whyCorrect: Separate a tag question from the rest of the sentence with a comma.
explanation.tip: Tag questions: isn't it? didn't you? won't they?

options.label: A
options.text: You finished, the report didn't you?
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: B
options.text: You finished the report, didn't you.
options.rationale: A question needs a question mark.

options.label: C
options.text: You finished the report didn't you?
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the tag.

options.label: D
options.text: You finished the report, didn't you?

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to write the title of a book?

explanation.whyCorrect: Book titles are italicized (or underlined when handwritten).
explanation.tip: Long works (books, movies) → italics; short works (poems, songs) → quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.text: My favorite book is Charlotte's Web.

options.label: B
options.text: My favorite book is charlotte's web.
options.rationale: Titles need capital letters.

options.label: C
options.text: My favorite book is “Charlotte's Web.”
options.rationale: Quotation marks are for short works such as stories and poems.

options.label: D
options.text: My favorite book is CHARLOTTE'S WEB.
options.rationale: Do not write titles in all capitals.

items.stem: Change to plural: one shelf, two ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: For many words ending in f, change f to v and add -es: shelf → shelves.
explanation.tip: f/fe → ves: leaf → leaves, knife → knives.

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Necessary has one c and two s's.
explanation.tip: Memory trick: one Collar and two Sleeves.

options.label: A
options.text: neccessary
options.rationale: Only one c.

options.label: B
options.text: necessary

options.label: C
options.text: necesary
options.rationale: Two s's are needed.

options.label: D
options.text: neccesary
options.rationale: One c and two s's.

items.stem: Which sentence best combines these? “The fox was hungry. The fox searched the field.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Moving hungry before fox combines the ideas into one clear sentence.
explanation.tip: Combine by turning a short sentence into an adjective or phrase.

options.label: A
options.text: The fox was hungry, the fox searched the field.
options.rationale: This is a comma splice that repeats the fox.

options.label: B
options.text: The fox was hungry and the fox searched.
options.rationale: This repeats the subject and drops a detail.

options.label: C
options.text: The hungry fox searched the field.

options.label: D
options.text: Hungry. The fox searched the field.
options.rationale: This creates a fragment.

items.stem: Choose the best transition: “Recycling saves resources. ____, it reduces the amount of trash in landfills.”

explanation.whyCorrect: In addition adds another supporting point.
explanation.tip: Transitions: adding (also, in addition), contrast (however), example (for instance), result (as a result).

options.label: A
options.text: As a result
options.rationale: The second idea is another benefit, not a result.

options.label: B
options.text: For instance
options.rationale: The second sentence is not an example of the first.

options.label: C
options.text: However
options.rationale: However shows a contrast; these ideas agree.

options.label: D
options.text: In addition

items.stem: Which phrase BEST links a reason to the opinion in an essay?

explanation.whyCorrect: Linking phrases such as “this matters because” or “consequently” connect reasons to opinions.
explanation.tip: W.5.1.c: link opinion and reasons with words, phrases, and clauses.

options.label: A
options.text: This matters because

options.label: B
options.text: Once upon a time
options.rationale: This begins a story, not an argument.

options.label: C
options.text: In my bedroom
options.rationale: This is a place, not a link.

options.label: D
options.text: The end
options.rationale: This ends a story.

items.stem: Put the sentences in order to show a clear sequence in a narrative.

explanation.whyCorrect: Transitions (At first, Then, Moments later, Finally) show the order of events.
explanation.tip: W.5.3.c: use transitional words to manage the sequence of events.

sequence: At first, the cave seemed silent and empty.
Then a faint drip echoed from the darkness.
Moments later, my flashlight caught the glitter of an underground pool.
Finally, I understood where the sound had been coming from.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most concrete and sensory details?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stung, sprinted, and slippery help readers feel and see the moment.
explanation.tip: Show, don't tell: use verbs and details the reader can sense.

options.label: A
options.text: It was raining a lot outside.
options.rationale: This tells, but doesn't show.

options.label: B
options.text: The cold rain stung my cheeks as I sprinted across the slippery bridge.

options.label: C
options.text: I didn't like the rain that day.
options.rationale: This states a feeling without details.

options.label: D
options.text: The weather was bad as I went across.
options.rationale: Bad and went are vague.

items.stem: Which is the best way to take notes from a source without plagiarizing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paraphrasing and listing sources shows respect for others' work.
explanation.tip: Read, cover the text, and write what you remember in your own words.

options.label: A
options.text: Change one word in each sentence.
options.rationale: Small changes are still copying.

options.label: B
options.text: Skip recording the source.
options.rationale: You must list sources you use.

options.label: C
options.text: Write the key facts in your own words and record the source.

options.label: D
options.text: Copy every sentence exactly.
options.rationale: Copying is plagiarism unless you quote and credit the source.

items.stem: What event sets the plot of “The Last Bus Home” in motion?

explanation.whyCorrect: Missing the 6:40 bus creates the problem that drives the rest of the story.
explanation.tip: The inciting incident is the first event that creates the story's problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Yusuf's phone battery dies.
options.rationale: This makes the problem worse, but it isn't the first event.

options.label: B
options.text: Mariam waits at the bakery.
options.rationale: This happens later, as part of the resolution.

options.label: C
options.text: Mrs. Qadri opens the door.
options.rationale: This happens near the end.

options.label: D
options.text: Yusuf misses the last bus after robotics club runs late.

items.stem: How does Yusuf respond to his problem during the walk home?

explanation.whyCorrect: The italic lines (“It wasn't my fault…”) show him preparing to defend himself.
explanation.tip: RL.6.3: notice how characters respond as the plot moves forward.

options.label: A
options.text: He rehearses excuses because he expects to be blamed.

options.label: B
options.text: He runs to catch the bus at the next stop.
options.rationale: He decides to walk the whole way.

options.label: C
options.text: He forgets about the problem completely.
options.rationale: He spends twenty minutes preparing a defense.

options.label: D
options.text: He calls his mother every few minutes.
options.rationale: His phone is dead.

items.stem: How does Yusuf change by the end of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last paragraph states his new understanding about Mariam.
explanation.tip: Character change is often revealed in the final thoughts of the main character.

options.label: A
options.text: He becomes angry at his mother for worrying.
options.rationale: He laughs and feels relieved.

options.label: B
options.text: He realizes his younger sister cares for him, not just the other way around.

options.label: C
options.text: He learns to always charge his phone.
options.rationale: This lesson is never stated.

options.label: D
options.text: He decides to quit the robotics club.
options.rationale: The club is never mentioned again.

items.stem: The story is told in third person but follows only Yusuf's thoughts. How does this affect the reader?

explanation.whyCorrect: A limited narrator lets readers discover the truth at the same moment as the character.
explanation.tip: RL.6.6: ask how the narrator's point of view develops the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Readers learn about every character equally.
options.rationale: The narration stays close to Yusuf.

options.label: B
options.text: Readers know from the start that his family is not angry.
options.rationale: We only learn this when Yusuf does.

options.label: C
options.text: Readers share Yusuf's worry, so they are surprised along with him that no one is angry.

options.label: D
options.text: Readers understand Mariam's thoughts during the whole story.
options.rationale: We don't hear Mariam's thoughts.

items.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yusuf prepares a defense, but discovers his family was only worried. That realization is the theme.
explanation.tip: A theme is a universal statement, not a summary of the plot.

options.label: A
options.text: Robotics clubs should end earlier.
options.rationale: This is a detail, not a universal message.

options.label: B
options.text: Phones should always be charged.
options.rationale: This is practical advice, not the theme.

options.label: C
options.text: Bakeries are good places to wait.
options.rationale: This is about the setting.

options.label: D
options.text: People who care about us may be worried rather than angry when things go wrong.

items.stem: “Yusuf felt the excuses dissolve.” What does the word dissolve suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Like sugar in water, the excuses vanish once he sees no one is angry.
explanation.tip: When a word is used figuratively, think about its literal meaning first, then apply it.

options.label: A
options.text: His prepared excuses disappeared because they were no longer needed.

options.label: B
options.text: He forgot how to speak.
options.rationale: He talks and laughs afterward.

options.label: C
options.text: He wrote his excuses on paper.
options.rationale: The excuses were only in his mind.

options.label: D
options.text: The cocoa melted his excuses.
options.rationale: Dissolve is figurative here.

items.stem: Which TWO details best support the idea that Mariam knows her brother well?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mariam predicted Yusuf's route because she knows his habits.
explanation.tip: RL.6.1: choose evidence that directly supports the specific claim.

options.label: A
options.text: “I told Mama you'd walk the bakery way.”

options.label: B
options.text: “You always do.”

options.label: C
options.text: “Your mother called every shop on this street.”
options.rationale: This is about the mother.

options.label: D
options.text: “She waved wildly.”
options.rationale: This shows excitement, not knowledge of Yusuf.

items.stem: Order these events from “The Last Bus Home.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The plot unfolds as a series of connected episodes from problem to resolution.
explanation.tip: Each episode leads to the next; look for cause and effect.

sequence: The robotics club stays late.
Yusuf watches the bus pull away.
His phone dies after a quick message.
He rehearses excuses while walking.
He finds Mariam waiting at the bakery.

items.stem: How does the second stanza contribute to the poem “Ladder”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stanza 2 links rung widths to specific years—an easy year, a hard year—developing the central metaphor.
explanation.tip: RL.6.5: ask what each stanza adds to the whole poem.

options.label: A
options.text: It describes how to build a ladder.
options.rationale: The poem is not instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: It explains that the different rungs stand for different years in the speaker's life.

options.label: C
options.text: It changes the topic to apple trees.
options.rationale: Apples appear in stanza 3.

options.label: D
options.text: It introduces the grandfather for the first time.
options.rationale: He appears in stanza 1.

items.stem: What does the ladder represent in the poem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each rung is “a year he gave to me,” so the ladder stands for years of the speaker's life shaped by the grandfather.
explanation.tip: A symbol is an object that stands for a bigger idea.

options.label: A
options.text: the storm that destroyed the tree
options.rationale: The storm only explains where the branches came from.

options.label: B
options.text: a tool the speaker needs to fix the house
options.rationale: The ladder is used to reach the grandfather's apples.

options.label: C
options.text: the speaker's life and the grandfather's care that supports it

options.label: D
options.text: the speaker's fear of heights
options.rationale: Fear is never mentioned.

items.stem: In “the third rung, thin and narrow,” what feeling do the words thin and narrow create?

explanation.whyCorrect: Thin and narrow connote fragility, matching “the winter I was sick and weak.”
explanation.tip: Connotation = the feeling a word suggests beyond its dictionary meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: a sense of joy
options.rationale: Joy would match words like wide and steady.

options.label: B
options.text: a sense of boredom
options.rationale: The year is described as hard, not dull.

options.label: C
options.text: a sense of anger
options.rationale: No words suggest anger.

options.label: D
options.text: a sense of difficulty and weakness

items.stem: What is the author's central claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: The introduction and conclusion both state the claim.
explanation.tip: The claim is the position the whole text argues for.

options.label: A
options.text: Schools should keep the five-day week until there is stronger evidence for a four-day week.

options.label: B
options.text: Four-day weeks save schools a lot of money.
options.rationale: The author argues the savings are small.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers should earn higher salaries.
options.rationale: Salaries are mentioned only to explain costs.

options.label: D
options.text: Students need more rest on weekends.
options.rationale: This is the supporters' argument.

items.stem: Which piece of evidence best supports the claim that a four-day week may hurt learning?

explanation.whyCorrect: A study comparing math growth is direct evidence about learning.
explanation.tip: Relevant evidence must connect directly to the specific claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Families must find care for the fifth day.
options.rationale: This is about families, not learning.

options.label: B
options.text: Math scores grew more slowly in districts that switched to four days.

options.label: C
options.text: Supporters believe students need rest.
options.rationale: This is the opposing view.

options.label: D
options.text: Districts save money on buses.
options.rationale: This is about cost, not learning.

items.stem: Which claim in the text is NOT supported by reasons or evidence?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Everyone knows” is a sweeping generalization with no evidence; it weakens the argument.
explanation.tip: RI.6.8: distinguish supported claims from unsupported ones. Watch for “everyone,” “always,” and “never.”

options.label: A
options.text: Savings are usually small because salaries do not change.
options.rationale: The author explains why with a reason.

options.label: B
options.text: Districts do save some money on buses and heating.
options.rationale: This is supported by reports.

options.label: C
options.text: Everyone knows that students would rather stay home anyway, so a four-day week would only make them lazier.

options.label: D
options.text: Students' math scores grew more slowly.
options.rationale: This is supported by a study.

items.stem: How does the author treat the claim that a four-day week saves money?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a concession and rebuttal: “Districts do save some money … but … these savings are usually small.”
explanation.tip: Strong arguments acknowledge the other side, then respond with evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: The author agrees it is the strongest reason.
options.rationale: The author argues the savings are small.

options.label: B
options.text: The author ignores it completely.
options.rationale: Paragraph 3 addresses it.

options.label: C
options.text: The author says it costs more money.
options.rationale: The author says districts do save some.

options.label: D
options.text: The author admits there are some savings, then shows they are small.

items.stem: True or false: The author's concluding paragraph restates the claim.

explanation.whyCorrect: The final sentence repeats that schools should keep the five-day schedule.
explanation.tip: Conclusions in arguments usually restate the claim.

items.stem: What is the central idea of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text explains why reefs matter, the threat of bleaching, and scientists' responses.
explanation.tip: RI.6.2: the central idea is developed across the whole text.

options.label: A
options.text: Coral reefs are vital to ocean life but are threatened by warming water, and scientists are working to protect them.

options.label: B
options.text: Coral polyps are tiny animals.
options.rationale: This is a supporting detail.

options.label: C
options.text: Algae make coral colorful.
options.rationale: This is a detail about the partnership.

options.label: D
options.text: Sea turtles eat reef plants.
options.rationale: This is one example of reef life.

items.stem: Which is the best summary of paragraph 3?

explanation.whyCorrect: A good summary keeps only the key ideas of the paragraph, without opinions.
explanation.tip: Summaries are short, objective, and include only the most important points.

options.label: A
options.text: Coral is beautiful and white.
options.rationale: White coral is bleached and starving.

options.label: B
options.text: Warm water causes coral to expel its algae and turn white; if the heat lasts, the coral can die.

options.label: C
options.text: Coral reefs protect coastlines from storms.
options.rationale: That is paragraph 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Scientists grow coral in nurseries.
options.rationale: That is paragraph 4.

items.stem: According to the text, what causes coral bleaching?

explanation.whyCorrect: “When ocean water becomes too warm … stressed corals expel their algae.”
explanation.tip: Look for “when” and “as a result” to find causes.

options.label: A
options.text: Polyps produce too much food.
options.rationale: The algae produce the food.

options.label: B
options.text: Storm waves break the coral.
options.rationale: Reefs break waves; this does not cause bleaching.

options.label: C
options.text: Water that is too warm makes corals expel their algae.

options.label: D
options.text: Fish eat the algae.
options.rationale: The text does not say this.

items.stem: How does paragraph 2 contribute to the development of ideas in the text?

explanation.whyCorrect: Without knowing the algae feed the coral, readers wouldn't see why losing them means starving.
explanation.tip: RI.6.5: analyze how a paragraph fits into the overall structure.

options.label: A
options.text: It introduces the scientists' solutions.
options.rationale: Solutions come in paragraph 4.

options.label: B
options.text: It lists animals that live on reefs.
options.rationale: That is paragraph 1.

options.label: C
options.text: It argues that reefs cannot be saved.
options.rationale: The text describes hopeful efforts.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains the coral–algae partnership so readers understand why bleaching is harmful.

items.stem: Bleached coral is “not dead, but it is starving.” What does expel mean in “stressed corals expel their algae”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Because the algae leave and the coral turns white and starves, expel must mean force out.
explanation.tip: L.6.4.a: use the overall meaning of the paragraph as a clue.

options.label: A
options.text: push out

options.label: B
options.text: protect
options.rationale: Protection would keep the algae inside.

options.label: C
options.text: feed
options.rationale: If the algae were fed, the coral would not starve.

options.label: D
options.text: grow
options.rationale: Growing would not lead to bleaching.

items.stem: What is the author's point of view about efforts to save reefs?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final sentence balances hope (“these efforts help”) with a limit (“only … if ocean temperatures stop rising”).
explanation.tip: RI.6.6: words like but and only signal the author's view.

options.label: A
options.text: The efforts are useless and should stop.
options.rationale: The author says they help.

options.label: B
options.text: The efforts are helpful, but reefs need ocean temperatures to stop rising to fully recover.

options.label: C
options.text: The efforts have already saved all reefs.
options.rationale: The author says large-scale recovery depends on temperature.

options.label: D
options.text: Only nurseries matter.
options.rationale: Two efforts are described.

items.stem: The Latin root aud means hear. Which word means “able to be heard”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Aud (hear) + -ible (able to be) = audible.
explanation.tip: L.6.4.b: Greek or Latin affixes and roots are clues to meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: auditorium
options.rationale: An auditorium is a place for hearing.

options.label: B
options.text: audition
options.rationale: An audition is a hearing for a performance.

options.label: C
options.text: audible

options.label: D
options.text: audience
options.rationale: An audience is a group that listens.

items.stem: Bio means life and logy means study of. What does a biologist study?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bio (life) + logy (study) + -ist (person) = a person who studies life.
explanation.tip: Split the word into parts and translate each one.

options.label: A
options.text: the past
options.rationale: That is history.

options.label: B
options.text: rocks and minerals
options.rationale: That is geology.

options.label: C
options.text: stars and planets
options.rationale: That is astronomy.

options.label: D
options.text: living things

items.stem: Match each word to its meaning using roots.

explanation.whyCorrect: chron = time, bene = good, trans = across + port = carry, auto = self + graph = write.
explanation.tip: Roots appear in many related words: chronic, beneficial, portable, automatic.

items.stem: Which part of a dictionary entry tells you how to say a word?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dictionaries show pronunciation with special symbols and stress marks.
explanation.tip: L.6.4.c: consult reference materials for pronunciation and meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: the pronunciation in parentheses or slashes

options.label: B
options.text: the example sentence
options.rationale: Examples show usage.

options.label: C
options.text: the guide words
options.rationale: Guide words help you find the page.

options.label: D
options.text: the definition
options.rationale: Definitions give meaning.

items.stem: The guide words on a dictionary page are cobalt and coconut. Which word would be on that page?

explanation.whyCorrect: Cockpit (co-c-k) comes after cobalt (co-b) and before coconut (co-c-o).
explanation.tip: Compare letter by letter until the words differ.

options.label: A
options.text: coffee
options.rationale: Coffee (co-f) comes after coconut (co-c).

options.label: B
options.text: cockpit

options.label: C
options.text: cozy
options.rationale: Cozy (co-z) comes after coconut.

options.label: D
options.text: coast
options.rationale: Coast (co-a) comes before cobalt (co-b).

items.stem: “The wind whispered secrets through the trees.” What figure of speech is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Whispering secrets is a human action given to the wind.
explanation.tip: L.6.5.a: interpret figures of speech in context.

options.label: A
options.text: hyperbole
options.rationale: Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration.

options.label: B
options.text: simile
options.rationale: No like or as.

options.label: C
options.text: personification

options.label: D
options.text: alliteration
options.rationale: The sentence doesn't repeat beginning sounds as its main effect.

items.stem: “I've told you a million times to close the door!” What does this hyperbole mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperbole exaggerates for emphasis.
explanation.tip: Ask: is this exaggeration meant to show a feeling?

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker is happy.
options.rationale: The tone is frustrated.

options.label: B
options.text: The door is broken.
options.rationale: The sentence is about repeated reminders.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker counted exactly a million reminders.
options.rationale: Hyperbole is not meant literally.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker has said it many times and is frustrated.

items.stem: Which pair shows a PART-to-WHOLE relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A page is one part of a whole book.
explanation.tip: L.6.5.b: relationships include cause/effect, part/whole, item/category.

options.label: A
options.text: page : book

options.label: B
options.text: rain : flood
options.rationale: This is cause and effect.

options.label: C
options.text: happy : joyful
options.rationale: These are synonyms.

options.label: D
options.text: hammer : tool
options.rationale: This is item and category.

items.stem: Match each word pair to its relationship.

explanation.whyCorrect: Identifying the relationship helps you understand both words.
explanation.tip: Make a sentence: “A spark CAUSES a fire,” “A wheel is PART OF a bicycle.”

items.stem: Which word has the most POSITIVE connotation for describing someone who saves money?

explanation.whyCorrect: Thrifty suggests wisely careful with money.
explanation.tip: Words with similar denotations can feel very different.

options.label: A
options.text: cheap
options.rationale: Cheap suggests being unwilling to spend, a negative feeling.

options.label: B
options.text: thrifty

options.label: C
options.text: greedy
options.rationale: Greedy is negative and means wanting too much.

options.label: D
options.text: stingy
options.rationale: Stingy is negative.

items.stem: Which sentence makes the speaker sound most critical of the plan?

explanation.whyCorrect: Scheme connotes a sneaky or dishonest plan.
explanation.tip: Check how each word makes you feel, not just what it means.

options.label: A
options.text: The committee's plan was announced on Monday.
options.rationale: Plan is neutral.

options.label: B
options.text: The committee's proposal was announced on Monday.
options.rationale: Proposal is neutral or positive.

options.label: C
options.text: The committee's scheme was announced on Monday.

options.label: D
options.text: The committee's strategy was announced on Monday.
options.rationale: Strategy sounds thoughtful.

items.stem: “Don't put all your eggs in one basket” advises you to —

explanation.whyCorrect: If the one basket falls, everything is lost.
explanation.tip: Proverbs give general advice about life.

options.label: A
options.text: buy more baskets
options.rationale: The saying isn't about baskets.

options.label: B
options.text: carry eggs carefully
