options.rationale: This is too literal.

options.label: C
options.text: eat eggs for breakfast
options.rationale: The saying gives advice about risk.

options.label: D
options.text: spread your risks instead of depending on one thing

items.stem: In which sentence does object mean “to disagree”?

explanation.whyCorrect: OBject (noun) = thing or goal; obJECT (verb) = to disagree.
explanation.tip: Homographs can change meaning AND stress.

options.label: A
options.text: I object to the new rule about phones.

options.label: B
options.text: The object of the game is to score.
options.rationale: Here object means goal.

options.label: C
options.text: That shiny object is a coin.
options.rationale: Here object is a thing.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the object on the table.
options.rationale: Here object is a thing.

items.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: “The coach gave the trophy to Laila and ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: To is a preposition, so its object must be in the objective case: me.
explanation.tip: L.6.1.a: subjective (I, he), objective (me, him), possessive (my, his).

options.label: A
options.text: myself
options.rationale: Myself is reflexive; there is no I in the sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: me

options.label: C
options.text: mine
options.rationale: Mine is possessive.

options.label: D
options.text: I
options.rationale: After a preposition (to), use the objective case.

items.stem: Which sentence uses pronoun case correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both pronouns are subjects, so both must be subjective: she and I.
explanation.tip: Test each pronoun alone: “She presented.” “I presented.”

options.label: A
options.text: She and me presented the science project.
options.rationale: Me cannot be a subject.

options.label: B
options.text: Me and her presented the science project.
options.rationale: Me and her are objective.

options.label: C
options.text: She and I presented the science project.

options.label: D
options.text: Her and me presented the science project.
options.rationale: Subjects need subjective pronouns.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an INTENSIVE pronoun?

explanation.whyCorrect: An intensive pronoun emphasizes a noun and could be removed without changing the meaning.
explanation.tip: Remove the -self word: if the sentence still works, it's intensive.

options.label: A
options.text: The principal handed out the awards.
options.rationale: There is no -self pronoun.

options.label: B
options.text: She handed out the awards.
options.rationale: She is a subject pronoun.

options.label: C
options.text: The principal handed herself an award.
options.rationale: Here herself is reflexive (the object).

options.label: D
options.text: The principal herself handed out the awards.

items.stem: Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in pronoun person?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence shifts from students (third person) to you (second person).
explanation.tip: L.6.1.c: keep pronoun number and person consistent.

options.label: A
options.text: When students study hard, you get better grades.

options.label: B
options.text: When I study hard, I get better grades.
options.rationale: Both are first person.

options.label: C
options.text: When you study hard, you get better grades.
options.rationale: Both are second person.

options.label: D
options.text: When students study hard, they get better grades.
options.rationale: Students and they are both third person.

items.stem: Which sentence has a VAGUE pronoun?

explanation.whyCorrect: He could mean Omar or Sami, so the reader can't tell who won.
explanation.tip: L.6.1.d: fix pronouns that could refer to more than one noun.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar told Sami that Sami had won the contest.
options.rationale: The noun is repeated, so it is clear.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar told Sami that he had won the contest.

options.label: C
options.text: Omar told Sami that Omar had won.
options.rationale: The noun makes it clear.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar told Sami, “You won the contest!”
options.rationale: The quotation makes it clear.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “It” has no clear antecedent—proud of what? Replace it with a specific noun.
explanation.tip: If you can't point to the exact noun a pronoun replaces, rewrite it.

segments: The teacher spoke to the students,
items.correction: were very proud of the results

items.stem: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Past perfect (had ended) shows the earlier of two past actions.
explanation.tip: Had + past participle = past perfect.

options.label: A
options.text: The game will have ended before we reached it.
options.rationale: Will have is future perfect.

options.label: B
options.text: The game ended before we had reach the stadium.
options.rationale: Reach should be reached.

options.label: C
options.text: The game had ended before we reached the stadium.

options.label: D
options.text: The game has ended before we reached the stadium.
options.rationale: Has ended is present perfect.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: After had, use the past participle: write → wrote → written.
explanation.tip: Irregular verbs have special past participles: go/gone, eat/eaten, write/written.

items.stem: Which is a run-on sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two independent clauses run together without punctuation.
explanation.tip: Fix with a period, semicolon, or comma + coordinating conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: The library closes at six, so we need to hurry.
options.rationale: A comma and so join the clauses correctly.

options.label: B
options.text: The library closes at six; we need to hurry.
options.rationale: A semicolon joins two clauses correctly.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the library closes at six.
options.rationale: This is a fragment, not a run-on.

options.label: D
options.text: The library closes at six we need to hurry.

items.stem: Which word is a collective noun? “The team celebrated after the final whistle.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A collective noun names a group as one unit: team, class, flock.
explanation.tip: Collective nouns are usually singular: The team IS ready.

options.label: A
options.text: team

options.label: B
options.text: celebrated
options.rationale: Celebrated is a verb.

options.label: C
options.text: final
options.rationale: Final is an adjective.

options.label: D
options.text: whistle
options.rationale: Whistle is a common noun but not collective.

items.stem: Which shows the correct plural possessive? “The ____ uniforms were washed.”

explanation.whyCorrect: For plural nouns ending in s, add only an apostrophe: players'.
explanation.tip: Singular: player's. Plural: players'.

options.label: A
options.text: players's
options.rationale: Do not add 's after a plural ending in s.

options.label: B
options.text: players'

options.label: C
options.text: players
options.rationale: This is plural without possession.

options.label: D
options.text: player's
options.rationale: This is singular possessive.

items.stem: Which word is a demonstrative adjective? “Those shoes belong to my brother.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Those points to specific nouns (shoes); demonstratives are this, that, these, those.
explanation.tip: Demonstrative adjectives come right before a noun.

options.label: A
options.text: shoes
options.rationale: Shoes is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: belong
options.rationale: Belong is a verb.

options.label: C
options.text: Those

options.label: D
options.text: my
options.rationale: My is a possessive pronoun/adjective.

items.stem: Which sentence is complex?

explanation.whyCorrect: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
explanation.tip: Subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when) start dependent clauses.

options.label: A
options.text: The storm knocked out power, and school was canceled.
options.rationale: This is compound.

options.label: B
options.text: Knocked out power during the storm.
options.rationale: This is a fragment.

options.label: C
options.text: The storm knocked out power.
options.rationale: This is simple.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the storm knocked out power, school was canceled.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates the nonrestrictive element?

explanation.whyCorrect: The clause adds extra information, so it is set off with commas.
explanation.tip: L.6.2.a: use commas, parentheses, or dashes for nonrestrictive elements.

options.label: A
options.text: My cousin, who lives in Jeddah, is visiting next week.

options.label: B
options.text: My cousin, who lives in Jeddah is visiting next week.
options.rationale: The closing comma is missing.

options.label: C
options.text: My cousin who lives, in Jeddah, is visiting next week.
options.rationale: The commas are in the wrong places.

options.label: D
options.text: My cousin who lives in Jeddah, is visiting next week.
options.rationale: A nonrestrictive clause needs commas on both sides.

items.stem: Which sentence uses dashes correctly to set off extra information?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pairs of dashes surround the interrupting element.
explanation.tip: Dashes, like commas, come in pairs around extra information in the middle of a sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The answer—which surprised everyone was zero.
options.rationale: A second dash is needed.

options.label: B
options.text: The answer—which surprised everyone—was zero.

options.label: C
options.text: The—answer which surprised everyone—was zero.
options.rationale: The dash splits the subject.

options.label: D
options.text: The answer which—surprised everyone—was zero.
options.rationale: The dash must come before which.

items.stem: True or false: In “Students who finish early may read quietly,” the clause who finish early should be set off with commas.

explanation.whyCorrect: The clause is restrictive—it tells WHICH students may read—so it does not take commas.
explanation.tip: If removing the clause changes the meaning, do not use commas.

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: When a quotation is interrupted by a speaker tag, use commas and keep the second part lowercase.
explanation.tip: Punctuation stays inside the quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.text: “I'll bring the map,” said Hana, “If you bring the snacks.”
options.rationale: The sentence continues, so if is lowercase.

options.label: B
options.text: “I'll bring the map, said Hana, if you bring the snacks.”
options.rationale: The speaker tag must be outside the quotation marks.

options.label: C
options.text: “I'll bring the map,” said Hana, “if you bring the snacks.”

options.label: D
options.text: “I'll bring the map” said Hana, “if you bring the snacks.”
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the closing quotation mark.

items.stem: Spell the word correctly: The tour guide will ____ (accommodate) twenty visitors.

explanation.whyCorrect: Accommodate has two c's and two m's.
explanation.tip: Memory trick: it accommodates two c's and two m's.

items.stem: Which revision best varies the sentence pattern? Original: “The sun set. The sky turned orange. Birds flew home.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Combining with an introductory clause creates variety and flow.
explanation.tip: L.6.3.a: vary sentence patterns for meaning, interest, and style.

options.label: A
options.text: The sun set. The sky turned orange. The birds flew home.
options.rationale: This keeps the same short pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: Sun set. Sky orange. Birds home.
options.rationale: These are fragments.

options.label: C
options.text: The sun set and the sky turned orange and birds flew home and it was evening.
options.rationale: Too many ands makes it stringy.

options.label: D
options.text: As the sun set, the sky turned orange and birds flew home.

items.stem: Which sentence keeps a consistent formal style in a research report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Formal writing uses precise, neutral language.
explanation.tip: L.6.3.b: maintain consistency in style and tone.

options.label: A
options.text: The results indicate that students who sleep eight hours perform better on tests.

options.label: B
options.text: The results show that kids who sleep a ton do way better.
options.rationale: A ton and way better are informal.

options.label: C
options.text: Sleep is awesome for tests, LOL.
options.rationale: LOL and awesome are informal.

options.label: D
options.text: So basically, sleep = good grades!
options.rationale: Casual and uses a symbol.

items.stem: Which evidence is most credible to support the claim that exercise improves concentration?

explanation.whyCorrect: Research from a reliable institution is credible and relevant.
explanation.tip: W.6.1.b: use credible sources and relevant evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: My friend says running makes him smarter.
options.rationale: One opinion is not credible evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: A university study found students focused longer after 20 minutes of activity.

options.label: C
options.text: Exercise is fun for most people.
options.rationale: Fun is not evidence about concentration.

options.label: D
options.text: An ad for sneakers says exercise boosts brain power.
options.rationale: Ads are biased sources.

items.stem: Which transition best introduces a counterclaim?

explanation.whyCorrect: Counterclaims present the other side before you respond to it.
explanation.tip: W.6.1.c: use words and phrases to clarify relationships among claims and reasons.

options.label: A
options.text: First of all,
options.rationale: This introduces a first reason.

options.label: B
options.text: In conclusion,
options.rationale: This ends an essay.

options.label: C
options.text: Some people argue that

options.label: D
options.text: For example,
options.rationale: This introduces evidence, not an opposing view.

items.stem: Choose the best transition: “Coral reefs protect coastlines. ____, they provide homes for thousands of species.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Furthermore adds another important idea.
explanation.tip: W.6.2.c: use transitions to clarify relationships among ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: Consequently
options.rationale: The second idea is not a result of the first.

options.label: B
options.text: Nevertheless
options.rationale: This shows contrast.

options.label: C
options.text: For instance
options.rationale: The second sentence isn't an example of the first.

options.label: D
options.text: Furthermore

items.stem: Which source would be most reliable for a report on coral bleaching?

explanation.whyCorrect: Research institutes have experts and publish evidence.
explanation.tip: W.6.8: assess the credibility of each source.

options.label: A
options.text: a marine research institute's website

options.label: B
options.text: a fictional story about mermaids
options.rationale: Fiction is not factual evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: an anonymous social media post
options.rationale: Anonymous sources cannot be checked.

options.label: D
options.text: a travel company's beach advertisement
options.rationale: Advertisements have a commercial purpose.

items.stem: Order the sentences to signal shifts in time and setting in a narrative.

explanation.whyCorrect: Transitions (That morning, By noon, Meanwhile, Hours later) signal shifts in time and place.
explanation.tip: W.6.3.c: use transitions to convey sequence and signal shifts.

sequence: That morning, the harbor was calm and gray.
By noon, dark clouds had gathered over the water.
Meanwhile, on the hill above town, my grandmother watched the sky.
Hours later, the storm finally passed.

items.stem: Which word is a noun? “The bird sang loudly.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A noun names a person, place, thing, or animal. Bird names an animal.
explanation.tip: Ask: can I put “a” or “the” in front of it?

options.label: A
options.text: loudly
options.rationale: Loudly is an adverb that tells how.

options.label: B
options.text: bird

options.label: C
options.text: sang
options.rationale: Sang is a verb—an action.

items.stem: Which end mark belongs at the end of this question? “Where is my pencil”

explanation.whyCorrect: Questions end with a question mark.
explanation.tip: Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why, or how.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A comma never ends a sentence.

options.label: C
options.rationale: An exclamation point shows strong feeling.

options.label: D
options.rationale: A period ends a statement, not a question.

items.stem: Which name needs a capital letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Egypt is the name of a specific place, so it is a proper noun.
explanation.tip: Specific names of people and places get capital letters.

options.label: A
options.text: river
options.rationale: River is a common noun.

options.label: B
options.text: country
options.rationale: Country is a common noun.

options.label: C
options.text: egypt

options.label: D
options.text: city
options.rationale: City is a common noun.

items.stem: Which word means the opposite of hot?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hot and cold are antonyms.
explanation.tip: Antonyms are opposites: up/down, fast/slow.

options.label: A
options.text: sunny
options.rationale: Sunny describes weather, not the opposite of hot.

options.label: B
options.text: big
options.rationale: Big is about size.

options.label: C
options.text: warm
options.rationale: Warm is close to hot.

options.label: D
options.text: cold

items.stem: What is the plural of box?

explanation.whyCorrect: Nouns ending in s, x, z, ch, or sh add -es.
explanation.tip: If you hear an extra syllable (box-es), add -es.

options.label: A
options.text: boxes

options.label: B
options.text: boxies
options.rationale: There is no y to change.

options.label: C
options.text: box
options.rationale: Box stays singular.

options.label: D
options.text: boxs
options.rationale: Words ending in x add -es.

items.stem: Read: “Grandpa's laugh was thunder rolling across the hills, and the children ran toward it like flowers turning to the sun.” Which statement best explains how the two comparisons work together?

explanation.whyCorrect: Thunder suggests a loud, booming laugh, while flowers turning to the sun suggests the children love being near it.
explanation.tip: With two comparisons, explain what EACH one describes, then how they connect.

options.label: A
options.text: Both comparisons describe the weather that day.
options.rationale: Thunder and sun are figurative, not real weather.

options.label: B
options.text: The metaphor shows Grandpa's laugh is big and powerful; the simile shows the children are drawn to its warmth.

options.label: C
options.text: Both comparisons show that the children are afraid of Grandpa.
options.rationale: Flowers turning to the sun shows attraction, not fear.

options.label: D
options.text: The simile describes the laugh and the metaphor describes the hills.
options.rationale: The metaphor describes the laugh; the simile describes the children.

items.stem: An article claims: “Our town should build bike lanes.” Which reason would be the WEAKEST support?

explanation.whyCorrect: The color of bikes has nothing to do with whether lanes should be built.
explanation.tip: Weak reasons are true but unrelated to the claim.

options.label: A
options.text: A nearby town's bike lanes cut pollution by 10%.
options.rationale: This is evidence from a similar place.

options.label: B
options.text: More people would bike to work, reducing traffic.
options.rationale: This explains a benefit.

options.label: C
options.text: Bikes come in many bright colors.

options.label: D
options.text: Bike lanes reduce accidents between cars and cyclists.
options.rationale: This is relevant safety evidence.

items.stem: Read: “Mira's explanation was so lucid that even her little brother understood the science experiment on the first try.” What does lucid mean, and which clue shows it?

explanation.whyCorrect: If a young child understood right away, the explanation must have been very clear.
explanation.tip: Use the RESULT described in the sentence as your clue.

options.label: A
options.text: funny — “her little brother”
options.rationale: Nothing suggests humor.

options.label: B
options.text: confusing — “science experiment”
options.rationale: The brother understood, so it was not confusing.

options.label: C
options.text: long — “explanation”
options.rationale: Explanation does not tell the meaning of lucid.

options.label: D
options.text: clear — “even her little brother understood … on the first try”

items.stem: A boy brags that he will win the race, skips practice, and loses to a quieter classmate who trained every day. Which theme fits best?

explanation.whyCorrect: The events show that effort, not boasting, leads to success.
explanation.tip: Themes come from what happens to characters because of their choices.

options.label: A
options.text: Hard work matters more than bragging.

options.label: B
options.text: Quiet people never win.
options.rationale: The quiet classmate wins.

options.label: C
options.text: Races are unfair to fast runners.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the race was unfair.

options.label: D
options.text: Practice is boring.
options.rationale: This is not a lesson shown by the events.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each is singular, so the verb must be has, even though puppies is plural.
explanation.tip: Words like each, every, and either are singular subjects.

items.stem: Which word is a proper noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: Jeddah names a specific city, so it is proper and capitalized.
explanation.tip: Proper nouns name specific people, places, or things.

options.label: A
options.text: market
options.rationale: Market is a common noun.

options.label: B
options.text: Jeddah

options.label: C
options.text: beach
options.rationale: Beach is a common noun.

options.label: D
options.text: city
options.rationale: City is a common noun.

items.stem: Which word is the verb in this sentence? “The happy children laughed.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Laughed tells what the children did.
explanation.tip: Verbs show action or being.

options.label: A
options.text: children
options.rationale: Children is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: happy
options.rationale: Happy is an adjective describing the children.

options.label: C
options.text: laughed

items.stem: Which sentence needs commas?

explanation.whyCorrect: Three items in a series need commas: lions, tigers, and bears.
explanation.tip: Count the items. Three or more? Use commas.

options.label: A
options.text: We saw lions.
options.rationale: One item needs no comma.

options.label: B
options.text: Lions roar.
options.rationale: This is a short simple sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: We saw lions tigers and bears.

options.label: D
options.text: We saw lions and tigers.
options.rationale: Two items joined by and need no comma.

items.stem: What does unhappy mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The prefix un- means not.
explanation.tip: Cover the prefix, read the base word, then add the prefix meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: happy again
options.rationale: Again is re-.

options.label: B
options.text: happy before
options.rationale: Before is pre-.

options.label: C
options.text: very happy
options.rationale: Un- does not mean very.

options.label: D
options.text: not happy

items.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Friend is spelled f-r-i-e-n-d.
explanation.tip: Memory trick: a friend to the end.

options.label: A
options.text: friend

options.label: B
options.text: frind
options.rationale: Missing the e.

options.label: C
options.text: freind
options.rationale: i before e in friend.

options.label: D
options.text: frend
options.rationale: Missing the i.

items.stem: A story about a soccer final is told by the goalkeeper who let in the winning goal. How would the description of the final minute most likely change if the scorer narrated it?

explanation.whyCorrect: A narrator's point of view shapes which feelings and details are emphasized.
explanation.tip: RL.5.6: ask how the narrator's experience colors the events.

options.label: A
options.text: It would describe the goalkeeper's thoughts in detail.
options.rationale: The scorer cannot know the goalkeeper's thoughts.

options.label: B
options.text: It would focus on excitement and pride instead of disappointment.

options.label: C
options.text: It would include no feelings at all.
options.rationale: First-person narrators share feelings.

options.label: D
options.text: It would describe exactly the same feelings.
options.rationale: Different narrators experience events differently.

items.stem: A text explains that honeybees pollinate crops, that bee numbers are falling, and that farmers are planting wildflower strips to help. Which statement best captures BOTH main ideas?

explanation.whyCorrect: Grade 5 texts can have two main ideas: why bees matter, and how people help them.
explanation.tip: Check that your summary statement covers every section.

options.label: A
options.text: Honeybees make honey.
options.rationale: Honey is not discussed.

options.label: B
options.text: Wildflowers are pretty.
options.rationale: This is a minor detail.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees are essential to farming, and people are acting to reverse their decline.

options.label: D
options.text: Farmers grow many crops.
options.rationale: This misses the bees' decline and the response.

items.stem: “The early bird catches the worm.” Which situation shows this proverb?

explanation.whyCorrect: The proverb means people who act early get the best opportunities.
explanation.tip: Match the proverb's lesson to a real-life example.

options.label: A
options.text: A bird ate a worm in the garden.
options.rationale: This is the literal meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar slept late and missed the bus.
options.rationale: This shows the opposite outcome, not the proverb.

options.label: C
options.text: Lina likes birds more than worms.
options.rationale: This has nothing to do with the advice.

options.label: D
options.text: Noura arrived first at the book sale and found the rarest book.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly combines the ideas using a dependent clause? “It was raining. We played inside.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Because it was raining is a dependent clause that explains why.
explanation.tip: Put the cause in the because-clause.

options.label: A
options.text: Because it was raining, we played inside.

options.label: B
options.text: It was raining because we played inside.
options.rationale: This reverses the cause and effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Because it was raining.
options.rationale: This is a fragment.

options.label: D
options.text: It was raining, we played inside.
options.rationale: This is a comma splice.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Their shows ownership (the students' notebooks); there tells where.
explanation.tip: their = belongs to them; there = place; they're = they are.

items.stem: Which word is a common noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: Teacher names a general person, not a specific one.
explanation.tip: Common nouns are not capitalized unless they start a sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Dammam
options.rationale: This is a specific city.

options.label: B
options.text: teacher

options.label: C
options.text: Ms. Amal
options.rationale: This is a specific name—a proper noun.

options.label: D
options.text: Friday
options.rationale: Days of the week are proper nouns.

items.stem: What kind of sentence is this? “Please close the window.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Imperative sentences give commands or requests.
explanation.tip: Declarative . | Interrogative ? | Exclamatory ! | Imperative (command).

options.label: A
options.text: declarative (a statement)
options.rationale: It tells someone to do something.

options.label: B
options.text: exclamatory (strong feeling)
options.rationale: It doesn't end with !

options.label: C
options.text: imperative (a command)

options.label: D
options.text: interrogative (a question)
options.rationale: There is no question mark.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for begin?

explanation.whyCorrect: Begin and start mean the same thing.
explanation.tip: Swap the words in a sentence: if the meaning stays, they're synonyms.

options.label: A
options.text: pause
options.rationale: Pause means stop for a while.

options.label: B
options.text: finish
options.rationale: Finish is an antonym.

options.label: C
options.text: forget
options.rationale: Forget is unrelated.

options.label: D
options.text: start

items.stem: Which word is an adjective? “A tall building shone brightly.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Tall describes what kind of building.
explanation.tip: Adjectives answer: what kind? which one? how many?

options.label: A
options.text: tall

options.label: B
options.text: building
options.rationale: Building is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: shone
options.rationale: Shone is a verb.

options.label: D
options.text: brightly
options.rationale: Brightly is an adverb; it tells how the building shone.

items.stem: Which word is more formal than kids?

explanation.whyCorrect: Children is the formal, standard word.
explanation.tip: Use formal words in reports and essays.

options.label: A
options.text: folks
options.rationale: Folks is casual.

options.label: B
options.text: children

options.label: C
options.text: guys
options.rationale: Guys is informal.

options.label: D
options.text: buddies
options.rationale: Buddies is informal.

items.stem: Which claim would require the strongest evidence to be convincing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Absolute claims (“no effect,” “any grade”) need broad, strong evidence because one counterexample can disprove them.
explanation.tip: The bigger the claim, the stronger the evidence it needs.

options.label: A
options.text: Many teachers assign reading homework.
options.rationale: This is an easily checked fact.

options.label: B
options.text: Some students prefer homework on weekends.
options.rationale: This is a modest claim about preference.

options.label: C
options.text: Homework has no effect on student learning at any grade level.

options.label: D
options.text: Homework can help students practise skills.
options.rationale: This is limited and widely supported.

items.stem: In a story, a girl lies to protect her friend; the lie grows, the friendship nearly breaks, and she finally confesses. The friend forgives her. Which theme is developed MOST fully?

explanation.whyCorrect: The plot moves from a lie, to consequences, to a confession that restores trust.
explanation.tip: RL.6.2: track how the theme develops through particular details.

options.label: A
options.text: Protecting friends is more important than anything.
options.rationale: The story shows the lie backfired.

options.label: B
options.text: Friends should never forgive each other.
options.rationale: The friend does forgive her.

options.label: C
options.text: Lying always works out in the end.
options.rationale: The lie nearly ruins the friendship.

options.label: D
options.text: Honesty, even when difficult, is necessary for trust between friends.

items.stem: A writer wants readers to admire a character who rarely gives up. Which word should the writer choose?

explanation.whyCorrect: Determined has a positive connotation for not giving up.
explanation.tip: Choose words whose feeling matches your purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: determined

options.label: B
options.text: inflexible
options.rationale: Inflexible suggests a weakness.

options.label: C
options.text: stubborn
options.rationale: Stubborn suggests unreasonable refusal—a negative connotation.

options.label: D
options.text: pigheaded
options.rationale: Pigheaded is insulting.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Between is a preposition, so it takes the objective case: between you and me.
explanation.tip: After prepositions (between, for, with, to), use me, him, her, us, them.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses to set off nonessential information?

explanation.whyCorrect: Parentheses go around extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence.
explanation.tip: Read the sentence without the parentheses—it should still make sense.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum open (since 1985) attracts, thousands of visitors.
options.rationale: The comma and parentheses are misplaced.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum (open since 1985) attracts thousands of visitors.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum (open since 1985 attracts) thousands of visitors.
options.rationale: The parentheses enclose part of the main sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The (museum open since 1985) attracts thousands of visitors.
options.rationale: The subject is inside the parentheses.

items.stem: What is the main problem in “The Stick Bridge”?

explanation.whyCorrect: When the bridge snaps at twelve seconds, Maya says, “It’s ruined.” That is the story’s problem.
explanation.tip: The conflict is the problem a character must solve. Look for the moment things go wrong.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya’s bridge breaks before the contest.

options.label: B
options.text: The class cannot find a dictionary.
options.rationale: The story never says the dictionary is missing.

options.label: C
options.text: Omar does not want to help Maya.
options.rationale: Omar helps from the start; he is not the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Maya cannot find any craft sticks.
options.rationale: She has forty sticks at the very beginning.

items.stem: How is the problem in “The Stick Bridge” solved?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story says they “replaced the weak stick and glued small triangles along both sides,” and the bridge holds.
explanation.tip: The resolution is how the problem is solved. Look near the end of the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar builds a different bridge by himself.
options.rationale: They fix Maya’s bridge together.

options.label: B
options.text: Maya and Omar replace the weak stick and add triangles.

options.label: C
options.text: The teacher lets Maya skip the contest.
options.rationale: Maya does enter the contest on Thursday.

options.label: D
options.text: Maya buys a new bridge kit from a store.
options.rationale: Nothing in the story mentions buying a kit.

items.stem: In “The Stick Bridge,” the problem is solved before the contest begins.

explanation.whyCorrect: They fix the bridge “that night,” and on Thursday it holds the dictionary for sixty seconds.
explanation.tip: Check when the fix happens compared with when the contest happens.

items.stem: Why does Maya say, “I don’t have time to start over”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The bridge breaks on Tuesday night and the contest is on Thursday, so there is little time.
explanation.tip: Use details about time and days to explain a character’s words.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar has hidden the craft sticks.
options.rationale: Omar is helping, not hiding anything.

options.label: B
options.text: She has already finished her homework.
options.rationale: That would give her more time, not less.

options.label: C
options.text: The contest is only two days away.

options.label: D
options.text: She has to go to bed right away.
options.rationale: The story does not say that; the issue is the contest date.

items.stem: Put the events of “The Stick Bridge” in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The crack comes first, then the break, then the idea, and finally the success at the contest.
explanation.tip: Problem, attempts to solve it, and resolution usually happen in that order.

sequence: Omar finds a cracked stick.
The bridge snaps during a test.
Omar shows a picture of triangles.
The bridge holds the dictionary for sixty seconds.

items.stem: How does solving the problem change Maya?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her last words are, “Next time, I’ll listen when you find a crack.”
explanation.tip: A character’s last words often show what they learned from the conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: She decides to build bridges only by herself.
options.rationale: She worked with Omar and thanks him.

options.label: B
options.text: She decides never to enter a contest again.
options.rationale: She is happy at the end, not discouraged.

options.label: C
options.text: She decides that triangles are too hard to make.
options.rationale: The triangles are what made the bridge strong.

options.label: D
options.text: She decides to listen more carefully to her brother.

items.stem: Which detail early in the story hints that the bridge will break?

explanation.whyCorrect: The cracked stick is the piece that later snaps, so the author hinted at the problem early.
explanation.tip: Foreshadowing is a clue that hints at what will happen later.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar finds a stick with a crack.

options.label: B
options.text: Maya spreads forty sticks on the table.
options.rationale: This sets up the project but does not hint at trouble.

options.label: C
options.text: Maya reads the rules.
options.rationale: Reading rules does not suggest a problem.

options.label: D
options.text: The contest is on Thursday.
options.rationale: This tells when, not what will go wrong.

items.stem: In “The Stick Bridge,” the cracked stick is a clue about what happens later.

explanation.whyCorrect: Omar points out the crack, and later “It was the cracked stick” that broke.
explanation.tip: Notice details the author repeats later in the story.

items.stem: Why does the author show Maya tossing the cracked stick into the pile “without looking”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her careless choice puts the weak stick in the bridge, and the bridge breaks because of it.
explanation.tip: Ask why the author included a small action. It often matters later.

options.label: A
options.text: To show that Omar is wrong about the crack.
options.rationale: The stick really was cracked; it broke later.

options.label: B
options.text: To show she is not paying attention, which leads to the problem.

options.label: C
options.text: To show that the contest is easy.
options.rationale: The contest turns out to be a challenge.

options.label: D
options.text: To show she is very careful with her work.
options.rationale: Tossing it without looking is the opposite of careful.

items.stem: Which sentence from the story is foreshadowing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Omar’s warning comes early and points to the break that happens later.
explanation.tip: Foreshadowing appears before the event it hints at.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya grinned at Omar.
options.rationale: This shows her feelings at the end.

options.label: B
options.text: Sixty seconds passed.
options.rationale: This tells the result at the end, not a hint about the future.

options.label: C
options.text: “This one has a crack,” he said.

options.label: D
options.text: The bridge did not even wobble.
options.rationale: This describes what happened, not a hint.

items.stem: In “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter,” Noura says she will count the stars “every night until you come home.” What does this suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Counting stars every night hints at many nights of waiting during a long season.
explanation.tip: A character’s promise can hint at what lies ahead.

options.label: A
options.text: Noura is learning about astronomy.
options.rationale: Counting stars here is about waiting, not science.

options.label: B
options.text: Her father will return the same night.
options.rationale: The text calls it “the long pearling season.”

options.label: C
options.text: Noura is afraid of the dark.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she fears the night.

options.label: D
options.text: Her father will be gone for a long time.

items.stem: An author writes: “The sky was clear, but the old fisherman kept looking at a small dark cloud in the west.” What is this most likely foreshadowing?

explanation.whyCorrect: A clear sky with one worrying cloud, and a character who keeps watching it, hints at bad weather ahead.
explanation.tip: When a character keeps noticing something, the author may be preparing you for it.

options.label: A
options.text: A storm may come later in the story.

options.label: B
options.text: The fisherman will catch many fish.
options.rationale: The dark cloud does not connect to fishing success.

options.label: C
options.text: The fisherman will move to the west.
options.rationale: He is watching the cloud, not planning a move.

options.label: D
options.text: The story will end at sunrise.
options.rationale: Nothing in the sentence points to the time of day.

items.stem: After Omar shows the picture of triangles, what will Maya and Omar most likely do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Omar says they need “stronger shapes” and shows a bridge made of triangles.
explanation.tip: Use what a character says and shows to predict what happens next.

options.label: A
options.text: Build a tower instead of a bridge.
options.rationale: The contest is for bridges.

options.label: B
options.text: Use triangles to make the bridge stronger.

options.label: C
options.text: Start reading the math book.
options.rationale: The picture is about bridges, not the lesson in the book.

options.label: D
options.text: Give up on the contest.
options.rationale: Omar has just offered an idea, so they are not giving up.

items.stem: Based on the ending of “The Stick Bridge,” what will Maya most likely do in her next project?

explanation.whyCorrect: She says, “Next time, I’ll listen when you find a crack.”
explanation.tip: Predictions should match what a character has learned.

options.label: A
options.text: Use only broken sticks.
options.rationale: She learned that weak sticks cause problems.

options.label: B
options.text: Work without anyone’s help.
options.rationale: She thanks Omar and wants his help next time.

options.label: C
options.text: Check her materials and listen to Omar’s warnings.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip reading the rules.
options.rationale: Reading the rules was not her mistake.

items.stem: At the end of “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter,” it makes sense to predict that Noura will keep the white shell safe.

explanation.whyCorrect: Her father asks her to keep it, and she holds it to her ear as he leaves.
explanation.tip: A good prediction is supported by details in the text.

items.stem: Which detail BEST supports the prediction that Noura will miss her father?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her fear of the empty months shows she will miss him while he is gone.
explanation.tip: Choose the detail that connects most directly to the prediction.

options.label: A
options.text: The dhows rocked in the harbor.
options.rationale: This describes the setting.

options.label: B
options.text: She had been five years old.
options.rationale: This is part of her memory, not her feelings now.

options.label: C
options.text: The summer sun was already hot.
options.rationale: This describes the weather, not her feelings.

options.label: D
options.text: She is “afraid of the empty months without him.”

items.stem: Read: “Sami studied his spelling words every night and asked his sister to quiz him.” What is the BEST prediction?

explanation.whyCorrect: Studying every night and practicing with a partner usually lead to success.
explanation.tip: Combine text clues with what you already know to make a prediction.

options.label: A
options.text: Sami will probably do well on his spelling test.

options.label: B
options.text: Sami will forget his spelling words.
options.rationale: His careful practice makes this unlikely.

options.label: C
options.text: Sami will stop studying tomorrow.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he will stop.

options.label: D
options.text: Sami’s sister will take the test for him.
options.rationale: She quizzes him; she does not take his test.

items.stem: Which TWO details help you predict that the bridge will hold at the contest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Removing the weak stick and adding triangles both make the bridge stronger.
explanation.tip: Look for details that show a problem has been fixed.

options.label: A
options.text: They glued triangles along both sides.

options.label: B
options.text: The contest was on Thursday.
options.rationale: The day does not tell us whether the bridge will hold.

options.label: C
options.text: Maya’s face felt hot.
options.rationale: This shows her feelings after the break, not the strength of the bridge.

options.label: D
options.text: They replaced the weak stick.

items.stem: When does “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” take place?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first paragraph names the season (summer) and the year (1932).
explanation.tip: Setting includes when a story happens. Look for years, seasons and times of day.

options.label: A
options.text: At night during a storm
options.rationale: The story happens in the hot daytime sun.

options.label: B
options.text: In the summer of 1932

options.label: C
options.text: In the present day
options.rationale: The story names the year 1932.

options.label: D
options.text: In the winter of 1932
options.rationale: The story says “The summer sun was already hot.”

items.stem: Where does “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” take place?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story mentions the shore, the harbor and dhows in “her small town on the Gulf.”
explanation.tip: Setting includes where a story happens. Look for places and objects.

options.label: A
options.text: In a busy city far from the sea
options.rationale: The story happens at the shore and harbor.

options.label: B
options.text: On a mountain farm
options.rationale: There are dhows and waves, not mountains.

options.label: C
options.text: At the shore of a small town on the Gulf

options.label: D
options.text: Inside a school classroom
options.rationale: Noura is at the shore with her father.

items.stem: Why is the setting important to the problem in this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Because the story takes place in a pearling town in summer, her father must sail away for the season.
explanation.tip: Ask how the time and place cause or shape the characters’ problems.

options.label: A
options.text: The hot sun makes Noura sick.
options.rationale: The heat is described, but no one gets sick.

options.label: B
options.text: The town has no market for dates.
options.rationale: Noura already has dates for her father.

options.label: C
options.text: The harbor is too small for the dhows.
options.rationale: The dhows fit; they are rocking in the harbor.

options.label: D
options.text: Pearling happens at sea, so Noura’s father must leave for months.

items.stem: The word “dhows” helps show that the story is set in a place where people sail on the sea.

explanation.whyCorrect: Dhows are wooden sailing boats, so the word shows that the setting is a seaside town.
explanation.tip: Special objects in a story are clues to its setting.

items.stem: How would the story be different if it were set in a desert town far from the sea?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pearling needs the sea, so the whole event of the story depends on the seaside setting.
explanation.tip: Imagine changing the setting. If the events no longer work, the setting is important.

options.label: A
options.text: Noura’s father could not go pearling from that town.

options.label: B
options.text: Noura would be five years old.
options.rationale: Her age does not depend on the place.

options.label: C
options.text: Noura would not have a father.
options.rationale: Changing the place does not change the characters.

options.label: D
options.text: The story would happen in the year 2032.
options.rationale: Changing the place does not change the year.

items.stem: Which detail shows that the story takes place in the past?

explanation.whyCorrect: Wooden sailing dhows used for a pearling season, together with the year 1932, show a time long ago.
explanation.tip: Look for objects or ways of life that belong to a particular time.

options.label: A
options.text: Noura has a father.
options.rationale: This would be true at any time.

options.label: B
options.text: The town’s boats are wooden dhows with sails.

options.label: C
options.text: Noura packed some dates.
options.rationale: People still pack dates today.

options.label: D
options.text: The sun is hot.
options.rationale: The sun is hot today too.

items.stem: Which part of “The Pearl Diver’s Daughter” is a flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story jumps back to when “She had been five years old.” That is a flashback.
explanation.tip: A flashback interrupts the story to show something that happened earlier.

options.label: A
options.text: Noura packs a bag of dates.
options.rationale: This happens in the present of the story.

options.label: B
options.text: Her father gives her a white shell.
options.rationale: This happens on the day he sails.

options.label: C
options.text: Noura remembers being five and crying at the waves.

options.label: D
options.text: The dhow’s sail fills with wind.
options.rationale: This is the story’s ending, not a memory.

items.stem: A flashback tells about events that happened before the main story.

explanation.whyCorrect: A flashback goes back in time to an earlier event.
explanation.tip: Flash = quick; back = to the past.

items.stem: Which words signal that the story is moving back in time?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Had been” and the younger age show that we are hearing about an earlier time.
explanation.tip: Words like “had,” “remembered” and earlier ages signal a flashback.

options.label: A
options.text: “The dhow’s sail filled with wind.”
options.rationale: This is the present action of the story.

options.label: B
options.text: “Keep this,” he said.
options.rationale: This is dialogue in the present.

options.label: C
options.text: “Now Noura was ten.”
options.rationale: “Now” brings the story back to the present.

options.label: D
options.text: “She had been five years old.”

items.stem: Why does the author include the flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The memory contrasts her old fear of the waves with her new fear of the months without her father.
explanation.tip: Ask what the flashback helps you understand about a character now.

options.label: A
options.text: To show that Noura once feared the sea but now fears missing her father.

options.label: B
options.text: To describe the market in the town.
options.rationale: The market is not in the flashback.

options.label: C
options.text: To explain how pearls are made.
options.rationale: The flashback is about Noura’s feelings, not pearls.

options.label: D
options.text: To show that her father is a good swimmer.
options.rationale: The memory is about her fear, not his swimming.

items.stem: What brings the story back to the present after the flashback?

explanation.whyCorrect: The word “Now” and her present age (ten) return the reader to the day of the story.
explanation.tip: Look for words like “now” and “today” after a flashback.

options.label: A
options.text: “From up there, the sea had looked like a sheet of blue glass.”
options.rationale: This is still part of the memory.

options.label: B
options.text: “Now Noura was ten, and she was not afraid of the sea.”

options.label: C
options.text: “She had stopped being afraid.”
options.rationale: This is still in the past.

options.label: D
options.text: “The waves had frightened her.”
options.rationale: This is still part of the memory.

items.stem: Put these events in the order they really happened in Noura’s life (not the order in which they are told).

explanation.whyCorrect: The flashback events happened five years before the day the father sails.
explanation.tip: A flashback is told later but happened earlier. Arrange events by time, not by page.

sequence: Noura cries at the waves when she is five.
Her father lifts her onto his shoulders.
Ten-year-old Noura walks to the shore.
Her father sails away on the dhow.

items.stem: How does Noura feel about her father leaving?

explanation.whyCorrect: She is “afraid of the empty months without him” and promises to count stars until he returns.
explanation.tip: A character’s perspective is how that character thinks and feels about events.

options.label: A
options.text: Angry because he forgot her dates
options.rationale: She packed the dates for him.

options.label: B
options.text: Excited because she wants to go pearling
options.rationale: She is not going; she will wait at home.

options.label: C
options.text: Sad and worried about the months without him

options.label: D
options.text: Afraid of the waves on the shore
options.rationale: She was afraid as a five-year-old, not now.

items.stem: How is Maya’s point of view different from Omar’s right after the bridge breaks?

explanation.whyCorrect: Maya says, “It’s ruined.” Omar says, “Maybe we just need stronger shapes.”
explanation.tip: Compare what two characters say about the same event.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya thinks it can be fixed; Omar wants to quit.
options.rationale: It is the other way around.

options.label: B
options.text: Both think the contest is not important.
options.rationale: Both care about the contest.

options.label: C
options.text: Both think the bridge is ruined.
options.rationale: Omar offers a solution, so he does not think that.

options.label: D
options.text: Maya thinks the bridge is ruined; Omar thinks it can be fixed.

items.stem: In “The Stick Bridge,” Maya and Omar react the same way when the bridge breaks.

explanation.whyCorrect: Maya is upset and wants to give up, while Omar calmly suggests a solution.
explanation.tip: Read each character’s words carefully to find their point of view.

items.stem: How does Noura’s father seem to feel about leaving?

explanation.whyCorrect: He kneels, takes her hand, smiles and gives her a shell so she will feel close to him.
explanation.tip: Actions can show a character’s feelings even when the character does not name them.

options.label: A
options.text: Calm and caring, wanting to comfort Noura

options.label: B
options.text: Angry that Noura came to the shore
options.rationale: He kneels and holds her hand, which is caring.

options.label: C
options.text: Uninterested in saying goodbye
options.rationale: He gives her a special shell.

options.label: D
options.text: Frightened of the sea
options.rationale: Nothing shows he is afraid; he smiles.

items.stem: Read: “Everyone cheered when the rain began, but Faisal stared at the soggy football field and sighed.” What is Faisal’s perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: While others cheer, Faisal stares at the field and sighs, showing a different feeling.
explanation.tip: When a character reacts differently from others, the author is showing a different point of view.

options.label: A
options.text: He is excited to play in the mud.
options.rationale: Sighing shows disappointment, not excitement.

options.label: B
options.text: He is disappointed because the rain may stop his game.

options.label: C
options.text: He is afraid of thunder.
options.rationale: Thunder is not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: He is happy about the rain like everyone else.
options.rationale: He sighs instead of cheering.

items.stem: The story is told from the outside (third person). How would the ending change if Omar told it?

explanation.whyCorrect: A first-person narrator shares his own thoughts and feelings, so we would know how Omar felt.
explanation.tip: Point of view decides whose thoughts the reader can hear.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya would no longer be in the story.
options.rationale: She would still be in the story; only the narrator changes.

options.label: B
options.text: The bridge would break at the contest.
options.rationale: Changing the narrator does not change the events.

options.label: C
options.text: We would hear Omar’s own thoughts about helping his sister.

options.label: D
options.text: We would learn the name of Maya’s teacher.
options.rationale: The narrator choice does not add new facts like this.

items.stem: Which words help you picture the bridge breaking?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sound of a snap and the image of the middle sagging help you see and hear the break.
explanation.tip: To visualize, look for words that appeal to your senses.

options.label: A
options.text: “the class bridge contest”
options.rationale: This names the event.

options.label: B
options.text: “forty craft sticks”
options.rationale: This describes the materials, not the break.

options.label: C
options.text: “Next time”
options.rationale: These words do not create a picture.

options.label: D
options.text: “a sharp snap” and “sagged down to the table”

items.stem: In the flashback, the sea “looked like a sheet of blue glass.” What should you picture?

explanation.whyCorrect: A sheet of glass is flat and shiny, so the sea looked calm and smooth.
explanation.tip: Comparisons help you build a picture in your mind.

options.label: A
options.text: A calm, smooth, shining sea

options.label: B
options.text: A sea full of big crashing waves
options.rationale: Glass is smooth, not wavy.

options.label: C
options.text: A dark, stormy sea
options.rationale: “Blue glass” suggests calm and bright.

options.label: D
options.text: A broken window
options.rationale: The sea is compared to glass; nothing is broken.

items.stem: At the end, the boat becomes “only a speck on the bright water.” What does this help you see?

explanation.whyCorrect: A speck is a tiny dot, so the boat has sailed so far that it looks tiny.
explanation.tip: Think about how things look smaller when they are far away.

options.label: A
options.text: The boat is very large.
options.rationale: A speck is tiny, so the boat looks small.

options.label: B
options.text: The boat is very far away.

options.label: C
options.text: The water is dark and dirty.
options.rationale: The water is described as “bright.”

options.label: D
options.text: The boat is sinking.
options.rationale: A speck shows distance, not sinking.

items.stem: In “Rain on the Roof,” the words “splashing puddles on the grass” help you picture the rain.

explanation.whyCorrect: You can see and hear the water splashing into puddles.
explanation.tip: Words that show action and sound help you visualize.

items.stem: Which line from “Rain on the Roof” helps you HEAR the rain?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tapping on tin makes a sound, so this line helps you hear the rain.
explanation.tip: Visualizing uses all your senses: sight, sound, touch, smell and taste.

options.label: A
options.text: “Slow and low, the gray clouds go”
options.rationale: This helps you see the clouds.

options.label: B
options.text: “rolling over the road below”
options.rationale: This shows the clouds moving.

options.label: C
options.text: “tapping tin roofs with tiny pins”

options.label: D
options.text: “Then the sun slides out to say”
options.rationale: This shows the sun coming out.

items.stem: What picture do the last two lines of the poem create?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sun “slides out” and tells the showers to “slip away,” so the rain ends.
explanation.tip: Picture what the words describe, not their literal meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: Silver coins fall from the sky.
options.rationale: “Silver showers” describes the shiny rain.

options.label: B
options.text: The night sky fills with stars.
options.rationale: The sun is out, so it is daytime.

options.label: C
options.text: A thunderstorm starts.
options.rationale: The sun is coming out, not a storm.

options.label: D
options.text: The rain stops and the sunshine returns.

items.stem: How is most of “How Honeybees Share Directions” organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article gives details about what the waggle dance and round dance are and what they show.
explanation.tip: A description structure gives details and features about one topic.

options.label: A
options.text: It describes how bees use dances to share information.

options.label: B
options.text: It tells events in time order from one bee’s life.
options.rationale: It does not follow one bee from birth to death.

options.label: C
options.text: It compares bees with ants.
options.rationale: Ants are not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains a problem and its solution.
options.rationale: There is no problem being solved.

items.stem: Which detail describes the waggle dance?

explanation.whyCorrect: The second paragraph tells exactly what the dance looks like.
explanation.tip: Descriptive details tell what something looks like or how it works.

options.label: A
options.text: Bees need food to survive.
options.rationale: This is not a description of the dance.

options.label: B
options.text: The bee walks in a straight line while shaking her body.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees live in colonies.
options.rationale: This is about bees in general, not the dance.

options.label: D
options.text: Scientists watched hives with glass walls.
options.rationale: This tells how people learned about the dance.

items.stem: A text with a description structure gives many details about one topic.

explanation.whyCorrect: Description gives features, characteristics and examples of a topic.
explanation.tip: Signal words for description include “for example,” “such as” and “looks like.”

items.stem: What does the round dance tell other bees?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article says the round dance is used when flowers “are very close to the hive.”
explanation.tip: Find the paragraph that describes the round dance.

options.label: A
options.text: It is time to sleep.
options.rationale: The dances are about food.

options.label: B
options.text: The food is very far away.
options.rationale: A long waggle shows food is far; the round dance shows it is near.

options.label: C
options.text: The food is very close to the hive.

options.label: D
options.text: The hive is in danger.
options.rationale: The article does not mention danger.

items.stem: Match each bee movement with what it tells other bees.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article describes what each part of the dances means.
explanation.tip: In a description, each detail explains one feature of the topic.

pairs.right: How far away the food is

items.stem: Why did the author describe the dances in so much detail?

explanation.whyCorrect: The details explain how direction and distance are shared through movement.
explanation.tip: Authors use description to help readers picture and understand a topic.

options.label: A
options.text: To explain how to build a beehive.
options.rationale: Building hives is not discussed.

options.label: B
options.text: To convince readers to buy honey.
options.rationale: The article informs; it does not sell anything.

options.label: C
options.text: To tell a story about one famous bee.
options.rationale: No single bee is the main character.

options.label: D
options.text: To help readers understand how bees communicate without words.

items.stem: Which is the BEST summary of “The Dripping Taps”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary tells the most important ideas from beginning to end in a few words.
explanation.tip: Include the main problem, the key actions and the result. Leave out small details.

options.label: A
options.text: Students found that taps wasted water, got them fixed, and helped the school save water.

options.label: B
options.text: Students like making bright signs.
options.rationale: This is not the main point and is not stated.

options.label: C
options.text: A cup was placed under a tap for one hour.
options.rationale: This is one detail, not a summary of the whole text.

options.label: D
options.text: Mrs. Hassan is the principal of Al-Noor Elementary.
options.rationale: This is a small detail.

items.stem: Which detail is LEAST important to include in a summary of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The cushion is a small detail; the main steps are mixing, rising, heating, shaping and baking.
explanation.tip: Summaries keep main ideas and drop small details.

options.label: A
options.text: The bread is baked on the hot wall of the oven.
options.rationale: This is the main baking step.

options.label: B
options.text: The baker uses a padded cushion.

options.label: C
options.text: The oven is heated with a fire.
options.rationale: This is an important step.

options.label: D
options.text: The dough must rise before baking.
options.rationale: This is a key step.

items.stem: A good summary includes your own opinion about the text.

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary retells the important ideas in your own words, without adding opinions.
explanation.tip: Summaries are short, accurate and objective.

items.stem: Which sentence BEST summarizes “The Stick Bridge”?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence includes the problem, the solution and the result.
explanation.tip: A story summary includes the main character, the problem and how it is solved.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya has forty craft sticks and a dictionary.
options.rationale: These are details from the beginning only.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar likes math books with pictures.
options.rationale: This is not stated and is not the main idea.

options.label: C
options.text: When Maya’s bridge breaks, she and Omar fix it with triangles, and it holds at the contest.

options.label: D
options.text: The bridge contest happens every year.
options.rationale: The story does not say this.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to make a summary of “How Honeybees Share Directions.”

explanation.whyCorrect: These sentences follow the article from finding food to how scientists learned about the dances.
explanation.tip: A summary follows the order of the main ideas in the text.

sequence: Bees that find food return to the hive.
They dance to show other bees where the food is.
A waggle dance shows direction and distance; a round dance shows food is close.
Scientists learned this by watching hives with glass walls.

items.stem: A student wrote: “The fourth graders measured, wrote, fixed, signed, checked and saved.” What is wrong with this summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: A useful summary explains the main problem (wasted water) and the result (saving water), not just a list of verbs.
explanation.tip: Check that a summary would make sense to someone who has not read the text.

options.label: A
options.text: It is too long.
options.rationale: It is very short; the problem is missing information.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses words from the text.
options.rationale: Using some key words is fine.

options.label: C
options.text: It includes the student’s opinion.
options.rationale: There is no opinion in it.

options.label: D
options.text: It lists actions but does not explain the problem or why it mattered.

items.stem: Which question is answered in the third paragraph of “How Honeybees Share Directions”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The third paragraph says the length of the waggle shows how far away the flowers are.
explanation.tip: Match the question to the paragraph that gives the answer.

options.label: A
options.text: How do bees show how far away the food is?

options.label: B
options.text: What color are honeybees?
options.rationale: Color is not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: How do beekeepers collect honey?
options.rationale: That is in a different article.

options.label: D
options.text: Why do bees live in colonies?
options.rationale: The text says they live in colonies but does not explain why.

items.stem: Which question can you answer using “The Dripping Taps”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says, “First, the students wrote a letter to the principal.”
explanation.tip: Good readers ask questions the text can answer, and find the evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: What is the principal’s favorite subject?
options.rationale: This is not in the text.

options.label: B
options.text: What did the class do first to solve the problem?

options.label: C
options.text: How much did the plumber charge?
options.rationale: The cost is not given.

options.label: D
options.text: How many students go to Al-Noor Elementary?
options.rationale: The number is not given.

items.stem: “The Dripping Taps” tells how full the cup was after one hour.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says that “By the end of the hour, the cup was almost full.”
explanation.tip: Find the exact sentence that answers the question.

items.stem: A reader asks, “How did scientists learn about the bee dances?” Which sentence answers this question?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence directly names how scientists studied the bees.
explanation.tip: Use key words from the question (scientists, learn) to find the answer.

options.label: A
options.text: A longer waggle means the food is farther away.
options.rationale: This explains the dance, not how it was discovered.

options.label: B
options.text: She moves in small circles.
options.rationale: This describes the round dance.

options.label: C
options.text: Scientists learned about these dances by watching bees in hives with glass walls.

options.label: D
options.text: Honeybees live and work together in large groups called colonies.
options.rationale: This does not mention scientists.

items.stem: Which question would be the MOST useful to ask before reading “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The title tells you the article explains a process, so asking about the steps guides your reading.
explanation.tip: Use the title and headings to ask questions that guide your reading.

options.label: A
options.text: Who wrote this article?
options.rationale: This does not help you understand the process.

options.label: B
options.text: Is the oven red?
options.rationale: This detail is too small to guide your reading.

options.label: C
options.text: Do I like bread?
options.rationale: Your opinion will not help you understand the text.

options.label: D
options.text: What steps are needed to bake bread in a clay oven?

items.stem: Which question CANNOT be answered from “Keeping Bees in the Mountains”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article never gives the number of beekeepers.
explanation.tip: Some questions need another source. Check whether the text really gives the answer.

options.label: A
options.text: How many beekeepers live in the mountains?

options.label: B
options.text: Where is the honey sold?
options.rationale: The text says it is sold at local markets.

options.label: C
options.text: Why do beekeepers use smoke?
options.rationale: The text says the smoke calms the bees.

options.label: D
options.text: Why do beekeepers move their hives?
options.rationale: The text says they move them closer to blooming flowers.

items.stem: You are not sure what the round dance means. What should you do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading the part that explains the round dance will clear up the confusion.
explanation.tip: When something is confusing, go back and reread that part slowly.

options.label: A
options.text: Skip to the end of the article.
options.rationale: The end does not explain the round dance.

options.label: B
options.text: Reread the paragraph about the round dance.

options.label: C
options.text: Guess and keep reading.
options.rationale: Rereading gives you real evidence instead of a guess.

options.label: D
options.text: Read only the title again.
options.rationale: The title does not explain the dance.

items.stem: Rereading can help you find details you missed the first time.

explanation.whyCorrect: Good readers reread to check their understanding and find evidence.
explanation.tip: Rereading is a fix-up strategy, not a sign of a weak reader.

items.stem: After reading “The Dripping Taps,” you are not sure why the bill was lower. Which part should you reread?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph about checking a month later explains the fixed taps and the lower bill.
explanation.tip: Reread the part of the text that matches your question.

options.label: A
options.text: The paragraph about the letter
options.rationale: The letter came before the results.

options.label: B
options.text: The title
options.rationale: The title does not explain the bill.

options.label: C
options.text: The paragraph about what happened a month later

options.label: D
options.text: The first sentence only
options.rationale: The first sentence introduces the problem.

items.stem: Rereading the second paragraph of “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven” helps you answer which question?

explanation.whyCorrect: The second paragraph says the dough rests “for about an hour.”
explanation.tip: Know which paragraph covers which idea before you reread.

options.label: A
options.text: Where is the bread stacked?
options.rationale: That is in the last paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: What is the oven made of?
options.rationale: That is in the title and first paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: How is the bread taken off the wall?
options.rationale: That is in the last paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: How long does the dough rest?

items.stem: Why might a reader reread the sentence “The length of time she waggles tells them how far away the flowers are”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence explains a key idea (distance), so rereading helps you understand it.
explanation.tip: Reread sentences that hold important or difficult ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: To understand how the dance shows distance

options.label: B
options.text: To find out what honey tastes like
options.rationale: The sentence is about distance.

options.label: C
options.text: To learn the bee’s name
options.rationale: Bees in the article are not named.

options.label: D
options.text: To count the paragraphs
options.rationale: Counting paragraphs does not help understanding.

items.stem: Which TWO are good reasons to reread a text?

explanation.whyCorrect: Readers reread to check understanding and to find evidence.
explanation.tip: Rereading is a tool for understanding.

options.label: A
options.text: To finish faster
options.rationale: Rereading takes extra time; it is for understanding.

options.label: B
options.text: To find evidence for an answer

options.label: C
options.text: To clear up a confusing part

options.label: D
options.text: To skip the hard words
options.rationale: Rereading helps with hard words; it does not skip them.

items.stem: Put the bread-making steps in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article describes mixing, rising, baking and removing, in that order.
explanation.tip: Signal words like “early,” “next” and “finally” show the order of steps.

sequence: Mix flour, water, salt and yeast.
Let the dough rise under a cloth.
Press the dough onto the hot oven wall.
Take the bread off with a long hook.

items.stem: What does the baker do WHILE the dough is rising?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article says, “While the dough rises, the baker lights a fire inside the oven.”
explanation.tip: “While” means two things happen at the same time.

options.label: A
options.text: Presses dough onto the wall
options.rationale: This happens after the dough has risen.

options.label: B
options.text: Lights a fire inside the oven

options.label: C
options.text: Takes the bread out of the oven
options.rationale: This happens at the very end.

options.label: D
options.text: Stacks bread in a basket
options.rationale: This is the last step.

items.stem: Which word in “The Dripping Taps” signals the second step the class took?

explanation.whyCorrect: First they wrote a letter; next the plumber fixed the taps; then they made signs.
explanation.tip: Sequence words: first, next, then, after that, finally.

options.label: A
options.text: Later
options.rationale: This word is not used for the steps.

options.label: B
options.text: Then
options.rationale: “Then” signals the third step.

options.label: C
options.text: Next

options.label: D
options.text: First
options.rationale: “First” signals the first step.

items.stem: Put the events of “The Dripping Taps” in time order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article tells the events in the order they happened.
explanation.tip: Follow time words and the order of paragraphs.

sequence: Students notice dripping taps.
They measure water with a cup.
They write to the principal.
A plumber fixes the taps.
They check again a month later.

items.stem: Why is a sequence structure a good choice for “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each step depends on the one before it, so time order helps readers follow the process.
explanation.tip: Authors choose sequence for processes, instructions and events over time.

options.label: A
options.text: It compares two kinds of bread.
options.rationale: The article explains one process; it does not compare.

options.label: B
options.text: It argues that bread is healthy.
options.rationale: The article does not give an opinion.

options.label: C
options.text: It tells a story with characters.
options.rationale: The article has no characters.

options.label: D
options.text: Making bread is a process that must be done in a certain order.

items.stem: What would MOST likely happen if the baker skipped heating the oven?

explanation.whyCorrect: The bread bakes on the “hot inner wall,” so a cool oven would not cook it.
explanation.tip: In a process, each step has a reason. Think about why a step is needed.

options.label: A
options.text: The bread would not bake properly on the cool walls.

options.label: B
options.text: The dough would rise faster.
options.rationale: Heating the oven does not affect rising.

options.label: C
options.text: The bread would turn golden more quickly.
options.rationale: Without heat, it cannot turn golden.

options.label: D
options.text: The bread would not need to be shaped.
options.rationale: Shaping happens no matter what.

items.stem: What problem did the fourth graders find?

explanation.whyCorrect: Taps dripped all day and some students left the water running.
explanation.tip: In a problem-and-solution text, the problem usually comes first.

options.label: A
options.text: The principal was not at school.
options.rationale: The students wrote to her; she was there.

options.label: B
options.text: Water was being wasted at the school sinks.

options.label: C
options.text: The cup was too small.
options.rationale: The cup was used to measure the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: The school had no sinks.
options.rationale: There were sinks with dripping taps.

items.stem: Which was one solution to the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Fixing the taps stopped the dripping, which solved part of the problem.
explanation.tip: A solution is an action that fixes the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: The cup was almost full.
options.rationale: This shows how big the problem was.

options.label: B
options.text: The taps dripped all day.
options.rationale: This is the problem.

options.label: C
options.text: A plumber fixed the leaking taps.

options.label: D
options.text: The students measured water in a cup.
options.rationale: Measuring showed the problem; it did not solve it.

items.stem: In “The Dripping Taps,” making signs was part of the solution.

explanation.whyCorrect: The signs reminded students to turn off the tap while soaping.
