explanation.tip: An author’s purpose shapes the structure of a text.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the author wanted to persuade readers to buy turtles
options.rationale: The article does not persuade.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the purpose is to inform readers about different parts of the topic

options.label: C
options.text: Because headings make articles longer
options.rationale: Structure is chosen for purpose, not length.

options.label: D
options.text: Because turtles cannot be argued about
options.rationale: Any topic can be argued; the purpose here is to inform.

items.stem: Which sense does “the bread oven breathes, warm and red” appeal to most?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Warm” appeals to touch, and “red” appeals to sight.
explanation.tip: Imagery uses details that appeal to the five senses.

options.label: A
options.text: Taste only
options.rationale: Bread is mentioned, but the line describes warmth and color.

options.label: B
options.text: Hearing only
options.rationale: There is no sound in this line.

options.label: C
options.text: Touch (feeling warmth) and sight

options.label: D
options.text: Smell only
options.rationale: The line focuses on warmth and redness.

items.stem: Which line from “Harbor at Dawn” appeals to the sense of smell?

explanation.whyCorrect: You can smell salt and diesel fuel carried on the wind.
explanation.tip: Ask which sense each image uses.

options.label: A
options.text: “the last stars folding up the night”
options.rationale: This appeals to sight.

options.label: B
options.text: “Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread”
options.rationale: This appeals to sight.

options.label: C
options.text: “Ropes creak like old men’s knees”
options.rationale: This appeals to hearing.

options.label: D
options.text: “salt and diesel ride the breeze”

items.stem: What does “Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread” help you picture?

explanation.whyCorrect: Like a needle going in and out, the gulls dart across the sky, catching silver light.
explanation.tip: Imagery often uses figurative language to create a picture.

options.label: A
options.text: Birds flying back and forth, flashing silver in the light

options.label: B
options.text: Birds sewing clothes
options.rationale: The image is a metaphor, not literal sewing.

options.label: C
options.text: Gulls sleeping on a boat
options.rationale: “Stitch” suggests movement.

options.label: D
options.text: A storm with lightning
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a storm.

items.stem: “Ropes creak like old men’s knees” appeals to the sense of hearing.

explanation.whyCorrect: A creak is a sound, and the comparison helps you hear it.
explanation.tip: Sound words such as creak, buzz and hiss create hearing images.

items.stem: Match each image from the poem with the sense it appeals to most.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each image uses a different sense to bring the harbor to life.
explanation.tip: Read each image and ask: Do I see, hear, smell, taste or feel this?

pairs.left: salt and diesel ride the breeze

items.stem: What overall mood does the imagery in “Harbor at Dawn” create?

explanation.whyCorrect: Words like “yawns,” “sleep” and “pearl-gray light” suggest a quiet morning waking up.
explanation.tip: The images together create the mood of a poem.

options.label: A
options.text: A sad farewell at sunset
options.rationale: The poem is about morning.

options.label: B
options.text: A calm, sleepy morning slowly waking up

options.label: C
options.text: A frightening, dangerous night
options.rationale: The poem describes dawn and gentle sounds.

options.label: D
options.text: A loud, busy afternoon
options.rationale: It is dawn and things are just waking.

items.stem: Which stage direction helps you picture Layla’s nervousness?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pacing back and forth is a picture of someone who is nervous.
explanation.tip: Stage directions help readers visualize characters’ actions.

options.label: A
options.text: [MS. DAWOOD walks in with a clipboard.]
options.rationale: This shows the teacher arriving.

options.label: B
options.text: [A clay volcano sits on a table.]
options.rationale: This describes the setting.

options.label: C
options.text: [LAYLA paces back and forth.]

options.label: D
options.text: [Red foam bubbles up.]
options.rationale: This shows the experiment working.

items.stem: What should you picture when you read “Red foam bubbles up and spills down the sides”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The verbs “bubbles up” and “spills down” show the foam moving.
explanation.tip: Strong verbs help you create a moving picture in your mind.

options.label: A
options.text: Smoke filling the classroom
options.rationale: The text describes foam, not smoke.

options.label: B
options.text: The volcano breaking into pieces
options.rationale: Nothing breaks.

options.label: C
options.text: Water dripping from the ceiling
options.rationale: The foam comes from the volcano.

options.label: D
options.text: Foam rising from the volcano and running down it

items.stem: In “The Last Repair,” the description “a silver curl no bigger than a fingernail” helps you picture the spring’s size.

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing it to a fingernail shows how tiny it is.
explanation.tip: Comparisons to familiar objects help you visualize size.

items.stem: Which detail helps you visualize Khalid’s panic?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sweeping hands and screws scattering show rushed, panicked movement.
explanation.tip: Look for actions that show feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: He swept his hands across the bench, knocking a box of screws to the floor.

options.label: B
options.text: He had opened the watch and cleaned every gear.
options.rationale: This shows careful work, not panic.

options.label: C
options.text: He closed the case and wound the crown.
options.rationale: This shows success.

options.label: D
options.text: He picked up the magnifying glass.
options.rationale: This shows calm searching.

items.stem: Reading the play aloud, how should the actor playing Layla say “The baking soda… is still in my backpack”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The ellipsis (…) and the direction “slowly lowering her hands” suggest a slow, embarrassed realization.
explanation.tip: Visualizing a scene includes imagining how lines are spoken.

options.label: A
options.text: In a whisper of fear
options.rationale: She is embarrassed, not frightened.

options.label: B
options.text: Slowly and with embarrassment, pausing at the dots

options.label: C
options.text: Quickly and excitedly
options.rationale: The ellipsis shows a slow, hesitant pause.

options.label: D
options.text: Loudly and angrily
options.rationale: She realizes her own mistake, so anger does not fit.

items.stem: How does visualizing the two scenes help you understand the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Picturing the actions in each scene shows Layla’s growth from Scene 1 to Scene 2.
explanation.tip: Picture how characters look and move at different points in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: You can see that Yusuf leaves the room.
options.rationale: Yusuf stays in both scenes.

options.label: B
options.text: You can see that the volcano never works.
options.rationale: It works in Scene 2.

options.label: C
options.text: You can see Layla change from panicked pacing to proudly standing beside the volcano.

options.label: D
options.text: You can see that Ms. Dawood is the main character.
options.rationale: Layla is the main character.

items.stem: Which is the BEST summary of “The Two Wells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary includes the problem, the key events and the resolution.
explanation.tip: Include the main character, the problem and the outcome.

options.label: A
options.text: The village had palm trees and a well.
options.rationale: This leaves out the conflict and resolution.

options.label: B
options.text: Salma’s hands blistered after seven days.
options.rationale: This is a detail, not a summary.

options.label: C
options.text: Hamdan was rich and had a gate.
options.rationale: This leaves out what happened.

options.label: D
options.text: When a merchant charges for the only well, Salma finds a new well, and the merchant learns to share.

items.stem: Which sentence BEST summarizes “Sea Turtles of the Red Sea”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The summary covers each main section: nesting, hatching and dangers.
explanation.tip: Use the headings to identify the main ideas to summarize.

options.label: A
options.text: Red Sea turtles nest on beaches, their hatchlings head to the sea, and bright lights can confuse them.

options.label: B
options.text: Warmer nests produce more females.
options.rationale: This is one sidebar fact.

options.label: C
options.text: A hatchling is a young animal just out of its egg.
options.rationale: This is the glossary definition.

options.label: D
options.text: Turtles have back flippers.
options.rationale: This is a small detail.

items.stem: A summary of “The Last Repair” should include what kind of fabric Khalid’s apron is made of.

explanation.whyCorrect: The fabric is not important and is not even mentioned; the apron matters only because the spring is found there.
explanation.tip: Summaries leave out small details.

items.stem: Which detail should be LEFT OUT of a summary of “Every School Needs a Garden”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The tomato line is a vivid example, not one of the main reasons.
explanation.tip: Keep the claim and main reasons; drop examples and descriptions.

options.label: A
options.text: Gardens make lessons real.
options.rationale: This is a main reason.

options.label: B
options.text: A tomato you have watered for weeks is more interesting.

options.label: C
options.text: Gardens can start small to save money.
options.rationale: This answers the counterclaim.

options.label: D
options.text: Gardens help students eat better.
options.rationale: This is a main reason.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to summarize “The Last Repair.”

explanation.whyCorrect: These four sentences give the beginning, problem, turning point and resolution.
explanation.tip: A story summary follows the plot from beginning to end.

sequence: Khalid must fix a captain’s watch before sunset.
He loses a tiny spring and panics.
He remembers his uncle’s lesson about patience.
He finds the spring and finishes just in time.

items.stem: A student summarized the garden article as “Gardens are great and everyone loves them.” What is the main problem with this summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary should state the author’s claim and main reasons, not a general opinion.
explanation.tip: Summaries are objective and include the main ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: It uses the author’s exact words.
options.rationale: It does not quote the author.

options.label: B
options.text: It includes too many facts.
options.rationale: It includes no facts.

options.label: C
options.text: It adds an opinion and leaves out the author’s actual reasons.

options.label: D
options.text: It is too long.
options.rationale: It is very short.

items.stem: You are unsure why hatchlings crawl the wrong way. Which section should you reread?

explanation.whyCorrect: This section explains that bright lights confuse hatchlings.
explanation.tip: Use headings to choose which part to reread.

options.label: A
options.text: Glossary
options.rationale: The glossary defines a word.

options.label: B
options.text: The title
options.rationale: The title does not explain the danger.

options.label: C
options.text: Where Turtles Nest
options.rationale: This section is about nesting beaches.

options.label: D
options.text: Dangers on the Beach

items.stem: Rereading can help you notice how one paragraph connects to another.

explanation.whyCorrect: A second reading often reveals connections you missed the first time.
explanation.tip: Reread slowly and look for links between ideas.

items.stem: After rereading “Every School Needs a Garden,” a student understands why the author mentions “donated seeds.” What did rereading help the student see?

explanation.whyCorrect: The donated seeds appear in the paragraph that responds to the cost argument.
explanation.tip: Reread to understand why the author includes a detail.

options.label: A
options.text: The detail answers the claim that gardens cost too much.

options.label: B
options.text: The author wants students to sell seeds.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests selling seeds.

options.label: C
options.text: Seeds grow faster when donated.
options.rationale: This is not stated.

options.label: D
options.text: Gardens need no seeds at all.
options.rationale: The text mentions seeds as a cheap way to start.

items.stem: Which question would rereading the first section of the turtle article help you answer?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first section names green turtles and hawksbill turtles.
explanation.tip: Know which section answers which question.

options.label: A
options.text: How long do eggs stay in the sand?
options.rationale: That is in “From Egg to Ocean.”

options.label: B
options.text: Which kinds of turtles swim in the Red Sea?

options.label: C
options.text: What does “hatchling” mean?
options.rationale: That is in the glossary.

options.label: D
options.text: Why do bright lights confuse hatchlings?
options.rationale: That is in “Dangers on the Beach.”

items.stem: A reader thinks the turtle article says lights help hatchlings. What should the reader do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading would show that lights confuse hatchlings; they do not help.
explanation.tip: Reread to check facts when you are not sure.

options.label: A
options.text: Trust their memory and move on.
options.rationale: Their memory is wrong; checking would show it.

options.label: B
options.text: Look only at the caption.
options.rationale: The caption alone does not explain the effect of lights.

options.label: C
options.text: Reread the section about dangers to check the information.

options.label: D
options.text: Read a different article.
options.rationale: This article has the answer.

items.stem: Which TWO details would a careful reread of “From Egg to Ocean” reveal?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both correct details are stated in the section; the others contradict it.
explanation.tip: Rereading helps you separate what the text says from what you assume.

options.label: A
options.text: The eggs stay in the sand for about two months.

options.label: B
options.text: Hatchlings usually dig out at night.

options.label: C
options.text: Hatchlings follow their mother to the water.
options.rationale: They follow the bright horizon.

options.label: D
options.text: The mother turtle stays to protect the nest.
options.rationale: She returns to the sea.

items.stem: Which question is answered in the sidebar of the turtle article?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sidebar says the temperature of the sand affects this.
explanation.tip: Match questions to the part of the text that answers them.

options.label: A
options.text: How many eggs does a turtle lay?
options.rationale: That is answered in “From Egg to Ocean.”

options.label: B
options.text: What is a caption?
options.rationale: The article does not define caption.

options.label: C
options.text: Where do turtles nest?
options.rationale: That is answered in the first section.

options.label: D
options.text: What affects whether hatchlings become males or females?

items.stem: Which question can be answered by quoting the garden article directly?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says gardens can start “with a few containers and donated seeds.”
explanation.tip: Ask questions that the text can answer with evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: What does the author suggest for schools with little money?

options.label: B
options.text: What does the author’s school garden look like?
options.rationale: The author does not describe a specific garden.

options.label: C
options.text: How many schools have gardens?
options.rationale: No number is given.

options.label: D
options.text: Which vegetables grow fastest?
options.rationale: Growth speed is not discussed.

items.stem: The turtle article explains exactly how many hatchlings survive to adulthood.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article does not give survival numbers; you would need another source.
explanation.tip: Notice when a text does NOT answer your question.

items.stem: A reader asks, “Why do hatchlings move toward the horizon?” Which sentence answers this?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence explains that the bright horizon leads them to the sea.
explanation.tip: Use the question’s key words to find the answer.

options.label: A
options.text: Warmer nests produce more females.
options.rationale: This is about temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: Hatchlings find the sea by moving toward the brightest horizon, which is normally the moonlit water.

options.label: C
options.text: She covers the nest and returns to the sea.
options.rationale: This is about the mother.

options.label: D
options.text: Green turtles and hawksbill turtles swim in the warm waters of the Red Sea.
options.rationale: This does not explain the movement.

items.stem: Which question shows the DEEPEST thinking about the garden article?

explanation.whyCorrect: This question applies the author’s ideas to a new situation.
explanation.tip: Strong readers ask questions that go beyond recall.

options.label: A
options.text: What is the title?
options.rationale: This is a simple recall question.

options.label: B
options.text: How many reasons are there?
options.rationale: This only counts.

options.label: C
options.text: Would the author’s reasons work for a school in a very dry climate?

options.label: D
options.text: Who argues that gardens cost too much?
options.rationale: The text says only “some people.”

items.stem: Which inference is BEST supported by the turtle article?

explanation.whyCorrect: If bright lights confuse hatchlings, darker beaches would help them find the moonlit water.
explanation.tip: Combine details from the text to answer a question it does not state directly.

options.label: A
options.text: Hawksbill turtles do not lay eggs.
options.rationale: Both species nest on beaches.

options.label: B
options.text: Turtles prefer cold beaches.
options.rationale: The article says warmer sand produces more females, not that turtles prefer cold.

options.label: C
options.text: Hatchlings are never in danger.
options.rationale: The article describes dangers.

options.label: D
options.text: Keeping beaches dark at night could help more hatchlings reach the sea.

items.stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has a subject (The new library) and a predicate (opens on Sunday) and expresses a complete thought.
explanation.tip: A sentence needs a subject, a verb and a complete thought.

options.label: A
options.text: The new library opens on Sunday.

options.label: B
options.text: The new library on Sunday.
options.rationale: This fragment has no verb.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the library opens.
options.rationale: This dependent clause is not a complete thought.

options.label: D
options.text: Opens on Sunday.
options.rationale: This fragment has no subject.

items.stem: Choose the end mark: “Have you ever seen a shooting star____”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Have you ever…” asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.
explanation.tip: Statements end with periods; questions end with question marks.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A semicolon cannot end a sentence.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A comma cannot end a sentence.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This sentence asks something, so it needs a question mark.

items.stem: Which interrogative word best begins this question? “____ did the museum close early today?”

explanation.whyCorrect: The question asks for a reason, so “Why” fits.
explanation.tip: Interrogatives: who (person), what (thing), when (time), where (place), why (reason), how (manner).

options.label: A
options.text: Who
options.rationale: “Who” asks about a person, not a reason.

options.label: B
options.text: Why

options.label: C
options.text: Whose
options.rationale: “Whose” asks about ownership.

options.label: D
options.text: Which
options.rationale: “Which” needs a noun after it here.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an appositive correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: An appositive that renames a noun in the middle of a sentence is set off by commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: Appositives explain a nearby noun and are usually set off with commas.

options.label: A
options.text: Our librarian Ms. Rahma, ordered, new atlases.
options.rationale: The commas are in the wrong places.

options.label: B
options.text: Ms. Rahma our librarian, ordered new atlases.
options.rationale: The appositive needs a comma on both sides.

options.label: C
options.text: Ms. Rahma, our librarian, ordered new atlases.

options.label: D
options.text: Ms. Rahma, our librarian ordered new atlases.
options.rationale: The appositive needs a closing comma.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of all the players, Majed had the ____ score.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Best” is the superlative of “good,” used when comparing more than two.
explanation.tip: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

options.label: A
options.text: bestest
options.rationale: Never add -est to an irregular superlative.

options.label: B
options.text: most best
options.rationale: Never add “most” to “best.”

options.label: C
options.text: better
options.rationale: “Better” compares two; this compares all the players.

options.label: D
options.text: best

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Worse” is already the comparative form of “bad,” so “more” must be removed.
explanation.tip: Never add more or most to an irregular comparative form.

items.stem: What is the complete predicate? “The friendly dog waited patiently for her owner.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The complete predicate includes the verb and all the words that tell about it.
explanation.tip: Complete predicate = everything that tells what the subject did or is.

options.label: A
options.text: The friendly dog
options.rationale: This is the complete subject.

options.label: B
options.text: dog
options.rationale: This is the simple subject.

options.label: C
options.text: her owner
options.rationale: This is part of the predicate only.

options.label: D
options.text: waited patiently for her owner

items.stem: What is the simple subject? “Several excited volunteers from the museum cleaned the beach.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Remove describing words and phrases; the main noun is “volunteers.”
explanation.tip: The simple subject is never inside a prepositional phrase.

options.label: A
options.text: volunteers

options.label: B
options.text: museum
options.rationale: This is part of a prepositional phrase.

options.label: C
options.text: excited
options.rationale: This describes the volunteers.

options.label: D
options.text: beach
options.rationale: This is part of the predicate.

items.stem: In “Under the old bridge lived a family of ducks,” the subject comes after the verb.

explanation.whyCorrect: The verb is “lived”; the subject “a family of ducks” comes after it.
explanation.tip: In inverted sentences, ask “Who or what lived?” to find the subject.

items.stem: Which sentence has BOTH a compound subject and a compound predicate?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two subjects (Reem, Dana) share two predicates (wrote…, directed…).
explanation.tip: Find the subjects first, then the verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: Reem wrote the script, and Dana directed the play.
options.rationale: This is a compound sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Reem and Dana wrote the script and directed the play.

options.label: C
options.text: Reem and Dana wrote the script.
options.rationale: This has a compound subject only.

options.label: D
options.text: Reem wrote the script and directed the play.
options.rationale: This has a compound predicate only.

items.stem: What is the simple predicate? “The students have been practicing their lines all week.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The simple predicate is the whole verb phrase: have been practicing.
explanation.tip: Include helping verbs in the simple predicate.

options.label: A
options.text: all week
options.rationale: This tells when.

options.label: B
options.text: their lines
options.rationale: This is the object of the verb.

options.label: C
options.text: have been practicing

options.label: D
options.text: practicing
options.rationale: The simple predicate includes the helping verbs.

items.stem: Add a simple subject that makes sense: “At dawn, the hungry ____ chirped loudly in the nest.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Something in a nest that chirps, such as “birds,” is a logical subject.
explanation.tip: The subject is who or what does the action.

items.stem: Which is a run-on sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete sentences are joined with no conjunction or punctuation.
explanation.tip: A run-on joins sentences without the proper conjunction and punctuation.

options.label: A
options.text: I went to the store, but it was closed.
options.rationale: This is a correct compound sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: When I went to the store.
options.rationale: This is a fragment, not a run-on.

options.label: C
options.text: I went to the store.
options.rationale: This is a correct simple sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: I went to the store it was closed.

items.stem: Which is a sentence fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has no subject and verb that complete a thought.
explanation.tip: A fragment leaves the reader asking, “What happened?”

options.label: A
options.text: After the long, rainy weekend.

options.label: B
options.text: We stayed inside all weekend.
options.rationale: This is a complete sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: It rained, so we played games.
options.rationale: This is a compound sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The weekend was long and rainy.
options.rationale: This is a complete sentence.

items.stem: Which is the best way to correct this run-on? “The museum was crowded we waited an hour.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma plus the conjunction “so” correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma plus and/but/or/so.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum was crowded, we waited an hour.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two sentences (comma splice).

options.label: B
options.text: The museum was crowded, so we waited an hour.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum was crowded we, waited an hour.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum crowded we waited.
options.rationale: This removes words and is still a run-on.

items.stem: “Running down the hallway with a heavy backpack” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: It has no subject and no complete verb; it is a fragment.
explanation.tip: Ask: Who is running? A complete sentence would tell you.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences; add a conjunction such as “and.”
explanation.tip: Two independent clauses need a comma AND a conjunction, or a period.

items.stem: Which revision fixes BOTH problems? “Because the bus was late. We missed the start of the play we were upset.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Attaching the fragment to the next clause and splitting the run-on fixes both errors.
explanation.tip: Fix fragments by joining them to a sentence; fix run-ons by separating or properly joining clauses.

options.label: A
options.text: The bus was late we missed the start. Of the play we were upset.
options.rationale: This creates new run-ons and fragments.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the bus was late. We missed the start of the play, we were upset.
options.rationale: The fragment and a comma splice remain.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the bus was late, we missed the start of the play. We were upset.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the bus was late, we missed the start of the play we were upset.
options.rationale: The run-on at the end remains.

items.stem: Choose the correct plural: “We packed our ____ for the trip.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Add -es to nouns ending in s, sh, ch or x: lunch → lunches.
explanation.tip: Words ending in s, sh, ch or x add -es.

options.label: A
options.text: lunches

options.label: B
options.text: lunchies
options.rationale: This is not a correct spelling.

options.label: C
options.text: lunchs
options.rationale: Nouns ending in ch add -es.

options.label: D
options.text: lunch’s
options.rationale: An apostrophe shows possession, not a plural.

items.stem: Choose the correct plural: “The library has three ____ of that book.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Copy ends in a consonant + y, so change y to i and add -es: copies.
explanation.tip: Vowel + y → add s (keys). Consonant + y → ies (copies).

options.label: A
options.text: copys
options.rationale: Consonant + y: change y to i and add -es.

options.label: B
options.text: copies

options.label: C
options.text: copy’s
options.rationale: An apostrophe does not form a plural.

options.label: D
options.text: copyes
options.rationale: Change the y to i first.

items.stem: Choose the correct plural: “Autumn ____ covered the path.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Some nouns ending in f change the f to v and add -es: leaf → leaves.
explanation.tip: Watch for f/fe words: leaf/leaves, knife/knives, half/halves.

options.label: A
options.text: leafs
options.rationale: Leaf changes f to v and adds -es.

options.label: B
options.text: leafes
options.rationale: The f must change to v.

options.label: C

items.stem: Which sentence uses an irregular plural correctly?

items.stem: Match each singular noun with its plural.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun with the correct verb?

items.stem: Choose the correct possessive: “____ bicycle has a flat tire.”

items.stem: Choose the correct possessive: “The ____ final project won first prize.”

items.stem: Choose the correct possessive: “The ____ uniforms were washed after the match.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses both a plural noun and a possessive noun?

items.stem: Choose the contraction for “are not”: “The shops ____ open on Fridays.”

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “____ going to love this museum!”

items.stem: Which word is a modal helping verb in “You should wear a helmet”?

options.label: B

options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: “The twins built the model by ____.”

explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, theirs) never use apostrophes.

items.stem: Which word is an adjective? “The tiny kitten slept on the rug.”

explanation.tip: Adjectives tell what kind, how many or how much.

options.label: A

options.rationale: This is a verb.

options.label: B

items.stem: Which sentence capitalizes the proper adjective correctly?

items.stem: Choose the article: “She ate ____ orange after lunch.”

options.label: B

items.stem: Choose the demonstrative adjective: “____ books right here on my desk are new.”

items.stem: Which phrase lists the adjectives in the correct order?

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas with adjectives correctly?

items.stem: Which sentence uses negatives correctly?

items.stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?

items.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

items.stem: What makes this a pun? “The baker quit because he couldn’t make enough dough.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A pun plays on a word with two meanings; “dough” can mean bread mixture or money.
explanation.tip: A pun is a joke that uses a word’s double meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: It repeats the same sound at the start.
options.rationale: That is alliteration.

options.label: B
options.text: It compares a baker to money using “like.”
options.rationale: That would be a simile.

options.label: C
options.text: It rhymes “baker” and “dough.”
options.rationale: These words do not rhyme.

options.label: D
options.text: “Dough” means both bread mixture and, informally, money.

items.stem: Which sentence is a pun?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Interest” means both money a bank pays and curiosity.

options.text: I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.

options.rationale: There is no double meaning here.

options.label: D
options.text: My bank is next to the bakery.
options.rationale: There is no wordplay.

options.label: B
options.text: flies

options.label: C
options.text: time
options.rationale: “Time” has one meaning here.

options.label: D
options.text: banana
options.rationale: “Banana” has one meaning here.

items.stem: Why might an author use a pun in a historical story?

options.label: A
options.text: To give exact dates and facts
options.rationale: Puns are wordplay, not facts.

options.label: B
options.text: To replace dialogue
options.rationale: Puns are often part of dialogue.

options.label: C
options.text: To show a character’s cleverness or add humor

options.label: D
options.text: To make the story sound more serious
options.rationale: Puns usually add humor.

options.rationale: Syllables do not tell the part of speech.

options.label: B
options.text: The guide words at the top of the page
options.rationale: Guide words help you find the page, not the word’s use.

options.label: C
