options.label: D
options.text: The part-of-speech label, such as (n.) or (v.)

items.stem: A digital thesaurus lists “glance, peek, scan, gaze” for “look.” Which word means to look for a long time?

explanation.whyCorrect: To gaze is to look steadily for a long time, often with wonder.
explanation.tip: Synonyms have shades of meaning; check the dictionary to choose precisely.

options.label: A
options.text: gaze

options.label: B
options.text: peek
options.rationale: A peek is a quick, secret look.

options.label: C
options.text: glance
options.rationale: A glance is a quick look.

options.label: D
options.text: scan
options.rationale: To scan is to look quickly over something.

items.stem: The dictionary shows “con·duct (noun) KON-dukt; (verb) kuhn-DUKT.” How should you say “conduct” in “The students will conduct an experiment”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Will conduct” is a verb, so the stress is on the second syllable.
explanation.tip: Some words change stress depending on their part of speech.

options.label: A
options.text: KON-dukt, because it is a noun
options.rationale: Here it is a verb (an action).

options.label: B
options.text: kuhn-DUKT, because it is a verb

options.label: C
options.text: Either way, because the meaning is the same
options.rationale: Stress changes with the part of speech.

options.label: D
options.text: KON-DUKT, stressing both syllables
options.rationale: Only one syllable is stressed.

items.stem: A glossary is found at the back of a book and defines words used in that book.

explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike a dictionary, a glossary only covers words from that book.
explanation.tip: Glossary = mini-dictionary for one book.

items.stem: Which source should you use to check whether “principal” or “principle” fits your sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: A dictionary gives each word’s meaning so you can choose correctly.
explanation.tip: Use a dictionary for meaning and spelling; a thesaurus for synonyms.

options.label: A
options.text: An almanac
options.rationale: An almanac gives yearly facts and data.

options.label: B
options.text: A table of contents
options.rationale: This lists chapters.

options.label: C
options.text: A dictionary, to compare the meanings

options.label: D
options.text: An atlas
options.rationale: An atlas contains maps.

items.stem: Put these words in dictionary order.

explanation.whyCorrect: Compare letter by letter: harb-i, harb-o, hard, harm, harv.
explanation.tip: When words begin the same way, keep comparing until a letter differs.

sequence: harbinger
harbor
hardship
harmony
harvest

items.stem: What does the suffix -less mean in “spotless”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Spotless means without spots, completely clean.
explanation.tip: -less = without; -ful = full of.

options.label: A
options.text: full of
options.rationale: That is the meaning of -ful.

options.label: B
options.text: one who
options.rationale: That is the meaning of -er or -or.

options.label: C
options.text: again
options.rationale: That is the meaning of the prefix re-.

options.label: D
options.text: without

items.stem: What does “washable” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The suffix -able means able to be: washable = able to be washed.
explanation.tip: Add the meaning of the suffix to the base word.

options.label: A
options.text: able to be washed

options.label: B
options.text: already washed
options.rationale: -able means able to be, not already done.

options.label: C
options.text: one who washes things
options.rationale: That would need -er.

options.label: D
options.text: full of water
options.rationale: That would need -ful.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “the state of being kind”: “Her ____ made everyone feel welcome.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The suffix -ness turns an adjective into a noun meaning “the state of being.”
explanation.tip: -ness = state or quality of.

options.label: A
options.text: kindness

options.label: B
options.text: kindly
options.rationale: -ly makes an adverb, not a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: kinder
options.rationale: -er compares two things.

options.label: D
options.text: unkind
options.rationale: un- means not.

items.stem: Match each suffix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Knowing suffix meanings helps you figure out new words.
explanation.tip: Think of a word you know with each suffix.

items.stem: Which word means “in a careful way”?

explanation.whyCorrect: care + -ful (full of) + -ly (in a … way) = in a careful way.
explanation.tip: Some words have two suffixes; build the meaning step by step.

options.label: A
options.text: careless
options.rationale: This means without care.

options.label: B
options.text: carefully

options.label: C
options.text: careful
options.rationale: This is an adjective; it does not describe how something is done.

options.label: D
options.text: caring
options.rationale: This has a different meaning.

items.stem: In “The government announced a new agreement,” how do the suffixes help you understand “government” and “agreement”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Govern → government; agree → agreement. Both become nouns naming a thing or result.
explanation.tip: Suffixes can change a word’s part of speech.

options.label: A
options.text: -ment turns the nouns into verbs.
options.rationale: It does the opposite.

options.label: B
options.text: -ment means “without.”
options.rationale: That is -less.

options.label: C
options.text: -ment turns the verbs “govern” and “agree” into nouns.

options.label: D
options.text: -ment makes the words plural.
options.rationale: Plurals use -s or -es.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “The scientist ____ through the microscope.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Scientist” is singular, so the verb adds -s: looks.
explanation.tip: Singular subject → verb + s. Plural subject → no -s.

options.label: A
options.text: look
options.rationale: A singular subject takes a verb ending in -s in the present tense.

options.label: B
options.text: looks

options.label: C
options.text: looking
options.rationale: This needs a helping verb.

options.label: D
options.text: are looking
options.rationale: “Are” does not agree with the singular subject.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “Audrey and her sister ____ catch in the field.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Two people joined by “and” make a plural subject, so the verb has no -s.
explanation.tip: Subject + and + subject = plural.

options.label: A
options.text: has played
options.rationale: “Has” does not agree with a plural subject.

options.label: B
options.text: plays
options.rationale: A compound subject joined by “and” is plural.

options.label: C
options.text: play

options.label: D
options.text: is playing
options.rationale: “Is” does not agree with a plural subject.

items.stem: Choose the verb: “The box of old toys ____ dust in the attic.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The prepositional phrase “of old toys” does not change the subject; “box” is singular.
explanation.tip: Cross out prepositional phrases to find the real subject.

options.label: A
options.text: are collecting
options.rationale: “Are” does not agree with “box.”

options.label: B
options.text: have collected
options.rationale: “Have” does not agree with “box.”

options.label: C
options.text: collect
options.rationale: The subject is “box,” which is singular.

options.label: D
options.text: collects

items.stem: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Flock” is a collective noun referring to the group as a whole, so it takes a singular verb.
explanation.tip: Collective nouns (flock, team, class) usually take singular verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: A flock of birds fly over the river every evening.
options.rationale: The subject “flock” is singular.

options.label: B
options.text: A flocks of birds flies over the river every evening.
options.rationale: “A flocks” is not correct.

options.label: C
options.text: A flock of birds flying over the river every evening.
options.rationale: This is a fragment with no main verb.

options.label: D
options.text: A flock of birds flies over the river every evening.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: In a compound sentence, each subject agrees with its own verb: “brother” is singular, so “watches.”
explanation.tip: Check the verb in each clause of a compound sentence separately.

items.stem: Which sentence is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: The subject is “Each,” which is singular, so the verb is “has.”
explanation.tip: Words like each, every and either are singular subjects.

options.label: A
options.text: Each of the students has a locker.

options.label: B
options.text: Each of the students having a locker.
options.rationale: This is a fragment.

options.label: C
options.text: Each of the student have a locker.
options.rationale: “Student” should be plural and the verb singular.

options.label: D
options.text: Each of the students have a locker.
options.rationale: “Each” is singular; “of the students” does not change it.

items.stem: What is the role of the NARRATOR in “The Interview”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator explains when and where the play takes place and why Sara is there.
explanation.tip: A narrator in a play speaks to the audience to provide background.

options.label: A
options.text: To interview Mr. Aziz
options.rationale: Sara conducts the interview.

options.label: B
options.text: To introduce the setting and situation before the action begins

options.label: C
options.text: To play a character in the interview
options.rationale: The narrator does not take part in the scenes.

options.label: D
options.text: To give stage directions to actors
options.rationale: Stage directions are in brackets.

items.stem: What is an aside, as used by Sara in Scene 1?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sara’s aside reveals her frustration to the audience without Mr. Aziz hearing it.
explanation.tip: Asides let the audience know a character’s private thoughts.

options.label: A
options.text: A change of scene
options.rationale: Scene changes are marked with scene headings.

options.label: B
options.text: A long speech to another character
options.rationale: That is a monologue.

options.label: C
options.text: A comment spoken to the audience that other characters do not hear

options.label: D
options.text: A stage direction about where to stand
options.rationale: An aside is spoken, not a direction.

items.stem: In “The Interview,” Scene 2 takes place two hours after Scene 1.

explanation.whyCorrect: The stage directions for Scene 2 say “Two hours later.”
explanation.tip: Scene headings and stage directions show changes in time and place.

items.stem: How does the stage direction [stopping, then smiling for the first time] contribute to the plot?

explanation.whyCorrect: After this moment his short answers change into a long story, which shifts the interview.
explanation.tip: Stage directions can mark important changes in a character or in the plot.

options.label: A
options.text: It explains why the gym flooded.
options.rationale: The flood is explained in his dialogue.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that Mr. Aziz is finished working for the day.
options.rationale: He continues to talk, not to leave.

options.label: C
options.text: It introduces a new character.
options.rationale: No new character appears.

options.label: D
options.text: It marks the turning point when Mr. Aziz begins to open up.

items.stem: Why did the playwright divide the play into two short scenes instead of one?

explanation.whyCorrect: Jumping two hours ahead lets the audience see how much the interview changed things.
explanation.tip: A scene break can compress time and highlight a change.

options.label: A
options.text: To skip the long interview and show its result: Sara’s full notebook and changed attitude

options.label: B
options.text: To show a different character’s point of view
options.rationale: Both scenes focus on Sara and Mr. Aziz.

options.label: C
options.text: To give the narrator more lines
options.rationale: The narrator speaks only at the start.

options.label: D
options.text: To introduce a second setting far from the school
options.rationale: Both scenes are in the storage room.

items.stem: Match each element of “The Interview” with how it contributes to the play.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each element plays a specific role in the structure and meaning of the drama.
explanation.tip: Ask what each part of a play does for the audience.

pairs.right: Sets the time, place and purpose
Reveals her private frustration to the audience
Expresses the play’s message about care

items.stem: What can you infer about Mr. Aziz at the start of Scene 1?

explanation.whyCorrect: He says, “There is not much to tell,” which suggests he undervalues his own story.
explanation.tip: An inference combines text evidence with what you already know.

options.label: A
options.text: He wants to stop working immediately.
options.rationale: He keeps polishing the doorknob.

options.label: B
options.text: He does not think his own work is interesting.

options.label: C
options.text: He is angry with Sara.
options.rationale: He is brief, not angry.

options.label: D
options.text: He has forgotten his years at the school.
options.rationale: He later remembers details from 1998.

items.stem: Why does Sara ask about the radio?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her aside shows she needs longer answers, so she tries a new question about an object in the room.
explanation.tip: Use a character’s goal to infer the reason for their actions.

options.label: A
options.text: She thinks the radio is broken and wants to fix it.
options.rationale: She is a writer, not fixing things.

options.label: B
options.text: She wants to listen to the news.
options.rationale: Her goal is the interview.

options.label: C
options.text: She is looking for a way to get Mr. Aziz talking.

options.label: D
options.text: She wants to buy the radio.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she wants to buy it.

items.stem: What does Mr. Aziz’s final line suggest about how he sees his job?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Some things last if you look after them” reflects pride in thirty years of care.
explanation.tip: Characters’ final lines often reveal their deeper values.

options.label: A
options.text: He wants Sara to become a custodian.
options.rationale: He is giving her a keepsake, not career advice.

options.label: B
options.text: He thinks doorknobs are worth a lot of money.
options.rationale: The value he means is not money.

options.label: C
options.text: He regrets working at the school.
options.rationale: His tone is proud and gentle.

options.label: D
options.text: He believes caring for things over time gives them lasting value.

items.stem: Which inference about the letter writer is BEST supported by the text?

explanation.whyCorrect: She mentions her grandfather’s spice stall and her first school bag bought there.
explanation.tip: Cite specific details that support your inference.

options.label: A
options.text: She feels a personal connection to the souq through her family.

options.label: B
options.text: She dislikes visitors to the city.
options.rationale: She suggests ways to welcome visitors.

options.label: C
options.text: She has never visited the souq.
options.rationale: She describes walking under its arches.

options.label: D
options.text: She works for the city council.
options.rationale: She is a sixth-grade student.

items.stem: The letter suggests that Huda believes old buildings and tourism can work together.

explanation.whyCorrect: She proposes repairs and signs in several languages to “protect our heritage and welcome visitors at the same time.”
explanation.tip: Inferences must be supported by evidence in the text.

items.stem: Which TWO details support the inference that Mr. Aziz has hidden depths?

explanation.whyCorrect: The vivid flood story and the full notebook show how much he had to share.
explanation.tip: Look for evidence that contrasts with first impressions.

options.label: A
options.text: Sara’s notebook is full after two hours.

options.label: B
options.text: He shrugs at the first question.
options.rationale: This shows his reserve, not depth.

options.label: C
options.text: He tells a detailed story about carrying two hundred chairs during a flood.

options.label: D
options.text: He polishes a brass doorknob.
options.rationale: This shows his work, not hidden depths.

items.stem: What is Huda’s main purpose in writing her letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: She writes, “I urge the council to change its plan.”
explanation.tip: Persuasive writing tries to convince readers to think or act in a certain way.

options.label: A
options.text: To entertain readers with a funny story
options.rationale: The letter is serious and persuasive.

options.label: B
options.text: To persuade the council to save the old souq

options.label: C
options.text: To explain how shopping centers are built
options.rationale: She argues against one; she does not explain construction.

options.label: D
options.text: To describe how spices are grown
options.rationale: Spices are mentioned only as part of family history.

items.stem: Why does Huda include the story of her grandfather’s stall?

explanation.whyCorrect: Personal history makes her argument about heritage feel real and emotional.
explanation.tip: Ask how each detail serves the author’s purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To complain about her grandfather
options.rationale: She speaks of him warmly.

options.label: B
options.text: To give directions to the souq
options.rationale: No directions are given.

options.label: C
options.text: To show that the souq is part of real families’ history

options.label: D
options.text: To prove that spices are expensive
options.rationale: Prices are not mentioned.

items.stem: How does Huda respond to the council’s argument about visitors?

explanation.whyCorrect: She turns the council’s own goal into a reason to keep the souq.
explanation.tip: Strong persuasive writers answer opposing arguments.

options.label: A
options.text: She agrees that a mall would bring more visitors.
options.rationale: She disagrees with this argument.

options.label: B
options.text: She ignores the council’s argument.
options.rationale: She addresses it directly with “However.”

options.label: C
options.text: She says visitors are not important.
options.rationale: She wants to welcome visitors.

options.label: D
options.text: She argues that visitors come for what is unique, which the souq offers and a mall does not.

items.stem: The closing image “disappear behind a glass wall” is meant to create an emotional reaction.

explanation.whyCorrect: The image of history vanishing behind glass appeals to readers’ feelings.
explanation.tip: Word choice can convey an author’s point of view.

items.stem: Which phrase BEST shows Huda’s point of view about the shopping center?

explanation.whyCorrect: The phrase suggests a mall is ordinary and replaceable, unlike the souq.
explanation.tip: Look for phrases that reveal what the author values.

options.label: A
options.text: “They can visit a shopping center in any city in the world”

options.label: B
options.text: “The city council plans to replace our old covered souq”
options.rationale: This states a fact about the plan.

options.label: C
options.text: “I am a sixth grader”
options.rationale: This introduces the writer.

options.label: D
options.text: “Respectfully”
options.rationale: This is a polite closing.

items.stem: How does Huda make her letter persuasive WITHOUT being rude to the council?

explanation.whyCorrect: Suggesting repairs, lighting and signs shows a constructive attitude, and “Respectfully” keeps a polite tone.
explanation.tip: An author’s purpose shapes tone as well as content.

options.label: A
options.text: She threatens the council with consequences.
options.rationale: She makes no threats.

options.label: B
options.text: She offers practical alternatives and closes respectfully.

options.label: C
options.text: She uses insults to show strong feeling.
options.rationale: She does not insult anyone.

options.label: D
options.text: She refuses to mention the council’s view.
options.rationale: She addresses their view directly.

items.stem: What theme do “The New Field” and “Transplant” share?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin learns the new field; the lemon tree grows new buds after a hard period.
explanation.tip: Compare how different genres approach the same theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Football is more important than gardening.
options.rationale: The poem is not about football.

options.label: B
options.text: Trees and people cannot change.
options.rationale: Both the tree and Yasmin change.

options.label: C
options.text: Adjusting to a new place takes time but can lead to growth.

options.label: D
options.text: Moving is always a terrible experience.
options.rationale: Both texts end with growth.

items.stem: How is the lemon tree’s experience similar to Yasmin’s?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin sits on the bench and misses home; the tree drops its leaves. Both later thrive.
explanation.tip: Look for parallel stages in each text.

options.label: A
options.text: Both are moved by a coach.
options.rationale: Only Yasmin has a coach.

options.label: B
options.text: Both live by the sea.
options.rationale: Yasmin moves away from the sea.

options.label: C
options.text: Both refuse to change.
options.rationale: Both change and grow.

options.label: D
options.text: Both struggle at first after being moved, then adapt.

items.stem: How does the poem’s form change the way the theme is presented compared with the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The poem compresses the idea into images; the story develops it through a character’s actions over time.
explanation.tip: Genre affects how an author develops a theme.

options.label: A
options.text: The poem uses a single image and rhyme to suggest the theme; the story shows it through events and dialogue.

options.label: B
options.text: The story uses rhyme and stanzas.
options.rationale: The story is prose.

options.label: C
options.text: The poem gives more details about football practice.
options.rationale: The poem does not mention football.

options.label: D
options.text: Both use the same characters.
options.rationale: The poem has a tree, not Yasmin.

items.stem: In both texts, a turning point shows the main subject beginning to thrive.

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin scores her first goal; the tree breaks out in new buds.
explanation.tip: Compare the structure as well as the theme.

items.stem: Match each detail from the story with a similar detail from the poem.

explanation.whyCorrect: The texts follow parallel stages: leaving, struggling, thriving.
explanation.tip: Pair details that play the same role in each text.

pairs.left: Yasmin leaves her team by the sea
pairs.right: The tree is lifted from its courtyard

pairs.left: Yasmin sits on the bench missing home
pairs.right: The tree drops its yellow light

items.stem: Which statement BEST explains a DIFFERENCE between the texts?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin practices every morning; the tree simply recovers “one morning.”
explanation.tip: Compare not only what happens but why it happens in each text.

options.label: A
options.text: The poem explains how to care for lemon trees.
options.rationale: The poem is not instructional.

options.label: B
options.text: The story credits effort and practice for the change, while the poem presents growth as something that comes with time.

options.label: C
options.text: The story is sad, but the poem is happy throughout.
options.rationale: Both move from hardship to hope.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the poem has a hopeful ending.
options.rationale: Both end hopefully.

items.stem: Which line from “Desert Night” appeals mainly to the sense of taste?

explanation.whyCorrect: The speaker tastes smoke and spice from the coffee.
explanation.tip: Sensory language appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.

options.label: A
options.text: “Somewhere a camel groans”
options.rationale: This appeals to hearing.

options.label: B
options.text: “A cool wind combs the ridges”
options.rationale: This appeals to touch and sight.

options.label: C
options.text: “and taste the smoke, the spice, the vast and silent dark”

options.label: D
options.text: “the sky unrolls its black carpet”
options.rationale: This appeals to sight.

items.stem: What does the simile “like a coin into a pocket” suggest about the sunset?

explanation.whyCorrect: A coin slips out of sight smoothly and fast, like the sun sinking.
explanation.tip: A simile compares two things using like or as.

options.label: A
options.text: The sun is made of metal.
options.rationale: The comparison is figurative.

options.label: B
options.text: Someone has stolen the sun.
options.rationale: The image is playful, not about theft.

options.label: C
options.text: The sunset is very slow.
options.rationale: A coin slipping into a pocket is quick.

options.label: D
options.text: The sun disappears quickly and neatly below the dunes.

items.stem: “The coffee pot hisses on the coals” appeals to the sense of hearing.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hisses” is a sound word.
explanation.tip: Sound words create auditory imagery.

items.stem: What does the metaphor “the sky unrolls its black carpet, scattered with salt” describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: The black carpet is the dark sky, and the scattered salt is the stars.
explanation.tip: A metaphor describes one thing as if it were another.

options.label: A
options.text: The night sky spreading out, full of white stars

options.label: B
options.text: A sandstorm covering the sky
options.rationale: The image is calm and dark, not stormy.

options.label: C
options.text: Salt being spilled on a rug
options.rationale: The language is figurative.

options.label: D
options.text: Black clouds before rain
options.rationale: The “salt” represents stars, not rain.

items.stem: Match each image from “Desert Night” with the sense it appeals to most.

explanation.whyCorrect: The poet uses every sense to place the reader in the desert.
explanation.tip: Identify the sense each detail relies on.

pairs.left: the sand gives back the day’s heat
a camel groans, low as a cello string
the sky unrolls its black carpet

items.stem: How does the imagery in the last two lines shift the poem’s focus?

explanation.whyCorrect: “I hold the small cup with both hands” brings the reader close to the speaker’s senses.
explanation.tip: Notice when a poem moves from wide images to close-up ones.

options.label: A
options.text: From night to morning
options.rationale: It is still night at the end.

options.label: B
options.text: From the wide desert landscape to the speaker’s close, personal experience

options.label: C
options.text: From calm to frightening
options.rationale: The tone remains peaceful.

options.label: D
options.text: From the speaker to the camel
options.rationale: The focus moves to the speaker, not away.

items.stem: What is the subject of the command “Close the window, please”?

explanation.whyCorrect: In an imperative sentence, the subject “you” is understood.
explanation.tip: Commands have an understood subject.

options.label: A
options.text: There is no subject.
options.rationale: Commands have an understood subject: you.

options.label: B
options.text: window
options.rationale: The window receives the action.

options.label: C
options.text: you (understood)

options.label: D
options.text: please
options.rationale: “Please” is a polite word, not the subject.

items.stem: What is the simple subject? “Neither of the answers on the board was correct.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Remove “of the answers on the board”; the subject is “Neither.”
explanation.tip: The subject is never inside a prepositional phrase.

options.label: A
options.text: answers
options.rationale: “Answers” is part of the prepositional phrase “of the answers.”

options.label: B
options.text: correct
options.rationale: This is a predicate adjective.

options.label: C
options.text: board
options.rationale: This is part of a prepositional phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither

items.stem: Find the subject: “Here are the results of the survey.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Rearranged: “The results of the survey are here.” The subject is “results.”
explanation.tip: In sentences beginning with here or there, the subject follows the verb.

options.label: A
options.text: results

options.label: B
options.text: survey
options.rationale: This is the object of the preposition “of.”

options.label: C
options.text: Here
options.rationale: “Here” is an adverb, not the subject.

options.label: D
options.text: are
options.rationale: This is the verb.

items.stem: In “The team and its coach celebrated and posed for photos,” the sentence has a compound subject and a compound predicate.

explanation.whyCorrect: Subjects: team, coach. Predicates: celebrated, posed.
explanation.tip: Find all subjects, then all verbs.

items.stem: What is the complete predicate? “During the storm, the old fishing boat drifted slowly toward the rocks.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The complete predicate is the verb and everything that tells about it.
explanation.tip: Introductory phrases are not part of the subject.

options.label: A
options.text: the old fishing boat
options.rationale: This is the complete subject.

options.label: B
options.text: drifted slowly toward the rocks

options.label: C
options.text: During the storm, the old fishing boat
options.rationale: This includes an introductory phrase and the subject.

options.label: D
options.text: toward the rocks
options.rationale: This is only part of the predicate.

items.stem: Write the simple predicate (main verb phrase): “By next June, the new library will have opened its doors.” ____

explanation.whyCorrect: The simple predicate includes all helping verbs: will have opened.
explanation.tip: Include every helping verb in the simple predicate.

items.stem: Which compound sentence is punctuated correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum closed early but, the café stayed open.
options.rationale: The comma goes before the conjunction.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum closed early, the café stayed open.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum closed early, but the café stayed open.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum, closed early but the café stayed open.
options.rationale: The comma is misplaced.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.
explanation.tip: Each side of a semicolon should be a complete sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The rain stopped the; players returned.
options.rationale: The semicolon is in the wrong place.

options.label: B
options.text: The rain; stopped the players returned.
options.rationale: The semicolon must separate two complete clauses.

options.label: C
options.text: The rain stopped; and the players returned.
options.rationale: Do not use a semicolon with a coordinating conjunction this way.

options.label: D
options.text: The rain stopped; the players returned to the field.

items.stem: Choose the conjunction: “He was exhausted, ____ he finished the race.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Yet” shows a surprising contrast.
explanation.tip: yet/but = contrast; so = result; for = reason; or = choice.

options.label: A
options.text: yet

options.label: B
options.text: or
options.rationale: “Or” gives a choice.

options.label: C
options.text: so
options.rationale: “So” shows a result, but finishing despite exhaustion is a contrast.

options.label: D
options.text: for
options.rationale: “For” gives a reason.

items.stem: Choose the conjunction: “Neither the coach was ready, ____ were the players.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Neither … nor” is a correlative pair.
explanation.tip: Pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also.

options.label: A
options.text: and
options.rationale: This does not complete the negative pair.

options.label: B
options.text: nor

options.label: C
options.text: or
options.rationale: “Neither” pairs with “nor.”

options.label: D
options.text: but
options.rationale: This does not complete “neither.”

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma create a comma splice; use a semicolon (or add a conjunction).
explanation.tip: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.

items.stem: Which revision best combines the ideas to show cause and effect? “The bridge was closed. Traffic moved slowly all morning.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “So” shows that the closed bridge caused the slow traffic.
explanation.tip: Choose the conjunction that matches the logical relationship.

options.label: A
options.text: The bridge was closed, so traffic moved slowly all morning.

options.label: B
options.text: The bridge was closed, but traffic moved slowly all morning.
options.rationale: “But” shows contrast, not cause.

options.label: C
options.text: The bridge was closed, traffic moved slowly all morning.
options.rationale: This is a comma splice.

options.label: D
options.text: The bridge was closed, or traffic moved slowly all morning.
options.rationale: “Or” shows a choice.

items.stem: Which word is an adverb? “The choir sang beautifully at the ceremony.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Beautifully” tells how the choir sang.
explanation.tip: Adverbs tell how, when, where or to what extent.

options.label: A
options.text: choir
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: beautifully

options.label: C
options.text: ceremony
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: sang
options.rationale: This is a verb.

items.stem: What question does the adverb answer? “We will leave tomorrow.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tomorrow” tells when we will leave.
explanation.tip: Adverbs of time: today, soon, later, tomorrow.

options.label: A
options.text: To what extent?
options.rationale: It does not show degree.

options.label: B
options.text: Where?
options.rationale: It does not name a place.

options.label: C
options.text: When?

options.label: D
options.text: How?
options.rationale: “Tomorrow” tells when, not how.

items.stem: Choose the relative adverb: “I still remember the day ____ we moved to a new city.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “When” introduces a clause that tells about a time: the day.
explanation.tip: Relative adverbs: where (place), when (time), why (reason).

options.label: A
options.text: where
options.rationale: “Where” refers to a place, not a time.

options.label: B
options.text: why
options.rationale: “Why” refers to a reason.

options.label: C
options.text: when

options.label: D
options.text: which
options.rationale: “Which” is a relative pronoun.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of all the runners, Nasser finished ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use “most” + adverb to compare three or more.
explanation.tip: -ly adverbs: more/most + adverb.

options.label: A
options.text: more quickly
options.rationale: “More” compares two; this compares all the runners.

options.label: B
options.text: quickliest
options.rationale: This is not a word.

options.label: C
options.text: most quick
options.rationale: An adverb is needed: quickly.

options.label: D
options.text: most quickly

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Well” is the adverb that describes how she did; “good” is an adjective.
explanation.tip: Use well (adverb) to describe actions; good (adjective) to describe nouns.

items.stem: Which word does the adverb “extremely” modify? “The extremely tired hikers rested by the stream.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Extremely” modifies the adjective “tired,” telling to what extent.
explanation.tip: Adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs.

options.label: A
options.text: stream
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: hikers
options.rationale: Adverbs do not modify nouns.

options.label: C
options.text: rested
options.rationale: “Extremely” describes how tired, not how they rested.

options.label: D
options.text: tired

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “____ turn is it to present?”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Whose” shows ownership: whose turn.
explanation.tip: Who’s = who is/who has; whose = belonging to whom.

options.label: A
options.text: Whose

options.label: B
options.text: Who
options.rationale: The sentence needs a possessive.

options.label: C
options.text: Who’s
options.rationale: “Who’s” means “who is.”

options.label: D
options.text: Whos
options.rationale: This is not a word.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The students said ____ ready to present their project.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “They are ready to present” makes sense, so the contraction “they’re” is correct.
explanation.tip: Expand the contraction to check if it fits.

options.label: A
options.text: theyre
options.rationale: The apostrophe is missing.

options.label: B
options.text: they’re

options.label: C
options.text: their
options.rationale: “Their” shows ownership.

options.label: D
options.text: there
options.rationale: “There” refers to a place.

items.stem: Which sentence uses its and it’s correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: It’s = it is; its = belonging to it.
explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes.

options.label: A
options.text: It’s clear that the team lost its focus.

options.label: B
options.text: It’s clear that the team lost it’s focus.
options.rationale: The second should be possessive “its.”

options.label: C
options.text: Its clear that the team lost its focus.
options.rationale: The first should be “It’s” (it is).

options.label: D
options.text: Its clear that the team lost it’s focus.
options.rationale: Both are reversed.

items.stem: Match each word with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Contractions contain apostrophes; possessive pronouns do not.
explanation.tip: Replace the word with its expanded form to test it.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “You’re” (you are) is needed: “If you are finished.” The second “your” is correct.
explanation.tip: Check each your/you’re in the sentence separately.

items.stem: Which sentence is completely correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: There (existence), they’re (they are), their (possession), its (possession) are all used correctly.
explanation.tip: Test every homophone in a long sentence one at a time.

options.label: A
options.text: There are two reasons why their late: there bus broke down, and its replacement was delayed.
options.rationale: “their late” and “there bus” are wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: There are two reasons why they’re late: their bus broke down, and its replacement was delayed.

options.label: C
options.text: There are two reasons why they’re late: there bus broke down, and it’s replacement was delayed.
options.rationale: “there bus” and “it’s replacement” are wrong.

options.label: D
options.text: Their are two reasons why there late: they’re bus broke down, and it’s replacement was delayed.
options.rationale: Every homophone is wrong.

items.stem: What does the prefix mis- mean in “misunderstand”?

explanation.whyCorrect: To misunderstand is to understand wrongly.
explanation.tip: mis- = wrongly or badly.

options.label: A
options.text: not
options.rationale: That is un- or in-.

options.label: B
options.text: before
options.rationale: That is pre-.

options.label: C
options.text: wrongly

options.label: D
options.text: again
options.rationale: That is re-.

items.stem: Using the prefix inter- (between), what does “international” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: inter- + national = between nations.
explanation.tip: inter- = between; intra- = within.

options.label: A
options.text: inside one nation
options.rationale: That would be intra- or domestic.

options.label: B
options.text: without a nation
options.rationale: No prefix here means “without.”

options.label: C
options.text: before nations existed
options.rationale: That would need pre-.

options.label: D
options.text: between or among nations

items.stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: These Greek and Latin prefixes appear in many academic words.
explanation.tip: Think of an example: submarine, transport, antibiotic, autograph.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “heat before”: “Please ____ the oven before you put the bread inside.”

explanation.whyCorrect: pre- means before: preheat = heat before.
explanation.tip: Combine the prefix meaning with the base word.

options.label: A
options.text: unheat
options.rationale: This is not a word.

options.label: B
options.text: overheat
options.rationale: over- means too much.

options.label: C
options.text: preheat

options.label: D
options.text: reheat
options.rationale: re- means again, not before.

items.stem: If “bi-” means two and “tri-” means three, what is a “tripod”?

explanation.whyCorrect: tri- (three) + pod (foot) = three-footed stand.
explanation.tip: Use both the prefix and the root to find the meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: a stand with three legs

options.label: B
options.text: a vehicle with three wheels
options.rationale: That is a tricycle; “pod” refers to feet or legs.

options.label: C
options.text: a stand with two legs
options.rationale: That would be “bipod.”

options.label: D
options.text: a book in three parts
options.rationale: That is a trilogy.

items.stem: In “The scientist’s findings were later proven to be a misinterpretation,” what does the prefix help you understand?

explanation.whyCorrect: mis- (wrongly) + interpretation = a wrong explanation.
explanation.tip: Prefixes change meaning even in long academic words.

options.label: A
options.text: The findings were explained before the study.
options.rationale: That would need pre-.

options.label: B
options.text: The findings had been explained incorrectly.

options.label: C
options.text: The findings were explained again.
options.rationale: That would be re-interpretation.

options.label: D
options.text: The findings were explained across many countries.
options.rationale: That would need trans- or inter-.

items.stem: Which word is an adjective? “A shiny bike leaned against the wall.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Shiny” describes the bike.
explanation.tip: Adjectives describe nouns: what kind, how many, which one.

options.label: A
options.text: bike
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: wall
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: shiny

options.label: D
options.text: leaned
options.rationale: This is a verb.

items.stem: Choose the adjective that tells HOW MANY: “We saw ____ camels near the road.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Seven” tells how many camels.
explanation.tip: Number words are adjectives that tell how many.

options.label: A
options.text: tall
options.rationale: “Tall” tells what kind.

options.label: B
options.text: slowly
options.rationale: This is an adverb.

options.label: C
options.text: brown
options.rationale: “Brown” tells what kind, not how many.

options.label: D
options.text: seven

items.stem: Which sentence uses “a” and “an” correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “An” comes before vowel sounds; “a” comes before consonant sounds.
explanation.tip: Say the next word aloud to hear its first sound.

options.label: A
options.text: I ate a apple and an banana.
options.rationale: Both articles are wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: I ate an apple and an banana.
options.rationale: Use “a” before a consonant sound: a banana.

options.label: C
options.text: I ate a apple and a banana.
options.rationale: Use “an” before a vowel sound: an apple.

options.label: D
options.text: I ate an apple and a banana.

items.stem: Choose the adjective: “That was the ____ storm we have had all year.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing more than two, the superlative of “bad” is “worst.”
explanation.tip: good–better–best; bad–worse–worst.

options.label: A
options.text: worst

options.label: B
options.text: most bad
options.rationale: Use the irregular form “worst.”

options.label: C
options.text: baddest
options.rationale: “Bad” is irregular: bad, worse, worst.

options.label: D
options.text: worse
options.rationale: “Worse” compares two; “all year” compares many.

items.stem: Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after the verb “smells”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Smells” links the bread to a describing word, so the adjective “wonderful” is correct.
explanation.tip: After linking verbs (is, seems, smells, tastes), use adjectives.

options.label: A
options.text: The fresh bread smells wonderful.

options.label: B
options.text: The fresh bread smells wonderfully.
options.rationale: After a linking verb like “smells,” use an adjective, not an adverb.

options.label: C
options.text: The freshly bread smells wonderful.
options.rationale: “Freshly” is an adverb; a noun needs the adjective “fresh.”

options.label: D
options.text: The fresh bread smell wonderful.
options.rationale: “Bread” is singular, so the verb is “smells.”

items.stem: Which word tells HOW the turtle moved? “The turtle moved slowly across the sand.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Slowly” is an adverb that tells how.
explanation.tip: Many adverbs end in -ly.

options.label: A
options.text: sand
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: slowly

options.label: C
options.text: turtle
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: moved
options.rationale: This is the verb.

items.stem: Choose the adverb that tells WHEN: “We will visit the museum ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tomorrow” tells when.
explanation.tip: Adverbs answer how, when or where.

options.label: A
options.text: quietly
options.rationale: This tells how.

options.label: B
options.text: tomorrow

options.label: C
options.text: upstairs
options.rationale: This tells where.

options.label: D
options.text: museum
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Which word is an adverb that tells WHERE? “The children played outside after lunch.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Outside” tells where they played.
explanation.tip: Where-adverbs: here, there, outside, inside, upstairs.

options.label: A
options.text: lunch
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: played
options.rationale: This is a verb.

options.label: C
options.text: outside

options.label: D
options.text: children
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Choose the relative adverb: “Nobody knows the reason ____ the bell rang early.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Why” goes with “the reason.”
explanation.tip: Relative adverbs: where (place), when (time), why (reason).

options.label: A
options.text: who
options.rationale: “Who” is a relative pronoun for people.

options.label: B
options.text: where
options.rationale: “Where” refers to a place.

options.label: C
options.text: why

options.label: D
options.text: when
options.rationale: “When” refers to a time.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Quickly” is the adverb that tells how he ran; “quick” is an adjective.
explanation.tip: Use an adverb to describe a verb.

items.stem: Choose the word: “A whale is ____ than a dolphin.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two animals uses -er: bigger.
explanation.tip: Two things: -er. Three or more: -est.

options.label: A
options.text: biggest
options.rationale: Use -est to compare three or more.

options.label: B
options.text: more big
options.rationale: Add -er to short adjectives.

options.label: C
options.text: big
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

options.label: D
options.text: bigger

items.stem: Choose the word: “Of the three puppies, Coco is the ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing three puppies uses -est.
explanation.tip: “Of the three” signals a superlative.

options.label: A
options.text: smallest

options.label: B
options.text: small
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

options.label: C
options.text: smaller
options.rationale: “Smaller” compares only two.

options.label: D
options.text: most small
options.rationale: Add -est to short adjectives.

items.stem: Which sentence compares two things correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Long adjectives use “more” to compare two things.
explanation.tip: Long words: more/most. Short words: -er/-est.

options.label: A
options.text: This puzzle is more difficulter than that one.
options.rationale: Do not use “more” and -er together.

options.label: B
options.text: This puzzle is most difficult than that one.
options.rationale: “Most” compares three or more.

options.label: C
options.text: This puzzle is difficulter than that one.
options.rationale: Long adjectives use “more,” not -er.

options.label: D
options.text: This puzzle is more difficult than that one.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Use -est OR most, never both: “the hottest.”
explanation.tip: Never double up comparing words.

items.stem: Which sentence uses comparing words correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: good → better → best.
explanation.tip: Irregular comparatives must be memorized.

options.label: A
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is better, and Sami’s is the best.

options.label: B
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is more better, and Sami’s is the best.
options.rationale: Do not add “more” to “better.”

options.label: C
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is gooder, and Sami’s is the goodest.
options.rationale: “Good” is irregular.

options.label: D
options.text: Huda’s drawing is good, Rami’s is better, and Sami’s is the bestest.
options.rationale: “Best” already means the most good.

items.stem: “Ran to the gate” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: It has no subject: who ran? It is a fragment.
explanation.tip: A sentence needs a subject and a verb.

items.stem: Which group of words is a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: There is a subject but no verb, so it is not a complete thought.
explanation.tip: Ask: What did the girl do?

options.label: A
options.text: It started to rain.
options.rationale: This is complete.

options.label: B
options.text: The girl with the red umbrella.

options.label: C
options.text: The girl opened her red umbrella.
options.rationale: This has a subject and a verb.

options.label: D
options.text: She stayed dry.
options.rationale: This is complete.

items.stem: Which is a correct way to fix this run-on? “The power went out we lit candles.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Splitting the run-on into two sentences fixes it.
explanation.tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma and a conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: The power went out and, we lit candles.
options.rationale: The comma belongs before “and.”

options.label: B
options.text: The power went out, we lit candles.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two sentences.

options.label: C
options.text: The power went out. We lit candles.

options.label: D
options.text: The power went out we, lit candles.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

items.stem: Which revision fixes the fragment? “When the bell rang. We lined up.”

explanation.tip: A clause starting with “When” needs a main clause.

options.text: The bell. When we lined up.
options.rationale: This creates new fragments.

options.label: B
options.text: When the bell rang we. Lined up.
options.rationale: This creates two fragments.

options.label: C
options.text: When the bell rang. we lined up.
options.rationale: The fragment is still separate.

options.label: D
options.text: When the bell rang, we lined up.

items.stem: Match each verb with its past tense.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Have you ever ____ a camel?”

items.stem: Which sentence uses irregular verbs correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: rang and began are correct past-tense forms.
explanation.tip: Past tense stands alone; past participles need has/have/had.

options.text: The bell rang, and the students began to write.

items.stem: Which word is a negative?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Never” means “not ever.”
explanation.tip: Negatives: no, not, never, nobody, nothing, nowhere.

options.label: A
options.text: often
options.rationale: This is positive.

options.label: B
options.text: never

options.label: C
options.text: always
options.rationale: This is positive.

options.label: D
options.text: sometimes
options.rationale: This is positive.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “I don’t have ____ homework tonight.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Use only one negative: “don’t” + “any.”
explanation.tip: One negative per sentence.

options.text: any

options.label: B
options.text: none

items.stem: “Nobody never cleans the board” is correct.

explanation.whyCorrect: Real data that matches one of the author’s reasons strengthens the claim.
explanation.tip: Facts and data are stronger than opinions.

options.label: A
options.text: A sentence saying gardens are pretty
options.rationale: This is an opinion, not evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: A list of all the classes in the school
options.rationale: This does not support any reason.

options.label: C
options.text: A survey showing students ate more vegetables after a nearby school started a garden

options.label: D
options.text: A picture of the author’s favorite flower

items.stem: How does the author of “Our School Needs a Garden” feel about the empty lot?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author calls it “wasted space right now.”
explanation.tip: Look for words that show feelings.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: It should stay empty.
options.rationale: The author wants to change it.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the best part of the school.
options.rationale: The author calls it “wasted space.”

options.label: D

items.stem: Which word in “The Dripping Taps” shows how the author first viewed the problem?

options.label: A
options.text: worrying

options.label: B
options.text: full

options.label: C
options.text: lower
options.rationale: This describes the bill.

options.label: D

options.rationale: This describes the signs.

items.stem: The author of “Nature’s Engineers” thinks beavers only cause problems.

explanation.whyCorrect: The author admits dams can flood roads but says many scientists think benefits are greater.
explanation.tip: Check whether the author presents more than one side.

items.stem: How does the author of “Nature’s Engineers” show a balanced point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last paragraph admits problems and weighs them against benefits.
explanation.tip: Balanced writing presents more than one side.

options.label: A
options.text: By describing only how beavers build lodges
options.rationale: That would show only one side.

options.label: B
options.text: By mentioning that dams can flood roads, then explaining why scientists still value beavers

options.label: C
options.text: By telling a story about one beaver
options.rationale: The article is not a story.

options.label: D
options.text: By saying beavers are dangerous to people
options.rationale: The text does not say this.

items.stem: How does the author of “The Dripping Taps” show the students’ success instead of just giving an opinion?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author points to evidence collected “a month later,” which shows a reporting point of view.
explanation.tip: Notice whether an author proves a point with facts or with opinions.

options.label: A
options.text: By saying the students were the best class in the school
options.rationale: This is an opinion the text does not state.

options.label: B
options.text: By telling the reader to save water at home
options.rationale: The author reports events rather than giving commands.

options.label: C
options.text: By reporting results that were checked: the taps stopped dripping and the water bill was lower.

options.label: D
options.text: By describing the colors of the signs
options.rationale: Sign colors do not show success.

items.stem: What is the author’s main purpose in “Baking Bread in a Clay Oven”?

options.label: A

options.rationale: The text explains; it does not persuade.

options.label: B
options.text: To tell a funny story about a baker
options.rationale: There is no story or humor.

options.label: C

options.rationale: Metal ovens are not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: To explain how bread is baked in a clay oven

items.stem: Why did the author write “Our School Needs a Garden”?

options.text: To persuade the school to build a garden

options.label: B
options.text: To entertain with a garden adventure
options.rationale: It is not a story.

options.label: C

options.rationale: The garden does not exist yet.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Growing steps are not explained.

items.stem: Why does the author of “How Honeybees Share Directions” explain how scientists studied bees?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last paragraph explains the source of the information.
explanation.tip: Authors include details for a reason.

options.text: To explain how honey is sold

options.label: B
options.text: To show readers how we know about the bee dances

options.label: C

options.rationale: Glass color is not mentioned.

options.label: D

options.rationale: The article does not persuade.

items.stem: Why does the author of “Nature’s Engineers” use headings?

options.rationale: Headings name topics.

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.rationale: Headings organize; they do not add length for its own sake.

items.stem: The author of “The Dripping Taps” ends with: “a small problem, noticed and measured, can lead to a big change.” What purpose does this ending serve?

options.label: B
options.text: To describe the plumber’s job
options.rationale: The plumber is not the focus.

options.label: C

options.rationale: The article is ending.

options.label: D
options.text: To share a lesson readers can use in their own lives

items.stem: In “The Dripping Taps,” what CAUSED the cup to fill?

items.stem: Which signal words show compare and contrast?

explanation.tip: Many antonyms are formed by adding a prefix or suffix like -less.
