options.text: neat
options.rationale: Neat describes tidiness, not care.

options.label: B
options.text: slow
options.rationale: Slow is not the opposite of careful.

options.label: C
options.text: careless

options.label: D
options.text: cautious
options.rationale: Cautious is close in meaning to careful.

items.stem: Match each word with its SYNONYM.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair has almost the same meaning.
explanation.tip: Try saying each word in the same sentence to check the meaning stays close.

items.stem: True or false: when describing a surface, “rough” and “smooth” are synonyms.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rough means bumpy or uneven, and smooth means even and flat — these are opposites, not synonyms.
explanation.tip: If two words describe opposite feelings when you touch something, they are antonyms.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for “gentle” in: “She gave the kitten a gentle pat”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A soft pat and a gentle pat both describe a light, kind touch.
explanation.tip: Picture the action in the sentence to check which word fits the same way.

options.label: A
options.text: fast
options.rationale: Fast describes speed, not gentleness.

options.label: B
options.text: loud
options.rationale: Loud describes sound, not touch.

options.label: C
options.text: rough
options.rationale: Rough is an antonym of gentle.

options.label: D
options.text: soft

items.stem: Choose the antonym: “The sky was sunny in the morning but ____ by noon.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Gloomy (dark and cloudy) is the opposite of sunny.
explanation.tip: Look for a word that paints the opposite picture in the sky.

options.label: A
options.text: clear
options.rationale: Clear is similar to sunny.

options.label: B
options.text: bright
options.rationale: Bright is similar to sunny, not opposite.

options.label: C
options.text: warm
options.rationale: Warm does not describe the sky’s look.

options.label: D
options.text: gloomy

items.stem: Which word means almost the same as “scared”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Scared and frightened both describe feeling afraid.
explanation.tip: Picture the feeling each word shows.

options.label: A
options.text: frightened

options.label: B
options.text: curious
options.rationale: Curious means wanting to know, not fear.

options.label: C
options.text: excited
options.rationale: Excited is a different feeling.

options.label: D
options.text: proud
options.rationale: Proud is a positive, different feeling.

items.stem: Which word is an antonym for “messy”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Messy means untidy; neat means tidy and organized — opposites.
explanation.tip: Picture a messy room, then picture its opposite.

options.label: A
options.text: cluttered
options.rationale: Cluttered means messy.

options.label: B
options.text: neat

options.label: C
options.text: dirty
options.rationale: Dirty is close in meaning to messy.

options.label: D
options.text: colorful
options.rationale: Colorful is about color, not tidiness.

items.stem: Match each word with its ANTONYM.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair has opposite meanings.
explanation.tip: Think of the exact opposite picture for each word.

items.stem: Read: “Dana felt upset when her kite got stuck in the tree.” Which word could replace “upset” without changing the meaning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Upset and unhappy both describe feeling bad about something.
explanation.tip: Replace the word in the sentence and check if the meaning stays the same.

options.label: A
options.text: thrilled
options.rationale: Thrilled means very excited and happy.

options.label: B
options.text: confused
options.rationale: Confused means not understanding, a different feeling.

options.label: C
options.text: unhappy

options.label: D
options.text: relieved
options.rationale: Relieved means feeling better, the opposite feeling.

items.stem: A friendly neighbor smiles and waves, while an unfriendly neighbor looks away without a word. True or false: this contrast shows that “friendly” and “unfriendly” are antonyms.

explanation.whyCorrect: Friendly means warm and kind to others; unfriendly means cold or unkind — opposite meanings.
explanation.tip: The prefix “un-” often creates an antonym, as in friendly/unfriendly.

items.stem: Choose the synonym: “The puppy was very ____ (small).”

explanation.whyCorrect: Tiny and small both describe something little in size.
explanation.tip: Match the word to the meaning given in parentheses.

options.label: A
options.text: tiny

options.label: B
options.text: heavy
options.rationale: Heavy describes weight, not size.

options.label: C
options.text: loud
options.rationale: Loud describes sound.

options.label: D
options.text: fast
options.rationale: Fast describes speed.

items.stem: Which word means almost the same as “repair”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Repair and fix both mean to make something work again.
explanation.tip: Think about what you do to something that is broken.

options.label: A
options.text: replace
options.rationale: Replace means to get a new one, not fixing the old one.

options.label: B
options.text: break
options.rationale: Break is an antonym of repair.

options.label: C
options.text: ignore
options.rationale: Ignore means to pay no attention, unrelated to repairing.

options.label: D
options.text: fix

items.stem: Read: “Elephants flap their large ears to cool down in the heat. The ears are full of blood vessels, and flapping them helps release heat into the air.” Which detail explains HOW elephants’ ears help them cool down?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence about blood vessels and releasing heat is the actual mechanism, which answers “how.”
explanation.tip: Look for the sentence that explains the process, not just the fact.

options.label: A
options.text: “The ears are full of blood vessels, and flapping them helps release heat into the air.”

options.label: B
options.text: “Elephants live in hot climates.”
options.rationale: This sentence is not in the text.

options.label: C
options.text: “Elephants flap their large ears to cool down in the heat.”
options.rationale: This states that they cool down, but not how the ears do it.

options.label: D
options.text: “Elephants are the largest land animals.”
options.rationale: This fact is not in the text and does not explain cooling.

items.stem: Read: “Spider silk comes in two kinds. Sticky silk traps insects, while non-sticky silk forms the frame. The spider is careful to walk only on the non-sticky strands.” Which TWO details explain why the spider does not get stuck in its own web?

explanation.whyCorrect: The web has two kinds of silk, and the spider only walks on the non-sticky kind.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that explains the SPECIFIC claim, not just related facts.

options.label: A
options.text: “non-sticky silk forms the frame”

options.label: B
options.text: “Sticky silk traps insects.”
options.rationale: This explains how prey gets caught, not how the spider avoids being caught.

options.label: C
options.text: “The spider is careful to walk only on the non-sticky strands.”

items.stem: Read: “Yara practiced her violin every afternoon for a month before the recital. The night before, her hands trembled as she packed her case.” Which detail shows that Yara felt nervous the night before the recital?

explanation.whyCorrect: Trembling hands are a physical sign of nervousness.
explanation.tip: Look for descriptions of feelings or body language.

options.label: A
options.text: “before the recital”
options.rationale: This only tells when the event happens, not how she felt.

options.label: B
options.text: “her hands trembled as she packed her case.”

options.label: C
options.text: “Yara practiced her violin.”
options.rationale: This states an action, not an emotion.

options.label: D
options.text: “Yara practiced her violin every afternoon for a month.”
options.rationale: This describes her practice routine, not her feelings the night before.

items.stem: Read: “Bees communicate by dancing. A figure-eight dance tells other bees the direction and distance to flowers.” True or false: the text says bees use sound, not movement, to share information about flowers.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says bees communicate by dancing (movement), not sound.
explanation.tip: Check whether the statement matches exactly what the text says.

items.stem: Read: “Rainforests cover about 6 percent of Earth’s land but are home to more than half of the world’s plant and animal species.” Which detail is evidence that rainforests are extremely important for wildlife?

explanation.whyCorrect: More than half of all species living there shows huge importance for wildlife.
explanation.tip: Match evidence to exactly what the claim is about.

options.label: A
options.text: “Earth’s land”
options.rationale: This is part of the sentence, not evidence of importance.

options.label: B
options.text: “cover about 6 percent of Earth’s land”
options.rationale: This describes size, not importance for wildlife.

options.label: C
options.text: “home to more than half of the world’s plant and animal species”

options.label: D
options.text: “Rainforests”
options.rationale: This is just the subject, not evidence.

items.stem: Read: “Khalid forgot his lunch at home. At recess, Fatima handed him half of her sandwich without saying a word, and Noor gave him one of her dates.” Which TWO details show that Khalid’s classmates were kind to him?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sharing food with Khalid shows kindness from his classmates.
explanation.tip: Look for actions that directly help someone.

options.label: A
options.text: “At recess”
options.rationale: This only tells when, not an act of kindness.

options.label: B
options.text: “Khalid forgot his lunch at home.”
options.rationale: This explains the problem, not kindness.

options.label: C
options.text: “Noor gave him one of her dates”

options.label: D
options.text: “Fatima handed him half of her sandwich without saying a word”

items.stem: Read: “Octopuses can change both the color and the texture of their skin in less than a second. This lets them blend in with rocks, sand, or coral to hide from predators.” Which detail explains WHY octopuses change their skin?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hiding from predators is the stated reason for changing color and texture.
explanation.tip: The word “why” means you need the reason, not just the action.

options.label: A
options.text: “Octopuses can change both the color and the texture of their skin.”
options.rationale: This describes what they do, not why.

options.label: B
options.text: “in less than a second”
options.rationale: This tells how fast, not why.

options.label: C
options.text: “with rocks, sand, or coral”
options.rationale: This names places, not the reason.

options.label: D
options.text: “This lets them blend in with rocks, sand, or coral to hide from predators.”

items.stem: Read: “Lina’s hands shook as she stepped onto the stage, but by the time she finished her poem, she was smiling and bowing to loud applause.” Which detail shows Lina’s feelings changed during her performance?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing the shaking hands at the start with the smiling at the end shows her feelings changed from nervous to happy.
explanation.tip: Compare the beginning and the end of the sentence to find a change.

options.label: A
options.text: she was smiling and bowing to loud applause

options.label: B
options.text: she finished her poem
options.rationale: This states an event, not a feeling.

options.label: C
options.text: she stepped onto the stage
options.rationale: This is an action, not a feeling.

options.label: D
options.text: her hands shook as she stepped onto the stage
options.rationale: This shows how she felt at the start, not the change.

items.stem: Read: “Most adult humans have 32 teeth, including four wisdom teeth that often appear in the late teenage years.” True or false: the text states that all 32 teeth appear by the age of five.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says wisdom teeth often appear in the late teenage years, not by age five.
explanation.tip: Watch for specific ages or numbers that do not match the text.

items.stem: Read: “A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through raindrops and separates into different colors.” Which detail tells you WHAT two things are needed to form a rainbow?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text names sunlight and raindrops as what must come together to form a rainbow.
explanation.tip: Find the exact words that answer the question being asked.

options.label: A
options.text: different colors
options.rationale: This is part of the result.

options.label: B
options.text: sunlight passes through raindrops

options.label: C
options.text: A rainbow forms
options.rationale: This names the event, not the two things needed.

options.label: D
options.text: separates into different colors
options.rationale: This describes the result, not what is needed.

items.stem: Read: “Jamal practiced his multiplication tables every night, even when his friends asked him to play. On test day, he finished early and checked his answers twice.” Which detail shows that Jamal resisted a distraction to keep studying?

explanation.whyCorrect: Despite being asked to play, Jamal kept studying — showing he resisted the distraction.
explanation.tip: Look for the exact moment the text shows a choice.

options.label: A
options.text: On test day
options.rationale: This only tells when, not about distraction.

options.label: B
options.text: he practiced his multiplication tables every night
options.rationale: This shows practice, not resisting distraction.

options.label: C
options.text: even when his friends asked him to play

options.label: D
options.text: he finished early and checked his answers twice
options.rationale: This happens on test day, not during practice.

items.stem: Read: “Volcanoes can be helpful as well as dangerous. The ash from eruptions makes soil rich for farming, but fast-moving lava and toxic gases can destroy everything in their path.” Which TWO details show that volcanoes can be dangerous?

explanation.whyCorrect: Lava and toxic gases are named as the dangerous parts of volcanoes.
explanation.tip: Separate the helpful details from the dangerous ones before choosing.

options.label: A
options.text: “ash from eruptions makes soil rich for farming”
options.rationale: This is a helpful effect, not dangerous.

options.label: B
options.text: “fast-moving lava”

options.label: C
options.text: “toxic gases can destroy everything in their path”

options.label: D
options.text: “Volcanoes can be helpful as well as dangerous.”
options.rationale: This states both ideas, not only danger.

items.stem: Read: “Honey never spoils if it is stored properly, because its low moisture and natural acidity stop bacteria from growing.” Which detail explains WHY honey does not spoil?

explanation.whyCorrect: Low moisture and acidity stopping bacteria is the scientific reason given.
explanation.tip: The word “because” often points straight to the reason.

options.label: A
options.text: Honey never spoils if it is stored properly.
options.rationale: This states the fact, not the reason.

options.label: B
options.text: if it is stored properly
options.rationale: This is a condition, not the reason.

options.label: C
options.text: Honey
options.rationale: This just names the subject.

options.label: D
options.text: its low moisture and natural acidity stop bacteria from growing

items.stem: Read: “Sara’s little brother broke her favorite model airplane. She clenched her fists, took a deep breath, and then helped him find the missing pieces.” Which detail shows that Sara controlled her anger?

explanation.whyCorrect: Taking a breath and helping, instead of reacting in anger, shows self-control.
explanation.tip: Look for what the character does AFTER feeling a strong emotion.

options.label: A
options.text: took a deep breath, and then helped him find the missing pieces

options.label: B
options.text: clenched her fists
options.rationale: This shows she felt angry, not that she controlled it.

options.label: C
options.text: broke her favorite model airplane
options.rationale: This describes the brother’s action, not Sara’s response.

options.label: D
options.text: her little brother
options.rationale: This names a character, not an action.

items.stem: Read: “Reusable water bottles can save a family hundreds of plastic bottles each year, since one bottle can be refilled thousands of times.” True or false: according to the text, a reusable bottle must be thrown away after just a few uses.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says a reusable bottle can be refilled thousands of times, which is the opposite of being thrown away quickly.
explanation.tip: Compare the statement word-for-word with what the text actually says.

items.stem: Read: “Even though Omar’s team lost the match, he shook hands with every player on the other team and congratulated them.” Which word best describes Omar?

explanation.whyCorrect: Congratulating the winning team after losing shows good sportsmanship.
explanation.tip: A character’s actions after disappointment reveal a trait.

options.label: A
options.text: shy
options.rationale: Shaking hands with everyone shows confidence, not shyness.

options.label: B
options.text: sportsmanlike

options.label: C
options.text: jealous
options.rationale: Jealousy would show resentment, not congratulating the winners.

options.label: D
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Nothing shows he is careless.

items.stem: Read: “Noor noticed a new student standing alone at lunch. She walked over, sat beside him, and asked about his favorite games.” Which word best describes Noor?

explanation.whyCorrect: Noor notices someone left out and includes him, showing she is welcoming.
explanation.tip: Watch how a character treats people who are left out.

options.label: A
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Noticing someone alone shows the opposite of carelessness.

options.label: B
options.text: nervous
options.rationale: Walking over confidently does not show nervousness.

options.label: C
options.text: welcoming

options.label: D
options.text: bossy
options.rationale: Asking kindly about his interests is not bossy.

items.stem: Read: “Hassan checked his backpack three times before school to make sure he had every book and pencil he needed.” True or false: this detail shows that Hassan is careless about his schoolwork.

explanation.whyCorrect: Checking three times shows Hassan is careful, the opposite of careless.
explanation.tip: Match the character’s actions to the trait, not the opposite.

items.stem: Read: “During the group project, Maya let her teammates choose the topic, then quietly did most of the research herself without complaining.” Which word best describes Maya?

explanation.whyCorrect: Doing the hard work quietly and without complaint shows Maya is hardworking.
explanation.tip: Look at what a character actually does, not just what they say.

options.label: A
options.text: selfish
options.rationale: Letting others choose and doing the work without complaint is not selfish.

options.label: B
options.text: lazy
options.rationale: Doing most of the research shows the opposite of lazy.

options.label: C
options.text: rude
options.rationale: Nothing in the text shows rudeness.

options.label: D
options.text: hardworking

items.stem: Read: “When the power went out during the storm, Yusuf calmly lit a candle, found the flashlight, and told his little sister it would be okay.” Which word best describes Yusuf?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yusuf’s steady, helpful actions during a stressful moment show he stays calm.
explanation.tip: A character’s behavior in a difficult moment often reveals a trait.

options.label: A
options.text: calm

options.label: B
options.text: confused
options.rationale: He knows exactly what to do, showing he is not confused.

options.label: C
options.text: angry
options.rationale: Nothing shows anger; he reassures his sister instead.

options.label: D
options.text: panicked
options.rationale: His calm actions are the opposite of panicked.

items.stem: Read: “Everyone else cheered when the school trip was canceled because of rain, but Huda sighed and looked down at her new hiking boots.” What is Huda’s perspective on the cancellation?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sighing and looking at the boots she wanted to wear shows she is upset about missing the trip.
explanation.tip: Notice when a character’s reaction is different from everyone else’s — it shows their own perspective.

options.label: A
options.text: She is angry at her classmates.
options.rationale: Nothing shows anger toward her classmates.

options.label: B
options.text: She is disappointed because she was looking forward to the trip.

options.label: C
options.text: She is relieved like everyone else.
options.rationale: Sighing and looking down shows disappointment, not relief.

options.label: D
options.text: She did not care about the trip.
options.rationale: Her reaction shows she did care.

items.stem: Read: “Mona thought the broken vase was ruined, but her brother Khalid saw the pieces and said, ‘We can glue this back together — it will look even more interesting.’” How is Khalid’s point of view different from Mona’s?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mona focuses on the damage, while Khalid focuses on the possibility of repair.
explanation.tip: Compare what each character says about the same event.

options.label: A
options.text: Mona wants to fix it, and Khalid wants to throw it away.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of what the text says.

options.label: B
options.text: Both are excited about the broken vase.
options.rationale: Mona is not excited; she thinks it is ruined.

options.label: C
options.text: Mona sees the vase as ruined, while Khalid sees a chance to fix and improve it.

options.label: D
options.text: Both think the vase cannot be fixed.
options.rationale: Khalid believes it can be fixed.

items.stem: Read: “The coach said the team played well despite losing, but Tariq kicked the ground and refused to look at the scoreboard.” True or false: Tariq shares the coach’s positive view of the game.

explanation.whyCorrect: Tariq’s actions show frustration and disappointment, not agreement with the coach’s positive view.
explanation.tip: A character’s actions can show a different perspective from what another character says.

items.stem: Read: “Sami’s grandmother smiled at the old photograph and said, ‘Those were simple, happy days.’ Sami looked at the black-and-white photo and thought it looked dull and plain.” How do Sami and his grandmother see the old photograph differently?

explanation.whyCorrect: The grandmother’s words show she values the memory, while Sami’s thought shows he only judges the photo’s look.
explanation.tip: A character’s own experience shapes how they see the same thing.

options.label: A
options.text: They both see the same happy memories.
options.rationale: Sami only sees the picture itself, not the memories.

options.label: B
options.text: Sami remembers the days in the photo better than his grandmother.
options.rationale: Sami was not alive then; the grandmother experienced it.

options.label: C
options.text: They both see the photo as boring.
options.rationale: The grandmother’s smile shows she feels happy, not bored.

options.label: D
options.text: His grandmother sees happy memories, while Sami sees only a dull, old picture.

items.stem: A story is told from Layla’s point of view only. How would readers’ understanding change if her little brother told the same story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator decides whose inner thoughts and feelings the reader gets to know.
explanation.tip: Point of view controls whose feelings the reader can directly hear.

options.label: A
options.text: Readers would learn the brother’s own thoughts and feelings instead of Layla’s.

options.label: B
options.text: The events in the story would be different.
options.rationale: Changing the narrator does not change what happened.

options.label: C
options.text: The setting of the story would change.
options.rationale: The setting stays the same no matter who narrates.

options.label: D
options.text: Layla would disappear from the story.
options.rationale: She would still appear; only whose thoughts we hear would change.

items.stem: Read: “Fatima watered the small seed every single day and made sure it got plenty of sunlight by the window.” What will most likely happen to the seed?

explanation.whyCorrect: Regular water and sunlight are what a seed needs to grow, so it will most likely grow into a plant.
explanation.tip: Think about what usually happens when you combine the clues in the text.

options.label: A
options.text: It will dry out and die.
options.rationale: Regular watering makes this unlikely.

options.label: B
options.text: It will probably grow into a healthy plant.

options.label: C
options.text: It will be eaten by a bird.
options.rationale: Nothing in the text mentions birds.

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing will happen to it.
options.rationale: Careful watering and sunlight usually cause a seed to grow.

items.stem: Read: “Khalid forgot his umbrella, and dark clouds were gathering quickly in the sky.” Based on this, it makes sense to predict that Khalid will probably get wet on his way home.

explanation.whyCorrect: Dark clouds usually mean rain is coming, and Khalid has no umbrella, so he will likely get wet.
explanation.tip: Good predictions connect text clues to what usually happens in real life.

items.stem: Read: “Noor had forgotten to study for her spelling test, but during recess she quickly asked her friend to quiz her on all the words.” What is the BEST prediction about Noor’s test?

explanation.whyCorrect: A quick review before a test usually helps, even if it is not as good as studying earlier.
explanation.tip: Use the clue about her action right before the test to judge the likely outcome.

options.label: A
options.text: She will fail the test no matter what.
options.rationale: Her last-minute review could still help.

options.label: B
options.text: Her friend will take the test for her.
options.rationale: Her friend is only quizzing her, not taking the test.

options.label: C
options.text: She may do better than if she had not reviewed the words at all.

options.label: D
options.text: She will refuse to take the test.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she will refuse.

items.stem: Read: “The hikers noticed the trail markers becoming fewer and the sky growing darker, but they kept walking deeper into the unfamiliar forest without checking their map.” Which detail BEST supports the prediction that the hikers might get lost?

explanation.whyCorrect: Continuing without checking a map, after noticing fewer markers, strongly suggests they will lose their way.
explanation.tip: Choose the detail that connects most directly to the exact prediction.

options.label: A
options.text: “The hikers noticed the trail markers becoming fewer.”
options.rationale: This is a warning sign, but choosing to keep going without checking the map is the stronger clue for getting lost.

options.label: B
options.text: “the sky growing darker.”
options.rationale: This is about light, not about losing the trail.

options.label: C
options.text: “trail markers.”
options.rationale: This alone is only part of the sentence, not full evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: “they kept walking deeper into the unfamiliar forest without checking their map.”

items.stem: Read: “Every afternoon, Yusuf fed the stray cat behind his building and slowly it began following him to the bus stop.” What will the cat most likely do next?

explanation.whyCorrect: Since the cat already follows Yusuf after being fed daily, it will likely continue trusting and following him.
explanation.tip: A pattern of behavior usually continues unless the text gives a reason for it to change.

options.label: A
options.text: It will probably keep following Yusuf and may even trust him more.

options.label: B
options.text: It will run away and never return.
options.rationale: The cat has been coming closer, not farther.

options.label: C
options.text: It will stop eating altogether.
options.rationale: The cat has been eating regularly, so this is unlikely.

options.label: D
options.text: It will attack Yusuf.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the cat is aggressive.

items.stem: Which word is an adverb? “The fox crept silently through the grass.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Silently” tells how the fox crept.
explanation.tip: Adverbs tell how, when, where or how often.

options.label: A
options.text: fox
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: silently

options.label: C
options.text: grass
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: crept
options.rationale: This is the verb.

items.stem: Choose the adverb that tells HOW OFTEN: “Our family ____ eats dinner together.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Always” tells how often.
explanation.tip: Frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, never.

options.label: A
options.text: delicious
options.rationale: This is an adjective.

options.label: B
options.text: always

options.label: C
options.text: hungry
options.rationale: This is an adjective.

options.label: D
options.text: kitchen
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Which word does the adverb “almost” describe in “The jar was almost empty”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Almost” tells to what extent the jar was empty.
explanation.tip: Adverbs can describe adjectives.

options.label: A
options.text: was
options.rationale: “Almost” tells how empty, not how it was.

options.label: B
options.text: The
options.rationale: This is an article.

options.label: C
options.text: empty

options.label: D
options.text: jar
options.rationale: Adverbs do not describe nouns.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of everyone in the choir, Reem sings ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing many people uses “most” + adverb.
explanation.tip: Two → more; three or more → most.

options.label: A
options.text: clearliest
options.rationale: This is not a word.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: “Dana’s heart pounded as she walked toward the microphone.”
options.rationale: This shows nervousness before her friend’s support.

options.label: D
options.text: “the front row.”
options.rationale: This only tells where her friend sat.

items.stem: Read: “Ancient cisterns carved from rock could hold over two million liters of rainwater. Archaeologists have found some still partly filled after thousands of years.” Which detail supports the idea that these cisterns were built extremely well?

explanation.whyCorrect: Still holding water after thousands of years proves the cisterns were extremely well built.
explanation.tip: Evidence of lasting quality usually mentions how something performs over time.

options.label: A
options.text: “rainwater.”
options.rationale: This names what they held, not evidence of quality.

options.label: B
options.text: “Archaeologists have found some still partly filled after thousands of years.”

options.label: C
options.text: “Ancient cisterns carved from rock could hold over two million liters of rainwater.”
options.rationale: This shows large capacity, not lasting quality.

options.label: D
options.text: “thousands of years.”
options.rationale: This only names a span of time without context.

items.stem: Read: “Khalid double-checked the rope, tested each knot twice, and only then let his younger cousin begin the climb.” True or false: this detail shows that Khalid was careless about his cousin’s safety.

explanation.whyCorrect: Double-checking the rope and testing each knot shows Khalid was extremely careful, not careless.
explanation.tip: Compare the statement to what the text actually describes.

items.stem: Read: “A single beehive can produce more than 25 kilograms of honey in one season, and the bees travel the equivalent of several times around the world to collect enough nectar.” Which detail shows how much effort bees put into making honey?

explanation.whyCorrect: Traveling the distance of several trips around the world shows an enormous amount of effort.
explanation.tip: Separate the result (honey) from the evidence about the process (travel).

options.label: A
options.text: “one season.”
options.rationale: This only names a time period.

options.label: B
options.text: “A single beehive can produce more than 25 kilograms of honey in one season.”
options.rationale: This shows the amount of honey, not the effort of travel.

options.label: C
options.text: “the bees travel the equivalent of several times around the world to collect enough nectar.”

options.label: D
options.text: “nectar.”
options.rationale: This names what they collect, not the amount of effort.

items.stem: Read: “During the group hike, Omar carried extra water for anyone who ran low, counted the trail markers out loud for fun, and gave up his own seat on the final bus ride.” Which TWO details show that Omar was thoughtful of others during the trip?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sharing water and giving up his seat are both actions that put others’ needs first.
explanation.tip: Look for actions that directly benefit someone else, not just personal habits.

options.label: A
options.text: “carried extra water for anyone who ran low”

options.label: B
options.text: “gave up his own seat on the final bus ride”

options.label: C
options.text: “During the group hike.”
options.rationale: This only tells when, not an action showing thoughtfulness.

options.label: D
options.text: “counted the trail markers out loud for fun.”
options.rationale: This is a personal habit, not an act of kindness toward others.

items.stem: Read: “Villagers built small stone walls across dry streambeds to slow rushing rainwater, giving it time to soak into the ground instead of running off.” Which detail explains the PURPOSE of the stone walls?

explanation.whyCorrect: Letting water soak in instead of running off is the stated purpose of the walls.
explanation.tip: A purpose explains WHY something was done, not just what was done.

options.label: A
options.text: “Villagers built small stone walls across dry streambeds.”
options.rationale: This describes the action, not the purpose.

options.label: B
options.text: “rushing rainwater.”
options.rationale: This names the problem, not the reason for the walls.

options.label: C
options.text: “dry streambeds.”
options.rationale: This only names the location.

options.label: D
options.text: “giving it time to soak into the ground instead of running off.”

items.stem: Read: “Layla read the instructions three times and laid out every tool in order before she finally picked up the screwdriver.” Which detail BEST shows that Layla was being methodical?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reading instructions multiple times and organizing tools before starting shows careful, methodical behavior.
explanation.tip: Look for repeated or extra careful actions before the main task begins.

options.label: A
options.text: “read the instructions three times and laid out every tool in order”

options.label: B
options.text: Layla
options.rationale: This just names the character.

options.label: C
options.text: “picked up the screwdriver.”
options.rationale: This is just the final step, not evidence of careful planning.

options.label: D
options.text: “only then.”
options.rationale: This is a transition word, not evidence by itself.

items.stem: Read: “Urban gardens can lower a neighborhood’s summer temperature by several degrees because plants release moisture that cools the surrounding air.” True or false: the text explains a reason why urban gardens cool their neighborhoods.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text gives the reason — plants releasing moisture — which explains how gardens cool the air.
explanation.tip: A ‘because’ clause usually signals the reason the text is giving.

items.stem: Read: “After the new traffic light was installed, the number of accidents at the intersection dropped from twelve per year to only two.” Which detail is the strongest evidence that the traffic light improved safety?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sharp drop in accidents, compared before and after, is the clearest evidence of improved safety.
explanation.tip: Look for numbers that are compared before and after a change.

options.label: A
options.text: “twelve per year.”
options.rationale: This is only part of the comparison, not the full evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: “the number of accidents at the intersection dropped from twelve per year to only two.”

options.label: C
options.text: “After the new traffic light was installed.”
options.rationale: This only tells when, not the result.

options.label: D
options.text: “the intersection.”
options.rationale: This only names the location.

items.stem: Read: “Hamdan insisted the new well belonged to everyone, even though he had paid for most of the digging himself.” Which detail shows that Hamdan valued the community over his own gain?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sharing something he paid for shows he values the community more than personal profit.
explanation.tip: Look for a contrast between what a character could have kept and what they chose to do.

options.label: A
options.text: “the new well.”
options.rationale: This only names the object.

options.label: B
options.text: “himself.”
options.rationale: This is only a pronoun, not evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: “he insisted the new well belonged to everyone, even though he had paid for most of the digging himself.”

options.label: D
options.text: “the digging.”
options.rationale: This names an action, not evidence of his values.

items.stem: Read: “Solar panels need very little maintenance, but they produce far less electricity on cloudy days, and the panels themselves are expensive to install at first.” Which TWO details describe a DRAWBACK of solar panels?

explanation.whyCorrect: Less electricity on cloudy days and high installation cost are both disadvantages mentioned in the text.
explanation.tip: Separate the advantages from the disadvantages before choosing.

options.label: A
options.text: “they produce far less electricity on cloudy days”

options.label: B
options.text: “Solar panels need very little maintenance.”
options.rationale: This describes an advantage, not a drawback.

options.label: C
options.text: “the panels themselves are expensive to install at first”

items.stem: Read: “Noor’s drawing won no ribbon at the fair, but she pinned it above her desk anyway and started sketching a new one that same evening.” Which detail shows that Noor did not let disappointment stop her?

explanation.whyCorrect: Starting a new drawing right away, instead of giving up, shows she kept going despite disappointment.
explanation.tip: Look for what a character does immediately AFTER a setback.

options.label: A
options.text: “the fair.”
options.rationale: This only names the event.

options.label: B
options.text: “Noor’s drawing won no ribbon at the fair.”
options.rationale: This describes the disappointment, not her response to it.

options.label: C
options.text: “a new one.”
options.rationale: This is only part of the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: “she pinned it above her desk anyway and started sketching a new one that same evening.”

items.stem: Read: “Public libraries lend more than just books; many now lend tools, musical instruments, and even seeds for home gardens.” Which detail supports the idea that libraries offer more than books?

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming specific items beyond books — tools, instruments, seeds — proves libraries offer more.
explanation.tip: The supporting evidence gives specific examples, not just a repeated claim.

options.label: A
options.text: “many now lend tools, musical instruments, and even seeds for home gardens.”

options.label: B
options.text: “home gardens.”
options.rationale: This is only part of the list, not full evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: “books.”
options.rationale: This is the opposite of what the detail should show.

options.label: D
options.text: “Public libraries lend more than just books.”
options.rationale: This states the claim itself, not the supporting evidence.

items.stem: Read: “When the team captain was injured, Rania quietly took over organizing practices without ever mentioning it to the coach, letting him think he had planned it himself.” Which word best describes Rania?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rania does important work without taking credit, showing she is modest.
explanation.tip: Notice whether a character seeks credit for their actions or avoids it.

options.label: A
options.text: boastful
options.rationale: Boastful would mean bragging, the opposite of hiding her role.

options.label: B
options.text: modest

options.label: C
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Taking over organizing shows responsibility, not carelessness.

options.label: D
options.text: jealous
options.rationale: Nothing shows jealousy of the captain.

items.stem: Read: “Faisal spent his Saturday rebuilding the neighbor’s fence that his dog had knocked down, refusing any payment for his time.” Which word best describes Faisal?

explanation.whyCorrect: Taking responsibility for his dog’s damage and fixing it himself shows Faisal is responsible.
explanation.tip: A character’s response to a mistake — theirs or someone else’s — often reveals a trait.

options.label: A
options.text: lazy
options.rationale: Spending a Saturday rebuilding a fence is the opposite of lazy.

options.label: B
options.text: stingy
options.rationale: Refusing payment shows generosity, the opposite of stingy.

options.label: C
options.text: responsible

options.label: D
options.text: proud
options.rationale: Nothing shows him bragging about it.

items.stem: Read: “Yara read the entire instruction manual twice before assembling the bookshelf, even though her brother said it was a waste of time.” True or false: this detail shows Yara is impulsive.

explanation.whyCorrect: Reading instructions carefully twice shows she is careful and thorough, not impulsive.
explanation.tip: Impulsive means acting quickly without thinking; look for the opposite behavior here.

items.stem: Read: “Even after losing the chess match for the third time, Khalid asked his opponent to explain the winning move so he could learn from it.” Which word best describes Khalid?

explanation.whyCorrect: Wanting to learn from repeated losses instead of giving up shows determination.
explanation.tip: Look at how a character handles failure to find a trait.

options.label: A
options.text: arrogant
options.rationale: Asking for help shows humility, not arrogance.

options.label: B
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Wanting to understand his mistake is the opposite of careless.

options.label: C
options.text: sore
options.rationale: Asking to learn shows he accepts the loss well, not that he is a bad loser.

options.label: D
options.text: determined

items.stem: Read: “Dalia noticed her little cousin struggling with his shoelaces at the party, so she knelt down and showed him the trick slowly, twice, without anyone asking her to.” Which word best describes Dalia?

explanation.whyCorrect: Noticing someone’s struggle and helping patiently, without being asked, shows caring.
explanation.tip: An unprompted act of kindness is strong evidence of a caring trait.

options.label: A
options.text: caring

options.label: B
options.text: shy
options.rationale: Kneeling down to help in front of others shows confidence, not shyness.

options.label: C
options.text: bossy
options.rationale: Helping gently is not the same as being bossy.

options.label: D
options.text: impatient
options.rationale: Showing him slowly and twice shows patience, not impatience.

items.stem: Read: “The whole class groaned when the teacher announced a surprise quiz, but Amira pulled out a pencil calmly, since she had reviewed her notes every night that week.” What is Amira’s perspective on the surprise quiz?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her calm reaction, explained by her nightly review, shows she feels prepared rather than worried.
explanation.tip: When a character reacts differently from the group, look for a reason given in the text.

options.label: A
options.text: She thinks the quiz is unfair.
options.rationale: Nothing in the text shows this opinion.

options.label: B
options.text: She is not worried, because she feels prepared.

options.label: C
options.text: She is upset like the rest of the class.
options.rationale: Her calm reaction is different from the class’s groaning.

options.label: D
options.text: She is confused about what a quiz is.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests confusion.

items.stem: Read: “Tariq thought the old clock tower should be torn down because it no longer worked, but his grandfather believed it should stay because it reminded the town of its history.” How do Tariq and his grandfather see the clock tower differently?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tariq judges the tower by whether it works; his grandfather judges it by its meaning to the town.
explanation.tip: Compare the REASON each character gives for their opinion.

options.label: A
options.text: Both think it should be torn down.
options.rationale: The grandfather wants it to stay.

options.label: B
options.text: Both value its history equally.
options.rationale: Tariq focuses on it no longer working, not its history.

options.label: C
options.text: Tariq values its usefulness, while his grandfather values its connection to history.

options.label: D
options.text: Tariq wants to keep it, and the grandfather wants it removed.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of what the text says.

items.stem: Read: “The coach called the scrimmage a success, but Sara kicked the grass and would not meet anyone’s eyes afterward.” True or false: Sara agrees with the coach’s view of the scrimmage.

explanation.whyCorrect: Sara’s frustrated body language shows she does not share the coach’s positive view.
explanation.tip: A character’s actions can reveal a perspective that contradicts what another character says.

items.stem: Read: “Grandma Zainab called the crowded, noisy souk ‘wonderfully alive,’ while her grandson Omar found it exhausting and could not wait to leave.” How is Omar’s perspective different from his grandmother’s?

explanation.whyCorrect: The same experience feels exciting to one character and exhausting to the other.
explanation.tip: The same event can feel different depending on who is experiencing it.

options.label: A
options.text: Neither of them likes the souk.
options.rationale: Grandma Zainab calls it wonderfully alive.

options.label: B
options.text: Both enjoy the souk equally.
options.rationale: Omar wants to leave, showing he does not enjoy it as much.

options.label: C
options.text: Omar loves the noise, and Grandma Zainab hates it.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the text.

options.label: D
options.text: Grandma Zainab enjoys the souk’s energy, while Omar finds it tiring.

items.stem: A story about a school trip is told only through the diary entries of one student, Huda. How would the story change if it also included her teacher’s diary entries?

explanation.whyCorrect: Adding a second point of view lets readers hear another character’s private thoughts, not just events.
explanation.tip: More than one perspective means readers hear more than one character’s inner thoughts.

options.label: A
options.text: Readers would also learn the teacher’s private thoughts and concerns about the trip.

options.label: B
options.text: The trip’s location would change.
options.rationale: Perspective does not affect where the story takes place.

options.label: C
options.text: Huda’s diary entries would disappear.
options.rationale: Her entries would likely remain alongside the teacher’s.

options.label: D
options.text: The events of the trip would change.
options.rationale: Adding another perspective does not change what happened.

items.stem: Read: “Sami had ignored every warning about the incoming sandstorm and left his bike outside the shed, uncovered, right next to the open gate.” What will most likely happen?

explanation.whyCorrect: Leaving a bike uncovered and exposed during a storm makes damage likely.
explanation.tip: Think about what usually happens when something is left exposed to a danger that was already warned about.

options.label: A
options.text: The sandstorm will not affect the bike at all.
options.rationale: This ignores the direct exposure described.

options.label: B
options.text: The bike will likely be damaged or blown around by the sandstorm.

options.label: C
options.text: The bike will stay perfectly clean.
options.rationale: Leaving it uncovered in a storm makes this unlikely.

options.label: D
options.text: The gate will close itself.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests this will happen.

items.stem: Read: “Lina had saved exactly half of the money for the bicycle and had three more months of allowance before the sale ended.” Based on this, it makes sense to predict that Lina will probably be able to afford the bicycle in time.

explanation.whyCorrect: If she already has half the money and has enough time left to save more, she will likely reach her goal.
explanation.tip: Predictions about money often depend on comparing what is saved with what is still needed and how much time is left.

items.stem: Read: “Scientists noticed a volcano’s steam vents releasing gas more quickly than usual and recorded several small tremors over the past week.” What is the BEST prediction based on these clues?

explanation.whyCorrect: Increasing gas release and small tremors are warning signs scientists use to predict a possible eruption.
explanation.tip: Combine several related clues, not just one, to make a stronger prediction.

options.label: A
options.text: The volcano will stop all activity permanently.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests activity is ending.

options.label: B
options.text: The tremors are unrelated to the volcano.
options.rationale: The tremors are reported alongside the volcano’s activity, suggesting a connection.

options.label: C
options.text: The volcano may be building toward a larger eruption soon.

options.label: D
options.text: The volcano has become completely safe.
options.rationale: Increased gas and tremors suggest rising activity, not safety.

items.stem: Read: “Despite being told the bridge was closed for repairs, two hikers decided to climb over the barrier and cross it anyway.” Which detail BEST supports the prediction that the hikers are taking a serious risk?

explanation.whyCorrect: Ignoring a warning about repairs, specifically, is what signals real danger ahead.
explanation.tip: Look for the exact detail that names the danger, not just the action taken.

options.label: A
options.text: “the bridge.”
options.rationale: This only names the object.

options.label: B
options.text: “and cross it anyway.”
options.rationale: This only confirms the action, not the specific danger.

options.label: C
options.text: “two hikers decided to climb over the barrier.”
options.rationale: This describes the action, but the warning about repairs is the stronger clue for risk.

options.label: D
options.text: “despite being told the bridge was closed for repairs”

items.stem: Read: “After weeks of drought, dark clouds finally gathered over the dry farmland, and the wind carried the smell of rain for the first time in a month.” What will most likely happen next?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dark clouds and the smell of rain are classic signs that rain is about to fall.
explanation.tip: Weather predictions often rely on recognizing familiar signs described in the text.

options.label: A
options.text: It will probably rain soon, bringing relief to the farmland.

options.label: B
options.text: The drought will continue with no change.
options.rationale: The clouds and smell of rain suggest a change is coming.

options.label: C
options.text: The farmland will flood immediately.
options.rationale: A first rain after a drought does not usually cause sudden flooding.

options.label: D
options.text: A sandstorm will begin instead.
options.rationale: Nothing in the text mentions sand or a storm of that kind.

items.stem: Which word describes the noun “camel” in “The patient camel waited in the shade”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Patient” tells what kind of camel.
explanation.tip: Adjectives describe nouns.

options.label: A
options.text: shade
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: patient

options.label: C
options.text: waited
options.rationale: This is the verb.

options.label: D
options.text: The
options.rationale: This is an article.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a predicate adjective?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Cool” follows the linking verb “felt” and describes the subject.
explanation.tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: The cool air arrived after sunset.
options.rationale: “Cool” comes before the noun here.

options.label: B
options.text: We watched the sunset.
options.rationale: There is no predicate adjective.

options.label: C
options.text: The desert air felt cool after sunset.

options.label: D
options.text: Sunset came quickly.
options.rationale: “Quickly” is an adverb.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “Of the two routes, the coastal road is ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing exactly two routes: more scenic.
explanation.tip: Two → comparative; three+ → superlative.

options.label: A
options.text: scenicer
options.rationale: Long adjectives use “more.”

options.label: B
options.text: most scenic
options.rationale: With two items, use the comparative.

options.label: C
options.text: more scenic

options.label: D
options.text: more scenicer
options.rationale: Never combine more with -er.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: No comma between adjectives that are not coordinate (you would not say “new and wooden jewelry box” naturally), and never a comma before the noun.
explanation.tip: Use commas only between coordinate adjectives, and never before the noun.

items.stem: Which clause is dependent? “Unless the bus arrives soon, we will be late.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Unless” makes the clause dependent.
explanation.tip: Dependent clauses begin with subordinating conjunctions or relative pronouns.

options.label: A
options.text: the bus arrives
options.rationale: This is part of the dependent clause.

options.label: B
options.text: we will be late
options.rationale: This can stand alone.

options.label: C
options.text: we will
options.rationale: This is incomplete.

options.label: D
options.text: Unless the bus arrives soon

items.stem: Which sentence contains a relative clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: “who trained us” describes the coach.
explanation.tip: Relative clauses begin with who, which, that, whose.

options.label: A
options.text: The coach who trained us retired this year.

options.label: B
options.text: The coach retired, and we were sad.
options.rationale: This is compound.

options.label: C
options.text: The coach retired this year.
options.rationale: No relative clause.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the coach retired, we were sad.
options.rationale: This has an adverb clause.

items.stem: Choose the relative pronoun: “The book ____ cover is torn belongs to the library.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Whose” shows the cover belongs to the book.
explanation.tip: whose = possession.

options.label: A
options.text: which
options.rationale: This does not show possession.

options.label: B
options.text: that
options.rationale: This does not show possession.

options.label: C
options.text: who’s
options.rationale: This means who is.

options.label: D
options.text: whose

items.stem: Which sentence is compound-complex?

explanation.whyCorrect: It has two independent clauses and one dependent clause.
explanation.tip: Compound-complex = 2+ independent + 1+ dependent.

options.label: A
options.text: We lit candles.
options.rationale: This is simple.

options.label: B
options.text: When the power failed, we lit candles, and Mariam told stories.

options.label: C
options.text: We lit candles, and Mariam told stories.
options.rationale: This is compound.

options.label: D
options.text: When the power failed, we lit candles.
options.rationale: This is complex.

items.stem: Which revision places the relative clause correctly to avoid confusion?

explanation.whyCorrect: A relative clause should sit right after the noun it describes.
explanation.tip: Place modifiers next to what they modify.

options.label: A
options.text: That my aunt made, the vase sat on the shelf.
options.rationale: The clause is misplaced.

options.label: B
options.text: The vase sat that my aunt made on the shelf.
options.rationale: This is confusing.

options.label: C
options.text: The vase that my aunt made sat on the shelf.

options.label: D
options.text: The vase sat on the shelf that my aunt made.
options.rationale: This suggests the aunt made the shelf.

items.stem: Which is a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: A dependent clause alone is a fragment.
explanation.tip: Ask: Because… what happened?

options.label: A
options.text: Yusuf missed the bus.
options.rationale: This is complete.

options.label: B
options.text: The robotics club stayed late.
options.rationale: This is complete.

options.label: C
options.text: He walked home.
options.rationale: This is complete.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the robotics club stayed late.

items.stem: Which is a comma splice?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice.
explanation.tip: Comma alone ≠ enough to join sentences.

options.label: A
options.text: The reef is fragile, it needs protection.

options.label: B
options.text: The reef is fragile, so it needs protection.
options.rationale: Correct with a conjunction.

options.label: C
options.text: The reef is fragile.
options.rationale: Simple sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The reef is fragile; it needs protection.
options.rationale: A semicolon is correct.

items.stem: Which revision fixes the run-on? “Scientists grow corals in nurseries they transplant them to reefs.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon correctly joins the two clauses.
explanation.tip: Use a period, semicolon, or comma + conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: Scientists grow corals in nurseries, they transplant them to reefs.
options.rationale: This is a comma splice.

options.label: B
options.text: Scientists grow corals in nurseries; then they transplant them to reefs.

options.label: C
options.text: Scientists grow corals. In nurseries they transplant them to reefs.
options.rationale: Changes meaning.

options.label: D
options.text: Scientists grow corals in nurseries they, transplant them.
options.rationale: Misplaced comma.

items.stem: “Hoping to finish the model before the deadline and working late every night” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: It contains only participial phrases; there is no subject and main verb.
explanation.tip: Long word groups can still be fragments.

items.stem: Which paragraph revision contains NO fragments or run-ons?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each sentence is complete and correctly joined.
explanation.tip: Check every sentence in a paragraph.

options.label: A
options.text: The souq is old. Its arches carved. Shops sell spices.
options.rationale: “Its arches carved” is a fragment.

options.label: B
options.text: The souq is old, its arches are carved, its shops sell spices.
options.rationale: Comma splices.

options.label: C
options.text: The souq is old. Its arches are carved, and its shops sell spices.

options.label: D
options.text: The souq is old its arches are carved.
options.rationale: Run-on.

items.stem: Choose the past tense: “The bell ____ at noon.”

explanation.whyCorrect: ring → rang → rung.
explanation.tip: Past participle needs has/have/had.

options.label: A
options.text: rang

options.label: B
options.text: rings
options.rationale: This is present.

options.label: C
options.text: rung
options.rationale: “Rung” needs a helping verb.

options.label: D
options.text: ringed
options.rationale: “Ring” is irregular.

items.stem: Match each verb with its past participle.

explanation.whyCorrect: These verbs form the past participle with -en.
explanation.tip: Test with “I have ___.”

items.stem: Choose: “By the time we arrived, the guests had already ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: had + gone (past participle of go).
explanation.tip: go → went → gone.

options.label: A
options.text: went
options.rationale: After “had,” use the past participle.

options.label: B
options.text: gone

options.label: C
options.text: goed
options.rationale: Not a word.

options.label: D
options.text: go

items.stem: Which is the best summary of “The Last Bus Home”?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.rationale: Too narrow.

options.label: D
options.text: Yusuf’s phone dies.
options.rationale: Detail.

items.stem: Which detail should be LEFT OUT of a summary of the four-day week article?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific examples are less essential than the main points.
explanation.tip: Keep main points; drop examples.

options.label: A
options.text: Families need childcare on the fifth day.
options.rationale: Key point.

options.label: B

options.rationale: Key point.

options.label: C
options.text: Buses and heating are examples of savings.

options.label: D
options.text: Math scores grew more slowly.
options.rationale: Key evidence.

items.stem: Which is the most objective summary of the souq letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Objective summaries avoid judgments.
explanation.tip: Report, don’t evaluate.

options.label: A
options.text: The souq has copper workshops.
options.rationale: Detail only.

options.label: B
options.text: The council is wrong and foolish.
options.rationale: Judgment.

options.label: C
options.text: A wise student bravely saves the best market ever.
options.rationale: Opinion words.

options.label: D
options.text: A student urges the council to repair the souq instead of replacing it, citing history and tourism.

items.stem: Which summary of “The Interview” keeps the important events in order?

explanation.whyCorrect: Correct sequence of key events.
explanation.tip: Keep events in order.

options.label: A
options.text: A student interviews a reserved custodian, a question about a radio unlocks his stories, and he gives her a doorknob as a keepsake.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.rationale: Detail only.

options.label: D
options.text: A custodian gives a student a doorknob, then she asks about the radio.
options.rationale: Order is wrong.

items.stem: Which sentence summarizes BOTH texts in the paired passage without adding opinions?

explanation.whyCorrect: It captures the shared pattern objectively.
explanation.tip: Summaries of paired texts note what both share.

options.label: A
options.text: Yasmin practices against a stone wall.
options.rationale: Detail from one text.

options.label: B
options.text: A girl and a transplanted tree each struggle after moving and eventually thrive.

options.label: C
options.text: Moving is the worst thing that can happen.
options.rationale: Opinion.

options.label: D
options.text: Lemon trees and football are both fun.
options.rationale: Opinion and inaccurate.

items.stem: Which sentence supports the claim that reefs protect coastlines?

explanation.whyCorrect: This states the protective function directly.
explanation.tip: Match evidence to the exact claim.

options.label: A
options.text: “Fish shelter in their branches.”
options.rationale: About fish.

options.label: B
options.text: “A reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps.”
options.rationale: About structure.

options.label: C
options.text: “Coastlines are protected because reefs break the force of storm waves.”

options.label: D

options.rationale: About bleaching.

items.stem: Which quotation supports the claim that four-day weeks may harm learning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Slower score growth is evidence about learning.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that matches the claim’s topic.

options.label: A
options.text: “Districts do save some money.”
options.rationale: About cost.

options.label: B
options.text: “families must find care for children.”
options.rationale: About families.

options.label: C
options.text: “More schools are considering a four-day week.”
options.rationale: Background.

options.label: D
options.text: “students’ math scores grew more slowly than in similar five-day schools.”

items.stem: Which detail shows that Yusuf expected to be in trouble?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rehearsing excuses shows he feared blame.
explanation.tip: Inner thoughts are strong evidence of feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: “It wasn’t my fault, he practiced.”

options.label: B
options.text: “The walk would take forty minutes.”
options.rationale: About distance.

options.label: C
options.text: “She waved wildly.”
options.rationale: About Mariam.

options.label: D
options.text: “Yusuf laughed.”
options.rationale: His later reaction.

items.stem: Which TWO quotations support the inference that Mr. Aziz takes pride in his work?

explanation.whyCorrect: His careful effort and his belief in looking after things show pride.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that clearly supports the inference.

options.label: A
options.text: “There is not much to tell.”
options.rationale: He downplays his work here.

options.label: B
options.text: “Some things last if you look after them.”

options.label: C
options.text: “I carried two hundred chairs to the library, one by one.”

options.label: D
options.text: “Sit closer. That was 1998…”
options.rationale: This begins the story but does not show pride.

items.stem: A reader claims Huda respects the council even while disagreeing. Which quotation is the STRONGEST evidence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her respectful closing and constructive tone support the claim; the closing states it directly.
explanation.tip: The best evidence most directly proves the claim.

options.label: A
options.text: “Please do not let our history disappear behind a glass wall.”
options.rationale: An emotional appeal.

options.label: B
options.text: “Respectfully, Huda Al-Mansour”

options.label: C
options.text: “The city council plans to replace our old covered souq.”
options.rationale: A fact.

options.label: D
options.text: “I urge the council to change its plan.”
options.rationale: Shows disagreement, not respect.

items.stem: Which theme does “Ladder” express?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each rung holds a year he gave; the speaker now reaches what he planted.
explanation.tip: Themes are messages about life.

options.label: A
options.text: Ladders are dangerous.
options.rationale: Not the message.

options.label: B
options.text: Apples are the best fruit.
options.rationale: Not a theme.

options.label: C
options.text: The love and lessons of family stay with us as we grow.

options.label: D
options.text: Storms destroy everything.
options.rationale: The tree became a gift.

items.stem: Which detail best develops the theme of “The Interview”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The gift connects to “Some things last if you look after them.”
explanation.tip: Find details tied to the message.

options.label: A
options.text: Sara sits on a bucket.
options.rationale: Setting detail.

options.label: B
options.text: The radio plays softly.
options.rationale: Atmosphere.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the last week of school.
options.rationale: Setting.

options.label: D
options.text: Mr. Aziz gives Sara the doorknob from the first door he fixed.

items.stem: What theme do “The New Field” and “Transplant” share?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both show struggle after moving, then success.
explanation.tip: Shared themes can appear in different genres.

options.label: A
options.text: Adapting to change takes time, but growth follows.

options.label: B
options.text: Football is better than gardening.
options.rationale: Not a theme.

options.label: C
options.text: Mountains are better than coasts.
options.rationale: Not a theme.

options.label: D
options.text: Never move away from home.
options.rationale: Both texts show growth after moving.

items.stem: How does the setting of “Desert Night” support its theme of peace and wonder?

explanation.whyCorrect: Quiet sounds, warm sand and a starry sky create calm wonder.
explanation.tip: Setting can help develop theme.

options.label: A
options.text: The storm creates fear.
options.rationale: There is no storm.

options.label: B
options.text: The vast, silent desert under the stars creates a feeling of calm awe.

options.label: C
options.text: The classroom creates focus.
options.rationale: There is no classroom.

options.label: D
options.text: The busy city noise creates excitement.
options.rationale: There is no city.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for “meticulous”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Meticulous and precise both describe extreme care with details.
explanation.tip: Formal synonyms like meticulous often replace simpler words such as careful.

options.label: A
options.text: careless
options.rationale: This is an antonym.

options.label: B
options.text: curious
options.rationale: This is unrelated.

options.label: C
options.text: precise

options.label: D
options.text: hasty
options.rationale: This is the opposite characteristic.

items.stem: Which word is an antonym for “reluctant”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reluctant means unwilling; eager means very willing — opposites.
explanation.tip: Picture someone dragging their feet versus someone racing to start.

options.label: A
options.text: quiet
options.rationale: Quiet is unrelated.

options.label: B
options.text: nervous
options.rationale: Nervous is a different meaning, about fear.

options.label: C
options.text: hesitant
options.rationale: Hesitant is a synonym of reluctant.

options.label: D
options.text: eager

items.stem: Choose the synonym: “The lawyer presented a ____ (convincing) argument to the jury.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Persuasive and convincing both describe an argument that changes people’s minds.
explanation.tip: Match the meaning in parentheses exactly, not just a related idea.

options.label: A
options.text: confusing
options.rationale: This describes the opposite effect.

options.label: B
options.text: persuasive

options.label: C
options.text: brief
options.rationale: This describes length, not persuasiveness.

options.label: D
options.text: loud
options.rationale: This describes volume, not the quality of the argument.

items.stem: Match each word with its SYNONYM.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair shares nearly the same meaning.
explanation.tip: Replace one word with its match in a sentence to check the meaning holds.

items.stem: A candid witness answers every question directly, while a deceptive witness twists the facts to hide the truth. True or false: this contrast means “candid” and “deceptive” are synonyms.

explanation.whyCorrect: Candid means open and honest; deceptive means misleading — opposites, not synonyms.
explanation.tip: If one word describes honesty and the other describes dishonesty, they are antonyms.

items.stem: Which word is an antonym for “abundant”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Abundant means existing in large amounts; scarce means existing in very small amounts — opposites.
explanation.tip: Think of a harvest with plenty of food compared to one with almost none.

options.label: A
options.text: scarce

options.label: B
options.text: fresh
options.rationale: Fresh is an unrelated meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: useful
options.rationale: Useful is an unrelated meaning.

options.label: D
options.text: plentiful
options.rationale: Plentiful is a synonym of abundant.

items.stem: Read: “Unlike his impulsive younger brother, Khalid always paused to weigh the consequences before acting.” Which word could replace “impulsive” without changing the sentence’s meaning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Impulsive and rash both describe acting quickly without thinking of consequences.
explanation.tip: Use the contrast in the sentence (Khalid pausing) as a clue to the opposite meaning of impulsive.

options.label: A
options.text: curious
options.rationale: This is an unrelated meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: rash

options.label: C
options.text: patient
options.rationale: This is the opposite quality.

options.label: D
options.text: cautious
options.rationale: This describes Khalid, the opposite of impulsive.

items.stem: Choose the antonym: “The committee’s decision was ____ (unanimous); several members strongly disagreed.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Unanimous means everyone agrees; divided means people disagree — opposites, which fits the sentence’s own contrast.
explanation.tip: Look for a word that fits the contrast the sentence itself describes.

options.label: A
options.text: official
options.rationale: This is an unrelated meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: quick
options.rationale: This describes speed, not agreement.

options.label: C
options.text: divided

options.label: D
options.text: agreed
options.rationale: This is similar to unanimous, not opposite.

items.stem: Which word is a synonym for “ambiguous”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Ambiguous and unclear both describe something that can be understood in more than one way, or not understood at all.
explanation.tip: Ambiguous is a more formal word for unclear or confusing.

options.label: A
options.text: obvious
options.rationale: This is an antonym of ambiguous.

options.label: B
options.text: formal
options.rationale: This is an unrelated meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: unclear

options.label: D
options.text: lengthy
options.rationale: This describes length, not clarity.

items.stem: Which pair of words are near-synonyms with DIFFERENT levels of intensity?

explanation.whyCorrect: Annoyed and furious both describe anger, but furious is a much stronger degree of the same feeling.
explanation.tip: Near-synonyms can share a meaning but differ in strength or degree.

options.label: A
options.text: fast / quick
options.rationale: These are near-synonyms, but at nearly the SAME level of intensity.

options.label: B
options.text: happy / sad
options.rationale: These are opposites, not near-synonyms.

options.label: C
options.text: hot / cold
options.rationale: These are opposites, not near-synonyms.

options.label: D
options.text: annoyed / furious

items.stem: Match each word with its ANTONYM.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair has opposite meanings.
explanation.tip: Check that each pair truly contrasts, not just that the words are different.

items.stem: Complete the analogy: honest : deceptive :: confident : ____

explanation.whyCorrect: Honest and deceptive are opposites, so confident should pair with its opposite: insecure.
explanation.tip: Analogies keep the same relationship — here, antonym pairs — on both sides.

options.label: A
options.text: insecure

options.label: B
options.text: humble
options.rationale: Humble is not necessarily an opposite of confident.

options.label: C
options.text: proud
options.rationale: Proud is similar to confident, not its opposite.

options.label: D
options.text: brave
options.rationale: Brave is similar to confident, not its opposite.

items.stem: True or false: “scarce” and “abundant” describe the same amount of something.

explanation.whyCorrect: Scarce means very little is available; abundant means a lot is available — these describe opposite amounts.
explanation.tip: Compare the actual quantities each word suggests.

items.stem: Read: “The witness gave a candid account of the accident, unlike the driver’s evasive answers.” Which word is an antonym for “candid” as used here?

explanation.whyCorrect: Candid means open and honest; evasive means avoiding giving a direct answer — opposites, as the sentence itself contrasts.
explanation.tip: The sentence’s own contrast (unlike) often names the antonym directly.

options.label: A
options.text: brief
options.rationale: This is unrelated to honesty.

options.label: B
options.text: evasive

options.label: C
options.text: honest
options.rationale: This is a synonym of candid.

options.label: D
options.text: loud
options.rationale: This is an unrelated meaning.

items.stem: Choose the synonym: “The volunteers showed ____ (plentiful) kindness toward the flood victims.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Abundant and plentiful both describe a large amount of something.
explanation.tip: Match the meaning in parentheses to the best synonym, not a similar-sounding word.

options.label: A
options.text: scarce
options.rationale: This is an antonym.

options.label: B
options.text: brief
options.rationale: This is an unrelated meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: formal
options.rationale: This is an unrelated meaning.

options.label: D
options.text: abundant

items.stem: Read: “Renewable energy sources like wind and solar now generate over 12 percent of global electricity, a figure that has tripled in the past decade.” Which detail is evidence that renewable energy use is growing rapidly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tripling in just ten years is direct evidence of rapid growth.
explanation.tip: Evidence of growth usually compares a past amount with a present one.

options.label: A
options.text: “generate over 12 percent of global electricity.”
options.rationale: This states the current amount, not the rate of growth.

options.label: B
options.text: “wind and solar.”
options.rationale: This only names the sources.

options.label: C
options.text: “a figure that has tripled in the past decade.”

options.label: D
options.text: “global electricity.”
options.rationale: This only names the category.

items.stem: Read: “The city’s new bike-sharing program cut traffic near downtown by 8 percent in its first year, though some residents complained that stations were often empty during rush hour.” Which TWO details give a balanced view of the program’s first year?

explanation.whyCorrect: A balanced view includes both the positive result (less traffic) and a real complaint (empty stations).
explanation.tip: A balanced summary uses evidence from both sides of an issue.

options.label: A
options.text: “stations were often empty during rush hour”

options.label: B
options.text: “its first year.”
options.rationale: This only tells the time frame.

options.label: C
options.text: “The city’s new bike-sharing program.”
options.rationale: This only names the program, not a result.

options.label: D
options.text: “cut traffic near downtown by 8 percent”

items.stem: Read: “Mr. Aziz ran his thumb along the cracked door frame he had repaired decades earlier and said nothing for a long moment before speaking again.” Which detail suggests that the repair held a deep personal meaning for Mr. Aziz?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pausing silently while touching his old work suggests a strong, quiet emotional connection to it.
explanation.tip: A long pause or silence in dialogue often signals strong, unspoken feeling.

options.label: A
options.text: “the door frame.”
options.rationale: This only names the object.

options.label: B
options.text: “before speaking again.”
options.rationale: This only marks a transition.

options.label: C
options.text: “he had repaired decades earlier.”
options.rationale: This gives a timeframe, not evidence of feeling.

options.label: D
options.text: “he ran his thumb along the cracked door frame... and said nothing for a long moment”
