items.stem: Read: “Deep-sea anglerfish produce their own light through a chemical reaction in a special organ, which attracts prey in the pitch-black water.” Which detail explains the PURPOSE of the anglerfish’s light?

explanation.whyCorrect: Attracting prey is the stated reason the anglerfish produces light.
explanation.tip: Separate the explanation of HOW something happens from the explanation of WHY.

options.label: A
options.text: “which attracts prey in the pitch-black water.”

options.label: B
options.text: “a special organ.”
options.rationale: This only names a body part.

options.label: C
options.text: “produce their own light through a chemical reaction.”
options.rationale: This explains how the light is made, not why.

options.label: D
options.text: “pitch-black water.”
options.rationale: This only describes the setting.

items.stem: Read: “Although four-day school weeks can save districts money on transportation and utilities, researchers found that younger students’ reading scores dropped slightly compared to five-day schools.” True or false: the text claims four-day school weeks have no drawbacks.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text names a specific drawback — a drop in younger students’ reading scores — so it does not claim there are no drawbacks.
explanation.tip: Watch for absolute claims like ‘no drawbacks’ when the text actually lists a cost.

items.stem: Read: “Huda crossed out her first three drafts of the letter, each one angrier than the last, before finally writing one that calmly explained her concerns.” Which detail shows that Huda chose to communicate respectfully rather than react in anger?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rewriting until she found a calm tone shows she deliberately chose respect over anger.
explanation.tip: Look at the FINAL version of a character’s words or actions, not just the early drafts.

options.label: A
options.text: “each one angrier than the last.”
options.rationale: This describes her early anger, not her final choice.

options.label: B
options.text: “crossed out her first three drafts... before finally writing one that calmly explained her concerns.”

options.label: C
options.text: “the letter.”
options.rationale: This only names the object.

options.label: D
options.text: “her concerns.”
options.rationale: This only names the topic.

items.stem: Read: “A single mature oak tree can absorb roughly 22 kilograms of carbon dioxide each year, which is why city planners increasingly favor planting them along busy streets.” Which detail supports the claim that oak trees help with pollution from traffic?

explanation.whyCorrect: Absorbing carbon dioxide — a pollutant released by traffic — is the direct evidence for the claim.
explanation.tip: Trace the claim back to the specific number or fact that supports it.

options.label: A
options.text: “city planners increasingly favor planting them along busy streets.”
options.rationale: This describes a decision made because of the fact, not the evidence itself.

options.label: B
options.text: “busy streets.”
options.rationale: This only names a location.

options.label: C
options.text: “can absorb roughly 22 kilograms of carbon dioxide each year”

options.label: D
options.text: “A single mature oak tree.”
options.rationale: This only names the subject.

items.stem: Read: “Yasmin woke at five every morning to practice before school, enjoyed listening to music on the bus, and kept a log of every mistake she made in rehearsal.” Which TWO details show Yasmin’s strong discipline?

explanation.whyCorrect: A strict daily routine and tracking her own mistakes both show serious self-discipline.
explanation.tip: Look for repeated habits and self-monitoring as strong evidence of discipline.

options.label: A
options.text: “kept a log of every mistake she made in rehearsal”

options.label: B
options.text: “woke at five every morning to practice before school”

options.label: C
options.text: “enjoyed listening to music on the bus.”
options.rationale: This is a personal preference, not evidence of discipline.

options.label: D
options.text: “before school.”
options.rationale: This only tells when, not evidence by itself.

items.stem: Read: “Lightning can heat the surrounding air to temperatures hotter than the surface of the sun, causing the air to expand explosively and produce the sound we hear as thunder.” Which detail explains WHY thunder happens?

explanation.whyCorrect: The explosive expansion of superheated air is the direct cause of the sound of thunder.
explanation.tip: Find the exact phrase describing the physical cause, not just a related fact.

options.label: A
options.text: “we hear as thunder.”
options.rationale: This only names the result, not the explanation.

options.label: B
options.text: “Lightning can heat the surrounding air to temperatures hotter than the surface of the sun.”
options.rationale: This explains the heat, but the explosive expansion is the direct cause of the sound.

options.label: C
options.text: “the surface of the sun.”
options.rationale: This is only a comparison, not the cause of thunder.

options.label: D
options.text: “causing the air to expand explosively”

items.stem: Read: “Huda signed her letter to the city council ‘Respectfully,’ even after writing three paragraphs disagreeing firmly with their plan.” Which detail shows that Huda disagreed without being disrespectful?

explanation.whyCorrect: Closing respectfully despite strong disagreement shows she kept a respectful, constructive tone.
explanation.tip: Compare the content of an argument with the TONE used to express it.

options.label: A
options.text: “signed her letter... ‘Respectfully,’ even after writing three paragraphs disagreeing firmly”

options.label: B
options.text: “the city council.”
options.rationale: This only names who received the letter.

options.label: C
options.text: “disagreeing firmly with their plan.”
options.rationale: This shows firm disagreement alone, not the respectful tone.

options.label: D
options.text: “three paragraphs.”
options.rationale: This only tells the length.

items.stem: Read: “Though bats are often feared, a single bat can eat more than a thousand insects in one night, making them valuable for controlling pests naturally.” True or false: the text presents bats as only dangerous to humans.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text actually presents bats as valuable pest controllers, not as dangerous.
explanation.tip: Check whether a statement matches the text’s actual claim, especially after a word like ‘though.’

items.stem: Read: “Switching a school’s lighting to LED bulbs cost the district $40,000 upfront, but the resulting savings on electricity paid back that cost within just three years.” Which detail shows that the LED switch was a good long-term investment?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paying back the cost in just three years, with savings continuing after, shows a strong long-term benefit.
explanation.tip: Compare the initial cost with the eventual payoff to judge whether something is a good investment.

options.label: A
options.text: “a school’s lighting.”
options.rationale: This only names what was changed.

options.label: B
options.text: “the resulting savings on electricity paid back that cost within just three years.”

options.label: C
options.text: “LED bulbs.”
options.rationale: This only names the product.

options.label: D
options.text: “cost the district $40,000 upfront.”
options.rationale: This states the cost, not evidence that it was worthwhile.

items.stem: Read: “Sara flipped through her notes one last time, closed the folder, and walked into the interview room without checking her phone even once.” Which detail shows that Sara stayed focused on the interview?

explanation.whyCorrect: Not checking her phone, a common distraction, shows she stayed mentally focused.
explanation.tip: Look for what a character avoids doing as evidence of focus or self-control.

options.label: A
options.text: “the interview room.”
options.rationale: This only names a location.

options.label: B
options.text: “flipped through her notes one last time.”
options.rationale: This shows preparation, not sustained focus during the walk.

options.label: C
options.text: “walked into the interview room without checking her phone even once.”

options.label: D
options.text: “closed the folder.”
options.rationale: This is a small action, not strong evidence of focus.

items.stem: Read: “Coastal mangrove forests can reduce the height of incoming storm waves by up to 66 percent, protecting the villages behind them from the worst flooding.” Which detail is the strongest evidence that mangroves protect coastal communities?

explanation.whyCorrect: The specific percentage reduction in wave height is the measurable evidence behind the claim.
explanation.tip: A number or statistic is often the strongest kind of evidence for a claim.

options.label: A
options.text: “Coastal mangrove forests.”
options.rationale: This only names the subject.

options.label: B
options.text: “storm waves.”
options.rationale: This only names the threat.

options.label: C
options.text: “protecting the villages behind them from the worst flooding.”
options.rationale: This states the result of the evidence, repeating the claim rather than giving new proof.

options.label: D
options.text: “can reduce the height of incoming storm waves by up to 66 percent”

items.stem: Read: “The region’s new desalination plant provides clean drinking water to 50,000 residents, but it also uses large amounts of electricity and releases concentrated salt water back into the sea.” Which TWO details describe a cost of the desalination plant?

explanation.whyCorrect: High electricity use and releasing concentrated salt water are both environmental costs of the plant.
explanation.tip: Separate the stated benefit from the stated costs before choosing.

options.label: A
options.text: “provides clean drinking water to 50,000 residents.”
options.rationale: This describes the benefit, not a cost.

options.label: B
options.text: “uses large amounts of electricity”

options.label: C
options.text: “releases concentrated salt water back into the sea”

items.stem: Read: “When the team’s presentation software crashed minutes before judging, Layla calmly grabbed a marker and sketched the diagrams by hand while her teammates panicked.” Which word best describes Layla?

explanation.whyCorrect: Finding a quick, creative solution under pressure shows Layla is resourceful.
explanation.tip: A character’s response to an unexpected problem often reveals a trait.

options.label: A
options.text: resourceful

options.label: B
options.text: anxious
options.rationale: She stays calm; her teammates panic instead.

options.label: C
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Her quick, calm solution shows the opposite of carelessness.

options.label: D
options.text: indifferent
options.rationale: She actively solves the problem, not ignoring it.

items.stem: Read: “Despite knowing the answer, Khalid let his quieter teammate present the group’s findings, coaching her through the key points beforehand instead of taking the spotlight himself.” Which word best describes Khalid?

explanation.whyCorrect: Giving up the spotlight to help a teammate shine shows generosity.
explanation.tip: Notice when a character gives up personal credit to help someone else.

options.label: A
options.text: insecure
options.rationale: Coaching her confidently shows the opposite of insecurity.

options.label: B
options.text: generous

options.label: C
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Preparing her carefully shows the opposite of carelessness.

options.label: D
options.text: competitive
options.rationale: Stepping back from the spotlight is the opposite of trying to compete for credit.

items.stem: Read: “Mariam re-checked the lab results three times before reporting them, even though her partner insisted the first result was obviously correct.” True or false: this detail shows Mariam is easily influenced by others’ opinions.

explanation.whyCorrect: Checking three times despite her partner’s pressure shows independence and thoroughness, not being easily influenced.
explanation.tip: Look for whether a character sticks to their own standards despite pressure from others.

items.stem: Read: “Omar admitted to the whole class that he had copied the homework answer, even though no one had noticed and he could easily have stayed silent.” Which word best describes Omar?

explanation.whyCorrect: Confessing a mistake no one would have noticed shows strong honesty.
explanation.tip: A character’s choice to tell the truth when they could easily hide it reveals honesty.

options.label: A
options.text: foolish
options.rationale: Telling the truth voluntarily is admirable, not foolish.

options.label: B
options.text: nervous
options.rationale: The text shows a choice to admit, not a feeling of fear.

options.label: C
options.text: honest

options.label: D
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Copying was the mistake, but admitting it shows the trait being tested: honesty.

items.stem: Read: “Even after three failed attempts to code the robot’s arm correctly, Dana reread the manual, asked a mentor one specific question, and tried a fourth approach before lunch.” Which word best describes Dana?

explanation.whyCorrect: Continuing to try new approaches after repeated failure shows persistence.
explanation.tip: Repeated attempts after failure are strong evidence of persistence.

options.label: A
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Rereading the manual and asking a focused question shows careful effort.

options.label: B
options.text: discouraged
options.rationale: Trying a fourth approach shows the opposite of giving up.

options.label: C
options.text: impatient
options.rationale: Taking time to reread and ask questions shows patience, not impatience.

options.label: D
options.text: persistent

items.stem: Read: “Yusuf noticed the new transfer student eating alone every day that week, so on Friday he invited him to sit with his usual group, even though it meant explaining the inside jokes all over again.” Which word best describes Yusuf?

explanation.whyCorrect: Actively including someone who was left out, despite the extra effort, shows Yusuf is inclusive.
explanation.tip: Notice how a character treats someone who does not belong to the usual group.

options.label: A
options.text: inclusive

options.label: B
options.text: annoyed
options.rationale: Nothing shows annoyance; he willingly includes the new student.

options.label: C
options.text: shy
options.rationale: Inviting someone over confidently is not shy behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: indifferent
options.rationale: Noticing and acting shows the opposite of indifference.

items.stem: Read: “Huda spent the entire bus ride rehearsing excuses for being late, even though her coach had texted that practice was cancelled.” True or false: this detail shows that Huda is confident she will not be blamed for anything.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rehearsing excuses, even unnecessarily, shows Huda expects to be blamed, not that she feels confident she is safe from blame.
explanation.tip: A character’s private thoughts, like rehearsed excuses, often reveal a hidden worry.

items.stem: Read: “Sami offered to carry the heaviest box up three flights of stairs without being asked, then went back down for a second trip while his friends rested.” Which word best describes Sami?

explanation.whyCorrect: Volunteering for the hardest task, twice, without being asked, shows Sami thinks of his tired friends — he is considerate.
explanation.tip: An unprompted offer to take on hard work for others is strong evidence of a considerate trait.

options.label: A
options.text: lazy
options.rationale: Volunteering for the heaviest box and a second trip is the opposite of lazy.

options.label: B
options.text: considerate

options.label: C
options.text: proud
options.rationale: Nothing shows him bragging about the task.

options.label: D
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Carrying boxes carefully does not show carelessness.

items.stem: Read: “Noura’s essay argued strongly against her own first opinion once new evidence changed her mind, and she rewrote the entire conclusion the night before it was due.” Which word best describes Noura?

explanation.whyCorrect: Being willing to change her opinion when new evidence appeared shows Noura is open-minded.
explanation.tip: A willingness to change one’s mind based on evidence often reveals open-mindedness.

options.label: A
options.text: stubborn
options.rationale: Changing her opinion based on evidence is the opposite of stubborn.

options.label: B
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Rewriting the conclusion carefully shows the opposite of carelessness.

options.label: C
options.text: open-minded

options.label: D
options.text: indecisive
options.rationale: She makes a firm decision based on evidence, not indecision.

items.stem: Read: “Tariq always double-checked the exits and the fire extinguisher locations whenever he entered an unfamiliar building, a habit his friends often teased him about.” Which word best describes Tariq?

explanation.whyCorrect: Consistently checking for safety exits, even when teased, shows Tariq is cautious.
explanation.tip: A repeated habit, even one that invites teasing, can reveal a consistent trait.

options.label: A
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Checking exits carefully is the opposite of careless.

options.label: B
options.text: lazy
options.rationale: The habit requires effort, not laziness.

options.label: C
options.text: arrogant
options.rationale: Nothing shows him bragging about this habit.

options.label: D
options.text: cautious

items.stem: Read: “Rather than arguing when the referee made a clearly wrong call against her team, Amal shook the referee’s hand after the match and thanked him for officiating.” Which word best describes Amal?

explanation.whyCorrect: Responding to an unfair call with respect, rather than anger, shows graciousness.
explanation.tip: How a character responds to being treated unfairly often reveals their true character.

options.label: A
options.text: gracious

options.label: B
options.text: indifferent
options.rationale: Choosing to thank him shows she cares about sportsmanship, not indifference.

options.label: C
options.text: resentful
options.rationale: Shaking hands and thanking him shows the opposite of resentment.

options.label: D
options.text: aggressive
options.rationale: Her calm, respectful reaction is the opposite of aggressive.

items.stem: Read: “Khalid volunteered to tutor the younger students every Tuesday for free, enjoyed drawing comics in his free time, kept a careful record of each student’s progress, and stayed late twice to help a struggling student catch up before an exam.” Which TWO details show that Khalid takes his tutoring role seriously?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tracking progress carefully and staying late to help show Khalid takes real, ongoing responsibility for his students’ learning.
explanation.tip: Look for evidence of sustained effort over time, not just the initial decision to help.

options.label: A
options.text: “enjoyed drawing comics in his free time.”
options.rationale: This is a personal hobby, unrelated to his tutoring role.

options.label: B
options.text: “volunteered to tutor the younger students every Tuesday for free.”
options.rationale: This shows generosity in starting, but is not itself evidence of ongoing seriousness and effort.

options.label: C
options.text: “kept a careful record of each student’s progress”

options.label: D
options.text: “stayed late twice to help a struggling student catch up before an exam”

items.stem: Read: “When her little brother accidentally deleted her science project files the night before the deadline, Rania took a breath, said, ‘It’s okay, accidents happen,’ and started rebuilding the project together with him.” Which word best describes Rania?

explanation.whyCorrect: Responding calmly to a stressful accident, instead of reacting in anger, shows patience.
explanation.tip: A character’s reaction to someone else’s mistake often reveals a trait.

options.label: A
options.text: indifferent
options.rationale: She actively helps rebuild, showing she cares about the outcome.

options.label: B
options.text: patient

options.label: C
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Rebuilding carefully with her brother shows responsibility, not carelessness.

options.label: D
options.text: furious
options.rationale: Her calm words show the opposite of fury.

items.stem: Read: “Yasmin refused to sign her name to the group project until every teammate’s contribution was listed accurately, even the smallest tasks.” Which word best describes Yasmin?

explanation.whyCorrect: Making sure every teammate gets accurate credit, even for small tasks, shows Yasmin values fairness.
explanation.tip: Look for a character’s insistence on fairness or accuracy toward others.

options.label: A
options.text: selfish
options.rationale: Insisting on crediting everyone equally is the opposite of selfish.

options.label: B
options.text: careless
options.rationale: Checking accuracy carefully is the opposite of careless.

options.label: C
options.text: fair

options.label: D
options.text: lazy
options.rationale: Checking every detail requires effort, not laziness.

items.stem: Read: “Mr. Aziz polished the same old doorknob he had installed decades earlier, smiling faintly, before telling Sara, ‘There is not much to tell.’” True or false: this detail suggests Mr. Aziz feels no pride in his long career.

explanation.whyCorrect: Smiling while polishing his old work suggests quiet pride, even though he downplays it in words.
explanation.tip: A character’s actions can reveal feelings that their words try to hide.

items.stem: How does the phrase “its red taillights shrinking down the hill” affect the tone of the opening of “The Last Bus Home”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Watching the lights shrink away pictures the bus as already out of reach, matching Yusuf's disappointment.
explanation.tip: Picture the image a word choice creates, then ask what feeling that image gives.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a comic tone meant to make the moment funny.
options.rationale: Nothing about missing the last bus is played for laughs.

options.label: B
options.text: It creates a frightening tone, warning of danger ahead.
options.rationale: The moment is disappointing, not dangerous.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates an exciting tone, as if Yusuf is about to catch up.
options.rationale: The bus is shrinking away, not getting closer.

options.label: D
options.text: It creates a quiet, disappointed tone by picturing the bus getting farther and farther out of reach.

items.stem: True or false: the author's tone toward the claim that students would rather stay home anyway, in “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?”, is accepting and respectful.

explanation.whyCorrect: The author calls it something “everyone knows” with no evidence, which is a dismissive, skeptical way to treat a claim, not a respectful one.
explanation.tip: Test a description of tone against the author's actual word choices, not just the topic.

items.stem: How does describing bleached coral as “starving” rather than simply “pale” affect the tone of paragraph 3 in “Coral Reefs Under Pressure”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Starving” frames bleaching as a survival crisis, which raises the emotional urgency of the paragraph.
explanation.tip: Compare a word choice to a plainer synonym to see what extra feeling it adds.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a more urgent, concerned tone by stressing that the coral is in real danger, not just changing color.

options.label: B
options.text: It creates a flat, purely clinical tone with no feeling at all.
options.rationale: A word like starving adds emotional weight that a clinical term would not.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates a hopeful tone, suggesting coral will recover quickly.
options.rationale: Starving emphasizes risk, not quick recovery.

options.label: D
options.text: It creates a playful tone, comparing coral to a picky eater.
options.rationale: Starving signals real danger, not a joke about appetite.

items.stem: How does Mr. Aziz's clipped dialogue in Scene 1 of “The Interview,” such as “I fix things. I clean things,” shape the tone of the opening?

explanation.whyCorrect: Short, simple sentences from a character often reflect a plain, modest attitude rather than drama or mystery.
explanation.tip: A character's sentence length and word choice can reveal their attitude before any action happens.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a comic tone meant to make the audience laugh at him.
options.rationale: His short answers are sincere, not played for laughs.

options.label: B
options.text: It creates a plain, modest tone that fits a man who does not think his own story is worth telling.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates a mysterious tone meant to confuse the audience.
options.rationale: His answers are plain and clear, just very short.

options.label: D
options.text: It creates an angry tone, showing he resents Sara's questions.
options.rationale: He is brief and shy, not hostile.

items.stem: How does listing specific details like “carved wooden doors,” “copper workshops,” and “spice sellers” affect the tone of paragraph 3 in the souq letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming specific, beloved details shows affection and pride rather than a plain inventory.
explanation.tip: Specific, well-chosen details often carry more feeling than a general statement would.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a flat, list-like tone with no feeling behind it.
options.rationale: Naming cherished, specific features adds warmth, not a neutral list.

options.label: B
options.text: It creates a sarcastic tone that mocks how old the souq is.
options.rationale: The details are offered with pride, not mockery.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates an admiring, affectionate tone by naming specific, cherished features that make the souq irreplaceable.

options.label: D
options.text: It creates a tone of complaint about buildings falling apart.
options.rationale: The details celebrate the souq's features, not its disrepair.

items.stem: Read: “The coach decided to bench the injured player for the rest of the match.” What does bench mean in this sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Benching a player means removing them from play, often because of injury.
explanation.tip: Multiple-meaning words can shift from naming an object (a bench) to naming an action (to bench someone).

options.label: A
options.text: to build a long seat for players
options.rationale: The sentence is about a decision affecting the player, not building furniture.

options.label: B
options.text: to sit calmly and watch quietly
options.rationale: Bench here is an action the coach takes, not a calm feeling.

options.label: C
options.text: to repair damaged sports equipment
options.rationale: Nothing in the sentence is being repaired.

options.label: D
options.text: to keep a player out of the game

items.stem: Read: “After the heavy rain, a fresh spring bubbled up at the base of the hill.” What does spring mean here?

explanation.whyCorrect: The surrounding words “bubbled up” and “base of the hill” describe water emerging from the ground.
explanation.tip: Look closely at the words right around a multiple-meaning word to find which definition fits.

options.label: A
options.text: a natural source of water flowing up from the ground

options.label: B
options.text: to jump upward suddenly
options.rationale: The sentence describes water, not a jumping motion.

options.label: C
options.text: a coiled piece of metal that stretches
options.rationale: Nothing mechanical is described here.

options.label: D
options.text: the season between winter and summer
options.rationale: No season is being described in this sentence.

items.stem: Read: “The boxer's trainer told him to guard his right side.” What does right mean in this sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: In a sentence about guarding a side of the body during boxing, right names a direction.
explanation.tip: Think about the overall topic of a sentence to narrow down which meaning of a word fits.

options.label: A
options.text: a legal entitlement, such as a right to vote
options.rationale: No laws or entitlements are mentioned here.

options.label: B
options.text: a direction, as opposed to left

options.label: C
options.text: correct or accurate
options.rationale: The sentence is about a body position, not accuracy.

options.label: D
options.text: immediately, as in “right now”
options.rationale: The sentence is not describing timing.

items.stem: Read: “The elephant's trunk was strong enough to lift the fallen branch.” What does trunk mean here?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence describes an elephant lifting something, which points to its long, flexible nose.
explanation.tip: Multiple-meaning words can mean very different things depending on the subject of the sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: the rear storage area of a car
options.rationale: No car appears in this sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: the thick main stem of a tree
options.rationale: The sentence is about an elephant, not a tree.

options.label: C
options.text: an elephant's long, flexible nose

options.label: D
options.text: a large box used for storage
options.rationale: Nothing about storage is described.

items.stem: Read: “Because he parked illegally, Omar had to pay a fine.” What does fine mean here?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paying something after parking illegally points directly to a monetary penalty.
explanation.tip: Look for words like “pay” or “penalty” nearby to identify this meaning of fine.

options.label: A
options.text: in good health or condition, as in “I feel fine”
options.rationale: The sentence describes a penalty for parking, not a feeling.

options.label: B
options.text: very thin or delicate, like fine sand
options.rationale: No texture or thinness is described.

options.label: C
options.text: to carefully adjust something, as in “fine-tune”
options.rationale: No adjustment of an object is described.

options.label: D
options.text: a sum of money paid as a penalty

items.stem: Choose the meaning that fits: in “Hassan will table the proposal until the next meeting,” table means ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: As a verb in a meeting context, table means to put something off until later.
explanation.tip: Check whether a multiple-meaning word is being used as a noun or a verb — that often changes its meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: to postpone discussing something

options.label: B
options.text: a piece of furniture with a flat top
options.rationale: Here table is a verb describing an action, not naming furniture.

options.label: C
options.text: to place food in front of guests
options.rationale: The sentence is about delaying a proposal, not serving food.

options.label: D
options.text: a chart that organizes numbers
options.rationale: No chart or data is being organized in this sentence.

items.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of the underlined multiple-meaning word as it is used in that sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: Context in each sentence shows which meaning of “table” and “bank” the author intends.
explanation.tip: Mentally replace the underlined word with its definition to check that the sentence still makes sense.

pairs.left: The committee will table the new policy until next month.
We set extra chairs around the table for our guests.
pairs.right: a piece of furniture with a flat top

pairs.left: The pilot had to bank sharply to avoid the storm clouds.
pairs.right: to tilt or turn to one side

pairs.left: Hassan opened a savings account at the local bank.
pairs.right: a business that holds and manages money

items.stem: Read these two sentences: “The students will note the date of the field trip on the calendar” and “Tariq left a short note on the fridge for his brother.” Which TWO meanings below correctly match note as used in the FIRST and SECOND sentence, in that order?

explanation.whyCorrect: In the first sentence note is a verb meaning to record; in the second it is a noun meaning a short written message.
explanation.tip: Check each sentence separately — a multiple-meaning word's part of speech often signals which meaning fits.

options.label: A
options.text: a single musical sound
options.rationale: This meaning does not fit either sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: to become famous or well known
options.rationale: This meaning does not fit either sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: a brief written message

options.label: D
options.text: to write something down so it is remembered

items.stem: Where does most of the action in “The Last Bus Home” take place?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story follows Yusuf's forty-minute walk, passing specific places like the bakery, after missing the bus.
explanation.tip: Track every place a character physically moves through to map out a story's setting.

options.label: A
options.text: along Yusuf's walk home, ending at Mrs. Qadri's bakery

options.label: B
options.text: at the robotics club meeting
options.rationale: The club is only mentioned; the meeting itself is never shown.

options.label: C
options.text: entirely inside Yusuf's house
options.rationale: Most of the story follows Yusuf's walk, not a scene at home.

options.label: D
options.text: on the bus itself
options.rationale: Yusuf misses the bus and never actually rides it in the story.

items.stem: How does the detail that the bakery's “lights were still on” late at night affect the mood of that scene in “The Last Bus Home”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A lit, open bakery appearing after a dark, worried walk feels safe and welcoming, setting up the warm ending.
explanation.tip: A setting detail, like light appearing in the dark, can build mood before the plot explains why it matters.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a frightening feeling of being watched.
options.rationale: The bakery is friendly and familiar, not threatening.

options.label: B
options.text: It creates a warm, welcoming feeling right after Yusuf's worried walk through the dark.

options.label: C
options.text: It suggests the bakery has been abandoned for the night.
options.rationale: Lights being on shows the bakery is open and active.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that Yusuf is in physical danger.
options.rationale: Nothing in this detail suggests danger.

items.stem: What is the setting of “The Interview”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narrator states both the time and the place at the very start of the play.
explanation.tip: In drama, the opening narration or stage directions usually establish the setting.

options.label: A
options.text: a busy newspaper office downtown
options.rationale: The narrator specifies a school storage room, not an office.

options.label: B
options.text: an empty school gym
options.rationale: The flooded gym is only mentioned in Mr. Aziz's story, not shown as the setting.

options.label: C
options.text: a quiet storage room at the school during the last week of the school year

options.label: D
options.text: Sara's home kitchen
options.rationale: No scene takes place at Sara's home.

items.stem: How are the settings of “The New Field” and “Transplant” similar?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yasmin moves from the coast to the mountains, and the lemon tree is lifted from its courtyard — both settings begin with displacement.
explanation.tip: Paired texts in different genres can still share a similar kind of setting or situation.

options.label: A
options.text: Both take place entirely at the seaside.
options.rationale: Yasmin moves away from the coast, and the tree leaves its courtyard.

options.label: B
options.text: Both take place within a single afternoon.
options.rationale: Both unfold over several weeks, not one afternoon.

options.label: C
options.text: Both are set inside a classroom.
options.rationale: Neither text is set in a classroom.

options.label: D
options.text: Both describe something being moved from a familiar place to a new, unfamiliar one.

items.stem: True or false: the poem “Desert Night” is set during the daytime.

explanation.whyCorrect: Details like the sun slipping under the dunes and the sky described as black and scattered with stars show a nighttime setting.
explanation.tip: Time-of-day clues, such as a setting sun or visible stars, reveal when a scene is taking place.

items.stem: Over what span of time is the setting of “The Old Olive Tree” described?

explanation.whyCorrect: References to “seasons of drought,” “wars that passed,” and “decades of patient toil” show a setting that spans a long time.
explanation.tip: A poem's setting can stretch across years or generations, not just a single scene.

options.label: A
options.text: many decades, spanning the grandfather's and the speaker's lifetimes

options.label: B
options.text: one autumn season only
options.rationale: Autumn is mentioned, but the setting's timespan reaches back much further.

options.label: C
options.text: the speaker's one birthday
options.rationale: No birthday or single-day event is mentioned in the poem.

options.label: D
options.text: a single afternoon
options.rationale: The poem describes seasons of drought and wars passing, far more than one afternoon.

items.stem: Where does the speaker stand while reflecting in the final stanza of “Ladder”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “I climb it now to reach the apples” places the speaker in a present-day setting built from a past memory.
explanation.tip: Look for present-tense verbs to find the “current” setting of a poem that also describes past memories.

options.label: A
options.text: watching a storm through a window
options.rationale: The storm already happened years before the poem's present moment.

options.label: B
options.text: climbing the ladder, reaching for apples in the present

options.label: C
options.text: sitting beside the storm-felled tree
options.rationale: The fallen tree became the ladder; the speaker now climbs it, in the present.

options.label: D
options.text: inside the grandfather's house
options.rationale: No indoor scene is described anywhere in the poem.

items.stem: Which pair shows a WHOLE-to-PART relationship — the reverse order of part-to-whole?

explanation.whyCorrect: A tree is the whole object, and a branch is one part of it — the whole is named first here.
explanation.tip: Decide which word names the whole object and which names a smaller piece of it, then check the order.

options.label: A
options.text: hour : minute
options.rationale: This is a relationship between units of time, not a whole object and its part.

options.label: B
options.text: fish : school
options.rationale: This is item-to-category: a fish is one member of the group called a school.

options.label: C
options.text: tree : branch

options.label: D
options.text: cold : hot
options.rationale: This is a pair of antonyms, not a whole and its part.

items.stem: Which pair shows a CAUSE-and-EFFECT relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: Practicing a skill is what causes improvement to happen over time.
explanation.tip: Test a pair by making the sentence “X causes Y” — if it makes sense, the pair shows cause and effect.

options.label: A
options.text: book : chapter
options.rationale: This is a part-to-whole relationship, not cause and effect.

options.label: B
options.text: hungry : food
options.rationale: Being hungry does not cause food to exist; it is simply a feeling about needing food.

options.label: C
options.text: teacher : student
options.rationale: This describes two roles in a classroom, not a cause and its effect.

options.label: D
options.text: practice : improvement

items.stem: Choose the word that completes the ITEM-to-CATEGORY analogy: trumpet : instrument :: oak : ____

explanation.whyCorrect: An oak is one specific example within the broader category “tree,” just as a trumpet is one example within “instrument.”
explanation.tip: Ask: is the first word ONE SPECIFIC EXAMPLE of the second, more general word?

options.label: A
options.text: leaf
options.rationale: A leaf would be a PART of an oak, which is a different relationship than item-to-category.

options.label: B
options.text: tree

options.label: C
options.text: forest
options.rationale: A forest is a group of many trees, not the general category that oak belongs to.

options.label: D
options.text: wood
options.rationale: Wood names a material, not the broader category an oak belongs to.

items.stem: Match each word pair with the relationship it shows.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each pair follows a different logical relationship between the two words.
explanation.tip: Say the relationship aloud as a full sentence, such as “A slice is PART OF a pizza,” to test it.

pairs.right: tool to the object it operates

items.stem: True or false: in the pair “spark : wildfire,” spark is the EFFECT and wildfire is the CAUSE.

explanation.whyCorrect: A spark is what starts, or causes, a wildfire; the wildfire itself is the effect, not the cause.
explanation.tip: Identify which event happens first in time — that event is usually the cause.

items.stem: Which TWO pairs below show a PART-to-WHOLE relationship? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: A chapter is one part of a whole novel, and an ingredient is one part of a whole recipe.
explanation.tip: Check whether the first word names a small piece contained within the second, larger thing.

options.label: A
options.text: ingredient : recipe

options.label: B
options.text: chapter : novel

options.label: C
options.text: hot : cold
options.rationale: This is a pair of antonyms, not part-to-whole.

options.label: D
options.text: author : reader
options.rationale: These name two different roles, not a part contained within a whole.

items.stem: Complete the analogy by writing one word: finger : hand :: toe : ____

explanation.whyCorrect: A finger is part of a hand, just as a toe is part of a foot — the same part-to-whole relationship on both sides.
explanation.tip: Keep the exact same relationship between the words on both sides of an analogy.

items.stem: Is the reasoning behind “schools should be cautious” adequately supported by the evidence that follows it in “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article backs its cautious claim with a study on scores, cost data, and a concrete family concern, which together make the reasoning well supported.
explanation.tip: To evaluate an argument, check whether specific evidence — not just a repeated claim — actually backs it up.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the article follows with a specific study on math scores, cost data, and a concern about childcare.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the author never gives any evidence to support caution.
options.rationale: The article provides a study, cost data, and a specific family concern.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but only because the author repeats the claim three times.
options.rationale: Repetition alone does not support a claim; specific evidence does.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because the article only offers one opinion with no facts.
options.rationale: Multiple kinds of evidence are given, not a single unsupported opinion.

items.stem: True or false: the four-day week article provides sufficient evidence to evaluate its claim about cost savings, because it cites a specific percentage from named reports.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article states that savings are “often less than two percent of the budget,” citing reports as its source, which counts as specific, checkable evidence.
explanation.tip: A specific number tied to a named source usually counts as sufficient evidence, unlike a vague, unsupported claim.

items.stem: A classmate claims the four-day week article is NOT persuasive because it never considers the supporters' point of view. Is this a fair evaluation of the argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article consistently states a supporting claim first, then responds to it with evidence — a structure that does consider the other side fairly.
explanation.tip: To evaluate a claim about an argument's fairness, check whether it actually addresses opposing views point by point.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the article only discusses cost, never learning.
options.rationale: Learning is actually the first and most developed point in the article.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the article states each of the supporters' claims before responding to it with evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: No, but only because the article ultimately agrees with the supporters.
options.rationale: The article disagrees with the supporters in its conclusion.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because the article completely ignores why anyone would want a four-day week.
options.rationale: The article opens each point by stating the supporters' claim first.

items.stem: Which type of support does Huda rely on MOST to persuade the council in her souq letter, based on the letter as a whole?

explanation.whyCorrect: Huda's strongest support comes from personal history and emotional appeal, since the letter contains no statistics, experts, or formal analysis.
explanation.tip: Evaluate what KIND of evidence — personal, statistical, or expert — an argument actually relies on.

options.label: A
options.text: statistical data about tourist numbers
options.rationale: No statistics or survey numbers are given anywhere in the letter.

options.label: B
options.text: expert testimony from historians
options.rationale: No outside experts are quoted or cited in the letter.

options.label: C
options.text: personal and emotional appeals, such as her family's connection to the souq

options.label: D
options.text: a formal economic comparison of both options
options.rationale: No cost or economic analysis appears in the letter.

items.stem: Is Huda's suggestion to “repair its roof, improve its lighting and add signs in several languages” a strong part of her argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: A persuasive argument is stronger when it offers a workable alternative rather than only a complaint, which is exactly what this paragraph does.
explanation.tip: Strong arguments often propose a specific solution, not just an objection to the opposing plan.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, but only because it is the longest paragraph in the letter.
options.rationale: Its practicality, not its length, is what makes the suggestion effective.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because she never explains what the council should do instead.
options.rationale: She lists three specific actions the council could take.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because repairs would clearly cost more than a new shopping center.
options.rationale: Costs are never compared anywhere in the letter.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because it offers the council a realistic alternative instead of only criticizing their plan.

items.stem: Which TWO qualities make Huda's souq-letter argument more convincing to a fair-minded reader? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Directly addressing the opposing reasoning and offering a workable solution are two hallmarks of a convincing, fair argument.
explanation.tip: Evaluate an argument's persuasiveness by looking for direct responses to the other side and practical solutions, not strong feelings alone.

options.label: A
options.text: She proposes a specific, practical alternative instead of only objecting.

options.label: B
options.text: She directly answers the council's own reasoning about attracting visitors.

options.label: C
options.text: She insults the council members personally.
options.rationale: She never insults anyone anywhere in the letter.

options.label: D
options.text: She repeats the same sentence many times for emphasis.
options.rationale: She does not rely on repeating a sentence for emphasis.

items.stem: Does the author of “Should Homework Be Optional?” adequately address the concern that optional homework could let struggling students fall behind?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author directly answers the concern with a new, specific reason — more precise, individualized teacher attention — rather than ignoring it or simply repeating the claim.
explanation.tip: A strong rebuttal offers a NEW reason to support its position, not just a restatement of the original claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the author offers a specific counter-reason: teachers could give struggling students more targeted attention.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the author admits optional homework would hurt struggling students.
options.rationale: The author argues the opposite — that support could actually improve.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because the author never mentions this concern at all.
options.rationale: Paragraph 4 directly raises and responds to exactly this concern.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, but only by repeating the original claim more forcefully.
options.rationale: The author gives a genuinely new reason, not just a louder repetition.

items.stem: Which organizational structure does the author use across paragraphs 2 and 3 of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paragraph 2 sets up the normal partnership, and paragraph 3 shows the effect of a cause — warm water — breaking that partnership down.
explanation.tip: Look for signal words like “when” or “because” that connect a cause to its effect.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — the two paragraphs compare two different reef locations
options.rationale: No two separate reef locations are compared anywhere in the text.

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect — paragraph 2 explains the coral-algae partnership, and paragraph 3 explains what happens when warm water breaks it down

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order — the paragraphs describe events on a historical timeline
options.rationale: No dates or historical timeline structure appear in these paragraphs.

options.label: D
options.text: problem and solution — paragraph 3 proposes a fix for a problem raised in paragraph 2
options.rationale: Paragraph 3 describes a problem; the proposed fix does not appear until paragraph 4.

items.stem: What is the OVERALL organizational structure of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text moves from the value of reefs, to the threat of bleaching, to the scientific response — a clear problem-and-solution pattern.
explanation.tip: Ask whether a whole informational text introduces a problem and then describes a response to find its overall structure.

options.label: A
options.text: a comparison between two very different kinds of coral reefs
options.rationale: Only one general kind of reef is discussed throughout the text.

options.label: B
options.text: a simple list of unrelated reef facts
options.rationale: The paragraphs build logically from importance, to threat, to response, rather than listing unrelated facts.

options.label: C
options.text: a problem-and-solution structure — it explains why reefs matter, the threat they face, and how scientists are responding

options.label: D
options.text: a step-by-step set of instructions for building a reef
options.rationale: The text explains and informs rather than giving instructions to follow.

items.stem: Put these paragraph functions from “Coral Reefs Under Pressure” in the order they appear in the text.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text builds logically: importance, how it normally works, what goes wrong, and how people are responding.
explanation.tip: Identify what JOB each paragraph does, then put those jobs in the order they appear.

sequence: Describe why reefs matter to ocean life
Explain how the coral-algae partnership normally works
Explain how warm water breaks down that partnership (bleaching)
Describe how scientists are responding to help reefs

items.stem: True or false: the final paragraph of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure” is organized as a physical description of what coral looks like.

explanation.whyCorrect: The final paragraph describes scientists' efforts and responses to bleaching, not a description of coral's appearance.
explanation.tip: Check what a paragraph is actually DOING — describing, explaining, or arguing — rather than assuming from its topic.

items.stem: How does the author organize the body paragraphs of “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each body paragraph follows a claim-and-response pattern: it states what supporters believe, then evaluates that claim with evidence.
explanation.tip: In argumentative texts, look for a repeating pattern across paragraphs, such as claim followed by a response.

options.label: A
options.text: The paragraphs are organized in simple time order, from Monday to Friday.
options.rationale: There is no day-by-day account of a school week.

options.label: B
options.text: Each paragraph compares two different countries' school systems.
options.rationale: No countries are compared in this article.

options.label: C
options.text: Each paragraph describes a different school's daily schedule.
options.rationale: No specific school schedules are described anywhere in the article.

options.label: D
options.text: Each body paragraph states one of the supporters' claims, then responds to it with evidence or reasoning.

items.stem: Match each paragraph's main structural job in “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?” with its paragraph number.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each numbered paragraph plays a specific structural role in building the overall argument.
explanation.tip: Identify the JOB each paragraph does within the text's overall structure.

pairs.right: introduces the issue and states the author's cautious claim
responds to the rest-and-achievement claim with learning evidence
responds to the money-saving claim with cost data
restates the claim to close the argument

items.stem: What organizational structure does Huda use across her souq letter as a whole?

explanation.whyCorrect: Huda explains the problem, argues the souq's importance, answers a counterargument, and proposes a specific solution — a problem-and-solution structure.
explanation.tip: In a persuasive letter, look for a shift from describing a problem to proposing a specific action.

options.label: A
options.text: problem-and-solution — she explains why the council's plan is a problem, then proposes a specific solution

options.label: B
options.text: a side-by-side comparison of two different cities' souqs
options.rationale: No second city's souq is described anywhere in the letter.

options.label: C
options.text: a plain physical description of the souq's architecture only
options.rationale: Architecture is only one supporting detail among several, not the letter's overall structure.

options.label: D
options.text: a strict chronological retelling of her grandfather's entire life
options.rationale: Her grandfather's story is one supporting detail, not the structure of the whole letter.

items.stem: True or false: Huda's souq letter uses a cause-and-effect structure, where each paragraph explains a different physical cause of damage to the building.

explanation.whyCorrect: The letter is organized as problem-and-solution, built around persuasion, rather than a chain of physical causes and effects on the building itself.
explanation.tip: Do not assume a structure type just from a text's topic — check how the paragraphs actually connect to one another.

items.stem: Which sentence best states the theme of “The Potter Who Outwitted the Governor”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tarek has no soldiers or riches, but a few clever words protect his workshop and his jar.
explanation.tip: A theme is the lesson a story teaches about life, not a fact from the setting.

options.label: A
options.text: Rivers are useful for making pottery.
options.rationale: The river is only part of the setting.

options.label: B
options.text: Cleverness can solve problems that strength or money cannot.

options.label: C
options.text: Governors always get what they want.
options.rationale: The ending shows the opposite is true.

options.label: D
options.text: Clay jars are more valuable than gold.
options.rationale: The story is not really about the value of jars.

items.stem: How does Tarek react when the guard threatens to take his workshop?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tarek “did not argue” and simply carried the jar to the palace himself—a calm, confident reaction.
explanation.tip: Look at what a character does right after a problem begins.

options.label: A
options.text: angrily, shouting at the guard
options.rationale: The text never shows him shouting.

options.label: B
options.text: sadly, by giving up pottery forever
options.rationale: He keeps his jar and his workshop in the end.

options.label: C
options.text: calmly, without arguing

options.label: D
options.text: fearfully, by running away
options.rationale: He walks straight to the palace instead of fleeing.

items.stem: What is the central conflict at the beginning of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The guard's threat creates the problem Tarek must solve using only his wits.
explanation.tip: The central conflict is the main problem a character faces and must resolve.

options.label: A
options.text: The river floods and destroys the workshop.
options.rationale: There is no flood in the story.

options.label: B
options.text: The jar cracks before Tarek can finish it.
options.rationale: The jar never actually cracks in the story.

options.label: C
options.text: Tarek wants to sell jars in a different village.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests Tarek wants to move.

options.label: D
options.text: The governor wants Tarek's best jar for free, and Tarek must find a way to keep it.

items.stem: Which clue tells you that this folktale is told in third person?

explanation.whyCorrect: Third-person narration uses he/she/names instead of I/me, which is exactly how this tale refers to both characters.
explanation.tip: Scan for pronouns like “he,” “she,” or “I” to identify a story's point of view.

options.label: A
options.text: The narrator refers to Tarek and the governor as “he,” never as “I.”

options.label: B
options.text: The governor explains his own plans using the word “I.”
options.rationale: The governor is also called “he,” not “I,” throughout.

options.label: C
options.text: Tarek describes his own feelings using the word “I.”
options.rationale: Tarek is always called “he” or by name, not “I.”

options.label: D
options.text: The narrator speaks directly to the reader as “you.”
options.rationale: This tale never addresses the reader this way.

items.stem: Why does the governor change his mind so quickly after hearing about the jar's “secret”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The text says he “loved his gold even more,” so the thought of filling the jar with gold scares him off.
explanation.tip: An inference combines a text clue with what you already know about the character.

options.label: A
options.text: He does not believe jars can be beautiful.
options.rationale: He clearly wanted the jar until he heard the warning.

options.label: B
options.text: He cares more about keeping his gold than about owning a beautiful jar.

options.label: C
options.text: He suddenly feels sorry for Tarek.
options.rationale: Nothing in the story suggests sympathy.

options.label: D
options.text: He plans to buy a different jar instead.
options.rationale: The story never mentions another jar.

items.stem: Which TWO details from the story are clues that Tarek is clever? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Tarek's invented warning is a clever trick, and his polite, bowing manner keeps him safe without conflict.
explanation.tip: Text evidence must directly support the specific idea being asked about.

options.label: A
options.text: He speaks politely while still protecting what is his.

options.label: B
options.text: He owns nothing else of much value.
options.rationale: This describes his wealth, not his cleverness.

options.label: C
options.text: He makes the finest clay jars in the land.
options.rationale: This shows skill as a potter, not cleverness in this situation.

options.label: D
options.text: He invents a warning about the jar instead of refusing the guard.

items.stem: Put the events of “The Potter Who Outwitted the Governor” in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The story moves from the threat, to Tarek's response, to his clever trick, to the result.
explanation.tip: Look for the order in which each character acts and speaks.

sequence: The governor sends a guard to demand Tarek's best jar.
Tarek wraps the jar and carries it to the palace himself.
Tarek warns the governor that the jar is cursed unless filled with gold.
The governor tells Tarek to keep the jar.

items.stem: True or false: The story suggests that greed can sometimes work against the greedy person.

explanation.whyCorrect: The governor's own love of gold is exactly what makes him refuse the jar, so his greed backfires.
explanation.tip: Ask whether a character's flaw ends up helping or hurting them by the end.

items.stem: In the last paragraph, what does outwitted mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence says Tarek outwitted the governor “with nothing but a few clever words,” which points to cleverness, not force.
explanation.tip: Look at HOW a character wins to figure out what a word like outwitted means.

options.label: A
options.text: beat someone by being faster
options.rationale: Speed is never mentioned in the story.

options.label: B
options.text: beat someone by being louder
options.rationale: Tarek speaks calmly and politely, not loudly.

options.label: C
options.text: beat someone by being smarter, not stronger

options.label: D
options.text: beat someone by being richer
options.rationale: Tarek has little money; his gold warning is a trick, not real wealth.

items.stem: In this story, the word crack means “to break apart.” Which sentence uses crack with a DIFFERENT meaning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Here crack describes a type of joke, not something breaking—a different meaning of the same word.
explanation.tip: Multiple-meaning words need the rest of the sentence to tell you which meaning fits.

options.label: A
options.text: Ice can crack if you stand on it too long.
options.rationale: This also means to break apart.

options.label: B
options.text: The jar will crack if it is not filled with gold.
options.rationale: This uses crack the same way the story does—to break.

options.label: C
options.text: The old plate had a crack down the middle.
options.rationale: This crack is a break in an object, the same meaning as in the story.

options.label: D
options.text: My brother always tells a crack joke at dinner.

items.stem: Based on how Tarek solves his first problem, what would he most likely do if the governor's guard returned next year?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tarek's calm, clever approach the first time is a strong clue to how he would act again.
explanation.tip: Predict future actions using a character's pattern of behavior earlier in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: Think of another clever, calm way to protect what is his

options.label: B
options.text: Move away from the village immediately
options.rationale: There is no hint that he plans to leave.

options.label: C
options.text: Yell at the guard and refuse to speak with him
options.rationale: He stayed calm and polite the first time.

options.label: D
options.text: Give up and hand over all of his jars
options.rationale: Nothing in his character suggests he would give up easily.

items.stem: How might the governor's opinion of Tarek differ from how the villagers see him?

explanation.whyCorrect: The governor avoids Tarek afterward, a sign of caution, while villagers celebrate his cleverness as a story worth retelling.
explanation.tip: Different characters can view the same event in very different ways.

options.label: A
options.text: The governor wants to reward Tarek, while the villagers are jealous.
options.rationale: The governor never offers a reward.

options.label: B
options.text: The governor may see Tarek as someone to be wary of, while the villagers see him as a hero.

options.label: C
options.text: The governor and the villagers both think Tarek is dishonest.
options.rationale: The villagers clearly admire him, retelling the story proudly.

options.label: D
options.text: Both the governor and villagers forget about Tarek quickly.
options.rationale: The story says villagers still come from far away to hear the tale.

items.stem: What is the central idea of “Camels: Built for the Desert”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every section—heat, water, and feet—explains a different way camels are built for desert survival.
explanation.tip: The central idea is supported by every section of an informational text, not just one.

options.label: A
options.text: Camels are called ships because they float on sand.
options.rationale: “Ships of the desert” is a nickname, not a literal fact.

options.label: B
options.text: Camels need to drink water every single day.
options.rationale: The text says camels can go up to two weeks without drinking.

options.label: C
options.text: Camels have special body features that help them survive and travel in the desert.

options.label: D
options.text: Camel feet are the most important desert animal feature.
options.rationale: Feet are one detail among several described in the text.

items.stem: Under which heading would you learn why a camel's hump is useful?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first section explains that the hump stores fat, which is used for energy and water.
explanation.tip: Headings preview what information appears in the section below them.

options.label: A
options.text: Wide, Soft Feet
options.rationale: That section explains how camels walk on sand.

options.label: B
options.text: Saving Every Drop
options.rationale: That section focuses on water and kidneys.

options.label: C
options.text: Camels: Built for the Desert
options.rationale: That is the title of the whole article.

options.label: D
options.text: A Body Made for Heat

items.stem: A reader is confused about the phrase “built-in snowshoes for sand.” Which heading should they reread to understand it?

explanation.whyCorrect: The snowshoe comparison appears in the section about feet, since both describe spreading weight out over sand.
explanation.tip: When a phrase is confusing, find the heading whose topic matches it, then reread that section.

options.label: A
options.text: Wide, Soft Feet

options.label: B
options.text: Saving Every Drop
options.rationale: That heading focuses on drinking and kidneys, not walking on sand.

options.label: C
options.text: Camels: Built for the Desert
options.rationale: This is only the article's title, not a specific section to reread.

options.label: D
options.text: A Body Made for Heat
options.rationale: That heading is about the hump and eyelashes, with no mention of snowshoes.

items.stem: According to the article, what is an EFFECT of a camel's hump storing fat?

explanation.whyCorrect: “It stores fat, which the camel's body slowly turns into energy and water” describes the effect of storing fat.
explanation.tip: Find the sentence right after the cause to locate its effect.

options.label: A
options.text: The camel needs to eat more often.
options.rationale: Storing fat actually helps the camel go longer without eating.

options.label: B
options.text: The fat can turn into energy and water when food is scarce.

options.label: C
options.text: The camel grows a second hump.
options.rationale: The article never mentions a second hump.

options.label: D
options.text: The hump fills completely with water.
options.rationale: The article corrects this common myth directly.

items.stem: Why does a camel sweat less than most animals during a hot day?

explanation.whyCorrect: “A camel's body temperature can rise several degrees during the day, which means it sweats less and saves water.”
explanation.tip: Signal words like “which means” connect a cause to its effect.

options.label: A
options.text: It drinks constantly throughout the day.
options.rationale: The article says camels can go up to two weeks without drinking.

options.label: B
options.text: Its thick eyelashes block sweat from forming.
options.rationale: Eyelashes protect the eyes from sand, not from sweating.

options.label: C
options.text: Its body temperature is allowed to rise several degrees instead of staying constant.

options.label: D
options.text: It stores extra water in its feet.
options.rationale: Feet are described for walking, not water storage.

items.stem: How is a camel's body temperature different from that of most animals, according to the article?

explanation.whyCorrect: The word “unlike” signals that the article is contrasting camels with most other animals.
explanation.tip: Words such as unlike and most often introduce a comparison.

options.label: A
options.text: A camel's temperature only changes at night.
options.rationale: The article specifies the rise happens during the day.

options.label: B
options.text: A camel's temperature never changes at all.
options.rationale: The article says it can rise several degrees.

options.label: C
options.text: Most animals' temperatures rise more than a camel's.
options.rationale: The article highlights the camel as unusual, not typical.

options.label: D
options.text: A camel's temperature can rise during the day, while most animals keep a steady temperature.

items.stem: In the article, what does scarce mean in “turns into energy and water when food is scarce”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The camel needs stored fat exactly when food is NOT easy to find, so scarce must mean hard to find.
explanation.tip: Think about why the camel would need a backup energy source.

options.label: A
options.text: hard to find; in short supply

options.label: B
options.text: spoiled or rotten
options.rationale: Nothing in the sentence is about spoiled food.

options.label: C
options.text: very tasty
options.rationale: Taste is not discussed in this sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: plentiful and easy to find
options.rationale: This is the opposite of how scarce is used here.

items.stem: What does efficient mean in “Their kidneys and intestines are so efficient that very little water is lost”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Because the kidneys lose “very little water,” efficient must mean they work well without waste.
explanation.tip: Use the result described in the sentence to figure out the word's meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: working only sometimes
options.rationale: The sentence suggests reliable, constant performance.

options.label: B
options.text: working very well without wasting anything

options.label: C
options.text: working very slowly
options.rationale: Slow would not explain why so little water is lost.

options.label: D
options.text: working loudly
options.rationale: Sound is never mentioned.

items.stem: Which TWO details show that a camel's body is good at saving water? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both chosen details directly describe how little water the camel's body loses or needs.
explanation.tip: Text evidence should match the exact idea the question asks about.

options.label: A
options.text: It can carry heavy loads across sand.
options.rationale: This is about strength and carrying, not water.

options.label: B
options.text: Its kidneys and intestines lose very little water.

options.label: C
options.text: It can go without drinking again for up to two weeks.

options.label: D
options.text: Its feet spread out wide when it steps.
options.rationale: This detail is about walking on sand, not water.

items.stem: True or false: According to the article, a camel's hump is mainly filled with water.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article directly corrects this idea: the hump stores fat, not water.
explanation.tip: Watch for sentences that correct a common myth; they often signal an important fact.

items.stem: Why did the author probably organize this article with three separate headings?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each heading introduces a different desert-survival feature, helping readers locate facts quickly.
explanation.tip: Authors use headings to organize information into clear, related groups.

options.label: A
options.text: to list the article in alphabetical order
options.rationale: The headings are grouped by topic, not alphabetically.

options.label: B
options.text: to make the article look longer than it is
options.rationale: Headings organize ideas; they do not just add length.

options.label: C
options.text: to group related facts about the camel's body so readers can find information easily

options.label: D
options.text: to show that camels have three legs
options.rationale: Camels have four legs; the headings are about body features.

items.stem: Which sentence best expresses the theme of “The Apprentice Scribe”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The father's final words directly state that fixing a mistake well is more valuable than avoiding risk entirely.
explanation.tip: Look for a character's closing statement—it often reveals the theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Scribes must count every number twice before writing.
options.rationale: This is a practical tip, not the theme.

options.label: B
options.text: Fathers should always check their children's work.
options.rationale: This describes an action, not the story's deeper message.

options.label: C
options.text: Papyrus is too expensive to ever use for practice.
options.rationale: Cost is mentioned, but it is not the story's lesson.

options.label: D
options.text: Fixing a mistake carefully can be more valuable than never taking a risk.

items.stem: How does Senwosret feel right after he realizes his mistake?

explanation.whyCorrect: “His stomach tightened,” showing worry, but he remembers his teacher's advice and stays calm enough to fix the error.
explanation.tip: A character can feel one emotion while still choosing a calm action.

options.label: A
options.text: anxious, but he manages to stay calm enough to fix it

options.label: B
options.text: relieved, because he decides to ignore it
options.rationale: He does not ignore the mistake; he carefully corrects it.

options.label: C
options.text: proud, because the mistake made his work look better
options.rationale: He is clearly worried, not proud, about the mistake.

options.label: D
options.text: angry at his father for giving him the task
options.rationale: He is scared of being caught, not angry at his father.

items.stem: What is the central conflict in the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The mistake on the papyrus creates the problem Senwosret must solve calmly and carefully.
explanation.tip: The central conflict is the main problem driving the character's choices.

options.label: A
options.text: The temple refuses to accept the harvest record.
options.rationale: The temple is not shown refusing anything.

options.label: B
options.text: Senwosret makes a costly mistake on an important document and must decide how to handle it.

options.label: C
options.text: Senwosret does not want to learn hieroglyphs.
options.rationale: He has studied for three years and wants to do this task.

options.label: D
options.text: Senwosret's father cannot read hieroglyphs.
options.rationale: The father reads and checks the column carefully.

items.stem: This story is told in third person. What does that allow the narrator to describe that a first-person account by only Senwosret might not easily show?

explanation.whyCorrect: A third-person narrator can describe other characters' reactions, like the father's, without being limited to only one character's own thoughts.
explanation.tip: Third-person narration can move beyond a single character's own perspective.

options.label: A
options.text: the moment Senwosret decides to fix the mark calmly
options.rationale: Senwosret could describe his own decision even if he told the story himself.

options.label: B
options.text: the worry Senwosret feels after making the mistake
options.rationale: Senwosret could easily describe his own worry even as a first-person narrator.

options.label: C
options.text: his father's calm, approving reaction after checking the corrected column

options.label: D
options.text: the trembling feeling in Senwosret's own hand
options.rationale: A first-person narrator could still describe his own physical feelings.

items.stem: Put the events of “The Apprentice Scribe” in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The story follows a clear time order: the task, the mistake, the fix, and the father's response.
explanation.tip: Look for time clues like “today,” “halfway down,” and “when his father finally checked.”

sequence: Senwosret's father gives him the first column of the harvest record to write.
Senwosret draws the wrong symbol for the number of baskets.
Senwosret carefully removes the wrong mark and redraws the correct symbol.
His father says a scribe who fixes mistakes is valuable, and sends him to the temple.

items.stem: Why does Senwosret's father say a scribe who fixes mistakes is “more valuable” than one who never takes risks?

explanation.whyCorrect: The father's comment suggests that avoiding all risk means never improving, while fixing mistakes shows real skill.
explanation.tip: An inference uses the character's exact words plus logical reasoning.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the temple prefers messy papyrus.
options.rationale: The temple expects careful, clear records.

options.label: B
options.text: Because risky scribes are paid more money.
options.rationale: Money is never mentioned in the story.

options.label: C
options.text: Because mistakes always look better than correct work.
options.rationale: The father values the correction, not the mistake itself.

options.label: D
options.text: Because a scribe who is too afraid to try difficult work will never grow skilled enough to do it well.

items.stem: Which TWO details show that Senwosret stays calm under pressure? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Remembering advice and carefully fixing the mark both show deliberate, calm problem-solving.
explanation.tip: Text evidence for “staying calm” should describe an action, not just a feeling.

options.label: A
options.text: He remembers his teacher's advice instead of panicking.

options.label: B
options.text: He carefully removes the wrong mark before it dries.

options.label: C
options.text: His stomach tightened when he saw the mistake.
options.rationale: This describes his feeling, not a calm action he takes.

options.label: D
options.text: His hand trembled as he dipped his pen in the ink.
options.rationale: This shows nervousness, not calm action.

items.stem: What does the phrase “his stomach tightened” most likely show about Senwosret?

explanation.whyCorrect: Writers often describe a physical feeling, like a tight stomach, to show a character's fear or nervousness.
explanation.tip: When a body part reacts strongly, think about what emotion usually causes that feeling.

options.label: A
options.text: He feels a sudden rush of worry or fear.

options.label: B
options.text: He is excited to finish his work.
options.rationale: The context after this phrase shows fear, not excitement.

options.label: C
options.text: He has a stomachache from the heat.
