options.rationale: No illness is mentioned in the story.

options.label: D
options.text: He is hungry and needs to eat soon.
options.rationale: The phrase describes an emotion, not actual hunger.

items.stem: In the story, what does papyrus mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The father “unrolls a fresh sheet of papyrus” and Senwosret writes a column on it, so papyrus must be a writing material.
explanation.tip: Picture what the character does with the object to figure out its meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: a type of hieroglyph symbol
options.rationale: Papyrus is the material, not a symbol drawn on it.

options.label: B
options.text: a material made for writing on, like paper

options.label: C
options.text: a tool used to grind soot into powder
options.rationale: That tool is separate; papyrus is what gets written on.

options.label: D
options.text: a king's official seal
options.rationale: Seals are not mentioned in the story.

items.stem: What does trembled mean in “Senwosret's hand trembled as he dipped his reed pen into the ink”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A trembling hand shakes slightly, which fits a nervous young scribe about to write something important.
explanation.tip: Think about how a nervous person's hand might move while doing something important.

options.label: A
options.text: moved very slowly
options.rationale: Trembling is about shaking, not speed.

options.label: B
options.text: reached forward
options.rationale: This describes motion, but not the shaking itself.

options.label: C
options.text: shook slightly

options.label: D
options.text: felt completely still
options.rationale: Trembling is the opposite of being still.

items.stem: True or false: Senwosret's father scolds him harshly for making the mistake.

explanation.whyCorrect: Instead of scolding him, the father praises the careful correction and calls him valuable.
explanation.tip: Compare what you expect a character to do with what actually happens in the text.

items.stem: How does the father's view of mistakes differ from what Senwosret feared he would think?

explanation.whyCorrect: Senwosret braces himself for a scolding, but his father's response shows a completely different, more understanding perspective.
explanation.tip: Compare a character's expectation with what another character actually says or does.

options.label: A
options.text: Both the father and Senwosret think the mistake ruined the papyrus.
options.rationale: The father does not see it as ruined once it is fixed.

options.label: B
options.text: The father is angrier about the mistake than Senwosret expected.
options.rationale: The father's reaction is calmer and more approving than expected.

options.label: C
options.text: Senwosret is proud of the mistake, but his father is not.
options.rationale: Senwosret braces for a scolding; he is not proud at first.

options.label: D
options.text: Senwosret expects a scolding, but his father actually values the careful correction.

items.stem: In “The Group Project,” which words are stage directions rather than dialogue?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stage directions appear in parentheses and describe a character's actions, tone, or movement.
explanation.tip: Dialogue is spoken aloud; stage directions in parentheses tell actors how to move or feel.

options.label: A
options.text: (frustrated, capping a marker)

options.label: B
options.text: MR. FARID enters, carrying a stack of graded tests.
options.rationale: This is a stage direction, but it is not in parentheses next to a character's line; the question asks about the bracketed action cue.

options.label: C
options.text: We have one day left, and half our poster is still blank.
options.rationale: This is dialogue—the words Nour says aloud.

options.label: D
options.text: NOUR:
options.rationale: This label shows who is speaking, not an action.

items.stem: What is the setting of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: The opening SCENE line describes a classroom after school with poster boards and markers scattered on a table.
explanation.tip: In a play script, the word SCENE introduces the setting before any dialogue begins.

options.label: A
options.text: Mr. Farid's office
options.rationale: The teacher enters the classroom; the scene never moves to an office.

options.label: B
options.text: a classroom after school, with poster boards and markers on a table

options.label: C
options.text: the school cafeteria during lunch
options.rationale: The scene is set in a classroom, not a cafeteria.

options.label: D
options.text: a stage at a spelling bee
options.rationale: That setting belongs to a different story.

items.stem: How does Nour feel at the start of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: The stage direction “(frustrated, capping a marker)” and her complaint about the blank poster both show frustration.
explanation.tip: In drama, stage directions and word choice both reveal a character's feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: confident that the project will be finished early
options.rationale: The stage direction and her words show worry, not confidence.

options.label: B
options.text: proud of how the poster looks so far
options.rationale: She says half the poster is still blank, which is not something to be proud of.

options.label: C
options.text: frustrated because she believes she is doing more than her fair share of the work

options.label: D
options.text: bored because the project is too easy
options.rationale: Her tone shows stress, not boredom.

items.stem: What is the central conflict in “The Group Project”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Their argument centers on what “our half” of the work was supposed to mean.
explanation.tip: The central conflict is the specific disagreement that drives the characters' dialogue.

options.label: A
options.text: Sami wants to switch partners.
options.rationale: Switching partners is never mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: Mr. Farid refuses to grade their project.
options.rationale: He offers advice, not a refusal to grade.

options.label: C
options.text: Nour and Sami disagree about which topic to research.
options.rationale: They already share the same topic, the volcano project.

options.label: D
options.text: Nour and Sami disagree about how much of the project each of them was supposed to finish.

items.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mr. Farid's comment and the partners' new plan to “check in along the way” both point to this lesson about communication.
explanation.tip: In drama, a character often states the theme directly in a key line of dialogue.

options.label: A
options.text: Good partners communicate clearly about their plans instead of assuming the other understands.

options.label: B
options.text: Working alone is always better than working with a partner.
options.rationale: The play never suggests this; it shows how to fix teamwork.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers should always check on group projects.
options.rationale: This describes Mr. Farid's action, not the deeper lesson.

options.label: D
options.text: Projects about volcanoes are more interesting than other topics.
options.rationale: The topic of the project is not the story's message.

items.stem: Why does Sami avoid looking up from his phone when Nour first complains?

explanation.whyCorrect: His later admission that they are stuck suggests he already sensed a problem, which explains his earlier avoidance.
explanation.tip: Combine a character's later words with an earlier action to make an inference.

options.label: A
options.text: He is finishing an important phone call for his family.
options.rationale: The play never mentions a phone call.

options.label: B
options.text: He may feel uncomfortable or guilty, suspecting the report is not actually finished.

options.label: C
options.text: He thinks the project is already perfect.
options.rationale: He later admits they are “stuck,” showing he knows it isn't finished.

options.label: D
options.text: He did not hear Nour speaking at all.
options.rationale: He answers her directly, so he clearly hears her.

items.stem: Which TWO details show that Nour and Sami's problem was caused by unclear communication, not laziness? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both lines show the two partners had different understandings of the plan, not that either one refused to work.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that explains the CAUSE of the conflict, not just any true detail.

options.label: A
options.text: Sami says, “We split the work, but we never really talked about what ‘our half’ meant.”

options.label: B
options.text: Sami says he already finished the volcano diagram.
options.rationale: This shows he did complete work, which argues against laziness.

options.label: C
options.text: Mr. Farid enters carrying graded tests.
options.rationale: This detail is about the teacher, not the cause of their problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Nour says, “I said I'd START it. Not finish the whole thing alone.”

items.stem: Put the events of “The Group Project” in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The play moves from the conflict, to the teacher's question, to the honest admission, to the resolution.
explanation.tip: Look for the moment each character's attitude or understanding changes.

sequence: Nour complains that the poster and report are still unfinished.
Mr. Farid asks how the project is going.
Sami admits that they never agreed on what “their half” meant.
Nour and Sami make a clear plan and agree to check in the next morning.

items.stem: Unlike a story with a narrator, how does the audience learn how Nour feels during the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Plays reveal feelings only through dialogue and stage directions, since there is no narrator.
explanation.tip: In drama, point of view is shown through what characters say and do, not through narration.

options.label: A
options.text: through a written letter Nour reads aloud
options.rationale: No letter appears in the play.

options.label: B
options.text: through Sami's opinion of her feelings
options.rationale: Sami never describes Nour's feelings for the audience.

options.label: C
options.text: through her own dialogue and the stage directions describing her tone and actions

options.label: D
options.text: through a narrator who explains her thoughts directly
options.rationale: A play script has no narrator explaining thoughts.

items.stem: What does hesitating mean in “NOUR: (hesitating) It's... coming along”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The pause shown by “...” and the stage direction together suggest Nour is unsure how honest to be.
explanation.tip: Stage directions and punctuation like “...” can both hint at a word's meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: leaving the room quickly
options.rationale: Nour stays in the scene and keeps speaking.

options.label: B
options.text: laughing at a joke
options.rationale: Nothing in the stage direction suggests humor.

options.label: C
options.text: speaking loudly and clearly
options.rationale: The pause and trailing “...” suggest the opposite of clear, confident speech.

options.label: D
options.text: pausing because of uncertainty or doubt

items.stem: In this play, Sami says they are “stuck.” What does stuck mean in this sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sami explains right after that they never agreed on the plan, which is why their progress has stopped.
explanation.tip: Read the sentence right after a tricky word—it often explains what is really happening.

options.label: A
options.text: unable to make progress on a problem

options.label: B
options.text: finished with all their work
options.rationale: They are NOT finished; that is the opposite of stuck here.

options.label: C
options.text: glued to an object
options.rationale: Nothing describes anything sticky in the play.

options.label: D
options.text: physically unable to move
options.rationale: No one in the play is physically trapped.

items.stem: How do Nour's and Sami's understandings of “our half” differ at the start of the play?

explanation.whyCorrect: Nour says she agreed only to START the report, while Sami believed she would finish the whole thing herself.
explanation.tip: Comparing two characters' expectations often reveals the true cause of a conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: Both of them thought Sami would write the entire report.
options.rationale: Sami believed Nour would do the writing, not himself.

options.label: B
options.text: Nour thought she only had to start the report, while Sami thought she would finish it alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Nour thought Sami would do the writing, and Sami agreed.
options.rationale: Sami believed NOUR would do the writing, which is the opposite.

options.label: D
options.text: Both of them thought the diagram still needed to be finished.
options.rationale: Sami already finished the diagram.

items.stem: What is the central idea of “Why Do We Get Goosebumps?”

explanation.whyCorrect: Every section builds on the idea that goosebumps are an old, now mostly useless, inherited reflex.
explanation.tip: A central idea is supported across the whole text, not just one paragraph.

options.label: A
options.text: Animals with fur never get goosebumps.
options.rationale: The article explains that fur made the reflex useful for animals, not that it doesn't happen to them.

options.label: B
options.text: Scientists do not understand why goosebumps happen.
options.rationale: The article explains the cause clearly, in detail.

options.label: C
options.text: Goosebumps are a leftover reflex from furrier ancestors that no longer serves the same purpose in humans.

options.label: D
options.text: Goosebumps only happen when people are cold.
options.rationale: The article explains that strong emotions can cause them too.

items.stem: Under which heading would you find out that fur makes animals look bigger to predators?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first section explains that raised fur traps warm air and makes an animal look larger to a threat.
explanation.tip: Headings organize an article's ideas into clearly labeled sections.

options.label: A
options.text: More Than Just Cold
options.rationale: That section is about emotional triggers, not predators.

options.label: B
options.text: Why Do We Get Goosebumps?
options.rationale: That is the title of the whole article.

options.label: C
options.text: Why Humans Still Have Them
options.rationale: That section explains why the reflex continues without fur.

options.label: D
options.text: A Useful Trick for Hairier Ancestors

items.stem: According to the article, what is an EFFECT of fur rising on a cold animal?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Raised fur traps a layer of warm air next to the skin,” which is the direct effect described.
explanation.tip: Look for the result that follows directly after a described cause.

options.label: A
options.text: A layer of warm air becomes trapped near the animal's skin.

options.label: B
options.text: The animal loses its sense of touch.
options.rationale: The article never mentions a change in touch.

options.label: C
options.text: The animal's temperature drops even lower.
options.rationale: The trapped air helps keep the animal warmer, not colder.

options.label: D
options.text: The tiny muscles under the skin disappear.
options.rationale: The muscles stay; they are what causes the fur to rise.

items.stem: Why do humans still get goosebumps even though they no longer have thick fur?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains that the ancient reflex stayed in our bodies even after it stopped being very useful.
explanation.tip: Look for words like “however” that signal why something continues despite no longer being useful.

options.label: A
options.text: Doctors have not found a way to stop the reflex.
options.rationale: The article frames this as an old, inherited reflex, not a medical problem to solve.

options.label: B
options.text: The tiny muscles under the skin still react the same old way, even though the reaction is no longer useful.

options.label: C
options.text: Goosebumps now help humans see better in the cold.
options.rationale: Goosebumps are never linked to eyesight in the article.

options.label: D
options.text: Human skin grows fur quickly when cold.
options.rationale: The article says humans no longer have thick fur.

items.stem: How is the goosebump reflex different in humans compared to furry animals?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article contrasts a useful ancient purpose in furry animals with an outdated, less useful reflex in humans today.
explanation.tip: Look for a paragraph that directly compares two groups' experience of the same feature.

options.label: A
options.text: In furry animals it is only caused by fear, never cold.
options.rationale: The article says cold is the main cause, and fear is a bonus survival effect.

options.label: B
options.text: In humans it keeps them warmer than furry animals.
options.rationale: The article says humans no longer have the fur needed for warmth.

options.label: C
options.text: In furry animals it provides warmth and protection, but in humans it no longer serves either purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: Humans and furry animals get goosebumps for exactly the same practical reason today.
options.rationale: The article clearly states the reflex is no longer useful for humans.

items.stem: What does reflex mean in “Our bodies kept this old reflex even after it stopped being very useful”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Goosebumps rising automatically, without anyone deciding to make them happen, is the clue that reflex means an automatic reaction.
explanation.tip: Think about whether the body's action happens on purpose or automatically.

options.label: A
options.text: a muscle used only for walking
options.rationale: The reflex described involves the skin's hair muscles, not walking.

options.label: B
options.text: a type of fur found on animals
options.rationale: Reflex describes a body reaction, not a body covering.

options.label: C
options.text: a decision someone makes carefully
options.rationale: A reflex happens automatically, not after careful thought.

options.label: D
options.text: an automatic reaction the body makes without thinking about it

items.stem: What does trigger mean in “can trigger the same nervous system signal that cold does”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Since both cold and strong emotion lead to the exact same nervous system signal, trigger must mean to cause or set off.
explanation.tip: Compare the word to something else in the sentence that causes the same result.

options.label: A
options.text: to cause or set off

options.label: B
options.text: to measure or record
options.rationale: Nothing about measuring is discussed here.

options.label: C
options.text: to weaken or slow down
options.rationale: The sentence compares two things that both cause the same signal.

options.label: D
options.text: to prevent or stop
options.rationale: The sentence says emotions CAUSE the signal, not stop it.

items.stem: Which TWO details show that emotions, not just cold, can cause goosebumps? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both details directly explain how emotional reactions can produce the very same goosebump response as cold.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that matches the exact claim—here, that emotions ALSO cause goosebumps.

options.label: A
options.text: Emotional reactions and temperature reactions share some of the same nerve pathways.

options.label: B
options.text: Fear, awe, or moving music can trigger the same nervous system signal that cold does.

options.label: C
options.text: Underneath each hair on your skin is a tiny muscle.
options.rationale: This describes the body part involved, not what triggers it.

options.label: D
options.text: Humans no longer have thick fur.
options.rationale: This explains why goosebumps are less useful, not what causes them.

items.stem: True or false: According to the article, goosebumps are caused only by cold temperatures.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article states that strong emotions, such as fear or awe, can trigger the same reaction as cold.
explanation.tip: Watch for words like “only” in true/false statements; informational texts often show more than one cause.

items.stem: What is the author's main purpose in explaining that fur made goosebumps useful for animals?

explanation.whyCorrect: Explaining the old purpose of the reflex helps readers understand why it survives in humans even without a clear use today.
explanation.tip: Ask why an author includes background information before explaining a modern mystery.

options.label: A
options.text: to convince readers that humans should grow more body hair
options.rationale: The article never suggests humans should change.

options.label: B
options.text: to help readers understand why humans still have a reflex that no longer fully makes sense for them

options.label: C
options.text: to list every animal that has fur
options.rationale: The article focuses on the purpose of fur, not a list of animals.

options.label: D
options.text: to argue that animals are smarter than humans
options.rationale: Intelligence is never compared in the article.

items.stem: Which is the best summary of the “More Than Just Cold” section?

explanation.whyCorrect: A good summary keeps only the key, factual point of the section without adding opinions.
explanation.tip: A summary should state the main scientific point in your own words.

options.label: A
options.text: Fear is the only emotion that can cause goosebumps.
options.rationale: The text also mentions awe and moving music as triggers.

options.label: B
options.text: Scientists do not know what causes goosebumps.
options.rationale: The section gives a clear scientific explanation.

options.label: C
options.text: Strong emotions can cause goosebumps because they trigger some of the same nerve pathways as cold does.

options.label: D
options.text: Music always feels better when you have goosebumps.
options.rationale: This is an opinion, not information from the text.

items.stem: Which sentence best expresses the theme of “The Spelling Bee”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final paragraph states directly that finding a way through panic “felt like its own kind of victory.”
explanation.tip: Look at the character's final realization to find the theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Practicing is a waste of time if you don't win.
options.rationale: Yasmin's practice clearly helps her get through her panic.

options.label: B
options.text: Judges are usually too strict during competitions.
options.rationale: The judge in the story is neutral, not strict or unfair.

options.label: C
options.text: Spelling bees are only fun for people who never make mistakes.
options.rationale: Yasmin does get eliminated, yet still feels successful.

options.label: D
options.text: Working through panic calmly, one small step at a time, is its own kind of success.

items.stem: How does Yasmin feel just before the spelling bee begins?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Yasmin's palms were sweating” and her memorized words “seemed to have evaporated,” both showing nervousness.
explanation.tip: Physical reactions, like sweating, are strong clues to a character's feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: nervous

options.label: B
options.text: bored
options.rationale: Sweating palms and racing thoughts show nerves, not boredom.

options.label: C
options.text: confident and relaxed
options.rationale: Her blank mind and sweating palms show the opposite of relaxed confidence.

options.label: D
options.text: angry
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she is upset with anyone.

items.stem: What is the central conflict Yasmin faces on stage?

explanation.whyCorrect: Despite weeks of practice, panic makes the word's letters seem to disappear from her memory.
explanation.tip: The central conflict is the specific obstacle the character must overcome in the moment.

options.label: A
options.text: Another speller cheats during the competition.
options.rationale: No cheating is mentioned in the story.

options.label: B
options.text: Panic makes her forget a word she had already memorized.

options.label: C
options.text: She forgets to study for the spelling bee.
options.rationale: She studied for three weeks, so this is not the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: The judge asks her an unfair question.
options.rationale: The judge simply gives her the next word on the list.

items.stem: The story is told in third person, but whose thoughts does the reader follow most closely?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narration stays close to Yasmin's thoughts and feelings throughout the passage.
explanation.tip: A third-person narrator can still focus closely on one character's inner thoughts.

options.label: A
options.text: the audience's
options.rationale: The audience's thoughts are never described.

options.label: B
options.text: the judge's
options.rationale: The judge only speaks a few words; we never hear the judge's thoughts.

options.label: C
options.text: Yasmin's

options.label: D
options.text: Ms. Adel's
options.rationale: Ms. Adel appears only in Yasmin's memory.

items.stem: Why does Yasmin feel a sense of victory even though she does not win the spelling bee?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last paragraph explains that overcoming the panic, not winning the whole event, is what felt like a victory to her.
explanation.tip: An inference about feelings should match the character's own stated realization.

options.label: A
options.text: She believes the word 'conscience' was unfair.
options.rationale: She never complains that the word was unfair.

options.label: B
options.text: She is happy the competition is finally over.
options.rationale: Relief that it's over is not the victory she describes.

options.label: C
options.text: She secretly did not want to win the competition.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she wanted to lose.

options.label: D
options.text: She successfully managed her panic instead of letting it defeat her completely.

items.stem: “Every word she had memorized seemed to have evaporated from her mind.” What does this figurative language suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing memorized words to evaporating water emphasizes how suddenly and completely they seemed to disappear.
explanation.tip: Picture the literal action in the figurative phrase, then apply that feeling to the character's situation.

options.label: A
options.text: Her memorized words suddenly felt completely gone, as if they had vanished into thin air.

options.label: B
options.text: Her memory turned into water.
options.rationale: The sentence is figurative, not literal.

options.label: C
options.text: She decided to stop studying.
options.rationale: The sentence describes a sudden panic, not a choice to quit.

options.label: D
options.text: She forgot how to spell forever.
options.rationale: She successfully spells the word moments later.

items.stem: Which TWO details show that Yasmin manages her panic instead of being completely controlled by it? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both chosen details show Yasmin taking a deliberate, calm step to work through her panic rather than freezing completely.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that shows an ACTION the character takes, not just a feeling she has.

options.label: A
options.text: Her palms were sweating before she reached the stage.
options.rationale: This shows she is nervous, not that she is managing the panic.

options.label: B
options.text: Sixty parents were watching the competition.
options.rationale: This describes the audience, not Yasmin's response to panic.

options.label: C
options.text: She remembers Ms. Adel's advice to break the word down.

options.label: D
options.text: She spells the easy part, “con,” first and then continues.

items.stem: Put the events of “The Spelling Bee” in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The story moves in time order from practice, to panic, to remembered advice, to success.
explanation.tip: Look for time clues such as “for three weeks,” “now,” and “she opened her mouth.”

sequence: Yasmin practices her spelling words for three weeks.
Her mind goes blank when the judge gives her the word 'conscience.'
She remembers her tutor's advice to break the word into smaller parts.
She spells the word correctly and hears applause.

items.stem: What does evaporated mean in “every word she had memorized seemed to have evaporated from her mind”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing memorized words to evaporating water suggests they felt like they had completely vanished.
explanation.tip: Think about what evaporating water actually does: it disappears into the air.

options.label: A
options.text: was written down on paper
options.rationale: The sentence is about memory, not writing.

options.label: B
options.text: disappeared completely, as if turned into vapor and gone

options.label: C
options.text: became easier to remember
options.rationale: This is the opposite of what the sentence describes.

options.label: D
options.text: grew much larger
options.rationale: Evaporating involves disappearing, not growing.

items.stem: What does ripple mean in “a small ripple of applause moved through the audience”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing the applause to a ripple suggests it spread gently and gradually through the crowd, like a ripple on water.
explanation.tip: Picture the literal meaning of a word (a ripple on water) to understand its figurative use.

options.label: A
options.text: a loud explosion
options.rationale: A ripple is usually small and gentle, not an explosion.

options.label: B
options.text: complete silence
options.rationale: Applause, even if small, is the opposite of silence.

options.label: C
options.text: a gradual spreading motion, like a small wave

options.label: D
options.text: a single loud clap from one person
options.rationale: The word “moved through the audience” suggests it spread, not from just one person.

items.stem: True or false: Yasmin wins the spelling bee at the end of the story.

explanation.whyCorrect: The text clearly states she “didn't win the spelling bee” and was eliminated two rounds later.
explanation.tip: Check the text carefully; a character can feel successful without actually winning a competition.

items.stem: How does Yasmin's idea of “winning” change from the beginning to the end of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final paragraph shows she has redefined success to include overcoming panic, not just placing first.
explanation.tip: Look for a shift in a character's thinking between the start and the end of a story.

options.label: A
options.text: Her idea of winning never changes in the story.
options.rationale: The final paragraph shows a clear shift in how she views success.

options.label: B
options.text: She believes only the judge's opinion matters.
options.rationale: The final paragraph is about her own realization, not the judge's view.

options.label: C
options.text: She decides winning does not matter to her at all.
options.rationale: She clearly values the moment; she just redefines what counts as success.

options.label: D
options.text: At first winning probably meant finishing first; by the end, she sees overcoming her panic as its own kind of win.

items.stem: Which sentence best expresses the theme of “The Lighthouse Keeper's Apprentice”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Yusra's choice to stop and work carefully, rather than force the mechanism, is what saves the night's light—exactly the theme the final paragraph emphasizes.
explanation.tip: Look at the character's key decision and its result to find the theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Careful patience in a difficult moment can matter more than speed.

options.label: B
options.text: Lighthouses are difficult machines to build.
options.rationale: This is a fact about the setting, not a lesson about life.

options.label: C
options.text: Sailors always trust what lighthouses tell them.
options.rationale: This describes the sailor's trust, not the story's deeper message.

options.label: D
options.text: Fevers can be dangerous for lighthouse keepers.
options.rationale: The uncle's illness starts the plot but is not the theme.

items.stem: How does Yusra feel as she climbs the stairs at the beginning of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her “damp” palms against the railing are a physical clue to her nervousness about this new responsibility.
explanation.tip: Physical details, like sweaty palms, often reveal a character's inner feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: excited to finally be rid of her uncle's rules
options.rationale: Her damp palms and careful memory of his warning show worry, not relief.

options.label: B
options.text: nervous, since this is her first time tending the lamp completely alone

options.label: C
options.text: bored, because she has done this job too many times to count
options.rationale: This is her FIRST time alone, so boredom does not fit.

options.label: D
options.text: confused about how the lamp mechanism works
options.rationale: She clearly knows the steps from watching her uncle many times.

items.stem: What is the setting of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The story opens by naming the place and year, and the lamp room's details confirm a historical, hand-operated lighthouse.
explanation.tip: Specific dates and location names at the start of a story usually establish its setting.

options.label: A
options.text: a classroom where Yusra studies mechanics
options.rationale: No classroom appears in the story.

options.label: B
options.text: a modern lighthouse run by machines
options.rationale: The story specifies 1887 and describes a hand-wound, old-fashioned mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: a harbor lighthouse in Alexandria in 1887

options.label: D
options.text: a merchant ship at sea in the present day
options.rationale: The ship appears only briefly, near the very end, from a distance.

items.stem: The story is told in third person. Whose thoughts and feelings does the narration follow most closely?

explanation.whyCorrect: The narration describes Yusra's memories, instincts, and physical sensations throughout the climb and repair.
explanation.tip: A third-person narrator can still stay close to a single character's experience.

options.label: A
options.text: her uncle's
options.rationale: Her uncle is sick in bed and does not appear in the lamp room scene.

options.label: B
options.text: the reader's
options.rationale: The reader is not a character whose thoughts the narration follows.

options.label: C
options.text: the sailor's
options.rationale: The sailor appears only in the final paragraph, and his thoughts are not described.

options.label: D
options.text: Yusra's

items.stem: Order these events from “The Lighthouse Keeper's Apprentice.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The plot unfolds in a clear sequence from the problem, to the warning, to the careful fix, to the result far out at sea.
explanation.tip: Look for details that show cause and effect between each event.

sequence: Yusra climbs the stairs alone because her uncle is sick with a fever.
She remembers her uncle's warning about the old, fragile clockwork.
She feels the mechanism catch and stops instead of forcing the crank.
A sailor sights the harbor light flashing correctly from three miles out.

items.stem: Why does Yusra stop turning the crank instead of forcing it when she feels it catch?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her uncle's exact warning about forcing a binding gear directly explains why she chooses to stop and investigate instead.
explanation.tip: Connect a character's earlier advice to a decision made later in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: She remembers her uncle's warning and infers that forcing it could break the gear completely.

options.label: B
options.text: She decides the lamp does not need to be lit tonight.
options.rationale: She continues working to get the lamp lit correctly.

options.label: C
options.text: She wants to let her uncle finish the job instead.
options.rationale: Her uncle is sick in bed and cannot help her.

options.label: D
options.text: She is too tired to keep turning the crank.
options.rationale: Tiredness is never mentioned as her reason for stopping.

items.stem: “The great lens loomed over her.” What does the word loomed suggest about the lens?

explanation.whyCorrect: Loomed is often used for something large that feels imposing, which fits Yusra's nervousness at facing this responsibility alone.
explanation.tip: A word like loomed adds feeling to a description beyond its literal meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: It was small and easy for her to overlook.
options.rationale: Loomed suggests something large and noticeable, not something small.

options.label: B
options.text: It appeared large and almost overwhelming, adding to the pressure Yusra feels.

options.label: C
options.text: It was actually moving toward her on its own.
options.rationale: The lens is a fixed object; loomed describes its appearance, not real motion.

options.label: D
options.text: It was glowing brightly with colored light.
options.rationale: The passage does not describe the lens glowing at this point.

items.stem: Which TWO details show that Yusra chooses patience over speed while fixing the mechanism? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both details describe a deliberate, careful choice Yusra makes instead of rushing through the repair.
explanation.tip: Choose evidence that describes an action taken in the key moment the question asks about.

options.label: A
options.text: The lens could bend a flame into a beam seen for twenty miles.
options.rationale: This is a fact about the lighthouse, not an action Yusra takes.

options.label: B
options.text: She stops and takes a slow breath instead of continuing to force the crank.

options.label: C
options.text: She works the metal sliver free carefully with the tip of a thin file.

options.label: D
options.text: She had watched her uncle tend the lamp a hundred times.
options.rationale: This shows her experience, not a choice made in this specific moment.

items.stem: What does reservoir mean in “check the oil reservoir”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Checking the oil reservoir makes sense only if it is a container that holds the oil supply for the lamp.
explanation.tip: Think about what object would logically need to be “checked” before lighting a lamp.

options.label: A
options.text: a tool used to wind machinery
options.rationale: Winding tools are mentioned separately in the passage.

options.label: B
options.text: a small flame used for light
options.rationale: A flame is lit from the oil; it is not the reservoir itself.

options.label: C
options.text: a container that holds a supply of liquid

options.label: D
options.text: a window that lets light escape
options.rationale: Windows or lenses are described elsewhere, not as part of the reservoir.

items.stem: What does wedged mean in “a sliver of displaced metal... wedged between two teeth of the largest gear”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sliver is causing a grinding problem by being caught tightly between the gear's teeth.
explanation.tip: Picture the small object causing a mechanical problem to understand what wedged means.

options.label: A
options.text: painted a bright color
options.rationale: Color is never mentioned in this description.

options.label: B
options.text: thrown far away from the gear
options.rationale: The sliver is stuck in place, not thrown elsewhere.

options.label: C
options.text: completely melted away
options.rationale: If the metal had melted, it would not be blocking the gear's motion.

options.label: D
options.text: tightly stuck in a narrow space

items.stem: What was the effect of removing the sliver of metal from the gear?

explanation.whyCorrect: Once Yusra removes the metal sliver, “it turned smoothly, and the great lens began its slow, steady rotation.”
explanation.tip: Find the sentence describing what happens immediately after the obstacle is removed.

options.label: A
options.text: The mechanism turned smoothly again, and the lens resumed its steady rotation.

options.label: B
options.text: The lamp went out completely for the rest of the night.
options.rationale: The story says the lens began rotating properly after the repair.

options.label: C
options.text: The uncle's fever immediately got better.
options.rationale: The fever and the gear repair are unrelated events.

options.label: D
options.text: The sailor's ship changed its course toward the harbor.
options.rationale: The ship's course is not described as changing because of the repair.

items.stem: The author describes the sound as “a faint grinding where smooth motion should have been.” What feeling does the word grinding create?

explanation.whyCorrect: Grinding connotes friction and malfunction, warning the reader—and Yusra—that something needs attention.
explanation.tip: Connotation is the feeling a word creates beyond its literal dictionary definition.

options.label: A
options.text: a sense of excitement and joy
options.rationale: Nothing about this moment is described as joyful.

options.label: B
options.text: a sense that something is wrong or damaged

options.label: C
options.text: a sense of calm and safety
options.rationale: Grinding usually signals trouble, not calm.

options.label: D
options.text: a sense of boredom
options.rationale: The moment is tense, not dull.

items.stem: How does the author's description in the final paragraph affect the story's tone?

explanation.whyCorrect: Describing what the sailor doesn't know creates quiet dramatic irony that highlights the importance of Yusra's careful choice.
explanation.tip: Notice when an author reveals something a character in the story does not know.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a comic tone by making fun of the sailor's confusion.
options.rationale: The sailor is not mocked; the passage is sincere, not comic.

options.label: B
options.text: It creates a frightening tone by describing a shipwreck.
options.rationale: No shipwreck happens; the light is successfully repaired.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates a quietly powerful tone by showing how little the sailor knows about the danger that was just avoided.

options.label: D
options.text: It creates a confusing tone that leaves the ending unclear.
options.rationale: The ending is clear: the light works, and the sailor is safe.

items.stem: What is the author's central claim in this article?

explanation.whyCorrect: The introduction and conclusion both state that optional, individualized homework is the author's main position.
explanation.tip: The central claim is the position the entire article is built to support.

options.label: A
options.text: Students should spend more hours on homework each night.
options.rationale: The author argues against heavy mandatory homework loads.

options.label: B
options.text: Only high school students should ever receive homework.
options.rationale: Grade level restrictions like this are not the author's claim.

options.label: C
options.text: Homework should be eliminated completely for all students.
options.rationale: The author says making homework optional does not mean eliminating it.

options.label: D
options.text: Homework should be optional, guided by what individual students actually need, rather than mandatory for everyone.

items.stem: Which evidence best supports the claim that mandatory homework may not improve achievement?

explanation.whyCorrect: A review of multiple research studies is strong, direct evidence connected specifically to the claim about achievement.
explanation.tip: Match evidence to the EXACT claim it is meant to support.

options.label: A
options.text: A review of multiple studies found a weak connection between homework and achievement in elementary and middle school.

options.label: B
options.text: Teachers could assign practice problems selectively.
options.rationale: This describes a proposed solution, not evidence of a weak connection.

options.label: C
options.text: Students spend seven hours in class already.
options.rationale: This describes students' schedules, not evidence about achievement.

options.label: D
options.text: Surveys link heavy homework to stress and reduced sleep.
options.rationale: This evidence supports a wellbeing claim, not the test-score claim specifically.

items.stem: How does the author respond to the concern that optional homework would let struggling students fall behind?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a concession-and-rebuttal structure: the author acknowledges the worry, then explains why the opposite may be true.
explanation.tip: Strong arguments respond directly to objections instead of ignoring them.

options.label: A
options.text: The author says struggling students should repeat the grade.
options.rationale: Repeating a grade is never mentioned in the article.

options.label: B
options.text: The author argues that a flexible system could actually help teachers target support more precisely.

options.label: C
options.text: The author ignores the concern completely.
options.rationale: Paragraph 4 directly addresses this concern.

options.label: D
options.text: The author agrees and abandons the main claim.
options.rationale: The author offers a counter-reason instead of agreeing.

items.stem: Which piece of evidence in the article is the MOST credible support for the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: A review of multiple studies is a stronger, more reliable form of evidence than a general observation or an assumed preference.
explanation.tip: Credible evidence usually comes from research, not from assumptions about what people want.

options.label: A
options.text: a claim that every teacher agrees homework should be optional
options.rationale: The article never states that every teacher agrees.

options.label: B
options.text: a general statement that students are often tired after school
options.rationale: This is a general observation, not evidence drawn from research.

options.label: C
options.text: a review of multiple research studies comparing homework loads and test scores

options.label: D
options.text: the idea that students would probably prefer less homework
options.rationale: A preference is an opinion, not evidence.

items.stem: According to the article, what is one effect of requiring the same homework for every student regardless of need?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains that uniform assignments make it harder for teachers to identify who truly needs more help.
explanation.tip: Look for the sentence describing what happens BECAUSE every assignment blends together.

options.label: A
options.text: Schools save money on classroom supplies.
options.rationale: Money and supplies are not mentioned in this article.

options.label: B
options.text: Parents are required to help with every assignment.
options.rationale: Parental involvement is not discussed in the article.

options.label: C
options.text: Students automatically get better grades.
options.rationale: The article argues the connection to achievement is weak.

options.label: D
options.text: Teachers have less time to notice which specific students actually need extra practice.

items.stem: What does mandatory mean in “Should Homework Be Optional?” when the article discusses “mandatory homework”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article contrasts mandatory homework with optional homework throughout, showing that mandatory means required for all.
explanation.tip: Look at the word the author contrasts it with to understand its meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: required for everyone, with no choice

options.label: B
options.text: assigned only to advanced students
options.rationale: Mandatory homework, as described, applies to all students, not just some.

options.label: C
options.text: graded very strictly
options.rationale: The article is about whether homework is required, not how it's graded.

options.label: D
options.text: suggested but not required
options.rationale: That meaning fits “optional,” the opposite of mandatory.

items.stem: What does documented mean in “excessive mandatory homework has a documented cost”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence immediately mentions “multiple surveys,” showing that documented means backed by recorded evidence.
explanation.tip: Check the words right after a tricky term for the proof or evidence being referenced.

options.label: A
options.text: imaginary and not actually true
options.rationale: The sentence specifically references surveys, meaning it is evidence-based.

options.label: B
options.text: recorded and supported by evidence, such as surveys or studies

options.label: C
options.text: illegal in most schools
options.rationale: Legality is never discussed in this article.

options.label: D
options.text: kept completely secret
options.rationale: A documented cost is the opposite of secret; it has been recorded and studied.

items.stem: Which TWO details support the claim that heavy mandatory homework can be harmful? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both chosen details are direct evidence the article uses to argue that heavy, required homework can cause harm without clear benefit.
explanation.tip: Select evidence that directly supports the specific harm the question describes.

options.label: A
options.text: Several studies found no meaningful difference in test scores between heavy and light homework loads.

options.label: B
options.text: Students already spend seven hours in class each day.
options.rationale: This describes students' schedules, not direct evidence of harm from homework.

options.label: C
options.text: Surveys link heavy homework loads to higher stress and reduced sleep.

options.label: D
options.text: Teachers could use quick in-class checks to see what students already know.
options.rationale: This describes a proposed solution, not harm caused by mandatory homework.

items.stem: True or false: The author wants homework eliminated completely for every student.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article clearly states that making homework optional “does not mean eliminating it altogether.”
explanation.tip: Watch for extreme words like “completely” or “always” that may not match a nuanced argument.

items.stem: What feeling does the phrase “one-size-fits-all approach” create in the final paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: “One-size-fits-all” connotes a rigid system that treats everyone the same, regardless of their actual needs.
explanation.tip: Some phrases carry a built-in judgment beyond their literal words.

options.label: A
options.text: a sense that the current system is carefully personalized
options.rationale: “One-size-fits-all” suggests the opposite of personalization.

options.label: B
options.text: a sense that the current system is extremely expensive
options.rationale: Cost is not what this phrase emphasizes.

options.label: C
options.text: a sense that the current system ignores individual students' different needs

options.label: D
options.text: a sense that the current system changes too often
options.rationale: The phrase suggests the system stays the same for everyone, not that it changes.

items.stem: How would you best describe the author's tone toward critics who disagree with optional homework?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author states the critics' worry fairly, then offers reasoning for a different conclusion—a respectful but firm tone.
explanation.tip: Look at how directly and fairly an author restates an opposing view before responding to it.

options.label: A
options.text: uninterested, ignoring critics' concerns entirely
options.rationale: The article specifically names and responds to a concern critics raise.

options.label: B
options.text: fully persuaded, agreeing that critics are right
options.rationale: The author offers a rebuttal rather than agreeing with the critics.

options.label: C
options.text: dismissive, mocking critics for disagreeing
options.rationale: The author engages with the concern seriously, rather than mocking it.

options.label: D
options.text: respectful but unconvinced, directly addressing their concern with a counterargument

items.stem: How many stanzas does “The Old Olive Tree” have?

explanation.whyCorrect: A stanza is a group of lines set apart from others; this poem has four such groups.
explanation.tip: Count the blocks of text separated by blank lines to find the number of stanzas.

options.label: A
options.text: four stanzas

options.label: B
options.text: sixteen stanzas
options.rationale: Sixteen is the total number of lines, not the number of stanzas.

options.label: C
options.text: three stanzas
options.rationale: Count the groups of lines separated by blank lines: there are four.

options.label: D
options.text: two stanzas
options.rationale: The poem has more than two separate groups of lines.

items.stem: Which pair of words from the poem rhyme?

explanation.whyCorrect: Soil and toil both end with the same “-oil” sound, making them a rhyming pair.
explanation.tip: Rhyming words share the same ending sound, even if spelled a little differently.

options.label: A
options.text: gate / birth
options.rationale: These words do not share an ending sound.

options.label: B
options.text: soil / toil

options.label: C
options.text: harvest / tends
options.rationale: These words end differently.

options.label: D
options.text: there / elder
options.rationale: These words do not rhyme with each other.

items.stem: In the last stanza, the speaker calls the tree “a kind of elder.” What type of figurative language is this, and what does it suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Calling the tree “a kind of elder” directly states it IS an elder, which is a metaphor suggesting wisdom and respect earned through age.
explanation.tip: A metaphor says one thing IS another, without using like or as.

options.label: A
options.text: a simile that compares the tree to a child
options.rationale: There is no like or as, and the comparison is to an elder, not a child.

options.label: B
options.text: an example of alliteration
options.rationale: Alliteration is about repeated beginning sounds, not comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: a metaphor that compares the tree to a wise, respected older person

options.label: D
options.text: a literal statement that the tree is an actual person
options.rationale: The tree is not literally a person; the comparison is figurative.

items.stem: What does the image “small fists of green and deepening black” most likely describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: Olives often appear green when unripe and turn dark, almost black, as they ripen—matching this vivid image.
explanation.tip: Use sensory details (shape and color) to picture what the poet is actually describing.

options.label: A
options.text: the tree's roots pushing into the ground
options.rationale: Roots are mentioned earlier, in a different stanza.

options.label: B
options.text: storm clouds gathering above the tree
options.rationale: Weather appears earlier as “wars that passed like weather,” not here.

options.label: C
options.text: the shadows the tree casts at sunset
options.rationale: Shadows are not described anywhere in the poem.

options.label: D
options.text: unripe and ripening olives on the tree

items.stem: What feeling does the phrase “bent low by time” create about the tree, rather than a purely negative idea of weakness?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paired with “but never disappears,” the phrase suggests the tree bends under time's weight yet endures with quiet dignity.
explanation.tip: Read the words right after a phrase to see whether they soften or change its connotation.

options.label: A
options.text: a sense of dignity and endurance despite age

options.label: B
options.text: a sense of confusion about its age
options.rationale: The poem states clearly how long the tree has stood; there's no confusion.

options.label: C
options.text: a sense of complete failure
options.rationale: The poem presents the tree with respect, not as a failure.

options.label: D
options.text: a sense of danger to people nearby
options.rationale: No danger from the tree is suggested anywhere in the poem.

items.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of “The Old Olive Tree”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The final stanza's shift from seeing the tree as “simply there” to seeing it as an elder reveals this central idea about respect for endurance.
explanation.tip: A theme in poetry often appears as a shift in how the speaker understands something by the end.

options.label: A
options.text: Grandparents know more about nature than anyone else.
options.rationale: The grandfather is a source of knowledge, but this is not the poem's central message.

options.label: B
options.text: Living things that quietly endure across generations deserve a new kind of respect and attention.

options.label: C
options.text: Olives are the most valuable crop a family can grow.
options.rationale: The poem's emphasis is on endurance and perspective, not crop value.

options.label: D
options.text: Trees need regular watering to survive drought.
options.rationale: This is a factual detail about plant care, not the poem's deeper message.

items.stem: From what point of view is this poem written?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pronouns like “I,” “my mother's,” and “my grandfather” show this poem is told from a first-person point of view.
explanation.tip: Look for I/me/my to identify first-person point of view.

options.label: A
options.text: third person — a narrator describes the speaker from outside
options.rationale: Words like “I” and “my” show the speaker is part of the poem, not an outside narrator.

options.label: B
options.text: second person — the poem speaks directly to “you”
options.rationale: The word “you” never appears in the poem.

options.label: C
options.text: first person — the speaker uses “I” and “my grandfather”

options.label: D
options.text: third person — the tree narrates its own life
options.rationale: The tree does not speak; the human speaker describes the tree.

items.stem: Why does the speaker's view of the tree change by the end of the poem?

explanation.whyCorrect: The middle stanzas about the tree's long memory and quiet labor explain why the speaker comes to see it differently by the final stanza.
explanation.tip: Trace how new information earlier in a poem can explain a change in the speaker's thinking later.

options.label: A
options.text: The tree suddenly grows taller than before.
options.rationale: No physical change in the tree is described in the poem.

options.label: B
options.text: The grandfather tells the speaker to stop visiting the tree.
options.rationale: The grandfather shares memories about the tree; he never tells the speaker to stay away.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker plants a brand-new tree nearby.
options.rationale: No new tree is mentioned anywhere in the poem.

options.label: D
options.text: Learning the tree's long history from the grandfather helps the speaker see it as something wise and enduring, not just an object.

items.stem: What does toil mean in “the quiet decades of patient toil”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pairing toil with “patient” and “decades” suggests a long, steady kind of hard work.
explanation.tip: Look at the words describing HOW LONG and HOW something is done to find a word's meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: hard, steady work

options.label: B
options.text: a short rest
options.rationale: “Patient toil” across “decades” suggests ongoing effort, not resting.

options.label: C
options.text: a type of fruit
options.rationale: Fruit (the olives) is described in a later stanza, not here.

options.label: D
options.text: a kind of storm
options.rationale: Weather is described separately as “wars that passed like weather.”

items.stem: Which TWO details from the poem show that the olive tree endures hardship? Choose two.

explanation.whyCorrect: Both details describe difficult conditions—drought and war—that the tree has lived through over time.
explanation.tip: Choose details that describe a difficulty, not simply a feature or a memory.

options.label: A
options.text: its trunk grown wide with seasons of drought

options.label: B
options.text: the wars that passed like weather overhead

options.label: C
options.text: small fists of green and deepening black
options.rationale: This describes the tree's harvest, not a hardship it survives.

options.label: D
options.text: the hands that first pressed seed to soil
options.rationale: This describes the tree's planting, not an ongoing hardship.

items.stem: How does describing the tree as “a kind of elder” affect the overall tone of the final stanza?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing the tree to a respected elder elevates it beyond a plant, creating a tone of quiet admiration.
explanation.tip: Notice how a single figurative comparison can shift the emotional tone of an entire stanza.

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a frightening tone, as if the tree were haunted.
options.rationale: Nothing in the stanza suggests fear or the supernatural.

options.label: B
options.text: It creates a respectful, almost reverent tone toward the tree.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates a neutral, purely factual tone with no feeling.
options.rationale: Calling the tree an “elder” adds clear emotional respect, not plain neutrality.

options.label: D
options.text: It creates a humorous tone that makes fun of old age.
options.rationale: The comparison is sincere and admiring, not mocking.

items.stem: What is the best first step before researching a report on volcanoes?

explanation.whyCorrect: Good research starts with clear questions that guide what you look for.
explanation.tip: Before you search, write down what you want to find out.

options.label: A
options.text: Copy a paragraph from a website.
options.rationale: Copying is not research; it is plagiarism.

options.label: B
options.text: Write the conclusion first.
options.rationale: You cannot conclude before you know what the research shows.

options.label: C
options.text: List questions you want to answer.

options.label: D
options.text: Pick the shortest book you can find.
options.rationale: The shortest source is not necessarily the best one.

items.stem: Choose the word: 'A ____ source is written by someone who saw or experienced the event.'

explanation.whyCorrect: A primary source comes directly from a witness or participant.
explanation.tip: Primary = present at the event; secondary = written about it later.

options.label: A
options.text: primary

options.label: B
options.text: fictional
options.rationale: A fictional source is made up, not a factual account.

options.label: C
options.text: secondary
options.rationale: A secondary source is written later, about the event, by someone else.

items.stem: Which source counts as a secondary source about ancient Egypt?

explanation.whyCorrect: The historian did not witness ancient Egypt; they wrote about it afterward using other sources.
explanation.tip: Secondary sources are written after the fact, often using primary sources.

options.label: A
options.text: a recording of an eyewitness
options.rationale: An eyewitness account is a primary source.

options.label: B
options.text: a diary written by a pharaoh's scribe
options.rationale: This was written at the time, so it is primary.

options.label: C
options.text: a photograph of a tomb wall
options.rationale: An original image from the time is primary evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: a textbook chapter written by a historian today

items.stem: You can use any website you find without checking who wrote it.

explanation.whyCorrect: Checking the author helps you judge whether the information is trustworthy.
explanation.tip: Always ask: who wrote this, and why?

items.stem: Mariam is researching sea turtles. Which keyword search will give the most useful results?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific keywords help a search engine find exactly the information you need.
explanation.tip: Use several specific words, not one broad word.

options.label: A
options.text: sea turtle nesting habits

options.label: B
options.text: animals
options.rationale: This is far too broad for her specific topic.

options.label: C
options.text: sea turtle sea turtle
options.rationale: Repeating a word does not narrow a search.

options.label: D
options.text: turtle
options.rationale: This is too broad and will return many unrelated results.

items.stem: Which note-taking method helps you avoid copying a source word-for-word?

explanation.whyCorrect: Restating the main idea in your own words is called paraphrasing, and it prevents plagiarism.
explanation.tip: Read, cover the text, then write what you remember.

options.label: A
options.text: Typing the article into your notes.
options.rationale: Typing the whole article is still copying it exactly.

options.label: B
options.text: Writing the main idea in your own words on a card

options.label: C
options.text: Highlighting the whole page.
options.rationale: Highlighting does not put anything into your own words.

options.label: D
options.text: Copying the first sentence of each paragraph.
options.rationale: Copying sentences, even just the first one, is still copying.

items.stem: Put the steps of a research project in the correct order.

explanation.whyCorrect: Research moves from asking questions, to gathering and sorting information, to writing.
explanation.tip: Plan before you search, and sort before you write.

sequence: Choose a topic and write research questions.
Find and read several reliable sources.
Take notes in your own words.
Organize notes under topic headings.
Write a draft using the notes.

items.stem: A list of all the sources you used at the end of a report is called a ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: This list lets readers see exactly where your facts and ideas came from.
explanation.tip: Keep a running list of sources as you research, not just at the end.

items.stem: Which source is most reliable for facts about climate change?

explanation.whyCorrect: A national agency has scientists and reviews its own data before publishing it.
explanation.tip: Look for sources backed by experts and institutions.

options.label: A
options.text: a blog post with no author listed
options.rationale: Without a known author, there is no way to check expertise.

options.label: B
options.text: a forum comment from a stranger
options.rationale: An anonymous comment cannot be checked for accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: a report published by a national weather agency

options.label: D
options.text: a cartoon about weather
options.rationale: A cartoon is entertainment, not a factual source.

items.stem: Tamer found two sources that disagree about when a bridge was built. What should he do?

explanation.whyCorrect: A third source can help confirm which date most evidence supports.
explanation.tip: When sources disagree, look for a tie-breaking source.

options.label: A
options.text: Guess which one sounds more official.
options.rationale: The sound of a source does not prove it is correct.

options.label: B
options.text: Use both dates in the same sentence without checking.
options.rationale: This would confuse readers and may spread an error.

options.label: C
options.text: Pick the date he likes better.
options.rationale: A date should be chosen based on evidence, not preference.

options.label: D
options.text: Check a third reliable source to see which date is supported

items.stem: When you take exact words from a source and use quotation marks, you are ____ the text.

explanation.whyCorrect: Quoting means copying someone's exact words and marking them with quotation marks.
explanation.tip: Quotation marks always signal someone's exact words.

options.label: A
options.text: skimming
options.rationale: Skimming means reading quickly for the main idea.

options.label: B
options.text: quoting

options.label: C
options.text: paraphrasing
options.rationale: Paraphrasing means restating ideas in your own words, not copying exact words.

items.stem: Which is an example of plagiarism?

explanation.whyCorrect: Using someone's exact words as if they were your own, with no credit, is plagiarism.
explanation.tip: Always quote or paraphrase, and always give credit.

options.label: A
options.text: Copying a paragraph from a website without quoting or crediting it

options.label: B
options.text: Summarizing an article in your own words.
options.rationale: A summary in your own words is proper paraphrasing.

options.label: C
options.text: Quoting a sentence and naming the source.
options.rationale: This correctly credits the original author.

options.label: D
options.text: Listing the website in your bibliography.
options.rationale: Listing a source you used is exactly what you should do.

items.stem: Which question is too broad to research in one short report?

explanation.whyCorrect: A topic as large as 'the ocean' cannot be fully answered in a short report.
explanation.tip: Narrow a broad topic into a specific question.

options.label: A
options.text: Why do coral reefs need sunlight?
options.rationale: This is a focused, answerable question.

options.label: B
options.text: What is the ocean?

options.label: C
options.text: How do clownfish protect themselves from predators?
options.rationale: This is specific and researchable.

options.label: D
options.text: How deep can a sea turtle dive?
options.rationale: This is a specific, researchable question.

items.stem: Yusuf wants facts about a local museum's history. Which source should he trust most?

explanation.whyCorrect: The museum's own history page is written by people with direct knowledge of its history.
explanation.tip: Go to the organization itself for facts about itself.

options.label: A
options.text: an advertisement for museum tickets
options.rationale: An advertisement's purpose is to sell, not to inform.

options.label: B
options.text: a rumor he heard from a classmate
options.rationale: A rumor cannot be checked or verified.

options.label: C
options.text: an article from the museum's official history page

options.label: D
options.text: a tourist's one-star review
options.rationale: A review shares opinions about a visit, not historical facts.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly paraphrases the source sentence 'Bees communicate through a dance called the waggle dance' without copying it word-for-word?

explanation.whyCorrect: A good paraphrase keeps the meaning but uses different wording and sentence structure.
explanation.tip: Say the idea aloud in your own words before writing it down.

options.label: A
options.text: Bees communicate through a dance called the waggle dance.
options.rationale: This copies the original sentence exactly.

options.label: B
options.text: Bees dance.
options.rationale: This is so short that it loses the original meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: The waggle dance is danced by bees who communicate.
options.rationale: This barely rearranges the same words as the original.

options.label: D
options.text: Bees use a special dance, called the waggle dance, to share information.

items.stem: Match each type of source to its example.

explanation.whyCorrect: Knowing these categories helps you judge how much to trust a source.
explanation.tip: Ask who wrote it, when, and why before trusting a source.

pairs.right: a letter written by a soldier
a history book written years later
a page with no author and many ads

items.stem: Reading only the title of an article is enough to know if it answers your research question.

explanation.whyCorrect: A title only hints at the topic; you must read enough of the article to check it truly answers your question.
explanation.tip: Skim the first paragraph, not just the title, before deciding to use a source.

items.stem: Which heading would you look under in a nonfiction book to find facts about a volcano's eruption history?

explanation.whyCorrect: A heading that names the topic directly is where that information will be found.
explanation.tip: Headings act like signposts for where facts are grouped.

options.label: A
options.text: History of Eruptions

options.label: B
options.text: Glossary
options.rationale: A glossary defines words; it does not list eruption events.

options.label: C
options.text: Index
options.rationale: An index lists page numbers for topics; it is not where the facts themselves are written.

options.label: D
options.text: About the Author
options.rationale: This section tells about the writer, not about volcanoes.

items.stem: Dalia is writing a report and has three sources that all agree on the same fact. What does this suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: When independent sources agree, it is stronger evidence that a fact is correct.
explanation.tip: Look for agreement across more than one trustworthy source.

options.label: A
options.text: She should ignore all three.
options.rationale: Agreeing sources are useful evidence, not something to ignore.

options.label: B
options.text: The fact is more likely to be accurate.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the newest source matters.
options.rationale: Agreement across sources matters more than any single source's age.

options.label: D
options.text: The fact must be false.
options.rationale: Agreement among independent sources usually supports a fact, not the opposite.

items.stem: Which is the best way to organize research notes gathered from several sources?

explanation.whyCorrect: Grouping by subtopic lets you see everything you know about one idea at once, no matter the source.
explanation.tip: Sort notes by idea, not by where each idea came from.

options.label: A
options.text: Keep notes in the order you found them with no labels.
options.rationale: Unlabeled notes in random order are hard to use when writing.

options.label: B
options.text: Write all notes on one long unlabeled page.
options.rationale: A single unlabeled page makes it hard to find anything later.

options.label: C
options.text: Group notes by subtopic, not by which source they came from

options.label: D
options.text: Only keep notes from the first source you read.
options.rationale: Ignoring later sources means missing important information.

items.stem: Which detail would you leave OUT of a list of keywords when searching for information about why bats sleep upside down?

explanation.whyCorrect: A search engine needs topic words, not personal details that have nothing to do with the subject.
explanation.tip: Keep search words focused only on the topic.

options.label: A
options.text: bats
options.rationale: This word is central to the topic and should stay in the search.

options.label: B
options.text: upside down
options.rationale: This phrase focuses the search on the exact question being asked.

options.label: C
options.text: sleep
options.rationale: This word narrows the search to the right behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: the student's own name

items.stem: Which citation shows you used an idea without directly quoting it, but still giving credit?

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming the source while restating the fact in your own words gives proper credit without quoting.
explanation.tip: A good paraphrase still names where the information came from.

options.label: A
options.text: According to the museum's website, the fossil is about 10,000 years old.

options.label: B
options.text: the fossil is about 10,000 years old (copied directly from the website with no quotation marks)
options.rationale: Copying exact wording without quotation marks is plagiarism, not paraphrasing.

options.label: C
options.text: The fossil is about 10,000 years old.
options.rationale: No source is named, so readers cannot tell where the fact came from.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum says the fossil is old.
options.rationale: This loses the specific fact and is too vague to be useful.

items.stem: Which research plan shows the best use of time?

explanation.whyCorrect: Planning questions first focuses the rest of the research so time is not wasted.
explanation.tip: Plan, then search, then write — in that order.

options.label: A
options.text: Collect fifteen sources without reading any of them.
options.rationale: Collecting sources without reading them wastes time and gathers nothing useful.

options.label: B
options.text: Spend the first day narrowing the topic and listing questions, then search for sources.

options.label: C
options.text: Choose the topic the night before the report is due.
options.rationale: Leaving the topic choice until the last night leaves no time for real research.

options.label: D
options.text: Start writing the report immediately, then find sources to match what you already wrote.
options.rationale: This risks writing facts that are not actually supported by real sources.

items.stem: A classmate says, 'I found one blog that disagrees with my science textbook, so the textbook must be wrong.' What is the problem with this reasoning?

explanation.whyCorrect: A single, unverified source is weaker evidence than a reviewed textbook, so it should not simply replace it.
explanation.tip: Weigh the reliability of each source, not just whether they disagree.

options.label: A
options.text: Textbooks are never allowed to be questioned.
options.rationale: Textbooks can contain errors, but a single unchecked blog is not strong enough evidence to overturn one.

options.label: B
options.text: The disagreement proves both sources are wrong.
options.rationale: A disagreement does not automatically prove either source is wrong.

options.label: C
options.text: One unreliable source should not outweigh a well-reviewed textbook.

options.label: D
options.text: Blogs are always more current than textbooks.
options.rationale: A blog's publish date does not automatically make it more accurate.

items.stem: Which domain ending most often signals a government source?

explanation.whyCorrect: Websites ending in .gov are run by government agencies.
explanation.tip: Check the domain ending as one quick clue about a site's purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: .biz
options.rationale: This ending is used for general business websites, not government ones.

options.label: B
options.text: .com
options.rationale: This ending is used by commercial, often for-profit, websites.

options.label: C
options.text: .fun
options.rationale: This ending is not associated with any official institution.

options.label: D
options.text: .gov

items.stem: Checking who wrote an article and what they know about the topic tests the author's ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: Authority means whether the author has the knowledge or experience to write accurately about the topic.
explanation.tip: Ask: is this person actually qualified to write about this?

options.label: A
options.text: popularity
options.rationale: How popular a source is does not tell you whether the author is an expert.

options.label: B
options.text: currency
options.rationale: Currency refers to how recent the information is, not the author's expertise.

options.label: C
options.text: authority

items.stem: Which clue suggests a website might be biased?

explanation.whyCorrect: A source that leaves out facts that disagree with its view is likely presenting only one side.
explanation.tip: Watch for one-sided sources that never mention opposing evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: It only presents facts that support one side of an issue.

options.label: B
options.text: It lists the author's name and credentials.
