options.rationale: Naming the author actually helps readers judge credibility.

options.label: C
options.text: It links to other sources for the same facts.
options.rationale: Linking to other sources can help readers verify the claims.

options.label: D
options.text: It includes a publication date.
options.rationale: A publication date helps readers judge how current the information is.

items.stem: Which is the BEST reason to check a source's publication date when researching medical treatments?

explanation.whyCorrect: Medical knowledge changes quickly, so an outdated source could give incorrect treatment information.
explanation.tip: For fast-changing topics, newer evidence usually matters more.

options.label: A
options.text: Newer sources never contain mistakes.
options.rationale: Being recent does not guarantee a source is free of errors.

options.label: B
options.text: Medical information can become outdated as research advances.

options.label: C
options.text: The date tells you how long the website has existed.
options.rationale: A publication date is about the content, not the website's age.

options.label: D
options.text: Older sources are always written better.
options.rationale: Age alone does not determine the quality of writing.

items.stem: A source funded by a company that sells a product can be fully objective about that product.

explanation.whyCorrect: A funder with something to sell has a reason to present the product favorably, which can affect objectivity.
explanation.tip: Ask who paid for a source and what they might gain from it.

items.stem: Put the steps for evaluating a website before using it in the correct order.

explanation.whyCorrect: Checking the author, the date, the purpose, and other sources together builds a full picture of reliability.
explanation.tip: No single check is enough — combine several before trusting a source.

sequence: Identify the author and their expertise.
Check the publication or update date.
Determine the purpose: to inform, persuade, or sell.
Compare the facts with another reliable source.

items.stem: Which is an example of synthesizing information from two sources?

explanation.whyCorrect: Synthesis means weaving ideas from multiple sources into one new explanation.
explanation.tip: Ask: how do these two sources' ideas fit together?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeating the same fact from one source twice.
options.rationale: Repeating one fact does not combine information from two sources.

options.label: B
options.text: Choosing only the source that is easiest to read.
options.rationale: Picking one source and ignoring the other is not synthesis.

options.label: C
options.text: Combining a historian's timeline with a scientist's data to explain why a city was abandoned.

options.label: D
options.text: Copying two paragraphs, one from each source, side by side.
options.rationale: Placing two copied paragraphs together is not the same as combining their ideas.

items.stem: Omar read a claim about a new vaccine on a page that sells vitamins. Why should he be cautious?

explanation.whyCorrect: A commercial page has a financial reason to favor claims that help sell its own products.
explanation.tip: Always ask what a source's purpose is before trusting its claims.

options.label: A
options.text: The page has a bright color scheme.
options.rationale: A website's colors have nothing to do with the accuracy of its claims.

options.label: B
options.text: The page uses complete sentences.
options.rationale: Good grammar does not by itself make a claim trustworthy.

options.label: C
options.text: The page is easy to navigate.
options.rationale: Easy navigation does not indicate whether the information is reliable.

options.label: D
options.text: The page's purpose is to sell products, which may bias its claims.

items.stem: Which is the clearest example of a scholarly source?

explanation.whyCorrect: Peer review means other experts checked the article's accuracy before it was published.
explanation.tip: Look for 'peer-reviewed' or 'journal' as signs of scholarly work.

options.label: A
options.text: a peer-reviewed article in an academic journal

options.label: B
options.text: a meme shared on social media
options.rationale: A meme is meant for humor, not as a researched source.

options.label: C
options.text: a personal travel blog
options.rationale: A blog shares one person's experience, not reviewed research.

options.label: D
options.text: a product review on a shopping site
options.rationale: A shopping review reflects a customer's opinion, not scholarship.

items.stem: Writing a short restatement of a whole article's main points, in your own words, is called a ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary condenses the most important ideas from a longer text.
explanation.tip: A summary is shorter than the original and covers only the main points.

items.stem: Using someone's exact words with quotation marks and a citation is called ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: Quoting preserves the original wording exactly, marked with quotation marks and credited to its source.
explanation.tip: Exact words always need quotation marks.

options.label: A
options.text: quoting

options.label: B
options.text: summarizing
options.rationale: Summarizing restates main ideas briefly in your own words, not word-for-word.

options.label: C
options.text: plagiarizing
options.rationale: Plagiarizing means using words or ideas without credit, which is the opposite of proper quoting.

items.stem: Two blogs cite each other as their only evidence for a claim, and neither names an original expert source. What problem does this show?

explanation.whyCorrect: When sources only cite each other in a loop, there may be no original, checkable evidence at all.
explanation.tip: Trace a claim back to its original source before trusting it.

options.label: A
options.text: The claim must come from a scientific study.
options.rationale: Nothing here shows the claim actually traces back to a study.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim may be circular reporting with no real evidence behind it.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is automatically true because two sources agree.
options.rationale: Two sources repeating each other is not the same as independent confirmation.

options.label: D
options.text: Blogs are always more reliable than books.
options.rationale: The format of a source does not determine its reliability.

items.stem: Which note-organizing method helps when writing a report from five different sources?

explanation.whyCorrect: Grouping by subtopic lets a writer see everything relevant to one idea, regardless of its source.
explanation.tip: Organize by idea, not by the order you found your sources.

options.label: A
options.text: Only taking notes from the longest source.
options.rationale: Ignoring four of the five sources wastes useful information.

options.label: B
options.text: Writing notes in the order the sources were found.
options.rationale: The order found rarely matches the order ideas should appear in a report.

options.label: C
options.text: Sorting notes into subtopics so ideas from different sources are grouped together

options.label: D
options.text: Keeping each source's notes completely separate with no overlap.
options.rationale: Separating sources entirely makes it hard to compare or combine related ideas.

items.stem: Which statement needs a citation in a research report?

explanation.whyCorrect: A specific statistic from a study is not common knowledge, so its source must be credited.
explanation.tip: Common knowledge needs no citation; specific data and claims do.

options.label: A
options.text: The fact that there are seven continents
options.rationale: This is widely known common knowledge.

options.label: B
options.text: The fact that water freezes at 0°C
options.rationale: This is common, well-known scientific knowledge that needs no citation.

options.label: C
options.text: The fact that plants need sunlight to grow
options.rationale: This basic fact is common knowledge that does not require a citation.

options.label: D
options.text: A statistic about how many coral reefs have died in the last decade

items.stem: Which is the best way to avoid plagiarism when using an idea (not exact words) from a source?

explanation.whyCorrect: A true paraphrase uses new wording and still names the original source.
explanation.tip: Close your source, write the idea from memory, then check it for accuracy.

options.label: A
options.text: Put the idea in your own words and credit the source.

options.label: B
options.text: Change a few words from the original sentence and use it as your own.
options.rationale: Lightly editing a sentence is still too close to the original wording.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the idea without naming where it came from.
options.rationale: Leaving out credit, even for an idea, is plagiarism.

options.label: D
options.text: Copy the idea exactly but leave out the quotation marks.
options.rationale: Exact wording without quotation marks looks like it is your own, which is plagiarism.

items.stem: Match each term to its definition.

explanation.whyCorrect: Knowing these terms helps you use and credit sources correctly.
explanation.tip: Mix up these terms and you risk accidentally plagiarizing.

pairs.right: a note that tells readers where information came from
restating someone's idea in your own words
someone's exact words, set off with quotation marks
using another's words or ideas without credit

items.stem: If a fact appears in several independent, reliable sources, it is more likely to be accurate.

explanation.whyCorrect: Agreement among separate, trustworthy sources is one of the strongest signs that a fact is correct.
explanation.tip: Cross-check important facts across more than one reliable source.

items.stem: Which search phrase, using quotation marks, helps find an exact phrase rather than separate words?

explanation.whyCorrect: Quotation marks tell a search engine to look for that exact phrase, which narrows the results.
explanation.tip: Use quotation marks to search for an exact phrase.

options.label: A
options.text: energy
options.rationale: This single word is far too broad for the intended topic.

options.label: B
options.text: "renewable energy sources"

options.label: C
options.text: renewable energy sources
options.rationale: Without quotation marks, a search engine looks for the words separately, not as one phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: renewable OR energy OR sources
options.rationale: This expands the search to any of the words, rather than narrowing it.

items.stem: Which is the strongest reason to prefer a library database over a general web search for a research report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Databases usually collect vetted, published work, which is more reliable than unfiltered web results.
explanation.tip: Library databases filter out much of the unreliable content found in a general search.

options.label: A
options.text: Library databases cannot be searched by keyword.
options.rationale: Library databases can be searched by keyword, just like a general search engine.

options.label: B
options.text: Library databases always load faster.
options.rationale: Loading speed has nothing to do with a source's reliability.

options.label: C
options.text: Library databases mainly index sources that have been reviewed for accuracy.

options.label: D
options.text: Library databases only have very short articles.
options.rationale: Many database articles are long, detailed, and well researched.

items.stem: A writer claims 'Most scientists agree' but names no scientists or studies. What should a careful researcher do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Vague claims about 'most scientists' need to be traced to real, named evidence before they are trusted.
explanation.tip: Vague appeals to unnamed experts are a signal to dig deeper.

options.label: A
options.text: Accept the claim because it sounds confident.
options.rationale: Confidence in wording is not evidence that a claim is true.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat the same claim in the report without checking it.
options.rationale: Repeating an unchecked claim can spread inaccurate information.

options.label: C
options.text: Assume the claim is false simply because no one is named.
options.rationale: A lack of names does not prove a claim is false, only that it needs checking.

options.label: D
options.text: Look for the specific studies or named experts behind the claim.

items.stem: Which fact would be considered common knowledge and would NOT usually need a citation?

explanation.whyCorrect: Widely known, basic facts that almost everyone learns do not need a citation.
explanation.tip: If nearly everyone already knows it, it is usually common knowledge.

options.label: A
options.text: The Earth orbits the Sun.

options.label: B
options.text: A particular researcher's theory about why a species went extinct
options.rationale: A specific researcher's theory is not common knowledge and needs credit.

options.label: C
options.text: A specific scientist's measurement of a planet's exact distance from the Sun this year
options.rationale: A precise, recent measurement is specific data that needs a citation.

options.label: D
options.text: A survey's percentage result about student sleep habits
options.rationale: A specific survey result is data from a study and needs a citation.

items.stem: Which revision best fixes a report that only cites one single source for every claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: Using more than one independent source strengthens a claim and reduces reliance on a single viewpoint.
explanation.tip: Relying on only one source leaves a report open to that source's errors or bias.

options.label: A
options.text: Remove the citation so the report looks more original.
options.rationale: Removing citations hides sources instead of fixing the lack of variety.

options.label: B
options.text: Add at least one additional independent source to confirm each major claim.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the source with an unrelated one on a different topic.
options.rationale: An unrelated source cannot support the same claims at all.

options.label: D
options.text: Cite the same source twice using different page numbers.
options.rationale: Citing the same source twice does not add any new, independent confirmation.

items.stem: Nour finds a sponsored article that looks like a news report but is paid for by a company. What should guide her evaluation?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sponsored content has a built-in reason to favor the sponsor, so its claims deserve extra scrutiny.
explanation.tip: Always notice when content is labeled 'sponsored' or 'paid partnership.'

options.label: A
options.text: The word 'sponsored' means the article has been fact-checked by a third party.
options.rationale: Being labeled sponsored only means it is paid promotion, not that it has been independently verified.

options.label: B
options.text: Paid articles are always less accurate than free ones.
options.rationale: Cost alone does not determine accuracy; the purpose and funding source matter more.

options.label: C
options.text: Sponsored content is designed to promote a product, so it should be checked against independent sources.

options.label: D
options.text: Sponsored articles follow the same review process as independent news.
options.rationale: Sponsored content is paid for and typically not reviewed the same way as independent journalism.

items.stem: Which research habit best protects against unintentional plagiarism while taking notes from several sources at once?

explanation.whyCorrect: Labeling every note with its source as you go prevents confusion and accidental plagiarism later.
explanation.tip: Label the source the moment you write a note, not afterward.

options.label: A
options.text: Taking all notes first and adding sources afterward from memory.
options.rationale: Relying on memory later risks mixing up or forgetting which source an idea came from.

options.label: B
options.text: Trusting that you'll remember which idea came from which source.
options.rationale: Memory is unreliable across many sources, making accidental plagiarism likely.

options.label: C
options.text: Only recording sources for direct quotations, not for paraphrased ideas.
options.rationale: Paraphrased ideas still need credit, not just exact quotations.

options.label: D
options.text: Recording the source next to every note, even brief ones, as you take them.

items.stem: Omar wanted to ride his bike, but it had a flat tire. What is the problem in this sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence states directly that the bike has a flat tire, which stops Omar from riding.
explanation.tip: Look for the word 'but' — it often signals the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar's bike has a flat tire.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar does not own a bike.
options.rationale: The sentence says it is his bike, just with a flat tire.

options.label: C
options.text: Omar does not like riding bikes.
options.rationale: The sentence says he wanted to ride, so he does like it.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar's friend took his bike.
options.rationale: No friend is mentioned in the sentence.

items.stem: Lina and her sister both wanted the last orange in the fruit bowl, and neither wanted to share. What kind of conflict is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two people want the same thing and are in conflict with each other.
explanation.tip: Character vs. character means two people are at odds.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. society
options.rationale: No rule or group of people is involved, just two sisters.

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. character

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. nature
options.rationale: No natural force like weather is part of this problem.

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. self
options.rationale: Two people disagree here, not one person struggling inside.

items.stem: A heavy storm knocked down the bridge that Farah needed to cross to get home. What kind of conflict does Farah face?

explanation.whyCorrect: The storm is a force of nature that creates the obstacle Farah must overcome.
explanation.tip: Weather, animals, and natural disasters point to character vs. nature.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. self
options.rationale: The problem comes from outside her, not from an inner struggle.

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. society
options.rationale: No rule or group of people caused this problem.

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. nature

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. character
options.rationale: No other person is causing Farah's problem.

items.stem: Youssef was afraid to speak in front of the class, even though he knew the answer. What kind of conflict is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Youssef is struggling with his own fear, which is an inner conflict.
explanation.tip: When the struggle is inside a character's own mind, it's character vs. self.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. nature
options.rationale: No natural force is part of this problem.

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. society
options.rationale: No rule or group of people is causing this fear.

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. character
options.rationale: No other person is opposing Youssef here.

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. self

items.stem: In Hassan's town, kids were not allowed to play soccer in the square, but Hassan believed the rule was unfair and wanted it changed. What kind of conflict is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hassan is in conflict with a rule made by his community, which is character vs. society.
explanation.tip: A fight against a rule, law, or tradition is usually character vs. society.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. society

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. nature
options.rationale: No natural force is part of this conflict.

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. character
options.rationale: No single person is opposing Hassan; it is a town rule.

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. self
options.rationale: Hassan is not struggling with his own feelings; he is pushing against a rule.

items.stem: Dalia practiced her lines every night because she was determined to win the lead role, even after she forgot a line at tryouts. How does Dalia respond to the conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dalia faces the setback by continuing to practice, showing determination.
explanation.tip: How a character reacts to a setback reveals their response to conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: She blames her friend for the mistake.
options.rationale: No friend is mentioned as the cause of her mistake.

options.label: B
options.text: She keeps practicing instead of giving up.

options.label: C
options.text: She refuses to try out again.
options.rationale: She already tried out; the sentence shows her continuing to prepare.

options.label: D
options.text: She quits the play completely.
options.rationale: The sentence says she keeps practicing, not that she quits.

items.stem: Zain built a sandcastle every day at the beach, but the tide kept washing it away before sunset. One evening, he dug a trench around his castle to block the water. The castle stood until morning. How is the conflict resolved?

explanation.whyCorrect: Zain's own solution, the trench, is what finally protects the castle.
explanation.tip: The resolution is the action that finally solves the conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: A friend rebuilds the castle for him.
options.rationale: No friend is mentioned; Zain solves the problem himself.

options.label: B
options.text: The tide stops coming in.
options.rationale: The text says Zain dug a trench; the tide itself does not stop.

options.label: C
options.text: Zain builds a trench that protects the castle from the tide.

options.label: D
options.text: Zain gives up building sandcastles.
options.rationale: The text shows him solving the problem, not giving up.

items.stem: Noor forgot her lunch at home. Her classmate Rami noticed she had nothing to eat and offered to share his sandwich. What is the resolution to Noor's problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rami's sharing is the action that solves Noor's lunch problem.
explanation.tip: Look for the character's action that actually fixes the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Noor goes home to get her lunch.
options.rationale: The text does not say she leaves school to get it.

options.label: B
options.text: Noor decides she is not hungry.
options.rationale: The problem is solved by sharing, not by Noor no longer being hungry.

options.label: C
options.text: The teacher buys Noor a new lunch.
options.rationale: No teacher is mentioned solving the problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Rami shares his sandwich with her.

items.stem: Karim's team was losing the final match by two points with one minute left. He felt like giving up, but his coach reminded him to focus on one play at a time. What internal conflict does Karim face?

explanation.whyCorrect: Karim's conflict happens inside his own mind, between quitting and persisting.
explanation.tip: An internal conflict is a struggle happening inside a character's own thoughts.

options.label: A
options.text: He struggles between wanting to give up and wanting to keep trying.

options.label: B
options.text: He is afraid of a storm during the game.
options.rationale: No storm or weather is mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: He disagrees with a rule set by the league.
options.rationale: No league rule is part of this conflict.

options.label: D
options.text: He argues with another player on his team.
options.rationale: No teammate is arguing with him in this scenario.

items.stem: Put the events of this conflict in the correct order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The events move from the problem appearing, to a failed attempt, to a successful solution.
explanation.tip: Look for the order that makes the attempts and solution make sense.

sequence: Sami's kite gets stuck in a tall tree.
Sami tries throwing a ball to knock it loose, but misses.
A neighbor lends Sami a long pole.
Sami uses the pole to free the kite.

items.stem: Maya wanted to win the art contest, but she also wanted to help her little brother, who was sick, instead of finishing her painting. She finally decided to stay home and finish the painting later that week. What does Maya's choice reveal about her?

explanation.whyCorrect: Maya chooses her brother's needs first, showing what matters most to her.
explanation.tip: A character's choice during a conflict often reveals their values.

options.label: A
options.text: She is afraid of losing the contest.
options.rationale: Her choice is about caring for her brother, not fear of losing.

options.label: B
options.text: She values caring for her family over winning a contest.

options.label: C
options.text: She blames her brother for being sick.
options.rationale: Nothing in the text shows her blaming her brother.

options.label: D
options.text: She does not care about the art contest at all.
options.rationale: She still plans to finish the painting, showing she still cares about it.

items.stem: Two neighbors, Huda and Tariq, disagreed about where to build a shared fence. After arguing for days, they asked an older neighbor to help them measure the yard fairly. How do Huda and Tariq resolve their conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bringing in a fair, neutral helper is how they finally settle the disagreement.
explanation.tip: A fair outside helper can resolve a disagreement between two people.

options.label: A
options.text: They flip a coin without discussing the problem.
options.rationale: The text describes asking for fair measurement, not a coin flip.

options.label: B
options.text: They stop speaking to each other.
options.rationale: The text shows them seeking help, not avoiding each other.

options.label: C
options.text: They ask a neutral person to help settle the disagreement.

options.label: D
options.text: They each build their own fence in secret.
options.rationale: The text describes them working together with a neighbor's help.

items.stem: In a character-vs-self conflict, the character struggles against another person.

explanation.whyCorrect: Character vs. self means the struggle happens inside the character's own mind or feelings, not against another person.
explanation.tip: Self conflicts are inner struggles, like fear, doubt, or a hard choice.

items.stem: Adam's village depended on one well for water, but it began to dry up during a long drought. What is the central conflict in this scenario?

explanation.whyCorrect: The drying well threatens the whole village's water supply, which is the main problem.
explanation.tip: The central conflict is the main problem that drives the whole plot.

options.label: A
options.text: A villager is arguing with Adam.
options.rationale: No argument between people is described.

options.label: B
options.text: Adam feels afraid of the dark.
options.rationale: Fear of the dark is not mentioned in this scenario.

options.label: C
options.text: The village has too many wells.
options.rationale: The scenario describes only one well, which is drying up.

options.label: D
options.text: The village's water supply is drying up.

items.stem: Reem discovered that her best friend had been chosen for the role she wanted in the school play. She felt jealous, but she also wanted to support her friend. Which sentence BEST describes the conflict Reem experiences?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reem's conflict is inside her own feelings, between two competing emotions.
explanation.tip: When two feelings pull a character in different directions, that's an internal conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: She struggles between jealousy and wanting to be supportive.

options.label: B
options.text: She is frightened of performing on stage.
options.rationale: Stage fright is not mentioned in this scenario.

options.label: C
options.text: She argues loudly with her friend about the role.
options.rationale: The text does not describe an argument between them.

options.label: D
options.text: She disagrees with the teacher's casting rules.
options.rationale: No disagreement with casting rules is described.

items.stem: A long drought dried up the farms near Noura's village. The farmers met to decide how to share the little water that was left fairly among all the families. What does the farmers' meeting suggest about how the conflict will be resolved?

explanation.whyCorrect: The farmers choosing to meet and share shows cooperation is how they plan to resolve the shortage.
explanation.tip: A meeting to find a fair solution often signals cooperative resolution.

options.label: A
options.text: The farmers will give up farming completely.
options.rationale: Meeting to share water shows an effort to keep farming, not give up.

options.label: B
options.text: The community will work together to solve the problem.

options.label: C
options.text: The drought will end on its own without any effort.
options.rationale: The farmers are actively meeting to solve the problem, not waiting.

options.label: D
options.text: One farmer will take all the remaining water.
options.rationale: The meeting is about sharing fairly, not one person taking everything.

items.stem: At the start of the story, Tamer refuses to ask for help with his broken bicycle because he is too proud. By the end, after falling twice, he finally asks his neighbor for help and fixes it together. How does Tamer change from the beginning to the end of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tamer's growth is shown by his shift from refusing help to accepting it.
explanation.tip: Compare how a character acts at the start and the end to see how they change.

options.label: A
options.text: He decides to stop trying to fix the bicycle.
options.rationale: The story shows him fixing it, not giving up.

options.label: B
options.text: He argues with his neighbor about the bicycle.
options.rationale: The story shows them fixing it together, not arguing.

options.label: C
options.text: He moves from refusing help out of pride to accepting it.

options.label: D
options.text: He becomes more afraid of riding bicycles.
options.rationale: The story does not mention a new fear of riding.

items.stem: Khalid wanted to join the school band, but he had never played an instrument before and was embarrassed to start lessons at his age. What kind of conflict is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Khalid's struggle is with his own embarrassment and doubt, an internal conflict.
explanation.tip: Embarrassment and self-doubt usually point to character vs. self.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. character
options.rationale: No other person is opposing Khalid in this scenario.

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. nature
options.rationale: No natural force is part of this conflict.

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. society
options.rationale: No rule or group of people is involved here.

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. self

items.stem: A wildfire spread quickly toward the cabin where Layla and her grandfather were staying, forcing them to leave everything behind. What kind of conflict is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: The wildfire is a natural force threatening the characters, making this character vs. nature.
explanation.tip: Fires, floods, and storms are classic character vs. nature conflicts.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. nature

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. society
options.rationale: No rule or group of people created this danger.

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. self
options.rationale: The danger comes from outside, not from an inner struggle.

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. character
options.rationale: No other person is causing this danger.

items.stem: Nadia disagreed with a new school rule that banned students from bringing homemade lunches, and she started a petition to change it. What kind of conflict is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Nadia is in conflict with a rule set by an institution, which is character vs. society.
explanation.tip: Petitions and protests against rules point to character vs. society.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. character
options.rationale: No single person is opposing Nadia; it is a school rule.

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. society

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. self
options.rationale: Nadia is not struggling internally; she is challenging a rule.

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. nature
options.rationale: No natural force is involved in this conflict.

items.stem: Samir accused his classmate Yara of losing the class pet turtle, but it turned out the turtle had simply hidden under a rock in its tank. What kind of conflict is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Samir's accusation puts him in conflict with Yara, which is character vs. character.
explanation.tip: When one character blames or opposes another person, it's character vs. character.

options.label: A
options.text: character vs. self
options.rationale: The conflict is between two classmates, not inside one person's mind.

options.label: B
options.text: character vs. nature
options.rationale: The turtle hiding is not a natural disaster or force threatening anyone.

options.label: C
options.text: character vs. character

options.label: D
options.text: character vs. society
options.rationale: No rule or group of people is involved; this is between two students.

items.stem: The rowers had trained for months for the regional race. Halfway through the race, their boat began taking on water, and they had to decide whether to keep paddling or turn back. What is the central conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: The damaged boat creates the urgent problem the rowers must solve.
explanation.tip: The central conflict is the main problem the characters must face and solve.

options.label: A
options.text: The rowers dislike the sport of rowing.
options.rationale: The text shows months of training, suggesting dedication, not dislike.

options.label: B
options.text: The rowers are arguing about who trained hardest.
options.rationale: No argument about training is described.

options.label: C
options.text: The rowers are competing against a rule that bans their boat.
options.rationale: No rule banning the boat is mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: The rowers must decide how to handle their damaged boat during the race.

items.stem: Dina's family had to move to a new city for her mother's job. Dina was upset about leaving her friends, but she also felt curious about exploring a new place. Which best describes Dina's internal conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dina experiences two competing feelings at once, which is an internal conflict.
explanation.tip: Internal conflicts often involve two feelings pulling a character in different directions.

options.label: A
options.text: She feels torn between sadness about leaving and curiosity about the new city.

options.label: B
options.text: She refuses to pack her belongings.
options.rationale: No refusal to pack is mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: She is afraid of a storm on moving day.
options.rationale: No storm or weather is part of this scenario.

options.label: D
options.text: She argues with her mother about the move.
options.rationale: No argument with her mother is described.

items.stem: The fishing village depended on the river, but a new factory upstream began polluting the water, killing fish the villagers needed. What is the central conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: The factory's pollution creates the main threat that drives the plot.
explanation.tip: Look for the problem that affects the whole community, not a small detail.

options.label: A
options.text: The villagers disagree about where to build new houses.
options.rationale: No disagreement about housing is mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: Pollution from the factory threatens the village's fish supply.

options.label: C
options.text: Two villagers compete to catch the most fish.
options.rationale: No competition between villagers is described.

options.label: D
options.text: A character is afraid of the river.
options.rationale: No fear of the river is described.

items.stem: Put the events of this conflict in the correct order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The events move from the cause, to the discovery, to the action taken, to the resolution.
explanation.tip: Find the cause first, then the discovery, then the response, then the fix.

sequence: The factory's waste starts killing fish in the river.
Villagers notice fewer fish each week.
A group of villagers reports the factory to local officials.
The factory agrees to clean its waste before releasing it.

items.stem: Hana trained for weeks to run the relay, but on race day she twisted her ankle during warm-ups. How might this conflict be resolved in a way that shows resilience?

explanation.whyCorrect: Finding a new way to contribute despite a setback shows resilience in facing the conflict.
explanation.tip: Resilient resolutions show a character adapting rather than giving up.

options.label: A
options.text: Hana quits the track team completely.
options.rationale: Quitting shows giving up, not resilience.

options.label: B
options.text: Hana blames her teammates for the injury.
options.rationale: An ankle injury during warm-ups is not caused by teammates.

options.label: C
options.text: Hana finds another way to support her team, such as cheering or coaching, despite the injury.

options.label: D
options.text: Hana pretends the injury did not happen and ignores the pain.
options.rationale: Ignoring an injury is not a realistic or healthy resolution.

items.stem: At the story's climax, Omar must choose between keeping the lost wallet he found, which has enough money to buy the bike he's wanted for months, or returning it to its owner. What is the central conflict at this moment?

explanation.whyCorrect: Omar's inner struggle between wanting the money and doing the honest thing is the central conflict.
explanation.tip: A choice between what a character wants and what is right often shows internal conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar is competing with a friend for the same bike.
options.rationale: No friend competing for the bike is mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar's town has a rule against owning bikes.
options.rationale: No such town rule is mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: Omar is lost and cannot find his way home.
options.rationale: Being lost is not part of this scenario.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar struggles between personal desire and honesty.

items.stem: Years of unequal rainfall meant one farm always had more water than its neighbor. The two farming families argued until an elder suggested they share the irrigation canal on alternating days. How is the conflict resolved?

explanation.whyCorrect: The elder's suggested schedule gives both families fair access, resolving the dispute.
explanation.tip: A fair compromise, like a schedule, often resolves a long-standing conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: The families agree to share the water on a schedule.

options.label: B
options.text: The families stop speaking to each other permanently.
options.rationale: The text shows them reaching an agreement, not permanent silence.

options.label: C
options.text: One family gives up farming entirely.
options.rationale: The text describes sharing, not one family quitting.

options.label: D
options.text: The drought ends before anyone has to act.
options.rationale: The resolution comes from the families' agreement, not from the weather changing.

items.stem: Soraya's team was behind in the quiz competition. She knew the next answer, but a teammate confidently (and incorrectly) answered before her. What is the conflict Soraya faces?

explanation.whyCorrect: Soraya faces an uncomfortable choice about whether to speak up and correct a mistake.
explanation.tip: A difficult choice a character must make is often the heart of a conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: She disagrees with the rules of the competition.
options.rationale: No disagreement with the rules is described.

options.label: B
options.text: She must decide whether to correct her teammate in front of everyone.

options.label: C
options.text: She competes against a rival school.
options.rationale: The conflict described is within her own team, not against a rival.

options.label: D
options.text: She is afraid of public speaking.
options.rationale: No fear of speaking is mentioned in this scenario.

items.stem: A story's climax is usually the point where the central conflict is at its most intense.

explanation.whyCorrect: The climax is the turning point of highest tension, right before the conflict begins to resolve.
explanation.tip: Climax = peak tension; resolution comes right after.

items.stem: Early in the story, Faris is too shy to perform his poem at the festival. Through the story, his sister encourages him, and by the final scene, he reads his poem confidently to the crowd. What role does the sister play in resolving Faris's internal conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sister's encouragement is what helps Faris overcome his own fear.
explanation.tip: A supportive character often helps resolve another character's internal conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: She convinces him to skip the festival.
options.rationale: The ending shows him performing, not skipping it.

options.label: B
options.text: She performs the poem in his place.
options.rationale: The text says Faris himself reads the poem in the end.

options.label: C
options.text: She helps him build the confidence he needs to face his fear.

options.label: D
options.text: She argues with the festival judges.
options.rationale: No argument with judges is described.

items.stem: A long-standing conflict between two neighboring towns over fishing rights in a shared lake finally ends when both towns agree to set seasonal limits recommended by marine scientists. What does the resolution suggest about solving the conflict?

explanation.whyCorrect: Relying on expert, evidence-based advice allowed both towns to agree on a fair solution.
explanation.tip: Expert guidance can help resolve a conflict between groups fairly.

options.label: A
options.text: The towns decided to split the lake with a wall.
options.rationale: No wall or physical division is mentioned in the resolution.

options.label: B
options.text: The lake dried up, ending the need to fish.
options.rationale: No mention is made of the lake drying up.

options.label: C
options.text: One town simply gave up fishing forever.
options.rationale: The resolution describes shared seasonal limits, not one town quitting entirely.

options.label: D
options.text: Using expert advice helped both towns find a fair compromise.

items.stem: Throughout the story, Mona resents having to care for her younger cousin during summer break. By the end, after they build a treehouse together, Mona looks forward to their time together. How does the resolution of the conflict change Mona?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mona's feelings shift from resentment to enjoyment after sharing a positive experience with her cousin.
explanation.tip: Look at how a character's feelings shift from the start to the end of a conflict.

options.label: A
options.text: She shifts from resentment to genuine enjoyment of her cousin's company.

options.label: B
options.text: She decides never to see her cousin again.
options.rationale: The ending shows her looking forward to time together, not avoiding her cousin.

options.label: C
options.text: She convinces her parents to end summer visits.
options.rationale: No such request is described in the text.

options.label: D
options.text: She remains annoyed by her cousin for the rest of the story.
options.rationale: The text explicitly shows her feelings changing to enjoyment.

items.stem: Two rival inventors raced to finish the same project first, each sabotaging small parts of the other's work out of jealousy. When their shared workshop caught fire, they had to work together to save both of their inventions. How does the external conflict (the fire) affect the inventors' personal rivalry?

explanation.whyCorrect: A shared external danger can push rival characters toward cooperation, easing their personal conflict.
explanation.tip: An outside crisis can bring characters together and change their relationship.

options.label: A
options.text: It ends the story without resolving either conflict.
options.rationale: The shared crisis begins to resolve their personal rivalry, as described.

options.label: B
options.text: It forces them to cooperate, which begins to resolve their rivalry.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes their rivalry even worse than before.
options.rationale: The shared danger pushes them to work together, not fight more.

options.label: D
options.text: It has no effect on their relationship with each other.
options.rationale: Having to cooperate during the fire directly changes how they interact.

items.stem: Which pronoun can replace 'Khalid' in 'Khalid plays chess every day'?

explanation.whyCorrect: He is the subject pronoun that replaces a single male name.
explanation.tip: Subject pronouns (he, she, I, we, they) take the place of the subject noun.

options.label: A
options.text: It
options.rationale: It is used for things, not people.

options.label: B
options.text: Him
options.rationale: Him is an object pronoun; the subject of the sentence needs He.

options.label: C
options.text: He

options.label: D
options.text: They
options.rationale: They is plural, but Khalid is only one person.

items.stem: Choose the pronoun: 'The parrot cleaned ____ feathers after the bath.'

explanation.whyCorrect: Its (no apostrophe) shows ownership by the parrot.
explanation.tip: Its shows ownership; it's means it is.

options.label: A
options.text: their
options.rationale: Their is plural; the parrot is one bird.

options.label: B
options.text: its

options.label: C
options.text: it's
options.rationale: It's means it is, which does not fit before a noun like feathers.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a possessive pronoun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mine is the possessive pronoun that stands alone to show ownership.
explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns that stand alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

options.label: A
options.text: This backpack is mines.
options.rationale: Mines is not a word; the correct possessive pronoun is mine.

options.label: B
options.text: This backpack is me.
options.rationale: Me is an object pronoun, not a possessive one.

options.label: C
options.text: This backpack is my.
options.rationale: My must come before a noun, like 'my backpack,' not stand alone.

options.label: D
options.text: This backpack is mine.

items.stem: Which word is a reflexive pronoun in this sentence? 'Lina made herself a sandwich.'

explanation.whyCorrect: Herself reflects the action back onto Lina, the subject of the sentence.
explanation.tip: Reflexive pronouns end in -self or -selves and refer back to the subject.

options.label: A
options.text: herself

options.label: B
options.text: Lina
options.rationale: This is a proper noun, the subject of the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: made
options.rationale: This is the verb in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: a
options.rationale: This is an article, not a pronoun.

items.stem: Choose the demonstrative pronoun: '____ are the shoes I want.'

explanation.whyCorrect: These is a plural demonstrative pronoun that points to something nearby.
explanation.tip: This/that are singular; these/those are plural.

options.label: A
options.text: This
options.rationale: This is singular, but shoes is plural.

options.label: B
options.text: That
options.rationale: That is singular and points to something far away.

options.label: C
options.text: These

items.stem: Which pronoun correctly replaces 'the twins' in 'The twins finished their project'?

explanation.whyCorrect: They is the plural subject pronoun that replaces two or more people.
explanation.tip: Use they for plural subjects, no matter who they are.

options.label: A
options.text: It
options.rationale: It is used for things, not people.

options.label: B
options.text: They

options.label: C
options.text: She
options.rationale: She is singular and feminine only; twins could be any gender.

options.label: D
options.text: He
options.rationale: He is singular; twins are two people.

items.stem: Which sentence has correct pronoun-antecedent agreement?

explanation.whyCorrect: Team is treated as one singular group, so it is matched with the singular pronoun its.
explanation.tip: A group acting as a single unit, like team or class, uses a singular pronoun.

options.label: A
options.text: The players celebrated its win.
options.rationale: Players is plural, so it needs the plural pronoun their.

options.label: B
options.text: The team celebrated their win.
options.rationale: Team is one group acting as a single unit, so it needs the singular pronoun its.

options.label: C
options.text: The team celebrated its win.

options.label: D
options.text: The team celebrated his win.
options.rationale: His refers to one person, but the whole team is being described.

items.stem: Which pronoun is indefinite in this sentence? 'Someone left an umbrella in the classroom.'

explanation.whyCorrect: Someone does not name a specific person, so it is an indefinite pronoun.
explanation.tip: Indefinite pronouns like someone, anyone, and everybody don't name a specific person.

options.label: A
options.text: classroom
options.rationale: This is a noun, the place where it was left.

options.label: B
options.text: left
options.rationale: This is the verb in the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: umbrella
options.rationale: This is a noun, the thing that was left.

options.label: D
options.text: Someone

items.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Between you and ____, I think the second plan is better.'

explanation.whyCorrect: After the preposition between, the object pronoun me is correct.
explanation.tip: Pronouns after a preposition are usually object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them.

options.label: A
options.text: me

options.label: B
options.text: myself
options.rationale: Myself is reflexive and isn't needed in this sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: I
options.rationale: After a preposition like between, use the object pronoun me, not I.

items.stem: Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun reference?

explanation.whyCorrect: Repeating the name Noor makes it completely clear who explained the plan.
explanation.tip: If a pronoun could point to more than one person, repeat the name instead.

options.label: A
options.text: When Noor met Hana, Noor explained the plan.

options.label: B
options.text: Noor met Hana, and then she left.
options.rationale: It is unclear whether 'she' means Noor or Hana.

options.label: C
options.text: When she met her, she explained the plan.
options.rationale: Both pronouns here are unclear about who is meant.

options.label: D
options.text: When Noor met Hana, she explained the plan.
options.rationale: It is unclear whether 'she' means Noor or Hana.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the relative pronoun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Who correctly refers to a person (the teacher) as the subject of the clause.
explanation.tip: Use who for people, which for things, and that for either.

options.label: A
options.text: The teacher which graded our tests gave helpful comments.
options.rationale: Which refers to things, not people.

options.label: B
options.text: The teacher who graded our tests gave helpful comments.

options.label: C
options.text: The teacher whose graded our tests gave helpful comments.
options.rationale: Whose shows ownership, not the subject of the clause.

options.label: D
options.text: The teacher who's graded our tests gave helpful comments.
options.rationale: Who's means who is or who has, which does not fit here.

items.stem: Which word is a pronoun in this sentence? 'She borrowed my pencil case.'

explanation.whyCorrect: She is a subject pronoun that takes the place of a person's name.
explanation.tip: Pronouns replace nouns so we don't repeat names over and over.

options.label: A
options.text: pencil
options.rationale: This is part of a noun, naming an object.

options.label: B
options.text: borrowed
options.rationale: This is the verb in the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: She

options.label: D
options.text: case
options.rationale: This is part of a noun, naming an object.

items.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: 'The prize belongs to ____.'

explanation.whyCorrect: After the preposition to, the object pronoun us is correct.
explanation.tip: Object pronouns (me, us, him, her, them) follow prepositions like to, for, and with.

options.label: A
options.text: ourselves
options.rationale: Ourselves is reflexive and is not needed in this sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: us

options.label: C
options.text: we
options.rationale: We is a subject pronoun; this sentence needs an object pronoun after 'to.'

items.stem: Which sentence uses an intensive pronoun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Myself emphasizes that I did the action alone, which is the job of an intensive pronoun.
explanation.tip: Intensive pronouns add emphasis and can usually be removed without changing the basic meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: Myself built the shelf.
options.rationale: Myself cannot be the subject of a sentence; use I.

options.label: B
options.text: I built the shelf myself for me.
options.rationale: Adding 'for me' repeats an idea myself already emphasizes.

options.label: C
options.text: I built the shelf hisself.
options.rationale: Hisself is not a standard word; the correct form is himself.

options.label: D
options.text: I built the shelf myself.

items.stem: Which pronoun correctly replaces 'Omar and Tariq' as the object of the sentence 'The coach praised ____'?

explanation.whyCorrect: Them is the plural object pronoun that replaces Omar and Tariq as the object of the verb.
explanation.tip: Object pronouns (him, her, them, us, me) receive the action of the verb.

options.label: A
options.text: them

options.label: B
options.text: it
options.rationale: It is used for things, not people.

options.label: C
options.text: they
options.rationale: They is a subject pronoun; this sentence needs an object pronoun.

options.label: D
options.text: him
options.rationale: Him is singular, but Omar and Tariq are two people.

items.stem: Which sentence fixes the unclear pronoun reference? 'Fatma told Reem that her essay needed more detail.'

explanation.whyCorrect: Using a direct quotation removes any confusion about whose essay is being discussed.
explanation.tip: Rewriting with a direct quotation or a name can clear up an ambiguous pronoun.

options.label: A
options.text: Fatma told Reem that the essay, hers, needed more detail.
options.rationale: 'Hers' is still unclear about which person it refers to.

options.label: B
options.text: Fatma told Reem, 'Your essay needs more detail.'

options.label: C
options.text: Fatma told Reem that her essay needed more detail, and she agreed.
options.rationale: 'She' is still unclear — it could mean Fatma or Reem.

options.label: D
options.text: Fatma told her that her essay needed more detail.
options.rationale: Both pronouns here are unclear about who is meant.

items.stem: Choose the pronoun: '____ of the puzzle pieces is missing.'

explanation.whyCorrect: One matches the singular verb is, showing a single missing piece.
explanation.tip: Match an indefinite pronoun to a singular or plural verb based on its meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: Many
options.rationale: Many would need the plural verb 'are,' not 'is.'

options.label: B
options.text: Several
options.rationale: Several would need the plural verb 'are,' not 'is.'

options.label: C
options.text: One

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses who vs. whom?

explanation.whyCorrect: After the preposition to, the object pronoun whom is correct.
explanation.tip: Who is a subject pronoun; whom is an object pronoun, often after a preposition.

options.label: A
options.text: To who should I address this letter?
options.rationale: After a preposition, use the object pronoun whom, not who.

options.label: B
options.text: Whom wrote this letter?
options.rationale: The subject of a sentence needs who, not whom.

options.label: C
options.text: To whom should I address this letter?

options.label: D
options.text: I wonder who to give this letter to, whom is my teacher.
options.rationale: This mixes who and whom incorrectly in the same sentence.

items.stem: Which sentence has correct pronoun-antecedent agreement?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every is a singular word, so it is matched here with the singular pronoun her.
explanation.tip: Words like every, each, and one are singular and need a singular pronoun.

options.label: A
options.text: Every player packed their own water bottles.
options.rationale: This still mismatches the singular antecedent 'every player.'

options.label: B
options.text: Every player packed their own water bottle.
options.rationale: Every is singular, so the matching pronoun should be singular, such as her or his.

options.label: C
options.text: The players packed her own water bottle.
options.rationale: Players is plural, so it needs the plural pronoun their.

options.label: D
options.text: Every player packed her own water bottle.

items.stem: Which sentence avoids an ambiguous pronoun?

explanation.whyCorrect: Repeating 'the captain' instead of using 'he' removes any confusion about who apologized.
explanation.tip: When two people of the same gender appear, repeat a name to avoid confusion.

options.label: A
options.text: After the coach spoke to the captain, the captain apologized to the team.

options.label: B
options.text: He told him that he was right.
options.rationale: All three pronouns here are unclear about who is meant.

options.label: C
options.text: After the coach spoke to the captain, he apologized to the team.
options.rationale: It's unclear whether 'he' means the coach or the captain.

options.label: D
options.text: The coach and the captain talked, and then he left.
options.rationale: It's unclear who 'he' refers to, the coach or the captain.

items.stem: Which revision best fixes the vague pronoun in this sentence? 'When the storm hit the coast, it caused a lot of damage, and they are still rebuilding it.'

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming 'the residents' and 'their homes' clears up who is acting and what is being rebuilt.
explanation.tip: Replace a string of vague pronouns with specific nouns to keep meaning clear.

options.label: A
options.text: It hit it, and they are rebuilding it.
options.rationale: Nearly every pronoun here is unclear about what or who it refers to.

options.label: B
options.text: When the storm hit the coast, it caused a lot of damage, and the residents are still rebuilding their homes.

options.label: C
options.text: When the storm hit the coast, it caused a lot of damage, and they are still rebuilding.
options.rationale: 'They' and the repeated 'it' are still unclear about who and what is meant.

options.label: D
options.text: The storm hit the coast, and it caused a lot of damage, and it is still being rebuilt by it.
options.rationale: Repeating 'it' for different things makes the sentence very confusing.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the correct object pronoun?

explanation.whyCorrect: After the preposition to, the object pronoun him is correct.
explanation.tip: Test it: remove 'Hana and' and see which pronoun still sounds right.

options.label: A
options.text: The teacher handed the certificates to Hana and he's.
options.rationale: He's means he is, which does not fit in this position.

options.label: B
options.text: The teacher handed the certificates to Hana and he.
options.rationale: After a preposition, use the object pronoun him, not he.

options.label: C
options.text: The teacher handed the certificates to Hana and him.

options.label: D
options.text: The teacher handed the certificates to Hana and his.
options.rationale: His is a possessive pronoun, not an object pronoun.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the correct subject pronoun?

explanation.whyCorrect: She and I are both subject pronouns, correctly matching their role as the subject.
explanation.tip: Test each pronoun alone: 'She finished' and 'I finished' both sound correct.

options.label: A
options.text: She and me finished the mural together.
options.rationale: Me is an object pronoun; the subject needs I.

options.label: B
options.text: Her and me finished the mural together.
options.rationale: Both pronouns are object pronouns; the subject needs she and I.

options.label: C
options.text: Her and I finished the mural together.
options.rationale: Her is an object pronoun; the subject needs she.

options.label: D
options.text: She and I finished the mural together.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses who or whom?

explanation.whyCorrect: Who correctly acts as the subject pronoun of the question.
explanation.tip: If the pronoun is the subject doing the action, use who, not whom.

options.label: A
options.text: Who finished the race first?

options.label: B
options.text: Whose finished the race first?
options.rationale: Whose shows ownership, not the subject of the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: Whom finished the race first?
options.rationale: Whom cannot be the subject of a sentence; the subject needs who.

options.label: D
options.text: Who's finished the race first?
options.rationale: Who's means who is or who has, which does not fit here.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses whom?

explanation.whyCorrect: Whom is the object of 'invite,' correctly using the object pronoun form.
explanation.tip: Try answering with 'him' or 'her' — if that fits, use whom in the question.

options.label: A
options.text: Who invited you to the party instead?
options.rationale: This question has a different meaning and does not test the object pronoun.

options.label: B
options.text: Whom did you invite to the party?

options.label: C
options.text: Whose did you invite to the party?
options.rationale: Whose shows ownership and does not fit this question.

options.label: D
options.text: Whom invited you to the party?
options.rationale: Whom cannot be the subject of a sentence; the subject needs who.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the possessive pronoun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Theirs is the possessive pronoun that stands alone to show ownership.
explanation.tip: Possessive pronouns that stand alone never use an apostrophe: theirs, his, hers, ours.

options.label: A
options.text: The trophy is their.
options.rationale: Their needs a noun after it, like 'their trophy'; theirs stands alone.

options.label: B
options.text: The trophy is their's.
options.rationale: Possessive pronouns never use an apostrophe.

options.label: C
options.text: The trophy is theirs.

options.label: D
options.text: The trophy is them.
options.rationale: Them is an object pronoun, not a possessive one.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the correct pronoun case after the preposition 'between'?

explanation.whyCorrect: After the preposition between, the object pronoun me is correct.
explanation.tip: Prepositions like between, with, and for are followed by object pronouns.

options.label: A
options.text: Keep this secret between you and I.
options.rationale: After a preposition, use the object pronoun me, not I.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep this secret between yourself and I.
options.rationale: Both pronouns in this sentence are used incorrectly.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep this secret between you and myself.
options.rationale: Myself is reflexive and isn't needed after a preposition here.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep this secret between you and me.

items.stem: Choose the correct pronoun: 'My brother runs faster than ____.'

explanation.whyCorrect: The comparison implies 'than I do,' so the subject pronoun I is correct.
explanation.tip: In comparisons, imagine the missing verb to choose the right pronoun case.

options.label: A
options.text: I

options.label: B
options.text: me
options.rationale: Me would only fit if the meaning were different; here the comparison implies 'than I do.'

options.label: C
options.text: myself
options.rationale: Myself is reflexive and does not fit a comparison like this.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the correct pronoun in a compound object?

explanation.whyCorrect: Her is the object pronoun correctly matching its role as part of the object of 'thanked.'
explanation.tip: Test it: remove 'Rami and' and see which pronoun still sounds right.

options.label: A
options.text: The coach thanked Rami and her for their effort.

options.label: B
options.text: The coach thanked Rami and she for their effort.
options.rationale: She is a subject pronoun; the object of 'thanked' needs her.

options.label: C
options.text: The coach thanked Rami and hers for their effort.
options.rationale: Hers is a possessive pronoun, not an object pronoun.

options.label: D
options.text: The coach thanked Rami and herself for their effort.
options.rationale: Herself is reflexive and isn't needed in this sentence.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the pronoun case after 'as'?

explanation.whyCorrect: He correctly serves as the subject pronoun of the clause 'he is.'
explanation.tip: Comparisons with as...as often need a subject pronoun before a verb.

options.label: A
options.text: Mariam is as tall as him is.
options.rationale: Him is an object pronoun; the comparison needs the subject pronoun he.

options.label: B
options.text: Mariam is as tall as he is.

options.label: C
options.text: Mariam is as tall as hisself.
options.rationale: Hisself is not a standard word.

options.label: D
options.text: Mariam is as tall as he's.
options.rationale: He's means he is, which creates an incomplete comparison here.

items.stem: Which sentence uses pronoun case correctly in all parts?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every pronoun matches its correct role: she as subject, me and her as objects.
explanation.tip: Check each pronoun separately for its job: subject, object, or possessive.

options.label: A
options.text: She gave the notes to Yusuf and I, and we both thanked her.
options.rationale: After 'to,' use the object pronoun me, not I.

options.label: B
options.text: She gave the notes to Yusuf and myself, and we both thanked her.
options.rationale: Myself is reflexive and shouldn't replace me as the object here.

options.label: C
options.text: She gave the notes to Yusuf and me, and we both thanked her.

options.label: D
options.text: Her gave the notes to Yusuf and me, and we both thanked she.
options.rationale: The subject needs she, and the object after 'thanked' needs her.

items.stem: An article says: 'Camels can go for many days without drinking water. Their humps store fat, not water, for energy.' What is the author's main purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article explains facts about how a camel's body helps it survive without water.
explanation.tip: Facts and explanations usually signal a purpose to inform.

options.label: A
options.text: To describe a camel's favorite food
options.rationale: Food is not mentioned in this passage.

options.label: B
options.text: To persuade readers to buy a camel
options.rationale: The article gives facts; it does not try to sell anything.

options.label: C
options.text: To tell a funny story about a camel
options.rationale: There is no story or humor here, only facts.

options.label: D
options.text: To inform readers about how camels survive

items.stem: A flyer reads: 'Join our recycling club today! Together we can keep our playground clean and help the planet.' What is the author's main purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The flyer urges readers to take an action, which is the goal of persuasive writing.
explanation.tip: Words like 'join today' and 'together we can' often signal persuasion.

options.label: A
options.text: To persuade students to join the recycling club

options.label: B
options.text: To describe the playground's size
options.rationale: The playground's size is not described.

options.label: C
options.text: To explain how recycling trucks work
options.rationale: No details about trucks or the recycling process are given.

options.label: D
options.text: To entertain readers with a story about trash
options.rationale: There is no story here, just a call to join.

items.stem: A paragraph reads: 'Rania laughed as the puppy chased its own tail around the yard, tumbling over its own paws.' What is the author's main purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The playful, funny description of the puppy is meant to amuse the reader.
explanation.tip: Humor and playful description usually signal a purpose to entertain.

options.label: A
options.text: To explain how puppies are trained
options.rationale: No training steps are described.

options.label: B
options.text: To entertain readers with a funny moment

options.label: C
options.text: To persuade readers to adopt a puppy
options.rationale: No request to adopt a puppy is made.

options.label: D
options.text: To list facts about dog breeds
options.rationale: No breed facts are mentioned.

items.stem: A science article explains: 'First, water evaporates into the air. Then it cools and forms clouds. Finally, it falls back to Earth as rain.' What is the author's main purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article walks through ordered steps to explain a scientific process.
explanation.tip: Step words like first, then, and finally often signal an explanation.

options.label: A
options.text: To entertain with a story about rain
options.rationale: There is no story here, only a process.

options.label: B
options.text: To describe a rainy day in detail
options.rationale: A specific rainy day is not described.

options.label: C
options.text: To explain the steps of the water cycle

options.label: D
options.text: To persuade readers to save water
options.rationale: No call to save water is made.

items.stem: An article states: 'Studies show that students who read for twenty minutes a day score higher on tests. Parents should set aside reading time every evening.' What is the author's main purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The word 'should' and the call to action show the author wants parents to act.
explanation.tip: Words like 'should' often signal a persuasive purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To entertain with a story about a book
options.rationale: There is no story here, only a recommendation.

options.label: B
options.text: To explain how books are printed
options.rationale: Printing is not mentioned at all.

options.label: C
options.text: To describe a library's layout
options.rationale: No library layout is described.

options.label: D
options.text: To persuade parents to set a daily reading time

items.stem: A travel guide reads: 'The coral reef stretches for miles, filled with bright fish and swaying sea plants.' Why might the author use words like 'bright' and 'swaying'?

explanation.whyCorrect: Vivid, descriptive words help readers imagine the scene clearly.
explanation.tip: Sensory, descriptive words often signal a purpose to describe.

options.label: A
options.text: To help readers picture and feel the scene

options.label: B
options.text: To list scientific facts about coral
options.rationale: No scientific data is given here.

options.label: C
options.text: To explain how coral reproduces
options.rationale: Coral reproduction is not discussed.

options.label: D
options.text: To persuade readers to stop swimming
options.rationale: There is no warning against swimming.

items.stem: An article about bridges begins with the heading 'How Bridges Are Built' and then lists each building step in order. Why does the author use this heading and order?

explanation.whyCorrect: A clear heading and ordered steps make an explanation easier for readers to follow.
explanation.tip: Headings and ordered steps usually support an informative purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To hide the most important details
options.rationale: A clear heading and order make details easier to find, not harder.

options.label: B
options.text: To help readers follow the steps clearly

options.label: C
options.text: To persuade readers to become engineers
options.rationale: No persuasion toward a career is included.

options.label: D
options.text: To entertain readers with a bridge story
options.rationale: There is no story here, only ordered steps.

items.stem: An opinion column ends: 'If we don't act now to protect the park, we may lose it forever. Please speak to your city council today.' What purpose does this ending serve?

explanation.whyCorrect: The direct call to 'speak to your city council' pushes readers toward taking action.
explanation.tip: A direct call to action at the end often reveals a persuasive purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To summarize facts about the park's history
options.rationale: No history facts are summarized here.

options.label: B
options.text: To entertain with a humorous ending
options.rationale: This ending is serious, not funny.

options.label: C
options.text: To urge readers to take action

options.label: D
options.text: To describe what the park looks like in spring
options.rationale: The park's appearance is not described.

items.stem: A nonfiction article about bees includes a diagram labeled 'Parts of a Beehive' next to the text. What is the most likely reason the author included this diagram?

explanation.whyCorrect: A labeled diagram supports the text by showing readers what words alone may not fully capture.
explanation.tip: Diagrams and labels usually support an informative purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To replace the need for any written explanation
options.rationale: The diagram works alongside the text, not instead of it.

options.label: B
options.text: To entertain readers with bee cartoons
options.rationale: A labeled diagram is informative, not a cartoon for fun.

options.label: C
options.text: To persuade readers to keep bees at home
options.rationale: No persuasion to keep bees is included.

options.label: D
options.text: To help readers visualize information that is hard to picture from words alone

items.stem: An author writes an article that begins by describing a dry, cracked field, then explains the science of drought, and ends by asking readers to conserve water. How do the different parts of the article work together?

explanation.whyCorrect: Together, the description, facts, and call to action build a purpose that both informs and persuades.
explanation.tip: A single article can use more than one purpose to build toward its goal.

options.label: A
options.text: The description draws readers in, the facts inform them, and the ending persuades them to act.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the ending matters; the rest is unnecessary.
options.rationale: The description and facts build the case that makes the ending persuasive.

options.label: C
options.text: The parts contradict each other and confuse the main purpose.
options.rationale: The parts build logically toward one combined purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: Each part has the same purpose: only to entertain.
options.rationale: The science and the call to action are not meant simply to entertain.

items.stem: An article states: 'Mangrove trees protect coastlines from erosion by trapping soil with their roots.' What is the author's main purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence explains a factual process, which shows an informative purpose.
explanation.tip: Explaining how or why something happens usually signals an informative purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To describe the taste of mangrove fruit
options.rationale: Taste is never mentioned in this passage.

options.label: B
options.text: To inform readers how mangroves protect coastlines

options.label: C
options.text: To persuade readers to plant mangroves in their yards
options.rationale: No request to plant mangroves is made.

options.label: D
options.text: To entertain with a story about a mangrove forest
options.rationale: There is no story here, only a factual explanation.

items.stem: A letter to a newspaper reads: 'Our town's only pool closes every winter, leaving kids with nowhere safe to swim. The town should build an indoor pool.' What is the author's point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: The letter's final sentence states directly what the author believes the town should do.
explanation.tip: An author's point of view is often stated directly in a claim like 'should.'

options.label: A
options.text: The outdoor pool should stay closed all year.
options.rationale: The author is arguing for a new pool, not for keeping the current one closed.

options.label: B
options.text: Swimming is not important for children.
options.rationale: The letter argues the opposite: that safe swimming matters.

options.label: C
options.text: The town needs an indoor pool.

options.label: D
options.text: The town already has enough pools.
options.rationale: The letter states the town has only one pool and needs another.

items.stem: A nonfiction piece opens: 'Few animals are as misunderstood as the bat. This article will separate bat myths from bat facts.' What is the author's main purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The opening directly states the goal of separating myths from facts.
explanation.tip: An opening sentence that states a goal often reveals the author's purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To entertain with a spooky bat story
options.rationale: There is no spooky story here, only a plan to share facts.

options.label: B
options.text: To persuade readers to fear bats
options.rationale: The article aims to clear up myths, not increase fear.

options.label: C
options.text: To describe a bat's habitat in detail
options.rationale: Habitat is not the stated focus of this opening.

options.label: D
options.text: To correct common misunderstandings about bats with facts

items.stem: An article about recycling uses the phrase 'a staggering 8 million tons of plastic' instead of just 'a lot of plastic.' Why might the author choose this phrase?

explanation.whyCorrect: A dramatic number and word like 'staggering' are chosen to make readers feel the scale of the issue.
explanation.tip: Strong, dramatic word choices often signal a persuasive purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To emphasize the scale of the problem and persuade readers to care

options.label: B
options.text: To entertain readers with a joke about plastic
options.rationale: There is no humor in this serious statistic.

options.label: C
options.text: To describe the shape of plastic waste
options.rationale: Shape is not mentioned in this phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: To simply state a neutral fact with no emotional effect
options.rationale: The word 'staggering' is chosen to create a strong emotional reaction.

items.stem: A science article presents both a scientist's claim that a lake is shrinking and a local fisherman's claim that it looks the same as always. Why might the author include both viewpoints?
