explanation.whyCorrect: Presenting both the scientist's and the fisherman's views gives readers a balanced picture.
explanation.tip: Including multiple viewpoints often signals a fair, informative purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: To persuade readers to stop fishing
options.rationale: No call to stop fishing is made.

options.label: B
options.text: To show readers more than one perspective on the issue

options.label: C
options.text: To prove the fisherman is wrong
options.rationale: Including both views does not argue that one is simply wrong.

options.label: D
options.text: To entertain readers with an argument
options.rationale: This is a balanced report, not entertainment.

items.stem: An author writes: 'Unlike earlier reports, this study used satellite images collected over ten years, giving a clearer picture of the glacier's retreat.' What does this sentence suggest about the author's point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: Describing the new study as giving a 'clearer picture' shows the author views it as more trustworthy.
explanation.tip: Word choices that favor one source over another reveal the author's point of view.

options.label: A
options.text: The author believes glaciers are not actually shrinking.
options.rationale: The sentence describes the glacier's retreat, meaning it is shrinking.

options.label: B
options.text: The author prefers the earlier, shorter studies.
options.rationale: The sentence favors the newer, longer study over earlier ones.

options.label: C
options.text: The author considers this study's evidence more reliable than earlier ones.

options.label: D
options.text: The author thinks satellite images are inaccurate.
options.rationale: The sentence presents satellite images as giving a clearer, more trustworthy picture.

items.stem: A persuasive article about school lunches states facts about nutrition, then adds, 'Isn't it time our cafeteria served meals that actually help kids learn?' What purpose does this question serve?

explanation.whyCorrect: A question like this is designed to make readers agree with the author's opinion.
explanation.tip: Rhetorical questions in persuasive writing are meant to sway the reader's opinion.

options.label: A
options.text: To entertain readers with a riddle
options.rationale: This is a serious argument, not a riddle for fun.

options.label: B
options.text: To simply ask for information the author does not know
options.rationale: The author already states a clear opinion, not a real request for information.

options.label: C
options.text: To summarize the nutrition facts already given
options.rationale: A summary would restate facts, not ask a leading question.

options.label: D
options.text: To push readers emotionally toward agreeing with the author's argument

items.stem: Two articles describe the same new bridge: one calls it 'a stunning achievement that will transform the city,' and the other calls it 'an expensive project that ignored cheaper options.' What do these word choices reveal?

explanation.whyCorrect: Positive words like 'stunning' and negative words like 'expensive... ignored' reveal two different viewpoints.
explanation.tip: Compare word choices across texts to find differing points of view.

options.label: A
options.text: The two authors have different points of view about the bridge.

options.label: B
options.text: The word choices show the bridge has not been built yet.
options.rationale: Nothing about whether the bridge is finished is suggested by the word choices.

options.label: C
options.text: Both authors agree completely about the bridge.
options.rationale: The word choices show clearly opposite opinions about the bridge.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither author has formed an opinion yet.
options.rationale: Both descriptions show a clear, formed opinion.

items.stem: An article about ocean plastic ends with a photo of a turtle caught in a net, captioned only with the turtle's location and species. Why might the author choose a factual caption instead of an emotional one?

explanation.whyCorrect: Letting a powerful image speak for itself can be a persuasive strategy that feels understated.
explanation.tip: Sometimes authors let strong images do the persuading instead of strong words.

options.label: A
options.text: To show the author has no opinion on ocean plastic
options.rationale: Choosing to include this striking photo at all shows the author has a clear purpose.

options.label: B
options.text: To let the image itself persuade readers without seeming to exaggerate

options.label: C
options.text: Because the author ran out of space for more text
options.rationale: A short caption is a deliberate choice, not a space problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Because captions are never allowed to relate to the author's purpose
options.rationale: A caption can absolutely support an author's overall purpose.

items.stem: An author researching a dam project interviews only engineers who built it and does not interview nearby residents who were displaced. How might this choice affect the article's point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: Choosing which people to interview shapes whose perspective the article ultimately reflects.
explanation.tip: Check whose voices are included, and whose are left out, to spot a possible one-sided view.

options.label: A
options.text: The missing interviews have no effect on the article's point of view.
options.rationale: Leaving out an entire group's perspective can significantly shape the article's point of view.

options.label: B
options.text: The article will automatically be balanced because engineers are experts.
options.rationale: Expertise alone does not guarantee a balanced point of view if other voices are left out.

options.label: C
options.text: The article may present a one-sided view that favors the engineers' perspective.

options.label: D
options.text: The article will focus entirely on the residents' experience.
options.rationale: Since no residents were interviewed, their experience would not be the focus.

items.stem: An editorial states: 'Cutting the library's hours will hurt the students who rely on it most. The city council must reconsider this decision.' What is the author's purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: The direct call for the council to 'reconsider' shows the author wants to change their decision.
explanation.tip: A direct call to action toward a specific group often signals persuasion.

options.label: A
options.text: To inform readers about library opening hours
options.rationale: Specific hours are not listed; the focus is on urging a change.

options.label: B
options.text: To describe the library's architecture
options.rationale: The building's design is never mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: To entertain readers with a story set in a library
options.rationale: There is no story here, only an argument.

options.label: D
options.text: To persuade the city council to reverse its decision

items.stem: A science magazine article explains photosynthesis using diagrams, labeled steps, and simple definitions in a side box. What does the format suggest about the author's purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: Using diagrams, labels, and simple definitions together helps break down a complex process for readers.
explanation.tip: Visual aids and definitions usually support a purpose to clearly inform.

options.label: A
options.text: The author wants to make a complex process clear and easy to follow.

options.label: B
options.text: The author is trying to entertain readers with a plant story.
options.rationale: Diagrams and definitions support explanation, not storytelling.

options.label: C
options.text: The author wants to hide the scientific details.
options.rationale: Diagrams, labels, and definitions make details clearer, not hidden.

options.label: D
options.text: The author wants to persuade readers to grow plants.
options.rationale: No call to grow plants is made in this format.

items.stem: An author writes about a factory's history: 'Some say the factory brought jobs; others say it brought pollution that still affects the river today.' What is the author's point of view in this sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mentioning both 'jobs' and 'pollution' equally shows the author is presenting a balanced view.
explanation.tip: Look for balanced wording, like 'some say... others say,' as a sign of a neutral point of view.

options.label: A
options.text: The author strongly supports the factory.
options.rationale: The sentence gives equal weight to both the jobs and the pollution.

options.label: B
options.text: The author is presenting both sides without clearly favoring one.

options.label: C
options.text: The author strongly opposes the factory.
options.rationale: The sentence does not lean only toward criticism; it also mentions jobs.

options.label: D
options.text: The author has no information about the factory's effects.
options.rationale: The sentence shows the author knows about both positive and negative effects.

items.stem: A columnist writes about a new law using phrases like 'common-sense protection' to support it and 'red tape' to describe compliance costs opponents mention. What does this word choice reveal?

explanation.whyCorrect: Calling the law 'common-sense' while dismissing opposing costs as 'red tape' reveals a favorable bias.
explanation.tip: Compare the connotation of words used for each side of an issue.

options.label: A
options.text: The columnist's word choice is completely neutral.
options.rationale: Positive phrases for one side and dismissive phrases for the other show a clear lean.

options.label: B
options.text: The word choice shows no clear point of view.
options.rationale: The contrasting word choices clearly reveal the columnist's favored side.

options.label: C
options.text: The columnist's word choice favors supporters of the law.

options.label: D
options.text: The columnist opposes the new law.
options.rationale: The columnist uses a positive phrase for the law and a dismissive one for its critics.

items.stem: An article on space exploration quotes three scientists who all work for the same space agency and no independent researchers. How might this affect the article's point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: Relying only on sources from one organization can shape the article's point of view toward that group's perspective.
explanation.tip: Notice whether all quoted sources come from the same organization or background.

options.label: A
options.text: Quoting scientists always removes any bias from an article.
options.rationale: Being a scientist does not remove the possibility of a shared institutional perspective.

options.label: B
options.text: The article's point of view cannot be affected by who is quoted.
options.rationale: The choice of whom to quote strongly shapes an article's point of view.

options.label: C
options.text: The article is guaranteed to be completely balanced.
options.rationale: Quoting only people from one agency makes a fully balanced view unlikely.

options.label: D
options.text: The article may lean toward the space agency's own perspective.

items.stem: A historical account states: 'The explorer bravely conquered the unknown wilderness,' while a later textbook states: 'The explorer traveled through land that Indigenous peoples had lived on for generations.' What do these differing descriptions reveal?

explanation.whyCorrect: The contrasting word choices, 'conquered' versus naming the land's original inhabitants, show two different viewpoints.
explanation.tip: Compare how different texts describe the same event to find differing points of view.

options.label: A
options.text: The two texts reflect different points of view about the same event.

options.label: B
options.text: The texts were written by the same author with the same purpose.
options.rationale: The contrasting descriptions suggest different authors with different perspectives.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the second text has any point of view at all.
options.rationale: The first text's word choice, like 'bravely conquered,' also reflects a clear point of view.

options.label: D
options.text: The two texts describe two completely different events.
options.rationale: Both texts describe the same explorer's journey, just from different viewpoints.

items.stem: An author writing about renewable energy includes statistics on cost savings but leaves out statistics on installation challenges that a rival article includes. What might this choice suggest about the author's purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: Selecting only statistics that support one side suggests a persuasive, rather than fully balanced, purpose.
explanation.tip: What an author leaves out can reveal their purpose just as much as what they include.

options.label: A
options.text: The author has no particular purpose in selecting information.
options.rationale: Choosing to include only favorable statistics is itself a meaningful choice.

options.label: B
options.text: The author may be trying to persuade readers by presenting a favorable picture.

options.label: C
options.text: The author is being fully objective by including only costs.
options.rationale: Leaving out challenges while including savings is not a fully objective approach.

options.label: D
options.text: The missing statistics prove renewable energy has no challenges.
options.rationale: Leaving out information does not prove that challenges do not exist.

items.stem: A report on a new policy opens with a personal story about a family affected by it, then presents data, and ends with a call to contact representatives. How do these parts work together to support the author's purpose?

explanation.whyCorrect: Together, the story, data, and call to action build toward persuading readers to take action.
explanation.tip: A text can combine emotional, factual, and direct appeals to build one overall purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: The data is included to confuse readers rather than inform them.
options.rationale: The data is included to support the argument with credible evidence, not to confuse.

options.label: B
options.text: The personal story is only there to entertain, with no connection to persuasion.
options.rationale: The story helps build an emotional case that supports the later call to action.

options.label: C
options.text: The story draws readers in emotionally, the data builds credibility, and the ending persuades them to act.

options.label: D
options.text: Each part is unrelated to the others and serves no shared purpose.
options.rationale: All three parts build logically toward one combined persuasive purpose.

items.stem: Comparing two authors' accounts of the same election, one emphasizes voter turnout numbers while the other emphasizes candidates' personal controversies. What does this comparison best reveal about author's purpose and point of view?

explanation.whyCorrect: The different emphases show how purpose and point of view shape which details an author highlights.
explanation.tip: Compare what two authors choose to emphasize about the same event to spot differing points of view.

options.label: A
options.text: Only one author can be telling the truth about the election.
options.rationale: Both accounts can report true facts while still choosing different emphases.

options.label: B
options.text: The choice of details has no connection to an author's purpose.
options.rationale: What an author chooses to emphasize is directly shaped by their purpose and point of view.

options.label: C
options.text: Both authors must be reporting false information.
options.rationale: Choosing different details to emphasize does not mean either account is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Authors select and emphasize different details based on their purpose and point of view.

items.stem: Which transition word best shows the order of events? “____, Lina fed the chickens. After that, she watered the garden.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “First” tells the reader which chore happened before the others.
explanation.tip: Order words like first, next, then, and finally show the sequence of events.

options.label: A
options.text: First

options.label: B
options.text: Although
options.rationale: “Although” shows a contrast, not a time order.

options.label: C
options.text: Unless
options.rationale: “Unless” shows a condition, not a time order.

options.label: D
options.text: Because
options.rationale: “Because” gives a reason, not the order of events.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a transition word to show that something happened unexpectedly in a story?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Suddenly” signals that an event happened quickly and without warning.
explanation.tip: Words like suddenly and all at once show a surprising moment in a story.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar liked the barn more than the house.
options.rationale: This compares two places and shows no sequence.

options.label: B
options.text: Suddenly, the lights in the barn went out.

options.label: C
options.text: The barn had lights and a loft.
options.rationale: This lists details without any time signal.

options.label: D
options.text: The lights in the barn were yellow.
options.rationale: This only describes the lights; it does not show a surprising moment.

items.stem: Choose the transition that shows time passed overnight: “We camped by the river. ____, the fish were jumping near our tent.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “The next morning” tells the reader a new day has begun.
explanation.tip: Look for words that answer “when,” not “why” or “where.”

options.label: A
options.text: Across the river
options.rationale: This tells where, not when.

options.label: B
options.text: Even though
options.rationale: This shows contrast, not time.

options.label: C
options.text: The next morning

options.label: D
options.text: Because of the rain
options.rationale: This gives a reason, not a time.

items.stem: Choose the transition that shows two things happening at the same time: “Hassan set up the tent. ____, Dalia gathered firewood.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Meanwhile” shows that Dalia's action happened at the same time as Hassan's.
explanation.tip: “Meanwhile” links two events that are happening together.

options.label: A
options.text: Afterward
options.rationale: “Afterward” shows something happened later, not at the same time.

options.label: B
options.text: Because
options.rationale: “Because” gives a reason, not timing.

options.label: C
options.text: Finally
options.rationale: “Finally” shows the last event, not something happening at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: Meanwhile

items.stem: Put the sentences from this camping story in the correct order.

explanation.whyCorrect: The events follow the order they happened: packing, driving, setting up camp, then the campfire.
explanation.tip: Look for time clues like “as the sun set” and “later that night” to find the order.

sequence: Karim packed the tent, flashlight, and snacks into the car.
The family drove two hours to reach the campsite.
As the sun set, Karim helped his father set up the tent.
Later that night, they roasted marshmallows over the fire.

items.stem: A student wrote a story about a lost dog. Put the sentences in the order that tells the story clearly.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences move from the problem, to the search, to a clue, to finding the dog.
explanation.tip: A clear narrative moves step by step from problem to solution.

sequence: Noor noticed that her dog Biscuit had slipped out of the yard.
She searched the street and called his name over and over.
A neighbor said he had seen a small dog near the park.
Noor ran to the park and finally spotted Biscuit chasing a squirrel.

items.stem: Which transition best shows that some time passed before the next event? “Tarek studied the map carefully. ____, he found the trailhead.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Before long” tells the reader that some time passed before Tarek found the trail.
explanation.tip: Phrases like before long and after a while show time passing without being exact.

options.label: A
options.text: Despite this
options.rationale: This shows contrast, not a time gap.

options.label: B
options.text: In other words
options.rationale: This restates an idea; it does not show time.

options.label: C
options.text: Before long

options.label: D
options.text: On the other hand
options.rationale: This shows contrast, not time passing.

items.stem: Choose the transition that shows an event happened at that exact moment: “Salma was about to give up. ____, she spotted the trail marker.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Just then” marks the exact instant the trail marker appeared.
explanation.tip: Just then and right then both signal one precise moment in a story.

options.label: A
options.text: Just then

options.label: B
options.text: On the contrary
options.rationale: This shows disagreement, not a moment in time.

options.label: C
options.text: In general
options.rationale: This makes a broad statement, not a single moment.

options.label: D
options.text: As usual
options.rationale: This shows something that happens often, not one exact moment.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence needs the past-tense verb “ate,” not “eating,” to flow with the other events.
explanation.tip: Check that every event in your sequence uses a matching, correct verb form.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: After “suddenly,” the verb should be the past-tense “started” to match the rest of the story.
explanation.tip: A sequence of events in a story usually stays in one consistent verb tense.

segments: to fall on the tin roof.

items.stem: Which transition best shows that something finally happened after a long search? “Rami checked every shelf in the library. ____, he found the missing book wedged behind a dictionary.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Eventually” shows that the event happened after some time and effort.
explanation.tip: Eventually and finally both signal the end of a long process.

options.label: A
options.text: For instance
options.rationale: This introduces an example, not a time shift.

options.label: B
options.text: On the other hand
options.rationale: This shows contrast, not the end of a search.

options.label: C
options.text: Similarly
options.rationale: This compares two things; it does not show time passing.

options.label: D
options.text: Eventually

items.stem: Choose the transition that shows a new part of the day has begun: “The team practiced all morning. ____, they reviewed the game plan in the gym.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Later that day” shows the second event happened after the first, within the same day.
explanation.tip: Watch for phrases naming a part of the day to track when events happen.

options.label: A
options.text: In contrast
options.rationale: This shows a difference, not a later time.

options.label: B
options.text: Later that day

options.label: C
options.text: For that reason
options.rationale: This gives a cause, not a time shift.

options.label: D
options.text: As a result
options.rationale: This shows a result, not simply a later time.

items.stem: Put these sentences about a school play rehearsal in the order that shows how the afternoon unfolded.

explanation.whyCorrect: The events move from preparation, to a problem, to help, to improvement.
explanation.tip: Look for words like during, just in time, and by the end to find the sequence.

sequence: Mariam arrived early to help set up the stage curtains.
During rehearsal, she forgot her lines and froze for a moment.
Her friend whispered the next line just in time.
By the end of practice, Mariam performed the scene without a single mistake.

items.stem: Which word tells the reader what happened right after the first event? “Yusuf brushed his teeth. ____, he put on his shoes.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Then” shows which action happened right after the first one.
explanation.tip: Then, next, and after that all point to what happens right after.

options.label: A
options.text: Then

options.label: B
options.text: Because
options.rationale: This tells a reason, not what happened next.

options.label: C
options.text: Unless
options.rationale: This shows a condition, not a sequence.

options.label: D
options.text: Although
options.rationale: This shows a contrast, not a time order.

items.stem: In a narrative about a storm, which transition best signals a sudden, surprising shift in the action? “The sky had been calm all afternoon. ____, thunder cracked and the wind tore through the tents.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “All of a sudden” signals an abrupt, unexpected change in the story's action.
explanation.tip: Phrases like all of a sudden and without warning mark sharp shifts in a narrative.

options.label: A
options.text: In the same way
options.rationale: This compares two ideas, not a sudden shift.

options.label: B
options.text: All of a sudden

options.label: C
options.text: As a result
options.rationale: This shows a cause-and-effect link, not surprise.

options.label: D
options.text: To sum up
options.rationale: This signals a conclusion, not a sudden event.

items.stem: Which transition best shows that this is the last event in the story? “We packed the car, said goodbye to the campsite, and ____, we drove home as the sun set.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Finally” signals that this is the last event in the sequence.
explanation.tip: Finally and in the end both mark the close of a sequence of events.

options.label: A
options.text: unless
options.rationale: This shows a condition, not an ending.

options.label: B
options.text: meanwhile
options.rationale: This shows something happening at the same time, not the last step.

options.label: C
options.text: finally

options.label: D
options.text: because

explanation.whyCorrect: “Had been monitoring” emphasizes the ongoing duration of an action before another past event.
explanation.tip: Past perfect progressive highlights how long an action continued before a past event.

options.label: A
options.text: The researchers have been monitoring the volcano for weeks before it erupted.
options.rationale: Present perfect progressive doesn't fit an action that ended before a past event.

options.label: B
options.text: The researchers were monitoring the volcano for weeks before it erupted.
options.rationale: Past progressive alone doesn't emphasize the duration leading up to the past event as clearly as the past perfect progressive.

options.label: C
options.text: The researchers monitored the volcano for weeks before it erupted.
options.rationale: Simple past doesn't emphasize the ongoing duration of the action.

options.label: D
options.text: The researchers had been monitoring the volcano for weeks before it erupted.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The rest of the sentence is in the past tense, so “concluded” keeps the verb tense consistent.
explanation.tip: Check that all verbs describing one event stay in the same tense unless there's a clear reason to shift.

items.stem: The sentence “I wish I were taller” correctly uses the subjunctive mood to express a wish contrary to fact.

explanation.whyCorrect: The subjunctive “were” (instead of “was”) is used after “wish” to describe something that is not true.
explanation.tip: After verbs like wish, the subjunctive mood often uses “were” even with singular subjects.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph, then answer the question.

“Our school should add ten more minutes to recess. Students come back from recess more focused and ready to learn. Teachers have noticed fewer disruptions in the afternoon when recess is longer. A longer recess also gives students more time for exercise.”

What is the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first sentence states exactly what the author wants to happen.
explanation.tip: An author's claim is often stated clearly in the first sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Recess should be ten minutes longer.

options.label: B
options.text: Students are unfocused in class.
options.rationale: This is a problem the author mentions, not the main claim.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers dislike disruptions.
options.rationale: This is a supporting detail, not the claim.

options.label: D
options.text: Exercise is good for students.
options.rationale: This is one reason given, not the overall claim.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Our classroom should get a pet fish. A fish teaches students responsibility because someone must feed it every day. Watching a fish swim can also calm students who feel nervous before a test. Fish are also easy to care for compared to other classroom pets.”

Which sentence gives a REASON that supports the claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence gives a specific reason—teaching responsibility—that supports getting a fish.
explanation.tip: A reason explains WHY the claim should be true.

options.label: A
options.text: Fish live in water.
options.rationale: This fact is not in the paragraph and does not support the claim.

options.label: B
options.text: A fish teaches students responsibility because someone must feed it every day.

options.label: C
options.text: Students enjoy recess.
options.rationale: This is unrelated to the claim about a classroom pet.

options.label: D
options.text: Our classroom should get a pet fish.
options.rationale: This states the claim, not a reason.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Teachers should not assign homework on weekends. Weekends are the only time many students have to spend with family. Some students also use weekends for sports practice or chores. Without weekend homework, students return to school on Monday feeling rested.”

Which detail would make the author's argument STRONGER?

explanation.whyCorrect: Evidence connecting the claim directly to test scores would give the strongest, most convincing support.
explanation.tip: Strong evidence directly connects to the claim, often with facts or data.

options.label: A
options.text: A list of students' favorite weekend activities.
options.rationale: This does not provide evidence that homework affects learning.

options.label: B
options.text: A story about a teacher who loves assigning homework.
options.rationale: This opposes the author's claim rather than supporting it.

options.label: C
options.text: A study showing that students who skip weekend homework score just as well on tests.

options.label: D
options.text: A description of what homework usually looks like.
options.rationale: This does not support the claim that weekend homework should stop.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Every school should offer a free breakfast. Students who eat breakfast pay better attention in morning classes. Free breakfast also means no student has to start the day hungry. Some families cannot afford to buy breakfast every morning.”

Which sentence is the author's CLAIM?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence states exactly what the author believes every school should do.
explanation.tip: Ask: what action does the author want readers to agree with?

options.label: A
options.text: Students who eat breakfast pay better attention.
options.rationale: This is a reason supporting the claim, not the claim itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Some families cannot afford breakfast.
options.rationale: This explains a problem, but it is not the main claim.

options.label: C
options.text: No student should start the day hungry.
options.rationale: This restates part of a reason, not the author's overall claim.

options.label: D
options.text: Every school should offer a free breakfast.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Middle schools should start classes later in the morning. Studies show that many students do not get enough sleep when school starts too early. Starting later would help students arrive more alert and ready to learn. However, some parents worry a later start would make after-school pickup harder.”

Which sentence shows the author addressing a counterargument?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence presents a concern from the other side of the argument—a counterargument.
explanation.tip: Look for words like however or but that often introduce an opposing view.

options.label: A
options.text: However, some parents worry a later start would make after-school pickup harder.

options.label: B
options.text: Middle schools should start classes later in the morning.
options.rationale: This is the claim, not a counterargument.

options.label: C
options.text: Starting later would help students arrive more alert.
options.rationale: This supports the claim rather than opposing it.

options.label: D
options.text: Studies show that many students do not get enough sleep.
options.rationale: This is supporting evidence, not an opposing view.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph, then choose ALL the reasons the author uses to support the claim.

“Our school should start a recycling program. Recycling would reduce the amount of trash sent to landfills each week. It would also teach students habits that help protect the environment. In addition, a recycling program could save the school money on trash collection fees.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The author gives three separate reasons: less landfill trash, better habits, and saved money.
explanation.tip: Count how many distinct reasons the author lists after stating the claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Recycling would reduce the amount of trash sent to landfills each week.

options.label: B
options.text: a recycling program could save the school money on trash collection fees

options.label: C
options.text: Our school should start a recycling program.
options.rationale: This is the claim itself, not one of the supporting reasons.

options.label: D
options.text: It would also teach students habits that help protect the environment.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Students should be allowed to vote for changes to the lunch menu. A recent survey found that most students throw away food they dislike, wasting both money and food. Giving students a vote would likely reduce this waste because the menu would better match their preferences. A cafeteria manager at another school reported a 20 percent drop in wasted food after students began voting on menu items.”

Which piece of evidence is the STRONGEST support for the claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: A real example with a specific result from another school gives the most convincing, concrete evidence.
explanation.tip: The strongest evidence is specific and shows that something similar already worked.

options.label: A
options.text: Students should be allowed to vote for changes to the lunch menu.
options.rationale: This is the claim, not evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: A cafeteria manager at another school reported a 20 percent drop in wasted food after students began voting on menu items.

options.label: C
options.text: A recent survey found that most students throw away food they dislike.
options.rationale: This shows a problem exists but does not prove that voting would fix it.

options.label: D
options.text: Giving students a vote would likely reduce this waste.
options.rationale: This is a prediction, not evidence that it has actually worked.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Our school needs smaller class sizes. Students learn best when teachers can give each child individual attention, which is harder in crowded classrooms. Smaller classes would also let teachers notice when a student is struggling before it becomes a bigger problem.”

Which detail would be the WEAKEST support for this claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: A detail about decorating has nothing to do with class size helping students learn, so it would weaken rather than strengthen the argument.
explanation.tip: Weak support strays from the actual claim being made.

options.label: A
options.text: Students learn best with individual attention from teachers.
options.rationale: This directly connects to why smaller classes would help.

options.label: B
options.text: Teachers can notice struggling students sooner in smaller classes.
options.rationale: This directly supports the benefit of smaller classes.

options.label: C
options.text: Many teachers say they enjoy decorating their classrooms.

options.label: D
options.text: Crowded classrooms make individual attention difficult.
options.rationale: This explains the problem that smaller classes would solve.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The city should build a skate park near the community center. Teenagers currently skateboard in the parking lot, which city officials say has caused several near-accidents with cars. A skate park would give teens a safe place to practice. Some nearby residents argue a skate park would bring noise and crowds to their quiet street.”

How does the author handle the opposing view about noise and crowds?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph states the concern about noise and crowds but stops without answering it, so the opposing view is acknowledged but not yet resolved.
explanation.tip: Not every text that mentions a counterargument goes on to refute it—check carefully.

options.label: A
options.text: The author provides data proving the opposing view is false.
options.rationale: No data is given to counter the concern about noise and crowds.

options.label: B
options.text: The author agrees that the skate park should not be built.
options.rationale: The author's claim is clearly that the park should be built.

options.label: C
options.text: The author ignores the opposing view completely.
options.rationale: The opposing view is stated directly in the final sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The author mentions it directly but does not yet offer a response to it.

items.stem: True or false: In the sentence “A new crosswalk would make it safer for students to cross the busy street near school,” the author is stating a REASON that supports a claim, not the claim itself.

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence explains WHY a crosswalk is needed, which functions as a supporting reason rather than the claim.
explanation.tip: Reasons usually begin with or imply “because” and explain the claim.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The school library should stay open an extra hour after school. Many students do not have internet access at home for research. Students who stay late to study report getting better grades on projects that require research. An extra hour would give more students a quiet place to work.”

What is the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first sentence states exactly what change the author wants.
explanation.tip: The claim is the main point the whole paragraph is built around.

options.label: A
options.text: The school library should stay open an extra hour after school.

options.label: B
options.text: Many students lack internet access at home.
options.rationale: This is a reason, not the claim itself.

options.label: C
options.text: A quiet place helps students focus.
options.rationale: This explains a benefit, but it is not the main claim.

options.label: D
options.text: Students who stay late get better grades.
options.rationale: This is supporting evidence, not the overall claim.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Our school should stop selling plastic water bottles in the cafeteria. Plastic bottles make up a large share of the trash collected on campus each week. Students could instead refill reusable bottles at the new water fountains. However, some students worry that reusable bottles are easy to forget at home.”

Which sentence presents a COUNTERARGUMENT to the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence raises a concern from the other side of the issue, which is a counterargument.
explanation.tip: Signal words like however often introduce a counterargument.

options.label: A
options.text: Plastic bottles make up a large share of the trash collected on campus.
options.rationale: This supports the claim rather than opposing it.

options.label: B
options.text: However, some students worry that reusable bottles are easy to forget at home.

options.label: C
options.text: Students could instead refill reusable bottles at the new water fountains.
options.rationale: This offers a solution supporting the claim, not an opposing view.

options.label: D
options.text: Our school should stop selling plastic water bottles in the cafeteria.
options.rationale: This is the claim itself.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“All high school students should complete twenty hours of community service before graduating. Volunteering helps students build skills like teamwork and responsibility that a classroom alone cannot teach. Several local colleges also give extra consideration to applicants who have volunteered. A few students argue that mandatory service feels less meaningful than service chosen freely.”

Which piece of evidence is the LEAST relevant support for the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence raises an objection to the claim rather than supporting it, making it the least relevant as support.
explanation.tip: Separate evidence that supports the claim from objections that challenge it.

options.label: A
options.text: Several local colleges give extra consideration to applicants who have volunteered.
options.rationale: This gives a concrete benefit that supports the claim.

options.label: B
options.text: All high school students should complete twenty hours of community service.
options.rationale: This is the claim itself, not a piece of evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: A few students argue that mandatory service feels less meaningful than service chosen freely.

options.label: D
options.text: Volunteering helps students build skills like teamwork and responsibility.
options.rationale: This directly supports why service should be required.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Schools should switch to a year-round calendar with shorter, more frequent breaks. Teachers report that students forget less material over a two-week break than over a ten-week summer. Shorter breaks spread throughout the year could also reduce teacher burnout from long, uninterrupted stretches of teaching. Critics point out that families would need to adjust vacation plans.”

How does the author acknowledge the opposing view?

explanation.whyCorrect: The last sentence states a real concern from critics, showing the author considered the other side.
explanation.tip: Acknowledging an opposing view means stating it clearly, even without fully answering it.

options.label: A
options.text: By proving that families prefer year-round school.
options.rationale: No proof like this is given in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: By arguing that vacations are not important to families.
options.rationale: The author does not dismiss vacations; the sentence simply notes an adjustment is needed.

options.label: C
options.text: By ignoring any possible objections.
options.rationale: The final sentence directly raises an objection.

options.label: D
options.text: By noting that families would need to adjust vacation plans.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph, then choose ALL the reasons the author uses to support the claim.

“The city should add protected bike lanes along Market Street. Three cyclists were injured on that street last year due to a lack of separation from traffic. A protected lane would also encourage more students to bike to school instead of being driven, reducing morning traffic near the school. Nearby cities that added similar lanes saw bike use double within a year.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The author gives three separate reasons: past injuries, reduced traffic, and results from nearby cities.
explanation.tip: A claim is the main idea; reasons are the separate points that back it up.

options.label: A
options.text: A protected lane would also encourage more students to bike to school instead of being driven, reducing morning traffic near the school.

options.label: B
options.text: Nearby cities that added similar lanes saw bike use double within a year.

options.label: C
options.text: Three cyclists were injured on that street last year due to a lack of separation from traffic.

options.label: D
options.text: The city should add protected bike lanes along Market Street.
options.rationale: This states the claim itself, not a supporting reason.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The district should restore funding for middle school music programs. Research cited in the district's own report links music participation to improved focus in other subjects, including math. A parent group collected over four hundred signatures supporting the program's return. One parent simply said, ‘My daughter loved band class.’”

Which piece of evidence provides the WEAKEST support for the claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: A single parent's personal opinion is far less convincing than research or a large petition.
explanation.tip: Personal opinions are weaker evidence than data or widely shared results.

options.label: A
options.text: One parent simply said, ‘My daughter loved band class.’

options.label: B
options.text: Research links music participation to improved focus in other subjects.
options.rationale: This is strong evidence because it connects music directly to academic benefits.

options.label: C
options.text: A parent group collected over four hundred signatures supporting the program.
options.rationale: This shows measurable, widespread support for the claim.

options.label: D
options.text: The district should restore funding for middle school music programs.
options.rationale: This is the claim itself, not evidence.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Teachers should be allowed to collect phones at the start of each class. A district-wide study found that classrooms with a no-phone policy had fewer reported distractions during lessons. Students also completed in-class assignments faster when phones were stored away. Some students argue they need their phones in case of a family emergency.”

Which sentence is the author's central claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence states the specific policy change the author is arguing for.
explanation.tip: The central claim usually appears early and states the change the author wants.

options.label: A
options.text: A district-wide study found fewer distractions with a no-phone policy.
options.rationale: This is supporting evidence, not the overall claim.

options.label: B
options.text: Teachers should be allowed to collect phones at the start of each class.

options.label: C
options.text: Some students argue they need their phones for emergencies.
options.rationale: This is a counterargument, not the author's claim.

options.label: D
options.text: Students completed assignments faster without phones.
options.rationale: This is a supporting detail, not the central claim.

items.stem: True or false: In the paragraph “The school should offer free tutoring twice a week. Test scores in math dropped last year across every grade level. Tutoring could help close the gap for students who are struggling the most,” the sentence about dropping test scores functions as evidence that the problem the claim addresses is real, not as the claim itself.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence about test scores explains WHY tutoring is needed, serving as supporting evidence rather than the claim.
explanation.tip: Evidence explains or proves a claim; it does not state the claim itself.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Vending machines at school should only sell healthy snacks. Students who ate the current vending machine snacks reported feeling sluggish by the end of the school day, according to a student health survey. Nutritionists hired by the district recommended removing sugary snacks entirely. A few students worry that healthy snacks will cost more than the current options.”

Which detail would make the author's argument even STRONGER?

explanation.whyCorrect: Addressing the cost concern directly with real numbers would remove the strongest objection and strengthen the case.
explanation.tip: The strongest additional evidence directly answers the opposing concern raised in the text.

options.label: A
options.text: A description of what the vending machines look like.
options.rationale: This is unrelated to whether the snacks should change.

options.label: B
options.text: A quote from a student who dislikes vegetables.
options.rationale: This works against the claim rather than strengthening it.

options.label: C
options.text: The actual price comparison showing that healthy snacks would cost about the same as current options.

options.label: D
options.text: A list of which snacks are currently sold in the machines.
options.rationale: This describes the current situation but does not strengthen the case for changing it.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The district should install solar panels on every school roof. Panels installed at two pilot schools cut electricity costs by nearly thirty percent within the first year. The savings could be redirected toward classroom supplies and technology. Installing panels does require a significant upfront cost, which some board members see as a drawback.”

Which sentence most clearly states the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence states the specific action the author wants the district to take.
explanation.tip: A claim is a specific, arguable statement the rest of the text supports.

options.label: A
options.text: The savings could be redirected toward classroom supplies.
options.rationale: This describes a benefit, not the central claim.

options.label: B
options.text: Panels installed at two pilot schools cut electricity costs by nearly thirty percent.
options.rationale: This is evidence supporting the claim, not the claim itself.

options.label: C
options.text: Installing panels does require a significant upfront cost.
options.rationale: This acknowledges a drawback, not the author's claim.

options.label: D
options.text: The district should install solar panels on every school roof.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Schools should ban the sale of energy drinks to students under sixteen. Pediatric health groups warn that high caffeine levels can cause heart palpitations and sleep problems in young teens. Several nearby districts have already removed energy drinks from vending machines without complaints from students. A small number of older teens argue they should be allowed to choose their own drinks.”

Which sentence functions as a counterargument the author includes?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence introduces a view opposing the ban, which is a counterargument.
explanation.tip: A counterargument represents a view that disagrees with the author's claim.

options.label: A
options.text: A small number of older teens argue they should be allowed to choose their own drinks.

options.label: B
options.text: Schools should ban the sale of energy drinks to students under sixteen.
options.rationale: This is the claim.

options.label: C
options.text: Several nearby districts have already removed energy drinks without complaints.
options.rationale: This supports the claim by showing the change works elsewhere.

options.label: D
options.text: Pediatric health groups warn that high caffeine levels can cause health problems.
options.rationale: This supports the claim rather than opposing it.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The passing period between classes should be extended from four minutes to six. Hallway monitors report that the current four minutes forces students to rush, leading to more minor injuries from collisions. Teachers note that students often arrive late and miss the first few minutes of instruction. Extending the passing period would reduce the total instructional minutes in the school day by about twelve minutes.”

Which sentence works AGAINST the strength of the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence reveals a real cost of the proposal, which weakens rather than strengthens the overall argument.
explanation.tip: A strong analysis of an argument notices details that complicate or weaken the claim, not just the ones that support it.

options.label: A
options.text: Hallway monitors report more minor injuries from rushing.
options.rationale: This supports the claim by describing a real problem.

options.label: B
options.text: Extending the passing period would reduce the total instructional minutes in the school day by about twelve minutes.

options.label: C
options.text: Teachers note that students often arrive late and miss instruction.
options.rationale: This supports the claim by describing another real problem.

options.label: D
options.text: The passing period should be extended from four minutes to six.
options.rationale: This is the claim itself.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The school board should add security cameras to the main hallways. A survey of similar schools found that hallway incidents, such as fights and vandalism, dropped by nearly forty percent after cameras were installed. Cameras would also help staff resolve disputes more quickly by reviewing footage instead of relying only on student accounts. Some students worry that constant monitoring would make the school feel less welcoming.”

Is the evidence in this paragraph SUFFICIENT to fully support the claim, or does it leave out an important consideration?

explanation.whyCorrect: Strong evaluation of an argument notices what is missing, such as cost, which is central to any real decision about installing cameras.
explanation.tip: Evaluate not just what evidence is given, but what important information might be missing.

options.label: A
options.text: The evidence is fully sufficient because it addresses every possible concern.
options.rationale: The paragraph does not mention cost, a major factor in any school board decision.

options.label: B
options.text: The evidence is insufficient because it ignores the opinions of teachers entirely.
options.rationale: The paragraph focuses on student safety data and student concerns, which is a reasonable scope, even though cost is still missing.

options.label: C
options.text: It leaves out cost information, such as how much the cameras and their monitoring would cost the district.

options.label: D
options.text: The evidence is insufficient because it never explains what cameras are.
options.rationale: A definition of cameras is unnecessary; the reader already understands what they are.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph, then choose ALL the reasons the author uses to support the claim.

“The district should replace printed textbooks with tablets in every classroom. Tablets can be updated instantly when information changes, unlike textbooks that stay outdated for years. A pilot program at one middle school reported that tablets weigh far less than a backpack full of textbooks, reducing complaints about back strain. The pilot program also saved the district printing costs after the first year.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The author gives three distinct reasons: faster updates, lighter weight, and lower long-term cost.
explanation.tip: Separate the main claim from each individual reason that supports it.

options.label: A
options.text: A pilot program at one middle school reported that tablets weigh far less than a backpack full of textbooks, reducing complaints about back strain.

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot program also saved the district printing costs after the first year.

options.label: C
options.text: The district should replace printed textbooks with tablets in every classroom.
options.rationale: This is the claim itself, not one of the supporting reasons.

options.label: D
options.text: Tablets can be updated instantly when information changes, unlike textbooks that stay outdated for years.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“Our school should prioritize building a new gym over renovating the cafeteria. The current gym cannot fit the entire student body for assemblies, forcing the school to split events across two days. Renovating the cafeteria, while nice, would mainly improve appearance rather than solve a functional problem. However, the cafeteria renovation has already been approved and partially funded.”

Which sentence most directly undermines the author's claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: This fact about existing approval and funding creates a practical obstacle to the author's proposed priority, undermining the claim.
explanation.tip: Look for facts that create real obstacles to what the author is proposing.

options.label: A
options.text: Renovating the cafeteria would mainly improve appearance rather than solve a problem.
options.rationale: This supports the claim by downplaying the alternative project.

options.label: B
options.text: The current gym cannot fit the entire student body for assemblies.
options.rationale: This supports the claim by describing a real functional problem.

options.label: C
options.text: Our school should prioritize building a new gym over renovating the cafeteria.
options.rationale: This is the claim itself.

options.label: D
options.text: However, the cafeteria renovation has already been approved and partially funded.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The state should reduce the number of standardized tests given each year. Teachers report spending nearly three weeks of class time on test preparation and testing itself. A national study found no strong link between the number of tests given and overall student achievement. Supporters of frequent testing argue that it helps identify struggling students early.”

How does the author respond to the idea that frequent testing helps identify struggling students early?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph states the opposing view in its final sentence but does not go on to argue against it directly.
explanation.tip: Notice when a text raises an opposing view but leaves it unanswered, rather than assuming it is always refuted.

options.label: A
options.text: The author does not directly respond to it; the paragraph ends by simply stating that view.

options.label: B
options.text: The author suggests testing should be increased instead of reduced.
options.rationale: This contradicts the stated claim at the start of the paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: The author fully agrees that frequent testing is the best way to identify struggling students.
options.rationale: This contradicts the author's claim that testing should be reduced.

options.label: D
options.text: The author provides a study proving that idea is completely false.
options.rationale: The cited study is about achievement overall, not specifically about identifying struggling students.

items.stem: True or false: In the paragraph “The school should allow students to wear any color sneakers instead of requiring plain white ones. A survey found that ninety percent of students support the change. Allowing more color choices would not affect learning in any measurable way,” the survey result functions as evidence rather than as the claim itself.

explanation.whyCorrect: The survey result supports the claim about sneaker color by showing student opinion, but it is not the claim itself.
explanation.tip: Evidence provides support for a claim; it is a separate sentence from the claim.

items.stem:
Read the paragraph.

“The high school should begin charging fifty dollars per semester for student parking permits. Visitor parking has become scarce because so many students drive to school. The fee could fund needed repaves of cracked and uneven sections of the lot. A small number of students who rely on cars for part-time jobs say the fee would be a financial burden for them.”

Which evaluation of this argument is most accurate?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph presents real reasons for the fee and acknowledges a concern, but it never resolves the hardship the fee could cause for some students.
explanation.tip: A careful evaluation checks whether a raised concern is actually resolved, not just mentioned.

options.label: A
options.text: The argument is irrelevant because parking has nothing to do with school operations.
options.rationale: Parking directly affects the school's lot conditions and visitor access, making it relevant.

options.label: B
options.text: The argument gives relevant reasons for the fee but does not address how it might affect students who truly cannot afford it.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument fully resolves every concern, including cost for low-income students.
options.rationale: The paragraph raises the cost concern but never proposes a solution for it, such as a reduced fee.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is completely one-sided and ignores any opposing view.
options.rationale: The paragraph does include a concern from students who rely on cars for jobs.

items.stem: What does the word “unfair” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Un-” reverses the meaning of “fair.”
explanation.tip: The prefix un- usually means “not.”

options.label: A
options.text: extremely fair
options.rationale: Un- does not add intensity; it reverses meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: very fair
options.rationale: “Un-” means not, so this is the opposite meaning.

options.label: C

options.label: D

items.stem: Choose the word that means “to heat again before eating”: “Mama will ____ the soup for dinner.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Re-” means again, so “reheat” means to heat again.
explanation.tip: The prefix re- usually means “again.”

options.label: A
options.text: reheat

options.label: B
options.text: misheat
options.rationale: “Mis-” means wrongly, not again.

options.label: C
options.text: unheat
options.rationale: This is not a real word formed this way.

options.label: D
options.text: preheat
options.rationale: “Pre-” means before, which doesn't fit this sentence—she's warming already-cooked soup again.

items.stem: What does “misbehave” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Mis-” means wrongly or badly.
explanation.tip: The prefix mis- usually means “wrongly.”

options.label: A
options.text: to behave extremely well
options.rationale: This is the opposite of what mis- signals.

options.label: B
options.text: to not behave at all
options.rationale: “Mis-” means wrongly, not “not at all.”

options.label: C
options.text: to behave again
options.rationale: That meaning uses the prefix re-, not mis-.

options.label: D
options.text: to behave in the wrong way

items.stem: Choose the word that means “to cook food before the main cooking step”: “Chefs often ____ vegetables before adding them to the stew.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Pre-” means before, so “precook” means to cook beforehand.
explanation.tip: The prefix pre- usually means “before.”

options.label: A
options.text: recook
options.rationale: “Re-” means again, not before.

options.label: B
options.text: precook

options.label: C
options.text: overcook
options.rationale: “Over-” means too much, not before.

options.label: D
options.text: undercook
options.rationale: “Under-” means not enough, not before.

items.stem: The captain gave the sailors a forecast of the coming storm. What does the prefix fore- contribute to a word like “forecast” or “forewarn”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Fore- attaches to a base word to show the action happens beforehand, as in warning or predicting ahead of time.
explanation.tip: The prefix fore- usually means “before” or “ahead of time.”

options.label: A
options.text: It signals that something happens ahead of time, earlier than the main event.

options.label: B
options.text: It signals that an event repeats itself.
options.rationale: Repetition describes re-, a completely different prefix.

options.label: C
options.text: It signals opposition to the main event.
options.rationale: Opposing something describes anti-, a completely different prefix.

options.label: D
options.text: It signals that an amount is insufficient.
options.rationale: A shortage in amount describes under-, a completely different prefix.

items.stem: What does “nonfiction” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Non-” means not, so “nonfiction” means not fiction.
explanation.tip: The prefix non- usually means “not.”

options.label: A
options.text: writing that is made up, like a fantasy story
options.rationale: This describes fiction, the opposite of nonfiction.

options.label: B
options.text: writing that is not made up; it is true

options.label: C
options.text: writing that is written again
options.rationale: That meaning uses re-, not non-.

options.label: D
options.text: writing that is too long
options.rationale: The length of writing has nothing to do with the prefix non-.

items.stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each prefix changes the meaning of the base word in a specific, consistent way.
explanation.tip: Learning common prefix meanings helps you figure out new words.

items.stem: What does “subway” suggest using the prefix sub- (meaning under)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Sub-” means under, matching an underground train system.
explanation.tip: The prefix sub- usually means “under” or “below.”

options.label: A
options.text: a train system that runs above the ground
options.rationale: “Sub-” means under, not above.

options.label: B

options.rationale: This matches a different, unrelated meaning of the word “sub,” not the prefix sub-.

options.label: C
options.text: a train system that runs under the ground

options.label: D

options.rationale: The prefix sub- says nothing about timing.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “larger than normal size”: “Scientists discovered a ____ star many times bigger than our sun.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Super-” means above or beyond normal, matching an unusually large star.
explanation.tip: The prefix super- usually means “above” or “beyond.”

options.label: A
options.text: antigiant
options.rationale: “Anti-” means against, which does not fit this meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: regiant
options.rationale: This is not a real word formed with a meaningful prefix.

options.label: C
options.text: supergiant

options.label: D
options.text: subgiant
options.rationale: “Sub-” means under or smaller, the opposite of what the sentence describes.

items.stem: What does the prefix anti- mean in “antifreeze”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Anti-” means against, so “antifreeze” works against freezing.
explanation.tip: The prefix anti- usually means “against.”

options.label: A
options.text: again
options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix re-, not anti-.

options.label: B
options.text: before
options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix pre-, not anti-.

options.label: C
options.text: together
options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix co-, not anti-.

options.label: D
options.text: against

items.stem: Choose the word that means “to write down automatically from speech”: “The program can ____ the entire interview in minutes.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Trans-” means across, matching the act of converting speech across into written form.
explanation.tip: The prefix trans- usually means “across” or “over.”

options.label: A
options.text: subscribe
options.rationale: This means to sign up for something, which does not fit this context.

options.label: B
options.text: prescribe
options.rationale: This means to officially recommend, which does not fit this context.

options.label: C
options.text: describe
options.rationale: This means to explain in words, not to convert speech into writing.

options.label: D
options.text: transcribe

items.stem: What does “cooperate” mean, using the prefix co- (meaning together)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Co-” means together, matching working jointly with others.
explanation.tip: The prefix co- usually means “together.”

options.label: A
options.text: to work together with someone

options.label: B
options.text: to work against someone
options.rationale: This is the opposite meaning of the prefix co-.

options.label: C
options.text: to stop working completely
options.rationale: The prefix co- has nothing to do with stopping.

options.label: D
options.text: to work alone without help
options.rationale: Co- signals joining others, not working alone.

items.stem: What does the word “postwar” mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Post-” means after, so “postwar” means after a war.
explanation.tip: The prefix post- usually means “after.”

options.label: A
options.text: happening during a war
options.rationale: Post- specifically means after, not during.

options.label: B
options.text: happening after a war

options.label: C
options.text: happening instead of a war
options.rationale: The prefix post- does not suggest a replacement.

options.label: D
options.text: happening before a war
options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix pre-, not post-.

items.stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each of these prefixes comes from Latin or Greek roots and changes a word's meaning in a predictable way.
explanation.tip: Recognizing these prefixes can help you guess the meaning of unfamiliar words.

items.stem: What does the prefix inter- mean in “international”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Inter-” means between or among, matching relations between nations.
explanation.tip: The prefix inter- usually means “between” or “among.”

options.label: B

options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix ultra- or trans-, not inter-.

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix circum-, not inter-.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “within the walls of one school”: “The debate was an ____ competition between classes rather than against other schools.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Intra-” means within, matching a competition held inside one school.
explanation.tip: The prefix intra- usually means “within.”

options.label: A
options.text: intramural

options.label: B
options.text: extramural
options.rationale: “Extra-” means outside, the opposite of within one school.

options.label: C
options.text: contramural
options.rationale: This is not a standard word formed this way.

options.label: D
options.text: intermural
options.rationale: This incorrectly combines inter- with the wrong root for this context.

items.stem: What does the word “hyperactive” mean, using the prefix hyper- (meaning excessive or over)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hyper-” means excessive, matching an unusually high level of activity.
explanation.tip: The prefix hyper- usually means “excessive” or “over.”

options.label: A
options.text: active only at night
options.rationale: The prefix hyper- says nothing about timing.

options.label: B
options.text: not active in any way
options.rationale: This is nearly the opposite of what hyper- signals.

options.label: C

options.rationale: That meaning would fit the prefix hypo-, which means under, not hyper-.

options.label: D
options.text: unusually and excessively active

items.stem: What does the prefix contra- mean in “contradict”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Contra-” means against, matching speaking against or opposite to something said.
explanation.tip: The prefix contra- usually means “against” or “opposite.”

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: together
options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix co-, not contra-.

options.label: C
options.text: before
options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix pre-, not contra-.

options.label: D
options.text: under
options.rationale: That meaning belongs to the prefix sub-, not contra-.

items.stem: Choose the word that means “a condition of having lower than normal body temperature”: “Doctors treated the hiker for severe ____ after the storm.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hypo-” means under or below, matching a dangerously low body temperature.
explanation.tip: The prefix hypo- usually means “under” or “below normal.”

options.label: A
options.text: thermohypo
options.rationale: This is not a correctly formed English word.

options.label: B
options.text: hypothermia

options.label: C

options.rationale: “Hyper-” means excessive, which would describe an unusually high temperature, not a low one.

options.label: D
