options.rationale: This term is not used to describe this medical condition.

items.stem: Match each prefix with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: These prefixes come from Latin roots and appear often in English science and everyday vocabulary.
explanation.tip: Breaking a long word into its prefix and root can reveal its meaning.

items.stem: Which sentence is the BEST topic sentence for a paragraph about why bees are important to gardens?

explanation.whyCorrect: A topic sentence gives a general statement that introduces the paragraph's main focus.
explanation.tip: Ask: does this sentence cover the WHOLE paragraph, or just one detail?

options.label: A
options.text: My aunt has a garden full of roses.
options.rationale: This is a personal detail, not a general introduction to the topic.

options.label: B
options.text: Bees help gardens grow by carrying pollen from flower to flower.

options.label: C
options.text: Gardens need water every day.
options.rationale: This sentence does not even mention bees, so it does not introduce the topic.

options.label: D
options.text: Bees have six legs.
options.rationale: This is too narrow—it is a detail, not an introduction.

items.stem: A paragraph explains that camels can close their nostrils in sandstorms, store fat in their humps, and have wide feet that don't sink in sand. Which added sentence does NOT belong in this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: A personal story about a zoo visit does not relate to how camels survive the desert.
explanation.tip: Every sentence in an informative paragraph should support the main topic.

options.label: A
options.text: Camels can close their nostrils during sandstorms.
options.rationale: This fits the paragraph's focus on desert survival, so it belongs.

options.label: B
options.text: A camel's hump stores fat, not water.
options.rationale: This fits the paragraph's focus on desert survival, so it belongs.

options.label: C
options.text: My brother visited a zoo last summer.

options.label: D
options.text: Thick eyelashes keep sand out of a camel's eyes.
options.rationale: This fits the paragraph's focus on desert survival, so it belongs.

items.stem: Which sentence is the BEST topic sentence for a paragraph about volcanoes?

explanation.whyCorrect: A good topic sentence states the paragraph's main focus before the details appear.
explanation.tip: Topic sentences are broad enough to introduce every detail that follows.

options.label: A
options.text: Rocks are hard.
options.rationale: This is too general and does not focus on volcanoes specifically.

options.label: B
options.text: Lava can reach temperatures of 1,200 degrees Celsius.
options.rationale: This is a supporting detail, not a general introduction.

options.label: C
options.text: Mount Vesuvius erupted long ago.
options.rationale: This is one specific example, too narrow for a topic sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: Volcanoes change the land in dramatic ways.

items.stem: A report about coral reefs has two headings: 'What Lives in a Reef' and 'Why Reefs Are in Danger.' Under which heading does the fact 'Warmer ocean water can cause coral to turn white and die' belong?

explanation.whyCorrect: Grouping facts under matching headings helps readers find information quickly.
explanation.tip: Ask what each fact is MOSTLY about before choosing its heading.

options.label: A
options.text: Why Reefs Are in Danger

options.label: B
options.text: Neither heading
options.rationale: The fact clearly fits under the danger heading, so it does belong somewhere.

options.label: C
options.text: What Lives in a Reef
options.rationale: This heading is about the creatures living in a reef, not threats to it.

options.label: D
options.text: The report's title
options.rationale: A title names the whole report, not one single fact.

items.stem: Put these sentences in the order that makes the clearest informative paragraph about recycling.

explanation.whyCorrect: A clear informative paragraph starts with a general topic sentence, groups related facts, then ends with a conclusion.
explanation.tip: Look for the sentence that introduces the whole topic—it comes first.

sequence: Recycling helps protect our environment in several ways.
First, recycling glass and plastic saves energy that factories would otherwise use to make new materials.
Second, recycling paper means fewer trees need to be cut down.
Because of these benefits, many communities now have recycling bins on every street.

items.stem: Which sentence gives a supporting detail for the topic sentence 'Spiders help control the number of insects around our homes'?

explanation.whyCorrect: Supporting details give facts that explain or prove the topic sentence.
explanation.tip: A supporting detail should answer the question the topic sentence raises.

options.label: A
options.text: Spiders have eight legs.
options.rationale: This is true, but it does not support the idea that spiders control insects.

options.label: B
options.text: A single spider can eat dozens of insects in one week.

options.label: C
options.text: My cousin found a spider in the garage.
options.rationale: This is a personal story, not a supporting fact.

options.label: D
options.text: Some people are afraid of spiders.
options.rationale: This is an opinion about feelings, not a fact supporting the topic.

items.stem: Grouping related facts under the same heading makes an informative report easier to understand.

explanation.whyCorrect: Readers can find information faster when similar facts are grouped together instead of scattered.
explanation.tip: Sort your facts into groups before you choose headings for them.

items.stem: A paragraph begins with 'Honeybees play an important role in nature' and then explains pollination and honey production. Which sentence BEST concludes the paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: A concluding sentence sums up the main idea the paragraph already explained.
explanation.tip: A strong ending refers back to the topic sentence's main idea.

options.label: A
options.text: Honey comes in different colors.
options.rationale: This adds a new fact rather than closing the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: My neighbor keeps three beehives.
options.rationale: This is a personal detail that does not conclude the main idea.

options.label: C
options.text: Because of all these benefits, honeybees deserve our protection.

options.label: D
options.text: Bees can sting when they feel threatened.
options.rationale: This introduces a new, unrelated idea instead of wrapping up the paragraph.

items.stem: A paragraph will explain that libraries offer free books, quiet study rooms, and computer access. Which topic sentence BEST introduces this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The topic sentence must be broad enough to cover all three supporting facts that follow.
explanation.tip: Check that your topic sentence fits every detail you plan to include.

options.label: A
options.text: I go to the library every Saturday.
options.rationale: This is a personal routine, not a general introduction to the topic.

options.label: B
options.text: The library computers are often slow.
options.rationale: This is a narrow complaint, not an introduction covering all three facts.

options.label: C
options.text: Books have covers and pages.
options.rationale: This is too general and does not focus on the library's resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Libraries offer many free resources that help the whole community.

items.stem: Put these sentences in the order that makes the clearest informative paragraph about baking bread.

explanation.whyCorrect: A clear paragraph introduces the topic first, then lists the steps in the order they happen.
explanation.tip: Sequence words like First, Next, and After signal the correct order.

sequence: Baking bread at home follows a few simple, important steps.
First, a baker mixes flour, water, yeast, and salt into a soft dough.
Next, the dough rests so the yeast can make it rise before it goes into a hot oven.
After about thirty minutes of baking, the loaf comes out golden brown and ready to eat.

items.stem: A report about the solar system includes three facts: planets' distances from the sun, how long each planet takes to orbit, and each planet's average temperature. Which heading BEST groups all three facts together?

explanation.whyCorrect: A heading should describe what all the grouped facts have in common.
explanation.tip: Choose a heading broad enough to cover every fact listed underneath it.

options.label: A
options.text: How the Planets Compare

options.label: B
options.text: Famous Astronauts
options.rationale: This heading is about people, not planet facts.

options.label: C
options.text: Our Favorite Planets
options.rationale: This heading is about opinions, not the measurable facts listed.

options.label: D
options.text: The History of Telescopes
options.rationale: This heading is about an instrument's history, unrelated to the three facts.

items.stem: A paragraph explains that Emperor penguins huddle together for warmth, have thick layers of fat, and have dense feathers that trap heat. Which sentence should be REMOVED because it does not belong?

explanation.whyCorrect: A fact about penguins' relatives does not explain how penguins stay warm, so it breaks the paragraph's focus.
explanation.tip: Remove any sentence that does not support the paragraph's main idea.

options.label: A
options.text: A thick layer of fat called blubber insulates penguins from cold water.
options.rationale: This supports the paragraph's focus on staying warm, so it belongs.

options.label: B
options.text: Penguins are closely related to seagulls, which also live near oceans.

options.label: C
options.text: Huddling in large groups helps penguins share body heat.
options.rationale: This directly supports how penguins stay warm, so it belongs.

options.label: D
options.text: Dense, oily feathers trap a layer of warm air next to a penguin's skin.
options.rationale: This explains another way penguins stay warm, so it belongs.

items.stem: Which revision turns this weak topic sentence into one with a clear general observation and focus? Weak: 'Museums have stuff in them.'

explanation.whyCorrect: A strong topic sentence replaces vague words with a specific, informative focus.
explanation.tip: Ask what the paragraph is really about, then name it precisely.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum was closed on Monday.
options.rationale: This is an unrelated detail, not a clear focus for the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: Museums have stuff in them, like old things.
options.rationale: This barely improves the vague wording and still lacks a clear focus.

options.label: C
options.text: Museums preserve objects that teach visitors about history and science.

options.label: D
options.text: I visited a museum last year.
options.rationale: This replaces the topic sentence with a personal story instead of a focus.

items.stem: A writer has two separate facts: 'Sea turtles hatch on sandy beaches.' and 'Sea turtles must crawl to the ocean right after hatching.' Which heading would BEST group these two related facts in a report?

explanation.whyCorrect: The best heading names exactly what both grouped facts have in common.
explanation.tip: A precise heading often names both the starting point and the ending point of a process.

options.label: A
options.text: The History of Turtle Research
options.rationale: This heading is about scientific study, not the two hatching facts given.

options.label: B
options.text: Sea Turtle Predators
options.rationale: This heading is about danger from other animals, not the hatching journey.

options.label: C
options.text: What Sea Turtles Eat
options.rationale: This heading is about diet, not hatching and reaching the ocean.

options.label: D
options.text: From Nest to Sea: A Hatchling's First Journey

items.stem: A report explains that sea otters wrap themselves in kelp so they don't drift away while sleeping, and that they crack open shellfish using rocks. Which heading BEST fits both facts?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both facts describe clever behaviors sea otters use to survive, which the heading names directly.
explanation.tip: A heading should match what the grouped facts actually describe, not just the general topic.

options.label: A
options.text: Clever Ways Sea Otters Survive

options.label: B
options.text: Where Sea Otters Live
options.rationale: That heading would fit facts about habitat, not these two survival behaviors.

options.label: C
options.text: Sea Otters in Danger
options.rationale: That heading would fit facts about threats, not these clever survival behaviors.

options.label: D
options.text: What Sea Otters Look Like
options.rationale: That heading would fit facts about appearance, not behavior.

items.stem: Put these sentences in the order that makes the clearest informative paragraph about the water cycle.

explanation.whyCorrect: A well-organized paragraph introduces the topic, explains the process step by step, then concludes with its significance.
explanation.tip: Look for the sentence that explains the overall significance—it usually comes last.

sequence: The water cycle moves water continuously between Earth's oceans, air, and land.
During evaporation, heat from the sun turns liquid water into vapor that rises into the atmosphere.
As that vapor cools and condenses into clouds, it eventually falls back to Earth as precipitation.
This endless cycle explains why the same water has been reused for billions of years.

items.stem: In a report about weather, which word precisely names the measurement of how much water is in the air?

explanation.whyCorrect: Humidity is the specific scientific term for moisture in the air.
explanation.tip: Precise domain words name an idea exactly—don't settle for a vague one.

options.label: A
options.text: visibility
options.rationale: Visibility measures how far a person can see.

options.label: B
options.text: humidity

options.label: C
options.text: pressure
options.rationale: Pressure measures the weight of the air, not its moisture.

options.label: D
options.text: temperature
options.rationale: Temperature measures heat, not the amount of water in the air.

items.stem: Choose the best transition to ADD an idea: 'Plants need sunlight to grow. ____, they need water and nutrients from the soil.'

explanation.whyCorrect: Additionally signals that a second, similar supporting idea is being added.
explanation.tip: L.5.6: choose transitions that match whether ideas add, contrast, or show a result.

options.label: A
options.text: As a result
options.rationale: The second idea is not a result caused by the first.

options.label: B
options.text: However
options.rationale: However signals contrast, but these two ideas agree and simply add on to each other.

options.label: C
options.text: Additionally

options.label: D
options.text: For example
options.rationale: The second sentence is not a specific example of the first.

items.stem: In a report about digestion, which word precisely names the organ that breaks down food using acid?

explanation.whyCorrect: The stomach is the specific organ that uses acid to begin breaking down food.
explanation.tip: Precise domain-specific nouns name the exact body part, not a general area.

options.label: A
options.text: esophagus
options.rationale: The esophagus only carries food down; it does not use acid to break it down.

options.label: B
options.text: liver
options.rationale: The liver filters blood and makes bile; it does not digest food with acid.

options.label: C
options.text: stomach

options.label: D
options.text: throat
options.rationale: The throat is a passage, not an organ that digests food with acid.

items.stem: Choose the best transition: 'Volcanoes release ash into the sky. ____, earthquakes shake the ground without releasing ash.'

explanation.whyCorrect: In contrast signals that the second sentence shows a difference from the first.
explanation.tip: Contrast words (however, in contrast) show that two ideas differ.

options.label: A
options.text: Similarly
options.rationale: Similarly signals agreement, but these two events are being contrasted.

options.label: B
options.text: For instance
options.rationale: This sentence is not an example of the first one.

options.label: C
options.text: Therefore
options.rationale: The second idea is not a result caused by the first.

options.label: D
options.text: In contrast

items.stem: In a report about government, which word precisely names a group of citizens chosen to make laws for a country?

explanation.whyCorrect: Legislature is the precise term for the lawmaking body of a government.
explanation.tip: Domain-specific vocabulary names an exact role, not a general group.

options.label: A
options.text: cabinet
options.rationale: A cabinet advises a leader but does not usually write the country's laws itself.

options.label: B
options.text: jury
options.rationale: A jury decides court cases; it does not make laws.

options.label: C
options.text: committee
options.rationale: Committee is a vaguer, more general term than the specific lawmaking body.

options.label: D
options.text: legislature

items.stem: In a report about rocks, which word precisely describes rock formed when melted rock cools and hardens?

explanation.whyCorrect: Igneous is the precise scientific term for rock formed from cooled, hardened magma or lava.
explanation.tip: Learn the exact science term instead of a general word like 'rock.'

options.label: A
options.text: igneous

options.label: B
options.text: sedimentary
options.rationale: Sedimentary rock forms from layers of settled particles, not cooled magma.

options.label: C
options.text: metamorphic
options.rationale: Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change existing rock.

options.label: D
options.text: mineral
options.rationale: Mineral is a broader term, not the specific rock type formed from cooled magma.

items.stem: In a report about trade, which word precisely names goods or services sent to another country to sell?

explanation.whyCorrect: Exports is the precise economic term for goods sent out of a country to be sold.
explanation.tip: Precise vocabulary helps readers picture the exact direction of trade.

options.label: A
options.text: imports
options.rationale: Imports are goods brought IN from another country, the opposite direction.

options.label: B
options.text: exports

options.label: C
options.text: profits
options.rationale: Profits are the money earned, not the goods themselves.

options.label: D
options.text: taxes
options.rationale: Taxes are fees collected by a government, not goods sent abroad.

items.stem: Choose the best transition: 'Bacteria multiply quickly in warm, moist places. ____, food left out in summer heat can spoil within hours.'

explanation.whyCorrect: As a result signals that spoiling food is a direct effect of bacteria multiplying quickly.
explanation.tip: Cause-and-effect words (as a result, therefore) connect a reason to its outcome.

options.label: A
options.text: As a result

options.label: B
options.text: For example
options.rationale: The second sentence states a general effect, not one specific instance.

options.label: C
options.text: Meanwhile

items.stem: In a report about ecosystems, which word precisely names an animal that eats only plants?

items.stem: Choose the best transition: 'Wind and water slowly wear away rock, a process called erosion. ____, when that worn-away material settles somewhere new, scientists call it deposition.'

items.stem: Choose the best transition: 'Electric cars produce no tailpipe pollution. ____, they are far quieter than gasoline cars.'

items.stem: Choose the best transition: 'Cutting down forests removes the trees that absorb carbon dioxide. ____, deforestation contributes to climate change.'

items.stem: Choose the best transition: 'Traders along the Silk Road carried silk and spices westward. ____, merchants moving east carried gold and glassware.'

items.stem: Choose the best transition: 'Teenagers often think they need less sleep than children do. ____, most teens need just as much sleep, or more.'

options.text: the caption must be a typing mistake
options.rationale: A reader should consider the information first, not assume an error without evidence.

items.stem: A diagram shows how a town's recycling process works, with an arrow path from 'collection truck' to 'sorting center' to 'recycling plant' for recyclable material. Put these four steps of that path in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: Following the arrows in a flowchart diagram in order shows the full recycling process for recyclable materials.
explanation.tip: In a flowchart, follow each arrow one at a time instead of skipping ahead.

sequence: collection truck picks up bins
sorting center separates materials by type
recyclable material is sent to the recycling plant
the recycling plant turns material into new products

items.stem: A nutrition label on a cereal box lists 'Calories: 120, Sugar: 8g, Fiber: 3g' in a table. What is the main purpose of this table?

explanation.whyCorrect: A nutrition table presents exact numbers so readers can compare facts quickly.
explanation.tip: Tables are best for presenting exact numbers that readers need to compare.

options.label: A
options.text: to list the ingredients in order
options.rationale: An ingredients list is usually separate text, not a nutrition facts table.

options.label: B
options.text: to let readers quickly compare specific nutrition facts

options.label: C
options.text: to show what the cereal tastes like
options.rationale: Taste cannot be shown by a table of numbers.

options.label: D
options.text: to show a picture of the cereal
options.rationale: A table shows numbers, not images.

items.stem: A table of contents lists chapter titles in the order they appear in a book.

explanation.whyCorrect: Readers use the table of contents to find which page a chapter starts on.
explanation.tip: Table of contents = front of book; index = back of book.

items.stem: An article about ocean currents includes a map with curved arrows showing warm and cold currents moving around the globe. What does this map help readers understand that words alone could not show as easily?

explanation.whyCorrect: Arrows on a map can show direction and path far more clearly than a written description alone.
explanation.tip: Maps with arrows are best for showing movement and direction.

options.label: A
options.text: the exact temperature of the water in degrees
options.rationale: A simple arrow map usually does not give exact temperature numbers.

options.label: B
options.text: the history of ocean exploration
options.rationale: A current map shows movement patterns, not historical events.

options.label: C
options.text: the direction and path each current travels around the globe

options.label: D
options.text: the number of fish living in each current
options.rationale: The map shows water movement, not fish populations.

items.stem: A report on ancient Mesopotamia has a heading 'Government and Law' followed by a paragraph about Hammurabi's Code. Under which heading would information about Mesopotamian farming methods belong?

explanation.whyCorrect: Farming information belongs under a heading that matches its own topic, not an unrelated one.
explanation.tip: Check whether a fact truly matches a heading's topic before grouping it there.

options.label: A
options.text: in the glossary
options.rationale: A glossary only defines words; it does not hold full explanations of farming methods.

options.label: B
options.text: in the book's title only
options.rationale: A title names the whole report, not one specific topic like farming.

options.label: C
options.text: still under 'Government and Law'
options.rationale: Farming methods are not about rulers or legal codes, so they don't fit this heading.

options.label: D
options.text: a different heading, such as 'Agriculture and Food'

items.stem: A line graph tracks a city's average monthly temperature: it rises steadily from January to July, then falls steadily from July to December. In which month is the temperature LIKELY highest?

explanation.whyCorrect: The graph rises until July and falls afterward, so July is the peak.
explanation.tip: On a line graph, the highest point on the line marks the highest value.

options.label: A
options.text: July

options.label: B
options.text: December
options.rationale: December is near the end of the falling trend, close to the lowest point.

options.label: C
options.text: January
options.rationale: The graph shows temperature rising FROM January, so January is a low point, not the highest.

options.label: D
options.text: April
options.rationale: April is in the middle of the rising trend, not the peak.

items.stem: A labeled diagram of a volcano shows, from bottom to top: magma chamber, pipe, vent, and crater. Which labeled part is closest to the magma chamber?

explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram lists the pipe directly above the magma chamber, making it the closest part.
explanation.tip: In a diagram, follow the order of labels from bottom to top, or vice versa.

options.label: A
options.text: the vent
options.rationale: The vent is near the top, farther from the magma chamber than the pipe.

options.label: B
options.text: the pipe

options.label: C
options.text: the label itself
options.rationale: A label is just text pointing to a part; it is not a physical part of the volcano.

options.label: D
options.text: the crater
options.rationale: The crater is at the very top, the farthest part from the magma chamber.

items.stem: Match each text feature with its purpose.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each feature presents information in a different way suited to its specific purpose.
explanation.tip: Ask what kind of information each feature is designed to highlight.

pairs.right: combines images, numbers, and short text to explain data quickly
gives extra information about a specific word or fact at the bottom of a page
shows a process as a series of connected steps
highlights an important sentence from the main text in larger print

items.stem: A history article has a timeline running along the bottom of the page and a separate paragraph describing causes of a war in detail. Why might an author include BOTH features instead of just one?

explanation.whyCorrect: Different features often answer different questions—a timeline answers 'when,' while a paragraph answers 'why.'
explanation.tip: Ask what unique question each text feature is answering.

options.label: A
options.text: the timeline and paragraph always repeat the exact same information
options.rationale: If they repeated each other exactly, one would be unnecessary; they serve different purposes.

options.label: B
options.text: the timeline is only decoration
options.rationale: A timeline presents real chronological information, not just decoration.

options.label: C
options.text: the timeline shows WHEN events happened, while the paragraph explains WHY they happened

options.label: D
options.text: the paragraph is only there to look longer
options.rationale: Paragraphs add explanation, not just length.

items.stem: A bar graph compares test scores across four subjects for one class: Math 82, Science 75, Reading 90, and Art 95. According to the graph, in which subject did the class score LOWEST?

explanation.whyCorrect: 75 is the lowest of the four scores shown on the bar graph.
explanation.tip: On a bar graph, the shortest bar shows the lowest value.

options.label: A
options.text: Math
options.rationale: Math's score of 82 is higher than Science's 75.

options.label: B
options.text: Reading
options.rationale: Reading's score of 90 is much higher than Science's 75.

options.label: C
options.text: Art
options.rationale: Art's score of 95 is the highest, not the lowest.

options.label: D
options.text: Science

items.stem: An article explains renewable energy and includes a diagram of a wind turbine with labeled parts: blades, rotor, generator, and tower. Which labeled part most likely converts spinning motion into electricity?

explanation.whyCorrect: The generator is the labeled part specifically designed to convert motion into electricity.
explanation.tip: In a labeled diagram, match each part's name to its specific job.

options.label: A
options.text: the generator

options.label: B
options.text: the rotor
options.rationale: The rotor connects the blades to the generator; the actual electricity is produced by the generator.

options.label: C
options.text: the tower
options.rationale: The tower only holds the turbine up high; it does not produce electricity.

options.label: D
options.text: the blades
options.rationale: The blades catch the wind and start the spinning motion, but they do not create electricity.

items.stem: Two infographics show the same statistic about plastic pollution. Infographic A uses a simple bar chart with clearly labeled numbers. Infographic B uses only large, colorful icons with no numbers. Which infographic would most reliably let a reader report an exact statistic?

explanation.whyCorrect: Exact numbers require a feature that actually labels those numbers, not just icons.
explanation.tip: Check whether a graphic gives exact labeled numbers before quoting a statistic from it.

options.label: A
options.text: Neither can be trusted for any report
options.rationale: A chart with clearly labeled numbers can reasonably be used to report a statistic.

options.label: B
options.text: Infographic A, because it shows exact labeled numbers

options.label: C
options.text: Infographic B, because it has more color
options.rationale: Color makes a graphic eye-catching but does not provide exact data.

options.label: D
options.text: Both are equally reliable for exact numbers
options.rationale: Only Infographic A actually labels numeric values; icons alone don't give exact figures.

items.stem: A table shows the boiling points of three liquids: water 100°C, ethanol 78°C, mercury 357°C. Based on the table, which liquid has the LOWEST boiling point?

explanation.whyCorrect: 78°C is the lowest of the three boiling points listed in the table.
explanation.tip: Scan every number in a table before deciding which is highest or lowest.

options.label: A
options.text: none of them boil
options.rationale: The table specifically lists each liquid's boiling point, so each one does boil.

options.label: B
options.text: water
options.rationale: Water's boiling point, 100°C, is higher than ethanol's 78°C.

options.label: C
options.text: ethanol

options.label: D
options.text: mercury
options.rationale: Mercury's boiling point, 357°C, is by far the highest of the three.

items.stem: A biography includes a sidebar titled 'In Her Own Words' with a direct quotation from the subject. What is the most likely purpose of this sidebar?

explanation.whyCorrect: A direct-quotation sidebar lets readers experience the subject's own words firsthand.
explanation.tip: Quotation sidebars add a personal voice that a summary cannot capture.

options.label: A
options.text: to correct errors made elsewhere in the biography
options.rationale: A quotation sidebar shares the subject's words; it isn't primarily for corrections.

options.label: B
options.text: to list the dates of the subject's life
options.rationale: Dates would more likely appear in a timeline, not a quotation sidebar.

options.label: C
options.text: to summarize the entire biography in one sentence
options.rationale: A short quotation cannot summarize an entire life story.

options.label: D
options.text: to let readers hear the subject's own voice and perspective directly

items.stem: A bar graph comparing two companies' profits has a y-axis that starts at $90,000 instead of $0, making a small difference in profit look huge. What problem does this create for readers?

explanation.whyCorrect: Starting a bar graph's axis above zero can exaggerate small differences visually.
explanation.tip: Always check where a graph's axis starts before judging how big a difference looks.

options.label: A
options.text: it can make a small difference appear much larger than it really is

options.label: B
options.text: it has no effect on how readers understand the data
options.rationale: Starting the axis above zero does change how large the difference appears.

options.label: C
options.text: it means the data must be completely false
options.rationale: The underlying numbers can still be accurate even though the scale is misleading.

options.label: D
options.text: it makes the numbers impossible to read
options.rationale: The numbers are still readable; the issue is how dramatic the difference looks.

items.stem: A graph shows two lines: one for a town's population and one for its number of schools, both from 1980 to 2020. The population line rises sharply, but the school line stays almost flat. What might a reader reasonably conclude?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing the two lines shows population growing much faster than the number of schools.
explanation.tip: When two lines on a graph diverge, think about what that gap might mean.

options.label: A
options.text: the town built far more schools than it needed
options.rationale: A flat school line alongside a rising population line does not suggest an oversupply of schools.

options.label: B
options.text: schools may have become more crowded as the population grew without new schools being built

options.label: C
options.text: the town's population and number of schools grew at exactly the same rate
options.rationale: The graph shows population rising sharply while schools stayed flat, which is not the same rate.

options.label: D
options.text: the number of schools has no connection to population at all
options.rationale: A reader can reasonably consider a connection when a growing population isn't matched by more schools.

items.stem: A map's legend uses a solid line for 'paved road' and a dashed line for 'unpaved trail.' The main text mentions hikers reaching a summit by trail only. Which lines on the map would show the hikers' likely route?

explanation.whyCorrect: The legend defines dashed lines as unpaved trails, matching the hikers' described route.
explanation.tip: Always check a map's legend before deciding what a line or symbol represents.

options.label: A
options.text: the solid lines
options.rationale: Solid lines represent paved roads, but the text says the hikers used a trail.

options.label: B
options.text: neither type of line, since hikers don't use mapped routes
options.rationale: The legend provides a specific symbol for trails, which the map would use to show the route.

options.label: C
options.text: the dashed lines

options.label: D
options.text: lines of any kind, since both represent paths
options.rationale: The legend specifically distinguishes trails from roads, so only one line type fits the text.

items.stem: An article argues that bats are important for farms. It includes a table of insect numbers eaten per night, a diagram of a bat's wing structure, and a caption noting a photographed bat near a cornfield. Which feature provides the STRONGEST evidence for the article's specific argument about farms?

explanation.whyCorrect: The table gives measurable evidence directly connected to the claim about bats benefiting farms.
explanation.tip: The strongest evidence for a specific claim is usually the feature that measures it directly.

options.label: A
options.text: none of the features relate to the argument
options.rationale: The table directly provides numeric evidence supporting the claim about bats helping farms.

options.label: B
options.text: the caption about the photo location
options.rationale: A caption noting a location is supporting detail, not quantitative evidence of benefit.

options.label: C
options.text: the diagram of wing structure
options.rationale: Wing structure explains flight, not the bat's benefit to farms.

options.label: D
options.text: the table of insect numbers eaten per night

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?

explanation.whyCorrect: Commas separate each item in a series of three or more things.
explanation.tip: Count the items in a list — three or more means commas between each one.

options.label: A
options.text: Omar packed a tent, a lantern, and a compass.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar packed a tent, a lantern and, a compass.
options.rationale: The second comma is placed right before the last item's word instead of before “and.”

options.label: C
options.text: Omar packed a tent a lantern and a compass.
options.rationale: Commas are missing between all the listed items.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar packed, a tent, a lantern, and a compass.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after the verb “packed.”

items.stem: The sentence “Yes, I finished my homework.” correctly uses a comma after an introductory word.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma follows a short introductory word like Yes, No, or Well at the start of a sentence.
explanation.tip: Introductory words are often followed by a comma.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a comma for direct address correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma follows the name of the person being spoken to directly.
explanation.tip: When a sentence speaks to someone by name, set the name off with a comma.

options.label: A
options.text: Layla can you, pass the salt?
options.rationale: The comma should come right after the name Layla, not later in the sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Layla, can you pass the salt?

options.label: C
options.text: Layla can you pass the salt?
options.rationale: A comma is needed after the name when speaking directly to someone.

options.label: D
options.text: Layla, can you pass, the salt?
options.rationale: There should be no comma before “the salt.”

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma separates the day from the year in a date.
explanation.tip: Dates written as month day, year need a comma after the day.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly between a city and a country?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma separates a city from its country, and another comma follows the country name.
explanation.tip: City, Country needs commas both before and after the country name.

options.label: A
options.text: My pen pal lives, in Aswan, Egypt, near the Nile.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “lives.”

options.label: B
options.text: My pen pal lives in Aswan, Egypt near the Nile.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after the country name.

options.label: C
options.text: My pen pal lives in Aswan, Egypt, near the Nile.

options.label: D
options.text: My pen pal lives in Aswan Egypt, near the Nile.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between the city and the country.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete sentences joined by “and” need a comma before the conjunction.
explanation.tip: Check if both parts could stand alone as sentences — if so, add a comma before the conjunction.

items.stem: Which sentence punctuates a letter greeting correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma follows the full greeting, right before the body of the letter begins.
explanation.tip: Letter greetings like “Dear ___,” always end with a comma.

options.label: A
options.text: Dear Grandma I miss you very much.
options.rationale: A comma is needed after the greeting, before the message begins.

options.label: B
options.text: Dear Grandma, I miss, you very much.
options.rationale: There should be no comma in the middle of the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: Dear, Grandma I miss you very much.
options.rationale: The comma belongs after the name, not after “Dear.”

options.label: D
options.text: Dear Grandma, I miss you very much.

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list of four items?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each item in the series needs a comma after it, including right before “and” plus the last item.
explanation.tip: A series of four items still follows the same comma rule as a series of three.

options.label: A
options.text: We need flour, sugar, butter, and eggs for the cake.

options.label: B
options.text: We need flour, sugar, butter and, eggs for the cake.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong spot; it should come before “and,” not after.

options.label: C
options.text: We need flour, sugar, butter, and, eggs for the cake.
options.rationale: There should not be a comma right after “and.”

options.label: D
options.text: We need flour sugar, butter, and eggs for the cake.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after the first item, flour.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma follows a longer introductory phrase before the main part of the sentence begins.
explanation.tip: If a sentence starts with a phrase telling when or where, add a comma before the main clause.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly joins two complete sentences with a comma and “but”?

explanation.whyCorrect: When two complete sentences are joined by “but,” a comma goes right before “but.”
explanation.tip: Test each half: if both could stand alone as sentences, add a comma before the joining word.

options.label: A
options.text: I wanted to go to the park, but, it started raining.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “but.”

options.label: B
options.text: I wanted to go to the park, but it started raining.

options.label: C
options.text: I wanted to go to the park but it started raining, heavily.
options.rationale: The comma is placed after the wrong word; it should come before “but,” which joins two complete sentences.

options.label: D
options.text: I wanted, to go to the park but it started raining.
options.rationale: The comma incorrectly splits the first clause instead of appearing before “but.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas to separate three descriptive adjectives in a row?

explanation.whyCorrect: Three describing words in a row before a noun are separated by commas, just like items in a list.
explanation.tip: Treat a row of adjectives like a short list — comma after each one except the last.

options.label: A
options.text: The old, dusty, forgotten, chest sat in the attic.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right before the noun “chest.”

options.label: B
options.text: The old dusty, forgotten chest sat in the attic.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between “old” and “dusty.”

options.label: C
options.text: The old, dusty, forgotten chest sat in the attic.

options.label: D
options.text: The old, dusty forgotten chest sat in the attic.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between “dusty” and “forgotten.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a series?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each item in a series of three or more needs a comma after it, except the final item.
explanation.tip: L.5.2.a: use commas to separate every item in a series.

options.label: A
options.text: The farmer grew carrots, potatoes and, onions in his garden.
options.rationale: The comma is placed after “and” instead of before it.

options.label: B
options.text: The farmer grew carrots potatoes, and onions in his garden.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between “carrots” and “potatoes.”

options.label: C
options.text: The farmer grew, carrots, potatoes, and onions in his garden.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “grew.”

options.label: D
options.text: The farmer grew carrots, potatoes, and onions in his garden.

items.stem: In a series of three or more items, a comma should be placed before the word “and” that comes right before the last item.

explanation.whyCorrect: This comma, often called the Oxford comma, separates the second-to-last item from the last.
explanation.tip: Count the items: three or more means you need commas between each one, including before “and.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a series of actions?

explanation.whyCorrect: A series can list actions as well as objects, and the same comma rule applies.
explanation.tip: Read the sentence aloud and pause where each action ends.

options.label: A
options.text: On Saturdays, Huda cleans her room, walks the dog, and practices piano.

options.label: B
options.text: On Saturdays, Huda cleans her room, walks the dog and, practices piano.
options.rationale: The comma is misplaced after “and” instead of before it.

options.label: C
options.text: On Saturdays, Huda cleans her room walks the dog, and practices piano.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between “room” and “walks.”

options.label: D
options.text: On Saturdays, Huda cleans her room, walks the dog, and, practices piano.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “and.”

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma is needed after each item in a series except the very last one.
explanation.tip: Read the sentence aloud and pause where each item ends.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly shows that NO comma is needed because there are only two items?

explanation.whyCorrect: A series comma rule applies to three or more items; two items joined by “and” need no comma.
explanation.tip: Count first: exactly two items joined by “and” usually need no comma at all.

options.label: A
options.text: Nadia packed her swimsuit, and sunscreen for the trip.
options.rationale: Two items joined only by “and” do not need a comma before it.

options.label: B
options.text: Nadia packed her swimsuit and sunscreen for the trip.

options.label: C
options.text: Nadia packed her swimsuit and, sunscreen for the trip.
options.rationale: A comma should not be placed right after “and.”

options.label: D
options.text: Nadia packed, her swimsuit and sunscreen for the trip.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “packed.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas to separate a series of descriptive words?

explanation.whyCorrect: A series of describing words before a noun follows the same comma rule as any other series.
explanation.tip: List adjectives the same way you would list objects — commas between each one.

options.label: A
options.text: The recipe called for ripe juicy red tomatoes.
options.rationale: Commas are missing between all three describing words.

options.label: B
options.text: The recipe called for ripe, juicy red, tomatoes.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right before the noun “tomatoes.”

options.label: C
options.text: The recipe called for ripe, juicy, red tomatoes.

options.label: D
options.text: The recipe called for ripe juicy, red tomatoes.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between “ripe” and “juicy.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a series joined by “or”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A series ending in “or” follows the same comma pattern as one ending in “and.”
explanation.tip: The last comma in a series comes right before the final connecting word, whether it's “and” or “or.”

options.label: A
options.text: For the field trip, the class can choose the zoo, the aquarium or, the science museum.
options.rationale: The comma is misplaced after “or” instead of before it.

options.label: B
options.text: For the field trip, the class can choose the zoo the aquarium, or the science museum.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between “zoo” and “the aquarium.”

options.label: C
options.text: For the field trip the class can choose, the zoo, the aquarium, or the science museum.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “choose,” and a comma is missing after the introductory phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: For the field trip, the class can choose the zoo, the aquarium, or the science museum.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each item in a series of three needs a comma after it, except the final item.
explanation.tip: A series can list actions, not just objects — the comma rule still applies.

segments: During the storm, the lights flickered
items.correction: During the storm, the lights flickered,

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a series, rather than mistakenly repeating “and” before every item?

explanation.whyCorrect: A standard series needs only one “and,” placed before the final item, with a comma right before it.
explanation.tip: Repeating “and” before every item is unnecessary; save it for right before the last item.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum displays ancient pottery, ceremonial masks, and carved statues.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum displays ancient pottery, and ceremonial masks, and carved statues.
options.rationale: Repeating “and” with a comma before each one is unnecessary; only the final “and” needs a comma before it.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum displays, ancient pottery, ceremonial masks, and carved statues.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “displays.”

options.label: D
options.text: The museum displays ancient pottery ceremonial masks, and carved statues.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between the first two items.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a series inside a longer sentence that begins with a clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both the introductory clause and the series inside the sentence need their own correct commas.
explanation.tip: Check introductory clauses and series commas separately — a sentence can need both.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the trail was steep, hikers needed sturdy boots plenty of water, and a walking stick.
options.rationale: A comma is missing between “boots” and “plenty of water.”

options.label: B
options.text: Because the trail was steep, hikers needed sturdy boots, plenty of water, and a walking stick.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the trail was steep hikers needed sturdy boots, plenty of water, and a walking stick.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after the introductory clause “Because the trail was steep.”

options.label: D
options.text: Because the trail was steep, hikers needed sturdy boots, plenty of water and, a walking stick.
options.rationale: The comma is misplaced after “and” instead of before it.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas for a series where some items are themselves pairs joined by “and”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each paired item in the series is treated as one unit, separated from the next pair by a comma.
explanation.tip: When series items are pairs, find the boundary between each whole pair before placing commas.

options.label: A
options.text: The study compared sleep and memory, diet and energy and, exercise and mood.
options.rationale: The comma is misplaced after “and” instead of before it.

options.label: B
options.text: The study compared, sleep and memory, diet and energy, and exercise and mood.
options.rationale: There should be no comma right after “compared.”

options.label: C
options.text: The study compared sleep and memory, diet and energy, and exercise and mood.

options.label: D
options.text: The study compared sleep and memory diet and energy, and exercise and mood.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after the first paired item, “sleep and memory.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates an appositive?

explanation.whyCorrect: A nonessential appositive is set off by commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: Find where the extra naming phrase begins and ends, then bracket it with commas.

options.label: A
options.text: Mount Everest, the tallest, mountain on Earth, attracts climbers from every country.
options.rationale: An extra comma incorrectly splits the appositive phrase itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Mount Everest the tallest mountain on Earth, attracts climbers from every country.
options.rationale: A comma is missing before the appositive “the tallest mountain on Earth.”

options.label: C
options.text: Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth attracts climbers from every country.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after the appositive.

options.label: D
options.text: Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth, attracts climbers from every country.

items.stem: A nonrestrictive clause adds extra information that could be removed without changing the sentence's basic meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: Nonrestrictive clauses are set off by commas because the sentence still makes sense without them.
explanation.tip: If you can delete the clause and the sentence still identifies the same thing, it's nonrestrictive.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a nonrestrictive clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: A nonrestrictive clause is extra information set off by commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: Both commas must appear — one before the clause and one right after it.

options.label: A
options.text: The novel, which won several awards, was translated into twelve languages.

options.label: B
options.text: The novel, which won, several awards, was translated into twelve languages.
options.rationale: An extra comma incorrectly splits the clause itself.

options.label: C
options.text: The novel, which won several awards was translated into twelve languages.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after the nonrestrictive clause, before “was.”

options.label: D
options.text: The novel which won several awards, was translated into twelve languages.
options.rationale: A comma is missing before “which,” at the start of the nonrestrictive clause.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly shows NO commas because the clause is restrictive, meaning it is needed to identify which students are meant?

explanation.whyCorrect: A restrictive clause is essential to the sentence's meaning, so it takes no commas.
explanation.tip: Ask: does removing the clause change WHICH ones are meant? If yes, it's restrictive — no commas.

options.label: A
options.text: The students, who finished the exam early, were allowed to leave.
options.rationale: Commas here wrongly suggest ALL students finished early, when the clause actually identifies only SOME students.

options.label: B
options.text: The students who finished the exam early were allowed to leave.

options.label: C
options.text: The students who, finished the exam early, were allowed to leave.
options.rationale: This incorrectly isolates part of the restrictive clause with commas.

options.label: D
options.text: The students who finished the exam, early were allowed to leave.
options.rationale: This comma incorrectly splits the restrictive clause itself.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A parenthetical interrupter like “of course” is set off by commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: If a word or phrase could be lifted out without changing the sentence's structure, set it off with commas.

segments: surprised every scientist on the team.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses dashes to set off a strong interruption?

explanation.whyCorrect: A pair of dashes, matching at both ends, sets off a strong interruption in a sentence.
explanation.tip: Dashes should come in matching pairs, just like parentheses or paired commas.

options.label: A
options.text: The experiment, despite months of careful planning—failed within minutes.
options.rationale: Mixing a comma and a dash to open and close the same interruption is inconsistent punctuation.

options.label: B
options.text: The experiment—despite months of careful planning failed within minutes.
options.rationale: A closing dash is missing before “failed.”

options.label: C
options.text: The experiment—despite months of careful planning—failed within minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: The experiment despite—months of careful planning—failed within minutes.
options.rationale: The dash is placed in the wrong spot, splitting the word “despite” from its own phrase.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses parentheses to add a brief clarifying fact?

explanation.whyCorrect: Parentheses enclose only the extra, clarifying detail, leaving the main sentence intact around them.
explanation.tip: Read the sentence without the parentheses — it should still make complete sense on its own.

options.label: A
options.text: The bridge (completed in 1937 remains) one of the most photographed landmarks in the world.
options.rationale: The closing parenthesis is in the wrong place, splitting the main sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: The bridge completed in 1937, remains one of the most photographed landmarks in the world.
options.rationale: Without parentheses or paired commas, this comma alone incorrectly separates the subject from its verb.

options.label: C
options.text: The (bridge completed in 1937) remains one of the most photographed landmarks in the world.
options.rationale: The parentheses incorrectly enclose part of the subject instead of just the extra detail.

options.label: D
options.text: The bridge (completed in 1937) remains one of the most photographed landmarks in the world.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates an appositive that names someone's title?

explanation.whyCorrect: An appositive renaming a person is set off by commas on both sides, just like other appositives.
explanation.tip: A title following a name is often a nonessential appositive needing paired commas.

options.label: A
options.text: Dr. Amina Farouk, the hospital's lead surgeon, performed the operation.

options.label: B
options.text: Dr. Amina Farouk, the hospital's lead surgeon performed the operation.
options.rationale: A comma is missing after the appositive, before the verb “performed.”

options.label: C
options.text: Dr. Amina Farouk, the hospital's, lead surgeon, performed the operation.
options.rationale: An extra comma incorrectly splits the appositive phrase itself.

options.label: D
options.text: Dr. Amina Farouk the hospital's lead surgeon, performed the operation.
options.rationale: A comma is missing before the appositive naming her title.

items.stem: A writer wants to STRONGLY emphasize an interruption, more than a comma would. Which sentence best achieves this using dashes?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dashes create a stronger, more dramatic pause than commas when setting off an interrupter.
explanation.tip: Choose dashes over commas when a writer wants extra emphasis on the interruption.

options.label: A
options.text: The invention, astonishingly, took less than a week to design.
options.rationale: Commas set off the interrupter gently; the sentence calls for the stronger emphasis of dashes.

options.label: B
options.text: The invention—astonishingly—took less than a week to design.

options.label: C
options.text: The invention astonishingly took less than a week to design.
options.rationale: With no punctuation at all, the interrupter isn't set off, so there is no emphasis.

options.label: D
options.text: The invention—astonishingly took less than a week to design.
options.rationale: A closing dash is missing, so the interruption is not properly set off on both sides.

items.stem: The nonrestrictive phrase in a sentence already contains a comma inside it: ‘...the capital, a city of nearly ten million people, which was founded...’ Why might a careful writer use dashes instead of commas to set off ‘a city of nearly ten million people, which was founded in the 16th century’ from the rest of the sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: When an interruption already contains a comma, dashes mark its start and end more clearly than more commas would.
explanation.tip: Switch to dashes when a nonrestrictive phrase has its own internal comma, to avoid confusion.

options.label: A
options.text: dashes are only used in informal writing and should be avoided
options.rationale: Dashes are a standard, formal punctuation tool for setting off interruptions.

options.label: B
options.text: commas and dashes always mean exactly the same thing, so it never matters
options.rationale: If it never mattered, careful writers wouldn't choose one over the other for clarity.

options.label: C
options.text: dashes make the boundaries of the long interruption clearer when it already contains its own comma

options.label: D
options.text: parentheses would always be a better choice in every case
options.rationale: The question asks specifically about dashes versus commas here, and parentheses can be just as confusing when a phrase already has internal punctuation.

items.stem: The root 'auto' means self. What is an autobiography?

explanation.whyCorrect: Auto (self) + bio (life) + graph (write) = a self-written account of one's own life.
explanation.tip: Auto always points back to the self doing the action.

options.label: A
options.text: a book written by someone else about a stranger
options.rationale: An autobiography is written BY the person about themselves, not by someone else about a stranger.

options.label: B
options.text: a book about cars
options.rationale: “Auto” here means self, not automobile.

options.label: C
options.text: a picture of a famous building
options.rationale: That would not involve the root “auto” or “bio.”

options.label: D
options.text: a book a person writes about their own life

items.stem: The root 'phon' means sound. Which word means 'a device that lets people talk to each other over long distances using sound'?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tele (far) + phon (sound) = a device for sending sound over a far distance.
explanation.tip: Phon always points to sound; look for it in words like phonics and symphony.

options.label: A
options.text: telephone

options.label: B
options.text: telescope
options.rationale: “Scope” means look, not sound; a telescope is for seeing far away.

options.label: C
options.text: photograph
options.rationale: “Graph” means write or draw, not sound.

options.label: D
options.text: thermometer
options.rationale: “Therm” means heat, which is unrelated to sound.

items.stem: Bio means life and graph means write. What is a biography?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bio (life) + graph (write) = a written account of a life, usually someone else's.
explanation.tip: Compare biography to autobiography: both use bio and graph, but only one adds auto.

options.label: A
options.text: a written account of your own life
options.rationale: That describes an autobiography, since “auto” means self.

options.label: B
options.text: a written account of someone else's life

options.label: C
options.text: a photograph of a living thing
options.rationale: A photograph uses light, not writing, to capture an image.

options.label: D
options.text: a list of scientific facts about animals
options.rationale: That would more likely be called a field guide or encyclopedia entry, not a biography.

items.stem: Match each root with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: These roots appear in words like dictate, scribble, conductor, and erupt.
explanation.tip: Think of one example word for each root to remember its meaning.

items.stem: The root 'therm' means heat. What does a thermometer measure?

explanation.whyCorrect: Therm (heat) + -meter (measure) = a tool that measures heat, or temperature.
explanation.tip: Therm shows up in thermal, thermos, and thermometer — all about heat.

options.label: A
options.text: weight
options.rationale: Weight is measured by a scale, which doesn't involve the root “therm.”

options.label: B
options.text: sound level
options.rationale: Sound level is measured by a different kind of instrument, unrelated to heat.

options.label: C
options.text: temperature

options.label: D
options.text: distance
options.rationale: A thermometer measures heat, not how far something is.

items.stem: Choose the word: A shape with ____ sides is called a decagon.

explanation.whyCorrect: Deca is the Greek root for ten, so a decagon has ten sides.
explanation.tip: Match each number-root to its matching polygon name.

options.label: A
options.text: five
options.rationale: A shape with five sides is a pentagon, using the root “penta.”

options.label: B
options.text: eight
options.rationale: A shape with eight sides is an octagon, using the root “octa.”

options.label: C
options.text: twelve
options.rationale: A shape with twelve sides is a dodecagon, a different root combination.

options.label: D
options.text: ten

items.stem: The Latin root 'ject' means throw. Which word means 'to throw something out or force it to leave'?

explanation.whyCorrect: E- (out) + ject (throw) = to throw or force something out.
explanation.tip: Match each prefix (e-, in-, pro-) to the direction it adds to the root ject.

options.label: A
options.text: inject
options.rationale: Inject means to force something IN, not throw it out.

options.label: B
options.text: project
options.rationale: Project means to throw forward, such as projecting an image, not force something out.

options.label: C
options.text: subject
options.rationale: Subject comes from a different root pairing meaning “thrown under,” not “thrown out.”

options.label: D
options.text: eject

items.stem: The Latin root 'cred' means believe. Which word describes someone who is easily fooled because they believe things too readily?

explanation.whyCorrect: Cred (believe) + -ulous (tending to) = tending to believe things too easily.
explanation.tip: Watch the suffix: -ulous often means “tending to” or “full of.”

options.label: A
options.text: credulous

options.label: B
options.text: credential
options.rationale: A credential is proof of qualification, not a description of someone's gullibility.

options.label: C
options.text: discredit
options.rationale: To discredit means to cause others to stop believing someone, which is different from being gullible oneself.

options.label: D
options.text: incredible
options.rationale: Incredible means hard to believe, which is the opposite idea.

items.stem: The Latin root 'mal' means bad. Which word describes a plan intended to cause harm?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mal (bad) combined with the idea of intent gives malicious its meaning of intending harm.
explanation.tip: Not every word with “mal” means exactly the same kind of “bad” — check the rest of the word too.

options.label: A
options.text: maladjusted
options.rationale: Maladjusted describes poor adjustment to a situation, not an intent to cause harm.

options.label: B
options.text: malicious

options.label: C
options.text: malleable
options.rationale: Malleable means easily shaped, which comes from a different root meaning to hammer, not “bad.”

options.label: D
options.text: malnourished
options.rationale: Malnourished describes poor nourishment, not harmful intent.

items.stem: The Latin root 'vis' means see. Which word describes something that cannot be seen?

explanation.whyCorrect: In- (not) + vis (see) + -ible (able to be) = not able to be seen.
explanation.tip: Look for the prefix in- or im- to spot when a root's meaning is being reversed.

options.label: A
options.text: revise
options.rationale: Revise means to “see again,” as in looking back over work, not describing invisibility.

options.label: B
options.text: supervisor
options.rationale: A supervisor “sees over” or oversees others; it doesn't mean something cannot be seen.

options.label: C
options.text: invisible

options.label: D
options.text: television
options.rationale: Television combines “tele” (far) and “vis” (see) to mean seeing from far away, not “unable to be seen.”

items.stem: Trans means across, and port means carry. What does transport mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Trans (across) + port (carry) = to carry something across a distance.
explanation.tip: Combine the prefix's direction with the root's action to build the meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: to stop something from moving
options.rationale: Transport describes movement, the opposite of stopping.

options.label: B
options.text: to carry something up high
options.rationale: Trans means across, not up; that meaning would need a different prefix.

options.label: C
options.text: to look at something closely
options.rationale: Looking closely would involve a root like “spect,” not “port.”

options.label: D
options.text: to carry something from one place to another

items.stem: The prefix 'sub' means under. What does 'submerge' mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sub (under) + merge (plunge into) = to plunge completely under the water.
explanation.tip: Sub always points downward or underneath, as in submarine and subway.

options.label: A
options.text: to put completely underwater

options.label: B
options.text: to float on the surface
options.rationale: Floating on the surface is the opposite of going under.

options.label: C
options.text: to freeze something solid
options.rationale: Freezing is not related to the root “sub” or the idea of going under.

options.label: D
options.text: to lift something out of water
options.rationale: Sub means under, so submerge means going under, not coming out.

items.stem: Re means again, and vis means see. What does revisit most likely mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: Re (again) + visit = to visit a second time, returning to a place already seen.
explanation.tip: The prefix re- almost always signals “again” or “back.”

options.label: A
options.text: to leave a place permanently
options.rationale: Revisit implies returning, not leaving for good.

options.label: B
options.text: to visit a place again

options.label: C
options.text: to see something for the very first time
options.rationale: Re means again, so revisit cannot mean a first-time visit.

options.label: D
options.text: to visit a place you have never heard of
options.rationale: Revisiting requires having been there before, which contradicts never having heard of it.

items.stem: Choose the number: 'uni' in words like unicorn and unicycle means ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: Uni is the Latin root for one, as in unicorn (one horn) and unicycle (one wheel).
explanation.tip: Compare uni-, bi-, and tri- to see how number roots change a word's meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: one

options.label: B
options.text: two
options.rationale: Two is shown by the root “bi,” as in bicycle.

options.label: C
options.text: many
options.rationale: Many is shown by roots like “multi” or “poly,” not “uni.”

options.label: D
options.text: three
options.rationale: Three is shown by the root “tri,” as in tricycle.

items.stem: The root 'contra' means against. What does it mean to contradict someone?

explanation.whyCorrect: Contra (against) + dict (say) = to say something that goes against what was said before.
explanation.tip: Contra shows up in contrast and contrary too, always carrying the idea of opposition.

options.label: A
options.text: to agree completely with someone
options.rationale: Contra means against, so contradicting means disagreeing, not agreeing.

options.label: B
options.text: to speak very loudly
options.rationale: Volume has nothing to do with the root “contra.”

options.label: C
options.text: to say the opposite of what someone else said

options.label: D
options.text: to repeat exactly what someone said
options.rationale: Repeating the same words is not “against” what they said.

items.stem: Match each root with its meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: These roots appear in words like flexible, fragment, convert, and motion.
explanation.tip: Think of a familiar word for each root to recall its meaning.

items.stem: Inter means between, and rupt means break. What does it mean to interrupt someone?

explanation.whyCorrect: Inter (between) + rupt (break) = to break in between, cutting into an ongoing action.
explanation.tip: Rupt always signals a break, as in erupt, disrupt, and rupture.

options.label: A
options.text: to help someone finish a sentence
options.rationale: Helping finish is cooperative, not a break caused by cutting in.

options.label: B
options.text: to repair something that is broken
options.rationale: Rupt means break, but “inter” plus “rupt” describes causing a break in an action, not fixing one.

options.label: C
options.text: to listen quietly without speaking
options.rationale: Listening quietly is the opposite of breaking into someone's speech.

options.label: D
options.text: to break into the middle of what someone is doing or saying

items.stem: The root 'circum' means around. What does it mean for a ship to circumnavigate the globe?

explanation.whyCorrect: Circum (around) + navigate (sail/steer) = to sail completely around something.
explanation.tip: Circum appears in circumference and circumstance, always pointing to “around.”

options.label: A
options.text: to sail all the way around the world

options.label: B
options.text: to sail across a narrow river
options.rationale: Circum means around, not across a narrow space.

options.label: C
options.text: to sail only along one coastline
options.rationale: Following one coastline is not the same as going all the way around.

options.label: D
options.text: to sail halfway around the world and stop
options.rationale: Circumnavigate specifically implies completing the full circle, not stopping halfway.

items.stem: The Latin root 'ambi' means both or around. What does it mean to be ambidextrous?

explanation.whyCorrect: Ambi (both) + dext (hand/right) = skilled with both hands.
explanation.tip: Ambi signals “both,” as in ambiguous, which can mean “both” or multiple ways to read something.

options.label: A
options.text: skilled in exactly one hand only
options.rationale: Ambidextrous means skilled with BOTH hands, not just one.

options.label: B
options.text: able to use both hands equally well

options.label: C
options.text: able to see in two directions at once
options.rationale: Ambidextrous relates to hand use, not vision.

options.label: D
options.text: confused about left and right
options.rationale: Being ambidextrous is a skill, not confusion.

items.stem: The root 'omni' means all. What does it mean for a narrator to be omniscient?

explanation.whyCorrect: Omni (all) + sci (know) = knowing all things, including private thoughts.
explanation.tip: Omni appears in omnivore and omnipresent — both built on the idea of “all.”

options.label: A
options.text: knowing only events that happen in the future
options.rationale: Omniscient means knowing everything, not only future events.

options.label: B
options.text: knowing only what one character says out loud
options.rationale: That describes a limited narrator, not one who is “all-knowing.”

options.label: C
options.text: knowing everything, including characters' private thoughts

options.label: D
options.text: knowing nothing about the story's events
options.rationale: Omni means all, so this is the opposite of omniscient.

items.stem: The root 'poly' means many. What is a polygon?

explanation.whyCorrect: Poly (many) + gon (angle/side) = a shape with many straight sides and angles.
explanation.tip: Poly shows up in polygon and polygamy, always pointing to “many.”

options.label: A
options.text: a shape with exactly one curved side
options.rationale: Poly means many, and a polygon's sides are straight, not curved.

options.label: B
options.text: a language spoken by many people
options.rationale: That would relate to “polyglot,” a different word, not “polygon.”

options.label: C
options.text: an animal with many legs
options.rationale: Polygon is a geometry term for a shape, not a living creature.

options.label: D
options.text: a shape with many straight sides

items.stem: The root 'hyper' means over or excessive. What does it mean to be hyperactive?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hyper (over) + active = having an excessive, over-the-top amount of energy.
explanation.tip: Hyper always signals “too much,” as in hypersensitive and hyperlink (a jump over to another page).

options.label: A
options.text: unusually and excessively active or energetic

options.label: B
options.text: unusually calm and still
options.rationale: Hyper means excessive, which is the opposite of calm and still.

options.label: C
options.text: active only during the night
options.rationale: Hyperactive describes a high level of energy, not a specific time of day.

options.label: D
options.text: active in only one activity
options.rationale: Hyperactive describes overall excess energy, not focus on a single activity.

items.stem: Choose the meaning: 'hypo' in hypothermia means ____, the opposite of 'hyper.'

explanation.whyCorrect: Hypo (under) + therm (heat) = a condition of dangerously low body heat.
explanation.tip: Hyper and hypo are opposite prefixes — one means too much, the other too little.

options.label: A
options.text: beside or next to
options.rationale: That describes the root “para,” not “hypo.”

options.label: B
options.text: under or below

options.label: C
options.text: around
options.rationale: That describes the root “circum” or “peri,” not “hypo.”

options.label: D
options.text: over or above
options.rationale: That is the meaning of “hyper,” the opposite of “hypo.”

items.stem: The root 'ante' means before. Which word means 'a room located before, or leading into, a larger room'?

explanation.whyCorrect: Ante (before) + chamber (room) = a room that comes before the main room.
explanation.tip: Ante shows up in antecedent — something that comes before.

options.label: A
options.text: antonym
options.rationale: Anti/ant means against, a different root from “ante” meaning before.

options.label: B
options.text: antechamber

options.label: C
options.text: postscript
options.rationale: Post means after, which is the opposite of “ante.”

options.label: D
options.text: antenna
options.rationale: Antenna is unrelated to the root “ante”; it refers to a sensory or signal-receiving part.

items.stem: The root 'post' means after. What does a postscript (P.S.) add to a letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: Post (after) + script (written) = something written after the main letter is finished.
explanation.tip: Post appears in postpone and postgame — both pointing to something after the main event.

options.label: A
options.text: the date the letter was written
options.rationale: A postscript is an added note, not simply a date.

options.label: B
options.text: the envelope the letter is mailed in
options.rationale: A postscript is written text, not the envelope.

options.label: C
options.text: a message added after the main letter has been signed

options.label: D
options.text: an introduction written before the letter begins
options.rationale: Post means after, so a postscript cannot be an introduction that comes first.

items.stem: The root 'para' means beside or alongside. What does it mean for two lines to be parallel?

explanation.whyCorrect: Para (beside) + allel (one another) = running beside one another at an equal distance.
explanation.tip: Para appears in paraphrase and paramedic — something existing alongside the main thing.

options.label: A
options.text: crossing each other at a sharp angle
options.rationale: Parallel lines specifically never cross; crossing lines are not parallel.

options.label: B
options.text: curving toward each other until they touch
options.rationale: Parallel lines keep the same distance apart and do not touch.

options.label: C
options.text: stacked directly on top of one another
options.rationale: Parallel describes lines running beside each other, not stacked vertically.

options.label: D
options.text: running beside each other at the same distance apart, never meeting

items.stem: The root 'peri' means around. What does the perimeter of a shape measure?
