options.rationale: “Exciting” and “good job” are still fairly vague compared to specific details.

options.label: B
options.text: The game was really good and the team played really well.
options.rationale: Adding “really” to vague words still leaves them vague.

options.label: C
options.text: The team executed crisp passes and scored three goals in a thrilling 3-1 victory.

items.stem: Which word is the most precise replacement for “good” in: “The chef made a good meal”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Flavorful” describes a specific quality of the meal.
explanation.tip: Replace vague judgment words with words that name an exact quality.

options.label: A
options.text: flavorful

options.label: B
options.text: fine
options.rationale: This word is just as vague as “good.”

options.label: C
options.text: okay
options.rationale: This word is even less precise than “good.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most precise verb to describe how the crowd reacted?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Erupted into cheers” shows exactly how loud and excited the crowd was.
explanation.tip: Precise verbs capture both the action and its intensity.

options.label: A
options.text: The crowd made noise when the home team scored.
options.rationale: “Made noise” is vague compared to “erupted into cheers.”

options.label: B
options.text: The crowd erupted into cheers when the home team scored.

options.label: C
options.text: The crowd did stuff when the home team scored.
options.rationale: This is far too vague to describe the crowd’s reaction.

items.stem: Which word choice has a more NEGATIVE connotation, even though both words have a similar basic meaning?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Stubborn” suggests the trait is unreasonable, giving it a negative feeling.
explanation.tip: Connotation is the feeling a word carries beyond its basic definition.

options.label: A
options.text: determined
options.rationale: This word has a positive connotation for the same basic trait.

options.label: B
options.text: persistent
options.rationale: This word also has a fairly positive connotation.

options.label: C
options.text: stubborn

items.stem: Which revision of “The ecosystem has a lot of different animals” uses more precise, domain-specific language for a science report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Terms like “predators,” “herbivores,” and “decomposers” are precise scientific vocabulary.
explanation.tip: Science writing should name specific categories instead of using vague words like “animals.”

options.label: A
options.text: The ecosystem supports a diverse population of predators, herbivores, and decomposers.

options.label: B
options.text: The ecosystem has many kinds of animals living in it.
options.rationale: This still uses vague, everyday wording instead of precise science terms.

options.label: C
options.text: The ecosystem has tons of animals doing their thing.
options.rationale: This is far too informal and vague for a science report.

items.stem: Which sentence would need to be revised to maintain a consistent FORMAL tone in a research report?

explanation.whyCorrect: Casual words like “anyway” and “kind of” break the formal tone the rest of the report uses.
explanation.tip: Check every sentence in a formal report for casual words that don’t belong.

options.label: A
options.text: Researchers observed a consistent rise in temperature over the study period.
options.rationale: This sentence is already formal and precise.

options.label: B
options.text: Anyway, the data kind of shows that temperatures went up a lot.

options.label: C
options.text: The data indicate a significant increase in temperature.
options.rationale: This sentence is already appropriately formal for a research report.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most precise dialogue tag to show how the character felt while speaking?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Exclaimed” along with the action of jumping shows Dana’s excitement precisely.
explanation.tip: Choose dialogue tags and actions that match the character’s actual emotion.

options.label: A
options.text: “I can’t believe we won!” Dana said.
options.rationale: “Said” is a neutral tag that doesn’t show her excitement.

options.label: B
options.text: “I can’t believe we won!” Dana stated.
options.rationale: “Stated” sounds formal and doesn’t match her excited reaction.

options.label: C
options.text: “I can’t believe we won!” Dana exclaimed, jumping with joy.

items.stem: Which revision replaces the vague phrase “a bunch of problems” with more precise language?

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming the specific problems is far more precise than the vague phrase “a bunch of problems.”
explanation.tip: Replace vague quantity phrases with the specific details they are hiding.

options.label: A
options.text: The old bridge had rusted beams, a cracked support pillar, and a weakened railing.

options.label: B
options.text: The old bridge had a bunch of problems that needed fixing.
options.rationale: “A bunch of problems” is vague and doesn’t specify what was wrong.

options.label: C
options.text: The old bridge had some issues here and there.
options.rationale: This is just as vague as the original phrase.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most precise comparative language to describe the two hiking trails?

explanation.whyCorrect: The specific comparison (“twice as steeply,” “first mile”) gives precise, measurable detail.
explanation.tip: Precise comparisons use specific measurements instead of vague intensifiers.

options.label: A
options.text: The northern trail is kind of worse than the southern trail.
options.rationale: “Kind of worse” is vague and informal.

options.label: B
options.text: The northern trail climbs twice as steeply as the southern trail in its first mile.

options.label: C
options.text: The northern trail is way harder than the southern trail.
options.rationale: “Way harder” is vague compared to a specific, measurable comparison.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the most precise sensory language to describe the kitchen?

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming the exact smells and sounds creates a precise, vivid picture for the reader.
explanation.tip: Precise sensory details name exact smells, sounds, and textures instead of vague labels.

options.label: A
options.text: The kitchen smelled nice and sounded like cooking.
options.rationale: This is vaguer and less specific than naming the exact smells and sounds.

options.label: B
options.text: The kitchen had a good smell and some sounds.
options.rationale: This phrasing is extremely vague and generic.

options.label: C
options.text: The kitchen smelled of cinnamon and simmering tomatoes, and the pan sizzled softly on the stove.

items.stem: Which revision maintains a consistent, precise, and formal style, unlike the original mixed version? Original: “The committee reviewed the budget, and honestly it was super confusing.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The revision removes casual filler words and replaces vague language with a precise, formal description.
explanation.tip: Scan for casual filler words (honestly, super, like) when formalizing a sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The committee reviewed the budget and found several sections difficult to interpret.

options.label: B
options.text: The committee reviewed the budget, and it was like really confusing, you know.
options.rationale: This remains casual and vague, which doesn’t fix the inconsistency.

options.label: C
options.text: The committee looked at the money stuff and it was confusing.
options.rationale: This is still casual and vague, not formal or precise.

items.stem: Original: “The storm was really bad and caused a lot of damage.” Which revision uses the MOST precise and vivid language while keeping a consistent, serious tone?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific numbers and concrete effects replace every vague word in the original sentence.
explanation.tip: Precise revisions replace both vague adjectives and vague verbs with exact, concrete details.

options.label: A
options.text: The storm was pretty intense and messed a lot of stuff up.
options.rationale: “Pretty intense” and “messed stuff up” are casual and vague, breaking a serious tone.

options.label: B
options.text: The storm’s hundred-mile-per-hour winds toppled power lines and stripped roofs from a dozen homes.

options.label: C
options.text: The storm was extremely bad and caused tons of damage.
options.rationale: Adding “extremely” and “tons” still leaves the language vague.

items.stem: Which sentence breaks the formal tone of this paragraph? “The museum’s new exhibit explores ancient trade routes. It’s pretty cool how merchants traveled so far. The exhibit also features rare artifacts from three continents.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Pretty cool” is casual and breaks the formal tone used in the rest of the paragraph.
explanation.tip: Scan a formal paragraph for casual phrases that don’t match the rest of the style.

options.label: A
options.text: The exhibit also features rare artifacts from three continents.
options.rationale: This sentence is formal and consistent with the rest of the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum’s new exhibit explores ancient trade routes.
options.rationale: This sentence is already formal and matches the rest of the paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: It’s pretty cool how merchants traveled so far.

items.stem: Which revision fixes the inconsistent tone in: “The scientist’s findings were groundbreaking, but honestly, some people just didn’t buy it.”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Replacing “honestly” and “didn’t buy it” with formal wording matches the serious tone of the first clause.
explanation.tip: Replace casual filler words and slang with formal equivalents to fix a tone shift.

options.label: A
options.text: The scientist’s findings were groundbreaking, but some critics remained skeptical.

options.label: B
options.text: The scientist’s findings were groundbreaking, but like, some people didn’t buy it.
options.rationale: This keeps the casual “like,” which still breaks the formal tone.

options.label: C
options.text: The scientist’s findings were groundbreaking, but honestly, some people disagreed, you know.
options.rationale: This adds another casual phrase, making the inconsistency worse.

items.stem: Which sentence maintains a consistent, objective tone appropriate for a news report?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence states the fact plainly without inserting personal opinion or uncertainty.
explanation.tip: News reports stay objective — avoid words that reveal the writer’s personal feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: City officials are apparently going to maybe fix the bridge sometime.
options.rationale: This is vague and uncertain, which doesn’t match a factual news report’s tone.

options.label: B
options.text: City officials announced the bridge repairs will begin next month.

options.label: C
options.text: City officials finally decided to fix that annoying bridge next month.
options.rationale: “Finally” and “annoying” introduce the writer’s personal opinion, breaking objectivity.

items.stem: Which sentence shows an inappropriate shift from formal to informal style within this paragraph? “The committee carefully reviewed every proposal submitted this year. They were super picky about budget details. In the end, three proposals were approved.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Super picky” is casual slang that doesn’t match the formal tone of the surrounding sentences.
explanation.tip: Look for a sudden slang word in an otherwise formal paragraph — that is usually the shift.

options.label: A
options.text: In the end, three proposals were approved.
options.rationale: This sentence is consistent with the formal, factual tone.

options.label: B
options.text: The committee carefully reviewed every proposal submitted this year.
options.rationale: This sentence matches the formal tone of the rest of the paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: They were super picky about budget details.

items.stem: Which word choice best maintains a formal, academic tone in: “The author’s argument ____ the reader to reconsider common assumptions”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Compels” is a precise, formal verb appropriate for academic analysis.
explanation.tip: Academic writing favors precise, formal verbs over casual, everyday ones.

options.label: A
options.text: compels

options.label: B
options.text: nudges
options.rationale: This word is too casual and understates the argument’s force for academic tone.

options.label: C
options.text: pushes
options.rationale: This word is more casual and less precise for academic writing.

items.stem: Which sentence would need revision to match the serious, respectful tone of an obituary? “Mrs. Hassan dedicated forty years to teaching and touched countless lives in her community. She was a total legend who never missed a day of work.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Total legend” is slang that clashes with the respectful, formal tone of an obituary.
explanation.tip: Formal tributes avoid slang, even when the sentiment behind it is positive.

options.label: A
options.text: Her dedication to her students will long be remembered by the community.
options.rationale: This sentence is consistent with a respectful, formal tone.

options.label: B
options.text: She was a total legend who never missed a day of work.

options.label: C
options.text: Mrs. Hassan dedicated forty years to teaching and touched countless lives in her community.
options.rationale: This sentence matches the respectful, formal tone of an obituary.

items.stem: Which revision corrects the tone shift while keeping the sentence’s meaning? Original: “The CEO’s decision was strategic, but kind of a bummer for the employees affected.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Replacing “kind of a bummer” with “a difficult impact” restores a consistent, professional tone.
explanation.tip: When fixing a tone shift, replace the casual phrase entirely rather than softening it.

options.label: A
options.text: The CEO’s decision was strategic, but employees were kind of upset about it.
options.rationale: This still keeps the casual phrase “kind of,” leaving the tone inconsistent.

options.label: B
options.text: The CEO’s decision was strategic, but it was a bummer and a half for employees.
options.rationale: This intensifies the casual slang instead of fixing it.

options.label: C
options.text: The CEO’s decision was strategic, but it had a difficult impact on the employees affected.

items.stem: Which sentence is written in a tone appropriate for a formal email to a potential employer?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentence uses polite, professional phrasing appropriate for communicating with an employer.
explanation.tip: Formal emails avoid casual greetings like “Hey” and vague phrases like “that thing.”

options.label: A
options.text: I am writing to follow up on my application for the summer internship position.

options.label: B
options.text: So did you guys decide about the internship yet or what?
options.rationale: This is overly casual and somewhat demanding in tone for a formal email.

options.label: C
options.text: Hey, just checking in about that internship thing I applied for!
options.rationale: This is far too casual for a formal email to an employer.

items.stem: A student’s persuasive essay shifts from a serious, formal tone to sarcasm partway through. Which sentence is the sarcastic shift? “Climate change is affecting ecosystems worldwide. Oh sure, because nobody could possibly care about that. Immediate policy changes are needed to address this crisis.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The sarcastic phrasing “oh sure” breaks the serious, formal tone used elsewhere in the essay.
explanation.tip: Sarcasm often signals an inappropriate shift away from a serious, persuasive tone.

options.label: A
options.text: Climate change is affecting ecosystems worldwide.
options.rationale: This sentence matches the serious, formal tone of the rest of the essay.

options.label: B
options.text: Oh sure, because nobody could possibly care about that.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate policy changes are needed to address this crisis.
options.rationale: This sentence is consistent with the serious, urgent tone.

items.stem: Original: “The novel’s themes are complex, but it’s basically a fun read if you’re into that kind of stuff.” Which revision fixes the tone shift while keeping it appropriate for a literary analysis essay?

explanation.whyCorrect: The revision removes all casual phrasing and uses formal, analytical language consistent with a literary essay.
explanation.tip: A full tone fix replaces every casual phrase, not just one word, with formal, analytical language.

options.label: A
options.text: The novel’s themes are complex, but honestly it’s just a fun read if you like that stuff.
options.rationale: This keeps multiple casual phrases, which still clash with a literary analysis tone.

options.label: B
options.text: The novel’s themes are complex, but it’s basically a pretty fun read overall.
options.rationale: This still contains the casual phrases “basically” and “pretty,” leaving the tone inconsistent.

options.label: C
options.text: The novel’s themes are complex, and its engaging narrative style rewards careful readers.

items.stem: What is the simple subject in: “The little boy raced down the hill”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Boy” is the one word that names who the sentence is about.
explanation.tip: The simple subject is just the main noun, without its describing words.

options.label: A
options.text: boy

options.label: B
options.text: little
options.rationale: This is an adjective describing the boy, not the subject itself.

options.label: C
options.text: hill
options.rationale: This is part of the predicate, not the subject.

items.stem: What is the complete predicate in: “Our neighbors painted their fence bright blue last weekend”?

explanation.whyCorrect: The complete predicate includes the verb and everything that tells more about the action.
explanation.tip: The complete predicate always starts with the verb and includes every word after it.

options.label: A
options.text: Our neighbors
options.rationale: This is the subject, not the predicate.

options.label: B
options.text: painted their fence bright blue last weekend

options.label: C
options.text: their fence bright blue
options.rationale: This leaves out the verb “painted,” so it isn’t the complete predicate.

items.stem: Which sentence has a compound subject?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Omar and his brother” are two subjects joined by “and,” forming a compound subject.
explanation.tip: A compound subject has two or more subjects joined by “and” or “or.”

options.label: A
options.text: Omar’s treehouse was built quickly.
options.rationale: This has a single subject, “treehouse.”

options.label: B
options.text: Omar built a treehouse with his brother.
