options.rationale: This is part of the falling action, after the main tension is resolved.

options.label: B
options.text: The team practicing all week.
options.rationale: This is part of the rising action, before the main problem happens.

options.label: C
options.text: The moment the spare baton is found just before the race.

items.stem: Which event is part of the RISING ACTION?

explanation.whyCorrect: Practicing all week builds up to the story's main problem.
explanation.tip: Rising action happens before the climax and builds toward the main tension.

options.label: A
options.text: The team practices handing off the baton all week.

options.label: B
options.text: The spare baton is found just before the race.
options.rationale: This is the climax, the turning point of tension.

options.label: C
options.text: The team crosses the finish line.
options.rationale: This is the falling action, after the climax.

items.stem: What CAUSES the family to search for candles?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sudden power outage is the direct cause of the candle search.
explanation.tip: Find the problem that happens right before a character takes action.

options.label: A
options.text: They want to make the dinner feel special.
options.rationale: The family searched for candles because of the outage, not to make things fancy on purpose.

options.label: B
options.text: The lights suddenly go out during dinner.

options.label: C
options.text: Dad always lights candles before dinner.
options.rationale: The story shows the candles were found only after the lights went out.

items.stem: Put the events of the story in order.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is the sequence the events happen in the story.
explanation.tip: The problem (lights going out) always comes before the solution (finding candles).

sequence: The family is cooking dinner together in the kitchen.
The lights suddenly go out.
Dad searches the kitchen drawer for candles.
They light the candles and keep cooking.
The family realizes the candlelit dinner was more fun than usual.

items.stem: How does the story's STRUCTURE build tension before the climax?

explanation.whyCorrect: Starting with a calm, ordinary scene makes the sudden outage feel more unexpected.
explanation.tip: Notice how a calm opening scene can make a sudden problem feel bigger.

options.label: A
options.text: It starts with the candles already lit.
options.rationale: The story starts with an ordinary dinner before the lights go out, not with candles already lit.

options.label: B
options.text: It explains the ending before anything else happens.
options.rationale: The story follows normal time order and does not reveal the ending first.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows an ordinary dinner first, which makes the sudden power outage feel more surprising.

items.stem: Where does the FLASHBACK occur in this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dalia's memory of leaving her notes at school is the flashback that opens the story.
explanation.tip: A flashback is a memory of something that already happened before the main action.

options.label: A
options.text: At the beginning, when Dalia remembers leaving her notes at school.

options.label: B
options.text: In the middle, when she finishes the project.
options.rationale: Finishing the project happens in the story's present time, not as a flashback.

options.label: C
options.text: At the end, when she presents her project.
options.rationale: The presentation happens in real time, not as a memory of the past.

items.stem: How does the flashback affect the story's structure?

explanation.whyCorrect: The flashback gives the reader the reason behind Dalia's nighttime rush.
explanation.tip: Ask what information the flashback gives the reader before the main events continue.

options.label: A
options.text: It replaces the climax of the story.
options.rationale: The climax is Dalia finishing just as the bell rings, not the flashback.

options.label: B
options.text: It explains WHY Dalia has to rebuild her notes, before the main action of the night begins.

options.label: C
options.text: It reveals how the story will end before it happens.
options.rationale: The flashback only explains a past event; it does not reveal the ending.

items.stem: Which event is the CLIMAX of the story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Finishing right as the bell rings is the moment of greatest tension and relief.
explanation.tip: The climax is usually the moment a race against time is finally won or lost.

options.label: A
options.text: Dalia remembers leaving her notes at school.
options.rationale: This flashback sets up the problem; it isn't the moment of highest tension.

options.label: B
options.text: Dalia presents her project calmly.
options.rationale: This is the falling action, after the climax has already passed.

options.label: C
options.text: Dalia finishes her project just as the morning bell rings.

items.stem: How do the SHORT sentences at the beginning affect the pacing of this excerpt?

explanation.whyCorrect: Short, clipped sentences slow the reader down and stretch out the tense waiting moment.
explanation.tip: Notice how sentence length can speed up or slow down the feeling of a scene.

options.label: A
options.text: They slow the pacing down and build suspense around the moment of waiting.

options.label: B
options.text: They have no effect on the pacing.
options.rationale: The short sentences clearly change the rhythm compared with the long sentence that follows.

options.label: C
options.text: They speed up the pacing to rush through the waiting.
options.rationale: The short, choppy sentences stretch out the tense moment rather than rushing it.

items.stem: Why does the final sentence become much LONGER than the ones before it?

explanation.whyCorrect: The flowing, longer sentence matches the slow unfolding of the letter after the tense pause.
explanation.tip: Ask why a writer would deliberately change sentence length at a key moment.

options.label: A
options.text: The author ran out of short sentences to use.
options.rationale: The sentence length is a deliberate structural choice to match the shift in action, not a random change.

options.label: B
options.text: It mirrors the moment tension finally breaks, as Mariam slowly opens and reads the letter.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows Mariam is now in a hurry.
options.rationale: The long sentence describes her moving slowly and carefully, not hurrying.

items.stem: Where does this excerpt most likely fit in the overall structure of a longer story about Mariam?

explanation.whyCorrect: The suspense and relief in this excerpt suggest a long-built tension is finally being resolved.
explanation.tip: Look for signs of built-up tension finally breaking to locate a scene near the climax.

options.label: A
options.text: In the middle of the rising action, before any tension has built.
options.rationale: The excerpt describes the resolution of built-up tension, which fits later in the structure.

options.label: B
options.text: At the very beginning, before any conflict is introduced.
options.rationale: The excerpt already shows a tense, resolved moment, which comes after a conflict has built up.

options.label: C
options.text: Near the climax, as the central tension (the exam result) is finally resolved.

items.stem: How does the PARALLEL structure (alternating between Khalid and Yara) affect the reader's understanding?

explanation.whyCorrect: Switching between Khalid and Yara lets the reader directly compare each path's result.
explanation.tip: Alternating between two characters is often used to set up a comparison.

options.label: A
options.text: It lets the reader compare the different results of each character's choice side by side.

options.label: B
options.text: It combines both characters into a single choice.
options.rationale: The structure keeps the two characters' separate choices and outcomes distinct.

options.label: C
options.text: It hides Khalid's choice from the reader until the end.
options.rationale: Khalid's choice is stated clearly at the beginning, not hidden.

items.stem: What does the structure of this excerpt suggest about the story's theme?

explanation.whyCorrect: Khalid arrives first but alone, while Yara arrives later but happier, suggesting speed isn't everything.
explanation.tip: Compare the outcomes, not just the speed, to find a story's deeper message.

options.label: A
options.text: Friendship is not important to the story.
options.rationale: Yara's enjoyable walk with a friend suggests friendship matters to the story's meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: Taking the faster path isn't always the better choice.

options.label: C
options.text: Taking the shortcut is always the best choice in any situation.
options.rationale: Khalid's shortcut left him alone, which does not support this being the better choice.

items.stem: The structure of alternating between the two characters builds toward a comparison rather than a single straight sequence of events.

explanation.whyCorrect: The excerpt switches between Khalid and Yara's choices and results, building a comparison instead of one continuous timeline.
explanation.tip: Look for alternating or parallel structure as a clue that a text is building a comparison.

items.stem: How does the contrast between the room's laughter and Sami's inner thoughts build tension?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sami's secret worry contrasts with the unaware laughter around him, creating suspense for the reader.
explanation.tip: Dramatic tension often comes from the reader knowing something the other characters don't yet.

options.label: A
options.text: It reveals that everyone already knows about the broken vase.
options.rationale: The sudden quiet when the aunt enters shows the others did NOT already know.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that Sami is also laughing at the joke on the inside.
options.rationale: Sami's racing thoughts are about the broken vase, not about the joke.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows the reader a hidden problem that the other characters don't yet know about.

items.stem: What is the function of the final sentence in the structure of this scene?

explanation.whyCorrect: The aunt's entrance is the structural turning point that finally reveals the hidden problem.
explanation.tip: The final sentence of a tense scene often delivers the moment the built-up suspense has been leading toward.

options.label: A
options.text: It delivers the reveal that resolves the suspense built by Sami's hidden worry.

options.label: B
options.text: It returns the scene to the calm mood from the very beginning.
options.rationale: The room going quiet is a tense moment, not a return to the earlier relaxed laughter.

options.label: C
options.text: It introduces a brand-new conflict unrelated to the rest of the scene.
options.rationale: The aunt's entrance directly resolves the tension already built around the broken vase.

items.stem: If this excerpt is the climax of a longer story, what would most likely come immediately AFTER it in the story's structure?

explanation.whyCorrect: After a climax, a story typically moves into falling action that resolves the tension just revealed.
explanation.tip: After the climax, expect the story to start resolving its central problem, not introduce a new one.

options.label: A
options.text: The very beginning of the story, introducing Sami for the first time.
options.rationale: A story's beginning would not logically follow after its climax.

options.label: B
options.text: The falling action, showing how Sami responds to being caught.

options.label: C
options.text: More rising action building up a brand-new problem before this one is addressed.
options.rationale: A climax is typically followed by falling action resolving the existing tension, not a new unrelated problem.

items.stem: Which group of words is an INDEPENDENT clause (a complete thought)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “The rain stopped” has a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought.
explanation.tip: An independent clause can stand alone as its own sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the rain stopped.
options.rationale: The word “because” makes this a dependent clause; it can't stand alone.

options.label: B
options.text: When the rain stopped.
options.rationale: “When” makes this a dependent clause; it needs a main clause to complete it.

options.label: C
options.text: The rain stopped.

items.stem: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: “After” begins the clause and leaves it needing a main clause to complete the thought.
explanation.tip: Words like after, when, and because often start dependent clauses.

options.label: A
options.text: After the bell rang

options.label: B
options.text: The students left the room.
options.rationale: This is also a complete thought on its own.

options.label: C
options.text: The bell rang.
options.rationale: This is a complete thought, so it is an independent clause.

items.stem: Choose the subordinating conjunction: “____ the sun set, the sky turned orange and pink.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “As” connects the time of the sunset to the main event.
explanation.tip: Subordinating conjunctions like as, when, and while introduce dependent clauses.

options.label: A
options.text: As

options.label: B
options.text: But
options.rationale: “But” also joins independent clauses, not a dependent clause here.

options.label: C
options.text: And
options.rationale: “And” joins two independent clauses, not a dependent clause to a main clause.

items.stem: Which sentence is a COMPLEX sentence (independent clause + dependent clause)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Although it was cold” is a dependent clause attached to the independent clause.
explanation.tip: A complex sentence has one dependent clause joined to one independent clause.

options.label: A
options.text: It was cold, and the children played outside.
options.rationale: This joins two independent clauses with “and,” making it a compound sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Although it was cold, the children played outside.

options.label: C
options.text: It was cold. The children played outside.
options.rationale: These are two separate simple sentences, not one complex sentence.

items.stem: “While the kettle boiled” can stand alone as a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: The word “while” starts a dependent clause, which needs a main clause to complete its meaning.
explanation.tip: If a clause starts with a word like while, because, or although, it usually cannot stand alone.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A dependent clause that starts a sentence needs a comma before the main clause.
explanation.tip: When a sentence begins with a dependent clause, add a comma after it.

segments: the first ten minutes of class.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly combines these two ideas using a dependent clause? “The lights went out. We lit candles.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “When” turns the first idea into a dependent clause that sets up the main clause.
explanation.tip: Use a subordinating conjunction like when, because, or although to join two related ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: The lights went out we lit candles.
options.rationale: This run-on has no conjunction or punctuation connecting the two ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: The lights went out, we lit candles.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this needs a conjunction.

options.label: C
options.text: When the lights went out, we lit candles.

items.stem: Match each dependent clause with the main clause that completes it best.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each dependent clause needs a main clause that logically completes its meaning.
explanation.tip: Read the dependent clause first and ask what main idea would make sense with it.

pairs.right: Hassan finished it with time to spare.
we studied at the park instead.
the game will go on as planned.

items.stem: Which group of words is an independent clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: “The museum opens at nine” has a subject and verb and is a complete thought.
explanation.tip: An independent clause can stand alone as its own sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum opens at nine.

options.label: B
options.text: Once the museum opens at nine.
options.rationale: “Once” makes this a dependent clause.

options.label: C
options.text: Before the museum opens at nine.
options.rationale: “Before” makes this a dependent clause.

items.stem: Choose the subordinating conjunction: “____ she practiced every day, Huda improved quickly at chess.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Since” shows the cause-and-effect link between practicing and improving.
explanation.tip: Since, because, and as often introduce a reason in a dependent clause.

options.label: A
options.text: Or
options.rationale: “Or” connects independent clauses or choices, not a dependent clause like this.

options.label: B
options.text: Since

options.label: C
options.text: Yet
options.rationale: “Yet” connects contrasting independent clauses, not a cause-and-effect dependent clause.

items.stem: Which sentence is complex?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Even though she was nervous” is a dependent clause attached to the main clause.
explanation.tip: A complex sentence joins one dependent clause to one independent clause.

options.label: A
options.text: She was nervous. Rana gave her speech confidently.
options.rationale: These are two separate simple sentences.

options.label: B
options.text: Even though she was nervous, Rana gave her speech confidently.

options.label: C
options.text: She was nervous, but Rana gave her speech confidently.
options.rationale: This joins two independent clauses with “but,” making it compound.

items.stem: “Whoever finishes first” expresses a complete thought on its own.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Whoever finishes first” depends on a main clause to complete its meaning, such as “gets a prize.”
explanation.tip: A clause beginning with whoever, whatever, or whichever is usually dependent.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: No comma is needed between the subject “captain” and the verb “turned.”
explanation.tip: Don't place a comma between a subject and its verb.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly combines these ideas with a dependent clause? “The power failed. The team lost their data.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Because” turns the first idea into a dependent clause explaining the cause.
explanation.tip: Use because to show that one event is the cause of another.

options.label: A
options.text: The power failed, the team lost their data.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

options.label: B
options.text: The power failed the team lost their data.
options.rationale: This run-on needs a conjunction or punctuation to connect the two ideas.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the power failed, the team lost their data.

items.stem: Which dependent clause best completes this sentence? “____, the hikers set up camp early.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Since” turns the reason into a dependent clause that fits before the main clause.
explanation.tip: A dependent clause often gives the reason behind the action in the main clause.

options.label: A
options.text: Since the trail was longer than expected

options.label: B
options.text: The trail was longer than expected
options.rationale: Without a subordinating word, this is an independent clause, not a dependent one.

options.label: C
options.text: The hikers set up camp early
options.rationale: This repeats the main clause instead of giving a reason for it.

items.stem: Match each dependent clause with the main clause that completes it best.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each dependent clause needs a logically matching main clause to form a complete sentence.
explanation.tip: Picture the situation described by the dependent clause, then find the matching result.

pairs.left: Because the bridge was under repair,
Even though the forecast predicted rain,
As soon as the bell rang,
pairs.right: students lined up at the door.

items.stem: Which group of words is a dependent clause?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Which” begins a relative clause that depends on a noun it describes.
explanation.tip: A relative clause beginning with who, which, or that is usually dependent.

options.label: A
options.text: The package arrived yesterday.
options.rationale: This is a complete, independent thought.

options.label: B
options.text: Which arrived yesterday

options.label: C
options.text: We opened the package.
options.rationale: This is also an independent clause.

items.stem: Which sentence contains a RELATIVE clause (starting with who, which, or that)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Who discovered the pattern” is a relative clause describing “the scientist.”
explanation.tip: Relative clauses describe a noun and start with who, which, or that.

options.label: A
options.text: The scientist discovered the pattern and won an award.
options.rationale: This joins two independent clauses with “and”; it has no relative clause.

options.label: B
options.text: The scientist discovered the pattern. She won an award.
options.rationale: These are two separate simple sentences with no relative clause.

options.label: C
options.text: The scientist who discovered the pattern won an award.

items.stem: Choose the correct relative pronoun: “The book, ____ was written in 1920, is still popular today.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Which” is the relative pronoun used for things, like a book.
explanation.tip: Use who/whom for people, which for things, and that for either.

options.label: A
options.text: who
options.rationale: “Who” refers to people, not a book.

options.label: B
options.text: because
options.rationale: “Because” introduces a reason, not a description of the book.

options.label: C
options.text: which

items.stem: In “The bridge, which was built last year, already needs repairs,” the clause “which was built last year” is essential to identifying which bridge is meant.

explanation.whyCorrect: There is only one bridge being discussed, so the clause just adds extra information set off by commas; it is nonrestrictive, not essential.
explanation.tip: A clause set off by commas usually adds extra, non-essential information.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The clause already names the subject (“the scientist”), so the extra pronoun “she” creates a repeated, ungrammatical subject.
explanation.tip: Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun after a relative clause.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a relative clause to combine these ideas? “The experiment failed. The experiment used the wrong chemical.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Which used the wrong chemical” is a relative clause that adds detail about the experiment.
explanation.tip: A relative clause can combine two related sentences about the same noun.

options.label: A
options.text: The experiment, which used the wrong chemical, failed.

options.label: B
options.text: The experiment failed used the wrong chemical.
options.rationale: This combines the two ideas without a relative pronoun, making the sentence unclear.

options.label: C
options.text: The experiment used the wrong chemical, it failed.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; this also unnecessarily repeats the subject with “it.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses a nonrestrictive clause correctly (set off with commas because it adds extra, non-essential information)?

explanation.whyCorrect: The clause “who lives in Alexandria” is extra, non-essential information, so it needs commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: A nonrestrictive clause describing a specific, already-identified noun needs commas on both sides.

options.label: A
options.text: My uncle who lives in Alexandria is visiting next week.
options.rationale: Since “my uncle” already identifies one specific person, the clause is extra information and needs commas.

options.label: B
options.text: My uncle, who lives in Alexandria, is visiting next week.

options.label: C
options.text: My uncle, who lives in Alexandria is visiting next week.
options.rationale: A nonrestrictive clause needs a comma on BOTH sides, not just before it.

items.stem: Match each sentence opening with the relative clause that completes it correctly.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each relative clause must logically and grammatically describe the noun it follows.
explanation.tip: Check whether the clause describes a person (who/whose), a thing (which), or either (that).

pairs.right: which surprised everyone, went to the youngest student.
who assigned the project gave clear instructions.
which sits along the river, floods every spring.
whose projects were chosen will present on Friday.

items.stem: Read: “Ant colonies are organized into different roles. The queen lays eggs deep inside the nest, worker ants gather food and build tunnels, and soldier ants defend the colony from danger. Each ant has a clear job that keeps the colony running smoothly.” How does the author mainly organize this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists separate roles — queen, workers, soldiers — within one colony.
explanation.tip: Description paragraphs list facts and details about one topic.

options.label: A
options.text: By telling the order in which an ant egg becomes an adult.
options.rationale: No growth stages or ages are described.

options.label: B
options.text: By comparing ant colonies to bee colonies.
options.rationale: No other insect is mentioned for comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: By describing the different roles ants have in a colony.

options.label: D
options.text: By explaining what causes ants to build tunnels.
options.rationale: No cause-and-effect relationship is described.

items.stem: Choose the word that signals another descriptive detail: “Worker ants gather food. ____, they build and repair tunnels.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Also” adds another detail about what worker ants do.
explanation.tip: Also, another, in addition — these words add description details.

options.label: A
options.text: First
options.rationale: “First” signals a step in a sequence, not an added detail.

options.label: B
options.text: Because
options.rationale: “Because” signals a cause.

options.label: C
options.text: Also

options.label: D
options.text: Later
options.rationale: “Later” signals time order.

items.stem: Read: “The Sahara Desert is extremely dry and hot during the day, but temperatures drop sharply at night. Sand dunes stretch for miles, and very little rain falls each year. Few plants can survive there except hardy shrubs and cactus-like plants.” How does the author organize information about the Sahara in this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph describes several features — temperature, dunes, rainfall, and plants — about one place.
explanation.tip: Description paragraphs pile up facts about a single subject.

options.label: A
options.text: By narrating a trip across the desert in time order.
options.rationale: No events or timeline are given.

options.label: B
options.text: By explaining what caused the desert to form.
options.rationale: The paragraph does not explain a cause.

options.label: C
options.text: By comparing the Sahara to a rainforest.
options.rationale: No other place is mentioned for comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: By listing physical features and conditions of the desert.

items.stem: Match each Sahara detail with what it tells you.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each detail describes a different aspect of the desert.
explanation.tip: Look for separate facts under one topic.

items.stem: Read: “Egyptian cotton is famous for its long, soft fibers. Farmers grow it along the fertile banks of the Nile, where the soil is rich and the weather is warm. The fine threads are woven into smooth sheets, towels, and shirts sold around the world.” Which sentence gives a descriptive detail about WHERE the cotton grows?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence names the Nile's banks as the growing location.
explanation.tip: Scan for the sentence naming a specific place.

options.label: A
options.text: Farmers grow it along the fertile banks of the Nile, where the soil is rich and the weather is warm.

options.label: B
options.text: Egyptian cotton is famous for its long, soft fibers.
options.rationale: This describes the fiber, not the growing location.

options.label: C
options.text: The fine threads are woven into smooth sheets, towels, and shirts sold around the world.
options.rationale: This describes products made from the cotton.

options.label: D
options.text: Egyptian cotton is grown only in one small village.
options.rationale: This sentence is not in the paragraph.

items.stem: Choose the word that adds another description detail: “Egyptian cotton has long, soft fibers. ____, it is known for being very strong.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “In addition” adds a further descriptive detail about the cotton.
explanation.tip: In addition, furthermore, also — all add more description.

options.label: A
options.text: Before this
options.rationale: This signals time order.

options.label: B
options.text: Unlike this
options.rationale: This signals a contrast.

options.label: C
options.text: As a result
options.rationale: This signals cause and effect.

options.label: D
options.text: In addition

items.stem: Read: “The Nile River flows north through Egypt for thousands of kilometers. Its banks are lined with green farmland, while its waters support fish, birds, and boats. Ancient and modern cities have grown along its edges.” What is the MAIN topic this paragraph describes?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every sentence adds a fact describing the river and its surroundings.
explanation.tip: Ask: what one subject do all the sentences describe?

options.label: A
options.text: A single boat trip down the Nile.
options.rationale: No specific trip or journey is narrated.

options.label: B
options.text: The features and importance of the Nile River.

options.label: C
options.text: The reasons the Nile sometimes floods.
options.rationale: No cause of flooding is explained.

options.label: D
options.text: The differences between the Nile and another river.
options.rationale: No other river is mentioned for comparison.

items.stem: A friend says the Nile paragraph above is organized as a list of facts, not as a sequence of events with a beginning and an end. Is the friend correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences list facts about the river's length, banks, and the cities near it, with no single timed sequence.
explanation.tip: A description structure gives facts, not a sequence of events.

items.stem: Read: “The school library has tall shelves filled with storybooks, atlases, and science magazines. Soft chairs sit near the big windows, and a quiet reading corner is set aside for younger students. A librarian helps students find books and use the computers.” Which detail describes the library's seating area?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence tells readers where students can sit.
explanation.tip: Match each detail to the part of the topic it describes.

options.label: A
options.text: A librarian helps students find books.
options.rationale: This describes the librarian's job.

options.label: B
options.text: Tall shelves filled with storybooks, atlases, and science magazines.
options.rationale: This describes the shelves, not the seating.

options.label: C
options.text: Soft chairs sit near the big windows.

options.label: D
options.text: The library closes at four o'clock.
options.rationale: This detail is not in the paragraph.

items.stem: Fill in: A paragraph that gives many facts about one topic, like the library above, uses a ____ structure. (one word)

explanation.whyCorrect: Listing many facts about a single topic is a description structure.
explanation.tip: Description = many details, one topic.

items.stem: Read: “Peregrine falcons have narrow wings built for speed and sharp eyes that can spot prey from far away. Their curved beaks tear meat easily, and their strong talons grip tightly onto branches or prey. These features make falcons skilled hunters.” Why did the author most likely describe the falcon's wings, eyes, beak, and talons separately?

explanation.whyCorrect: Breaking the description into separate body parts helps readers picture the whole bird.
explanation.tip: Authors often describe a subject part by part.

options.label: A
options.text: To compare falcons with eagles.
options.rationale: No other bird is mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: To explain why falcons are becoming rare.
options.rationale: No information about falcon populations is given.

options.label: C
options.text: To tell the order in which falcons are born and grow.
options.rationale: No growth stages or time order are described.

options.label: D
options.text: To give readers a clear picture of each body part that helps the falcon hunt.

items.stem: Match each falcon body part with what it is used for.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each body part has its own descriptive detail about its purpose.
explanation.tip: Look for a feature paired with its function.

items.stem: Read: “Camels can survive for days without water because they store fat in their humps. Thick eyelashes and nostrils that close protect them from blowing sand. Wide, tough feet keep them from sinking into loose sand.” Which structure does this paragraph use to explain camels?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists separate features — humps, eyelashes, nostrils, feet — that help camels survive.
explanation.tip: Count the separate features listed about one subject.

options.label: A
options.text: It describes several physical features that help camels survive in the desert.

options.label: B
options.text: It explains the order in which a camel grows from birth to adulthood.
options.rationale: No growth stages or ages are mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: It argues that camels should be protected.
options.rationale: The paragraph states facts, not an opinion.

options.label: D
options.text: It compares camels to horses.
options.rationale: No other animal is named for comparison.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Also” adds another descriptive detail; “First” wrongly suggests a step in a sequence.
explanation.tip: Check whether a transition adds a detail or shows a step in order.

segments: Camels can survive for days without water.
they also have thick eyelashes that protect their eyes.

items.stem: Read: “Coral reefs are home to colorful fish, sea turtles, and tiny shrimp. The coral itself looks like branching rock but is actually built by millions of tiny living animals. Reefs also shelter young fish from larger predators.” What is this paragraph mostly about?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every sentence adds a fact describing the reef and the animals living there.
explanation.tip: Ask what single topic every sentence describes.

options.label: A
options.text: Why coral reefs are disappearing.
options.rationale: No cause of reef loss is explained.

options.label: B
options.text: The living things and shelter found in a coral reef.

options.label: C
options.text: A story about a diver exploring a reef.
options.rationale: No character or events are narrated.

options.label: D
options.text: The difference between coral reefs and rainforests.
options.rationale: No other habitat is compared.

items.stem: Choose the best word: “Coral reefs shelter fish. ____, they protect young sea turtles.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Furthermore” adds another fact about what reefs protect.
explanation.tip: Also/furthermore/in addition add more description.

options.label: A
options.text: Furthermore

options.label: B
options.text: Finally
options.rationale: This signals the last step in a sequence.

options.label: C
options.text: Therefore
options.rationale: This signals a cause-and-effect result.

options.label: D
options.text: Unlike
options.rationale: This signals a contrast.

items.stem: Read: “A volcano is a mountain with an opening that can release melted rock called lava. Thick clouds of ash sometimes rise from the opening, and the ground around it can tremble before an eruption. Some volcanoes stay quiet for hundreds of years.” Which detail describes what happens to the ground near a volcano?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence specifically describes the trembling ground.
explanation.tip: Match each detail to exactly what it is describing.

options.label: A
options.text: Some volcanoes stay quiet for hundreds of years.
options.rationale: This describes how long volcanoes can be inactive.

options.label: B
options.text: Thick clouds of ash sometimes rise from the opening.
options.rationale: This describes the ash, not the ground.

options.label: C
options.text: The ground around it can tremble before an eruption.

options.label: D
options.text: A volcano is a mountain with an opening that can release lava.
options.rationale: This defines a volcano, not the ground's behavior.

items.stem: A classmate claims the volcano paragraph above narrates a single eruption from start to finish, step by step. Is the classmate right?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists general facts about volcanoes, not a single eruption unfolding in order.
explanation.tip: Description gives facts; sequence tells a time-ordered story.

items.stem: Read: “A bicycle has two wheels connected by a frame, with pedals that turn a chain to move the back wheel. Handlebars let the rider steer, and brakes squeeze the wheels to slow down. Some bicycles also have gears to make hills easier to climb.” How does the author mainly organize this paragraph about bicycles?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph names separate parts — wheels, pedals, handlebars, brakes, gears — and what each does.
explanation.tip: Look for a list of parts, each with its own detail.

options.label: A
options.text: By telling the history of when bicycles were invented.
options.rationale: No dates or historical events are mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: By comparing bicycles to cars.
options.rationale: No other vehicle is mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: By explaining the steps to fix a flat tire.
options.rationale: No repair steps are given.

options.label: D
options.text: By describing each part of a bicycle and what it does.

items.stem: Read the paragraph above about bicycles. Which detail explains how a bicycle's gears help the rider?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence specifically explains what the gears are for.
explanation.tip: Match the question to the exact detail that answers it.

options.label: A
options.text: Some bicycles also have gears to make hills easier to climb.

options.label: B
options.text: Handlebars let the rider steer.
options.rationale: This describes steering, not gears.

options.label: C
options.text: A bicycle has two wheels connected by a frame.
options.rationale: This describes the frame, not the gears.

options.label: D
options.text: Brakes squeeze the wheels to slow down.
options.rationale: This describes braking, not gears.

items.stem: Read: “A lighthouse is a tall tower built near dangerous coastlines. A bright, rotating light at the top warns ships of rocks below. Many lighthouses also have a foghorn that sounds when visibility is poor.” Which statement best explains the structure of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph describes the tower, the light, and the foghorn as separate features.
explanation.tip: Count how many separate features are described about the subject.

options.label: A
options.text: It explains why lighthouses are no longer used today.
options.rationale: The paragraph does not discuss whether lighthouses are still used.

options.label: B
options.text: It lists separate features of a lighthouse and what each one does for ships.

options.label: C
options.text: It compares lighthouses built in different countries.
options.rationale: No other lighthouses are named for comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: It tells a story about a ship that crashed near a lighthouse.
options.rationale: No specific event or characters are described.

items.stem: Read the paragraph above about lighthouses. Which detail tells how the lighthouse warns ships in fog?

explanation.whyCorrect: The foghorn detail specifically addresses poor visibility.
explanation.tip: Find the sentence that matches the exact condition asked about.

options.label: A
options.text: A bright, rotating light at the top warns ships of rocks below.
options.rationale: This light is used mainly when it can be seen, not in heavy fog.

options.label: B
options.text: Lighthouses are painted in bright colors.
options.rationale: This detail is not in the paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: Many lighthouses also have a foghorn that sounds when visibility is poor.

options.label: D
options.text: A lighthouse is a tall tower built near dangerous coastlines.
options.rationale: This describes the tower's location, not the fog warning.

items.stem: Read: “Tropical rainforests are warm and extremely wet, with rain falling almost every day. Tall trees form a thick canopy that blocks most sunlight from reaching the ground. Thousands of plant and animal species live in the many layers of the forest.” What is the MAIN topic described in this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every sentence adds a general fact about the rainforest itself.
explanation.tip: Ask what single place or thing every sentence is about.

options.label: A
options.text: A single hike through a rainforest trail.
options.rationale: No specific trip or characters are described.

options.label: B
options.text: A comparison between rainforests and deserts.
options.rationale: No other biome is named for comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: The reasons rainforests are being cut down.
options.rationale: No cause of deforestation is explained.

options.label: D
options.text: The climate and layers of a tropical rainforest.

items.stem: Match each rainforest detail with what it describes.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each detail describes a different part of the rainforest.
explanation.tip: Sort details by what part of the topic they belong to.

pairs.left: A thick canopy of tall trees

items.stem: Read: “Most spiders have eight legs and two body sections. Many spin silk webs to trap insects, while others hunt their prey by chasing it. Spider silk is extremely strong for its thin size.” Which detail describes how some spiders catch food?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence names two different hunting methods.
explanation.tip: Find the sentence that directly answers the question asked.

options.label: A
options.text: Many spin silk webs to trap insects, while others hunt their prey by chasing it.

options.label: B
options.text: Spider silk is extremely strong for its thin size.
options.rationale: This describes the silk's strength, not a hunting method.

options.label: C
options.text: Most spiders have eight legs and two body sections.
options.rationale: This describes a spider's body, not how it catches food.

options.label: D
options.text: Spiders live mostly in cold climates.
options.rationale: This detail is not stated in the paragraph.

items.stem: Choose the best word: “A spider has eight legs. ____, it has two main body sections.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Additionally” adds another physical detail about the spider.
explanation.tip: Also/additionally/another signal more description, not order or cause.

options.label: A
options.text: Next
options.rationale: This signals a step in a sequence.

options.label: B
options.text: Additionally

options.label: C
options.text: Instead
options.rationale: This signals a contrast or substitution.

options.label: D
options.text: So
options.rationale: This signals a result, not an added detail.

items.stem: Read: “A bakery fills its shelves with warm loaves of bread, flaky pastries, and sweet cakes. The smell of fresh dough drifts through the open door, and large ovens hum in the back room. Bakers knead dough early each morning before customers arrive.” How is information about the bakery mainly organized in this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists sensory details — sight, smell, sound — about the bakery.
explanation.tip: Look for details grouped by the senses they describe.

options.label: A
options.text: By telling the steps to bake a cake, in order.
options.rationale: No numbered steps or recipe is given.

options.label: B
options.text: By describing sights, smells, and sounds found inside the bakery.

options.label: C
options.text: By explaining why fresh bread costs more than packaged bread.
options.rationale: No price comparison or cause is discussed.

options.label: D
options.text: By comparing this bakery to a restaurant.
options.rationale: No other business is named for comparison.

items.stem: Read the paragraph above about the bakery. Which detail appeals to the reader's sense of smell?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence directly names a smell.
explanation.tip: Look for words naming what you would smell, see, or hear.

options.label: A
options.text: Warm loaves of bread, flaky pastries, and sweet cakes fill the shelves.
options.rationale: This appeals to sight, not smell.

options.label: B
options.text: Bakers knead dough early each morning.
options.rationale: This describes an action, not a smell.

options.label: C
options.text: The smell of fresh dough drifts through the open door.

options.label: D
options.text: Large ovens hum in the back room.
options.rationale: This appeals to hearing, not smell.

items.stem: Read: “A freight train pulls dozens of long cars loaded with coal, grain, or steel. Powerful engines at the front provide the strength to pull such heavy loads. Loud horns warn nearby cars and pedestrians at crossings.” Which detail describes how the train warns people nearby?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence directly describes the horn as a warning.
explanation.tip: Match the question to the exact detail that answers it.

options.label: A
options.text: A freight train pulls dozens of long cars loaded with coal, grain, or steel.
options.rationale: This describes the cargo, not a warning.

options.label: B
options.text: Freight trains travel only at night.
options.rationale: This detail is not in the paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: Powerful engines at the front provide the strength to pull heavy loads.
options.rationale: This describes the engine's power, not a warning.

options.label: D
options.text: Loud horns warn nearby cars and pedestrians at crossings.

items.stem: Someone argues the freight-train paragraph above is built from general facts rather than from a story about one particular trip. Do you agree?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences give general facts about freight trains, not a single timed event.
explanation.tip: Facts about a subject in general signal a description structure.

items.stem: Read: “Many mosques have a tall tower called a minaret, where the call to prayer can be heard. Inside, patterned carpets cover the floor, and arched doorways lead into a large open hall. Domes on the roof help carry sound throughout the building.” Which detail describes a feature of the mosque's roof?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence names the domes as a roof feature.
explanation.tip: Check which part of the building each detail belongs to.

options.label: A
options.text: Domes on the roof help carry sound throughout the building.

options.label: B
options.text: Patterned carpets cover the floor.
options.rationale: This describes the floor, not the roof.

options.label: C
options.text: Arched doorways lead into a large open hall.
options.rationale: This describes the doorways, not the roof.

options.label: D
options.text: Many mosques have a tall tower called a minaret.
options.rationale: This describes the tower, not the roof.

items.stem: Match each mosque feature with what it is used for.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each architectural feature has its own descriptive purpose.
explanation.tip: Pair each feature with its function.

items.stem: Read: “A glacier is a huge, slow-moving sheet of ice formed from packed snow. Deep cracks called crevasses can form as the ice moves over uneven ground. Glaciers can carve valleys and leave behind piles of rock called moraines.” What is the author's purpose in listing the crevasses and moraines in this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both features are described as results of the glacier's movement, adding detail to the description.
explanation.tip: Ask why the author added each extra fact about the topic.

options.label: A
options.text: To warn readers about the dangers of climbing glaciers.
options.rationale: The paragraph states facts, not a warning.

options.label: B
options.text: To describe specific features that form as a glacier moves.

options.label: C
options.text: To explain the order in which the glacier melts each year.
options.rationale: No yearly melting timeline is given.

options.label: D
options.text: To compare glaciers in different countries.
options.rationale: No specific countries or other glaciers are named.

items.stem: Choose the best word: “A glacier moves slowly over land. ____, it can carve out deep valleys.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “On top of that” adds another descriptive fact about what glaciers do.
explanation.tip: Also/in addition/on top of that add more description.

options.label: A
options.text: Because
options.rationale: This signals a cause.

options.label: B
options.text: However
options.rationale: This signals a contrast.

options.label: C
options.text: On top of that

options.label: D
options.text: Before
options.rationale: This signals time order.

items.stem: Read: “An orchard is a large area planted with rows of fruit trees such as apple, orange, or fig trees. Bees fly between the blossoms, helping the trees produce fruit. Workers pick the ripe fruit by hand each season.” Which sentence structure best describes how this paragraph is organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each sentence adds a separate fact about a different part of the orchard.
explanation.tip: Count the separate facts given about one overall topic.

options.label: A
options.text: It explains the cause of poor fruit harvests.
options.rationale: No cause of a poor harvest is discussed.

options.label: B
options.text: It narrates one specific day of picking fruit.
options.rationale: No single day or event with a timeline is described.

options.label: C
options.text: It lists separate facts about the trees, the bees, and the workers in an orchard.

options.label: D
options.text: It compares an orchard to a vegetable garden.
options.rationale: No other type of farm is named for comparison.

items.stem: Read the paragraph above about the orchard. Which detail describes how fruit trees get help producing fruit?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence explains the bees' role in fruit production.
explanation.tip: Find the exact sentence that answers the question.

options.label: A
options.text: Workers pick the ripe fruit by hand each season.
options.rationale: This describes harvesting, not fruit production.

options.label: B
options.text: Orchards are always found near rivers.
options.rationale: This detail is not stated in the paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: An orchard is a large area planted with rows of fruit trees.
options.rationale: This defines an orchard, not how fruit is produced.

options.label: D
options.text: Bees fly between the blossoms, helping the trees produce fruit.

items.stem: Read: “A natural history museum displays dinosaur bones, sparkling rocks, and preserved animals behind glass cases. Guided tours explain how each exhibit connects to the history of life on Earth. Interactive screens let visitors test their own knowledge.” What does this paragraph mainly describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every sentence names a different feature found inside the museum.
explanation.tip: Ask what overall subject every sentence describes.

options.label: A
options.text: The exhibits and features found inside a natural history museum.

options.label: B
options.text: A field trip a class took last spring.
options.rationale: No specific class or trip is narrated.

options.label: C
options.text: Why some museums charge an entrance fee.
options.rationale: No reason for fees is explained.

options.label: D
options.text: The difference between two museums in different cities.
options.rationale: No second museum is named for comparison.

items.stem: Could the museum paragraph above be rewritten as a timeline of one visitor's single afternoon at the museum, step by step?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sentences describe general features of the museum, not a single visit's timeline.
explanation.tip: General facts about a place, not events in order, signal description.

items.stem: Read: “The solar system includes the sun at its center, eight planets, and many moons and asteroids. Some planets, like Mercury, are small and rocky, while others, like Jupiter, are huge balls of gas. Each planet travels around the sun on its own path called an orbit.” Which detail describes a difference among the planets themselves?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence directly compares planet sizes and materials.
explanation.tip: Look for the sentence naming specific differences.

options.label: A
options.text: The solar system includes the sun at its center, eight planets, and many moons and asteroids.
options.rationale: This lists the parts of the solar system, not a difference among planets.

options.label: B
options.text: Some planets, like Mercury, are small and rocky, while others, like Jupiter, are huge balls of gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Each planet travels around the sun on its own path called an orbit.
options.rationale: This describes orbits, not size or makeup.

options.label: D
options.text: The sun is the brightest star we can see.
options.rationale: This detail is not in the paragraph.

items.stem: Match each solar system term with what it describes.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each term is paired with the detail that defines it.
explanation.tip: Match vocabulary with its description in the text.

pairs.right: the center of the solar system
smaller objects in the solar system
a planet's path around the sun

items.stem: Read: “A recycling center sorts paper, glass, plastic, and metal into separate bins. Large machines crush cans and shred paper into smaller pieces. Trucks then carry the sorted materials to factories where they are made into new products.” How does the author mainly organize facts about the recycling center?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists separate facts about sorting, machines, and transport.
explanation.tip: Look for a list of related facts about one process or place.

options.label: A
options.text: By explaining what caused people to start recycling.
options.rationale: No historical cause is discussed.

options.label: B
options.text: By comparing recycling centers in two different towns.
options.rationale: No second recycling center is named for comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: By describing the separate materials, machines, and steps found at the center.

options.label: D
options.text: By arguing that recycling should be mandatory everywhere.
options.rationale: The paragraph states facts, not an opinion or argument.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Also” adds another fact; “First” wrongly implies a time-ordered step.
explanation.tip: Check whether a transition adds a fact or shows a sequence step.

segments: The center sorts materials into bins.
it also uses machines to crush cans.

items.stem: Read: “A playground usually has swings, a slide, and a climbing structure with bars and ladders. Soft rubber mats or sand cover the ground to cushion falls. Benches nearby let parents sit and watch their children play.” Which detail describes what covers the playground ground?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence specifically names what covers the ground.
explanation.tip: Find the exact sentence matching the question.

options.label: A
options.text: Playgrounds are only open during the summer.
options.rationale: This detail is not in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: A playground usually has swings, a slide, and a climbing structure.
options.rationale: This describes the equipment, not the ground covering.

options.label: C
options.text: Benches nearby let parents sit and watch their children play.
options.rationale: This describes the benches, not the ground.

options.label: D
options.text: Soft rubber mats or sand cover the ground to cushion falls.

items.stem: Looking back at that same playground paragraph, where does it say grown-ups can watch the kids from?

explanation.whyCorrect: The benches are the spot named for parents to sit and watch.
explanation.tip: Find the exact sentence matching the question.

options.label: A
options.text: Benches nearby let parents sit and watch their children play.

options.label: B
options.text: A cushioned layer keeps falls from hurting.
options.rationale: This names the ground's safety layer, not a seat.

options.label: C
options.text: A fence surrounds the whole play area.
options.rationale: No fence is mentioned anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: Swings, a slide, and bars for climbing fill the play area.
options.rationale: This names the equipment itself, not a spot for watching.

items.stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Layla is a proper noun naming a specific person, and the sentence's first word must also be capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize the first word of every sentence and every proper noun.

options.label: A
options.text: My friend layla came over after school.
options.rationale: “Layla” is a specific person's name and must start with a capital letter.

options.label: B
options.text: My friend Layla came over after school.

options.label: C
options.text: my friend Layla came over after school.
options.rationale: The first word of a sentence must be capitalized.

options.label: D
options.text: My Friend Layla came over after school.
options.rationale: “Friend” is a common noun and should not be capitalized.

items.stem: Choose the correctly capitalized word: “Our class trip is on ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Days of the week are proper nouns, so only the first letter is capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize days, months, and holidays.

options.label: A
options.text: thursday
options.rationale: Days of the week are proper nouns and need a capital letter.

options.label: B
options.text: THURSDAY
options.rationale: Only the first letter of a day name is capitalized, not all letters.

options.label: C
options.text: thurday
options.rationale: This is misspelled.

options.label: D
options.text: Thursday

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Eid al-Fitr is the specific name of a holiday, so its main words are capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize the names of holidays.

items.stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Languages are proper nouns and are always capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize the names of languages and nationalities.

options.label: A
options.text: Fatima speaks arabic, english, and french.
options.rationale: Languages are proper nouns and must be capitalized.

options.label: B
options.text: fatima speaks Arabic, English, and French.
options.rationale: The first word of the sentence must be capitalized.

options.label: C
options.text: Fatima speaks Arabic, English, and French.

options.label: D
options.text: Fatima Speaks Arabic, English, and French.
options.rationale: “Speaks” is a verb, not a proper noun, and should not be capitalized.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a title correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dr. is a title directly before a name, so both the title and the name are capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize a title only when it comes right before a specific name.

options.label: A
options.text: dr. Hassan examined the patient carefully.
options.rationale: A title before a name, like Dr., is capitalized.

options.label: B
options.text: Dr. hassan examined the patient carefully.
options.rationale: A person's name is always capitalized.

options.label: C
options.text: The Dr. examined the patient carefully.
options.rationale: Without a name attached, “doctor” is a common noun and should not be capitalized.

options.label: D
options.text: Dr. Hassan examined the patient carefully.

items.stem: Which book title is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: In a title, the first word and all important words are capitalized, but short connecting words are usually lowercase.
explanation.tip: Capitalize the first, last, and all major words in a title.

options.label: A
options.text: The Secret of the Lost City

options.label: B
options.text: The Secret Of The Lost City
options.rationale: Short words like “of” and “the” inside a title are usually not capitalized.

options.label: C
options.text: The secret of the Lost city
options.rationale: Major words like “Secret” and “City” must also be capitalized.

options.label: D
options.text: the secret of the lost city
options.rationale: The first word and all major words of a title must be capitalized.

items.stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: The names of planets are proper nouns and are always capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize the names of planets, but not general sky words like sun, moon, or sky.

options.text: Mars and Jupiter are easier to see in the Night Sky than Mercury.

options.label: D
options.text: mars and jupiter are easier to see in the night sky than mercury.
options.rationale: Planet names are proper nouns and must be capitalized.

items.stem: The sentence “my sister and i went to the market” is capitalized correctly.

explanation.whyCorrect: The pronoun “I” is always capitalized, and the sentence should begin with a capital letter: “My sister and I went to the market.”
explanation.tip: Always capitalize the pronoun I, wherever it appears in a sentence.

items.stem: Choose the correctly capitalized word: “We visited the ____ last summer.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Cairo Tower names one specific landmark, so it is fully capitalized.
explanation.tip: Capitalize every important word in the name of a specific place.

options.label: A
options.text: Cairo Tower

options.label: B
options.text: cairo tower
options.rationale: A specific landmark's name is a proper noun and must be capitalized.

options.label: C
options.text: CAIRO TOWER
options.rationale: Only the first letter of each word is capitalized, not the whole name.

options.label: D
options.text: Cairo tower

options.label: C
options.text: Scrawny

options.label: D
options.text: Thin
options.rationale: This is the plain, neutral original word.

items.stem: A dictionary entry shows “child (noun) pl. children.” What does “pl.” tell you?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Pl.” marks the plural form, which for “child” is the irregular word “children.”
explanation.tip: Learn common entry abbreviations, including pl. for plural.

options.label: A
options.text: That “child” can be used as a verb
options.rationale: “Pl.” refers to plural nouns, not verbs.

options.label: B
options.text: That “children” is a synonym for “child”
options.rationale: “Pl.” does not mean synonym.

options.label: C
options.text: That “children” is pronounced differently from “child”
options.rationale: “Pl.” is about the plural form, not pronunciation.

options.label: D
options.text: That “children” is the irregular plural form of “child”

items.stem: A dictionary entry for “frog” ends with “see also: amphibian.” What should you do with this note?

explanation.whyCorrect: A “see also” note points to a related entry that adds useful background.
explanation.tip: Follow cross-references to learn how a word connects to a broader category.

options.label: A
options.text: Look up “amphibian” for related information about the larger animal group frogs belong to

options.label: B
options.text: Ignore it, because it is not part of the definition
options.rationale: Cross-references point to useful related entries.

options.label: C
options.text: Look for “amphibian” in the index instead of the dictionary
options.rationale: The note is a dictionary cross-reference, not an index instruction.

options.label: D
options.text: Assume “frog” and “amphibian” mean exactly the same thing
options.rationale: They are related but not identical terms.

items.stem: Which resource would best explain the exact scientific meaning of the word “photosynthesis”?

explanation.whyCorrect: A subject-specific dictionary or glossary gives the precise meaning used in that field.
explanation.tip: Choose a reference tool that matches the subject you are studying.

options.label: A
options.text: An atlas
options.rationale: An atlas shows maps, not word meanings.

options.label: B
options.text: A science dictionary or glossary written for that subject

options.label: C
options.text: A rhyming dictionary
options.rationale: A rhyming dictionary lists words that sound alike, not definitions.

options.label: D
options.text: A thesaurus
options.rationale: A thesaurus lists similar words, not exact scientific definitions.

items.stem: Put these words in the order they would appear in a dictionary.

explanation.whyCorrect: Compare letters one by one: brid, brie, brig, bril, brin.
explanation.tip: After matching letters, compare the next different letter.
