options.label: A
options.text: Watch the race from the stands.
options.rationale: He is a runner lining up to compete, not a spectator in the stands.

options.label: B
options.text: Go back home to sleep.
options.rationale: He is at the starting line, ready to race, not heading home.

options.label: C
options.text: Start running the race.

options.label: D
options.text: Take off his running shoes.
options.rationale: He just put them on to prepare for the race he is about to run.

items.stem: Read: "The chess champion studied her opponent’s last ten moves carefully and noticed he always protected his queen the same way." What is the BEST prediction about her next move?

explanation.whyCorrect: Noticing a predictable pattern in an opponent is exactly the kind of clue a skilled player would use strategically.
explanation.tip: When a character gathers specific information, predict they will use it to their advantage.

options.label: A
options.text: She will give up the match.
options.rationale: Careful study of her opponent suggests she is preparing to win, not quit.

options.label: B
options.text: She will switch to a completely different game.
options.rationale: There is no indication she wants to stop playing chess.

options.label: C
options.text: She will ignore everything she noticed.
options.rationale: Noticing a clear pattern is useful information she would likely use, not ignore.

options.label: D
options.text: She will use a strategy that targets the opponent’s predictable pattern.

items.stem: Read: "Despite months of rehearsal, the lead actor lost her voice the night before opening night." Based on this, it makes sense to predict that the show might face a last-minute challenge.

explanation.whyCorrect: Losing a voice right before a performance is a clear sign of a last-minute problem the show must handle.
explanation.tip: A sudden setback right before an event is a strong clue that a challenge is coming.

items.stem: Read: "The young falcon had practiced short flights from branch to branch all week and was now perched at the very top of the tall cliff." What will the falcon most likely do next?

explanation.whyCorrect: A week of practice followed by climbing to a higher point suggests the falcon is ready to try a bigger flight.
explanation.tip: Track a character’s progress over time to predict their next, bigger step.

options.label: A
options.text: Attempt a longer flight from the cliff.

options.label: B
options.text: Forget how to fly.
options.rationale: A full week of practice makes forgetting how to fly very unlikely.

options.label: C
options.text: Stay on the branch forever.
options.rationale: It has already moved up to the cliff, showing clear progress beyond the branch.

options.label: D
options.text: Build a nest instead of flying.
options.rationale: Nothing in the passage suggests the falcon is building a nest.

items.stem: Read: "The scientists recorded rising temperatures in the lake for the third summer in a row and saw fewer fish eggs each year." Which detail BEST supports the prediction that the fish population will keep declining?

explanation.whyCorrect: A three-year pattern of declining fish eggs is strong, repeated evidence that the trend will likely continue.
explanation.tip: A trend repeated over several years is stronger evidence than a single data point.

options.label: A
options.text: The temperature was measured in summer.
options.rationale: The season of measurement does not by itself predict the population decline.

options.label: B
options.text: Fewer fish eggs were found each of the three years.

options.label: C
options.text: The scientists took careful notes.
options.rationale: Taking notes itself does not predict a change in the fish population.

options.label: D
options.text: The lake is popular with tourists.
options.rationale: Tourism is unrelated to the data about fish eggs.

items.stem: Read: "Despite practicing her speech every night for two weeks, Maya’s hands still shook and her voice cracked during the final rehearsal." What is the BEST prediction for the actual speech?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two weeks of practice with some lingering nervousness suggests a realistic mix of continued nerves and gradual improvement.
explanation.tip: Realistic predictions often combine a character’s weakness with the progress they have already made.

options.label: A
options.text: Maya will suddenly become a completely confident speaker overnight.
options.rationale: Nervousness built up over two weeks rarely disappears instantly.

options.label: B
options.text: Maya will refuse to give the speech.
options.rationale: Nothing in the passage suggests she plans to back out of giving it.

options.label: C
options.text: Maya will likely feel nervous but may still improve with more practice.

options.label: D
options.text: The speech topic will be changed entirely.
options.rationale: There is no mention anywhere of changing the topic of the speech.

items.stem: Read: "The explorers packed extra water, checked the weather forecast twice, and told rangers their exact route before entering the canyon." Which TWO details help you predict the explorers are preparing carefully for a safe trip?

explanation.whyCorrect: Packing extra supplies and informing rangers of their route are both clear safety precautions.
explanation.tip: Focus on the specific actions a character takes, not general background facts.

options.label: A
options.text: They have hiked before.
options.rationale: Past hiking experience is not a detail from this specific preparation described.

options.label: B
options.text: They packed extra water.

options.label: C
options.text: They told rangers their exact route.

options.label: D
options.text: They entered the canyon in the morning.
options.rationale: The time of day they entered does not show careful safety preparation.

items.stem: Read: "The startup’s app crashed during its first public demo, but the engineers found and fixed the bug within an hour and ran three flawless tests afterward." What is the BEST prediction about the next public demo?

explanation.whyCorrect: Fixing the known problem and then passing several tests strongly suggests the next demo will go better.
explanation.tip: A fixed problem followed by successful tests is strong evidence of improvement.

options.label: A
options.text: The company will shut down the project.
options.rationale: Fixing the bug and running successful tests shows the team is continuing their effort.

options.label: B
options.text: The engineers will stop testing the app.
options.rationale: Running three flawless tests shows they are still actively and carefully testing it.

options.label: C
options.text: The app will crash again in exactly the same way.
options.rationale: The specific bug that caused that crash has already been found and fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: The next demo will likely go more smoothly.

items.stem: Read: "Every volunteer who signed up early for the beach cleanup brought their own gloves and bags, while the city promised extra supplies for latecomers." Which detail BEST supports the prediction that the cleanup will have enough supplies for everyone?

explanation.whyCorrect: The city’s promise specifically addresses the group that might otherwise be left without supplies.
explanation.tip: Look for the detail that directly solves the potential shortage, not just a related fact.

options.label: A
options.text: The city promised extra supplies for latecomers.

options.label: B
options.text: The cleanup is at the beach.
options.rationale: The location of the cleanup does not relate to the supply levels.

options.label: C
options.text: Volunteers signed up early.
options.rationale: Signing up early does not by itself guarantee enough supplies for everyone.

options.label: D
options.text: Some volunteers brought their own gloves.
options.rationale: This helps some volunteers but does not address supplies for the latecomers.

items.stem: Read: "The city council reviewed traffic data showing accidents had dropped sharply at every intersection where new crosswalk signals were installed last year." What is the BEST prediction if more signals are installed citywide?

explanation.whyCorrect: Since signals reduced accidents at every intersection where they were installed, more installations should have a similar effect.
explanation.tip: A result that repeats “at every” location is a strong basis for predicting the same result elsewhere.

options.label: A
options.text: Traffic will completely disappear.
options.rationale: Crosswalk signals reduce accidents; they do not eliminate traffic volume.

options.label: B
options.text: Accidents will likely decrease at the newly equipped intersections.

options.label: C
options.text: Accidents will increase everywhere.
options.rationale: This directly contradicts the data showing a sharp drop in accidents.

options.label: D
options.text: The council will remove all the signals.
options.rationale: The positive data gives a strong reason to add more signals, not remove them.

items.stem: Read: "The marathon runner had battled a knee injury for months but finished every training run in the two weeks leading up to race day without any pain." Which detail BEST supports the prediction that she will be able to complete the marathon?

explanation.whyCorrect: Recent, consistent pain-free training is the strongest and most current evidence of her readiness.
explanation.tip: The most recent, repeated evidence usually outweighs older background facts.

options.label: A
options.text: She has run marathons before.
options.rationale: Past marathons do not address her recent injury recovery specifically.

options.label: B
options.text: The marathon is a long race.
options.rationale: The length of the race is not evidence about her recent recovery.

options.label: C
options.text: She finished every training run pain-free in the two weeks before the race.

options.label: D
options.text: She battled a knee injury for months.
options.rationale: This detail suggests risk and past difficulty, not current readiness.

items.stem: Read: "The negotiating team had resolved every disagreement except one minor clause, and both sides had already scheduled a signing ceremony for the following week." Which detail BEST supports the prediction that the agreement will be signed as planned?

explanation.whyCorrect: Already scheduling the ceremony shows both sides expect and are planning for the agreement to be finalized.
explanation.tip: A concrete, planned next step is stronger evidence than how smooth or rocky the process was before.

options.label: A
options.text: Both teams argued about many issues earlier.
options.rationale: Past disagreements do not predict the outcome of the final signing by themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: Only one minor clause remained unresolved.
options.rationale: This shows the sides are close, but alone it does not show a ceremony is already arranged.

options.label: C
options.text: The negotiation took several months.
options.rationale: The length of the process does not predict whether the signing will happen as planned.

options.label: D
options.text: Both sides had already scheduled a signing ceremony for the following week.

items.stem: Read: "The orchestra had performed the symphony flawlessly in six straight rehearsals, and the conductor told the musicians there was nothing left to change." Based on this, it makes sense to predict that the upcoming concert will likely go well.

explanation.whyCorrect: Six flawless rehearsals in a row, with no changes needed, strongly suggests the concert will go well.
explanation.tip: A long streak of success right before an event is strong evidence that the event will likely go well too.

items.stem: Read: "Farid practiced his handwriting every night even though his letters were messy at first. By the end of the term, his teacher praised his neat, careful writing." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Farid’s messy start and improved ending show that consistent effort, not natural skill, led to his success.
explanation.tip: Look at how a character changes from the beginning to the end of the story to find the theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Hard work pays off over talent alone.

options.label: B
options.text: Teachers are always strict.
options.rationale: The story shows encouragement from the teacher, not strictness.

options.label: C
options.text: Writing neatly is impossible for beginners.
options.rationale: The story shows the opposite: improvement was possible with practice.

options.label: D
options.text: Only naturally talented students succeed.
options.rationale: Farid succeeded through steady practice, not natural talent.

items.stem: In the story where Mona shared half of her lunch with a classmate who had forgotten his own, and the two became close friends afterward, the theme is best described as: small acts of kindness can make a big difference.

explanation.whyCorrect: Mona’s small act of sharing led to a meaningful new friendship, which is exactly what the theme describes.
explanation.tip: A small action with a big result is often a clue pointing to the story’s theme.

items.stem: Read: "Lina almost quit her science project after her first volcano model collapsed, but her friend convinced her to rebuild it. The rebuilt volcano won first prize at the fair." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Lina nearly quit right before her eventual success, showing how close giving up came to costing her that success.
explanation.tip: Notice moments when a character almost quits to find a theme about persistence.

options.label: A
options.text: Volcanoes are difficult to build.
options.rationale: This is a detail about the project, not the lesson the story teaches.

options.label: B
options.text: Giving up too soon can cost you a success that was within reach.

options.label: C
options.text: Friends should always agree with you.
options.rationale: The friend encouraged Lina to keep trying, not simply to agree with her.

options.label: D
options.text: Science fairs are only for experts.
options.rationale: The story is about persistence after a setback, not about expertise.

items.stem: Read: "Each rower on the boat pulled at a different pace until the coach told them to count together out loud. Once they rowed in rhythm, the boat sliced through the water and won the heat." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The rowers only succeeded once they stopped pulling separately and worked together in rhythm.
explanation.tip: Watch what changes right before a story’s success to find its lesson.

options.label: A
options.text: Only the fastest rower matters in a race.
options.rationale: The story shows that working together, not one person’s speed, led to winning.

options.label: B
options.text: Rowing boats are heavier than they look.
options.rationale: This is a physical detail, not the lesson of the story.

options.label: C
options.text: Working as a team accomplishes more than working alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Coaches should never give instructions.
options.rationale: The coach’s instruction is exactly what helped the team succeed.

items.stem: Read: "The new student wore old, patched clothes, and some classmates avoided him until they learned he had built his own telescope from scrap metal and was the best in the astronomy club." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The classmates’ early judgment based on clothing turned out to be completely wrong once they learned the truth.
explanation.tip: Look for a mistaken first impression that gets corrected later in the story.

options.label: A
options.text: New students are always unpopular.
options.rationale: The story actually shows the classmates were wrong to avoid him.

options.label: B
options.text: Astronomy clubs only accept experts.
options.rationale: The story does not suggest any membership requirement for the club.

options.label: C
options.text: Telescopes are expensive to build.
options.rationale: This is a detail about the student’s project, not the main lesson.

options.label: D
options.text: Judging others by appearances can lead to mistakes.

items.stem: In the story where Rami’s bread dough collapsed twice before he discovered he needed to let it rise longer, the theme is that mistakes are valuable because they teach important lessons.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rami’s two failures directly led him to the discovery that solved his problem, showing mistakes can be valuable teachers.
explanation.tip: When a character learns something useful specifically from a failure, that points to a theme about mistakes.

items.stem: Read: "Instead of hiding his torn backpack from his parents, Adam showed them right away, and together they found a simple way to fix it with a sewing kit." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Adam’s choice to show the problem right away, instead of hiding it, led to a quick and easy solution.
explanation.tip: Compare what a character chooses to do with what might have happened if they had chosen differently.

options.label: A
options.text: Facing a problem directly is better than avoiding it.

options.label: B
options.text: Parents are always upset about small problems.
options.rationale: The parents helped calmly, showing the opposite of being upset.

options.label: C
options.text: Sewing kits can fix almost anything.
options.rationale: This is a detail about the solution, not the lesson the story teaches.

options.label: D
options.text: Backpacks should never be repaired.
options.rationale: This directly contradicts what actually happens in the story.

items.stem: Read: "When the well in the village ran low, each family brought a bucket of water from their own supply to fill the school’s water tank until the rains returned." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every family contributing from their own supply shows how sharing helped the whole community get through a hard time.
explanation.tip: Notice when many characters each give a little to solve a shared problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Rain never returns to dry villages.
options.rationale: The story actually mentions that the rains eventually returned.

options.label: B
options.text: Sharing what you have can bring a community together.

options.label: C
options.text: Villages always run out of water in summer.
options.rationale: This is a setting detail, not the lesson of the story.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the school needed water.
options.rationale: The story shows the whole community helped meet a shared need, not just the school.

items.stem: Read: "Reem found an expensive watch on the bus and could have kept it, but she gave it to the driver, who tracked down its owner and thanked her publicly." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reem chose honesty over keeping something valuable for herself, and that choice led to a good outcome.
explanation.tip: Look at the choice a character makes when tempted, to uncover the theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Drivers should keep lost items for themselves.
options.rationale: This directly contradicts the honest choice made in the story.

options.label: B
options.text: Buses are good places to find valuables.
options.rationale: This is a setting detail, not the lesson of the story.

options.label: C
options.text: Honesty is more valuable than a quick advantage.

options.label: D
options.text: Expensive items are always returned to their owners.
options.rationale: This is not guaranteed in general; Reem’s honest choice is what made the return possible.

items.stem: Read: "Hadi wanted to repaint the fence in one afternoon, but his grandfather convinced him to do two thin coats over two days. The finished fence looked smooth with no drips." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Taking the slower, patient approach of two thin coats led to a smoother result than rushing would have.
explanation.tip: Compare the rushed plan to the patient plan to find the lesson about results.

options.label: A
options.text: Painting fences is always a two-day job.
options.rationale: This describes only this specific case, not a lesson that applies more broadly.

options.label: B
options.text: Thin paint never covers properly.
options.rationale: In the story, the thin coats actually worked very well.

options.label: C
options.text: Grandfathers always know more than grandsons.
options.rationale: The story’s point is about taking time, not about age or experience in general.

options.label: D
options.text: Patience often leads to better results than rushing.

items.stem: In the story where fishermen agreed to let smaller fish go so the lake would have enough fish next season, the theme is that respecting nature protects the people who depend on it.

explanation.whyCorrect: By protecting the smaller fish now, the fishermen are protecting their own future catches, showing how respecting nature helps people too.
explanation.tip: When characters give something up now to protect a resource for later, think about themes connecting nature and people.

items.stem: Read: "Before the storm warning was even issued, Layla’s family had already stocked candles, water, and a radio. When the power went out for two days, they were comfortable while neighbors scrambled for supplies." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Layla’s family prepared before anyone knew for certain a storm was coming, and that early preparation paid off.
explanation.tip: Notice what a character does before trouble arrives to find a theme about preparation.

options.label: A
options.text: Preparation turns luck into success.

options.label: B
options.text: Storms always last exactly two days.
options.rationale: This is a specific detail from the story, not a general lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: Only wealthy families can prepare for storms.
options.rationale: Nothing in the story suggests that wealth was the reason for their preparation.

options.label: D
options.text: Candles are the most important emergency supply.
options.rationale: This names one item, not the broader lesson about preparing ahead.

items.stem: Read: "Karim spent his Saturday mornings tutoring younger students for free. Years later, when he struggled in his first job, one of those former students, now a manager, helped him get hired." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Karim’s years of free tutoring eventually came back to help him when he needed it most.
explanation.tip: Look for an action early in a story that quietly returns to help the character later.

options.label: A
options.text: Managers only hire people they already know.
options.rationale: The story’s point is about kindness coming back around, not about favoritism.

options.label: B
options.text: Helping others in need often helps you in return.

options.label: C
options.text: Tutoring always leads to a job offer.
options.rationale: This specific outcome is not guaranteed; the lesson is broader than one exact result.

options.label: D
options.text: Saturdays are the best day to volunteer.
options.rationale: This is a detail about timing, not the lesson of the story.

items.stem: Read: "When the kitchen’s main oven broke an hour before the banquet, the head chef calmly reorganized the stovetop burners instead of panicking, and the meal was served on time." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The chef’s calm response, rather than panic, is exactly what allowed the meal to be served on time.
explanation.tip: Compare a calm reaction to a panicked one to find the story’s lesson.

options.label: A
options.text: Ovens break down more often than stoves.
options.rationale: This is a detail about kitchen appliances, not the story’s lesson.

options.label: B
options.text: Banquets should always have backup ovens.
options.rationale: This suggests one specific solution, not the broader lesson about staying calm.

options.label: C
options.text: Staying calm under pressure leads to better decisions.

options.label: D
options.text: Head chefs never make mistakes.
options.rationale: The story is about handling a problem calmly, not about avoiding mistakes entirely.

items.stem: Read: "When Dina’s project partner was hospitalized the week before the science fair, Dina finished both of their parts and then insisted both names stay on the winning project." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dina did extra work and still shared the credit, showing she helped her friend without wanting anything extra for herself.
explanation.tip: Notice when a character gives credit away instead of keeping it, to find a theme about friendship.

options.label: A
options.text: Hospitals always interfere with school projects.
options.rationale: This is a plot detail, not the lesson the story teaches.

options.label: B
options.text: Winning is only possible by working alone.
options.rationale: Dina’s actions show the opposite: she helped her partner instead of taking credit alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Science fairs should only list one name per project.
options.rationale: This directly contradicts what Dina insisted on at the end of the story.

options.label: D
options.text: True friendship means helping without expecting anything back.

items.stem: Read: "At seventy, Mr. Aziz enrolled in a beginner’s coding class alongside teenagers, insisting he wanted to build a website for his old bookshop before he retired for good." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mr. Aziz’s choice to learn a brand-new skill late in life shows that age does not have to limit new learning.
explanation.tip: Pay attention to a character’s age compared with what they choose to try, to find the theme.

options.label: A
options.text: It’s never too late to learn something new.

options.label: B
options.text: Coding classes are only useful for teenagers.
options.rationale: Mr. Aziz disproves this by learning successfully at seventy years old.

options.label: C
options.text: Older people should not use computers.
options.rationale: The story clearly shows the opposite is true.

options.label: D
options.text: Bookshops cannot have websites.
options.rationale: This directly contradicts Mr. Aziz’s goal in the story.

items.stem: Read: "Though her hands trembled before every competition, the gymnast stepped onto the mat and performed her routine exactly as she had practiced." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The gymnast performed well even though she was clearly afraid, showing that courage does not require the absence of fear.
explanation.tip: Look for a character acting despite a feeling, rather than without that feeling at all.

options.label: A
options.text: Trembling hands always ruin a performance.
options.rationale: She still performed the routine successfully despite her trembling hands.

options.label: B
options.text: Courage means acting despite fear, not feeling no fear at all.

options.label: C
options.text: Gymnasts never feel nervous before a competition.
options.rationale: Her trembling hands clearly show that she does feel nervous.

options.label: D
options.text: Only fearless people become champions.
options.rationale: The story shows she succeeded despite fear, not because she had none.

items.stem: Read: "Teased for his unusual left-handed grip, the young fencer refused to switch hands and later used that same unconventional angle to defeat the regional champion." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The very trait that made him a target of teasing turned out to be the advantage that helped him win.
explanation.tip: Notice when a character’s unusual trait becomes an advantage instead of a flaw.

options.label: A
options.text: Teasing always makes athletes quit a sport.
options.rationale: He did not quit despite being teased for his grip.

options.label: B
options.text: Fencing requires switching grips often.
options.rationale: This contradicts his choice to keep using his own unusual grip.

options.label: C
options.text: Being different from others can be a strength, not a weakness.

options.label: D
options.text: Left-handed people are naturally better at fencing.
options.rationale: The story is about his specific unique style, not a general rule about left-handed fencers.

items.stem: In the story where a merchant secretly watered down his oil to sell more bottles but lost all his regular customers once they noticed, the theme is that greed can cause people to lose more than they gain.

explanation.whyCorrect: The merchant gained a little extra product to sell but lost his entire customer base, showing greed cost him far more than it gained.
explanation.tip: Compare what a greedy character gains in the short term with what they ultimately lose.

items.stem: Read: "After a bitter argument split two lifelong friends apart for a year, one of them finally apologized at a reunion, and the two spent the rest of the evening laughing like old times." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: A single apology was able to undo a full year of distance caused by anger, showing the power of forgiveness.
explanation.tip: Compare the length of the conflict with how quickly it was resolved to find the theme.

options.label: A
options.text: Reunions are only for strangers.
options.rationale: The reunion in the story brought together old friends, not strangers.

options.label: B
options.text: Arguments always end friendships forever.
options.rationale: The story actually shows that the friendship was repaired, not ended forever.

options.label: C
options.text: Apologies never change how people feel.
options.rationale: The apology clearly changed the mood of the reunion for the better.

options.label: D
options.text: Forgiveness can repair a friendship that anger would destroy.

items.stem: Read: "While testing an unrelated chemical mixture out of simple curiosity, the young researcher stumbled onto a discovery that years of planned experiments had failed to produce." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The unplanned, curious experiment succeeded where years of careful, planned experiments had not.
explanation.tip: Notice when an accidental or curious action succeeds where careful planning did not.

options.label: A
options.text: Curiosity can lead to discoveries that careful planning alone would miss.

options.label: B
options.text: Planned experiments always fail.
options.rationale: The story only shows that this particular planned approach had not yet succeeded, not that all planning fails.

options.label: C
options.text: Discoveries only happen by following strict steps.
options.rationale: The discovery in the story happened outside of the strict planned steps.

options.label: D
options.text: Curiosity is dangerous in a laboratory.
options.rationale: The story presents curiosity as valuable here, not as something dangerous.

items.stem: Read: "Despite her coach’s doubts about her chances, the swimmer kept believing she could qualify, trained before dawn every day, and shaved two full seconds off her best time at the trials." Which sentence best states the theme of this story?

explanation.whyCorrect: The swimmer’s own belief in herself, not her coach’s doubts, is what carried her to an improved result.
explanation.tip: Compare what a character believes about themselves with what others around them believe.

options.label: A
options.text: Coaches are always right about their swimmers.
options.rationale: The coach’s doubts turned out to be mistaken in this story.

options.label: B
options.text: Believing in yourself helps you overcome doubt from others.

options.label: C
options.text: Training before dawn guarantees success.
options.rationale: The lesson is about her self-belief, not specifically about the training schedule.

options.label: D
options.text: Doubt from others always comes true.
options.rationale: The swimmer’s success in the story disproves this statement.

items.stem: Which pair shows a PART-to-WHOLE relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A page is one part that makes up the whole book.
explanation.tip: Ask: is the first word physically contained inside the second?

options.label: A
options.text: library : shelf
options.rationale: This reverses the order; a shelf is a part of a library, not the other way around.

options.label: B
options.text: author : reader
options.rationale: This names two different people, not a part contained within a whole.

options.label: C
options.text: page : book

options.label: D
options.text: pencil : eraser
options.rationale: These are two separate tools used together, not a part of a whole.

items.stem: Which pair shows a PART-to-WHOLE relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A petal is one part of the whole flower.
explanation.tip: The part should be something that is physically attached to or inside the whole.

options.label: A
options.text: stem : soil
options.rationale: Both of these are separate things a plant needs, not a part and the whole it belongs to.

options.label: B
options.text: garden : petal
options.rationale: This reverses the order; the petal is the part, and it comes first in a true part-to-whole pair.

options.label: C
options.text: bee : hive
options.rationale: A bee is one member of a group that lives in a hive, which is member-to-group, not part-to-whole.

options.label: D
options.text: petal : flower

items.stem: Which pair shows the SAME relationship as “wing : bird”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Just as a wing is one part of the whole bird, a verse is one part of the whole song.
explanation.tip: Restate the pair as “a ___ is one part of a ___” and test each choice.

options.label: A
options.text: verse : song

options.label: B
options.text: audience : song
options.rationale: An audience listens to a song, but it is not a part of the song itself.

options.label: C
options.text: instrument : musician
options.rationale: This shows a tool and the person who uses it, not a part and its whole.

options.label: D
options.text: radio : station
options.rationale: A radio plays a station's broadcast; it is not a piece contained inside the station.

items.stem: Choose the word that completes the PART-to-WHOLE analogy: branch : ____ :: wave : ocean

explanation.whyCorrect: A branch is one part of the whole tree, just as a wave is one part of the whole ocean.
explanation.tip: The second word in each pair should be the complete thing that contains the first.

options.label: A
options.text: tree

options.label: B
options.text: forest
options.rationale: A forest is a group of many trees, which is member-to-group, not part-to-whole.

options.label: C
options.text: root
options.rationale: A root is a different part of the tree, not the whole tree itself.

options.label: D
options.text: leaf
options.rationale: A leaf is also a part of a tree, so this pairs two parts instead of a part and its whole.

items.stem: Which pair shows a PART-to-WHOLE relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A hinge is a small part that is built into the whole door.
explanation.tip: Picture taking the object apart: is the first word one of the pieces you would find?

options.label: A
options.text: window : curtain
options.rationale: These are two separate objects often used together, but neither is a piece of the other.

options.label: B
options.text: hinge : door

options.label: C
options.text: house : neighborhood
options.rationale: A house is one member of a neighborhood, which is member-to-group, not part-to-whole.

options.label: D
options.text: tool : carpenter
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the tool they use, not a part and its whole.

items.stem: Which pair shows a PART-to-WHOLE relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A spoke is one of the thin parts that make up the whole wheel.
explanation.tip: If you removed the first word's object, would the second word's object still be complete?

options.label: A
options.text: axle : engine
options.rationale: An axle and an engine are both separate parts of a car; neither is the whole that contains the other.

options.label: B
options.text: driver : wheel
options.rationale: This names a person and an object, not a part and the whole it belongs to.

options.label: C
options.text: spoke : wheel

options.label: D
options.text: tire : road
options.rationale: A tire touches a road, but the road is not a whole object that contains the tire.

items.stem: Which pair shows a WHOLE-to-PART relationship, with the whole named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The necklace, the whole object, is named first, followed by the bead, one of its many parts.
explanation.tip: Check the order: does the first word contain the second, or is it the other way around?

options.label: A
options.text: jeweler : necklace
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the object they make, not a whole and one of its parts.

options.label: B
options.text: necklace : jewelry box
options.rationale: A jewelry box stores a necklace; it is not a piece of the necklace itself.

options.label: C
options.text: bead : bracelet
options.rationale: This lists the part first and the whole second, which is the reverse order being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: necklace : bead

items.stem: Which pair shows a WHOLE-to-PART relationship, with the whole named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The orchestra, the whole group, is named first, followed by the violin, one of its instruments.
explanation.tip: Say the pair as a sentence: “The ___ is made up of many ___s.”

options.label: A
options.text: orchestra : violin

options.label: B
options.text: conductor : orchestra
options.rationale: A conductor leads the orchestra but is not one of the orchestra's component parts.

options.label: C
options.text: violin : orchestra
options.rationale: This lists the part first and the whole second, the reverse of what is being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: violin : musician
options.rationale: This shows an object and the person who plays it, not a whole and one of its parts.

items.stem: Choose the word that completes the WHOLE-to-PART analogy: forest : ____ :: fleet : ship

explanation.whyCorrect: A forest is made up of many trees, just as a fleet is made up of many ships.
explanation.tip: Match the level of the comparison: forest relates to tree the way fleet relates to ship.

options.label: A
options.text: jungle
options.rationale: This renames the whole with a similar word instead of naming one of its parts.

options.label: B
options.text: tree

options.label: C
options.text: leaf
options.rationale: A leaf is a part of a tree, not a part of the forest at this level of the comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: ranger
options.rationale: A ranger works in a forest but is not one of the forest's physical parts.

items.stem: Which pair shows a WHOLE-to-PART relationship, with the whole named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The skeleton, the whole structure, is named first, followed by the bone, one of its parts.
explanation.tip: Ask which word names a single piece and which word names the full structure.

options.label: A
options.text: doctor : skeleton
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the object they study, not a whole and one of its parts.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.rationale: This lists the larger whole first and the skeleton second, but the skeleton is itself a whole made of bones, which is the relationship asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: bone : marrow
options.rationale: This compares two things found inside a body, but it does not match the skeleton-and-bone pair being described.

items.stem: Which pair shows a WHOLE-to-PART relationship, with the whole named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: A committee, the whole group, is made up of its individual members.
explanation.tip: The whole should be a single unit, and the part should be one piece inside it.

options.label: A
options.text: member : committee
options.rationale: This lists the part first and the whole second, the reverse of what is being asked for.

options.label: B
options.text: chairperson : committee
options.rationale: A chairperson has a special role within the group, but the question asks for the group and any ordinary part of it.

options.label: C
options.text: committee : member

options.label: D
options.text: member : vote
options.rationale: This shows a role and an action, not a whole and one of its parts.

items.stem: Which pair shows an ITEM-to-CATEGORY relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A salmon is one specific example that belongs to the broader category of fish.
explanation.tip: Ask: is the second word a general group that the first word is a type of?

options.label: A
options.text: salmon : dinner
options.rationale: A salmon can become a meal, but “dinner” is not the biological category it belongs to.

options.label: B
options.text: fisherman : salmon
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the thing they catch, not an item and its category.

options.label: C
options.text: ocean : salmon
options.rationale: An ocean is a habitat, not the general group or category that salmon belongs to.

options.label: D
options.text: salmon : fish

items.stem: Which pair shows an ITEM-to-CATEGORY relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: An oak is one specific kind of tree, so it belongs to the broad category “tree.”
explanation.tip: The category word should describe a whole group the first word is a member of, by type.

options.label: A
options.text: oak : tree

options.label: B
options.text: tree : forest
options.rationale: This is item-to-group, since a tree is a member of a forest, not an item and its general category.

options.label: C
options.text: acorn : oak
options.rationale: An acorn grows into an oak, which is more of a cause-and-growth relationship, not item-to-category.

options.label: D
options.text: oak : furniture
options.rationale: Furniture can be made from oak wood, but “furniture” is not the category oak itself belongs to.

items.stem: Choose the word that completes the ITEM-to-CATEGORY analogy: tulip : flower :: python : ____

explanation.whyCorrect: A tulip belongs to the category “flower,” and a python belongs to the matching category “snake.”
explanation.tip: Pick the category that is at the same level of detail on both sides of the analogy.

options.label: A
options.text: predator
options.rationale: This describes how the python behaves, not the general group it belongs to.

options.label: B
options.text: reptile
options.rationale: A python is also a reptile, but “snake” is the more exact match to how specific “flower” is for tulip.

options.label: C
options.text: snake

options.label: D
options.text: desert
options.rationale: A desert is a habitat where some pythons live, not the category of animal it belongs to.

items.stem: Which pair shows an ITEM-to-CATEGORY relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: Cumulus is one specific kind of cloud, so it belongs to the broad category “cloud.”
explanation.tip: The first word should be a specific example, and the second should be the broader group.

options.label: A
options.text: weather : forecast
options.rationale: These two words describe a general topic and a type of report about it, not an item and its category.

options.label: B
options.text: cumulus : cloud

options.label: C
options.text: rain : cumulus
options.rationale: Rain can fall from some clouds, but this names an effect, not the category the cloud belongs to.

options.label: D
options.text: sky : cumulus
options.rationale: This reverses the order; the cloud type should be named first as the specific item.

items.stem: Which pair shows an ITEM-to-CATEGORY relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A sonata is one specific type of musical composition, so it belongs to the category “composition.”
explanation.tip: Check that the second word names a broad type the first word fits into.

options.label: A
options.text: composer : sonata
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the thing they create, not an item and its category.

options.label: B
options.text: orchestra : sonata
options.rationale: An orchestra can perform a sonata, but the orchestra is not the category the sonata belongs to.

options.label: C
options.text: sonata : composition

options.label: D
options.text: symphony : orchestra
options.rationale: A symphony is performed by an orchestra, but this pairs a piece with a performing group, not an item with its category.

items.stem: Which pair shows an ITEM-to-CATEGORY relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: Diesel is one specific kind of fuel, so it belongs to the broad category “fuel.”
explanation.tip: Say the pair as “a ___ is a type of ___” and see if it still makes sense.

options.label: A
options.text: fuel : diesel
options.rationale: This lists the category first and the item second, the reverse of what is being asked for.

options.label: B
options.text: engine : diesel
options.rationale: This shows a machine and the fuel it uses, not an item and its category.

options.label: C
options.text: gallon : fuel
options.rationale: A gallon is a unit used to measure fuel, not a type of fuel itself.

options.label: D
options.text: diesel : fuel

items.stem: Which pair shows a CAUSE-and-EFFECT relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A drought causes crops to dry out and wilt from lack of water.
explanation.tip: Ask which event happens first and makes the second event happen.

options.label: A
options.text: drought : wilted crops

options.label: B
options.text: farmer : crops
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the thing they grow, not a cause and its effect.

options.label: C
options.text: rain : drought
options.rationale: Rain actually helps prevent a drought rather than causing one, so this is not a true cause-and-effect pair.

options.label: D
options.text: crops : harvest
options.rationale: These are two steps in a farming process, not a single cause producing one effect.

items.stem: Which pair shows a CAUSE-and-EFFECT relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: The shaking from the earthquake is what caused the bridge to collapse.
explanation.tip: The cause should be the event, and the effect should be the result of that event.

options.label: A
options.text: bridge : river
options.rationale: This shows an object and the place it is built over, not a cause and its effect.

options.label: B
options.text: earthquake : collapsed bridge

options.label: C
options.text: collapse : earthquake
options.rationale: This lists the effect before the cause, the reverse of the order being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: engineer : bridge
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the structure they build, not a cause and its effect.

items.stem: Choose the word or phrase that completes the CAUSE-and-EFFECT analogy: frost : frozen pipes :: heat wave : ____

explanation.whyCorrect: Just as frost causes pipes to freeze, extreme heat can cause asphalt roads to melt.
explanation.tip: The second word in each pair should describe something that happens because of the first.

options.label: A
options.text: sunscreen
options.rationale: This is something people use during a heat wave, not an effect the heat wave causes.

options.label: B
options.text: thermometer
options.rationale: A thermometer measures temperature; it is not an effect caused by extreme heat.

options.label: C
options.text: summer
options.rationale: This names a season, not a specific effect caused by the heat wave.

options.label: D
options.text: melted asphalt

items.stem: Which pair shows a CAUSE-and-EFFECT relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: Years of neglect, such as never cleaning or oiling it, is what caused the gate to rust.
explanation.tip: Picture the first word as an ongoing condition and the second as its lasting result.

options.label: A
options.text: paint : gate
options.rationale: Paint and a gate are an object and a material used on it, not a cause and its effect.

options.label: B
options.text: gate : fence
options.rationale: A gate is usually part of a fence, which is part-to-whole, not cause-and-effect.

options.label: C
options.text: neglect : rusted gate

options.label: D
options.text: rust : metal
options.rationale: This describes a property that can affect metal, but it does not name a cause producing a distinct result.

items.stem: Which pair shows a CAUSE-and-EFFECT relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: Catching too many fish over time is what causes the overall fish population to shrink.
explanation.tip: Ask: does the first idea explain why the second idea happened?

options.label: A
options.text: fisherman : boat
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the tool they use, not a cause and its effect.

options.label: B
options.text: ocean : fish
options.rationale: This shows a habitat and the animals that live there, not a cause and its effect.

options.label: C
options.text: population : decline
options.rationale: This only restates the effect by itself, without naming the cause that produced it.

options.label: D
options.text: overfishing : declining fish population

items.stem: Which pair shows a CAUSE-and-EFFECT relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: Removing trees leaves soil unprotected, which causes it to wash or blow away.
explanation.tip: Tree roots normally hold soil in place; removing them removes that protection.

options.label: A
options.text: deforestation : soil erosion

options.label: B
options.text: logger : tree
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the object they cut down, not a cause and its effect.

options.label: C
options.text: erosion : deforestation
options.rationale: This lists the effect before the cause, the reverse of the order being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: forest : wildlife
options.rationale: This shows a habitat and the animals that live in it, not a cause and its effect.

items.stem: Which pair shows an EFFECT-to-CAUSE relationship, with the effect named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sunburn is the effect, and spending too long in the sun is the cause that produced it.
explanation.tip: Read the pair as “___ happened because of ___” to check the order.

options.label: A
options.text: sun exposure : sunburn
options.rationale: This lists the cause before the effect, the reverse of the order being asked for.

options.label: B
options.text: sunburn : too much sun exposure

options.label: C
options.text: tan : summer
options.rationale: This is a loose association between a season and a skin change, not a precise effect naming its cause.

options.label: D
options.text: sunscreen : skin
options.rationale: This shows a protective item and the body part it protects, not an effect and its cause.

items.stem: Which pair shows an EFFECT-to-CAUSE relationship, with the effect named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The shattered window is the effect, and the thrown rock is what caused it to break.
explanation.tip: Find the result first, then ask what event made that result happen.

options.label: A
options.text: window : house
options.rationale: This is part-to-whole, since a window is part of a house, not an effect and its cause.

options.label: B
options.text: glass : window
options.rationale: This shows a material and the object made from it, not an effect and its cause.

options.label: C
options.text: shattered window : thrown rock

options.label: D
options.text: thrown rock : shattered window
options.rationale: This lists the cause before the effect, the reverse of the order being asked for.

items.stem: Which pair shows an EFFECT-to-CAUSE relationship, with the effect named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The traffic jam is the effect, caused by the stalled truck blocking the road.
explanation.tip: The effect word usually names a problem or change; the cause word explains why it happened.

options.label: A
options.text: highway : truck
options.rationale: This shows a location and an object on it, not an effect and its cause.

options.label: B
options.text: stalled truck : traffic jam
options.rationale: This lists the cause before the effect, the reverse of the order being asked for.

options.label: C
options.text: driver : truck
options.rationale: This shows a person and the vehicle they operate, not an effect and its cause.

options.label: D
options.text: traffic jam : stalled truck blocking the highway

items.stem: Which pair shows an EFFECT-to-CAUSE relationship, with the effect named first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The power outage is the effect, caused directly by the electrical line that fell during the storm.
explanation.tip: Look for the exact event that directly caused the problem, not just the general situation around it.

options.label: A
options.text: power outage : downed electrical line during the storm

options.label: B
options.text: electrician : line
options.rationale: This shows a worker and the object they repair, not an effect and its cause.

options.label: C
options.text: downed line : power outage
options.rationale: This lists the cause before the effect, the reverse of the order being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: storm : outage
options.rationale: The storm is a broader trigger, but it is not the precise, direct cause of the outage described here.

items.stem: Which pair shows a TOOL-to-USER relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A scalpel is the tool that a surgeon uses to perform surgery.
explanation.tip: The tool should be an object, and the user should be the person who operates it.

options.label: A
options.text: hospital : surgeon
options.rationale: This shows a workplace and a worker, not a tool and the person who uses it.

options.label: B
options.text: scalpel : surgeon

options.label: C
options.text: surgeon : scalpel
options.rationale: This lists the user first and the tool second, the reverse of what is being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: patient : surgeon
options.rationale: These are two people in a medical setting, not a tool and its user.

items.stem: Which pair shows a TOOL-to-USER relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A telescope is the tool that an astronomer uses to study the sky.
explanation.tip: Ask which word names an object you hold and which names the person who holds it.

options.label: A
options.text: astronomer : telescope
options.rationale: This lists the user first and the tool second, the reverse of what is being asked for.

options.label: B
options.text: star : telescope
options.rationale: This shows the object being observed and the tool used to observe it, not a tool and its user.

options.label: C
options.text: telescope : astronomer

options.label: D
options.text: observatory : astronomer
options.rationale: This shows a workplace and a worker, not a tool and the person who uses it.

items.stem: Choose the word that completes the TOOL-to-USER analogy: stethoscope : doctor :: whisk : ____

explanation.whyCorrect: Just as a doctor uses a stethoscope, a baker uses a whisk.
explanation.tip: Match each tool to the type of person who would naturally hold and use it.

options.label: A
options.text: baker

options.label: B
options.text: bakery
options.rationale: A bakery is a workplace, not the person who actually uses the tool.

options.label: C
options.text: oven
options.rationale: An oven is a different tool entirely, not the person using the whisk.

options.label: D
options.text: flour
options.rationale: Flour is an ingredient a baker might use, not the person who uses the whisk.

items.stem: Which pair shows a TOOL-to-USER relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A gavel is the small tool a judge uses to call for order in the courtroom.
explanation.tip: The first word in a tool-to-user pair should be something the second word physically holds.

options.label: A
options.text: courtroom : judge
options.rationale: This shows a workplace and a worker, not a tool and the person who uses it.

options.label: B
options.text: lawyer : judge
options.rationale: These are two different professional roles, not a tool and its user.

options.label: C
options.text: judge : gavel
options.rationale: This lists the user first and the tool second, the reverse of what is being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: gavel : judge

items.stem: Which pair shows a TOOL-to-USER relationship?

explanation.whyCorrect: A chisel is the tool a sculptor uses to carve and shape stone or wood.
explanation.tip: Picture the object in someone's hand; the hand it belongs in is the user.

options.label: A
options.text: chisel : sculptor

options.label: B
options.text: studio : sculptor
options.rationale: This shows a workplace and a worker, not a tool and the person who uses it.

options.label: C
options.text: sculptor : chisel
options.rationale: This lists the user first and the tool second, the reverse of what is being asked for.

options.label: D
options.text: marble : sculptor
options.rationale: Marble is a material a sculptor shapes, not a tool they hold and use.

items.stem: A weather reporter needs a word pair for the same kind of heat, going from mild to extreme. Which pair fits?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Warm” and “scorching” both describe heat, but “scorching” describes a much more intense heat.
explanation.tip: Both words should describe the exact same quality, just to different strengths.

options.label: A
options.text: scorching : freezing
options.rationale: Both words here already describe extremes, just at opposite ends, not a mild-to-strong climb.

options.label: B
options.text: warm : scorching

options.label: C
options.text: warm : sunny
options.rationale: A quality (heat) and an unrelated weather trait don't belong on a single shared scale.

options.label: D
options.text: warm : cold
options.rationale: This pair sits at opposite ends of the temperature scale, not two points on the same side.

items.stem: A counselor wants to rank one emotion from a mild spark up to its most extreme version. Which pair fits?

explanation.whyCorrect: Being furious is a much stronger version of the mild irritation you feel when annoyed.
explanation.tip: Rank the two feelings on one scale from mild to extreme.

options.label: A
options.text: annoyed : calm
options.rationale: Calm is the absence of irritation, the opposite direction from building anger.

options.label: B
options.text: annoyed : happy
options.rationale: Happiness is an unrelated emotion, not a milder point on the anger scale.

options.label: C
options.text: annoyed : furious

options.label: D
options.text: furious : relaxed
options.rationale: Relaxed sits at the opposite end from rage, not a milder step toward it.

items.stem: Choose the word that shows a STRONGER version of “tired”: She wasn't just tired, she was ____ after the race.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Exhausted” describes an extreme level of tiredness, far beyond ordinary tiredness.
explanation.tip: Look for context clues like “wasn't just ___” that signal a stronger word is needed.

options.label: A
options.text: awake
options.rationale: This does not describe tiredness at all.

options.label: B
options.text: exhausted

options.label: C
options.text: bored
options.rationale: This describes a different feeling entirely, not a greater amount of tiredness.

options.label: D
options.text: rested
options.rationale: This is the opposite of tired, not a stronger version of it.

items.stem: Which pair shows two words that describe the SAME quality, but the second word is much STRONGER?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both words describe wetness, but “drenched” means far wetter than merely “damp.”
explanation.tip: Ask whether both words sit on the same scale, just at different points.

options.label: A
options.text: drenched : parched
options.rationale: These are opposite extremes of wetness and dryness, not a mild and a stronger version of the same quality.

options.label: B
options.text: damp : dry
options.rationale: These describe opposite amounts of wetness, not two strengths of the same quality.

options.label: C
options.text: damp : cool
options.rationale: These describe two different qualities, not the same quality at two different strengths.

options.label: D
options.text: damp : drenched

items.stem: A writing coach asks for a pair tracking ONE emotion from a slight worry up to total panic. Which pair fits?

explanation.whyCorrect: Terror is a far more extreme version of the mild worry described as “concerned.”
explanation.tip: Picture a thermometer for the feeling: where would each word land?

options.label: A
options.text: concerned : terrified

options.label: B
options.text: terrified : confident
options.rationale: Confidence is unrelated to fear, not a milder step back from panic.

options.label: C
options.text: concerned : fearless
options.rationale: Fearless describes having no fear at all, moving away from the feeling rather than deeper into it.

options.label: D
options.text: concerned : curious
options.rationale: Curiosity is an unrelated feeling, not a weaker version of worry.

items.stem: Which pair of words are ANTONYMS (opposites)?

explanation.whyCorrect: Someone who is generous freely gives, while someone who is stingy refuses to give; these describe opposite behaviors.
explanation.tip: Check each pair against a simple test: does one word mean roughly the opposite of the other?

options.label: A
options.text: generous : kind
options.rationale: These two words are close in meaning, not opposites.

options.label: B
options.text: generous : stingy

options.label: C
options.text: stingy : cheap
options.rationale: These two words are close in meaning, not opposites.

options.label: D
options.text: generous : wealthy
options.rationale: Being generous and being wealthy describe unrelated qualities, not opposite ones.

items.stem: Which pair of words are ANTONYMS (opposites)?

explanation.whyCorrect: Something transparent lets light pass through it, while something opaque blocks light completely.
explanation.tip: Opposite pairs should describe two qualities that cannot both be fully true at once.

options.label: A
options.text: opaque : dark
options.rationale: These two words are related in meaning, but “dark” is not the true opposite of “transparent.”

options.label: B
options.text: transparent : clear
options.rationale: These two words are close in meaning, not opposites.

options.label: C
options.text: transparent : opaque

options.label: D
options.text: transparent : glass
options.rationale: This pairs a quality with a material, not two opposite qualities.

items.stem: Choose the ANTONYM that completes the sentence: The hallway was so ____ that we could barely see, unlike the brilliantly lit lobby.
