options.text: Reread only the glossary, if there is one, and nothing else.
options.rationale: A glossary alone may define terms but not fully explain the cause.

options.label: D
options.text: Decide tectonic plates move randomly for no reason.
options.rationale: Assuming no cause ignores a scientific explanation the text likely gives.

items.stem: A text states that the Great Barrier Reef is made of billions of tiny coral polyps. A reader wants to know how such small creatures build something so large. What should the reader do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading can reveal how the text explains gradual reef-building over long periods of time.
explanation.tip: When a fact feels surprising, reread for the text’s explanation of how it happens.

options.label: A
options.text: Assume the number given must be a typo.
options.rationale: Dismissing the number ignores a possible explanation the text provides.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop reading because it seems unbelievable.
options.rationale: Giving up prevents the reader from finding the text’s own explanation.

options.label: C
options.text: Reread the text to find the explanation of how polyps build the reef over time.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to reading about a different ocean topic.
options.rationale: Switching topics avoids answering the original question.

items.stem: After finishing an article about ancient trade routes, a student cannot explain why merchants traveled in large groups called caravans. Which part should the student reread?

explanation.whyCorrect: The section about grouping reasons directly answers why caravans formed.
explanation.tip: Match your specific question to the section most likely to address it.

options.label: A
options.text: The map caption alone
options.rationale: A caption is unlikely to fully explain a social or safety reason.

options.label: B
options.text: The section listing trade goods only
options.rationale: A list of goods does not explain why merchants traveled in groups.

options.label: C
options.text: The concluding sentence about trade today
options.rationale: A sentence about modern trade would not explain the historical reason for caravans.

options.label: D
options.text: The section explaining the reasons merchants grouped together

items.stem: A reader is confused by the sentence “Suspension bridges use cables to transfer the weight of traffic to the towers at each end.” What should the reader do first?

explanation.whyCorrect: Slowly rereading the whole sentence helps connect cables, weight, and towers.
explanation.tip: Break a complex sentence into its parts during a careful reread.

options.label: A
options.text: Reread the sentence slowly, focusing on each part of the process.

options.label: B
options.text: Reread only the word “bridge.”
options.rationale: Rereading a single word will not clarify the whole process described.

options.label: C
options.text: Decide the sentence is unimportant.
options.rationale: The sentence explains a key part of how the bridge works, so it matters.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip ahead without rereading.
options.rationale: Skipping would not resolve confusion about this specific process.

items.stem: A text about bacteria explains that some bacteria are helpful while others cause illness. A reader wonders if this applies to all microscopic organisms. What is the best step?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading can reveal whether the text draws distinctions between organism types.
explanation.tip: Reread to check whether the text actually answers your broader question.

options.label: A
options.text: Assume all tiny organisms behave the same way.
options.rationale: The text may distinguish between types, so assuming sameness could be wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: Reread the text to see if it compares bacteria to other microscopic organisms.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the subject to something unrelated.
options.rationale: Changing the subject avoids answering the original question.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop reading because the question feels too broad.
options.rationale: Giving up prevents finding any comparison the text might offer.

items.stem: Which TWO are good reasons to reread a section about how glaciers carve valleys?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading helps with both vocabulary and understanding cause-and-effect processes.
explanation.tip: Reread to connect ideas and clarify terms, not to stall.

options.label: A
options.text: To notice how one process leads to another

options.label: B
options.text: To clarify a confusing geology term

options.label: C
options.text: To make the section shorter
options.rationale: Rereading does not shorten text.

options.label: D
options.text: To avoid finishing the article
options.rationale: Rereading should support finishing the article, not avoiding it.

items.stem: A student reads that early bicycles had no pedals and riders pushed off the ground with their feet. The student is confused about how this was safer or less safe than modern bikes. What should the student do?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph may directly compare safety features of early and modern bicycles.
explanation.tip: Reread for direct comparisons the text makes between two things.

options.label: A
options.text: Guess that early bicycles were always safer.
options.rationale: Guessing ignores any comparison the text might directly provide.

options.label: B
options.text: Reread only the picture caption.
options.rationale: A caption alone may not include the full comparison described in the text.

options.label: C
options.text: Reread the paragraph to look for a comparison to modern bicycles.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip ahead to an unrelated article.
options.rationale: Switching articles avoids answering the question.

items.stem: An article says the human heart has four chambers that each play a different role. A reader cannot remember which chamber does what. What should the reader do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading carefully lets the reader match each chamber to the role the text describes.
explanation.tip: When a text lists several similar parts, reread slowly to tell them apart.

options.label: A
options.text: Guess the roles from memory.
options.rationale: Guessing risks mixing up the chambers’ specific functions.

options.label: B
options.text: Skip to a paragraph about a different organ.
options.rationale: A different organ’s paragraph will not explain heart chambers.

options.label: C
options.text: Decide the chambers all do the same thing.
options.rationale: The text likely explains that each chamber has a distinct role.

options.label: D
options.text: Reread the paragraph, matching each chamber to its specific role.

items.stem: A reader who already understands a passage perfectly the first time should still reread it ten times before moving on.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading is meant to resolve confusion, not a required number of repeats regardless of understanding.
explanation.tip: Reread based on need, not a fixed number of times.

items.stem: A text explains that some fish can detect electric fields produced by other animals. A reader wants to know how this ability works. What should the reader do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading can reveal details about the specialized organ that senses electric fields.
explanation.tip: When an ability seems surprising, reread for the text’s explanation of the mechanism.

options.label: A
options.text: Reread the text looking for the explanation of the sensing organ involved.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume the text is exaggerating.
options.rationale: Assuming exaggeration skips the chance to find a real scientific explanation.

options.label: C
options.text: Ignore the detail and move on.
options.rationale: Ignoring the detail leaves real confusion unresolved.

options.label: D
options.text: Reread only the diagram, not the words.
options.rationale: A diagram alone may not fully explain the biological process described in the text.

items.stem: A student rereads a paragraph about forest fires and notices a sentence they missed: “Some seeds only sprout after being exposed to intense heat.” What did rereading help the student do?

explanation.whyCorrect: A careful second read can surface sentences that were skipped the first time.
explanation.tip: Rereading slowly can catch details your eyes glossed over at first.

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid new information.
options.rationale: Rereading helped the student gain new information, not avoid it.

options.label: B
options.text: Find an important detail that was missed during the first reading.

options.label: C
options.text: Shorten the paragraph.
options.rationale: Rereading does not change a paragraph’s length.

options.label: D
options.text: Change the author’s original wording.
options.rationale: Rereading does not alter the original text.

items.stem: An article explains that medieval castles had moats, drawbridges, and thick walls. A reader does not understand the specific purpose of a moat. What should the reader do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading the sentence likely reveals that the moat was meant to slow or stop attackers.
explanation.tip: Look for the stated purpose near the term you are confused about.

options.label: A
options.text: Skip to an article about a different building.
options.rationale: Switching topics would not explain this specific defensive feature.

options.label: B
options.text: Guess that the moat was for swimming.
options.rationale: Guessing a recreational use ignores the defensive context of the article.

options.label: C
options.text: Reread the sentence about the moat to look for its stated purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: Decide the moat was just decoration.
options.rationale: Decoration is unlikely to be the stated reason in a text about defense.

items.stem: A paragraph about solar panels explains how sunlight, electrons, and wiring work together to create electricity, in that order. A reader mixes up the sequence. What is the best fix?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading with attention to sequence clues clarifies the correct order of the process.
explanation.tip: Reread for words like first, then, and finally to track a process.

options.label: A
options.text: Make up an order that sounds logical.
options.rationale: Making up an order risks contradicting what the text actually states.

options.label: B
options.text: Only reread the heading of the section.
options.rationale: A heading is unlikely to list the full three-part sequence.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip the paragraph entirely.
options.rationale: Skipping would leave the confusing sequence unresolved.

options.label: D
options.text: Reread the paragraph, tracking the order each part is introduced.

items.stem: A student rereads an article about submarines twice and now understands why they must carefully control both their weight and air supply underwater. What is the BEST explanation for this improvement?

explanation.whyCorrect: A slower, more careful second reading allows focus on previously confusing details.
explanation.tip: Careful, attentive rereading—not speed—builds deeper understanding.

options.label: A
options.text: The second reading let the student focus on details that were confusing at first.

options.label: B
options.text: The student read it much faster the second time.
options.rationale: Reading faster typically reduces, not increases, careful understanding.

options.label: C
options.text: The student skipped the confusing parts both times.
options.rationale: Skipping confusing parts twice would not explain improved understanding.

options.label: D
options.text: The article’s content changed between readings.
options.rationale: A text does not change simply because it is read a second time.

items.stem: Rereading is useful only for science articles and never helps with history or social studies texts.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading is a general strategy that helps with confusing text in any subject, not just science.
explanation.tip: Rereading works across all subjects, not just one.

items.stem: After reading about satellites orbiting Earth, a student is confused about why satellites do not fall out of the sky. What should the student do?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading the section can reveal how a satellite’s speed balances Earth’s gravity to keep it in orbit.
explanation.tip: When a fact seems to defy common sense, reread for the text’s scientific explanation.

options.label: A
options.text: Assume gravity does not affect satellites.
options.rationale: Gravity does affect satellites; the text likely explains how orbit balances this force.

options.label: B
options.text: Reread the section explaining the balance between gravity and speed.

options.label: C
options.text: Guess that satellites have engines running constantly.
options.rationale: Constant engine use is not the explanation most texts give for staying in orbit.

options.label: D
options.text: Skip the whole section about orbits.
options.rationale: Skipping would leave the confusion unresolved.

items.stem: A writer claims, “Our school should start an hour later because teenagers need more sleep.” What is the claim in this argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: The claim is the specific position the writer wants readers to accept.
explanation.tip: The claim is usually the main opinion the whole argument is trying to prove.

options.label: A
options.text: Our school has classes.
options.rationale: This is an unrelated fact, not the claim.

options.label: B
options.text: Sleep is healthy.
options.rationale: This is a general idea, not the specific claim being argued.

options.label: C
options.text: The school should start an hour later.

options.label: D
options.text: Teenagers need more sleep.
options.rationale: This is the reasoning that supports the claim, not the claim itself.

items.stem: A student argues against homework by saying, “Homework is just busywork, and everyone knows busywork is pointless.” What is weak about this reasoning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Claiming “everyone knows” something is a bandwagon appeal, not real evidence.
explanation.tip: Watch for arguments that rely on popularity instead of facts.

options.label: A
options.text: It uses too many big words.
options.rationale: Word choice is not the issue; the reasoning itself is weak.

options.label: B
options.text: It does not mention homework at all.
options.rationale: The argument does mention homework directly.

options.label: C
options.text: It is too short to be an argument.
options.rationale: Length is not the problem; the logic itself is flawed.

options.label: D
options.text: It assumes something is true just because many people supposedly believe it.

items.stem: An article argues cities should add more bike lanes and supports this with data showing bike injuries dropped 40% in cities that added protected lanes. Is this evidence relevant to the claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: The statistic shows a direct link between the proposed action and a real safety outcome.
explanation.tip: Relevant evidence directly supports the specific claim being made.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because it directly connects bike lanes to fewer injuries, supporting the claim’s safety benefit.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the article does not mention bike lanes at all.
options.rationale: The article’s central topic is bike lanes, so this option misstates the argument.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because injury statistics have nothing to do with bike lanes.
options.rationale: The statistic directly links bike lanes to a drop in injuries, so it is clearly related.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, but only because it mentions a percentage.
options.rationale: A percentage alone is not what makes evidence relevant; its connection to the claim does.

items.stem: A letter to the editor says, “We must ban plastic bags immediately, or our oceans will be completely dead within five years.” What technique does this sentence use?

explanation.whyCorrect: The extreme claim about oceans being “completely dead” in five years is an exaggeration meant to scare readers.
explanation.tip: Watch for absolute, dramatic predictions that lack supporting evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: A balanced comparison of two solutions
options.rationale: Only one option, banning bags, is discussed; no comparison is made.

options.label: B
options.text: An extreme, exaggerated prediction to create fear

options.label: C
options.text: A direct quotation from a marine scientist
options.rationale: No source or quotation is given for this prediction.

options.label: D
options.text: A calm explanation of recycling methods
options.rationale: The sentence is alarming, not calm or explanatory.

items.stem: An essay claims school uniforms reduce bullying and supports this only by saying, “My cousin’s school has uniforms, and nobody there gets bullied.” Why is this evidence weak?

explanation.whyCorrect: One anecdote is not enough evidence to support a broad claim about all schools.
explanation.tip: A single example, or anecdote, is weaker evidence than data from many cases.

options.label: A
options.text: It is weak because it is written in first person.
options.rationale: Point of view does not determine whether evidence is strong or weak.

options.label: B
options.text: It is weak because uniforms are mentioned.
options.rationale: Mentioning uniforms is necessary since that is the topic of the claim.

options.label: C
options.text: A single personal example cannot prove something is true for schools in general.

options.label: D
options.text: It is weak because the cousin attends school.
options.rationale: Attending school is irrelevant to the strength of the evidence.

items.stem: An opinion piece argues against raising the driving age by saying, “Lowering the driving age last year clearly caused the rise in traffic jams this year.” What is the flaw in this reasoning?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a false-cause fallacy: one event happening before another does not prove it caused the other.
explanation.tip: Just because B follows A does not prove A caused B.

options.label: A
options.text: It fails to mention traffic jams at all.
options.rationale: Traffic jams are directly mentioned in the argument.

options.label: B
options.text: It focuses only on pedestrians, not drivers.
options.rationale: The argument is entirely about drivers and the driving age, not pedestrians.

options.label: C
options.text: It uses too much statistical data.
options.rationale: No statistical data is actually provided in this argument.

options.label: D
options.text: It assumes one event caused another just because it happened first, without real proof.

items.stem: A city council member argues for a new community garden, citing a university study of 50 cities showing gardens reduced local food costs by 15% on average. Compared to a single resident’s opinion, why is this evidence stronger?

explanation.whyCorrect: A large study across many cities is more reliable than one person’s limited experience.
explanation.tip: Evidence from many cases is generally stronger than a single opinion or example.

options.label: A
options.text: It is based on data from many cities rather than one person’s impression.

options.label: B
options.text: It is stronger because it mentions gardens.
options.rationale: Simply mentioning the topic does not make evidence strong.

options.label: C
options.text: It is stronger because it includes a percentage.
options.rationale: A number alone is not what makes evidence strong; its broad, studied basis does.

options.label: D
options.text: It is stronger because a council member said it.
options.rationale: Who states the evidence does not make data more reliable; the data itself does.

items.stem: A debate speaker says, “My opponent wants to cut the art budget, so clearly she hates creativity and wants children to suffer.” What is wrong with this statement?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is an ad hominem attack: it insults the opponent’s character instead of addressing her reasoning.
explanation.tip: A fair argument responds to ideas, not insults aimed at a person.

options.label: A
options.text: It correctly summarizes the opponent’s budget proposal.
options.rationale: The statement exaggerates and distorts the opponent’s actual position rather than summarizing it fairly.

options.label: B
options.text: It unfairly attacks the opponent’s character instead of addressing her actual argument.

options.label: C
options.text: It provides strong evidence for cutting the art budget.
options.rationale: No evidence about the budget itself is given; it is an attack on character.

options.label: D
options.text: It focuses only on factual spending numbers.
options.rationale: No spending numbers are mentioned at all.

items.stem: An article claims, “Video games cause violence,” and supports this only by describing one teenager who played violent games and later got in a fight. Is this evidence sufficient to prove the claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: A single example is not enough to support a sweeping claim about video games in general.
explanation.tip: A broad claim needs broad evidence, not just one story.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because fights are a serious topic.
options.rationale: The seriousness of a topic does not make limited evidence sufficient.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because video games are not mentioned.
options.rationale: Video games are directly mentioned as part of the example.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because one isolated case cannot prove a broad claim about all video games.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because the teenager definitely played video games.
options.rationale: Confirming the teenager played games does not establish a broad cause-and-effect claim.

items.stem: A persuasive essay about ocean cleanup states, “According to a 2023 marine biology study, plastic debris in the Pacific has tripled since 2000.” Why might this source be considered credible?

explanation.whyCorrect: Naming a specific, dated study gives readers a way to verify the claim, which builds credibility.
explanation.tip: Specific, named sources are generally more credible than vague references.

options.label: A
options.text: It is credible because it uses the word “tripled.”
options.rationale: A dramatic-sounding word does not establish credibility; the cited study does.

options.label: B
options.text: It is credible because it appears in an essay.
options.rationale: Simply appearing in an essay does not make a claim credible without a named, specific source.

options.label: C
options.text: It is credible because the topic is about the ocean.
options.rationale: The topic itself does not make a source credible; its basis in named research does.

options.label: D
options.text: It cites a specific, dated scientific study rather than a vague or unnamed claim.

items.stem: A classmate argues, “If we allow students to use phones during lunch, soon they’ll want phones during tests, and eventually school will have no rules at all.” What flaw does this argument show?

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a slippery-slope fallacy: it assumes a small change must lead to a drastic, unproven outcome.
explanation.tip: Be suspicious of arguments claiming one step must lead to an extreme chain reaction.

options.label: A
options.text: It assumes one small change will lead to extreme, unlikely consequences.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses a specific statistic about phone use.
options.rationale: No statistic is used anywhere in this argument.

options.label: C
options.text: It correctly predicts a realistic and likely chain of events.
options.rationale: The chain of extreme outcomes described is unlikely and not supported by evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: It focuses only on lunchtime rules, ignoring other topics.
options.rationale: The argument actually expands far beyond lunchtime rules to extreme, unrelated outcomes.

items.stem: An article argues for mandatory recess and acknowledges, “Some worry recess cuts into learning time, but studies show short breaks actually improve focus afterward.” What does acknowledging this counterargument do for the essay?

explanation.whyCorrect: Addressing and responding to an opposing view shows the writer has considered multiple sides fairly.
explanation.tip: A strong argument often anticipates objections and explains why they do not outweigh the claim.

options.label: A
options.text: It weakens the essay by admitting the writer is wrong.
options.rationale: Addressing and refuting a concern is not the same as admitting the whole argument is wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the argument more credible by showing the writer considered an opposing view.

options.label: C
options.text: It is irrelevant because recess is unrelated to learning.
options.rationale: The counterargument is directly about how recess relates to learning time.

options.label: D
options.text: It contradicts the main claim entirely.
options.rationale: The writer refutes the concern, which supports rather than contradicts the main claim.

items.stem: A speech claims cafeteria food should be healthier, citing a nutritionist’s expert opinion, a survey of 500 students, and a comparison to three other districts’ menus. What makes this argument strong?

explanation.whyCorrect: Using expert opinion, a large survey, and real comparisons together builds a well-rounded, convincing case.
explanation.tip: Arguments that combine multiple kinds of credible evidence are generally stronger than those relying on one type.

options.label: A
options.text: It is strong because it is a speech, not an essay.
options.rationale: The format of a speech versus essay does not determine the strength of its evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: It is strong because it mentions the number three.
options.rationale: A specific number alone is not what makes the evidence strong.

options.label: C
options.text: It combines several different, credible types of evidence rather than relying on just one.

options.label: D
options.text: It is strong because it is about food.
options.rationale: The topic itself does not determine the strength of the argument’s evidence.

items.stem: A blog post argues against zoos, stating only, “Zoos are sad places.” Which revision would make this argument more convincing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific, factual evidence about animal welfare would support the claim far better than an unsupported feeling.
explanation.tip: Vague emotional claims become convincing arguments only once specific evidence is added.

options.label: A
options.text: Repeating the phrase “zoos are sad” three more times.
options.rationale: Repetition without new evidence does not make an argument stronger.

options.label: B
options.text: Making the font of the claim larger.
options.rationale: Formatting changes do not affect the logical strength of an argument.

options.label: C
options.text: Adding more exclamation points to the sentence.
options.rationale: Punctuation for emphasis does not provide evidence for the claim.

options.label: D
options.text: Adding specific evidence about animal stress levels or enclosure sizes compared to natural habitats

items.stem: An editorial argues for a four-day school week and provides this evidence: a pilot program in one district showed improved test scores. What additional information would help evaluate whether this evidence is sufficient?

explanation.whyCorrect: Checking for other possible causes helps determine whether the schedule change, and not something else, truly caused the improvement.
explanation.tip: Before accepting a cause-and-effect claim, consider whether other factors could explain the result.

options.label: A
options.text: Whether other factors in that district, besides the schedule, might explain the improved scores

options.label: B
options.text: The exact date the editorial was published
options.rationale: The publication date does not help evaluate whether the schedule itself caused the improvement.

options.label: C
options.text: The name of the newspaper that printed it.
options.rationale: The name of the newspaper does not determine whether the cause-and-effect claim is sound.

options.label: D
options.text: How many pages the editorial is.
options.rationale: Length has nothing to do with the strength of the evidence.

items.stem: A student writer claims minimum wage for teens should rise, using a single friend's unfairly low paycheck as the only evidence, while the article overall discusses national wage statistics elsewhere. Which revision would most improve the argument's evidence?

explanation.whyCorrect: Broader regional data would make the case far more representative than one friend's experience.
explanation.tip: When an argument relies on a single story, ask what wider data could replace or support it.

options.label: A
options.text: Repeating the claim at the end of every paragraph
options.rationale: Repeating the claim does not add any new supporting evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: Replacing or supplementing the anecdote with broader data on teen wages across the region

options.label: C
options.text: Mentioning the friend's favorite school subject
options.rationale: A detail unrelated to wages does not strengthen the argument's evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Describing the friend's paycheck in greater emotional detail
options.rationale: Adding more emotional detail to one story does not make the evidence more representative or sufficient.

items.stem: An article about youth sports argues early specialization in one sport increases injury risk, citing a sports-medicine association’s position statement and three peer-reviewed studies. A reader claims this argument is weak because “sports articles are always biased.” Is this a fair evaluation?

explanation.whyCorrect: Dismissing credible, cited evidence with a vague generalization is not a fair or specific critique.
explanation.tip: A fair evaluation points to a specific weakness in the evidence, not a blanket dismissal.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because all articles about sports are untrustworthy.
options.rationale: This is an unsupported generalization, not a specific flaw in this argument's evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the article never mentions any evidence.
options.rationale: The article clearly cites a position statement and three peer-reviewed studies.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because it dismisses solid medical evidence without pointing to any specific flaw in it.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because peer-reviewed studies are rarely accurate.
options.rationale: Peer-reviewed studies are generally considered reliable; this claim is unsupported.

items.stem: A flyer states, “Vote for the new playground proposal because it will make our park better.” What is missing from this argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: The flyer states an opinion but gives no specific reasons or evidence to support it.
explanation.tip: A claim without supporting reasons is an opinion, not yet a complete argument.

options.label: A
options.text: Any mention of voting.
options.rationale: The flyer directly mentions voting for the proposal.

options.label: B
options.text: A claim about the park.
options.rationale: The flyer does state a claim about improving the park.

options.label: C
options.text: A title for the flyer.
options.rationale: Whether the flyer has a title is not the issue with its argument.

options.label: D
options.text: Specific evidence or reasons explaining how the playground will improve the park

items.stem: An article about renewable energy states, “Solar panels are getting cheaper, and some cities report lower electricity bills after installing them.” Is this evidence relevant to an argument for using more solar energy?

explanation.whyCorrect: Falling cost and lower bills are directly relevant facts for deciding whether solar energy is worthwhile.
explanation.tip: Ask whether the evidence actually bears on the specific claim being made.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because cost and savings are directly related to whether solar energy is worth adopting.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because electricity bills have nothing to do with solar panels.
options.rationale: Electricity bills are directly affected by whether a city uses solar panels.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because cities are not involved in solar energy use.
options.rationale: Several cities installing solar panels are directly described in the evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, but only because the sentence is short.
options.rationale: The length of the sentence has nothing to do with whether the evidence is relevant.

items.stem: A letter about protecting coral reefs says, “Reefs are beautiful, so we should ban all boats near them.” What is the weakness in this reasoning?

explanation.whyCorrect: The reasoning jumps from an emotional appeal (beauty) straight to an extreme solution without real evidence connecting the two.
explanation.tip: A strong solution needs evidence linking the problem to that specific fix, not just an appeal to emotion.

options.label: A
options.text: It focuses only on economic costs.
options.rationale: No economic costs are discussed in this sentence at all.

options.label: B
options.text: A reef’s beauty alone does not logically prove that banning all boats is the right solution.

options.label: C
options.text: It fails to mention coral reefs.
options.rationale: Coral reefs are directly and repeatedly mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses a scientific study as evidence.
options.rationale: No scientific study is cited anywhere in this sentence.

items.stem: A writer argues against a new highway, stating, “Every single person I asked at the grocery store opposes it, so clearly the whole town is against it.” What is the flaw here?

explanation.whyCorrect: A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion about a whole town from a very small, biased sample.
explanation.tip: A small sample from one location cannot represent an entire population's views.

options.label: A
options.text: It focuses only on cost estimates.
options.rationale: No cost estimates are mentioned in this sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: It fails to mention the highway at all.
options.rationale: The highway is directly and clearly the subject of the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: A small, unrepresentative group cannot reliably stand for the opinion of an entire town.

options.label: D
options.text: It relies on a government report.
options.rationale: No government report or similar formal source is mentioned.

items.stem: An op-ed about space exploration funding cites NASA’s publicly released budget reports and interviews with three astrophysicists. Compared to an anonymous online comment making the same claim, why would this evidence be considered more trustworthy?

explanation.whyCorrect: Named experts and official reports can be checked and verified, unlike an anonymous, unsupported comment.
explanation.tip: Evidence from identifiable, qualified sources is generally more trustworthy than anonymous claims.

options.label: A
options.text: It is more trustworthy because it is longer.
options.rationale: Length alone does not determine how trustworthy a source is.

options.label: B
options.text: It is more trustworthy because it discusses space.
options.rationale: The topic itself does not make a source more or less trustworthy.

options.label: C
options.text: It is more trustworthy because it was published online.
options.rationale: Being published online, like the anonymous comment, does not by itself establish trustworthiness.

options.label: D
options.text: It comes from named, verifiable sources with relevant expertise.

items.stem: An argument for self-driving cars states, “Self-driving cars will eliminate all car accidents forever.” What is problematic about this claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: Claiming a technology will eliminate something “forever” and completely is an unsupported, extreme overstatement.
explanation.tip: Be cautious of arguments using words like “always,” “never,” or “forever” without strong evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: It makes an absolute, overly confident prediction that no technology could realistically guarantee.

options.label: B
options.text: It fails to mention cars at all.
options.rationale: Cars, specifically self-driving cars, are the entire subject of the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: It cites too many statistics.
options.rationale: No statistics are cited in this claim at all.

options.label: D
options.text: It focuses only on pedestrian safety.
options.rationale: Pedestrian safety is not specifically mentioned in this general claim.

items.stem: An article supports remote learning by describing one student who improved grades while learning from home, without mentioning any other students' experiences. Why might this evidence be considered one-sided?

explanation.whyCorrect: Presenting only a positive example while ignoring students who struggled gives an incomplete, biased picture.
explanation.tip: A balanced argument should acknowledge both successes and struggles, not just one side.

options.label: A
options.text: It is one-sided because the student is named.
options.rationale: Whether the student is named or not does not create one-sidedness.

options.label: B
options.text: It presents only a success story without acknowledging students who may have struggled with remote learning.

options.label: C
options.text: It is one-sided because it mentions grades.
options.rationale: Mentioning grades is directly relevant to evaluating the effectiveness of remote learning.

options.label: D
options.text: It is one-sided because it is about school.
options.rationale: The subject of school itself does not create a one-sided argument.

items.stem: An article arguing for later school start times cites a sleep-medicine association’s guidelines and a three-year study across twelve school districts. A critic claims the argument is weak because it is “too long.” Is this a fair critique?

explanation.whyCorrect: A fair critique addresses the quality or relevance of evidence, not simply how long the argument is.
explanation.tip: Length is not a valid reason to dismiss an argument; focus on the evidence itself.

options.label: A
options.text: No, because the article never actually cites any evidence.
options.rationale: The article clearly cites both expert guidelines and a multi-year, multi-district study.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because twelve districts is too small a number to matter.
options.rationale: Twelve districts over three years is actually a fairly substantial and broad sample.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because length does not determine whether evidence is strong or relevant.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because longer arguments are always less convincing.
options.rationale: Length alone does not make an argument weaker or stronger; the quality of evidence does.

items.stem: A proposal to add a school garden includes a farmer’s expert advice, a cost estimate from the district budget office, and results from three similar school gardens elsewhere. What makes this combination of evidence effective?

explanation.whyCorrect: Combining expert advice, financial facts, and real outcomes addresses the proposal from multiple important angles.
explanation.tip: Strong proposals often combine expert opinion, practical cost data, and real examples.

options.label: A
options.text: It is effective only because it was written for school.
options.rationale: The context of being written for school does not determine the strength of the evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: It is effective only because it mentions a garden.
options.rationale: Simply naming the topic does not make the combination of evidence effective.

options.label: C
options.text: It is effective only because three numbers are used.
options.rationale: The number of examples alone is not what makes the evidence effective; its variety and credibility do.

options.label: D
options.text: It draws on expert knowledge, financial reality, and real-world results together.

items.stem: A speaker argues, “Anyone who disagrees with building the new stadium clearly doesn’t care about our town’s future.” Why is this reasoning flawed, even if the speaker also provides some economic data later?

explanation.whyCorrect: This statement unfairly dismisses valid objections by implying only one bad motive explains disagreement.
explanation.tip: Watch for arguments that insult opposing views instead of responding to their actual reasons.

options.label: A
options.text: It unfairly implies that any disagreement must come from not caring, ignoring other valid reasons someone might object.

options.label: B
options.text: It is flawed because it is addressed to the town.
options.rationale: Addressing the town as the audience is not a flaw in the reasoning.

options.label: C
options.text: It is flawed because it mentions a stadium.
options.rationale: Mentioning the subject of the debate is necessary and not itself a flaw.

options.label: D
options.text: It is flawed because it includes economic data.
options.rationale: Including economic data elsewhere is not the flaw being identified here.

items.stem: An article claims a town’s new recycling program failed because “litter on Main Street increased the same month the program began.” A classmate points out that a large festival also happened that month. How does this affect the article’s argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: Identifying another possible cause, like the festival, shows the original argument may have overlooked a more likely explanation.
explanation.tip: Before accepting a single cause, check whether another event could explain the same result.

options.label: A
options.text: It strengthens the article’s claim about the program.
options.rationale: An alternative explanation would weaken, not strengthen, the original cause-and-effect claim.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows another likely cause exists, weakening the claim that the recycling program caused the increase.

options.label: C
options.text: It proves the recycling program is working perfectly.
options.rationale: Nothing in this situation proves the program is working; it only questions the stated cause of the litter.

options.label: D
options.text: It has no effect, because festivals never produce litter.
options.rationale: Festivals commonly generate significant litter, so this ignores a likely cause.

items.stem: A reviewer argues a new library policy is bad, writing only, “I don’t like change.” What is the main problem with this argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: Simply disliking change says nothing specific about why the policy itself is actually harmful.
explanation.tip: A real argument needs reasons tied to the specific issue, not just a general preference.

options.label: A
options.text: It includes too much data about the library.
options.rationale: No data about the library is included at all.

options.label: B
options.text: It fails to state an opinion.
options.rationale: The sentence clearly states the reviewer's personal opinion.

options.label: C
options.text: It gives a personal preference instead of a reason connected to the actual policy.

options.label: D
options.text: It focuses only on other libraries.
options.rationale: No other libraries are mentioned in this statement.

items.stem: An essay favoring community service requirements cites a single star student who loved volunteering, then concludes, “So every student will love community service.” What is the flaw in this conclusion?

explanation.whyCorrect: One enthusiastic student's experience cannot reliably predict how an entire student body will react.
explanation.tip: A conclusion about “everyone” needs evidence from many people, not just one example.

options.label: A
options.text: It uses a large, representative survey.
options.rationale: No survey of any kind, large or small, is used; only one student's experience is described.

options.label: B
options.text: It focuses only on students who dislike volunteering.
options.rationale: The essay actually focuses only on a student who loved volunteering, not one who disliked it.

options.label: C
options.text: It fails to mention community service.
options.rationale: Community service is directly and repeatedly the subject of the essay.

options.label: D
options.text: It generalizes one enthusiastic student's experience to predict how every student will feel.

items.stem: An article defending a longer lunch period states, “Students who eat lunch for 45 minutes report feeling less rushed and more focused in afternoon classes, according to a survey of 300 students.” Is this evidence relevant and sufficient?

explanation.whyCorrect: A sizable survey directly linking lunch length to focus is both relevant and reasonably strong evidence.
explanation.tip: Check both whether evidence connects to the claim and whether it comes from a reasonably large, credible source.

options.label: A
options.text: It is relevant and reasonably sufficient, since it directly connects lunch length to a measurable outcome across many students.

options.label: B
options.text: It is relevant but not sufficient, because surveys are never useful evidence.
options.rationale: Surveys of a meaningful size are a legitimate and commonly used form of evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: It is irrelevant, because lunch length has nothing to do with focus.
options.rationale: The survey directly connects lunch length to a measurable change in focus.

options.label: D
options.text: It is sufficient only because the number 300 is mentioned.
options.rationale: The number alone does not make evidence sufficient; its clear connection to the claim does.

items.stem: A speaker claims, “Everyone knows that students who play sports get worse grades,” without citing any source. What is the main issue with this argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: Saying “everyone knows” something does not make it true; it simply avoids providing real evidence.
explanation.tip: A claim is not proven just because it is stated as common knowledge.

options.label: A
options.text: It fails to mention sports at all.
options.rationale: Sports are directly and repeatedly the topic of this statement.

options.label: B
options.text: It presents an unsupported generalization as if it were an established fact.

options.label: C
options.text: It focuses only on grades in one specific class.
options.rationale: The statement is about grades in general, not one specific class.

options.label: D
options.text: It cites a peer-reviewed study.
options.rationale: No study or source of any kind is cited in this statement.

items.stem: An argument for banning junk-food ads aimed at children states, “Removing these ads will instantly make every child healthy.” What makes this claim weak?

explanation.whyCorrect: Health depends on many factors besides advertising, so claiming an “instant” and total fix is an overstatement.
explanation.tip: Watch for claims that promise a single simple fix will solve a complicated problem entirely.

options.label: A
options.text: It fails to mention children.
options.rationale: Children are directly and repeatedly mentioned as the subject.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses a specific, cited statistic.
options.rationale: No specific statistic is cited in this particular claim.

options.label: C
options.text: It overstates what removing ads could realistically achieve, ignoring other factors in children's health.

options.label: D
options.text: It focuses only on advertising techniques.
options.rationale: The claim is about the outcome of banning ads, not a description of advertising techniques.

items.stem: An editorial favoring solar panels on school roofs discusses a pilot program’s energy savings, addresses the concern about installation cost by citing a ten-year payback estimate, and compares outcomes to two similar schools. What makes this a strong argument overall?

explanation.whyCorrect: Combining evidence, a response to objections, and real comparisons builds a well-rounded, convincing argument.
explanation.tip: The strongest arguments present evidence, address objections, and offer comparable real examples.

options.label: A
options.text: It is strong only because panels are mentioned twice.
options.rationale: Simply repeating a term does not make an argument well-supported.

options.label: B
options.text: It is strong only because it is about schools.
options.rationale: The subject itself does not determine the strength of the argument's reasoning.

options.label: C
options.text: It is strong only because it mentions ten years.
options.rationale: A single number alone is not what makes the overall argument strong.

options.label: D
options.text: It presents evidence, directly responds to a likely objection, and provides comparable real-world examples.

items.stem: A town-hall speaker argues against a curfew for teens, stating, “Curfews insult every responsible teenager in this town.” What logical problem does this statement show?

explanation.whyCorrect: The statement assumes a strong emotional reaction without any evidence that teens in general actually feel insulted.
explanation.tip: An emotional assumption is not the same as evidence that something is actually true.

options.label: A
options.text: It assumes all responsible teens would be personally insulted, without evidence that this is actually true.

options.label: B
options.text: It fails to mention teenagers.
options.rationale: Teenagers are directly the subject of this statement.

options.label: C
options.text: It focuses only on curfews for adults.
options.rationale: The statement is specifically about a curfew for teens, not adults.

options.label: D
options.text: It cites a city council report.
options.rationale: No city council report or similar source is cited.

items.stem: An article about lowering the voting age cites political-science research showing 16-year-olds in test programs voted at similar informed rates as adults. How does this evidence support the argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific research comparing informed voting rates directly supports the claim about younger teens' readiness to vote.
explanation.tip: Look for evidence that directly measures the exact outcome the claim is about.

options.label: A
options.text: It does not support the argument at all.
options.rationale: The research directly addresses and supports the claim about younger voters' informed participation.

options.label: B
options.text: It provides specific, research-based data suggesting younger teens can vote responsibly.

options.label: C
options.text: It supports the argument only because it is from an article.
options.rationale: Simply appearing in an article does not establish the strength of evidence.

options.label: D
options.text: It supports the argument only because it mentions an age.
options.rationale: A number alone does not make evidence supportive; its research basis and relevance do.

items.stem: An op-ed opposing a proposed amusement park states, “The one time I visited a similar park, the lines were long, so this park will definitely fail.” What is the flaw in this reasoning?

explanation.whyCorrect: One unrelated experience at a different park is not strong evidence for predicting this new park's success or failure.
explanation.tip: A single, unrelated personal experience is weak evidence for predicting an unrelated future outcome.

options.label: A
options.text: It fails to mention an amusement park.
options.rationale: An amusement park is clearly and repeatedly the subject of the statement.

options.label: B
options.text: It focuses only on ticket prices.
options.rationale: Ticket prices are not mentioned anywhere in this statement.

options.label: C
options.text: It bases a broad prediction about a different, new park on a single unrelated past experience.

options.label: D
options.text: It cites a formal business analysis.
options.rationale: No formal business analysis or similar study is cited.

items.stem: An essay in favor of grading on a curve addresses the objection that curving is “unfair to top students” by explaining that curves are recalculated so top scores are never lowered, only middle and low scores adjusted upward. Does this response adequately address the concern?

explanation.whyCorrect: Explaining exactly how the method works directly answers the specific fairness objection raised.
explanation.tip: A strong rebuttal explains precisely why a specific objection does not hold up, not just that the writer disagrees.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, but only because it uses the word “fair.”
options.rationale: Using a word is not what makes a response adequate; its direct explanation does.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because it ignores the concern completely.
options.rationale: The response directly engages with and explains the specific concern raised.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because curves are always unfair by definition.
options.rationale: This is an unsupported assertion, not a response to the specific explanation given.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because it directly explains why the specific fairness concern raised does not actually apply.

items.stem: A student argues that mandatory summer homework improves fall test scores, citing a study from one small private school with unusually small class sizes. A classmate says the evidence is “fine because it’s a real study.” Is this classmate’s evaluation complete?

explanation.whyCorrect: A study's being real does not guarantee its findings apply broadly; unusual conditions can limit how general the results are.
explanation.tip: Consider whether a study’s specific conditions might limit how well its findings apply to other situations.

options.label: A
options.text: No, because it overlooks whether the small school’s unique conditions might limit how well the results apply elsewhere.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because any real study is automatically sufficient evidence.
options.rationale: Being a real study does not guarantee the results generalize to very different schools.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because private schools are always representative of all schools.
options.rationale: Private schools, especially with unusual class sizes, are not necessarily representative of schools generally.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because the study does not mention test scores.
options.rationale: The study is specifically about homework's effect on test scores.

items.stem: An argument for building a new skate park states, “A few teens wrote supportive letters, so clearly the whole community wants this.” A second argument for the same park cites a city survey of 2,000 residents showing 68% support. How do these two pieces of evidence compare in strength?

explanation.whyCorrect: A large, broad survey represents the community far better than a handful of individual letters.
explanation.tip: When comparing evidence, consider how well each piece represents the whole group being discussed.

options.label: A
options.text: Neither piece of evidence is relevant to the skate park.
options.rationale: Both pieces of evidence are directly about support for the skate park.

options.label: B
options.text: The survey of 2,000 residents is far stronger evidence of community-wide support than a few letters.

options.label: C
options.text: The letters are stronger because they are personal and emotional.
options.rationale: Emotional appeal does not make evidence more reliable than a large, representative survey.

options.label: D
options.text: Both pieces of evidence are equally strong.
options.rationale: A small number of letters and a large, representative survey are not equally strong evidence.

items.stem: An investigative report argues a factory’s new filter reduced river pollution, citing water-quality data from upstream and downstream testing stations over eighteen months, expert analysis from an environmental engineer, and acknowledgment that a nearby farm’s runoff could also affect results. How does acknowledging the farm’s runoff affect the overall strength of this argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: Honestly acknowledging another possible cause, while still presenting strong supporting data, makes an argument more credible, not less.
explanation.tip: A thorough argument considers alternative explanations rather than ignoring them.

options.label: A
options.text: It proves the filter had no effect on pollution at all.
options.rationale: The data and expert analysis still support the filter's effect; acknowledging another factor does not erase that evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: It is irrelevant because farms have nothing to do with rivers.
options.rationale: Farm runoff is a well-known and directly relevant source of river pollution.

options.label: C
options.text: It strengthens the argument’s credibility by showing the writer considered and weighed another possible cause.

options.label: D
options.text: It completely destroys the argument’s claim about the filter.
options.rationale: Acknowledging another factor does not destroy the claim; it shows careful, honest consideration of alternatives.

items.stem: Two articles both argue for stricter coral reef protections. Article A cites a single tour guide’s opinion that “tourists are ruining the reefs.” Article B cites peer-reviewed marine biology data on coral bleaching rates near high-traffic tourist sites over ten years. Which argument provides stronger support for action, and why?

explanation.whyCorrect: Peer-reviewed, long-term data is far more reliable and representative than a single person’s personal opinion.
explanation.tip: When comparing arguments, weigh systematic data more heavily than a single, unverified opinion.

options.label: A
options.text: Both articles are equally strong since they reach the same conclusion.
options.rationale: Reaching the same conclusion does not mean the evidence supporting each argument is equally strong.

options.label: B
options.text: Article A, because tour guides see the reefs most often.
options.rationale: Frequent observation does not substitute for systematic, long-term scientific data.

options.label: C
options.text: Article A, because opinions are always more persuasive than data.
options.rationale: Opinions are generally considered less reliable than long-term, peer-reviewed data.

options.label: D
options.text: Article B, because long-term, peer-reviewed data provides far more reliable evidence than one person’s opinion.

items.stem: True or false style check turned question: does paragraph 2 of “Should Homework Be Optional?” tell a story about one specific student’s day, or does it use research to respond to a claim?

explanation.whyCorrect: Paragraph 2 states a common claim and then counters it with a review of research studies.
explanation.tip: In argument paragraphs, check whether a claim is being tested against evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: It uses research evidence to respond to a claim — it counters the idea that homework improves scores with findings from multiple studies.

options.label: B
options.text: It describes what a typical homework assignment looks like.
options.rationale: The paragraph evaluates a claim with research, not describe assignment contents.

options.label: C
options.text: It lists homework rules from several different countries.
options.rationale: No countries or their homework rules are compared in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: It tells a story about one specific student’s homework routine.
options.rationale: No single student’s personal routine is described anywhere in paragraph 2.

items.stem: True or false: paragraph 3 of “Should Homework Be Optional?” is organized as a chronological account of a single school year.

explanation.whyCorrect: Paragraph 3 explains what an optional-homework system would look like in practice, not a year-by-year account.
explanation.tip: Check what a paragraph is actually doing, not just its general topic.

items.stem: Which structure describes paragraph 5 of “Should Homework Be Optional?” (the one about stress and sleep) on its own?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph links one cause (heavy mandatory homework) to two effects (stress and poor sleep).
explanation.tip: Look for words like “linked to” that connect a cause to its effects.

options.label: A
options.text: problem and solution — it proposes a specific fix for student stress
options.rationale: This paragraph names a cost of mandatory homework; the proposed fix appears earlier, in paragraph 3.

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect — heavy mandatory homework is shown to cause higher stress and less sleep in students

options.label: C
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares two different named schools’ homework policies
options.rationale: No two specific named schools are compared anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it lists stress levels recorded each month of the school year
options.rationale: No month-by-month data or timeline is given in this paragraph.

items.stem: How does the author organize paragraph 4 of “Should Homework Be Optional?”, the one addressing the worry about struggling students falling behind?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph names a worry (falling behind), then offers a new, specific reason why flexible homework could actually help.
explanation.tip: A strong rebuttal paragraph often follows a worry with a fresh reason, not a repeated claim.

options.label: A
options.text: It simply restates the article’s main claim three times in a row.
options.rationale: The paragraph introduces a specific counterargument and a new reason, not a repeated restatement.

options.label: B
options.text: It compares struggling students in two different grade levels.
options.rationale: No specific grade levels are compared against each other in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: It raises a counterargument and then answers it with a new reason, rather than simply repeating the original claim.

options.label: D
options.text: It lists the exact daily schedule of a struggling student.
options.rationale: No daily schedule for any student is described in this paragraph.

items.stem: Put these paragraph functions from “Should Homework Be Optional?” in the order they appear in the text.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article builds step by step: claim, evidence against mandatory homework, a practical explanation, a rebuttal, a wellbeing cost, and a closing restatement.
explanation.tip: Identify the JOB each paragraph does, then put those jobs in the order they appear.

sequence: Introduce the issue and state the author’s claim that homework should be optional
Counter the claim that mandatory homework improves achievement, using research
Explain what an optional-homework system would actually look like in practice
Answer the worry that struggling students would fall behind
Link heavy mandatory homework to stress and poor sleep
Restate that flexible homework would likely help both wellbeing and learning

items.stem: Match each paragraph’s main structural job in “Should Homework Be Optional?” with its paragraph number.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each numbered paragraph plays a specific structural role in building the overall argument.
explanation.tip: Identify the JOB each paragraph does within the text’s overall structure.

pairs.right: introduces the issue and states the author’s claim
counters the achievement claim using research evidence
raises and answers the falling-behind counterargument
restates the claim to close the argument

items.stem: What is paragraph 1 of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure” primarily organized to do?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists several distinct examples of why reefs matter, one after another.
explanation.tip: A paragraph that names several separate examples about one topic is usually a description structure.

options.label: A
options.text: list the exact steps scientists use to study a reef
options.rationale: No research steps or scientific procedures are described in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: explain a single cause-and-effect chain about reef damage
options.rationale: Paragraph 1 lists reasons reefs matter; the cause-and-effect chain about damage appears later, in paragraph 3.

options.label: C
options.text: compare two different oceans’ reef populations
options.rationale: No second ocean is named or compared anywhere in paragraph 1.

options.label: D
options.text: describe several specific ways reefs matter to ocean life, using examples such as fish shelter, sea turtle food and storm protection

items.stem: True or false: paragraph 4 of “Coral Reefs Under Pressure” describes two different solutions scientists are trying to help reefs recover.

explanation.whyCorrect: Paragraph 4 names both growing corals in nurseries and breeding heat-tolerant corals as two separate responses.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph lists more than one fix for the same problem, it is still organized as problem-and-solution.

items.stem: Which structure best describes paragraph 3 of “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?”, the paragraph about saving money?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph states supporters’ money-saving claim and then responds with specific cost figures.
explanation.tip: In argumentative texts, check whether a paragraph tests a claim with evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: claim and evidence — it states the money-saving claim, then presents cost data that undercuts it

options.label: B
options.text: description only — it simply lists what a school budget contains
options.rationale: The paragraph tests a specific claim with evidence, rather than just listing budget categories.

options.label: C
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares bus costs in two different districts
options.rationale: No two specific districts’ bus costs are directly compared against each other.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it lists a school’s budget month by month
options.rationale: No month-by-month budget figures are given in this paragraph.

items.stem: True or false: the article as a whole, “Should Schools Switch to a Four-Day Week?”, uses chronological order, describing how a single school week changes hour by hour.

explanation.whyCorrect: The article is organized around testing supporters’ separate claims with evidence, not around an hour-by-hour account of one week.
explanation.tip: Do not assume a structure just from a text’s topic — check how the paragraphs actually connect.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Houseplants kept away from windows often grow pale and droopy. Without enough sunlight, a plant cannot make the food it needs, so its leaves turn yellow and its stems grow weak.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph explains that one condition (low light) produces a specific effect (weak, pale growth).
explanation.tip: Signal words like “so” often point to cause and effect.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares plants in sunlight to plants without sunlight
options.rationale: Only plants without enough light are described; no second case is directly compared.

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect — a lack of sunlight causes the plant’s leaves and stems to weaken

options.label: C
options.text: problem and solution — it proposes a fix for pale houseplants
options.rationale: No fix or solution for the pale houseplants is offered anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it lists what happens to a plant day by day
options.rationale: No specific days or a day-by-day timeline are given in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “The fennec fox has several features suited to desert life. Its huge ears release body heat. Thick fur on its paws protects against hot sand. Its kidneys are built to need very little water.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists separate traits of one animal rather than connecting them by cause, time or comparison.
explanation.tip: A paragraph listing several traits about one subject is usually a description structure.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares the fox to another desert animal
options.rationale: Only the fennec fox is discussed; no second animal is named for comparison.

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect — each feature causes the next feature to develop
options.rationale: The features are not shown causing one another to develop; each is simply listed.

options.label: C
options.text: description — it lists several separate features that help the fox survive the desert

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — the features are listed in the order the fox develops them
options.rationale: No growth timeline for the fox’s features is given anywhere in the paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “First, workers collect used paper and soak it in water until it breaks apart into pulp. Next, the pulp is pressed flat into thin sheets. Finally, the sheets are dried and rolled onto large spools.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Words like “first,” “next” and “finally” signal a step-by-step, time-ordered process.
explanation.tip: Order words (first, next, then, finally) are the clearest clue to chronological structure.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares old paper to new paper
options.rationale: No comparison between old and new paper is made anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: description — it simply describes what a paper mill looks like
options.rationale: The paragraph describes a process in order, not the appearance of a building.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — each step is a cause that explains why paper is recycled
options.rationale: No cause for WHY paper is recycled is explained; the paragraph only lists the steps.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it describes the steps of recycling paper in the order they happen

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Bicycles have two wheels and are pedaled by the rider’s legs. Electric scooters also have wheels, but a small motor powers them instead of leg muscles. Both are used for short trips around a neighborhood.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph points out a shared feature (wheels, short trips) and a key difference (legs versus motor).
explanation.tip: Watch for words like “also” and “but” that signal similarities and differences.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it shows how bicycles and scooters are alike and different

options.label: B
options.text: chronological order — it tells the history of how scooters were invented
options.rationale: No invention history or dates for scooters are given in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: problem and solution — it explains a transportation problem and a fix
options.rationale: No transportation problem or fix is presented anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: cause and effect — pedaling causes the scooter’s motor to run
options.rationale: The scooter is described as motor-powered, not powered by pedaling, so there is no such cause-effect link.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Students at Rawda Middle School complained that the library was too noisy to study in during lunch. The librarian set up a separate quiet room with a sign-in sheet and moved group projects to the cafeteria instead. Within a week, students reported the library felt calm enough to focus.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A specific problem (noise) is named, followed by the concrete actions taken to solve it.
explanation.tip: Look for a named problem followed by a fix — that pattern signals problem and solution.

options.label: A
options.text: description — it only describes what the library building looks like
options.rationale: No physical description of the building is given anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: problem and solution — it describes a noise problem and the specific steps taken to fix it

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order — it lists the school’s full daily schedule
options.rationale: No full daily schedule for the school is described in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares the library to the cafeteria
options.rationale: The cafeteria is mentioned only as part of the fix, not compared feature by feature to the library.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “When more cars idle in traffic, engines burn fuel without actually moving anywhere. This wasted fuel releases extra exhaust into the air, and in cities with heavy traffic jams, air quality often gets worse during rush hour.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: One condition (idling traffic) leads directly to a result (worse air quality).
explanation.tip: Ask: does one event make another event happen? That is cause and effect.

options.label: A
options.text: chronological order — it lists what happens during each hour of a commute
options.rationale: No specific hour-by-hour timeline of a commute is given in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares traffic in two different cities
options.rationale: No second city’s traffic is named or compared against the first.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — idling cars in traffic cause more exhaust, which worsens air quality

options.label: D
options.text: description — it simply describes what a traffic jam looks like
options.rationale: The paragraph explains a cause-and-result relationship, not the appearance of traffic.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Clouds come in several basic shapes. Cumulus clouds look like puffy cotton balls. Stratus clouds spread out in flat, gray sheets. Cirrus clouds form thin, feathery streaks high in the sky.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph simply lists separate categories and their features, without connecting them by cause, time or problem.
explanation.tip: A paragraph naming several types or categories, one after another, usually uses a description structure.

options.label: A
options.text: problem and solution — it explains a weather problem clouds create
options.rationale: No problem related to clouds is raised in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect — each cloud type causes the next type to form
options.rationale: No causal chain between the cloud types is described anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order — it describes clouds in the order they appear each day
options.rationale: No daily order for when each cloud type appears is given in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: description — it lists different types of clouds and describes what each one looks like

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Keeping savings in a jar at home means the money is easy to reach anytime, but it earns nothing extra over time. Putting the same money in a savings account makes it slightly harder to access quickly, but the bank adds a small amount of interest every year.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph sets two options side by side and names an advantage and disadvantage of each.
explanation.tip: Look for “but” paired with matching features — that is comparison.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it weighs the trade-offs of keeping money in a jar versus a bank account

options.label: B
options.text: chronological order — it explains the history of how banks were invented
options.rationale: No invention history or dates for banks are given in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: problem and solution — it identifies one single correct way to save money
options.rationale: The paragraph weighs trade-offs between two options, rather than solving one problem with one fix.

options.label: D
options.text: cause and effect — saving in a jar causes people to open a bank account
options.rationale: No causal link between the two storage methods is stated in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “When a hillside is cleared of trees, there are no longer any roots to hold the soil in place. Heavy rain then washes the loose topsoil downhill, leaving the land harder for new plants to grow in. Over time, the bare hillside can become almost impossible to farm.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each sentence shows one event producing the next: no trees, then loose soil, then erosion, then unfarmable land.
explanation.tip: When one effect becomes the cause of the next effect, that is a cause-and-effect chain.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares hillsides with trees to hillsides without rain
options.rationale: Rainfall amount is not being compared between two hillsides; only one chain of events is described.

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect — clearing trees sets off a chain of results, from loose soil to erosion to land that is hard to farm

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order — it lists the exact dates when hillsides were cleared
options.rationale: No dates or a specific calendar timeline are given in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: description — it only describes what a bare hillside looks like
options.rationale: The paragraph explains a chain of results, not just the hillside’s appearance.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Many students who rode bikes to Al-Nour School left them leaning against the fence, where they often got knocked over or blocked the sidewalk. The student council proposed installing numbered bike racks near the main gate, and the school agreed to install twenty of them before the new term began.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A specific problem (poorly parked bikes) is followed by a concrete plan that solves it.
explanation.tip: Problem-and-solution paragraphs usually name a difficulty, then describe exactly what fixed it.

options.label: A
options.text: cause and effect — leaning bikes against the fence caused the fence to break
options.rationale: No damage to the fence is mentioned anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares bike racks at two different schools
options.rationale: Only one school’s bike-parking situation is discussed in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: problem and solution — it names a bike-parking problem and the specific solution the council proposed and the school carried out

options.label: D
options.text: description — it only describes what the bikes looked like
options.rationale: No physical description of the bikes themselves is given in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “In the 1950s, farmers in Deir al-Wadi sold vegetables from the backs of trucks parked along the main road.
