By the 1980s, the town had built a covered market with permanent stalls. Today, the same market also hosts a weekend crafts fair alongside the vegetable sellers.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific time markers (1950s, 1980s, today) trace the market’s development across decades.
explanation.tip: Dates or decades lined up in order are a strong signal of chronological structure.

options.label: A
options.text: problem and solution — it describes a problem with the covered market
options.rationale: No problem with the covered market is raised anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: description — it only describes what the market stalls look like
options.rationale: The paragraph traces change over time, not just the stalls’ appearance.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — the crafts fair caused the vegetable sellers to leave
options.rationale: The vegetable sellers are still present today alongside the crafts fair, so nothing shows them leaving.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it traces how the town’s market changed from the 1950s to today

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A violin has four main parts. The body is a hollow wooden box that makes the sound louder. The neck holds the fingerboard where a player presses the strings. The bridge lifts the strings above the body. The scroll at the top holds the tuning pegs.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each sentence introduces one labeled part and what it does, without connecting them by time or cause.
explanation.tip: A list of labeled parts, each explained separately, is a description structure.

options.label: A
options.text: description — it names and explains each main part of a violin, one at a time

options.label: B
options.text: chronological order — it explains the steps for building a violin over time
options.rationale: No construction process or build-time sequence is described in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — the bridge causes the scroll to hold the tuning pegs
options.rationale: These parts are not linked by cause and effect anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares a violin to another instrument
options.rationale: No second instrument is mentioned for comparison in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Basketball requires a hoop at a fixed height and rewards players who can dribble while running. Volleyball, on the other hand, is played over a net and depends on quick reactions rather than ball-handling while moving. Both games, however, reward teamwork and communication between teammates on the move.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph sets the two sports side by side, naming a difference for each and then a shared trait.
explanation.tip: Phrases like “on the other hand” and “both … however” are strong compare-and-contrast signals.

options.label: A
options.text: chronological order — it explains the history of each sport
options.rationale: No historical background or dates for either sport are given in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast — it points out key differences between basketball and volleyball while noting one shared quality

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — dribbling in basketball causes volleyball players to react quickly
options.rationale: The two sports are not linked to each other by cause and effect anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: problem and solution — it solves a disagreement about which sport is better
options.rationale: No disagreement or solution about which sport is better is presented in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “During deep sleep, the brain strengthens connections between neurons that were active while a person was learning something new that day. Students who sleep fewer than six hours tend to remember less of what they studied the day before, because this strengthening process is cut short. Over weeks of poor sleep, this effect can add up to noticeably weaker test performance.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph traces a chain: less sleep interrupts a brain process, which lowers memory, which lowers test scores.
explanation.tip: When a result keeps leading to a further result, trace the whole chain of causes and effects.

options.label: A
options.text: description — it only describes what happens physically inside the brain during sleep
options.rationale: The paragraph traces a chain of results from poor sleep, not just brain anatomy.

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares students who sleep six hours to students who sleep eight hours
options.rationale: Only one amount, fewer than six hours, is actually discussed in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — too little sleep interrupts memory strengthening, which weakens memory and eventually test performance

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it lists the stages of a person’s sleep cycle in order
options.rationale: No stage-by-stage account of a sleep cycle is described in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Fishing fleets off one coastal town had been catching so many young sardines that the overall sardine population began shrinking every year. Marine officials introduced a seasonal catch limit and required nets with wider holes so young fish could escape. Within three years, sardine numbers in the area had begun to recover.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A clear problem (shrinking sardine population) is followed by the specific actions that reversed it.
explanation.tip: Look for a result (recovery, improvement) that follows directly after a described fix.

options.label: A
options.text: description — it only describes what a fishing net looks like
options.rationale: The net is mentioned only as part of the solution, not described in detail.

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares sardine fishing to tuna fishing
options.rationale: No other fish or fishing method is named for comparison in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order — it lists every year’s exact catch numbers
options.rationale: No year-by-year catch data is listed anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: problem and solution — it names a shrinking-fish-population problem and the specific rules that helped fix it

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “In 1876, the first working telephone could only connect two specific points joined by a single wire. By the 1890s, cities had built switchboards so that any customer’s call could be connected to any other customer in town. By the mid-1900s, long-distance cables let callers reach other cities and even other countries.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Specific years (1876, 1890s, mid-1900s) mark each stage of the network’s growth in order.
explanation.tip: A string of dates or eras, each building on the last, signals chronological structure.

options.label: A
options.text: chronological order — it traces how telephone networks expanded from 1876 through the mid-1900s

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares telephones to telegraphs
options.rationale: Telegraphs are never mentioned anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — switchboards caused the invention of the telephone
options.rationale: The telephone already existed before switchboards in this timeline, so this cause-effect order is reversed.

options.label: D
options.text: problem and solution — it describes one single problem with modern phones
options.rationale: No modern-day problem with phones is raised in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A rural village had no streetlights, so people avoided walking after dark because of poor visibility. The village council installed solar-powered lamps along the main road, which charge during the day and turn on automatically at dusk. Since the lamps needed no wiring to the village's main power grid, installation took only two weeks. Residents now report walking after dark far more often than before.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A specific problem (unsafe darkness) is followed by a specific, quickly installed fix (solar lamps) and a result (more walking after dark).
explanation.tip: Look for a named problem followed by an action that fixes it.

options.label: A
options.text: cause and effect only, with no solution described
options.rationale: The paragraph explicitly describes the lamps being installed as a specific fix, not just a cause-and-effect description without any solution.

options.label: B
options.text: problem and solution — it names a safety problem from the dark and explains how solar lamps solved it quickly

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order — it lists the full history of solar lamp technology
options.rationale: No invention history or technology timeline for solar lamps is described in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares solar lamps to lamps connected to the power grid
options.rationale: No grid-connected lamps are actually installed or compared feature by feature; the grid is mentioned only as something avoided.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A few years after zebra mussels were accidentally introduced to a freshwater lake, fishers noticed the water had become unusually clear. The mussels filter huge amounts of plankton from the water as they feed, and plankton is the main food source for many small native fish. As plankton grew scarce, several native fish species that once thrived in the lake began to decline sharply.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The clearer water, the mussels’ feeding, the shrinking plankton and the declining fish form one connected chain of causes and effects.
explanation.tip: In nature articles, trace how one species’ feeding habit can ripple through to affect other species.

options.label: A
options.text: description — it only describes what zebra mussels look like
options.rationale: The paragraph explains a chain of ecological effects, not the mussels’ appearance.

options.label: B
options.text: problem and solution — it proposes a way to remove the mussels from the lake
options.rationale: No removal plan or solution for the mussels is described in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect — the mussels’ feeding reduces plankton, which then causes native fish populations to decline

options.label: D
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares zebra mussels to a native mussel species
options.rationale: No native mussel species is mentioned for comparison anywhere in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Solar panels generate the most electricity around midday, when sunlight is strongest, but produce almost nothing at night. Wind turbines can generate power at any hour, as long as the wind is blowing, but calm days leave them nearly idle. Because the two sources tend to be weak at different times, many power grids combine both to keep electricity flowing more steadily.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lines up a weakness of each source and shows how pairing them offsets those weaknesses.
explanation.tip: When two things are each strong where the other is weak, that pairing itself is a form of comparison.

options.label: A
options.text: cause and effect — solar panels cause wind turbines to generate more power
options.rationale: The two technologies are not shown causing each other to work in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: chronological order — it explains the order in which solar and wind technology were invented
options.rationale: No invention history or dates for either technology are given in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: description — it only describes what a wind turbine looks like
options.rationale: The paragraph compares timing and reliability, not the turbine’s physical appearance.

options.label: D
options.text: compare and contrast — it contrasts when solar and wind power are strong or weak, then explains why combining them helps

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Patients at a busy clinic were often waiting more than two hours past their scheduled appointment time, mostly because urgent walk-in cases kept interrupting the daily schedule. The clinic began setting aside two short blocks each day reserved only for walk-ins, so scheduled appointments would no longer be bumped. Average wait times for scheduled patients dropped by almost half within a month.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A specific cause of delay is diagnosed, a scheduling fix is applied, and a clear result (reduced wait time) follows.
explanation.tip: Good problem-and-solution paragraphs often name why the problem happened, not just what the problem was.

options.label: A
options.text: problem and solution — it identifies the cause of long waits and explains the scheduling change that reduced them

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast — it compares this clinic’s wait times to another clinic’s
options.rationale: Only one clinic’s results are discussed in this paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: description — it only describes what the clinic’s waiting room looks like
options.rationale: No physical description of the waiting room is given in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it lists the clinic’s exact opening and closing times
options.rationale: No daily opening or closing times for the clinic are described in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Coffee cherries are first picked by hand when they turn deep red. They are then either dried whole in the sun for several weeks or washed to remove the outer fruit immediately after picking. Once dried, the inner beans are hulled, sorted by size, and finally roasted just before shipping.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph moves step by step through the stages a coffee cherry passes through, ending in roasting.
explanation.tip: Process paragraphs that move from raw material to finished product are chronological in structure.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it only compares sun-dried coffee to washed coffee
options.rationale: Both drying methods are mentioned as one step within a larger process, not weighed against each other in depth.

options.label: B
options.text: chronological order — it follows coffee cherries through each stage of processing, from picking to roasting

options.label: C
options.text: problem and solution — it explains a problem with roasting coffee too early
options.rationale: No such problem is raised anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: cause and effect — picking the cherries causes them to turn red
options.rationale: The cherries turn red before they are picked, so this cause-and-effect order is reversed.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Canned vegetables can sit safely in a pantry for a year or more because the sealed can and the heat used during canning kill the bacteria that cause spoilage. Fresh vegetables keep their vitamins and texture better, but they spoil within days unless refrigerated, since nothing stops bacteria from growing on them right away. Because of this trade-off, many families buy some of each, choosing fresh vegetables for the week ahead and canned ones for longer storage.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph names an advantage and disadvantage of each storage method, then shows how that comparison shapes a real choice.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph ends by explaining how people act because of a trade-off, trace back to the comparison that created it.

options.label: A
options.text: chronological order — it explains the history of how canning was invented
options.rationale: No invention history or dates for canning are mentioned anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: problem and solution — it identifies one single best way to store all vegetables
options.rationale: The paragraph says families use a mix of both methods, not one universal fix.

options.label: C
options.text: compare and contrast — it weighs shelf life against freshness for canned versus fresh vegetables and explains how that trade-off affects shopping choices

options.label: D
options.text: cause and effect only — refrigeration is shown as the one cause of all food spoilage
options.rationale: The paragraph explains two separate storage methods and their trade-offs, not a single cause-effect chain.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Dark asphalt and concrete absorb far more sunlight than grass or trees do, and they release that heat back into the surrounding air for hours after sunset. Because many cities are covered mostly in these materials, nighttime temperatures downtown can stay several degrees warmer than in nearby suburbs with more greenery. Some cities have responded by painting rooftops white and planting trees along streets to reduce this effect.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Most of the paragraph builds a cause-and-effect chain (dark materials, trapped heat, warmer nights), and the last sentence briefly shifts to a solution being tried.
explanation.tip: A paragraph can blend two structures — look at where a shift happens, often in the final sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: pure description — it only describes what asphalt looks like
options.rationale: The paragraph explains why temperatures rise and what is being done, not just appearance.

options.label: B
options.text: pure compare and contrast — it only compares two specific named cities to each other
options.rationale: No two specific cities are named and compared; only general city-versus-suburb patterns are discussed.

options.label: C
options.text: pure chronological order — it lists the exact hour each city planted its first tree
options.rationale: No specific hours or planting dates are given anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: cause and effect, with a brief problem-and-solution ending — dark surfaces trap heat and raise city temperatures, and the final sentence adds a response some cities have tried

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Rain-fed farms depend entirely on seasonal rainfall, so a dry year can cut their harvest drastically, but farmers save on the cost and labor of watering. Irrigated farms water their crops on a steady schedule regardless of rainfall, which protects yields during dry years, but the pumps and canals needed are expensive to build and maintain. Because of this trade-off, many regions use rain-fed farming where rainfall is reliable and irrigation only where it is not.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph sets the two farming methods side by side, naming a benefit and a drawback for each, then explains how that comparison guides a choice.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph names a trade-off for each option and then draws a conclusion from comparing them, that is compare and contrast.

options.label: A
options.text: compare and contrast — it weighs the risks and costs of rain-fed versus irrigated farming and explains how that trade-off shapes farmers’ choices

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect only — dry years are shown as the single cause of all farming decisions
options.rationale: The paragraph weighs costs and benefits of both methods, not just one cause producing one effect.

options.label: C
options.text: problem and solution — it identifies irrigation as the one correct fix for all farms
options.rationale: The paragraph says irrigation is useful only where rainfall is unreliable, not a universal fix.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order — it explains how irrigation technology developed over the centuries
options.rationale: No historical timeline or invention dates for irrigation are described in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Many recycling programs found that bins meant only for paper and plastic were filled with food waste, greasy pizza boxes and broken glass, ruining otherwise recyclable material. Several cities responded by printing clear picture guides on every bin lid and fining repeat offenders who ignored the rules. Contamination rates in those cities fell by nearly a third within two years, though officials noted that ongoing public education remained necessary to keep rates low.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A specific problem (contamination) leads to specific fixes (guides, fines) and a measured result, with a closing note about ongoing effort.
explanation.tip: A strong problem-and-solution paragraph often ends by noting whether the fix was complete or still needs more work.

options.label: A
options.text: description only — it simply describes what is typically found inside a recycling bin
options.rationale: The paragraph explains a problem and response, not just an inventory of bin contents.

options.label: B
options.text: problem and solution — it names the contamination problem, describes two specific fixes, and reports a result while noting the fix still needs upkeep

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order only — it lists each city’s recycling program by the year it was founded
options.rationale: No founding dates for any recycling program are given in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: compare and contrast only — it compares recycling rules in different countries
options.rationale: No countries are named or compared against each other in this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “After a severe flood destroyed hundreds of homes along the river in 1962, the city built its first levee system within five years. A second, larger flood in 1998 revealed that the original levees were too low, so engineers raised and reinforced them throughout the early 2000s. Because of these upgrades, a comparably large flood in 2019 caused far less damage to the same neighborhoods.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: Three dated floods are presented in order, and each one’s cause-and-effect relationship to the city’s levee response is tracked across time.
explanation.tip: When dates anchor a chain of causes and effects, the structure is chronological but driven by cause and effect.

options.label: A
options.text: problem and solution with no time order — it treats all three floods as happening at the same time
options.rationale: The floods are clearly dated and occur in sequence, not simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: pure description — it only describes what a levee looks like
options.rationale: The paragraph traces events and their consequences over decades, not the physical appearance of a levee.

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order built around cause and effect — each flood (1962, 1998, 2019) prompts a response, and the paragraph tracks how those responses changed outcomes over time

options.label: D
options.text: pure compare and contrast — it only compares the 1962 flood to the 2019 flood, ignoring everything else
options.rationale: The 1998 flood and the engineering response in between are also central to the paragraph, not left out.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Bacteria reproduce so quickly that a population exposed to an antibiotic may include a few individuals with a random mutation that happens to resist the drug. Because the antibiotic kills off the non-resistant bacteria, the resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing the resistance trait to their offspring. Over many rounds of this process, especially when antibiotics are overused or not finished as prescribed, a bacterial population can become mostly or entirely resistant. Doctors have responded by prescribing antibiotics more selectively and completing full treatment courses to reduce how often this cycle repeats.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph explains a repeating mechanism (mutation, survival, reproduction, repeat) that builds toward a problem, then closes with how doctors are addressing it.
explanation.tip: Some structures repeat in a cycle rather than happening only once — look for words like “over many rounds” or “repeats.”

options.label: A
options.text: chronological order with specific dates for each stage of resistance
options.rationale: No specific years or dates mark any stage of the process described in this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: a single, one-time cause and effect — one antibiotic dose permanently makes all bacteria resistant forever
options.rationale: The paragraph describes a repeating, multi-round process, not one dose causing permanent resistance all at once.

options.label: C
options.text: compare and contrast between two different bacteria species
options.rationale: No second bacteria species is introduced for comparison anywhere in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: a repeating cause-and-effect cycle that builds to a problem, followed by a brief solution — each round of antibiotic use causes resistant bacteria to multiply, and the final sentence adds how doctors are responding

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “When a key factory that supplied a specific computer chip shut down after a storm, several electronics companies that depended on that single supplier could not finish assembling their products, even though every other part was ready. Prices for finished electronics using that chip rose within weeks, since the remaining chip supply could not meet demand. In response, some companies began sourcing the same chip from two or more factories instead of just one, even though this raised their costs slightly, in order to avoid being stopped completely by a single factory’s shutdown again.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A single cause (the shutdown) triggers a chain of effects (shortage, price rise), and the paragraph ends by describing a solution companies adopted to prevent a repeat.
explanation.tip: In cause-and-effect writing about business or systems, look for a shift at the end toward prevention — that often signals an added problem-and-solution layer.

options.label: A
options.text: cause and effect leading into a problem-and-solution ending — the factory shutdown causes a supply shortage and price increase, and companies then adopt a strategy to prevent the same cause from stopping them again

options.label: B
options.text: compare and contrast between two competing computer chip brands
options.rationale: Only one type of chip and its single original supplier are discussed; no competing chip brand is compared.

options.label: C
options.text: description only, detailing what the factory building looked like after the storm
options.rationale: The paragraph explains a chain of economic consequences and a strategic response, not the factory’s physical condition.

options.label: D
options.text: chronological order listing the exact date of every price increase
options.rationale: No specific dates for any price changes are given, only a general “within weeks.”

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A species of migratory bird has relied for centuries on wetlands along its route to rest and refuel during a journey of several thousand kilometers. As many of those wetlands have been drained for farmland over the past fifty years, the birds now face longer stretches without a safe place to stop, and researchers have recorded a steady decline in the number of birds completing the full migration each year. Conservation groups in several countries along the route have begun restoring small sections of wetland and coordinating the timing of protections so that no single country’s efforts are undone by another’s lack of action.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph traces how a decades-long cause (wetland loss) produces a specific effect (fewer successful migrations), then closes with a coordinated, multi-country solution.
explanation.tip: When several separate causes (draining wetlands in different places) combine to create one large effect, solving it usually also requires coordinated action.

options.label: A
options.text: a simple list of facts about the bird’s appearance and diet
options.rationale: The paragraph focuses on a historical change and its ecological consequences, not the bird’s appearance or diet.

options.label: B
options.text: cause and effect across a long time span, ending with a solution that requires coordination among several causes of the original problem — wetland loss (cause) reduces migration success (effect), and the final sentence describes a multi-country response

options.label: C
options.text: chronological order with each country’s protection law dated individually
options.rationale: No specific laws or dates for individual countries are given in this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: compare and contrast between two different bird species that share the same route
options.rationale: Only one species of migratory bird is discussed throughout this paragraph.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Bus ridership in one mid-sized city fell by nearly a third after routes were cut and fares were raised during a budget shortfall, forcing many riders to rely on cars instead and worsening downtown traffic. City planners later restored the cut routes and froze fares for two years while also adding real-time arrival screens at major stops so riders could trust the schedule again. Ridership slowly climbed back over the following three years, though it still has not fully returned to its earlier levels.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: A budget cut causes a specific effect (falling ridership), and the city’s later actions address that problem, though the paragraph notes the fix is still incomplete.
explanation.tip: Look for a result described as only partly fixed, such as “still has not fully returned” — that often signals a blended cause-effect and problem-solution structure.

options.label: A
options.text: pure compare and contrast between bus ridership in two different cities
options.rationale: Only one city’s transit system is discussed throughout this paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: pure description of what the city’s buses and bus stops look like
options.rationale: The paragraph explains why ridership changed over several years, not what the vehicles or stops look like.

options.label: C
options.text: cause and effect followed by problem and solution — budget cuts cause falling ridership and worse traffic, and the city’s multi-part response only partially reverses that effect over time

options.label: D
options.text: pure chronological order with no cause-and-effect connections between events
options.rationale: The events are explicitly linked by cause and effect — the cuts cause the ridership drop, and the response causes partial recovery — not just listed without connection.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Along one stretch of coastline, a storm destroyed homes built behind a cleared beach, while homes behind a stretch of mangrove forest just a few kilometers away suffered far less damage, because the mangroves’ dense roots absorbed much of the wave energy before it reached land. Engineers initially proposed building a concrete seawall to replace the lost protection, but a mangrove-restoration project turned out to cost less and also created a fish nursery that supported the area’s fishing economy. Because of these added benefits, the restoration plan was eventually chosen over the seawall.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph blends three patterns: a cause-and-effect explanation for the damage difference, a comparison of two proposed fixes, and a final choice based on added benefits.
explanation.tip: Longer paragraphs often blend structures — identify each piece (why something happened, what options were compared, what was finally decided) separately.

options.label: A
options.text: pure chronological order, with every event dated to a specific year
options.rationale: No specific years or dates are given for the storm, the proposal or the final decision.

options.label: B
options.text: pure description of what a mangrove tree looks like
options.rationale: The paragraph explains a cause-and-effect difference and a decision between two solutions, not the tree’s physical features.

options.label: C
options.text: pure problem and solution, with no comparison between the two proposed solutions
options.rationale: The paragraph explicitly weighs the seawall against the mangrove-restoration project before choosing one, which is a comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: cause and effect combined with compare and contrast, ending in problem and solution — the mangroves’ root structure explains the damage difference, two solutions are compared, and one is chosen for its added benefits

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A disease that spreads easily needs a certain percentage of a population to be immune before outbreaks stop spreading widely, a point researchers call the herd immunity threshold; for a highly contagious disease, that percentage can be quite high. When vaccination rates in one region fell below that threshold after a period of low turnout at clinics, a localized outbreak spread quickly among unvaccinated children, even though most adults in the same region were already immune. Health officials responded with a focused campaign at schools specifically, rather than a general public campaign, because the gap was concentrated almost entirely among that one age group.” How is this paragraph organized?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph opens by defining a concept, then traces how falling below that threshold caused a specific outbreak, then explains a solution matched to the specific group affected.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph defines a term before explaining an event, check whether the definition itself is doing structural work — setting up the cause that follows.

options.label: A
options.text: a definition followed by cause and effect and then a targeted solution — the paragraph first explains a concept, then shows how falling below it caused an outbreak in one group, then describes a response matched specifically to that group

options.label: B
options.text: pure chronological order, with the outbreak and the campaign given specific calendar dates
options.rationale: No specific dates are given for when vaccination rates fell, when the outbreak began, or when the campaign started.

options.label: C
options.text: pure compare and contrast between two different diseases
options.rationale: Only one disease and one herd immunity threshold are discussed throughout this paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: pure description of what the disease’s symptoms look like
options.rationale: The paragraph explains a concept, a cause-and-effect outbreak, and a targeted response, not a list of symptoms.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a possessive noun correctly?

explanation.tip: Read the sentence aloud — does it sound like “belonging to”?

options.rationale: This is missing the apostrophe needed to show ownership.

options.label: B

options.rationale: This adds an extra, incorrect s.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ shells were scattered on the beach.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Many turtles own the shells, so the plural turtles takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.tip: Plural already ending in s: add only an apostrophe.

options.label: A
options.text: turtle’s

options.label: B
options.text: turtle

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ boots were covered in mud.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Men” is already plural and does not end in s, so add ’s: men’s.
explanation.tip: Irregular plurals (men, women, mice, geese) add ’s just like singular nouns.

options.label: A
options.text: men’s

options.label: B
options.text: mens’

options.rationale: This misspells the plural of man.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a possessive noun correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Geese” is the irregular plural of goose, and since it does not end in s, add ’s.

explanation.tip: Singular owner: add an apostrophe and s.

items.stem: Which sentence shows that a set of bikes is owned by MORE THAN ONE girl?

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The ____ shell was spotted with brown.”

explanation.whyCorrect: One snail owns the shell, so add ’s: snail’s.

options.label: D
options.text: “My uncle used to say, “A clean workshop is a safe workshop,”” Laila recalled.
options.rationale: Use single quotation marks for a quotation nested inside another quotation.

items.stem: Put the pieces in order to make a correctly punctuated sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: The speaker tag interrupts the quotation and is set off by commas on both sides.
explanation.tip: Interrupted quotation: “part one,” tag, “part two.”

sequence: “Once the paint dries,”
said the foreman,
“we can move the shelves back.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly integrates a short quotation from a text into your own sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: An integrated quotation blends smoothly into your sentence without an extra comma or capital, and end punctuation stays inside the marks.
explanation.tip: If the quotation completes your own sentence grammatically, treat it like a normal phrase, not a full quoted sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The report notes that the bridge’s cables were “showing early signs of rust”.
options.rationale: The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

options.label: B
options.text: The report notes that the bridge’s cables were, “showing early signs of rust.”
options.rationale: No comma is needed when a quoted phrase flows directly into your own sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: The report notes that the bridge’s cables were “Showing early signs of rust.”
options.rationale: A quoted phrase blended into your sentence is not capitalized unless it begins a full quoted sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The report notes that the bridge’s cables were “showing early signs of rust.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates dialogue where the quotation is interrupted and the two parts form ONE sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: When the two quoted parts form a single sentence, commas surround the tag and the second part stays lowercase.
explanation.tip: One interrupted sentence: lowercase after the tag. Two separate sentences: capitalize after the tag.

options.label: A
options.text: “If we hurry,” the guide said, “we can still catch the sunset.”

options.label: B
options.text: “If we hurry,” the guide said “we can still catch the sunset.”
options.rationale: A comma is needed after the speaker tag, before the second quotation begins.

options.label: C
options.text: “If we hurry,” the guide said, “We can still catch the sunset.”
options.rationale: Since both parts form one sentence, the second part should not start with a capital letter.

options.label: D
options.text: “If we hurry” the guide said, “we can still catch the sunset.”
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the closing quotation mark after the first part.

items.stem: A writer wants to show that two characters spoke, one right after the other. Which formatting choice is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: A new paragraph for each new speaker is the standard convention that keeps dialogue clear.
explanation.tip: New speaker, new paragraph — this is true even for one-word responses.

options.label: A
options.text: Keep every line of dialogue from different speakers in one paragraph to save space.
options.rationale: Mixing different speakers’ lines in one paragraph makes it unclear who is talking.

options.label: B
options.text: Start a new paragraph each time the speaker changes, even if a line of dialogue is short.

options.label: C
options.text: Add a new paragraph only every third exchange between the two speakers.
options.rationale: Readers need a new paragraph at every change of speaker, not just periodically.

options.label: D
options.text: Only start a new paragraph when a speaker’s line is longer than one sentence.
options.rationale: Paragraph breaks in dialogue depend on who is speaking, not on how long the line is.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates dialogue where the second quoted part is a new, separate sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: When the second quoted part is its own complete sentence, the tag ends with a period, and the new sentence begins with a capital letter.
explanation.tip: Two separate sentences in dialogue each need their own capital letter and end mark.

options.label: A
options.text: “The generator finally started” Dunia said. “Now we can finish the wiring.”
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the closing quotation mark after the first part.

options.label: B
options.text: “The generator finally started,” Dunia said, “now we can finish the wiring.”
options.rationale: Since the second part is a separate sentence, it needs its own capital letter and end punctuation, not a comma and lowercase.

options.label: C
options.text: “The generator finally started,” Dunia said. “Now we can finish the wiring.”

options.label: D
options.text: “The generator finally started,” Dunia said. “now we can finish the wiring.”
options.rationale: The second quoted sentence must begin with a capital letter.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Ants work together to build their homes. Some ants dig tunnels underground. Other ants carry leaves and dirt to make walls. A few ants guard the entrance to keep the colony safe.” What is the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every sentence describes a different job that helps build and protect the ant colony as a team.
explanation.tip: Ask: what one idea do all the sentences have in common?

options.label: A
options.text: Ants only dig tunnels and do nothing else.
options.rationale: The paragraph also describes ants building walls and guarding the entrance.

options.label: B
options.text: Ants build their homes above ground only.
options.rationale: The paragraph says some ants dig tunnels underground.

options.label: C
options.text: Each ant works completely alone without any teamwork.
options.rationale: The paragraph shows ants working together, each with a different job.

options.label: D
options.text: Ants work together, with different jobs, to build and protect their home.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Many families plant a small vegetable garden in their backyard. Growing your own vegetables can save money at the store. Garden vegetables often taste fresher than ones bought in a store. Taking care of a garden also teaches children patience.” What is the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists several separate benefits that all support one main idea about backyard gardens.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph lists several good things about one topic, that is usually the main idea.

options.label: A
options.text: Growing a backyard vegetable garden offers several benefits to a family.

options.label: B
options.text: Children dislike taking care of gardens.
options.rationale: The paragraph says gardening teaches patience, not that children dislike it.

options.label: C
options.text: Backyard gardens always cost more money than store vegetables.
options.rationale: The paragraph says gardens can save money, not cost more.

options.label: D
options.text: Store-bought vegetables always taste better than garden vegetables.
options.rationale: The paragraph says garden vegetables often taste fresher.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A lighthouse helps ships find their way at night. Its bright light can be seen from far away across the water. The light often flashes in a special pattern so sailors know exactly which harbor it marks. Without lighthouses, many ships could crash into rocky coastlines in the dark.” What is the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: Every detail connects back to the central idea that lighthouses keep ships safe at night.
explanation.tip: Find the idea that explains why every detail in the paragraph is included.

options.label: A
options.text: Lighthouses are only built during the daytime.
options.rationale: The paragraph is entirely about how lighthouses help at night.

options.label: B
options.text: Lighthouses help guide ships safely by warning them of the coastline at night.

options.label: C
options.text: Ships never need help finding their way.
options.rationale: The paragraph explains that ships rely on lighthouses to avoid crashing.

options.label: D
options.text: All lighthouses flash in exactly the same pattern.
options.rationale: The paragraph says the pattern helps sailors tell harbors apart, meaning patterns differ.

items.stem: Which TWO details support the main idea that camels are well suited for desert travel?

explanation.whyCorrect: These two details directly explain physical features that help camels survive desert travel.
explanation.tip: Choose details that explain WHY the animal survives the desert, not just what it looks like.

options.label: A
options.text: Some camels live in zoos far from any desert.
options.rationale: This is unrelated to how camels are suited for desert travel.

options.label: B
options.text: Thick pads on a camel's feet keep it from sinking into loose sand.

options.label: C
options.text: Camels are usually brown or tan in color.
options.rationale: This describes appearance, not survival in the desert.

options.label: D
options.text: A camel can go many days without drinking water.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Rainwater that falls on a roof usually just runs off into the street and is wasted. Some families now attach a large barrel under a gutter to catch this rainwater instead. The collected water can be used to water a garden or wash a car. Over a rainy season, a single barrel can save a surprising amount of water that would otherwise be lost.” What is the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph's details all build toward the idea that catching rainwater helps families avoid wasting it.
explanation.tip: Look for the problem a paragraph raises and the idea that solves it.

options.label: A
options.text: Gutters are only used to make roofs look nice.
options.rationale: The paragraph describes gutters as part of a water-saving system, not decoration.

options.label: B
options.text: Every family already owns a rain barrel.
options.rationale: The paragraph says some families, not all, use this method.

options.label: C
options.text: Collecting rainwater in a barrel lets families reuse water that would otherwise be wasted.

options.label: D
options.text: Rainwater is never useful for anything around the house.
options.rationale: The paragraph explains several uses for collected rainwater.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Reading aloud to young children helps them learn new words faster than reading alone later. It also helps children understand how a story is put together, with a beginning, middle and end. Many children remember stories better when they hear a parent's voice. For these reasons, many teachers encourage parents to read aloud every day.” Which sentence BEST restates the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence combines the paragraph's separate benefits — vocabulary, story structure and memory — into one main idea.
explanation.tip: A good restatement combines the separate details into one general sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Children only enjoy stories without any pictures.
options.rationale: Pictures are never mentioned anywhere in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: Teachers discourage parents from reading to their children.
options.rationale: The paragraph says teachers encourage this practice, not discourage it.

options.label: C
options.text: Reading aloud works best only with very long books.
options.rationale: The length of the books is never discussed in the paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: Reading aloud to young children helps them learn language and understand stories in ways that benefit them.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Some schools have started ten-minute recess breaks between every class instead of one long recess at midday. Teachers noticed that students focused better in class right after a short break than they did after sitting for a long time. Short, frequent breaks also meant fewer students asked to leave class to use the restroom or get water. Because of these changes, several schools plan to keep the new schedule next year.” What is the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph explains a specific change and the two benefits that followed it, which together form the main idea.
explanation.tip: Watch for a change described in a paragraph, followed by the results of that change.

options.label: A
options.text: Switching to short, frequent breaks improved student focus and reduced classroom interruptions.

options.label: B
options.text: Students only asked to leave class during the new short breaks.
options.rationale: The paragraph says fewer students asked to leave class under the new schedule, not more.

options.label: C
options.text: The new schedule made no difference in how students behaved.
options.rationale: The paragraph explains two clear improvements noticed by teachers.

options.label: D
options.text: Schools removed recess completely to save class time.
options.rationale: The paragraph describes more frequent breaks, not the removal of recess.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Volunteers at an animal shelter noticed that many dogs stayed longer when their photos online looked blurry or dark. The shelter began taking brighter, better-lit photos of every new dog and writing a short, friendly description for each one. Within two months, dogs were being adopted almost twice as quickly as before. The shelter now trains every new volunteer in basic photography before letting them help with adoptions.” What is the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph connects a specific change (better photos) to a clear result (faster adoptions), which is its main idea.
explanation.tip: Find the change a paragraph describes, then the result that followed.

options.label: A
options.text: The shelter stopped posting photos of dogs online entirely.
options.rationale: The paragraph describes improving photos, not removing them.

options.label: B
options.text: Improving online photos and descriptions helped shelter dogs get adopted much faster.

options.label: C
options.text: Volunteers were no longer needed once the new photos were posted.
options.rationale: The paragraph says volunteers are now trained in photography, showing they are still needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Dogs with blurry photos were adopted faster than other dogs.
options.rationale: The paragraph says dogs stayed longer, meaning they were adopted more slowly, when photos were blurry.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A small coastal town used to lose several fishing boats every year when sudden storms caught sailors by surprise far from shore. After installing a simple weather-warning siren at the harbor, boats could return to safety before a storm fully formed. Boat losses dropped sharply in the years after the siren was installed, though a few sailors still ignored the warning when fish were plentiful.” What is the main idea of this paragraph, including the detail about sailors who ignored the siren?

explanation.whyCorrect: A complete main idea should include both the siren's clear benefit and the detail that it did not solve the problem for every sailor.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph ends with an exception, a strong main-idea statement should mention it too.

options.label: A
options.text: Sailors ignored the siren because it was too quiet to hear.
options.rationale: No reason involving the siren's volume is given; the paragraph says some sailors ignored it when fish were plentiful.

options.label: B
options.text: The siren completely ended all boat losses in the town forever.
options.rationale: The paragraph notes that a few sailors still ignored the warning, so losses were reduced but not fully ended.

options.label: C
options.text: A harbor warning siren greatly reduced storm-related boat losses, although not every sailor heeded it.

options.label: D
options.text: The town removed the siren because it did not work.
options.rationale: The paragraph never says the siren was removed; it says losses dropped after it was installed.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A small bakery began offering free bread to anyone who came by just before closing time, rather than throwing away unsold loaves. At first, only a handful of neighbors came by each evening, but word spread, and soon a small line formed every night. The owner noticed that many of these same visitors became regular paying customers earlier in the day, since they now trusted the bakery and visited more often. What began as a way to reduce waste ended up growing the bakery's daily business as well.” Which statement BEST captures the main idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: A full main-idea statement should include both the original goal (reducing waste) and the surprising additional benefit (growing the daytime business).
explanation.tip: When a paragraph describes an unexpected extra result, a strong main-idea statement captures both the original purpose and that result.

options.label: A
options.text: The bakery stopped selling bread during the day to focus on giving it away at night.
options.rationale: The paragraph says the same visitors became paying customers earlier in the day, so daytime selling continued and grew.

options.label: B
options.text: Giving away bread caused the bakery to lose money overall.
options.rationale: The paragraph describes the bakery's daily business growing, not losing money.

options.label: C
options.text: Only strangers who never returned came for the free bread.
options.rationale: The paragraph says many visitors became regular customers, meaning they did return.

options.label: D
options.text: Giving away unsold bread not only reduced waste but also unexpectedly helped the bakery gain more regular daytime customers.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Octopuses are known for their remarkable intelligence among invertebrates. They can solve simple puzzles to reach hidden food. Many octopuses have escaped from aquarium tanks by figuring out how to open lids. Scientists have even observed them using tools, such as carrying shells to use as shelter later.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each example — puzzle-solving, escaping tanks and tool use — supports the same overall claim about octopus intelligence.
explanation.tip: Look for the one idea that connects every specific example in a paragraph.

options.label: A
options.text: Octopuses show several signs of surprising intelligence for an invertebrate.

options.label: B
options.text: Octopuses cannot solve any kind of puzzle.
options.rationale: The paragraph says they can solve simple puzzles to reach food.

options.label: C
options.text: No other invertebrate has ever been studied by scientists.
options.rationale: The paragraph only discusses octopuses and does not compare them to other invertebrates.

options.label: D
options.text: Aquariums are specially designed so octopuses can never escape.
options.rationale: The paragraph says octopuses have escaped by opening lids.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Many cities are adding more bicycle lanes to busy streets. Protected lanes with a physical barrier reduce accidents between cyclists and cars. Cities with more bike lanes often see fewer traffic jams, since some drivers switch to biking instead. Bike lanes can also encourage more people to exercise as part of their daily commute.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists three separate benefits of bike lanes, all supporting one overall claim about their value to a city.
explanation.tip: When several distinct benefits are listed, the central idea usually ties them together.

options.label: A
options.text: Protected bike lanes have no effect on cyclist safety.
options.rationale: The paragraph says protected lanes reduce accidents.

options.label: B
options.text: Adding bicycle lanes brings several benefits to a city, from safety to traffic to health.

options.label: C
options.text: Bicycle lanes always make traffic jams worse.
options.rationale: The paragraph says cities with more bike lanes often see fewer traffic jams.

options.label: D
options.text: People who bike to work rarely get any exercise.
options.rationale: The paragraph says biking to work encourages exercise.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Icebergs form when large chunks of ice break off from glaciers or ice shelves and drift into the ocean. Only about one-tenth of an iceberg is visible above the water's surface, while the rest remains hidden below. This hidden mass makes icebergs especially dangerous to ships, since a vessel can misjudge how far the ice actually extends underwater. Sailors have used sonar for decades to measure an iceberg's true size before sailing nearby.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph's details about hidden mass and sonar use both support the central idea about hidden danger.
explanation.tip: Find the idea that explains why the paragraph includes the detail about sonar.

options.label: A
options.text: Sonar was invented specifically to study icebergs.
options.rationale: The paragraph says sailors use sonar to measure icebergs, not that it was invented for that purpose.

options.label: B
options.text: Icebergs form only from ocean water freezing in place.
options.rationale: The paragraph says icebergs form from ice breaking off glaciers or ice shelves, not from ocean water freezing.

options.label: C
options.text: Icebergs are more dangerous than they appear because most of their size is hidden underwater.

options.label: D
options.text: Icebergs are completely visible above the water's surface.
options.rationale: The paragraph says only about one-tenth is visible above the surface.

items.stem: Which TWO details support the central idea that coral reefs face serious threats from warming oceans?

explanation.whyCorrect: These two details directly explain how warming water damages and can kill coral.
explanation.tip: Choose details that explain the THREAT itself, not background facts about reefs.

options.label: A
options.text: Warm water causes coral to expel the algae that give it color and food.

options.label: B
options.text: Some tourists enjoy snorkeling near coral reefs.
options.rationale: This describes a human activity, not a threat to reefs from warming water.

options.label: C
options.text: Coral reefs are found in oceans all around the world.
options.rationale: This describes where reefs are located, not a threat they face.

options.label: D
options.text: Prolonged high temperatures can cause bleached coral to die.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Public libraries have begun offering more than just books to borrow. Many now lend out tools, sewing machines and even telescopes for a short period. Some libraries host free coding classes and resume-writing workshops for adults. These added services have drawn in visitors who might never have come in for books alone.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph lists several new services and ends by connecting them to a central claim about attracting new visitors.
explanation.tip: Look at the final sentence of a paragraph — it often restates the central idea in general terms.

options.label: A
options.text: Telescopes are the most popular item libraries now lend.
options.rationale: The paragraph does not say which borrowed item is most popular.

options.label: B
options.text: Libraries have stopped lending books to focus on other services.
options.rationale: The paragraph says libraries now offer more THAN books, not that they stopped lending books.

options.label: C
options.text: Only children are interested in the new library services.
options.rationale: The paragraph mentions coding classes and resume workshops, which are described as being for adults.

options.label: D
options.text: Libraries are attracting new visitors by offering services beyond just lending books.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Researchers studying ant colonies have found that ants use chemical trails, called pheromones, to communicate with each other. When an ant finds food, it leaves a pheromone trail back to the colony. Other ants follow the strongest trail, which helps the colony quickly focus on the best food source. Over time, weaker trails to less useful food fade away entirely.” Which sentence BEST restates the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence combines the paragraph's details about pheromones, trail-following and fading trails into one general idea.
explanation.tip: A strong restatement should combine separate details into one overall claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Ants use chemical trails to communicate and efficiently guide the colony toward the best food sources.

options.label: B
options.text: Every ant trail leads to a different food source forever.
options.rationale: The paragraph says weaker trails fade away over time, so they do not last forever.

options.label: C
options.text: Ants communicate only through physical touch, never chemicals.
options.rationale: The paragraph is entirely about chemical pheromone trails, not touch.

options.label: D
options.text: Ants cannot tell the difference between a strong and a weak trail.
options.rationale: The paragraph says ants follow the strongest trail, meaning they can tell the difference.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A regional airline began charging passengers a small fee to check a bag, while making the fee free for passengers who booked online a week in advance. Ticket sales rose for flights booked early, since the discount gave travelers a clear reason to plan ahead instead of waiting until the last minute. Flights booked at the last minute, which used to fill up with checked bags, now carry noticeably less luggage overall. The airline credits the new fee structure with both steadier bookings and lighter planes.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph connects one policy change to two distinct results — steadier bookings and lighter planes — which together form the central idea.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph names two separate results from one cause, the central idea usually covers both.

options.label: A
options.text: Passengers who book early now check more bags than before.
options.rationale: The paragraph says last-minute flights carry less luggage, and does not describe early bookers checking more bags.

options.label: B
options.text: A new baggage fee structure changed passenger behavior in ways that benefited the airline in two separate ways.

options.label: C
options.text: The new fee structure had no effect on when people booked flights.
options.rationale: The paragraph explicitly says ticket sales rose for flights booked early because of the fee structure.

options.label: D
options.text: The airline removed baggage fees for all passengers.
options.rationale: The paragraph describes a fee that is only waived for passengers who book a week in advance, not removed for everyone.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A community garden project initially struggled because most plots sat empty during the hottest summer weeks, when volunteers avoided working outside. Organizers moved the main watering and harvesting schedule to early morning and evening instead of midday. Plot usage rose significantly once volunteers no longer had to work during the worst heat, though a few plots near the garden's shadeless edge remained harder to keep staffed.” What is the central idea of this paragraph, including the detail about the shadeless plots?

explanation.whyCorrect: A complete central-idea statement should include both the main improvement and the specific detail about the remaining exception.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph closes with “though” or “however,” check whether that detail belongs in a complete central-idea statement.

options.label: A
options.text: The shadeless plots were the only ones that were ever used.
options.rationale: The paragraph implies the opposite — most plots improved, while the shadeless ones remained a harder exception.

options.label: B
options.text: Changing the schedule solved every single staffing problem completely.
options.rationale: The paragraph notes that plots near the shadeless edge remained harder to staff, so the problem was not fully solved.

options.label: C
options.text: Rescheduling garden work around the hottest hours fixed most of the staffing problem, though a few especially hot plots stayed harder to maintain.

options.label: D
options.text: Volunteers avoided the garden entirely, even after the schedule changed.
options.rationale: The paragraph says plot usage rose significantly after the change, meaning volunteers did return.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A regional hospital introduced color-coded wristbands to flag patients with specific allergies, replacing handwritten notes that staff sometimes missed during busy shifts. Allergy-related medication errors dropped noticeably within the first six months of using the wristbands. However, the hospital later found that wristbands sometimes slipped off during long procedures, so staff began double-checking allergy status in the patient's digital chart as well.” What is the central idea of this paragraph, including the limitation that was discovered later?

explanation.whyCorrect: A full central-idea statement should include both the wristbands' clear benefit and the specific limitation that led to an added safeguard.
explanation.tip: When a text reports a fix and then a later discovered flaw, the central idea usually needs to mention both.

options.label: A
options.text: The wristbands completely replaced every other safety check at the hospital.
options.rationale: The paragraph says staff added a digital chart check as well, so the wristbands did not replace every other safety measure.

options.label: B
options.text: The hospital stopped using wristbands once the slipping problem was discovered.
options.rationale: The paragraph says staff added a backup check, not that they abandoned the wristbands.

options.label: C
options.text: Handwritten notes were found to be more reliable than the wristbands.
options.rationale: The paragraph says errors dropped after switching away from handwritten notes, suggesting the wristbands were actually more reliable overall.

options.label: D
options.text: Color-coded wristbands reduced allergy-related errors, but the hospital had to add a digital backup check after discovering the wristbands could slip off.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A small publishing company began offering authors a choice between a traditional contract with a larger upfront payment and a smaller upfront payment paired with a higher share of ongoing sales. Most new authors chose the larger upfront payment, valuing certainty over a book's uncertain future sales. Authors whose first books had sold unusually well, however, increasingly chose the second option for their next book, trusting their track record to earn more over time. The company found that offering both options kept both new and established authors satisfied in different ways.” Which statement BEST captures the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: A full central-idea statement should capture that the options appealed to different groups for different, text-stated reasons.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph explains WHY different groups made different choices, the central idea should reflect that reasoning, not just the choices themselves.

options.label: A
options.text: Giving authors a choice between two payment structures satisfied different authors differently, based on their experience and confidence in future sales.

options.label: B
options.text: Authors with successful first books always regretted choosing the second option.
options.rationale: The paragraph says these authors trusted their track record and chose the option deliberately; no regret is mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: The company eliminated the traditional upfront-payment contract entirely.
options.rationale: The paragraph says most new authors still chose the larger upfront payment, so that option was not eliminated.

options.label: D
options.text: Every author at the company always prefers the same payment option.
options.rationale: The paragraph says new and established authors tended to choose differently, not the same option.

items.stem: What is the central idea of “Should Homework Be Optional?”

explanation.whyCorrect: Every paragraph builds toward the idea that flexible, needs-based homework serves students better than a required, one-size-fits-all approach.
explanation.tip: The central idea usually appears near the beginning and is restated at the end.

options.label: A
options.text: Teachers dislike grading homework assignments.
options.rationale: Teacher opinions about grading are never mentioned anywhere in the article.

options.label: B
options.text: Homework should be optional and matched to each student's needs rather than required for everyone the same way.

options.label: C
options.text: All homework should be eliminated completely.
options.rationale: The article says homework could still be assigned, just not required for students who already show mastery.

options.label: D
options.text: Students who get less homework always score higher on tests.
options.rationale: The article says there is little difference in scores, not that less homework guarantees higher scores.

items.stem: Which detail BEST supports the central idea that mandatory homework may not actually raise achievement?

explanation.whyCorrect: This research finding directly challenges the claim that homework improves test scores.
explanation.tip: Look for the detail that is evidence, not just background information.

options.label: A
options.text: Heavy homework loads are linked to stress and poor sleep.
options.rationale: This supports a different point, about wellbeing, not achievement.

options.label: B
options.text: Teachers could still assign practice problems under an optional system.
options.rationale: This describes how optional homework would work, not evidence about achievement.

options.label: C
options.text: A review of multiple studies found a weak connection between homework and achievement for younger students.

options.label: D
options.text: Students spend hours on homework after a full school day.
options.rationale: This describes the current situation, not evidence about achievement.

items.stem: Which TWO sentences belong in an objective summary of the homework article's central ideas?

explanation.whyCorrect: Objective summaries include only facts and findings stated in the text, not opinions.
explanation.tip: Ask whether the article itself states the sentence as evidence, or whether it is an added opinion.

options.label: A
options.text: Every teacher secretly agrees that homework should end.
options.rationale: Teachers' private opinions are never described in the article.

options.label: B
options.text: Heavy mandatory homework is linked to higher stress and less sleep for students.

options.label: C
options.text: Research shows a weak link between required homework and achievement, especially for younger students.

options.label: D
options.text: Homework is the most stressful part of being a student.
options.rationale: This states an opinion rather than a fact reported in the article.

items.stem: How does the central idea of “Should Homework Be Optional?” develop across the text?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article layers several different kinds of evidence, each supporting the same central recommendation.
explanation.tip: Track how each new paragraph adds a different kind of support for the same idea.

options.label: A
options.text: It lists homework rules from several different countries.
options.rationale: No other countries' homework rules are compared or listed in the article.

options.label: B
options.text: It focuses only on one single piece of evidence, repeated five times.
options.rationale: Four distinct kinds of evidence are introduced in the article, not one point repeated.

options.label: C
options.text: It tells a personal story about one struggling student.
options.rationale: No single student's personal story is told anywhere in the article.

options.label: D
options.text: Each paragraph adds a new piece of evidence — achievement, flexibility, targeted support and wellbeing — building toward the same recommendation.

items.stem: Which sentence would BEST conclude a summary of the central idea of “Should Homework Be Optional?”?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence captures the article's final recommendation, which ties together all the evidence presented.
explanation.tip: A strong concluding sentence should connect back to the article's opening claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Matching homework to what each student actually needs would likely help both learning and wellbeing more than requiring the same amount for everyone.

options.label: B
options.text: Homework should always be assigned on Fridays.
options.rationale: No particular day for assigning homework is discussed anywhere in the article.

options.label: C
options.text: Students who finish homework quickly should receive extra assignments.
options.rationale: This directly contradicts the article's suggestion that such students use the time differently.

options.label: D
options.text: Parents should check their children's homework every night.
options.rationale: Parental involvement in checking homework is never addressed in the article.

items.stem: A reader claims the homework article argues homework should be banned entirely for all grade levels. Is this an accurate statement of the article's central idea?

explanation.whyCorrect: The article's actual claim is for flexibility and optionality, not elimination, and it is specific about which age groups the evidence applies to.
explanation.tip: Check a restated central idea carefully against both WHAT the text claims and WHO it is about.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the article never mentions homework being assigned at all.
options.rationale: The article explicitly discusses teachers still assigning practice problems under an optional system.

options.label: B
options.text: No — the article argues homework should become optional and flexible, not banned, and it focuses specifically on elementary and middle school students.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because test scores always drop when homework is assigned.
options.rationale: The article reports a weak connection for younger students, not that scores always drop.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because the article argues homework should increase for struggling students only.
options.rationale: The article proposes more flexibility and targeted support, not simply increasing homework for one group.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Urban beekeeping has grown quickly in several major cities over the past decade. Rooftop hives give bees access to park flowers without competing with rural farmland. City-produced honey often sells at a premium because customers see it as a novelty. Beyond honey, these urban bee colonies help pollinate street trees and community gardens that might otherwise produce less fruit.” What is the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph names several distinct benefits — honey, novelty value and pollination — that together support one overall idea about the value of urban beekeeping.
explanation.tip: When several different benefits are listed, the central idea usually ties them together with one general claim.

options.label: A
options.text: Urban honey always costs less than honey from rural farms.
options.rationale: The paragraph says city honey sells at a premium, meaning it costs more, not less.

options.label: B
options.text: Rooftop hives compete directly with rural farms for the same bees.
options.rationale: The paragraph says rooftop hives avoid competing with rural farmland.

options.label: C
options.text: Keeping bees in cities benefits both beekeepers and the surrounding urban environment in more than one way.

options.label: D
options.text: Community gardens cannot survive without rooftop beehives nearby.
options.rationale: The paragraph says pollination helps gardens produce more, not that gardens cannot survive at all without bees.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “A growing number of companies now let employees choose between working from an office, working from home, or splitting their week between the two. Early data suggests that fully remote workers report the most flexibility but also the most difficulty feeling connected to coworkers. Employees who split their time report feeling nearly as flexible while staying better connected to their teams, which is why many companies are now encouraging this hybrid option over either extreme.” Which sentence BEST states the central idea of this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph compares three work arrangements and builds toward a recommendation for the middle option, which is the central idea.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph compares options and ends by favoring one, that favored option is usually the central idea.

options.label: A
options.text: Fully remote work is always the best option for every employee.
options.rationale: The paragraph says fully remote workers struggle with connection, so it is not described as the best option for everyone.

options.label: B
options.text: Working in an office at all times guarantees strong teamwork.
options.rationale: Full-time office work is not described as guaranteed to produce strong teamwork; it is barely mentioned at all.

options.label: C
options.text: Companies should let employees choose any schedule without tracking results.
options.rationale: The paragraph is based on data companies are using to guide a specific recommendation, not on avoiding tracking altogether.

options.label: D
options.text: A mix of in-office and remote work may balance flexibility and connection better than choosing only one extreme.

items.stem: Read this paragraph: “Several hospitals recently began offering patients a short recovery survey by text message instead of a lengthy phone call days after a procedure. Response rates rose sharply because patients could reply in a free moment rather than scheduling a call, and hospitals received feedback faster, letting staff address complications sooner.
