However, patients without reliable phone access or who were less comfortable with texting were sometimes missed entirely, so several hospitals also kept a phone-call option available for those patients.” Which statement BEST captures the central idea of this paragraph, including its limitation?

explanation.whyCorrect: A full statement of the central idea must include both the main benefit (faster, better feedback) and the stated limitation (some patients were missed), since the paragraph explicitly balances both.
explanation.tip: When a paragraph ends with a limitation or exception, a strong central-idea statement should account for it, not just the main benefit.

options.label: A
options.text: Text-message surveys sped up and improved patient feedback overall, though hospitals still had to keep a phone option to avoid leaving some patients out.

options.label: B
options.text: Hospitals abandoned the text-message survey once they noticed a problem.
options.rationale: The paragraph says hospitals kept BOTH options, rather than abandoning the new text-message method.

options.label: C
options.text: Text-message surveys completely replaced phone calls at every hospital.
options.rationale: The paragraph explicitly says hospitals kept a phone-call option for some patients, so phone calls were not entirely replaced.

options.label: D
options.text: Patients overwhelmingly prefer phone calls to text messages after a procedure.
options.rationale: The paragraph reports that response rates rose with texting, suggesting many patients preferred it, not phone calls.

items.stem: Which word is an action verb? “The puppy barked loudly at the mail truck.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Barked” tells what the puppy did.
explanation.tip: Action verbs show what someone or something does.

options.label: A
options.text: loudly
options.rationale: This is an adverb.

options.label: B
options.text: barked

options.label: C
options.text: puppy
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: truck
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Which word is a linking verb? “The cookies appeared delicious as soon as they left the oven.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Appeared” links the cookies to the word that describes them.
explanation.tip: Linking verbs: am, is, are, was, were, seem, become, appear.

options.label: A
options.text: delicious
options.rationale: This is an adjective.

options.label: B
options.text: cookies
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: appeared

options.label: D
options.text: oven
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Choose the helping verb that completes this sentence correctly: “By sunset, the neighbors ____ repaired the old fence.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Had repaired” is a verb phrase using the helping verb had to show an action completed before another past moment.
explanation.tip: Helping verbs: have, has, had, is, are, will, can.

options.label: A
options.text: is
options.rationale: “Is repaired” does not fit a completed past action.

options.label: B
options.text: had

options.label: C
options.text: has
options.rationale: “Neighbors” is plural, and this event already finished before another past moment.

options.label: D
options.text: having
options.rationale: This is not a complete verb on its own.

items.stem: Which modal verb shows PERMISSION? “You ____ leave early if you finish your work.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “May” shows that permission is being given.
explanation.tip: may/can = permission; must = requirement.

options.label: A
options.text: shall
options.rationale: “Shall” is used for offers or plans.

options.label: B
options.text: would
options.rationale: “Would” is used for imagined situations.

options.label: C
options.text: must
options.rationale: “Must” shows something required.

options.label: D
options.text: may

items.stem: Which TWO words are verbs? “Mariam whispered the answer, so she felt proud.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Whispered” is an action verb; “felt” links Mariam to “proud.”
explanation.tip: Find every word that shows action or links ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: whispered

options.label: B
options.text: answer
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: felt

options.label: D
options.text: proud
options.rationale: This is an adjective.

items.stem: Which sentence uses a linking verb correctly after a verb of the senses?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tastes” links the soup to the describing word “delicious.”
explanation.tip: After linking verbs (taste, smell, look, feel), use adjectives.

options.label: A
options.text: The soup tastes delicious.

options.label: B
options.text: The soup tastes deliciously.
options.rationale: After a linking verb like “tastes,” use an adjective, not an adverb.

options.label: C
options.text: The soup taste delicious.
options.rationale: “Soup” is singular, so the verb is “tastes.”

options.label: D
options.text: The soup tasting delicious.
options.rationale: This is not a complete verb.

items.stem: Choose the modal verb: “Students ____ bring a pencil to the exam.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Must” shows the pencil is required.
explanation.tip: must = required; might/could = possible.

options.label: A
options.text: would
options.rationale: “Would” is for imagined actions.

options.label: B
options.text: could
options.rationale: “Could” shows ability or possibility.

options.label: C
options.text: must

options.label: D
options.text: might
options.rationale: “Might” shows something possible, not required.

items.stem: In the sentence “The farmers have planted rice near the river,” which word is the MAIN verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Planted” shows the action; “have” helps show the tense.
explanation.tip: The main verb carries the meaning; helping verbs add detail about time.

options.label: A
options.text: farmers
options.rationale: This is the subject, a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: planted

options.label: C
options.text: have
options.rationale: This is the helping verb.

options.label: D
options.text: river
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Choose the correct helping verb: “The letter ____ delivered yesterday, since it is already in the mailbox.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Must have been” shows a confident conclusion based on strong evidence.
explanation.tip: must have + past participle = a confident conclusion about the past.

options.label: A
options.text: could have been
options.rationale: “Could” also suggests weaker certainty.

options.label: B
options.text: might have been
options.rationale: “Might” suggests weaker certainty than the clear evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: should have been
options.rationale: “Should” implies obligation, not a logical conclusion.

options.label: D
options.text: must have been

items.stem: Which modal verb shows the SMALLEST chance something will happen? “It ____ snow in the desert this winter.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Might” shows only a small possibility.
explanation.tip: might/may = possible; will/must = more certain.

options.label: A
options.text: will
options.rationale: “Will” shows certainty.

options.label: B
options.text: can
options.rationale: “Can” shows ability, not a small chance.

options.label: C
options.text: might

options.label: D
options.text: must
options.rationale: “Must” shows strong certainty or a requirement.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the irregular verb “to be” correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Was” agrees with the singular subject “weather” in the past tense.
explanation.tip: Match “to be” to the subject and the time of the action.

options.label: A
options.text: The weather be unusually cold last March.
options.rationale: “Be” alone is not a complete verb here.

options.label: B
options.text: The weather were unusually cold last March.
options.rationale: “Weather” is singular, so use “was.”

options.label: C
options.text: The weather is unusually cold last March.
options.rationale: “Last March” shows the past, so use “was.”

options.label: D
options.text: The weather was unusually cold last March.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Twins” is plural, so the helping verb must be “have,” not “has.”
explanation.tip: Match the helping verb to the subject.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “After the race, Tariq ____ exhausted.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Looked” links Tariq to the describing word “exhausted” in the past tense.
explanation.tip: Sense verbs like look, seem and feel can act as linking verbs.

options.label: A
options.text: looked

options.label: B
options.text: look
options.rationale: This does not agree with one person in the past.

options.label: C
options.text: looks
options.rationale: The race already happened, so use the past tense.

options.label: D
options.text: looking
options.rationale: This needs a helping verb.

items.stem: Match each verb with the type of verb it is.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each verb plays a different role: showing action, linking, helping, or showing possibility.
explanation.tip: Ask what job the verb is doing in the sentence.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a helping verb with the main verb “finished”?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Had finished” correctly shows an action completed before another point in the past.
explanation.tip: Had + past participle shows one past action finished before another.

options.label: A
options.text: By noon, the workers had finished painting the fence.

options.label: B
options.text: By noon, the workers had finish painting the fence.
options.rationale: After “had,” use the past participle “finished.”

options.label: C
options.text: By noon, the workers has finished painting the fence.
options.rationale: “Workers” is plural, so use “had,” not “has.”

options.label: D
options.text: By noon, the workers have finished painting the fence, yesterday.
options.rationale: “Have” does not match an action placed firmly in the past with “yesterday.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses a modal verb to express a POLITE request?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Would” softens the request and makes it sound polite.
explanation.tip: Would/could often make requests sound more polite than will/can.

options.label: A
options.text: Must you please pass the water jug?
options.rationale: “Must” sounds demanding, not polite.

options.label: B
options.text: Would you please pass the water jug?

options.label: C
options.text: Can you please pass the water jug, immediately?
options.rationale: “Immediately” makes this sound like an order, not a request.

options.label: D
options.text: Will you please pass the water jug, now?
options.rationale: “Will” sounds like a command here.

items.stem: Choose the correct verb form: “By the time the bus arrived, Noor ____ waiting for twenty minutes.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Had been waiting” shows an action that continued up until another past event.
explanation.tip: Had been + -ing shows a longer past action interrupted by a later one.

options.label: A
options.text: was
options.rationale: This does not show the action continuing before the bus arrived.

options.label: B
options.text: had been

options.label: C
options.text: is
options.rationale: This is present tense.

options.label: D
options.text: has been
options.rationale: “Has been” is used for actions continuing into the present, not the past.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive mood with a verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Were” is used after “if” for conditions that are not true, even with a singular subject.
explanation.tip: Unreal “if” clauses use “were,” no matter the subject.

options.label: A
options.text: If I am taller, I could reach the top shelf.
options.rationale: This mixes the present tense with an unreal condition.

options.label: B
options.text: If I were taller, I can reach the top shelf.
options.rationale: The result clause needs “could,” not “can,” to match the unreal condition.

options.label: C
options.text: If I were taller, I could reach the top shelf.

options.label: D
options.text: If I was taller, I could reach the top shelf.
options.rationale: The subjunctive uses “were,” not “was,” after “if” for an unreal condition.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly distinguishes a transitive verb from an intransitive one?

explanation.whyCorrect: A transitive verb passes its action to a direct object; an intransitive verb does not need one.
explanation.tip: Ask “verb + what?” — if there is an answer, it is transitive.

options.label: A
options.text: In both sentences, the verbs are intransitive because no helping verb is used.
options.rationale: Having no helping verb does not make a verb intransitive.

options.label: B
options.text: In “Samir mailed the package,” mailed is intransitive because “package” is a noun.
options.rationale: A noun receiving the action is a direct object, which makes the verb transitive.

options.label: C
options.text: In “Samir arrived,” arrived is transitive because it describes an action.
options.rationale: Showing action alone does not make a verb transitive; it needs a direct object.

options.label: D
options.text: In “Samir mailed the package,” mailed is transitive because it has a direct object; in “Samir arrived,” arrived is intransitive because it has no object.

items.stem: Which word is an action verb? “Lina sketched a map of the old souq.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Sketched” tells what Lina did.
explanation.tip: Action verbs show what someone does.

options.label: A
options.text: sketched

options.label: B
options.text: Lina
options.rationale: This is a proper noun.

options.label: C
options.text: map
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: souq
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Choose the linking verb: “The bread ____ warm right out of the oven.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Seemed” links the bread to the describing word “warm.”
explanation.tip: Linking verbs connect a subject to a word that describes it.

options.label: A
options.text: bread
options.rationale: This is the noun subject.

options.label: B
options.text: oven
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: seemed

options.label: D
options.text: warm
options.rationale: This is the adjective, not the verb.

items.stem: Which sentence contains a helping verb and a main verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Were setting” is a verb phrase: “were” helps and “setting” is the main verb.
explanation.tip: Verb phrases combine a helping verb with a main verb.

options.label: A
options.text: The scouts' tents stood near the river.
options.rationale: “Stood” is the only verb here.

options.label: B
options.text: The scouts were setting up their tents before sunset.

options.label: C
options.text: The scouts set up their tents before sunset.
options.rationale: This has only one main verb, no helping verb.

options.label: D
options.text: The scouts packed their tents at dawn.
options.rationale: “Packed” is the only verb here.

items.stem: Choose the modal verb that shows ABILITY: “Khaled ____ solve the puzzle in under a minute.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Can” shows Khaled is able to solve the puzzle.
explanation.tip: can/could = ability; must = requirement; should = advice.

options.label: A
options.text: should
options.rationale: “Should” shows advice.

options.label: B
options.text: must
options.rationale: “Must” shows requirement, not ability.

options.label: C
options.text: would
options.rationale: “Would” shows a hypothetical choice, not current ability.

options.label: D
options.text: can

items.stem: Which TWO words are verbs? “The kitten pounced on the yarn and tumbled across the rug.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Pounced” and “tumbled” both show what the kitten did.
explanation.tip: Look for every word that shows an action.

options.label: A
options.text: kitten
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: pounced

options.label: C
options.text: yarn
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: tumbled

items.stem: Which sentence uses a modal verb to express NECESSITY rather than possibility?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Must” shows the rule is required, not optional.
explanation.tip: must = required; might/could/may = possible or allowed.

options.label: A
options.text: Visitors might remove their shoes before entering the mosque.
options.rationale: “Might” shows possibility, not a requirement.

options.label: B
options.text: Visitors could remove their shoes before entering the mosque.
options.rationale: “Could” shows ability or possibility.

options.label: C
options.text: Visitors must remove their shoes before entering the mosque.

options.label: D
options.text: Visitors may remove their shoes before entering the mosque.
options.rationale: “May” shows permission, not a strict rule.

items.stem: Choose the correct helping verb: “By next June, Hoda ____ graduated from secondary school.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Will have graduated” shows an action completed by a specific point in the future.
explanation.tip: will have + past participle = future perfect tense.

options.label: A
options.text: will have

options.label: B
options.text: had
options.rationale: “Had” places the action in the past, before now.

options.label: C
options.text: is
options.rationale: This is present tense.

options.label: D
options.text: has
options.rationale: This does not show an action finishing by a future point.

items.stem: Which sentence has a transitive verb (an action passed to a direct object)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Repaired” passes its action onto the direct object “fence.”
explanation.tip: Ask “verb + what?” to find a direct object.

options.label: A
options.text: Adel arrived early.
options.rationale: “Arrived” has no direct object.

options.label: B
options.text: Adel smiled at the puppy.
options.rationale: “Smiled” does not take a direct object here; “at the puppy” is a prepositional phrase.

options.label: C
options.text: Adel worked all afternoon.
options.rationale: “Worked” has no direct object.

options.label: D
options.text: Adel repaired the broken fence.

items.stem: Choose the correct verb: “Neither the players nor the coach ____ satisfied with the result.”

explanation.whyCorrect: With “neither…nor,” the verb agrees with the closer subject, “coach,” which is singular.
explanation.tip: neither/nor: match the verb to the nearer subject.

options.label: A
options.text: is
options.rationale: The sentence describes the past, not the present.

options.label: B
options.text: was

options.label: C
options.text: were
options.rationale: With “neither…nor,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject, “coach.”

options.label: D
options.text: are
options.rationale: The sentence describes the past, not the present.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a linking verb to compare?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Seems” links the recipe to the comparing adjective “easier.”
explanation.tip: Linking verbs take adjectives, not adverbs.

options.label: A
options.text: This recipe seems easier than the last one.

options.label: B
options.text: This recipe seem easier than the last one.
options.rationale: “Recipe” is singular, so the verb is “seems.”

options.label: C
options.text: This recipe seems easily than the last one.
options.rationale: After a linking verb, use an adjective, not an adverb.

options.label: D
options.text: This recipe seeming easier than the last one.
options.rationale: This is not a complete verb.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: An action completed before another past event needs “had,” not “has.”
explanation.tip: Past perfect (had + past participle) shows one past action before another.

items.stem: Which sentence shows the correct use of a modal verb for a logical conclusion?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Must” shows a confident conclusion based on strong evidence.
explanation.tip: must (for conclusions) shows near certainty based on clues.

options.label: A
options.text: The lights are off and the car is gone, so Samir could be at work.
options.rationale: “Could” suggests only a weak possibility, not a strong conclusion.

options.label: B
options.text: The lights are off and the car is gone, so Samir must be at work.

options.label: C
options.text: The lights are off and the car is gone, so Samir might have never arrived.
options.rationale: This ignores the strong evidence already given.

options.label: D
options.text: The lights are off and the car is gone, so Samir should be at work.
options.rationale: “Should” suggests advice, not a conclusion drawn from evidence.

items.stem: Choose the correct verb: “The committee ____ its decision at the end of the meeting.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Committee” acts as one group, so it takes the singular verb “announces.”
explanation.tip: Collective nouns usually take a singular verb when acting as one unit.

options.label: A
options.text: have announced
options.rationale: “Has announced” would be needed, not “have,” for a singular unit.

options.label: B
options.text: announcing
options.rationale: This needs a helping verb.

options.label: C
options.text: announces

options.label: D
options.text: announce
options.rationale: “Committee” is treated as a single unit, so the verb needs -s.

items.stem: Match each verb phrase with the verb tense it shows.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each helping verb combination signals a different time relationship.
explanation.tip: Identify the helping verb first, then the tense it creates.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the verb “lie” (to rest or recline)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Lie” means to rest and takes no direct object.
explanation.tip: lie (no object) = rest; lay (needs object) = put something down.

options.label: A
options.text: The cat likes to lay in the warm sunlight.
options.rationale: “Lay” needs a direct object; use “lie” when nothing is being placed.

options.label: B
options.text: The cat likes to laid in the warm sunlight.
options.rationale: “Laid” is the past tense of “lay,” which needs a direct object.

options.label: C
options.text: The cat likes to lie in the warm sunlight.

options.label: D
options.text: The cat likes to lied in the warm sunlight.
options.rationale: “Lied” means “told an untruth,” not “rested.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a verb in the passive voice?

explanation.whyCorrect: In passive voice, the subject (“bridge”) receives the action instead of performing it.
explanation.tip: Passive voice: subject + be verb + past participle (+ by someone).

options.label: A
options.text: The old bridge repaired a team of engineers last spring.
options.rationale: This reverses the subject and object illogically.

options.label: B
options.text: The old bridge was repair by a team of engineers last spring.
options.rationale: The past participle “repaired,” not “repair,” is needed after “was.”

options.label: C
options.text: A team of engineers repaired the old bridge last spring.
options.rationale: This is active voice; the subject performs the action.

options.label: D
options.text: The old bridge was repaired by a team of engineers last spring.

items.stem: Choose the correct form: “If the museum ____ open later, more visitors would come.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Were” is the subjunctive form used after “if” for conditions that are not true.
explanation.tip: Hypothetical “if” clauses use “were,” regardless of subject.

options.label: A
options.text: is
options.rationale: This describes a real, present condition, not a hypothetical one.

options.label: B
options.text: be
options.rationale: “Be” alone is not a complete verb form here.

options.label: C
options.text: was
options.rationale: The subjunctive after “if” for an unreal condition uses “were.”

options.label: D
options.text: were

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a gerund as the subject, distinguishing it from a verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Swimming” is a gerund — a verb form acting as a noun — serving as the subject of the sentence.
explanation.tip: A gerund (verb + -ing) can act as a noun, unlike an ordinary verb.

options.label: A
options.text: Swimming in the cold sea energized the whole team.

options.label: B
options.text: Swimming in the cold sea energize the whole team.
options.rationale: The subject “swimming” is singular, so the verb must be “energized,” matching tense.

options.label: C
options.text: Swim in the cold sea energized the whole team.
options.rationale: “Swim” alone cannot act as a noun subject here; it needs the -ing form.

options.label: D
options.text: Swum in the cold sea energized the whole team.
options.rationale: “Swum” is a past participle, not a noun form that can serve as a subject.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses an infinitive verb form?

explanation.whyCorrect: “To postpone” is an infinitive — “to” plus the base form of the verb.
explanation.tip: Infinitives = to + the base form of the verb.

options.label: A
options.text: The committee decided postpone the trip until the weather improved.
options.rationale: The infinitive marker “to” is missing before “postpone.”

options.label: B
options.text: The committee decided to postpone the trip until the weather improved.

options.label: C
options.text: The committee decided postponing the trip until the weather improved.
options.rationale: After “decided,” the infinitive “to postpone” is the standard form, not the gerund.

options.label: D
options.text: The committee decided to postponed the trip until the weather improved.
options.rationale: An infinitive uses the base form of the verb: “to postpone,” not “to postponed.”

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Ants kept getting into the kitchen through a crack under the door. Mama placed a thin strip of rubber along the bottom of the door, and the ants stopped coming in.” What problem does the paragraph describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first sentence names the problem: ants entering through the crack.
explanation.tip: The problem is usually named early in a problem-solution paragraph.

options.label: A
options.text: Mama could not find the crack.
options.rationale: She found the crack right away.

options.label: B
options.text: The kitchen door would not close.
options.rationale: The door is not described as broken.

options.label: C
options.text: Ants were getting into the kitchen.

options.label: D
options.text: The rubber strip was too thin.
options.rationale: The strip worked; it is not described as a problem.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The classroom was too hot every afternoon because the window stuck shut. The custodian oiled the window track, and now it opens easily to let in a breeze.” What was the SOLUTION?

explanation.whyCorrect: Oiling the track fixed the stuck window so a breeze could cool the room.
explanation.tip: Look for the action that fixes the stated problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Closing the curtains
options.rationale: Curtains are not mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: Moving the class to another room
options.rationale: The class stayed in the same room.

options.label: C
options.text: Turning on a fan
options.rationale: No fan is mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: Oiling the window track so it would open

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Books kept disappearing from the classroom shelf without being signed out. Ms. Nabil added a sign-out sheet by the shelf, and after that every book that left the room was recorded.” What problem is described?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph states books disappeared without being signed out.
explanation.tip: Find the sentence that names what is going wrong.

options.label: A
options.text: Books were going missing without being recorded.

options.label: B
options.text: The sign-out sheet was lost.
options.rationale: The sheet was added as the fix, not lost.

options.label: C
options.text: Students did not like to read.
options.rationale: Reading interest is not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: The shelf was too small for the books.
options.rationale: Shelf size is not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The soccer field flooded every time it rained because there was nowhere for the water to drain. Workers dug a shallow ditch along one edge, and now the water drains away within an hour.” Choose the solution: the workers ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: Digging the ditch gave the rainwater a path to drain away.
explanation.tip: The solution directly removes the cause of the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: dug a drainage ditch

options.label: B
options.text: covered the field with sand
options.rationale: Sand covering is not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: moved the field to higher ground
options.rationale: The field was not moved.

options.label: D
options.text: built a roof over the field
options.rationale: A roof is not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Stray cats kept knocking over the trash cans behind the bakery, scattering wrappers across the alley. The baker started using a can with a locking lid, and the alley has stayed clean since.” Why did the new trash can solve the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: The lid locked shut, so cats could no longer open the can and spill trash.
explanation.tip: Ask how the solution removes the exact cause of the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: It was painted a bright color.
options.rationale: Color is not mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: Its locking lid kept the cats from knocking it open.

options.label: C
options.text: It was placed indoors.
options.rationale: The can stayed outside, just with a lock.

options.label: D
options.text: It was bigger than the old one.
options.rationale: Size is not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Every morning, students crowded around one water fountain and were late getting to class. The school installed two more fountains along the hallway, and the lines disappeared.” What was the ROOT CAUSE of the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Adding more fountains fixed the shortage, showing the real cause was too few fountains.
explanation.tip: The best-fitting solution often reveals the true cause of a problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Classes started too early.
options.rationale: Class start time is not blamed in the text.

options.label: B
options.text: Students did not want water.
options.rationale: Students clearly wanted water, since they crowded the fountain.

options.label: C
options.text: There were not enough fountains for the number of students.

options.label: D
options.text: The fountain was broken.
options.rationale: The fountain worked; there just were not enough.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The community garden's tomato plants kept wilting because nobody watered them on weekends. The gardeners made a watering schedule so someone always came on Saturdays and Sundays.” Choose the word that completes the solution: the gardeners made a watering ____ for weekends.

explanation.whyCorrect: A schedule ensured someone watered the plants every weekend.
explanation.tip: The solution should directly supply what was missing.

options.label: A
options.text: basket
options.rationale: A basket is not mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: schedule

options.label: C
options.text: sign
options.rationale: A sign alone would not water the plants.

options.label: D
options.text: fence
options.rationale: A fence would not provide water.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The library's returned books piled up on the front desk because there was no cart to carry them back to the shelves. The librarian borrowed a rolling cart from the office, and the books were reshelved the same day.” What EFFECT did the cart have?

explanation.whyCorrect: With a cart, the librarian could move books to shelves right away.
explanation.tip: The effect of a solution undoes the original problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer students returned books.
options.rationale: The problem was about shelving, not returning.

options.label: B
options.text: The front desk was removed.
options.rationale: The desk is not mentioned as removed.

options.label: C
options.text: The library bought more books.
options.rationale: Buying books is not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: Books were returned to the shelves quickly instead of piling up.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Farmers near the canal lost part of their crop every summer when the water level dropped too low to reach their fields. They pooled money to build a small pump station, which now lifts water into the irrigation channels even in dry months.” Which sentence BEST summarizes the problem and solution?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence captures both the stated cause (low water) and the fix (the pump station).
explanation.tip: A good summary names both the problem and the matching solution.

options.label: A
options.text: Low water levels were hurting crops, so farmers built a pump station to lift water to their fields.

options.label: B
options.text: Crops failed because of pests, so farmers used a spray.
options.rationale: Pests are not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: Farmers argued over water rights, so the government stepped in.
options.rationale: No argument or government action is mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: The canal dried up completely, so farmers dug a new one.
options.rationale: The canal did not dry up completely; only the level dropped.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The school's recycling bins filled up within a day because they were never emptied until Friday. The janitor switched to emptying them every morning instead, and the bins stopped overflowing.” What is the problem-solution structure signal in this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph names a cause of overflow and then the change that fixed it.
explanation.tip: Problem-solution paragraphs link a specific cause to a matching fix.

options.label: A
options.text: A description of what the bins look like
options.rationale: The paragraph focuses on the fix, not appearance.

options.label: B
options.text: A cause (bins emptied only once a week) is followed by a fix (daily emptying).

options.label: C
options.text: A list of steps in time order
options.rationale: The paragraph is not a sequence of steps for one task.

options.label: D
options.text: A comparison between two kinds of bins
options.rationale: No second type of bin is compared.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Visitors kept getting lost in the museum because the signs pointed in confusing directions. Staff repainted the floor with colored lines leading to each exhibit, and visitors stopped asking for directions.” Choose the best word: the floor lines acted as a ____ for visitors.

explanation.whyCorrect: The colored lines guided visitors to each exhibit.
explanation.tip: Ask what job the solution performs for the people affected.

options.label: A
options.text: barrier
options.rationale: Lines do not block movement; they direct it.

options.label: B
options.text: warning
options.rationale: The lines are not described as a warning.

options.label: C
options.text: guide

options.label: D
options.text: decoration
options.rationale: The lines served a practical purpose, not just looks.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The town's single bridge became dangerously crowded every market day, and two near-accidents were reported last month. The council added a second, narrower bridge for pedestrians only, separating foot traffic from carts.” Which detail BEST supports that the solution addressed safety, not just crowding?

explanation.whyCorrect: The near-accidents show the real danger that the new bridge was built to prevent.
explanation.tip: Look for evidence in the problem that matches the goal of the solution.

options.label: A
options.text: The bridge is described as narrow.
options.rationale: Narrowness describes the bridge, not the safety reason.

options.label: B
options.text: The bridge is only for pedestrians.
options.rationale: This describes who uses it, not why it was needed.

options.label: C
options.text: The mention of two near-accidents shows the danger the new bridge was meant to prevent.

options.label: D
options.text: The council made the decision.
options.rationale: Who decided is not evidence about safety.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Shoppers at the weekend market often could not find a specific stall because none of the aisles were labeled. Organizers hung numbered signs above each row and printed a small map at the entrance.” Why did organizers use TWO solutions instead of one?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each solution helps at a different moment: planning ahead and finding a stall once inside.
explanation.tip: Sometimes two solutions work together to solve one problem from different angles.

options.label: A
options.text: The first solution did not work at all.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a failed first attempt.

options.label: B
options.text: Shoppers complained about both problems separately.
options.rationale: Only one unlabeled-aisle problem is described.

options.label: C
options.text: One solution was too expensive to use alone.
options.rationale: Cost is not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: Signs help shoppers already inside, and a map helps them plan before they even enter.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The apartment building's elevator broke down twice a month because it was overloaded during rush hour. The building manager posted a weight limit sign and asked residents to use the stairs for short trips.” The manager's solution mainly targets the ____ of the problem.

explanation.whyCorrect: Reducing overload (the cause of breakdowns) directly targets why the elevator failed.
explanation.tip: The strongest solutions remove the actual cause, not just a symptom.

options.label: A
options.text: history
options.rationale: No history of the elevator is given.

options.label: B
options.text: location
options.rationale: Where the elevator is located is not the issue.

options.label: C
options.text: cost
options.rationale: Repair cost is not discussed.

options.label: D
options.text: cause

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Every rainy season, muddy water from the hillside washed across the only road into the village, sometimes stranding cars for hours. Villagers dug a drainage channel along the hillside to redirect the runoff into a nearby stream.” What would happen if the channel were removed?

explanation.whyCorrect: The channel was built specifically to redirect runoff away from the road; removing it would bring the flooding back.
explanation.tip: Imagine undoing the solution to check that it truly addresses the cause.

options.label: A
options.text: The road would likely flood with muddy runoff again during rainy season.

options.label: B
options.text: The village would need a new road entirely.
options.rationale: The paragraph never suggests building a new road.

options.label: C
options.text: The stream would dry up.
options.rationale: The stream receiving water is not the problem being solved.

options.label: D
options.text: Cars would travel faster on the road.
options.rationale: Speed is not related to the channel.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A small fishing village noticed its catch shrinking each year as larger boats from other towns fished the same waters daily. Local fishermen agreed among themselves to fish only every other day and to avoid certain breeding areas during spawning season.” Which word BEST describes the type of solution chosen?

explanation.whyCorrect: The fishermen chose to limit themselves through an agreement, not through an outside law or fine.
explanation.tip: Notice whether a solution comes from a rule, a tool, or people's own choices.

options.label: A
options.text: a law passed by the government
options.rationale: No government law is mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: a voluntary agreement among the fishermen themselves

options.label: C
options.text: a new type of fishing boat
options.rationale: No new equipment is described.

options.label: D
options.text: a fine for overfishing
options.rationale: No fine or punishment is mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “After several students complained that the cafeteria ran out of the healthy lunch option by noon, the school began preparing twice as many of that meal and moved the serving station closer to the entrance.” Which solution addresses SUPPLY, and which addresses ACCESS?

explanation.whyCorrect: Supply means how much food exists; access means how easily students can reach it.
explanation.tip: Separate a solution's effect on quantity from its effect on availability or location.

options.label: A
options.text: Both solutions address only access.
options.rationale: Doubling the meal changes how much food exists, which is about supply, not location.

options.label: B
options.text: Both solutions address only supply.
options.rationale: Moving the station changes where students can reach the food, which is about access.

options.label: C
options.text: Doubling the meal addresses supply; moving the station closer addresses access.

options.label: D
options.text: Moving the station addresses supply; doubling the meal addresses access.
options.rationale: These are reversed; doubling the amount is about supply, not location.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A coastal town's beach shrank noticeably each year as waves carried sand out to sea faster than it was replaced naturally. Engineers proposed two options: building a long wall of boulders to block the waves, or regularly trucking in new sand from a nearby quarry. The town chose the second option because the wall might change wave patterns and harm nearby reefs.” Why did the town reject the FIRST option, even though it would also fix the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph explains the wall was rejected because of its possible harm to wave patterns and reefs, not cost or preference.
explanation.tip: A solution can solve one problem while risking a new one — weigh both effects.

options.label: A
options.text: It would take longer to build than trucking in sand.
options.rationale: Construction time is not compared.

options.label: B
options.text: It was the option residents preferred.
options.rationale: Resident preference is not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: It would cost less than trucking in sand.
options.rationale: Cost is not compared in the paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: It could create a new problem by disrupting wave patterns and damaging the reefs.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A clinic in a small town struggled to see every patient because only one doctor was available most days, and patients sometimes waited since early morning. The clinic began scheduling appointments by phone the day before, and added a part-time nurse to handle minor concerns, freeing the doctor for serious cases.” Which sentence BEST explains why TWO separate solutions were needed to fully solve the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: The two causes — unpredictable crowding and an overloaded doctor — each needed a different fix.
explanation.tip: When a problem has more than one cause, look for a solution that addresses each cause.

options.label: A
options.text: Scheduling reduced crowding from walk-ins, while the nurse reduced the doctor's workload — together solving both the waiting and the overload.

options.label: B
options.text: Scheduling alone would have solved everything.
options.rationale: Scheduling does not address the doctor's heavy workload for minor cases.

options.label: C
options.text: Neither solution was actually necessary.
options.rationale: The paragraph presents both as effective in combination.

options.label: D
options.text: The nurse alone would have solved everything.
options.rationale: A nurse alone does not fix the problem of unpredictable walk-in crowding.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The rooftop garden's herbs kept dying because the black plastic pots absorbed too much heat in the afternoon sun. The gardener switched to light-colored ceramic pots, and the herbs stayed healthy all summer.” What problem does the paragraph describe?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph states the plastic pots absorbed too much heat, harming the herbs.
explanation.tip: Identify exactly what is causing harm before looking for the fix.

options.label: A
options.text: The ceramic pots were too expensive.
options.rationale: Cost is not discussed.

options.label: B
options.text: The herbs were dying from overheated pots.

options.label: C
options.text: The rooftop had no sunlight.
options.rationale: Too much heat, not lack of sunlight, is the issue.

options.label: D
options.text: The herbs were not getting enough water.
options.rationale: Watering is not mentioned as the issue.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Visitors to the aquarium often missed feeding time because it was not announced anywhere. Staff began posting the schedule at the entrance and announcing it over the speakers ten minutes before.” Choose the solution: staff ____ the feeding schedule.

explanation.whyCorrect: Announcing and posting the schedule let visitors know when feeding time would happen.
explanation.tip: The solution should give people the missing information.

options.label: A
options.text: announced

options.label: B
options.text: hid
options.rationale: Hiding the schedule would make the problem worse.

options.label: C
options.text: delayed
options.rationale: Delaying is not mentioned as the fix.

options.label: D
options.text: cancelled
options.rationale: Feeding time was not cancelled.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A rural school's only computer lab had internet so slow that videos froze constantly during lessons. The district installed a stronger signal booster on the roof, and streaming became smooth within days.” What was the CAUSE of the problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: The weak signal is identified as the reason streaming kept freezing.
explanation.tip: The solution (a booster) targets exactly what was weak: the signal.

options.label: A
options.text: Old, broken computers
options.rationale: The computers themselves are not described as broken.

options.label: B
options.text: Too many computers in the lab
options.rationale: The number of computers is not blamed.

options.label: C
options.text: A weak internet signal reaching the school

options.label: D
options.text: A shortage of teachers
options.rationale: Teacher shortage is not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Fruit vendors near the train station lost customers because their stalls blocked the sidewalk, forcing shoppers to walk in the street. The city moved the stalls to a designated row along one side, keeping the sidewalk clear.” What EFFECT did moving the stalls have?

explanation.whyCorrect: Moving the stalls cleared the sidewalk, so shoppers no longer had to walk in the street.
explanation.tip: Match the solution's effect directly to the original danger or inconvenience.

options.label: A
options.text: The train station closed early.
options.rationale: Station hours are not mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: The street became wider.
options.rationale: The street's width did not change.

options.label: C
options.text: Vendors sold less fruit than before.
options.rationale: The paragraph does not say sales dropped.

options.label: D
options.text: Shoppers could walk safely without stepping into the street.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The community pool's filter clogged every week because swimmers tracked in sand from the nearby beach. The pool added a rinse station with a small shower at the entrance, and clogging dropped sharply.” Choose the word: the rinse station removed sand ____ swimmers entered the pool.

explanation.whyCorrect: Rinsing before entry removed the sand before it could reach the filter.
explanation.tip: Timing matters: a solution often works by acting before the problem occurs.

options.label: A
options.text: without
options.rationale: This does not fit the sentence's meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: before

options.label: C
options.text: after
options.rationale: Rinsing after would not prevent sand from entering the pool.

options.label: D
options.text: despite
options.rationale: This does not fit the sentence's meaning.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “An orchard's apple trees produced fewer apples each year as the local bee population shrank, likely due to a nearby pesticide spray drifting onto wildflowers the bees depended on. The orchard owner planted a wide strip of pesticide-free wildflowers along the property's edge to draw bees back.” What is the ROOT CAUSE identified in the paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph traces the shrinking bee population to pesticide drift harming their food supply.
explanation.tip: Trace the chain: fewer apples, then fewer bees, then why bees declined.

options.label: A
options.text: Pesticide drift was destroying the bees' food source.

options.label: B
options.text: The apple trees were too old to produce fruit.
options.rationale: Tree age is not blamed.

options.label: C
options.text: A disease was spreading among the apple trees.
options.rationale: No disease is mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: The orchard owner stopped watering the trees.
options.rationale: Watering is not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A warehouse's shipments were delayed each week because workers spent hours searching for misplaced boxes in a disorganized storage room. Managers introduced a labeling system with numbered shelves and a digital inventory list.” How does the labeling system solve the underlying problem?

explanation.whyCorrect: Numbered shelves and a digital list let workers locate a box directly, ending the lengthy searches.
explanation.tip: Ask whether the solution removes the need for the wasted effort, not just adds more effort.

options.label: A
options.text: It hires more workers to search faster.
options.rationale: No new workers are mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: It lets workers find exactly where a box is instead of searching the whole room.

options.label: C
options.text: It reduces the number of shipments sent out.
options.rationale: Shipment quantity is not changed.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes boxes smaller so they fit on shelves.
options.rationale: Box size is not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A riverside village lost several meters of farmland every flood season as fast-moving water ate away at the unprotected riverbank. Villagers planted rows of deep-rooted reeds along the bank, which held the soil firmly in place.” The reeds mainly act to ____ the soil.

explanation.whyCorrect: The reeds' deep roots hold, or anchor, the soil in place against the river's current.
explanation.tip: Think about the physical action a solution performs on the problem.

options.label: A
options.text: cover
options.rationale: Covering alone would not stop fast-moving water from eroding soil.

options.label: B
options.text: soften
options.rationale: Softer soil would erode more easily, not less.

options.label: C
options.text: anchor

options.label: D
options.text: dry
options.rationale: Drying the soil is not the goal.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A busy intersection near a new mall caused traffic jams every evening because the single traffic light cycle did not account for the sudden rise in cars. Engineers reprogrammed the light to extend the green signal during peak hours and added a dedicated left-turn lane.” Which sentence BEST summarizes the problem and solution together?

explanation.whyCorrect: This option correctly links the stated cause (traffic growth outpacing the old timing) with the stated fix.
explanation.tip: A strong summary mentions both why the problem happened and exactly how it was fixed.

options.label: A
options.text: The mall was too far from the main road, so a new road was built.
options.rationale: No new road is mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: The intersection had no traffic light at all, so one was installed.
options.rationale: A light already existed; it just needed adjusting.

options.label: C
options.text: Increased traffic overwhelmed an outdated light cycle, so engineers adjusted the timing and added a turn lane.

options.label: D
options.text: Drivers ignored the traffic light, so police were stationed there.
options.rationale: No police action is mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A small fishing cooperative noticed its total catch dropping for three straight years, even though the number of boats going out stayed the same. Marine biologists found that certain fish species were being caught before they were old enough to reproduce. The cooperative agreed to use nets with larger holes, letting younger fish escape.” What is the problem-solution relationship shown here?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph explains that catching young fish reduced future stock, and larger net holes addressed exactly that cause.
explanation.tip: Look for the specific cause named by the experts, not just the general problem.

options.label: A
options.text: Fish were migrating elsewhere, so boats traveled farther.
options.rationale: Migration is not mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: Too many boats were going out, so the cooperative reduced the fleet.
options.rationale: The number of boats stayed the same.

options.label: C
options.text: The water had become too polluted, so fishing was paused.
options.rationale: Pollution is not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: Catching young fish before they could reproduce was reducing future fish stock, so larger net holes let young fish survive.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A seaside town's underground parking garage flooded during every heavy storm because its drainage pipes were too narrow for sudden downpours. The town installed wider pipes and added a backup pump as a second line of defense.” The backup pump exists mainly as a ____ in case the pipes still cannot keep up.

explanation.whyCorrect: The pump is a backup safeguard in case the wider pipes are still overwhelmed.
explanation.tip: A second solution added 'just in case' usually serves as a safeguard, not a full replacement.

options.label: A
options.text: decoration
options.rationale: A pump serves a functional purpose, not decoration.

options.label: B
options.text: shortcut
options.rationale: A pump is not described as speeding anything up.

options.label: C
options.text: replacement
options.rationale: The pump works alongside the pipes, not instead of them.

options.label: D
options.text: safeguard

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A manufacturing plant's workers reported frequent headaches, and an inspection found carbon monoxide levels slightly above safe limits near one machine. Rather than simply installing air filters, engineers traced the issue to a cracked exhaust pipe on that machine and replaced it.” Why did engineers choose to replace the pipe instead of just adding filters?

explanation.whyCorrect: Fixing the cracked pipe addressed the actual source of the gas, rather than managing its symptoms.
explanation.tip: A solution that targets the source is usually stronger than one that only manages the symptom.

options.label: A
options.text: Filters would only reduce the gas already leaking, while replacing the pipe stopped the leak at its source.

options.label: B
options.text: Filters were too expensive to install.
options.rationale: Cost is not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: Workers refused to wear filter masks.
options.rationale: Masks are not mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: The machine itself needed to be replaced entirely.
options.rationale: Only the pipe, not the whole machine, needed replacement.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “An animal shelter became overcrowded within a year of opening because it accepted every stray brought in, with no limit on intake. The shelter partnered with three nearby clinics to offer free spay-and-neuter days, hoping to reduce the number of strays born each year.” Which detail shows this solution targets a LONG-TERM cause rather than the immediate overcrowding?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reducing future births addresses the underlying cause of overcrowding over time, rather than solving today's crowding directly.
explanation.tip: Some solutions fix a problem's root cause over time instead of the immediate symptom.

options.label: A
options.text: The shelter stopped accepting new animals.
options.rationale: The shelter is not described as refusing intake.

options.label: B
options.text: The partnership aims to reduce future strays being born, not to immediately empty the shelter.

options.label: C
options.text: The clinics charged a small fee for the service.
options.rationale: The service is described as free, and fees are not the focus anyway.

options.label: D
options.text: The shelter built a bigger building.
options.rationale: No construction is mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A software company's servers kept overheating during summer months because the server room's air conditioning unit was never upgraded as more servers were added over the years. The company installed a second, larger cooling unit and added vents to improve airflow.” The overheating problem grew worse over time mainly because the cooling system failed to ____ with the growing number of servers.

explanation.whyCorrect: The cooling system did not grow, or scale, to match the increasing number of servers.
explanation.tip: Look for a mismatch between a fixed resource and a growing demand.

options.label: A
options.text: scale

options.label: B
options.text: compete
options.rationale: Competition between systems is not the issue.

options.label: C
options.text: decorate
options.rationale: Appearance is irrelevant to cooling capacity.

options.label: D
options.text: communicate
options.rationale: Communication between machines is not the issue.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A well that supplied drinking water to several farms tested positive for a mild contaminant believed to come from fertilizer runoff on nearby fields. Rather than closing the well immediately, officials installed a filtration system at the wellhead while working with farmers to create a buffer zone of unfertilized land.” Why did officials use TWO different solutions?

explanation.whyCorrect: Together, the two solutions address both the current contamination and its future cause.
explanation.tip: Immediate fixes and long-term prevention often work together to fully solve a problem.

options.label: A
options.text: One solution failed completely before the other was tried.
options.rationale: Nothing indicates the filter failed.

options.label: B
options.text: The well needed to be relocated entirely.
options.rationale: Relocating the well is never discussed.

options.label: C
options.text: The filter solves the immediate water-safety problem, while the buffer zone prevents future contamination.

options.label: D
options.text: Farmers refused to cooperate with just one plan.
options.rationale: No refusal is mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Residents near a regional airport filed repeated noise complaints after a new, more frequent flight schedule began. Rather than reducing flights, which airline officials said would hurt the local economy, the airport adjusted flight paths to avoid flying directly over the densest neighborhoods during early morning and late night hours.” Which word BEST describes the airport's approach to balancing two competing needs?

explanation.whyCorrect: Adjusting flight paths let the airport reduce noise for residents without cutting flights the economy relied on.
explanation.tip: When a solution partly satisfies two different groups' needs, it is usually a compromise.

options.label: A
options.text: apology
options.rationale: An apology alone would not change the flight paths.

options.label: B
options.text: relocation
options.rationale: The airport itself was not moved.

options.label: C
options.text: refusal
options.rationale: The airport did take action, so it did not simply refuse to respond.

options.label: D
options.text: compromise

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A coastal fishing fleet noticed its squid catch dropping sharply, and researchers linked the decline to warmer-than-usual water temperatures pushing squid populations farther offshore. Rather than fighting the warming water directly, which was beyond their control, fishermen began tracking satellite temperature maps to locate where squid had migrated.” Why was this solution chosen over trying to fix the water temperature?

explanation.whyCorrect: Since the fishermen could not control ocean temperature, they adapted their methods to the new conditions instead.
explanation.tip: Some solutions work around a cause that cannot be controlled, rather than removing it.

options.label: A
options.text: The cause (ocean warming) was outside the fishermen's control, so they adapted to it instead.

options.label: B
options.text: Fixing the temperature would have been cheaper.
options.rationale: Cost comparison is not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: Researchers were unable to find the cause.
options.rationale: The cause is clearly identified.

options.label: D
options.text: The fleet preferred using new technology regardless of cost.
options.rationale: Preference for technology alone is not the stated reason.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A lake once famous for clear water began turning murky green each summer as an invasive algae species spread rapidly, fed partly by fertilizer runoff and partly by warmer summer temperatures that let the algae grow faster. Officials introduced fertilizer-use limits for nearby farms, but acknowledged this alone would not fully solve the problem.” Why does the paragraph suggest the fertilizer limit is only a PARTIAL solution?

explanation.whyCorrect: Since the algae has two causes, fixing only one (fertilizer runoff) leaves the other (warm temperatures) unaddressed.
explanation.tip: When a problem has multiple causes, a solution addressing only one cause is only a partial fix.

options.label: A
options.text: The lake had too little water to dilute the algae.
options.rationale: Water volume is not discussed.

options.label: B
options.text: Warmer temperatures, a second cause of the algae growth, are not addressed by limiting fertilizer.

options.label: C
options.text: The farmers refused to follow the new limit.
options.rationale: No refusal is mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: The algae had already spread to other lakes.
options.rationale: Spreading to other lakes is not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A city's downtown delivery trucks caused constant congestion because drivers had no reliable way to know which loading zones were free, often circling blocks while searching for space. The city installed sensors in each loading zone connected to an app that showed real-time availability, and congestion dropped noticeably within a month, though a few drivers still circled out of habit.” What does the detail about drivers 'still circling out of habit' reveal about the solution?

explanation.whyCorrect: The lingering habit shows that fixing the information gap does not instantly change old behaviors.
explanation.tip: A solution can remove a problem's cause while people's habits take longer to catch up.

options.label: A
options.text: The app was too difficult for drivers to use.
options.rationale: Difficulty using the app is not mentioned.

options.label: B
options.text: The sensors did not actually work.
options.rationale: Congestion dropped, showing the sensors worked.

options.label: C
options.text: Even a strong technical solution may take time to fully change people's established behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: The city planned to remove the sensors soon.
options.rationale: Removal plans are not mentioned.

items.stem: Read the sentence. “The new playground is finally finished, and it is wonderful to see children laughing on the bright blue slide again.” How does the author feel about the new playground?

explanation.whyCorrect: Words like “wonderful” and “laughing” show the author's positive feeling.
explanation.tip: Look for feeling words to find an author's view.

options.label: A
options.text: The author is confused by it.
options.rationale: There is no confusion in the sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: The author does not care about it.
options.rationale: Describing it as “wonderful” shows care.

options.label: C
options.text: The author is upset about it.
options.rationale: Words like “wonderful” and “laughing” show happiness, not anger.

options.label: D
options.text: The author is happy about it.

items.stem: Read the sentence. “Sadly, the old oak tree by the school gate had to be cut down after the storm damaged its roots.” What word shows the author's feeling about the tree being cut down?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Sadly” directly states the author's feeling about the event.
explanation.tip: Feeling words often appear at the very start of a sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Sadly

options.label: B
options.text: Storm
options.rationale: This names what caused damage.

options.label: C
options.text: Old
options.rationale: This describes the tree's age.

options.label: D
options.text: Roots
options.rationale: This names a part of the tree.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Every classroom should have a recycling bin. Paper waste piles up fast, and a simple bin would keep useful material out of the trash.” What is the author's PURPOSE in this paragraph?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author argues that schools “should” add bins, which is persuasive writing.
explanation.tip: Words like “should” often signal an author trying to persuade.

options.label: A
options.text: To compare two kinds of bins
options.rationale: Only one kind of bin is discussed.

options.label: B
options.text: To persuade schools to add recycling bins

options.label: C
options.text: To describe how paper is made
options.rationale: Paper-making is not explained.

options.label: D
options.text: To entertain with a story about trash
options.rationale: There is no story.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The bakery down the street raised its prices again this month. Families who used to stop by every week now walk right past the window.” What is the author's attitude toward the price increase?

explanation.whyCorrect: Describing families walking past instead of stopping shows the author sees the price increase as harmful.
explanation.tip: Authors often reveal their view through the details and effects they choose to describe.

options.label: A
options.text: The author is excited about the new prices.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests excitement.

options.label: B
options.text: The author has no opinion about the prices.
options.rationale: The detail about families walking past shows a clear concern.

options.label: C
options.text: The author views it as a problem driving customers away.

options.label: D
options.text: The author thinks the bakery deserves more customers.
options.rationale: The paragraph shows customers leaving, not increasing.

items.stem: An author's choice of words, like calling something “wonderful” instead of just “new,” can reveal the author's perspective.

explanation.whyCorrect: Descriptive words beyond plain facts often show how an author feels.
explanation.tip: Compare a neutral word to an emotional one to spot perspective.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The city finally repaired the cracked sidewalk on Palm Street, three years after residents first reported it. While the repair is welcome, many wonder why such a simple fix took so long.” How would you describe the author's perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph praises the fix but questions the long delay, showing a mixed view.
explanation.tip: An author's perspective can include both approval and criticism in the same paragraph.

options.label: A
options.text: Entirely positive about the city's quick action
options.rationale: The three-year delay is criticized, so the view is not entirely positive.

options.label: B
options.text: Completely neutral with no opinion at all
options.rationale: The questioning tone shows the author does have an opinion.

options.label: C
options.text: Entirely negative about the repair itself
options.rationale: The repair itself is called “welcome,” so the view is not entirely negative.

options.label: D
options.text: Mixed — glad the sidewalk is fixed but critical of the long delay

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Some say the new museum downtown is too expensive to visit often. Still, anyone who has seen the dinosaur hall knows it is worth every coin.” Which phrase BEST reveals the author's own perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: By calling it “worth every coin,” the author pushes back against the cost complaint and shares a personal view.
explanation.tip: Watch for a turn like “still” that signals the author's true opinion.

options.label: A
options.text: “worth every coin”

options.label: B
options.text: “anyone who has seen”
options.rationale: This introduces the author's claim rather than stating it.

options.label: C
options.text: “the new museum downtown”
options.rationale: This simply names the museum.

options.label: D
options.text: “too expensive to visit often”
options.rationale: This states what “some say,” not the author's own view.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Supporters of the new highway argue it will cut travel time in half. Opponents point out it will pass within a hundred meters of the elementary school, filling the playground with exhaust fumes during recess.” How does the author present this issue?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph gives a benefit from supporters and a concern from opponents, showing balance.
explanation.tip: A balanced author presents more than one perspective on an issue.

options.label: A
options.text: By only showing the highway's benefits
options.rationale: The paragraph also raises a concern about the school.

options.label: B
options.text: By showing both sides of the argument instead of taking one side

options.label: C
options.text: By refusing to mention any opinions at all
options.rationale: Both supporters' and opponents' opinions are included.

options.label: D
options.text: By only showing the highway's dangers
options.rationale: The paragraph also mentions the benefit of cutting travel time.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The factory's new filters have reduced smoke above the town by half, a real improvement worth celebrating. Even so, residents living closest to the factory still report trouble breathing some mornings.” Which detail SHIFTS the paragraph from praise toward concern?

explanation.whyCorrect: After praising the improvement, the author adds the breathing complaints to show the problem is not fully solved.
explanation.tip: Look for the sentence that turns a positive statement into a more complicated one.

options.label: A
options.text: The phrase “worth celebrating”
options.rationale: This phrase is part of the praise, not the shift away from it.

options.label: B
options.text: The fact that filters were installed
options.rationale: Installing filters supports the praise, not the shift.

options.label: C
options.text: The mention of residents still having trouble breathing

options.label: D
options.text: The claim that smoke was reduced by half
options.rationale: This is also part of the praise.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Proponents of the four-day school week insist students return refreshed and more focused. Critics counter that a longer school day leaves younger children exhausted by the final class, undercutting any gain in focus.” What rhetorical technique does the author use to present this debate?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph states a benefit, then immediately presents an opposing concern that challenges it directly.
explanation.tip: A claim followed by a direct counterclaim is a common way authors frame debates.

options.label: A
options.text: Using only statistics to prove one side right
options.rationale: No statistics are given in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeating the same claim using different words
options.rationale: The second sentence introduces a new, opposing idea, not a repeat.

options.label: C
options.text: Telling a personal story about one student
options.rationale: No personal story is included.

options.label: D
options.text: Presenting a claim and then a counterclaim that directly challenges it

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Few would deny that the new toll road eases congestion on the old highway. What goes unmentioned in most official reports, however, is that the toll itself falls hardest on commuters who can least afford the extra cost each week.” What does the phrase “goes unmentioned in most official reports” suggest about the author's perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pointing out what reports leave out shows the author believes an important perspective, the cost burden on commuters, is being overlooked.
explanation.tip: Noticing what a text leaves out can reveal an author's critical perspective.

options.label: A
options.text: The author is critical that an important downside is being left out of the official discussion.

options.label: B
options.text: The author believes the toll road has no real downsides.
options.rationale: The author points directly to a downside: the cost burden on commuters.

options.label: C
options.text: The author is simply restating what the official reports already say.
options.rationale: The author adds a point the reports do not include, rather than repeating them.

options.label: D
options.text: The author fully supports the official reports' conclusions.
options.rationale: The phrase signals disagreement, not support.

items.stem: Read the sentence. “Thankfully, the leaky roof over the gym was finally patched before the rainy season began.” How does the author feel about the roof being patched?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Thankfully” shows the author's relief that the repair happened in time.
explanation.tip: A single feeling word at the start of a sentence often reveals the author's attitude.

options.label: A
options.text: Annoyed
options.rationale: “Thankfully” shows relief, not annoyance.

options.label: B
options.text: Relieved

options.label: C
options.text: Indifferent
options.rationale: A feeling word like “thankfully” shows the author does care.

options.label: D
options.text: Embarrassed
options.rationale: Nothing suggests embarrassment.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Plastic bags clog storm drains and end up tangled in riverbank plants for years. Banning them from stores is a small step that could make a real difference.” What is the author's position on banning plastic bags?

explanation.whyCorrect: Calling the ban “a real difference” shows the author favors it.
explanation.tip: Look for words that show approval or disapproval of a specific action.

options.label: A
options.text: The author opposes the ban.
options.rationale: The paragraph argues banning bags “could make a real difference,” showing support.

options.label: B
options.text: The author is undecided about the ban.
options.rationale: Calling it “a small step that could make a real difference” shows a clear position.

options.label: C
options.text: The author supports the ban.

options.label: D
options.text: The author only discusses storm drains, not bags.
options.rationale: Storm drains are mentioned as evidence for the author's position on bags.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The town's only bookstore closed last week after thirty years, and the empty storefront already feels like a missing tooth on Main Street.” Which phrase BEST reveals the author's feeling about the closing?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing the empty storefront to a missing tooth shows the author's sense of loss.
explanation.tip: Comparisons can carry an author's emotional view.

options.label: A
options.text: “after thirty years”
options.rationale: This gives a fact about the bookstore's history.

options.label: B
options.text: “the empty storefront”
options.rationale: This describes the scene without the feeling comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: “closed last week”
options.rationale: This states a fact without revealing feeling.

options.label: D
options.text: “a missing tooth on Main Street”

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Supporters of later school start times cite research showing teenagers need more sleep. Still, some parents worry a later schedule would clash with work hours and after-school sports.” How would you describe the author's approach here?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph includes a reason for later starts and a concern against them, showing a balanced approach.
explanation.tip: A balanced paragraph usually includes both support and concerns on an issue.

options.label: A
options.text: Presenting both the research in favor and the concerns against the change

options.label: B
options.text: Avoiding the topic of school start times entirely
options.rationale: The entire paragraph focuses on this exact topic.

options.label: C
options.text: Arguing only that schools should keep the current schedule
options.rationale: The paragraph also presents research favoring a change.

options.label: D
options.text: Arguing only that schools should start later
options.rationale: The paragraph also raises parents' concerns.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Drone deliveries promise packages within the hour, a convenience many customers welcome. Yet residents near the new delivery hub describe a constant buzzing overhead that makes afternoons on the porch far less peaceful.” Which sentence reveals a perspective DIFFERENT from the customers mentioned?

explanation.whyCorrect: The buzzing complaint shows a different, more negative perspective held by nearby residents.
explanation.tip: A paragraph can shift between perspectives of different groups affected by the same thing.

options.label: A
options.text: The sentence naming drone deliveries directly
options.rationale: This simply introduces the topic.

options.label: B
options.text: The sentence about residents hearing constant buzzing overhead

options.label: C
options.text: The sentence calling fast delivery a convenience
options.rationale: This also reflects the customers' positive view.

options.label: D
options.text: The sentence about packages arriving within the hour
options.rationale: This reflects the customers' welcomed convenience.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The city's new electric buses are, by most measures, a success: quieter streets and cleaner air near every stop. The one persistent complaint is that charging delays have caused several routes to run late during the coldest winter mornings.” What is the author's OVERALL perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author calls the buses a success overall but still notes one real problem, showing a mostly positive but not uncritical view.
explanation.tip: An author's overall perspective can lean one way while still including a fair concern.

options.label: A
options.text: Entirely negative about the buses
options.rationale: The paragraph calls the buses “a success” overall.

options.label: B
options.text: Completely neutral, stating only facts
options.rationale: Calling it “a success” expresses a clear positive judgment.

options.label: C
options.text: Largely positive, with one specific concern noted

options.label: D
options.text: Entirely positive with no concerns at all
