options.rationale: The charging delay complaint is clearly mentioned.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Standardized tests, their defenders argue, offer a fair way to compare students across different schools. Critics respond that a single test score ignores everything from a student's home situation to their native language.” Which word signals that the author is introducing an OPPOSING view?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Critics” signals that a different, opposing group's perspective is about to be presented.
explanation.tip: Words like supporters/critics or proponents/opponents often mark a shift in perspective.

options.label: A
options.text: “standardized”
options.rationale: This simply names the type of test.

options.label: B
options.text: “fair”
options.rationale: This word is part of the first view's claim, not the signal of a shift.

options.label: C
options.text: “defenders”
options.rationale: This word introduces the first view, not the opposing one.

options.label: D
options.text: “Critics”

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Public art installations downtown have drawn praise from visitors who photograph the murals for social media. Longtime residents, however, note that the funding for these murals came from a budget once used for sidewalk repairs in their neighborhood.” What does the author achieve by including the residents' point?

explanation.whyCorrect: Including the residents' concern about lost sidewalk funding reveals a cost that the visitors' enthusiasm overlooks.
explanation.tip: An author broadens perspective by including a viewpoint the first group might not see.

options.label: A
options.text: It shows a cost of the project that the visitors' praise alone would not reveal.

options.label: B
options.text: It explains how the murals were painted.
options.rationale: The painting process is not discussed.

options.label: C
options.text: It proves the murals should be removed immediately.
options.rationale: The paragraph does not call for removal.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that visitors and residents actually agree completely.
options.rationale: Their views contrast rather than agree.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Few argue that youth sports build teamwork and discipline. Less discussed is how specializing in a single sport before age ten correlates with higher injury rates among young athletes, according to several pediatric studies.” What does the phrase “less discussed” suggest about the author's perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Less discussed” signals the author thinks an important downside is not getting enough attention.
explanation.tip: Phrases like “less discussed” or “often overlooked” reveal an author's critical perspective.

options.label: A
options.text: The author believes pediatric studies are unreliable.
options.rationale: The studies are cited as support, not doubted.

options.label: B
options.text: The author believes an important risk is being overlooked in the usual conversation about youth sports.

options.label: C
options.text: The author believes youth sports have no benefits at all.
options.rationale: The paragraph opens by agreeing sports build teamwork and discipline.

options.label: D
options.text: The author believes specialization should start even earlier.
options.rationale: The paragraph raises a concern about early specialization, not a push for more of it.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Advocates of water conservation rebates point to a measurable drop in household usage wherever the program has run. Opponents counter that the rebates mostly benefit homeowners who can already afford efficient appliances, leaving renters with the highest bills and no rebate to claim.” Which rhetorical move does the author use?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author first grants the program's measurable success, then raises a fairness concern that complicates a simple positive view.
explanation.tip: Authors often complicate a stated benefit by raising who is left out of it.

options.label: A
options.text: Telling a single homeowner's personal story
options.rationale: No individual story is included.

options.label: B
options.text: Presenting only statistics with no counterargument
options.rationale: A clear counterargument about fairness follows the statistic.

options.label: C
options.text: Presenting a measurable benefit, then a fairness concern that complicates it

options.label: D
options.text: Dismissing the rebate program entirely without evidence
options.rationale: The program's measurable benefit is acknowledged, not dismissed.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Few dispute that homework-free weekends give students time to rest. What rarely appears in these discussions is that students whose families can afford tutors or enrichment programs often use that same free time to get ahead, widening a gap the policy was never meant to create.” What does the author's framing suggest about their perspective on the policy?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author acknowledges the intended benefit of rest while pointing to an unequal effect the policy was not designed to cause.
explanation.tip: Authors can support a policy's intent while still raising a concern about its real-world effect.

options.label: A
options.text: The author believes all students benefit from the policy equally.
options.rationale: The author specifically points out that some students benefit more than others.

options.label: B
options.text: The author believes tutoring programs should be banned.
options.rationale: Banning tutoring programs is never suggested.

options.label: C
options.text: The author believes homework-free weekends are a complete failure.
options.rationale: The author grants that rest time is a real, if partial, benefit.

options.label: D
options.text: The author supports the policy's goal but is concerned about an unintended consequence it may cause.

items.stem: Read the sentence. “Finally, after years of delay, the new wind farm began supplying power to the coastal towns this spring.” How does the author seem to feel about the wind farm's completion?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Finally” expresses satisfaction that a long-awaited project is complete.
explanation.tip: A single word like “finally” can reveal relief or satisfaction.

options.label: A
options.text: Pleased that the long wait is over

options.label: B
options.text: Doubtful that it will work
options.rationale: Nothing in the sentence expresses doubt.

options.label: C
options.text: Unconcerned either way
options.rationale: “Finally” shows the author does care about the outcome.

options.label: D
options.text: Angry about the delay
options.rationale: The focus is on the completion, not lingering anger.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Gig work offers flexibility that a traditional nine-to-five job cannot match. That flexibility, though, often comes without health insurance or a guaranteed minimum income.” What is the author's perspective on gig work?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author names a genuine advantage (flexibility) alongside a genuine disadvantage (lost benefits).
explanation.tip: A balanced perspective often lists a benefit immediately followed by a cost.

options.label: A
options.text: It should be banned immediately.
options.rationale: No call to ban gig work appears in the paragraph.

options.label: B
options.text: It has real benefits but also real drawbacks worth noting.

options.label: C
options.text: It is identical to a traditional job in every way.
options.rationale: The paragraph explicitly contrasts it with a traditional job.

options.label: D
options.text: It is entirely beneficial with no downsides.
options.rationale: The lack of health insurance and guaranteed income are clear downsides.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “The rewilding project reintroduced wolves to the valley eight years ago, and elk populations have since spread more evenly across the landscape instead of overgrazing a few favored spots.” Which word would BEST describe the author's tone toward the project's results?

explanation.whyCorrect: Describing the balanced grazing as a positive outcome of the reintroduction shows an approving tone.
explanation.tip: Look at whether the described outcome is framed as good or bad.

options.label: A
options.text: alarmed
options.rationale: Nothing in the description suggests danger or alarm.

options.label: B
options.text: mocking
options.rationale: The description is straightforward, not mocking.

options.label: C
options.text: approving

options.label: D
options.text: confused
options.rationale: The explanation is clear, not confused.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Some school districts now use AI tools to grade student essays, citing faster turnaround for teachers buried in paperwork. Teachers who have tried the tools report that the software often rewards long, formulaic sentences over genuinely original ideas.” How does the author balance this issue?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph grants a real efficiency benefit while raising a real concern teachers have observed firsthand.
explanation.tip: Balanced writing often follows a stated benefit with a firsthand concern.

options.label: A
options.text: By ignoring teachers' direct experience with the tools
options.rationale: Teachers' experience is the main source of the concern raised.

options.label: B
options.text: By claiming AI grading has no advantages at all
options.rationale: Faster turnaround is clearly presented as an advantage.

options.label: C
options.text: By arguing that AI grading should replace teachers completely
options.rationale: Replacing teachers is never suggested.

options.label: D
options.text: By presenting the efficiency argument alongside a concern about what the AI actually rewards

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Few dispute that social media age limits aim to protect younger users from harmful content. What gets less attention is how easily such limits are bypassed with a fake birth date, raising the question of whether the policy protects anyone at all.” What does the phrase “gets less attention” reveal about the author's stance?

explanation.whyCorrect: By noting what “gets less attention,” the author signals a critical view that the policy's weakness is underexamined.
explanation.tip: Phrases pointing out what is overlooked often reveal an author's underlying criticism.

options.label: A
options.text: The author believes a major flaw in the policy is being overlooked by most discussions.

options.label: B
options.text: The author believes younger users need no protection at all.
options.rationale: The intended goal of protection is acknowledged, not dismissed.

options.label: C
options.text: The author believes fake birth dates are rare and unimportant.
options.rationale: The ease of bypassing the limit is presented as a serious concern, not a minor one.

options.label: D
options.text: The author believes the policy works perfectly as written.
options.rationale: The author directly questions the policy's effectiveness.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Genetically modified crops can resist pests without heavy pesticide use, a clear win for both farmers and nearby ecosystems. Critics note, however, that a handful of large companies control most of the patented seeds, leaving small farmers with little choice but to pay rising licensing fees.” What perspective does the author add by including the critics' point?

explanation.whyCorrect: The critics' point shifts the discussion from an environmental win to an economic concern about control and cost.
explanation.tip: An added perspective can complicate an otherwise simple positive claim.

options.label: A
options.text: A second environmental benefit of the crops
options.rationale: The added point is about economics, not the environment.

options.label: B
options.text: A concern about economic control that complicates the environmental benefit

options.label: C
options.text: A suggestion that pesticide use should increase again
options.rationale: Returning to heavy pesticide use is never suggested.

options.label: D
options.text: Proof that the crops do not actually resist pests
options.rationale: Pest resistance is accepted as true throughout.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “A pilot program paying residents a guaranteed monthly income reported that most recipients used the funds for rent, food and job training, not leisure spending as some had predicted. Skeptics still argue that a small trial cannot prove the approach would work if applied to an entire country's budget.” How does the author frame the skeptics' argument?

explanation.whyCorrect: The author presents the skeptics' point as a fair caution about generalizing a small trial, not as an attack on the program itself.
explanation.tip: Notice whether an author treats an opposing view as reasonable or as simply wrong.

options.label: A
options.text: As an attack on the recipients' honesty
options.rationale: The skeptics question scale, not the recipients' behavior.

options.label: B
options.text: As proof that the entire pilot program was a failure
options.rationale: The pilot's actual results are described as disproving a prediction, not failing.

options.label: C
options.text: As a reasonable limitation on how far the pilot's results can be generalized

options.label: D
options.text: As evidence that monthly payments caused more spending on leisure
options.rationale: The paragraph states the opposite: spending went to necessities.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “City planners praise green roofs for lowering indoor temperatures and absorbing stormwater that would otherwise flood streets. Building owners, who must cover the higher upfront installation cost, are far less enthusiastic, especially when the savings on energy bills take years to offset that cost.” What rhetorical structure does the author use to present this issue?

explanation.whyCorrect: The paragraph sets the planners' civic view against the owners' financial view without endorsing either side outright.
explanation.tip: Look for two different groups and what each one weighs most heavily.

options.label: A
options.text: Siding entirely with building owners against the planners
options.rationale: Both perspectives are presented without the author clearly favoring one.

options.label: B
options.text: Ignoring the cost concerns raised by building owners
options.rationale: The cost concern is given as much weight as the civic benefit.

options.label: C
options.text: Presenting only one group's perspective throughout
options.rationale: Two distinct groups' perspectives are both presented.

options.label: D
options.text: Contrasting the planners' long-term civic benefits with the owners' short-term financial burden

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Proponents of commercial space tourism point to the technological advances that trickle down from private rocket development. Rarely mentioned alongside this praise is the sheer carbon output of a single rocket launch, which can exceed the yearly emissions of thousands of cars, a cost quietly absorbed while the benefits are loudly announced.” What does the phrase “quietly absorbed while the benefits are loudly announced” reveal about the author's perspective?

explanation.whyCorrect: The contrast between “quietly absorbed” and “loudly announced” shows the author's critical view that costs are being underplayed.
explanation.tip: Contrasting verbs like “quietly” and “loudly” can reveal an author's judgment about fairness in a debate.

options.label: A
options.text: The author believes the industry's environmental cost is being downplayed relative to how its benefits are promoted.

options.label: B
options.text: The author believes the industry should be praised more often.
options.rationale: The phrasing criticizes the imbalance in attention, not a lack of praise.

options.label: C
options.text: The author believes carbon emissions from rockets are exaggerated by critics.
options.rationale: The author presents the emissions figure as a fact, not an exaggeration to dismiss.

options.label: D
options.text: The author believes space tourism has produced no technological benefits.
options.rationale: The technological advances are acknowledged as real.

items.stem: Read the paragraph. “Hospital administrators defend rotating night shifts as necessary for round-the-clock patient care, a need few would question. Occupational health researchers, studying the same nurses for over a decade, have quietly built a case that chronic shift rotation carries long-term health costs rarely weighed against the convenience it offers administrators.” What does the word “quietly” suggest about how the author views the researchers' findings compared to the administrators' position?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Quietly” suggests the long-term research has been overshadowed by the administrators' more prominent justification, revealing the author's concern about this imbalance.
explanation.tip: Words suggesting something was done “quietly” often signal the author thinks it deserves more attention.

options.label: A
options.text: The administrators have no real justification for the current system.
options.rationale: Round-the-clock care is called a need “few would question.”

options.label: B
options.text: The researchers' well-supported findings have received far less attention than the administrators' more visible justification.

options.label: C
options.text: The researchers' findings are less reliable than the administrators' claims.
options.rationale: A decade-long study is presented as solid evidence, not unreliable.

options.label: D
options.text: The word “quietly” suggests the researchers kept their study secret on purpose.
options.rationale: “Quietly” describes a lack of attention, not intentional secrecy.

items.stem: “Jumped over the fence” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: There is no subject telling who jumped, so it is a fragment.
explanation.tip: Every sentence needs a subject and a verb.

items.stem: Which group of words is a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: There is no subject or verb telling what happened underneath the bridge.
explanation.tip: Ask: who or what did something, and what did they do?

options.label: A
options.text: The water looked calm today.
options.rationale: This is complete.

options.label: B
options.text: The fish swam underneath the bridge.
options.rationale: This has a subject and a verb.

options.label: C
options.text: Underneath the old wooden bridge.

options.label: D
options.text: We crossed the bridge quickly.
options.rationale: This is complete.

items.stem: Which sentence is a run-on?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete ideas are joined with no punctuation or connecting word.
explanation.tip: A run-on jams two sentences together without a period, comma, or conjunction.

options.label: A
options.text: The bell rang. The students grabbed their bags.
options.rationale: Two separate sentences are correctly punctuated.

options.label: B
options.text: The bell rang, so the students grabbed their bags.
options.rationale: A comma and “so” correctly join the two ideas.

options.label: C
options.text: When the bell rang, the students grabbed their bags.
options.rationale: This is one correctly joined sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The bell rang the students grabbed their bags.

items.stem: Which is the best way to fix this run-on? “Nour finished her chores she went to the park.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma plus the conjunction “and” correctly joins the two complete ideas.
explanation.tip: Fix run-ons with a period, or a comma plus a conjunction like and, but, or so.

options.label: A
options.text: Nour finished her chores, and she went to the park.

options.label: B
options.text: Nour finished her chores and, she went to the park.
options.rationale: The comma belongs before “and,” not after.

options.label: C
options.text: Nour finished her chores she, went to the park.
options.rationale: The comma is in the wrong place.

options.label: D
options.text: Nour finished her chores, she went to the park.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two sentences.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete ideas are joined with no punctuation, creating a run-on; adding a comma and “so” fixes it.
explanation.tip: Look for two complete ideas joined with no connecting word.

items.stem: Which sentence contains a sentence fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Standing by the old gate” has no subject performing an action; it is a fragment on its own.
explanation.tip: Check that every group of words set off as a sentence has its own subject and verb.

options.label: A
options.text: Samir waved to his friends; they waved back.
options.rationale: A semicolon correctly joins two complete sentences.

options.label: B
options.text: Samir waved to his friends. Standing by the old gate.

options.label: C
options.text: Samir waved to his friends standing by the old gate.
options.rationale: This is one complete sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: Samir, who was standing by the old gate, waved to his friends.
options.rationale: This is one complete sentence with a clause.

items.stem: “Before the sun rose over the dunes and painted the sand gold” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a dependent clause with no main clause attached; it cannot stand alone.
explanation.tip: Clauses starting with words like “before” need a main clause to complete the thought.

items.stem: Which revision fixes BOTH the fragment and the run-on? “Because the ferry was delayed. We waited at the dock we watched the waves.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Joining the dependent clause to the main clause and adding “and” between the two complete ideas fixes both problems.
explanation.tip: Fix one error at a time, then check the whole sentence again.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the ferry was delayed we waited at the dock. We watched the waves.
options.rationale: The fragment is fixed, but a comma is still missing after “delayed.”

options.label: B
options.text: Because the ferry was delayed, we waited at the dock we watched the waves.
options.rationale: The run-on between “dock” and “we watched” is not fixed.

options.label: C
options.text: Because the ferry was delayed, we waited at the dock, and we watched the waves.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the ferry was delayed. We waited at the dock, and we watched the waves.
options.rationale: The first fragment is never joined to a main clause.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete ideas are run together with no punctuation; adding a comma and “so” fixes the run-on.
explanation.tip: A comma alone between two complete sentences is not enough; add a conjunction too.

segments: The museum closes early on Fridays

items.stem: Which paragraph contains NO fragments or run-ons?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each sentence has its own subject and verb and is correctly separated with end punctuation.
explanation.tip: Check each sentence alone: does it have a subject, a verb, and a complete thought?

options.label: A
options.text: The storm knocked out power. Across the village. Families lit candles and waited.
options.rationale: “Across the village” is a fragment on its own.

options.label: B
options.text: The storm knocked out power across the village families lit candles. Waited for the lines to be repaired.
options.rationale: This has both a run-on and a fragment.

options.label: C
options.text: The storm knocked out power across the village, families lit candles and waited for the lines to be repaired.
options.rationale: A comma alone cannot join these two complete ideas; this is a comma splice.

options.label: D
options.text: The storm knocked out power across the village. Families lit candles and waited for the lines to be repaired. By morning, the lights flickered back on.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon to join two related, complete ideas without creating a comma splice?

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon alone can correctly join two closely related complete sentences.
explanation.tip: Use a semicolon between two complete sentences without a conjunction after it.

options.label: A
options.text: The tide was rising fast; the fishermen hurried to pull in their nets.

options.label: B
options.text: The tide was rising fast; and the fishermen hurried to pull in their nets.
options.rationale: A semicolon should not be followed by “and”; use either the semicolon or a comma plus “and,” not both.

options.label: C
options.text: The tide was rising fast the fishermen hurried to pull in their nets.
options.rationale: With no punctuation at all, this is a run-on.

options.label: D
options.text: The tide was rising fast, the fishermen hurried to pull in their nets.
options.rationale: A comma alone between two complete sentences creates a comma splice.

items.stem: “Although the trail looked easy at first” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a dependent clause starting with “although” and has no main clause to finish the thought.
explanation.tip: Words like although, because, and when start clauses that need a main clause.

items.stem: Which group of words is a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: There is a subject but no verb telling what the lighthouse keeper did.
explanation.tip: A describing phrase after a subject is not enough; the sentence still needs a verb.

options.label: A
options.text: The old lighthouse keeper retired after decades of storms.
options.rationale: This has a subject and a verb.

options.label: B
options.text: The old lighthouse keeper, tired after decades of storms.

options.label: C
options.text: He watched the waves from his window.
options.rationale: This is complete.

options.label: D
options.text: After decades of storms, he retired.
options.rationale: This is complete.

items.stem: Which sentence is a comma splice?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences; that creates a comma splice.
explanation.tip: A comma splice is a run-on fixed with only a comma, which is not enough.

options.label: A
options.text: The hikers reached the summit, and the view stretched for miles.
options.rationale: A comma plus “and” correctly joins the two ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: The hikers reached the summit. The view stretched for miles.
options.rationale: Two correctly punctuated separate sentences.

options.label: C
options.text: The hikers reached the summit, the view stretched for miles.

options.label: D
options.text: After the hikers reached the summit, the view stretched for miles.
options.rationale: This is one correctly joined sentence.

items.stem: Which is the best way to correct this run-on? “The ferry arrived late the passengers missed their connecting bus.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma plus the conjunction “so” correctly joins the two related ideas.
explanation.tip: Check that a comma is paired with a conjunction, not left alone.

options.label: A
options.text: The ferry arrived late. the passengers missed their connecting bus.
options.rationale: The second sentence needs a capital letter to start correctly.

options.label: B
options.text: The ferry arrived late so the passengers missed their connecting bus.
options.rationale: A comma is needed before the conjunction “so.”

options.label: C
options.text: The ferry arrived late, the passengers missed their connecting bus.
options.rationale: A comma alone still creates a comma splice.

options.label: D
options.text: The ferry arrived late, so the passengers missed their connecting bus.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete ideas are joined with no punctuation, creating a run-on; a comma and “so” fix it.
explanation.tip: Look for two complete thoughts crammed together with nothing between them.

segments: The bridge had been closed for repairs

items.stem: Which sentence contains a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Searching for the exact cause of the crack” has no subject of its own and cannot stand as a sentence.
explanation.tip: A phrase describing an earlier sentence is still a fragment if it stands alone.

options.label: A
options.text: The engineers studied the bridge for months. Searching for the exact cause of the crack.

options.label: B
options.text: The engineers studied the bridge for months, searching for the exact cause of the crack.
options.rationale: This is one complete sentence with a phrase attached correctly.

options.label: C
options.text: The engineers studied the bridge for months; they searched for the crack's cause.
options.rationale: A semicolon correctly joins two complete sentences.

options.label: D
options.text: The engineers, searching for the exact cause of the crack, studied the bridge for months.
options.rationale: This is one complete sentence.

items.stem: Which revision fixes BOTH problems? “Because the generator failed during the storm. The clinic lost power for six hours it ran on backup batteries.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Joining the dependent clause to the main clause and adding a comma plus “and” between the two complete ideas fixes both problems.
explanation.tip: Work through a long error one join at a time.

options.label: A
options.text: Because the generator failed during the storm. The clinic lost power for six hours, and it ran on backup batteries.
options.rationale: The opening fragment is never joined to a main clause.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the generator failed during the storm, the clinic lost power for six hours, and it ran on backup batteries.

options.label: C
options.text: The generator failed during the storm the clinic lost power for six hours, and it ran on backup batteries.
options.rationale: Removing “because” creates a new run-on at the start.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the generator failed during the storm, the clinic lost power for six hours it ran on backup batteries.
options.rationale: The run-on between “hours” and “it ran” is never fixed.

items.stem: Which paragraph contains NO fragments or run-ons?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each sentence has its own subject, verb, and correct end punctuation.
explanation.tip: Read each sentence alone; does it stand as a complete thought?

options.label: A
options.text: The bakery ran out of flour by mid-morning, customers lined up anyway, hoping a delivery would arrive soon.
options.rationale: A comma alone joining the first two ideas creates a comma splice.

options.label: B
options.text: The bakery ran out of flour. By mid-morning. Customers lined up anyway, hoping for a delivery.
options.rationale: “By mid-morning” on its own is a fragment.

options.label: C
options.text: The bakery ran out of flour by mid-morning. Customers lined up anyway, hoping a new delivery would arrive soon. By noon, a truck finally pulled up outside.

options.label: D
options.text: The bakery ran out of flour by mid-morning customers lined up anyway. Hoping a new delivery would arrive soon.
options.rationale: This has both a run-on and a fragment.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon to join two related, complete ideas?

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related, complete sentences without a conjunction.
explanation.tip: A semicolon replaces a period between two closely related complete sentences.

options.label: A
options.text: The negotiations dragged on for weeks, neither side wanted to compromise first.
options.rationale: A comma alone creates a comma splice.

options.label: B
options.text: The negotiations dragged on for weeks; because neither side wanted to compromise first.
options.rationale: A semicolon should not be followed by a dependent clause starting with “because.”

options.label: C
options.text: The negotiations dragged on for weeks neither side wanted to compromise first.
options.rationale: With no punctuation, this is a run-on.

options.label: D
options.text: The negotiations dragged on for weeks; neither side wanted to compromise first.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly joins two independent clauses with a semicolon and a transition word?

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon before a transition word like “therefore,” followed by a comma, correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: Transition words like therefore, however, and moreover need a semicolon before and a comma after when joining two sentences.

options.label: A
options.text: The river had flooded twice that year; therefore, the village council approved funding for a new levee.

options.label: B
options.text: The river had flooded twice that year, therefore, the village council approved funding for a new levee.
options.rationale: A comma alone before “therefore” is not strong enough to join two complete sentences.

options.label: C
options.text: The river had flooded twice that year; therefore the village council approved funding for a new levee.
options.rationale: A comma is needed after a transition word like “therefore” when it follows a semicolon.

options.label: D
options.text: The river had flooded twice that year therefore the village council approved funding for a new levee.
options.rationale: With no punctuation at all around “therefore,” this is a run-on.

items.stem: “Even though the harvest had been poor that year” is a complete sentence.

explanation.whyCorrect: This dependent clause starting with “even though” has no main clause to finish the idea.
explanation.tip: A clause beginning with a subordinating word needs an independent clause attached.

items.stem: Which group of words is a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: There is a subject, “committee members,” but no verb showing what they did.
explanation.tip: A describing phrase attached to a subject is not a verb.

options.label: A
options.text: The committee members left exhausted after the five-hour debate.
options.rationale: This has a subject and a verb.

options.label: B
options.text: The committee members, exhausted after the five-hour debate.

options.label: C
options.text: The debate lasted five hours.
options.rationale: This is complete.

options.label: D
options.text: Exhausted, the committee members finally left.
options.rationale: This is complete.

items.stem: Which sentence is a comma splice?

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences, creating a comma splice.
explanation.tip: Check whether both halves of a sentence could stand alone; if so, a comma alone is not enough.

options.label: A
options.text: Once the treaty was signed, both nations celebrated the end of the conflict.
options.rationale: This is one correctly joined sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: The treaty was signed, and both nations celebrated the end of the conflict.
options.rationale: A comma plus “and” correctly joins the ideas.

options.label: C
options.text: The treaty was signed, both nations celebrated the end of the conflict.

options.label: D
options.text: The treaty was signed. Both nations celebrated the end of the conflict.
options.rationale: Two correctly separated sentences.

items.stem: Which is the best way to correct this run-on? “The committee reviewed the proposal twice they still could not reach an agreement.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A comma plus the conjunction “but” correctly joins the two contrasting, complete ideas.
explanation.tip: Choose a conjunction that matches the relationship between the two ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: The committee reviewed the proposal twice but, they still could not reach an agreement.
options.rationale: The comma belongs before “but,” not after.

options.label: B
options.text: The committee reviewed the proposal twice, they still could not reach an agreement.
options.rationale: A comma alone creates a comma splice.

options.label: C
options.text: The committee reviewed the proposal twice they still, could not reach an agreement.
options.rationale: The comma is misplaced and does not fix the run-on.

options.label: D
options.text: The committee reviewed the proposal twice, but they still could not reach an agreement.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Two complete ideas are joined with no punctuation, creating a run-on; adding “when” and a comma shows the time relationship and fixes it.
explanation.tip: Look for two full sentences crammed together with nothing connecting them.

segments: The excavation had uncovered pottery shards for weeks

items.stem: Which sentence contains a fragment?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Frustrated by the lack of progress after three days” has no subject performing an action and cannot stand alone.
explanation.tip: A descriptive phrase separated by a period is still a fragment if it has no subject and verb of its own.

options.label: A
options.text: The negotiators left the room abruptly. Frustrated by the lack of progress after three days.

options.label: B
options.text: Frustrated by the lack of progress, the negotiators left the room abruptly.
options.rationale: This is one complete sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: The negotiators left the room abruptly; they were frustrated by the lack of progress.
options.rationale: A semicolon correctly joins two complete sentences.

options.label: D
options.text: The negotiators left the room abruptly, frustrated by the lack of progress after three days.
options.rationale: This is one complete sentence with a phrase attached correctly.

items.stem: Which revision fixes BOTH problems? “Although the committee had warned residents for months. Few believed the dam could actually fail it collapsed within hours of the flood warning.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Joining the dependent clause to the main clause and adding a comma plus “and” between the two complete ideas fixes both errors.
explanation.tip: Untangle a long error one connection at a time, checking each join separately.

options.label: A
options.text: Although the committee had warned residents for months, few believed the dam could actually fail it collapsed within hours of the flood warning.
options.rationale: The run-on between “fail” and “it collapsed” is never fixed.

options.label: B
options.text: Although the committee had warned residents for months, few believed the dam could actually fail, and it collapsed within hours of the flood warning.

options.label: C
options.text: The committee had warned residents for months few believed the dam could actually fail, and it collapsed within hours of the flood warning.
options.rationale: Removing “although” creates a new run-on at the start.

options.label: D
options.text: Although the committee had warned residents for months. Few believed the dam could actually fail, and it collapsed within hours of the flood warning.
options.rationale: The opening fragment is never joined to a main clause.

items.stem: Which paragraph contains NO fragments or run-ons?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each sentence has its own subject, verb, and correct end punctuation, with no gaps or improper joins.
explanation.tip: Isolate each sentence and confirm it has a subject, a verb, and a complete thought.

options.label: A
options.text: The city council debated the proposal for hours, residents packed the chamber hoping to sway the vote.
options.rationale: A comma alone joining the first two ideas creates a comma splice.

options.label: B
options.text: The city council debated the proposal for hours residents packed the chamber. Hoping to sway the final vote.
options.rationale: This has both a run-on and a fragment.

options.label: C
options.text: The city council debated the proposal for hours. Residents on both sides packed the chamber, hoping to sway the final vote. In the end, the measure passed by a narrow margin.

options.label: D
options.text: The city council debated the proposal. For hours. Residents packed the chamber, hoping to sway the vote.
options.rationale: “For hours” standing alone is a fragment.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon to join two related, complete ideas?

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon alone correctly joins two closely related, complete sentences.
explanation.tip: Make sure both halves joined by a semicolon could stand as their own sentences.

options.label: A
options.text: The old factory had sat empty for a decade developers finally saw potential in its brick walls.
options.rationale: With no punctuation at all, this is a run-on.

options.label: B
options.text: The old factory had sat empty for a decade, developers finally saw potential in its brick walls.
options.rationale: A comma alone creates a comma splice.

options.label: C
options.text: The old factory had sat empty for a decade; because developers finally saw potential in its brick walls.
options.rationale: A semicolon should not be followed by a dependent clause starting with “because.”

options.label: D
options.text: The old factory had sat empty for a decade; developers finally saw potential in its brick walls.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly joins two independent clauses with a semicolon and a transition word?

explanation.whyCorrect: A semicolon before the transition word “consequently,” followed by a comma, correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.tip: Transition words like consequently, however, and therefore take a semicolon before and a comma after when joining two sentences.

options.label: A
options.text: The company's profits had fallen for three straight quarters; consequently, the board voted to replace the chief executive.

options.label: B
options.text: The company's profits had fallen for three straight quarters consequently the board voted to replace the chief executive.
options.rationale: With no punctuation around “consequently,” this is a run-on.

options.label: C
options.text: The company's profits had fallen for three straight quarters, consequently, the board voted to replace the chief executive.
options.rationale: A comma alone before “consequently” is too weak to join two complete sentences.

options.label: D
options.text: The company's profits had fallen for three straight quarters; consequently the board voted to replace the chief executive.
options.rationale: A comma is needed after a transition word like “consequently” following a semicolon.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Yusuf's hands shook as he opened the envelope. When he saw the winning number, he let out a loud whoop and jumped off the couch.” What can you infer about Yusuf's feelings?

explanation.whyCorrect: Shaking hands, a loud whoop, and jumping all show strong excitement.
explanation.tip: Use a character's actions to infer their feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: He felt sleepy.
options.rationale: Shaking hands and jumping do not show sleepiness.

options.label: B
options.text: He felt excited and surprised.

options.label: C
options.text: He felt bored.
options.rationale: Jumping and whooping do not show boredom.

options.label: D
options.text: He felt angry.
options.rationale: Nothing in the actions shows anger.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Mariam set two extra plates at the table even though only she and her mother would be eating. She kept glancing at the front door.” What can you infer?

explanation.whyCorrect: Extra plates and watching the door both suggest she expects someone else to arrive.
explanation.tip: Look for small clues a character's actions give about what they expect.

options.label: A
options.text: Mariam does not like using plates.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests dislike of plates.

options.label: B
options.text: Mariam forgot how many people live in her house.
options.rationale: Setting extra plates on purpose does not suggest forgetting.

options.label: C
options.text: Mariam is expecting more guests to arrive.

options.label: D
options.text: Mariam is cleaning the table.
options.rationale: Setting plates and watching the door do not show cleaning.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Khaled walked past the bakery three times before finally going inside. Once there, he stared at the price list for a long time before ordering just one roll.” What can you infer about Khaled?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hesitating outside and studying prices before buying just one item suggest he was watching his spending.
explanation.tip: Hesitation before a purchase often suggests concern about cost.

options.label: A
options.text: He was in a hurry.
options.rationale: Walking past three times and staring at prices does not show hurrying.

options.label: B
options.text: He did not like bread.
options.rationale: He went inside and bought a roll, so he does like bread.

options.label: C
options.text: He forgot his money at home.
options.rationale: He did order and presumably pay for a roll.

options.label: D
options.text: He was being careful with his money.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Lina's older brother usually teased her about her drawings, but today he pinned her newest sketch to the refrigerator without saying a word.” It can be inferred that Lina's brother secretly liked the drawing.

explanation.whyCorrect: Pinning the sketch up, instead of teasing, suggests he admired it even without saying so.
explanation.tip: A changed action can hint at a changed feeling, even without words.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Samir kept checking his watch during the soccer match, even glancing at the exit twice. When his phone buzzed, he answered it before the referee had even blown the whistle for halftime.” What can you infer about Samir?

explanation.whyCorrect: Repeatedly checking his watch, glancing at the exit, and answering quickly all suggest he was anxiously waiting for a call.
explanation.tip: Repeated small actions can reveal what a character is anxiously anticipating.

options.label: A
options.text: He was waiting for an important call and was distracted from the game.

options.label: B
options.text: He was the referee's assistant.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he had an official role.

options.label: C
options.text: He was hoping the game would be cancelled.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he wanted the game cancelled.

options.label: D
options.text: He had lost interest in sports altogether.
options.rationale: Watching the match and checking his watch show he was still there, just distracted.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Hoda's grandmother handed her the old recipe card without looking up, her voice tighter than usual as she described the steps. When Hoda asked if something was wrong, her grandmother just smiled and said the onions were strong today.” What can you infer about the grandmother's true feelings?

explanation.whyCorrect: A tight voice and an excuse about onions suggest she was hiding deeper emotion while sharing something meaningful.
explanation.tip: A character's excuse can hint at a feeling they are not stating directly.

options.label: A
options.text: She did not want to share the recipe at all.
options.rationale: She hands over the card and describes the steps willingly.

options.label: B
options.text: She was likely feeling emotional about sharing the recipe, not just affected by onions.

options.label: C
options.text: She genuinely disliked cutting onions.
options.rationale: The onion comment is likely an excuse, not the real reason for her tight voice.

options.label: D
options.text: She was angry at Hoda for asking a question.
options.rationale: Smiling while answering does not suggest anger.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Adel's little sister asked him for the fifth time that afternoon to play outside, and each time he said he was too busy with his model airplane. When she finally gave up and went to her room, he glanced at the door for a long moment before going back to his glue and plastic pieces.” What does Adel's glance toward the door suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pausing to glance at the door right after his sister leaves disappointed suggests a moment of guilt.
explanation.tip: A pause after disappointing someone often hints at a feeling the character does not say aloud.

options.label: A
options.text: He wanted to go outside himself.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he wanted to play outside.

options.label: B
options.text: He was waiting for a friend to arrive.
options.rationale: No friend is mentioned at all.

options.label: C
options.text: He felt a flicker of guilt about turning his sister away.

options.label: D
options.text: He was worried someone would steal his model.
options.rationale: No threat to the model is mentioned.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “The coach announced the starting lineup without once glancing toward Noor, who had scored the winning goal in practice all week. Noor gripped her water bottle tighter and stared at the grass instead of the clipboard.” What can you infer about Noor's situation?

explanation.whyCorrect: The coach avoiding eye contact and Noor's tense reaction both suggest she was passed over and is upset about it.
explanation.tip: Notice what a character avoids looking at; it often points to what is bothering them.

options.label: A
options.text: She was chosen as team captain.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she received an honor; the clues point to disappointment.

options.label: B
options.text: She did not care at all about the lineup.
options.rationale: Her physical reactions show she cared a great deal.

options.label: C
options.text: She was excited to be benched to rest before a big game.
options.rationale: Gripping the bottle tighter and avoiding the clipboard suggest tension, not calm acceptance.

options.label: D
options.text: She was likely left out of the starting lineup and felt hurt by it.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Tariq's father read the acceptance letter twice, folded it carefully along its original creases, and placed it back in the envelope before setting it on the kitchen counter rather than the family bulletin board where every other important letter went. He said only, “We'll talk about it after dinner.”” What does the father's handling of the letter most strongly suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reading it twice, handling it carefully, and setting it apart from routine letters all suggest the news matters deeply but is complicated for him.
explanation.tip: Where and how a character places an object can reveal unspoken feelings about it.

options.label: A
options.text: He has complicated feelings about the news and needs time before discussing it.

options.label: B
options.text: He did not read the letter carefully.
options.rationale: Reading it twice shows careful attention, not carelessness.

options.label: C
options.text: He thinks the letter is unimportant.
options.rationale: Folding it carefully along its creases shows he considers it significant.

options.label: D
options.text: He is proud and plans to celebrate immediately.
options.rationale: Delaying the conversation and avoiding the usual bulletin board do not suggest immediate celebration.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Dalia reread the letter three times, tracing each line with her finger before folding it and tucking it under her pillow instead of in her desk drawer.” What can you infer about the letter's importance to Dalia?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rereading it carefully and keeping it somewhere special, under her pillow, shows it matters deeply to her.
explanation.tip: Where a character keeps an object can reveal how much they value it.

options.label: A
options.text: It is a letter she plans to throw away.
options.rationale: Keeping it under her pillow instead of discarding it shows she values it.

options.label: B
options.text: It means a great deal to her.

options.label: C
options.text: It contains instructions for a school assignment.
options.rationale: The emotional care taken suggests something more personal than an assignment.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a letter from a stranger she does not know.
options.rationale: The careful, repeated reading suggests a personal connection.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Every time the teacher mentioned the upcoming science fair, Youssef's pencil stopped moving and his eyes dropped to his desk. He was the only student who never raised his hand to volunteer a project idea.” What can you infer about Youssef?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stopping his work and avoiding eye contact whenever the topic comes up suggest the science fair makes him anxious.
explanation.tip: A character's physical reaction to a topic can reveal their hidden feelings about it.

options.label: A
options.text: He is the most excited student in class.
options.rationale: Dropping his eyes and staying silent do not show excitement.

options.label: B
options.text: He already finished his project early.
options.rationale: His reaction suggests worry, not confidence from being finished.

options.label: C
options.text: He feels anxious or unprepared about the science fair.

options.label: D
options.text: He thinks science fairs are a waste of time.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests indifference; his reaction suggests nervousness.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Rania's coach benched her for the first half without explanation. During the break, Rania sat at the far end of the bench, arms crossed, answering her teammates' questions with one word each.” What can you infer about Rania's feelings?

explanation.whyCorrect: Sitting apart, crossing her arms, and giving short answers all show she is upset and pulling away from the team.
explanation.tip: Physical distance from others can mirror a character's emotional distance.

options.label: A
options.text: She is relieved to have a rest.
options.rationale: Crossed arms and short answers do not show relief or relaxation.

options.label: B
options.text: She agrees completely with the coach's decision.
options.rationale: Her distant behavior suggests frustration, not agreement.

options.label: C
options.text: She is focused on planning her next play.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests she is strategizing; her behavior shows withdrawal.

options.label: D
options.text: She feels upset and is withdrawing from her teammates.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Khalil's mother set his favorite dinner on the table without being asked, then sat across from him instead of eating in the kitchen as usual. She kept starting sentences and stopping before finishing them.” What can you infer about what is happening?

explanation.whyCorrect: A favorite meal, sitting unusually close, and unfinished sentences together suggest she is preparing to share difficult news.
explanation.tip: Unusual changes in routine often signal that a character has something important to say.

options.label: A
options.text: She has something difficult to tell him and is working up to it.

options.label: B
options.text: She is simply hungry and wants company.
options.rationale: The unfinished sentences suggest she is building up to say something, not just socializing.

options.label: C
options.text: She is testing a new recipe for a cooking class.
options.rationale: The emotional cues point to a difficult announcement, not a recipe test.

options.label: D
options.text: She forgot that Khalil already ate dinner.
options.rationale: Preparing his favorite meal shows deliberate planning, not forgetfulness.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Sami's older cousin had always borrowed his tools without asking, but today he returned them all, cleaned and oiled, with a short note that just said, “Thanks for everything.”” It can be inferred that the cousin is leaving or moving away soon.

explanation.whyCorrect: Returning borrowed items, cleaning them carefully, and writing a farewell-sounding note together suggest the cousin is preparing to leave.
explanation.tip: A sudden return of borrowed things, paired with a thankful note, often signals a goodbye.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “The shopkeeper slid the broken toy back across the counter to Nadia without a word, then quietly placed a different, nicer one in her bag while pretending to wrap her original purchase.” What can you infer about the shopkeeper?

explanation.whyCorrect: Quietly swapping in a better toy without announcing it suggests a private act of kindness.
explanation.tip: A quiet, unannounced act can reveal generosity a character does not want recognized.

options.label: A
options.text: He is trying to trick Nadia into paying more.
options.rationale: Secretly giving a nicer toy is generous, not deceptive toward her.

options.label: B
options.text: He is kindly replacing the broken toy without wanting to be thanked for it.

options.label: C
options.text: He did not notice the toy was broken.
options.rationale: Sliding it back silently suggests he noticed and is quietly handling it.

options.label: D
options.text: He wants Nadia to return later and buy more toys.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a plan to bring her back as a customer.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “During the interview, Omar answered every question about the award with short, polite sentences, but when a reporter mentioned his late grandfather's old workshop, Omar's voice caught, and he asked for a moment before continuing.” What does Omar's reaction to the mention of the workshop suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: His composed answers elsewhere contrast sharply with his reaction to the workshop, showing it touches something deeply personal.
explanation.tip: Compare a character's reaction to one topic against their reactions to others to find what truly matters to them.

options.label: A
options.text: He is uncomfortable discussing his award at all.
options.rationale: He answered the award questions smoothly; the reaction is specific to the workshop mention.

options.label: B
options.text: He is annoyed that the reporter changed the subject.
options.rationale: Asking for a moment suggests emotion, not irritation at the topic change.

options.label: C
options.text: The workshop holds a deep personal and emotional connection for him.

options.label: D
options.text: He has never heard of the workshop before.
options.rationale: A reaction this strong suggests familiarity, not unfamiliarity.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Layla's manuscript came back from the publisher with a single line of feedback: “Not quite ready yet, but keep going.” She read it standing in the hallway, then sat down right there on the floor and began rewriting the first page on the back of the rejection letter itself.” What does Layla's choice to write on the back of the rejection letter most strongly suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Writing new work directly on the rejection letter, rather than putting it away, shows she is channeling disappointment into immediate action.
explanation.tip: A character's unusual, symbolic choice of action often reveals their deeper resolve.

options.label: A
options.text: She plans to frame the letter as a souvenir.
options.rationale: Writing over it suggests using it as a tool, not preserving it as a keepsake.

options.label: B
options.text: She has decided to give up writing entirely.
options.rationale: Immediately rewriting the first page shows renewed effort, not giving up.

options.label: C
options.text: She has run out of paper and had no other option.
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a shortage of paper; the choice is symbolic, not practical.

options.label: D
options.text: She is transforming the disappointment into immediate determination to improve.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Hassan read the test results form twice, set it face-down on the table, and walked to the window before saying anything to his sister waiting on the phone.” What can you infer about Hassan's reaction to the results?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reading it twice, turning it over, and pausing before speaking all suggest he needed time to process a strong reaction.
explanation.tip: A pause before speaking often signals a character is processing a strong reaction.

options.label: A
options.text: The results affected him strongly, and he needed a moment before responding.

options.label: B
options.text: He was relieved and wanted to celebrate right away.
options.rationale: Setting it face-down and pausing suggest hesitation, not immediate celebration.

options.label: C
options.text: He had not yet opened the envelope.
options.rationale: He already read the form twice.

options.label: D
options.text: He found the results boring and unimportant.
options.rationale: Reading it twice and pausing before speaking suggest strong, not indifferent, feelings.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Every evening that week, Mona's father came home later than usual, his tie loosened before he even reached the door, and went straight to his study without the usual greeting.” What can you infer about Mona's father?

explanation.whyCorrect: Coming home later, loosening his tie early, and skipping his usual greeting together suggest he is under unusual strain.
explanation.tip: A break in a character's normal routine often signals something is weighing on them.

options.label: A
options.text: He has started a new hobby he enjoys.
options.rationale: Nothing about his behavior suggests enjoyment; it points to strain.

options.label: B
options.text: He is dealing with unusual stress or pressure at work.

options.label: C
options.text: He is planning a surprise celebration for Mona.
options.rationale: Nothing hints at planning a celebration; the details suggest stress instead.

options.label: D
options.text: He forgot where the study is located.
options.rationale: Going straight there shows he knows exactly where it is.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “The council member who had always voted against funding the new clinic stood up first at the meeting and moved to approve the budget without a single amendment.” What can you infer about this council member?

explanation.whyCorrect: A sudden reversal from consistent opposition to immediate, full support suggests a real change of mind.
explanation.tip: A character's unexpected reversal usually signals a meaningful change in their view.

options.label: A
options.text: They have always supported the clinic.
options.rationale: The sentence states they “always voted against” it before.

options.label: B
options.text: They misunderstood what was being voted on.
options.rationale: Standing up first to propose the motion shows clear intent, not confusion.

options.label: C
options.text: Something has changed their mind about the clinic's importance.

options.label: D
options.text: They are trying to delay the vote further.
options.rationale: Moving to approve without amendments speeds up the process rather than delaying it.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “Zein kept the acceptance letter from the university in his jacket pocket for three days without telling his parents, even as they asked at dinner each night whether any news had arrived.” What can you infer about Zein's situation?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hiding the letter for days while being directly asked suggests he feels conflicted about the news, not simply excited or dismissive.
explanation.tip: A gap between what a character does and what they say reveals their true uncertainty.

options.label: A
options.text: He plans to reject the offer and sees no reason to mention it.
options.rationale: Keeping the letter rather than discarding it suggests he is still weighing the decision.

options.label: B
options.text: He has not yet received any letter.
options.rationale: He already has the letter in his pocket.

options.label: C
options.text: He is certain his parents will be thrilled and is planning a surprise party.
options.rationale: Hiding the letter for days while being asked directly suggests hesitation, not excited planning.

options.label: D
options.text: He is uncertain or conflicted about sharing or accepting the news.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “The usually talkative tour guide grew quiet as the group approached the old courthouse, pointing only briefly at the building before leading everyone quickly toward the next stop.” It can be inferred that the courthouse holds a difficult or painful memory for the guide.

explanation.whyCorrect: A sudden, uncharacteristic silence and a rushed pace past a specific building suggest the guide is avoiding something painful.
explanation.tip: A character avoiding a topic, especially one usually talkative, often signals a sensitive memory.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “After the verdict was read, the lawyer closed her briefcase slowly, shook hands with the opposing counsel for an unusually long moment, and left through the side door instead of facing the reporters waiting at the main entrance.” What can you infer about the lawyer's feelings about the case's outcome?

explanation.whyCorrect: The long handshake and avoiding reporters suggest complex emotions that go beyond a simple reaction to winning or losing.
explanation.tip: Deliberate, unusual actions after a major event often reveal complicated, mixed feelings.

options.label: A
options.text: She has complicated feelings about the result, beyond simple victory or defeat.

options.label: B
options.text: She believes the verdict was completely wrong and plans to appeal immediately.
options.rationale: Nothing about her calm, deliberate actions suggests outrage or an immediate plan to appeal.

options.label: C
options.text: She has no opinion about the case at all.
options.rationale: Her deliberate, unusual actions show she is affected, not indifferent.

options.label: D
options.text: She is thrilled and eager to speak with reporters.
options.rationale: Avoiding the main entrance suggests she is not eager to face the press.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “The scientist's hands trembled slightly as she adjusted the microscope for the final confirmation, though she had run this exact test dozens of times before without incident.” What does her trembling, despite her experience, most strongly suggest?

explanation.whyCorrect: Trembling despite having performed the same test many times before suggests this particular result matters unusually much to her.
explanation.tip: A skilled character's uncharacteristic nervousness often signals the unusual importance of a specific moment.

options.label: A
options.text: She has forgotten how to use the microscope properly.
options.rationale: Running the test “dozens of times” shows clear familiarity with the equipment.

options.label: B
options.text: This particular result carries unusually high stakes or significance for her.

options.label: C
options.text: The microscope is broken and difficult to adjust.
options.rationale: No mechanical problem with the microscope is mentioned.

options.label: D
options.text: She is simply tired after a long day of work.
options.rationale: Trembling specifically despite extensive experience points to the significance of this result, not general fatigue.

items.stem: Read the sentences. “The retired general answered every question about the battle in precise, clipped detail, military terms intact, until a young reporter asked simply, “Were you scared?” He looked past the camera for a long moment before answering, “Every single day,” in a voice far softer than before.” What does the shift in the general's voice and gaze most strongly reveal?

explanation.whyCorrect: The sudden shift from precise military language to a soft, simple answer reveals real emotion beneath his composed exterior.
explanation.tip: A sudden change in a character's tone or precision often signals a break from a practiced persona into genuine feeling.

options.label: A
options.text: He is exaggerating his fear for dramatic effect in the interview.
options.rationale: The softened, genuine tone suggests sincerity rather than performance.

options.label: B
options.text: He considers the question disrespectful and is ending the interview.
options.rationale: He answers the question honestly rather than refusing or objecting to it.

options.label: C
options.text: Beneath his composed, professional exterior, he carries genuine, long-held fear and vulnerability.

options.label: D
options.text: He did not understand the reporter's question.
options.rationale: His direct, honest answer shows clear understanding, not confusion.

items.stem: Which word is a preposition? “The frog jumped into the pond.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Into” shows where the frog jumped.
explanation.tip: Prepositions often show position or direction.

options.label: A
options.text: jumped
options.rationale: This is a verb.

options.label: B
options.text: frog
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: pond
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: into

items.stem: Choose the preposition of place: “The keys are ____ the drawer.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “In” shows the keys are inside the drawer.
explanation.tip: “In” is used for enclosed spaces.

options.label: A
options.text: of
options.rationale: “Of” does not show place.

options.label: B
options.text: in

options.label: C
options.text: at
options.rationale: “At” names a point, not inside a space.

options.label: D
options.text: to
options.rationale: “To” shows direction, not location.

items.stem: Which word is a preposition? “She walked across the bridge every morning.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Across” shows how she moved over the bridge.
explanation.tip: Prepositions can show movement over or through something.

options.label: A
options.text: across

options.label: B
options.text: bridge
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: morning
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: walked
options.rationale: This is a verb.

items.stem: Choose the preposition of time: “The bakery opens ____ sunrise.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Before” tells us the bakery opens earlier than sunrise.
explanation.tip: Time prepositions: before, after, during, at.

options.label: A
options.text: between
options.rationale: This needs two points in time.

options.label: B
options.text: onto
options.rationale: This shows movement, not time.

options.label: C
options.text: before

options.label: D
options.text: of
options.rationale: This does not fit time.

items.stem: What is the prepositional phrase in this sentence? “The kitten hid beneath the old couch.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The phrase starts with the preposition “beneath” and ends with the noun “couch.”
explanation.tip: A prepositional phrase: preposition + its object.

options.label: A
options.text: the old couch
options.rationale: A phrase begins with the preposition.

options.label: B
options.text: beneath the old couch

options.label: C
options.text: The kitten hid
options.rationale: This is the subject and verb.

options.label: D
options.text: kitten hid beneath
options.rationale: This mixes the subject into the phrase.

items.stem: Choose the preposition of direction: “The hikers climbed ____ the steep hill.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Up” shows the direction the hikers climbed.
explanation.tip: Direction prepositions: up, down, through, across.

options.label: A
options.text: of
options.rationale: “Of” does not show direction.

options.label: B
options.text: at
options.rationale: “At” names a point, not direction.

options.label: C
options.text: by
options.rationale: “By” usually shows nearness.

options.label: D
options.text: up

items.stem: In the sentence “The birds flew over the lake,” the word “over” is a preposition.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Over” shows the birds’ position in relation to the lake, so it is a preposition.
explanation.tip: Check if the word connects a noun to the rest of the sentence showing place, time or direction.

items.stem: What is the object of the preposition in this sentence? “We planted flowers around the fountain.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The noun right after “around” is “fountain,” so it is the object of the preposition.
explanation.tip: The object of a preposition is the noun that follows it.

options.label: A
options.text: flowers
options.rationale: This is the object of the verb “planted.”

options.label: B
options.text: planted
options.rationale: This is the verb.

options.label: C
options.text: fountain

options.label: D
options.text: We
options.rationale: This is the subject.

items.stem: Choose the preposition: “The library is ____ the post office.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Next to” correctly shows the library’s location beside the post office.
explanation.tip: Some location phrases, like “next to,” act as one preposition.

options.label: A
options.text: next to

options.label: B
options.text: near to
options.rationale: This repeats the idea; use “near” alone.

options.label: C
options.text: close of
options.rationale: This is not a correct phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: beside of
options.rationale: This is not a correct phrase; drop “of.”

items.stem: Which TWO are prepositional phrases? “During the storm, the sailors stayed inside the cabin.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “During” and “inside” each begin a phrase ending in a noun.
explanation.tip: Look for a preposition followed by a noun.

options.label: A
options.text: During the storm

options.label: B
options.text: the storm
options.rationale: A phrase must include its preposition.

options.label: C
options.text: the sailors stayed
options.rationale: This is the subject and verb.

options.label: D
options.text: inside the cabin

items.stem: Which word is a preposition that shows time? “The guests arrived after the ceremony began.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “After” tells us when the guests arrived.
explanation.tip: Time prepositions tell when something happens.

options.label: A
options.text: ceremony
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: arrived
options.rationale: This is a verb.

options.label: C
options.text: guests
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: after

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Under” alone is the correct preposition; “of” should not follow it.
explanation.tip: Some prepositions never need a second word like “of” after them.

items.stem: Choose the preposition: “The team practiced ____ dawn until dusk.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “From … until” shows the whole span of time the team practiced.
explanation.tip: “From” pairs naturally with “until” to show a time range.

options.label: A
options.text: by
options.rationale: “By” shows a deadline, not a starting point.

options.label: B
options.text: from

options.label: C
options.text: at
options.rationale: “At” names one point, not a span.

options.label: D
options.text: since
options.rationale: “Since” pairs with a specific starting time, not “until.”

items.stem: Which phrase works as an adverb telling HOW in this sentence? “The engineer explained the plan with great care.”

options.label: B
