explanation.tip: Think of a dog chasing prey up the wrong tree entirely.

options.label: A
options.text: Accusing someone correctly.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the idiom’s meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: Pursuing a mistaken idea or the wrong course of action.

options.label: C
options.text: Climbing a tree to search for clues.
options.rationale: The idiom is not literal about trees.

options.label: D
options.text: Making a loud noise on purpose.
options.rationale: The idiom is not about actual barking.

items.stem: Even though the team lost the semifinal, their coach told them to keep their chin up. What does this idiom mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The idiom encourages someone to remain hopeful after a setback.
explanation.tip: Picture someone lifting their chin instead of hanging their head in disappointment.

options.label: A
options.text: Hold your head high to look taller.
options.rationale: The idiom is about attitude, not literal posture.

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid looking down while walking.
options.rationale: The idiom has nothing to do with walking safely.

options.label: C
options.text: Stay positive and don’t become discouraged.

options.label: D
options.text: Ignore the loss completely.
options.rationale: The idiom encourages staying positive, not pretending nothing happened.

items.stem: Even after apologizing, the dishonest merchant tried the same trick again the next week, proving that a leopard can’t change its spots. What does this adage mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The adage compares a person’s unchanging habits to a leopard’s permanent spots.
explanation.tip: Think about why the leopard’s spots are a good symbol for something that stays the same.

options.label: A
options.text: Apologies are always insincere.
options.rationale: The adage describes a pattern, not every apology.

options.label: B
options.text: Leopards cannot be trained at all.
options.rationale: The adage is not literal zoology; it is about human character.

options.label: C
options.text: Spots on animals change with age.
options.rationale: The adage relies on the fact that leopard spots do NOT change.

options.label: D
options.text: People’s basic character or habits rarely change.

items.stem: Before announcing the winner, the host said, “Hold your horses,” to the excited crowd. What does this idiom mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The idiom tells people to be patient and avoid acting too quickly.
explanation.tip: Think about pulling back on a horse’s reins to slow it down.

options.label: A
options.text: Wait patiently; don’t rush.

options.label: B
options.text: Ride a horse to the stage.
options.rationale: The idiom has nothing to do with riding.

options.label: C
options.text: Take care of horses properly.
options.rationale: The idiom is not about real horses.

options.label: D
options.text: Stop watching the show.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of what the host intended.

items.stem: Instead of stopping at the nearest shelter, the volunteers went the extra mile and drove two more hours to deliver supplies. What does this idiom mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The idiom describes doing more than what is required or expected.
explanation.tip: Think of a mile as a symbol for any extra effort, not an exact distance.

options.label: A
options.text: To complete the minimum required work.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of making extra effort.

options.label: B
options.text: To make a greater effort than is expected.

options.label: C
options.text: To drive exactly one more mile than planned.
options.rationale: The idiom is not a literal measurement of distance.

options.label: D
options.text: To take the shortest possible route.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the idiom’s meaning.

items.stem: The students who loved chess, puzzles, and coding naturally became close friends, since birds of a feather flock together. What does this adage mean?

explanation.whyCorrect: The adage compares people who share interests to birds of the same species that stay together.
explanation.tip: Think about how birds of the same kind naturally travel in the same flock.

options.label: A
options.text: People with different interests always become friends.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the adage’s meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: Birds and people behave in the same way.
options.rationale: The adage uses birds only as a comparison, not a literal claim about behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: People with similar interests or qualities tend to group together.

options.label: D
options.text: Only birds benefit from staying in groups.
options.rationale: The adage is really about people, not literal birds.

items.stem: A summary should include every single detail from the text.

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary only includes the most important ideas, not every detail.
explanation.tip: Summaries are short word sketches, not full copies of the text.

items.stem: Read: “Bees collect nectar from flowers. They carry the nectar back to the hive. Inside the hive, bees turn the nectar into honey. Other bees store the honey in wax cells.” Which sentence BEST summarizes this passage?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence captures the whole process described, from collecting nectar to making honey.
explanation.tip: A good summary covers the main steps, not just one small detail.

options.label: A
options.text: Bees never leave the hive.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, since bees collect nectar outside the hive.

options.label: B
options.text: Wax cells are the most interesting part of a hive.
options.rationale: This is a minor detail, not the main idea.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees only eat flowers.
options.rationale: This is not stated in the passage.

options.label: D
options.text: Bees collect nectar and turn it into honey to store in their hive.

items.stem: Read: “Mariam’s class visited a farm. They fed the goats, watched a cow being milked, and collected eggs from the hens. Mariam said it was the best day ever.” Which detail is LEAST important to include in a summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: Mariam’s personal feeling is a small detail, not one of the main farm activities.
explanation.tip: Focus a summary on the main events, not on personal reactions.

options.label: A
options.text: Mariam said it was the best day ever.

options.label: B
options.text: They collected eggs from the hens.
options.rationale: This is one of the main activities on the trip.

options.label: C
options.text: They watched a cow being milked.
options.rationale: This is one of the main activities on the trip.

options.label: D
options.text: They fed the goats.
options.rationale: This is one of the main activities on the trip.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to summarize this passage: “First, Sami gathered old newspapers and glue. Next, he shaped the papier-mâché over a balloon. Then he let it dry overnight. Finally, he painted it bright colors.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary of a process should keep the steps in the same order as the original text.
explanation.tip: Reread the passage and note the order signal words.

sequence: Sami gathered newspapers and glue.
He shaped the papier-mâché over a balloon.
He let it dry overnight.
He painted it bright colors.

items.stem: Read: “A camel can go for many days without drinking water. Its hump stores fat, not water, which the camel’s body can use for energy. Camels also have thick eyelashes that protect their eyes from sand.” Which is the BEST summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This summary combines both adaptations described in the passage into one main idea.
explanation.tip: A strong summary pulls together the key points, not just one detail.

options.label: A
options.text: Camels store water in their humps.
options.rationale: The passage says the hump stores fat, not water.

options.label: B
options.text: Camels survive the desert because their bodies are specially adapted, like humps for energy and eyelashes for protection.

options.label: C
options.text: Camels never need to eat.
options.rationale: This is not stated in the passage.

options.label: D
options.text: Desert sand is dangerous for camels’ eyes.
options.rationale: This covers only one detail, missing the passage’s main idea.

items.stem: Read: “Volunteers cleaned the beach for three hours. They collected plastic bottles, old fishing nets, and bits of broken glass. By the end of the day, they had filled twenty bags with trash.” Which sentence is the BEST summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence captures the main activity and its result from the whole passage.
explanation.tip: Combine the main action and its outcome into one summary sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: The beach was completely clean by noon.
options.rationale: This detail is not stated in the passage.

options.label: B
options.text: Fishing nets are dangerous to sea animals.
options.rationale: This is true but is not stated or the main point of this passage.

options.label: C
options.text: Volunteers spent three hours cleaning trash from the beach and filled twenty bags.

options.label: D
options.text: Volunteers enjoyed finding glass on the beach.
options.rationale: Enjoyment is not mentioned, and finding glass is not the main idea.

items.stem: A good summary is usually shorter than the original text.

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary condenses the main ideas, so it is naturally shorter than the full text.
explanation.tip: If your summary is as long as the original, you probably included too many details.

items.stem: Read: “Rania’s robot kit came with wheels, a small motor, and wires. She first attached the wheels to the base, then connected the motor, and finally wired it to a battery. When she turned it on, the robot rolled across the table.” Which detail should be LEFT OUT of a summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: Listing the wires separately is less important than the main building steps and the result.
explanation.tip: Keep the steps and the outcome; drop minor supply details.

options.label: A
options.text: She connected the motor.
options.rationale: This is a key step in building the robot.

options.label: B
options.text: The robot rolled across the table.
options.rationale: This is the key result of the whole process.

options.label: C
options.text: She attached the wheels to the base.
options.rationale: This is a key step in building the robot.

options.label: D
options.text: The kit came with wires.

items.stem: A student summarized a passage about solar panels by writing only: “Solar panels are good.” What is the main problem with this summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary must still capture the key information, not just a vague opinion.
explanation.tip: A one-sentence opinion is not enough; include the main facts too.

options.label: A
options.text: It leaves out the important facts and details explained in the passage.

options.label: B
options.text: It is too long.
options.rationale: The summary is actually far too short, not too long.

options.label: C
options.text: It uses too many quotes from the text.
options.rationale: The summary does not use any quotes at all.

options.label: D
options.text: It focuses only on unimportant details.
options.rationale: The summary has no details at all, important or not.

items.stem: Read: “Coral reefs are home to thousands of species of fish. They form when tiny coral animals called polyps build hard skeletons over many years. Reefs also protect coastlines by slowing down powerful waves.” Which sentence BEST summarizes the whole passage?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence combines all three main ideas: habitat, formation, and protection.
explanation.tip: Look for a summary sentence that touches every main idea, not just one.

options.label: A
options.text: Coral polyps are a type of fish.
options.rationale: The passage describes polyps as tiny coral animals, not fish.

options.label: B
options.text: Coral reefs, built slowly by polyps, support ocean life and protect coastlines.

options.label: C
options.text: Reefs form in just a few days.
options.rationale: The passage says reefs form over many years, not days.

options.label: D
options.text: Waves are the biggest danger to coral reefs.
options.rationale: This is not stated in the passage; reefs actually protect against waves.

items.stem: Why should a summary avoid including the reader’s own opinion?

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary should reflect the text itself, not the reader’s personal reaction to it.
explanation.tip: Save your opinions for a response or review, not a summary.

options.label: A
options.text: Opinions always make summaries longer.
options.rationale: Length is not the real reason opinions are avoided.

options.label: B
options.text: Only teachers are allowed to have opinions.
options.rationale: This is not a real rule about summaries.

options.label: C
options.text: A summary should objectively restate the author’s main ideas, not personal feelings.

options.label: D
options.text: Opinions are impossible to include in writing.
options.rationale: Opinions can certainly be written; they just don’t belong in an objective summary.

items.stem: A summary restates the main ideas of a text in your own words.

explanation.whyCorrect: Summarizing means putting the key ideas into your own words, not copying the text.
explanation.tip: If your summary matches the text word for word, you are copying, not summarizing.

items.stem: Read: “Lighthouses once used oil lamps and mirrors to create a strong beam of light. Keepers had to climb many stairs to refuel the lamp every few hours. Today, most lighthouses use automatic electric lights that need little maintenance.” Which is the BEST summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This summary captures the contrast between past oil lamps and present electric lights.
explanation.tip: A summary of change over time should mention both the past and the present.

options.label: A
options.text: Lighthouse keepers enjoyed climbing stairs.
options.rationale: This is not stated, and enjoyment is not mentioned at all.

options.label: B
options.text: Electric lights are the only ones ever used.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says lighthouses once used oil lamps.

options.label: C
options.text: All lighthouses have been torn down.
options.rationale: This is not stated in the passage.

options.label: D
options.text: Lighthouses have changed from oil lamps that needed constant care to automatic electric lights.

items.stem: Read: “Volcanoes form where melted rock, called magma, rises through cracks in the Earth’s crust. Over time, pressure builds until the magma erupts as lava. Some volcanoes are found underwater and create new islands when they erupt repeatedly.” Which detail is LEAST essential to a summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: The detail about underwater volcanoes is an interesting extra fact, not part of the basic formation process.
explanation.tip: Keep the core cause-and-effect steps; leave out extra examples.

options.label: A
options.text: Some volcanoes are found underwater.

options.label: B
options.text: Eruptions release lava.
options.rationale: This describes the main result of the process, so it is essential.

options.label: C
options.text: Magma rises through cracks in the crust.
options.rationale: This explains the basic cause of volcano formation, so it is essential.

options.label: D
options.text: Pressure builds until it erupts.
options.rationale: This explains a key part of the eruption process, so it is essential.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to summarize this passage: “Workers first mix cement, sand, and water to make concrete. Next, they pour it into wooden molds. Then they let it cure for several days. Finally, they remove the molds to reveal the hardened shape.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A summary of a process should follow the same step order as the original passage.
explanation.tip: Look for the order words first, next, then and finally to guide the sequence.

sequence: Workers mix cement, sand, and water.
They pour the concrete into molds.
They let it cure for several days.
They remove the molds.

items.stem: Read: “Monarch butterflies travel thousands of kilometers every year to escape the cold winter. They fly from North America to warmer forests in Mexico. In spring, their offspring make the journey back north.” Which sentence BEST captures the main idea?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence captures both the direction and the reason for the monarchs’ migration.
explanation.tip: A strong summary combines the “what” and the “why” of the main event.

options.label: A
options.text: Monarch offspring never travel at all.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says offspring make the return journey.

options.label: B
options.text: Monarch butterflies migrate long distances between North America and Mexico to avoid winter.

options.label: C
options.text: Monarch butterflies cannot survive in Mexico.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says they fly there to survive winter.

options.label: D
options.text: Butterflies only migrate in the spring.
options.rationale: The passage describes migration in both directions, not only in spring.

items.stem: Read: “To purify water in an emergency, people can boil it for one minute to kill germs, or add purification tablets to clean it. Bottled water bought from a store is already safe to drink without extra steps.” Which detail is LEAST necessary for a summary of the purification methods?

explanation.whyCorrect: Since this item only summarizes the purification methods, the fact about store-bought water is not one of those methods.
explanation.tip: Match the summary to exactly what the question is asking you to summarize.

options.label: A
options.text: Purification tablets can also clean water.
options.rationale: This is the second main method described, so it belongs in the summary.

options.label: B
options.text: Boiling water for one minute kills germs.
options.rationale: This is one of the two main purification methods described, so it belongs in the summary.

options.label: C
options.text: Bottled water from a store is already safe.

items.stem: When summarizing an informational text, you should focus on the author’s most important points rather than minor examples.

explanation.whyCorrect: A good summary highlights the key points instead of getting lost in small examples.
explanation.tip: Ask yourself: would the passage still make sense without this detail?

items.stem: A student summarized an article about hurricanes by copying three full sentences directly from the text. What is the main problem with this summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: Summarizing means restating ideas in your own words, which shows you understood them.
explanation.tip: If you are copying sentences exactly, you are quoting, not summarizing.

options.label: A
options.text: The summary includes too many unrelated ideas.
options.rationale: Copying from the text does not necessarily add unrelated ideas.

options.label: B
options.text: The summary is too short.
options.rationale: Copying three full sentences is not unusually short.

options.label: C
options.text: A summary should be written in the student’s own words, not copied directly.

options.label: D
options.text: The summary is written in the wrong tense.
options.rationale: Verb tense is not the issue described here.

items.stem: Read: “Researchers tagged sea turtles with tracking devices to study their migration. The data showed that turtles travel thousands of kilometers to return to the beach where they were born in order to lay their eggs. This behavior is called natal homing.” Which is the BEST summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence names the key finding and the scientific term used to describe it.
explanation.tip: Include both the discovery and any special term the passage defines.

options.label: A
options.text: Tracking devices harm sea turtles.
options.rationale: This is not stated in the passage.

options.label: B
options.text: Natal homing means turtles avoid laying eggs.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the passage’s description of natal homing.

options.label: C
options.text: Sea turtles never return to the same beach twice.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which describes turtles returning to their birth beach.

options.label: D
options.text: Tracking data revealed that sea turtles migrate long distances back to their birth beach to nest, a behavior called natal homing.

items.stem: Why is it important for a summary to keep events in the same order as the original text?

explanation.whyCorrect: Keeping the original order helps readers understand relationships between events, like cause and effect.
explanation.tip: If a summary reorders events, readers may misunderstand what led to what.

options.label: A
options.text: Changing the order can confuse readers about what caused what or what happened first.

options.label: B
options.text: Order only matters in fictional stories.
options.rationale: Order matters for informational texts too, especially cause-and-effect or sequence passages.

options.label: C
options.text: Summaries are always written backward.
options.rationale: This is not a real rule for summaries.

options.label: D
options.text: Order does not matter in a summary.
options.rationale: This is the opposite of the real reason order matters.

items.stem: An objective summary avoids the writer’s personal opinions and biases.

explanation.whyCorrect: An objective summary sticks to the facts and ideas in the text, not the writer’s own feelings.
explanation.tip: Remove words like “I think” or “this is good/bad” from a summary.

items.stem: Read: “A four-day school week is being tested in some districts. Supporters argue it saves money on busing and utilities. Critics worry that longer school days are tiring for younger students.” Which is the most OBJECTIVE summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This summary reports both the supporters’ and critics’ views without taking a side.
explanation.tip: An objective summary represents every viewpoint the text presents, not just one.

options.label: A
options.text: Four-day school weeks are clearly a bad idea.
options.rationale: This states a personal opinion rather than reporting both sides.

options.label: B
options.text: Some districts are testing a four-day school week, which supporters say saves money while critics worry it tires younger students.

options.label: C
options.text: Everyone agrees a four-day week saves money.
options.rationale: This ignores the critics mentioned in the passage.

options.label: D
options.text: Longer school days are definitely too tiring.
options.rationale: This states a personal opinion rather than reporting both sides.

items.stem: Read: “Urban gardens let city residents grow vegetables on rooftops and empty lots. They can lower grocery costs and bring neighbors together. One garden in the story was painted a cheerful shade of yellow.” Which detail is LEAST essential to a summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: The color of one garden is a small, specific detail that does not affect the main ideas.
explanation.tip: Ask whether removing a detail changes the passage’s overall meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: Gardens can bring neighbors together.
options.rationale: This is one of the main benefits described, so it is essential.

options.label: B
options.text: Urban gardens can lower grocery costs.
options.rationale: This is one of the main benefits described, so it is essential.

options.label: C
options.text: One garden was painted a cheerful shade of yellow.

options.label: D
options.text: Gardens grow on rooftops and empty lots.
options.rationale: This explains where gardens are located, so it is essential.

items.stem: Put these sentences in order to summarize this passage: “City planners first studied traffic patterns for a month. Next, they proposed adding a bike lane downtown. Then they held public meetings to gather feedback. Finally, the city council approved the new lane.”

explanation.whyCorrect: A process summary should match the order the steps happened in the original text.
explanation.tip: Use the order words first, next, then and finally as a guide.

sequence: Planners studied traffic patterns for a month.
They proposed adding a downtown bike lane.
They held public meetings for feedback.
The city council approved the new lane.

items.stem: Read: “Microplastics are tiny plastic fragments smaller than five millimeters. They come from larger plastic items breaking down, as well as from synthetic clothing fibers released during washing. Scientists have found microplastics in ocean water, soil, and even drinking water.” Which is the BEST summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence combines the definition, sources, and locations of microplastics into one idea.
explanation.tip: A strong summary of a science passage often combines definition, cause, and evidence.

options.label: A
options.text: Microplastics are larger than five millimeters.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says they are smaller than five millimeters.

options.label: B
options.text: Microplastics only come from clothing.
options.rationale: The passage says they come from clothing fibers AND larger plastic items breaking down.

options.label: C
options.text: Scientists have not found microplastics in drinking water.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage directly.

options.label: D
options.text: Microplastics, tiny plastic fragments from broken-down items and clothing fibers, have been found in water, soil, and drinking water.

items.stem: A student summarizing a debate article wrote only the side they personally agreed with. What is the main problem with this summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: Leaving out an opposing viewpoint makes the summary biased and incomplete.
explanation.tip: A summary of a debate should give fair space to each side presented.

options.label: A
options.text: A fair summary should represent all major viewpoints presented in the text, not just one.

options.label: B
options.text: The summary uses too much evidence.
options.rationale: Leaving out an entire side is not caused by using too much evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: The summary should have included even more personal opinions.
options.rationale: Adding more personal opinion would make the summary less objective, not better.

options.label: D
options.text: The summary is too long.
options.rationale: Focusing on only one side is not primarily a length problem.

items.stem: Read: “A new app helps farmers track rainfall and soil moisture. It sends alerts when soil moisture drops too low, helping farmers decide when to irrigate. The app’s icon is colored green. Early tests showed some farmers saved up to twenty percent on water use.” Which detail should be LEFT OUT of a short summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: The icon’s color is a cosmetic detail that has nothing to do with how the app helps farmers.
explanation.tip: Focus on function and results, not minor cosmetic details.

options.label: A
options.text: The app alerts farmers about low soil moisture.
options.rationale: This describes the app’s main purpose, so it is essential.

options.label: B
options.text: The app’s icon is colored green.

options.label: C
options.text: Farmers use the alerts to decide when to irrigate.
options.rationale: This describes how the app is used, so it is essential.

options.label: D
options.text: Tests showed water savings of up to twenty percent.
options.rationale: This describes the main result of using the app, so it is essential.

items.stem: Read: “Researchers studied two groups of students: one that took short breaks every 25 minutes while studying, and one that studied for two hours straight. The group that took breaks remembered more information on a test given a week later.” Which is the BEST summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This sentence states the comparison and the study’s main finding accurately.
explanation.tip: Include both groups being compared and the actual result of the comparison.

options.label: A
options.text: The study tested only one group of students.
options.rationale: The passage clearly describes two separate groups.

options.label: B
options.text: Breaks had no effect on memory.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage’s main finding.

options.label: C
options.text: A study found that students who took short, regular breaks while studying remembered more than those who studied without breaks.

options.label: D
options.text: Students who studied for two hours straight remembered the most.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says the break-taking group remembered more.

items.stem: Why must a summary of a persuasive article still remain objective?

explanation.whyCorrect: An objective summary reports the article’s argument accurately, without trying to convince readers of it.
explanation.tip: A summary describes what an article argues; it should not argue the point itself.

options.label: A
options.text: Objectivity is only required for fiction.
options.rationale: Objectivity applies to summaries of both fiction and nonfiction.

options.label: B
options.text: Persuasive articles do not need summaries.
options.rationale: Persuasive articles can still be summarized objectively.

options.label: C
options.text: A summary should persuade readers to agree with the article.
options.rationale: This confuses the summary’s job with the original article’s job.

options.label: D
options.text: So readers can understand the article’s argument without the summary adding its own bias.

items.stem: Read: “A city council debated whether to replace a historic bridge. Engineers said the bridge was structurally unsafe and needed replacement within five years. Preservationists argued the bridge was a cultural landmark worth the cost of repair. The council postponed a final decision pending further inspection.” Which is the BEST summary?

explanation.whyCorrect: This summary captures both viewpoints and the council’s actual decision to wait.
explanation.tip: When a passage ends without a final resolution, your summary should reflect that too.

options.label: A
options.text: Facing competing engineering and preservation concerns about a historic bridge, the city council postponed its decision pending further inspection.

options.label: B
options.text: The council voted to tear down the bridge immediately.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says the decision was postponed.

options.label: C
options.text: Engineers said the bridge was perfectly safe.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says engineers called it unsafe.

options.label: D
options.text: Preservationists wanted the bridge replaced quickly.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which says preservationists wanted it repaired, not replaced.

items.stem: Because Fatima left her bike outside in the rain, it became rusty. What is the EFFECT in this sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: The rust is the result of leaving the bike out in the rain.
explanation.tip: The effect is what happens because of the cause.

options.label: A
options.text: She left her bike outside.
options.rationale: This is the cause, not the effect.

options.label: B
options.text: The bike became rusty.

options.label: C
options.text: Fatima rode her bike.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: It started raining.
options.rationale: This is a condition in the sentence, not the stated effect.

items.stem: The ice cream melted because the sun was very hot. What is the CAUSE?

explanation.whyCorrect: The heat from the sun is what made the ice cream melt.
explanation.tip: The cause is the reason something happens.

options.label: A
options.text: The ice cream melted.
options.rationale: This is the effect, not the cause.

options.label: B
options.text: It was a cold day.
options.rationale: This contradicts the sentence, which says the sun was hot.

options.label: C
options.text: The sun was very hot.

options.label: D
options.text: Someone ate the ice cream.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

items.stem: Choose the word that signals a cause: “The plants grew tall ____ they received plenty of sunlight and water.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Because” introduces the reason the plants grew tall.
explanation.tip: “Because” answers the question “why?”

options.label: A
options.text: but
options.rationale: “But” signals a contrast, not a cause.

options.label: B
options.text: so
options.rationale: “So” usually introduces the effect, not the cause.

options.label: C
options.text: then
options.rationale: “Then” signals time order, not a reason.

options.label: D
options.text: because

items.stem: Noor forgot to charge her tablet, so it turned off during class. What is the EFFECT of Noor forgetting to charge her tablet?

explanation.whyCorrect: The tablet turning off is the result of it not being charged.
explanation.tip: Find the word “so” — it usually introduces the effect.

options.label: A
options.text: Noor bought a new tablet.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Noor forgot to charge it.
options.rationale: This is the cause, not the effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Class started late.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The tablet turned off during class.

items.stem: Match each cause with its most likely effect.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each cause naturally leads to its matching result.
explanation.tip: Ask yourself, “What would happen next?” for each cause.

pairs.left: A pot of water is left boiling too long.
A plant is kept in a dark closet.
pairs.right: The plant’s leaves turn yellow and weak.

pairs.left: A bicycle tire is never filled with air.
A classroom window is left open in winter.

items.stem: Because the farmers built a canal from the river, their dry fields could finally be watered. What is the CAUSE?

explanation.whyCorrect: Building the canal is what allowed the fields to be watered.
explanation.tip: The cause usually comes right after the word “because.”

options.label: A
options.text: The farmers built a canal from the river.

options.label: B
options.text: The river dried up.
options.rationale: This contradicts the sentence, which says the canal came from the river.

options.label: C
options.text: Their fields could be watered.
options.rationale: This is the effect, not the cause.

options.label: D
options.text: The farmers planted new crops.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

items.stem: In a cause-and-effect relationship, the cause always happens after the effect.

explanation.whyCorrect: The cause happens first and makes the effect happen; the effect follows the cause.
explanation.tip: Ask “why did this happen?” to find the cause, and “what happened as a result?” to find the effect.

items.stem: A town built a taller sea wall after a storm flooded Main Street the previous year. What was the EFFECT of the flood?

explanation.whyCorrect: Building a taller sea wall was the town’s response, caused by the earlier flood.
explanation.tip: Look for what happened as a direct result of the stated event.

options.label: A
options.text: Main Street flooded.
options.rationale: This is itself an effect of the storm, but the question asks about the town’s response to the flood.

options.label: B
options.text: The town built a taller sea wall.

options.label: C
options.text: A storm hit the town.
options.rationale: This is part of the cause, not the town’s response.

options.label: D
options.text: The storm ended.
options.rationale: This is not the focus of the sentence.

items.stem: Because the old bridge could no longer support heavy trucks, the city closed it and built a detour road. Which sentence shows a CHAIN of causes and effects?

explanation.whyCorrect: The weakness led to the closure, and the closure led to building the detour, forming a chain.
explanation.tip: A chain of cause and effect has one effect become the cause of the next event.

options.label: A
options.text: The city built the detour before the bridge weakened.
options.rationale: This reverses the actual timeline described.

options.label: B
options.text: The bridge was closed for no particular reason.
options.rationale: This ignores the stated cause of weakness.

options.label: C
options.text: The bridge’s weakness caused the closure, which in turn caused the detour to be built.

options.label: D
options.text: The detour road caused the bridge to weaken.
options.rationale: This reverses the actual order of events.

items.stem: Because the power line was damaged in the storm, the whole neighborhood lost electricity. What is the CAUSE?

explanation.whyCorrect: The damaged power line is the reason the neighborhood lost electricity.
explanation.tip: The cause is usually introduced by the word “because.”

options.label: A
options.text: The neighborhood lost electricity.
options.rationale: This is the effect, not the cause.

options.label: B
options.text: Workers repaired the line.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: The storm ended quickly.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The power line was damaged in the storm.

items.stem: Overfishing in the bay caused the fish population to drop sharply. What is the EFFECT?

explanation.whyCorrect: The drop in fish population is the direct result of overfishing.
explanation.tip: The word “caused” signals that an effect will follow.

options.label: A
options.text: The fish population dropped sharply.

options.label: B
options.text: The bay became larger.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: New fishing laws were passed.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: Overfishing happened in the bay.
options.rationale: This is the cause, not the effect.

items.stem: Choose the word that signals an effect: “The bridge was old and weak; ____, engineers closed it to traffic.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Therefore” introduces the engineers’ decision as a result of the bridge’s condition.
explanation.tip: “Therefore” and “as a result” both signal an effect is coming.

options.label: A
options.text: therefore

options.label: B
options.text: unless
options.rationale: “Unless” signals a condition, not a result.

options.label: C
options.text: although
options.rationale: “Although” signals a contrast, not an effect.

options.label: D
options.text: meanwhile
options.rationale: “Meanwhile” signals events happening at the same time, not a result.

items.stem: Because the factory released untreated waste into the river, fish downstream began to die. What is the EFFECT?

explanation.whyCorrect: The dying fish are the direct result of the polluted water.
explanation.tip: Ask what happened because of the stated action.

options.label: A
options.text: New factories were built.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Fish downstream began to die.

options.label: C
options.text: The river became wider.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The factory released waste.
options.rationale: This is the cause, not the effect.

items.stem: Match each cause with its most likely effect.

explanation.whyCorrect: Each cause leads naturally to the effect that matches it.
explanation.tip: Think about the most realistic outcome of each situation.

pairs.left: A region experiences a long drought.
A city plants thousands of trees downtown.
pairs.right: Summer temperatures in the city decrease.

pairs.left: A factory updates to more efficient machines.
pairs.right: Energy costs for the factory fall.

pairs.left: An invasive species is introduced to a lake.

items.stem: Because a new highway bypassed the small town, fewer travelers stopped at local shops, so several businesses closed. What is the FIRST cause in this chain?

explanation.whyCorrect: The highway bypassing the town is the event that starts the whole chain.
explanation.tip: In a chain, find the very first event that sets everything else in motion.

options.label: A
options.text: The town built a new highway.
options.rationale: The sentence does not say the town itself built the highway.

options.label: B
options.text: Several businesses closed.
options.rationale: This is the final effect in the chain.

options.label: C
options.text: The new highway bypassed the town.

options.label: D
options.text: Fewer travelers stopped at local shops.
options.rationale: This is a middle effect in the chain, caused by the highway.

items.stem: A marine biologist explains that warmer ocean water causes coral to expel the algae living inside it, which causes the coral to turn white and lose its main food source. Which event in this passage ALSO acts as a cause for a later event?

explanation.whyCorrect: The coral expelling its algae is an effect of warm water, but it also causes the coral to turn white.
explanation.tip: In a causal chain, a middle event is both an effect of what came before and a cause of what comes after.

options.label: A
options.text: Warmer ocean water
options.rationale: This is only a cause; the passage does not describe anything causing it.

options.label: B
options.text: Coral turning white
options.rationale: This is described only as an effect, not as a cause of a further event in the passage.

options.label: C
options.text: Coral losing its food source
options.rationale: This is the final effect described, not a cause of something else.

options.label: D
options.text: Coral expelling its algae

items.stem: Rising global temperatures are causing glaciers to melt faster, which is raising sea levels, which is increasing coastal flooding. If temperatures stopped rising, what would this causal chain predict about coastal flooding?

explanation.whyCorrect: Since each effect depends on the one before it, removing the first cause should slow or reverse the whole chain.
explanation.tip: Follow a causal chain backward to predict what happens if the starting cause changes.

options.label: A
options.text: Coastal flooding would likely decrease, since each effect in the chain depends on the one before it.

options.label: B
options.text: Coastal flooding would stay exactly the same.
options.rationale: This ignores how each step in the chain depends on the one before it.

options.label: C
options.text: Glaciers would melt even faster.
options.rationale: This contradicts the chain, since the original cause has stopped.

options.label: D
options.text: Coastal flooding would increase even more.
options.rationale: This contradicts the logic of the causal chain described.

items.stem: Because the city reduced bus fares, more residents began using public transportation. What is the EFFECT?

explanation.whyCorrect: The increase in riders is the direct result of the lower fares.
explanation.tip: The word “because” points to the cause; the rest of the sentence usually states the effect.

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer buses were purchased.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: More residents began using public transportation.

options.label: C
options.text: Bus routes were extended.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The city reduced bus fares.
options.rationale: This is the cause, not the effect.

items.stem: A drop in bee populations is causing some crops to produce less fruit, since bees pollinate many flowering plants. What is the CAUSE of the lower fruit production?

explanation.whyCorrect: Fewer bees means less pollination, which leads directly to less fruit.
explanation.tip: Look for the explanation introduced by “since,” which often signals a cause.

options.label: A
options.text: A rise in bee populations.
options.rationale: This contradicts the passage, which describes a drop, not a rise.

options.label: B
options.text: Farmers planting more crops.
options.rationale: This is not mentioned in the passage.

options.label: C
options.text: The drop in bee populations.

options.label: D
options.text: The crops producing less fruit.
options.rationale: This is the effect, not the cause.

items.stem: Choose the best transition for cause and effect: “The river’s water level dropped sharply; ____, several boats could no longer dock at the pier.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “As a result” introduces the direct consequence of the dropping water level.
explanation.tip: “As a result” and “consequently” both signal that an effect is about to be stated.

options.label: A
options.text: for example
options.rationale: “For example” signals an illustration, not a result.

options.label: B
options.text: as a result

options.label: C
options.text: similarly
options.rationale: “Similarly” signals a comparison, not a result.

options.label: D
options.text: in contrast
options.rationale: “In contrast” signals a difference, not a result.

items.stem: Because the company switched to recycled packaging, its shipping costs decreased and its reputation improved among environmentally conscious customers. Which TWO effects are described?

explanation.whyCorrect: Both lower costs and improved reputation are results of the switch to recycled packaging.
explanation.tip: Look for the outcomes listed after the cause is introduced.

options.label: A
options.text: The company switched to recycled packaging.
options.rationale: This is the cause, not an effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Shipping costs decreased.

options.label: C
options.text: Its reputation improved among environmentally conscious customers.

options.label: D
options.text: The company went out of business.
options.rationale: This is not stated and contradicts the positive outcomes described.

items.stem: A historian explains that a severe drought led to crop failures, which led to food shortages, which eventually led to mass migration from the region. Which of these is a MIDDLE link in the causal chain — both an effect and a cause?

explanation.whyCorrect: Food shortages are an effect of the crop failures, but they also cause the mass migration that follows.
explanation.tip: A middle link in a chain is caused by the step before it and causes the step after it.

options.label: A
options.text: The historian’s explanation
options.rationale: The explanation itself is not part of the events in the chain.

options.label: B
options.text: The mass migration
options.rationale: This is only the final effect of the whole chain.

options.label: C
options.text: The severe drought
options.rationale: This is only the starting cause of the whole chain.

options.label: D
options.text: The food shortages

items.stem: Because social media algorithms show users more of what they already agree with, some researchers argue this causes people’s opinions to become more extreme over time. According to this passage, what is being proposed as a LONG-TERM effect?

explanation.whyCorrect: The passage states this outcome as the long-term result researchers are concerned about.
explanation.tip: Look for the outcome the passage frames as happening gradually, “over time.”

options.label: A
options.text: People’s opinions becoming more extreme over time.

options.label: B
options.text: Users disagreeing with algorithms.
options.rationale: This is not stated in the passage.

options.label: C
options.text: Algorithms showing agreeable content.
options.rationale: This is the cause, not the proposed long-term effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Researchers studying social media.
options.rationale: This describes the researchers’ activity, not an effect of the algorithms.

items.stem: A single effect can have more than one contributing cause.

explanation.whyCorrect: Many real-world events, like a forest fire, result from multiple causes working together, such as dry weather and a spark.
explanation.tip: Look for words like “also” and “in addition” that signal more than one cause.

items.stem: An economist notes that rising fuel prices increase shipping costs, which increases the price of imported goods, which then reduces how much consumers are able to buy. If fuel prices suddenly fell instead, which outcome would this causal chain predict?

explanation.whyCorrect: Reversing the first cause in a chain should reverse the effects that follow it.
explanation.tip: Trace a causal chain forward with the opposite starting condition to predict the outcome.

options.label: A
options.text: Imported goods would become more expensive.
options.rationale: This contradicts the logic of the causal chain if the starting cause reverses.

options.label: B
options.text: Shipping costs would likely fall, making imported goods cheaper and increasing how much consumers can buy.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers would buy less regardless of fuel prices.
options.rationale: This ignores how the whole chain depends on the starting cause.

options.label: D
options.text: Shipping costs would rise even though fuel got cheaper.
options.rationale: This contradicts the direct relationship described in the passage.

items.stem: Choose the word: “A giraffe is ____ than a zebra.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two animals uses the comparative form -er: taller.
explanation.tip: Two things: add -er. Three or more: add -est.

options.label: A
options.text: more tall
options.rationale: Short adjectives like “tall” add -er instead of “more.”

options.label: B
options.text: tallest
options.rationale: Comparing only two animals needs -er, not -est.

options.label: C
options.text: taller

options.label: D
options.text: tall
options.rationale: You need a comparing word here.

items.stem: Choose the word: “Of the three bags, the blue one is the ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing three bags needs the superlative -est: heaviest.
explanation.tip: “Of the three” signals a superlative.

options.label: A
options.text: most heavy
options.rationale: Short adjectives like “heavy” change y to i and add -est.

options.label: B
options.text: heavy
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

options.label: C
options.text: heavier
options.rationale: “Heavier” compares only two bags.

options.label: D
options.text: heaviest

items.stem: Which sentence compares two drawings correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Colorful” is a long adjective, so “more” is used to compare two drawings.
explanation.tip: Long adjectives (three or more syllables) take more/most, not -er/-est.

options.label: A
options.text: Lina’s drawing is colorfuler than Hana’s.
options.rationale: Long adjectives use “more,” not -er.

options.label: B
options.text: Lina’s drawing is more colorfuller than Hana’s.
options.rationale: Never use “more” and -er together.

options.label: C
options.text: Lina’s drawing is more colorful than Hana’s.

options.label: D
options.text: Lina’s drawing is most colorful than Hana’s.
options.rationale: “Most” compares three or more, and “than” signals only two.

items.stem: Choose the word: “This path is ____ than that one.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two paths uses -er: shorter.
explanation.tip: Short one-syllable adjectives usually add -er/-est.

options.label: A
options.text: shorter

options.label: B
options.text: short
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

options.label: C
options.text: shortest
options.rationale: Comparing two paths needs -er.

options.label: D
options.text: more short
options.rationale: Short adjectives like “short” add -er.

items.stem: Which sentence uses comparing words correctly for three runners?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing three or more runners needs the superlative -est: fastest.
explanation.tip: Never use “than” right after a superlative like fastest.

options.label: A
options.text: Of the three runners, Sara finished faster.
options.rationale: “Faster” compares only two runners.

options.label: B
options.text: Of the three runners, Sara finished fastest than the others.
options.rationale: Never use “than” after a superlative.

options.label: C
options.text: Of the three runners, Sara finished the most fast.
options.rationale: “Fast” is short, so it takes -est, not “most.”

options.label: D
options.text: Of the three runners, Sara finished the fastest.

items.stem: “Older” correctly compares the ages of two brothers.

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing exactly two people uses the comparative -er form: older.
explanation.tip: Check how many things are being compared before choosing -er or -est.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Never pair “more” with an -er ending; “heavier” by itself already shows the comparison.
explanation.tip: Double comparatives (more + -er) are always wrong.

items.stem: Choose the word: “This riddle is ____ than the last one.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two riddles uses -er, changing y to i: trickier.
explanation.tip: For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to i before adding -er/-est.

options.label: A
options.text: more tricky
options.rationale: Short adjectives ending in y change to i and add -er.

options.label: B
options.text: trickier

options.label: C
options.text: tricky
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

options.label: D
options.text: trickiest
options.rationale: Comparing two riddles needs -er.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the irregular comparative correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bad changes to worse to worst; comparing two days uses worse.
explanation.tip: Memorize irregular forms: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst.

options.label: A
options.text: My cold is worse today than it was yesterday.

options.label: B
options.text: My cold is worst today than it was yesterday.
options.rationale: “Worst” compares three or more, not two.

options.label: C
options.text: My cold is more bad today than it was yesterday.
options.rationale: “Bad” is irregular: bad, worse, worst.

options.label: D
options.text: My cold is badder today than it was yesterday.
options.rationale: “Badder” is not a word; use “worse.”

items.stem: Choose the word: “Please speak ____ than you did before.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Adverbs ending in -ly form comparatives with more: more quietly.
explanation.tip: Adverbs ending in -ly almost always use more/most.

options.label: A
options.text: most quietly
options.rationale: “Most” compares three or more.

options.label: B
options.text: quieter
options.rationale: “Quieter” compares the adjective, not how someone speaks.

options.label: C
options.text: more quietly

options.label: D
options.text: quietlier
options.rationale: Adverbs ending in -ly use “more,” not -er.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly compares how two sisters sing?

explanation.whyCorrect: More plus beautifully compares how two sisters sing.
explanation.tip: Compare adverbs the same way as long adjectives: more/most.

options.label: A
options.text: Mona sings beautifullier than her sister.
options.rationale: -ly adverbs use “more,” not -er.

options.label: B
options.text: Mona sings more beautifully than her sister.

options.label: C
options.text: Mona sings most beautifully than her sister.
options.rationale: “Most” is for three or more, but “than” signals a two-way comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: Mona sings beautifuller than her sister.
options.rationale: “Beautiful” is a long word; its adverb form also needs “more.”

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Short adjectives like “hot” double the final consonant and add -er instead of using “more.”
explanation.tip: One-syllable adjectives ending in one vowel plus one consonant double that consonant before -er/-est.

items.stem: Choose the word: “This is the ____ day of the whole year.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “The whole year” signals a superlative with a doubled consonant: hottest.
explanation.tip: Double the final consonant before -er/-est when a short adjective ends in one vowel plus one consonant.

options.label: A
options.text: hotter
options.rationale: “Hotter” compares only two days, not the whole year.

options.label: B
options.text: most hot
options.rationale: Short adjectives like “hot” double the consonant and add -est, not “most.”

options.label: C
options.text: hot
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

options.label: D
options.text: hottest

items.stem: Which sentence makes an equal comparison correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Equal comparisons use the pattern as + adjective + as.
explanation.tip: Look for “as…as” to compare two equal things.

options.label: A
options.text: This bridge is as longer as that one.
options.rationale: Do not add -er inside an “as…as” comparison.

options.label: B
options.text: This bridge is so long as that one.
options.rationale: Equal comparisons use “as…as,” not “so…as.”

options.label: C
options.text: This bridge is as long as that one.

options.label: D
options.text: This bridge is as long than that one.
options.rationale: Equal comparisons use “as” on both sides, not “than.”

items.stem: Choose the word: “This hallway was ____ than I remembered.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two states (now and before) uses -er: narrower.
explanation.tip: Watch for comparisons across time, not only between two objects.

options.label: A
options.text: narrower

options.label: B
options.text: more narrow
options.rationale: “Narrow” is a short adjective and takes -er.

options.label: C
options.text: narrowest
options.rationale: This still compares just two states, so -er is needed, not -est.

options.label: D
options.text: narrow
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

items.stem: Which sentence compares distance correctly using “farther”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Far is irregular; “farther” compares physical distance between two places.
explanation.tip: Use “farther” for physical distance and “further” for additional or figurative ideas.

options.label: A
options.text: The library is farthest from school than the park is.
options.rationale: A superlative cannot be followed by “than.”

options.label: B
options.text: The library is further from school than the park is.
options.rationale: “Further” is usually used for figurative distance, not physical distance.

options.label: C
options.text: The library is more far from school than the park is.
options.rationale: “Far” is irregular: far, farther, farthest.

options.label: D
options.text: The library is farther from school than the park is.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “More” and the -er ending cannot be combined; “clearer” alone is the correct comparative.
explanation.tip: A double comparative (more + -er) is always incorrect.

segments: sitting near the back of the room.

items.stem: Choose the correct comparative adverb: “The detective solved the case ____ than anyone expected.”

explanation.whyCorrect: The -ly adverb cleverly forms its comparative with more: more cleverly.
explanation.tip: To compare an action, check whether the word ends in -ly; if so, use more/most.

options.label: A
options.text: cleverlier
options.rationale: -ly adverbs cannot take -er; use “more.”

options.label: B
options.text: more cleverly

options.label: C
options.text: most cleverly
options.rationale: “Most” compares three or more, but “than anyone” signals a two-way comparison.

options.label: D
options.text: more clever
options.rationale: This compares the adjective, not how the detective solved it.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly compares three essays using the irregular word for “little”?

explanation.whyCorrect: Little changes to less to least, an irregular pattern; three or more items need the superlative least.
explanation.tip: Little is irregular: little, less, least — just like good, better, best.

options.label: A
options.text: Of the three essays, this one has the least detail.

options.label: B
options.text: Of the three essays, this one has less detail than the others.
options.rationale: Comparing three or more items needs the superlative “least,” not “less.”

options.label: C
options.text: Of the three essays, this one has the littlest detail.
options.rationale: “Littlest” is not standard; the irregular superlative is “least.”

options.label: D
options.text: Of the three essays, this one has the less detail.
options.rationale: “Less” compares only two things; use “least” for three or more.

items.stem: Choose the word: “This novel is ____ than the one I read last month.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two novels uses -er: longer.
explanation.tip: Two things compared uses -er; three or more uses -est.

options.label: A
options.text: longest
options.rationale: Comparing two novels needs -er.

options.label: B
options.text: more long
options.rationale: Short adjectives like “long” add -er, not “more.”

options.label: C
options.text: longer

options.label: D
options.text: long
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

items.stem: Choose the word: “Of all the rivers on the map, the Nile is the ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing many rivers needs the superlative -est: longest.
explanation.tip: “Of all” signals a superlative.

options.label: A
options.text: most long
options.rationale: Short adjectives add -est, not “most.”

options.label: B
options.text: longer
options.rationale: “Longer” compares only two rivers.

options.label: C
options.text: long
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

options.label: D
options.text: longest

items.stem: Choose the word: “Dana looked ____ after the surprise party than she had all week.”

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing two states uses -er, changing y to i: happier.
explanation.tip: For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to i before adding -er/-est.

options.label: A
options.text: happier

options.label: B
options.text: happiest
options.rationale: This compares only two states (before and after), so use -er.

options.label: C
options.text: more happy
options.rationale: Short adjectives ending in y change to i and add -er.

options.label: D
options.text: happy
options.rationale: You need a comparing word.

items.stem: Which sentence compares the triplets correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing three triplets needs the superlative -est: happiest.
explanation.tip: A group of three or more always needs the superlative form.

options.label: A
options.text: Of the triplets, Ahmed is happier.
options.rationale: “Happier” compares only two people, but there are three triplets.

options.label: B
options.text: Of the triplets, Ahmed is the happiest.

explanation.tip: Formal letters use a colon after the greeting; friendly letters use a comma.

options.label: A
options.text: Dear Sir or Madam:

options.label: B
options.text: Dear sir or madam:

options.label: C
options.text: dear Sir or Madam:

options.label: D
options.text: Dear Sir or Madam,

options.label: B

items.stem: Put the parts of a formal business letter in the correct order.

explanation.whyCorrect: A formal business letter follows this order: heading, inside address, greeting, body, closing, signature.

the inside address
the greeting

items.stem: Which sentence uses the abbreviation “etc.” correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Etc.” is short for “and so on” and is spelled with a period after it, usually followed by a comma in a list.
explanation.tip: “Etc.” always ends with a period, even in the middle of a sentence.

options.label: A
options.text: Bring snacks, Etc., for the trip.
options.rationale: “Etc.” is not capitalized in the middle of a sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: Bring snacks, drinks, etc for the trip.
options.rationale: The abbreviation etc. needs a period after it.

options.label: C
options.text: Bring snacks, drinks, ect., for the trip.
options.rationale: This abbreviation is misspelled; the correct form is etc.

options.label: D
options.text: Bring snacks, drinks, etc., for the trip.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the comparative form of an adverb correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: Adverbs ending in -ly form their comparative with more: more gracefully.
explanation.tip: -ly adverbs always use more/most, never -er/-est.

options.label: A
options.text: She explained the puzzle most gracefully than her partner did.
options.rationale: “Most” compares three or more, but “than” signals only two.

options.label: B
options.text: She explained the puzzle gracefullier than her partner did.
options.rationale: -ly adverbs cannot take -er; use “more.”

options.label: C
options.text: She explained the puzzle more gracefuller than her partner did.
options.rationale: Never combine “more” with an -er ending.

options.label: D
options.text: She explained the puzzle more gracefully than her partner did.

explanation.tip: “Of all” is a clue to use the superlative most + adverb.

options.label: A
options.text: Of all the dancers, Yara moved the most gracefully.

options.label: B
options.text: Of all the dancers, Yara moved the most gracefulliest.
options.rationale: Never combine “most” with an -est ending.

options.label: C
options.text: Of all the dancers, Yara moved more gracefully.
options.rationale: “More” compares only two dancers, but “of all” signals a group.

options.label: D
options.text: Of all the dancers, Yara moved the gracefullest.
options.rationale: -ly adverbs cannot take -est; use “most.”

items.stem: Which sentence is an interrogative sentence (asks a question)?

explanation.whyCorrect: An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark.
explanation.tip: Interrogative sentences usually begin with words like what, who, when, or do.

options.label: A
options.text: What a long wait that was!
options.rationale: This sentence shows strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

options.label: B
options.text: Wait for the bus here.
options.rationale: This sentence gives a command, so it is imperative.

options.label: C
options.text: The bus leaves at eight.
options.rationale: This sentence makes a statement, so it is declarative.

options.label: D
options.text: What time does the bus leave?

items.stem: Which sentence is an imperative sentence (gives a command)?

explanation.whyCorrect: An imperative sentence gives a command or makes a request.
explanation.tip: Imperative sentences often begin with the verb itself, as if “you” is understood.

options.label: A
options.text: Please hand me the scissors.

options.label: B
options.text: I need the scissors now.
options.rationale: This sentence makes a statement, so it is declarative.

options.label: C
options.text: Could you hand me the scissors?
options.rationale: This sentence asks a question, so it is interrogative.

options.label: D
options.text: Those scissors are so sharp!
options.rationale: This sentence shows strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

items.stem: Which sentence is an exclamatory sentence?

explanation.whyCorrect: An exclamatory sentence shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation point.
explanation.tip: Exclamatory sentences often begin with “what” or “how” and express excitement.

options.label: A
options.text: This is a wonderful surprise.
options.rationale: This sentence simply states a fact, so it is declarative.

options.label: B
options.text: What a wonderful surprise this is!

options.label: C
options.text: Is this a wonderful surprise?
options.rationale: This sentence asks a question, so it is interrogative.

options.label: D
options.text: Tell me about the surprise.
options.rationale: This sentence gives a command, so it is imperative.

options.label: B

items.stem: Match each sentence with the way it begins.

items.stem: Which sentence has a compound SUBJECT?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Sara and Tom” are two subjects joined by “and,” making a compound subject.
explanation.tip: A compound subject has two or more subjects doing the same action.

options.label: A
options.text: Sara washed the car carefully and quickly.
options.rationale: This sentence has one subject, one verb, and two adverbs.

options.label: B
options.text: Sara washed the car and the bike.
options.rationale: This sentence has one subject and one verb with two objects.

options.label: C
options.text: Sara washed and waxed the car together.
options.rationale: This sentence has one subject but two verbs, so it has a compound predicate.

options.label: D
options.text: Sara and Tom washed the car together.

items.stem: Which sentence has a compound PREDICATE?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Stretched” and “yawned” are two verbs joined by “and,” making a compound predicate.
explanation.tip: A compound predicate has two or more verbs for the same subject.

options.label: A
options.text: The cat stretched and yawned in the sun.

options.label: B
options.text: The cat and the dog slept in the sun.
options.rationale: This sentence has two subjects joined by “and,” so it has a compound subject.

options.label: C
options.text: The cat stretched in the warm, bright sun.
options.rationale: This sentence has only one verb and two adjectives.

options.label: D
options.text: The sleepy cat stretched in the sun.
options.rationale: This sentence has only one verb, “stretched.”
