options.text: It confirms the explorer’s route was always safe.
options.rationale: The flashback actually explains a danger connected to the old map, not safety.

options.label: B
options.text: It removes any need for a conclusion.
options.rationale: The story still needs a conclusion after the flashback is revealed.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes the ending less important than the middle of the story.
options.rationale: Placing key information at the end usually increases, not decreases, its importance.

options.label: D
options.text: It delivers a twist that reframes everything readers thought they understood about the mapmaker.

items.stem: A lighthouse keeper’s daughter keeps her father’s old, cracked lantern on her shelf, flashing back to the storm when he used it to guide a ship to safety; the story ends with her lighting her own new lantern during a storm. Why might the author include both lanterns?

explanation.whyCorrect: The old and new lanterns mirror each other, showing the daughter continuing her father’s role.
explanation.tip: When an object reappears across a flashback and the present, compare what it represents each time.

options.label: A
options.text: To show that the daughter is carrying on her father’s legacy of guiding others safely.

options.label: B
options.text: To prove that lanterns are no longer useful.
options.rationale: Both lanterns are shown being used successfully, not as useless objects.

options.label: C
options.text: To suggest the daughter plans to leave the lighthouse.
options.rationale: The ending shows her actively continuing the work, not leaving it.

options.label: D
options.text: To explain how electricity was invented.
options.rationale: The passage focuses on legacy and duty, not the history of electricity.

items.stem: A village storyteller is first shown as grumpy and unwelcoming, but a flashback reveals that he lost his own family in a flood years ago and has been alone since. How does this flashback likely change a reader’s judgment of the storyteller?

explanation.whyCorrect: Learning about the storyteller’s painful loss helps readers understand his grumpy behavior with more sympathy.
explanation.tip: A flashback revealing past pain often shifts readers’ judgment of a character.

options.label: A
options.text: It shows that the flood was the storyteller’s own fault.
options.rationale: Nothing in the passage blames the storyteller for causing the flood.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes readers feel more sympathy for him by explaining the pain behind his behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes readers trust him less because he lied about his past.
options.rationale: There is no indication the storyteller lied; the flashback simply reveals unknown pain.

options.label: D
options.text: It proves that the storyteller was always a cheerful person.
options.rationale: The flashback reveals loss and sorrow, not a cheerful past.

items.stem: In a flashback, a young pilot notices a strange rattling sound in an old plane just before a minor crash landing; years later, as an experienced pilot, she hears the same sound and immediately lands safely. Which flashback detail connects to the safe ending?

explanation.whyCorrect: The rattling sound links the two moments: ignoring it caused trouble once, and recognizing it later prevents trouble.
explanation.tip: Look for a specific sensory detail that repeats between the flashback and the present.

options.label: A
options.text: The color of the old plane she flew as a young pilot.
options.rationale: The color of the plane is never mentioned as important to either landing.

options.label: B
options.text: The number of passengers on her very first flight.
options.rationale: Passenger count is not connected to recognizing the rattling sound.

options.label: C
options.text: The strange rattling sound she first heard and ignored as a young pilot.

options.label: D
options.text: The name of the airport where she first trained.
options.rationale: The airport’s name is not the detail linked to the safe landing.

items.stem: A flashback must always appear at the very beginning of a story.

explanation.whyCorrect: A flashback can appear anywhere in a story — at the start, in the middle, or near the end — wherever the author needs it.
explanation.tip: Don’t assume a flashback only opens a story; check the whole passage for one.

items.stem: “A tiny lizard hid under the warm rock.” Which word describes HOW BIG the lizard is?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tiny” tells the size of the lizard.
explanation.tip: Size adjectives answer the question “how big or small?”

options.label: A
options.text: rock
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: lizard
options.rationale: This is the noun being described.

options.label: C
options.text: hid
options.rationale: This is the verb.

options.label: D
options.text: tiny

items.stem: Choose the correctly ordered adjectives: “We adopted a ____ puppy.”

explanation.whyCorrect: English adjective order usually places size before color: a small brown puppy.
explanation.tip: Remember a rough order: opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material, purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: puppy small
options.rationale: A noun cannot be placed before its own adjectives.

options.label: B
options.text: small brown

options.label: C
options.text: brown little
options.rationale: This repeats the size idea with two different words in the wrong order.

options.label: D
options.text: brown small
options.rationale: Size adjectives usually come before color adjectives: small brown, not brown small.

items.stem: “Those mountains look snowy today.” Which word is a demonstrative adjective?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Those” points out which mountains, so it is a demonstrative adjective.
explanation.tip: Demonstrative adjectives: this, that, these, those.

options.label: A
options.text: Those

options.label: B
options.text: snowy
options.rationale: This is an adjective, but it describes a quality, not “which one.”

options.label: C
options.text: look
options.rationale: This is the verb.

options.label: D
options.text: mountains
options.rationale: This is the noun being described.

items.stem: “After the long hike, the campers felt exhausted.” Which word is the predicate adjective describing the campers?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Exhausted” follows the linking verb “felt” and describes the campers.
explanation.tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs like feel, seem, look, taste.

options.label: A
options.text: long
options.rationale: This describes the hike, not the campers.

options.label: B
options.text: exhausted

options.label: C
options.text: campers
options.rationale: This is the noun being described, not the adjective.

options.label: D
options.text: hike
options.rationale: This is a noun.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A compound adjective made of two words before a noun usually needs a hyphen: well-seasoned.
explanation.tip: Hyphenate two-word adjectives that work together before a noun.

items.stem: “Egyptian cotton is famous worldwide.” Which word is a proper adjective?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Egyptian” comes from the proper noun Egypt and is capitalized, making it a proper adjective.
explanation.tip: Proper adjectives come from proper nouns and are always capitalized.

options.label: A
options.text: cotton
options.rationale: This is a noun.

options.label: B
options.text: famous
options.rationale: This is an adjective, but it is not formed from a proper noun.

options.label: C
options.text: Egyptian

options.label: D
options.text: worldwide
options.rationale: This is an adverb.

items.stem: There are ____ clouds in the sky today than yesterday.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Clouds” can be counted, so the correct comparing word is “fewer.”
explanation.tip: Use fewer for countable nouns and less for uncountable nouns.

options.label: A
options.text: little
options.rationale: “Little” does not fit before a plural countable noun like “clouds.”

options.label: B
options.text: less
options.rationale: Use “less” for amounts you cannot count, like “less rain,” not countable clouds.

options.label: C
options.text: fewer

options.label: D
options.text: much
options.rationale: “Much” is used with uncountable nouns, not countable ones like clouds.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the irregular comparative correctly?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Good” changes irregularly: good → better → best.
explanation.tip: Memorize irregular comparatives like good/better/best and bad/worse/worst.

options.label: A
options.text: The new bridge is bestest than the old wooden one.
options.rationale: “Bestest” is not a real word; the superlative of good is best.

options.label: B
options.text: The new bridge is gooder than the old wooden one.
options.rationale: “Good” is irregular: good, better, best, not gooder.

options.label: C
options.text: The new bridge is more better than the old wooden one.
options.rationale: Never use “more” together with “better.”

options.label: D
options.text: The new bridge is better than the old wooden one.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: A person who feels curiosity about something is “interested,” while “interesting” describes the thing that causes the feeling.
explanation.tip: -ed adjectives describe feelings; -ing adjectives describe what causes the feeling.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the adjective correctly after a linking verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Feels” is a linking verb here, so it should be followed by the adjective “soft,” not an adverb.
explanation.tip: After linking verbs (is, seems, tastes, feels, smells), use adjectives.

options.label: A
options.text: The blanket feels soft against her cheek.

options.label: B
options.text: The blanket feels softly against her cheek.
options.rationale: After a linking verb like “feels,” use an adjective, not an adverb.

options.label: C
options.text: The blanket feel soft against her cheek.
options.rationale: “Blanket” is singular, so the verb should be “feels.”

options.label: D
options.text: The blanket feels soft against her cheekly.
options.rationale: “Cheekly” is not a real word; the correct word is “cheek.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses “looks” correctly, keeping in mind that “looks” can act as a linking verb or an action verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Looks” links “barn” to a quality, so the adjective “shaky” is correct.
explanation.tip: If a verb describes a quality rather than an action, follow it with an adjective.

options.label: A
options.text: The old barn looks shakily in the strong wind.
options.rationale: Here “looks” is a linking verb describing a quality, so it needs the adjective “shaky,” not the adverb “shakily.”

options.label: B
options.text: The old barn looks shaky in the strong wind.

options.label: C
options.text: The old barn look shaky in the strong wind.
options.rationale: “Barn” is singular, so the verb must be “looks,” not “look.”

options.label: D
options.text: The old barn looks shaky in the strongly wind.
options.rationale: “Wind” is a noun, so it needs the adjective “strong,” not the adverb “strongly.”

items.stem: “The curious explorer studied the ancient, crumbling wall.” Which two words are coordinate adjectives (adjectives of equal importance, separated by a comma, both describing “wall”)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Ancient” and “crumbling” are both adjectives of equal weight describing the wall, so they are separated by a comma.
explanation.tip: Coordinate adjectives can usually be swapped or joined with “and” and still make sense.

options.label: A
options.text: the, ancient
options.rationale: “The” is an article, not a coordinate adjective.

options.label: B
options.text: studied, wall
options.rationale: “Studied” is a verb and “wall” is a noun.

options.label: C
options.text: ancient, crumbling

options.label: D
options.text: curious, explorer
options.rationale: “Explorer” is a noun, not an adjective.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: Three or more coordinate adjectives in a series usually need “and” before the last one, plus commas between the others.
explanation.tip: In a list of three or more adjectives, use commas and “and” before the final item.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly avoids comparing an absolute adjective (one that cannot logically have degrees, like “perfect” or “round”)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Perfect” describes a complete, flawless state, so it should not be compared with “more” or “-er.”
explanation.tip: Absolute adjectives like perfect, round, and complete usually cannot be compared.

options.label: A
options.text: Her solution to the puzzle was the most perfect.
options.rationale: “Perfect” already means complete, so it cannot have a superlative degree.

options.label: B
options.text: Her solution to the puzzle was perfecter.
options.rationale: “Perfecter” is not a correct or real comparative form.

options.label: C
options.text: Her solution to the puzzle was more perfect.
options.rationale: “Perfect” is an absolute adjective; it cannot logically be “more perfect.”

options.label: D
options.text: Her solution to the puzzle was perfect.

items.stem: Choose the article: “She is ____ honest witness in this case.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Honest” starts with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes “an.”
explanation.tip: Choose a/an based on the SOUND of the next word, not just its first letter.

options.label: A
options.text: a
options.rationale: “Honest” begins with a silent h, so it has a vowel sound and needs “an.”

options.label: B
options.text: the
options.rationale: “The” would not fit the meaning of introducing one witness among many.

options.label: C
options.text: some
options.rationale: “Some” does not fit before a singular countable noun like “witness.”

options.label: D
options.text: an

items.stem: Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct order?

explanation.whyCorrect: The usual order is quantity, size, condition, then color: two, small, ripe, green.
explanation.tip: Build a mental checklist: quantity, size, age/condition, shape, color, origin, material.

options.label: A
options.text: The chef used two small ripe green mangoes.

options.label: B
options.text: The chef used green small two ripe mangoes.
options.rationale: Color adjectives usually come near the end of the order, not near the beginning.

options.label: C
options.text: The chef used ripe small two green mangoes.
options.rationale: Size adjectives usually come before age/condition adjectives like “ripe.”

options.label: D
options.text: The chef used small two ripe green mangoes.
options.rationale: Numbers usually come before size adjectives: two small, not small two.

items.stem: A predicate adjective always comes directly before the noun it describes.

explanation.whyCorrect: A predicate adjective comes AFTER a linking verb and describes the subject, not directly before a noun.
explanation.tip: Predicate adjectives follow linking verbs: The sky is clear.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Eggs” is a countable noun, so the correct comparing word is “fewer,” not “less.”
explanation.tip: Fewer for things you can count; less for things you cannot count.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a possessive adjective?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Their” is the possessive adjective that correctly shows ownership of the tent.
explanation.tip: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) come directly before a noun.

options.label: A
options.text: There tent blew away in the sudden wind.
options.rationale: “There” points to a place; the possessive word needed here is “Their.”

options.label: B
options.text: Their tent blew away in the sudden wind.

options.label: C
options.text: Them tent blew away in the sudden wind.
options.rationale: “Them” is an object pronoun and cannot be used as an adjective before a noun.

options.label: D
options.text: They’re tent blew away in the sudden wind.
options.rationale: “They’re” means “they are” and cannot describe a noun like “tent.”

items.stem: Which sentence uses “smells” correctly, keeping in mind it can act as a linking verb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Smells” describes a quality of the bakery here, so the adjective “wonderful” follows it correctly.
explanation.tip: When a sense verb describes a quality, follow it with an adjective, not an adverb.

options.label: A
options.text: The bakery smells wonderful this morningly.
options.rationale: “Morningly” is not a real word; “this morning” is correct as written.

options.label: B
options.text: The bakery smells wonderfully this morning.
options.rationale: “Smells” links the bakery to a quality here, so it needs the adjective “wonderful,” not the adverb “wonderfully.”

options.label: C
options.text: The bakery smells wonderful this morning.

options.label: D
options.text: The bakery smell wonderful this morning.
options.rationale: “Bakery” is singular, so the verb must be “smells.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly compares three or more items?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Of the three” signals a comparison among three or more items, which requires the superlative “most difficult.”
explanation.tip: Two items: comparative (more/-er). Three or more: superlative (most/-est).

options.label: A
options.text: Of the three trails, this one is the more difficult.
options.rationale: Comparing three or more items needs “the most,” not “the more.”

options.label: B
options.text: Of the three trails, this one is more difficult.
options.rationale: “More difficult” compares only two things; “of the three” needs the superlative.

options.label: C
options.text: Of the three trails, this one is difficulter.
options.rationale: Long adjectives like “difficult” use “more/most,” not -er/-est endings.

options.label: D
options.text: Of the three trails, this one is the most difficult.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphenated compound adjective before a noun?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Ten-minute” is a compound adjective describing the presentation and is hyphenated before the noun.
explanation.tip: Hyphenate a number-plus-unit adjective before a noun, and keep the unit singular.

options.label: A
options.text: The team built a ten-minute presentation for the contest.

options.label: B
options.text: The team built a ten-minutes presentation for the contest.
options.rationale: In a hyphenated compound adjective before a noun, the unit word stays singular: ten-minute, not ten-minutes.

options.label: C
options.text: The team built a ten minute’s presentation for the contest.
options.rationale: An apostrophe is not used to form this kind of compound adjective.

options.label: D
options.text: The team built a ten minute presentation for the contest.
options.rationale: A two-word adjective made of a number and a unit before a noun usually needs a hyphen: ten-minute.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses an absolute adjective without comparing it illogically?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Round” describes a complete state and is generally not compared using more/most or -er/-est.
explanation.tip: Absolute adjectives (round, perfect, complete) resist comparison because they describe an all-or-nothing quality.

options.label: A
options.text: The circle drawn by the compass was the roundest.
options.rationale: A true circle is already fully round; “roundest” illogically suggests varying degrees of roundness.

options.label: B
options.text: The circle drawn by the compass was round.

options.label: C
options.text: The circle drawn by the compass was very most round.
options.rationale: Stacking “very” and “most” together is incorrect, and “round” should not be compared at all.

options.label: D
options.text: The circle drawn by the compass was more round.
options.rationale: “Round” is an absolute adjective describing a complete shape, so it should not be compared with “more.”

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The two-word compound adjective “well researched” needs a hyphen when it comes directly before the noun it describes: well-researched.
explanation.tip: Hyphenate a compound adjective made of an adverb and participle only when it sits right before the noun.

items.stem: Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct conventional order?

explanation.whyCorrect: The conventional order is opinion, then age, then material: stunning, antique, wooden.
explanation.tip: Memorize the general order: opinion, size/shape, age, color, origin, material, purpose.

options.label: A
options.text: We admired a wooden stunning antique chest.
options.rationale: Material adjectives like “wooden” come last, not first, in the usual order.

options.label: B
options.text: We admired an antique wooden stunning chest.
options.rationale: Opinion adjectives like “stunning” come first, not last, in the usual order.

options.label: C
options.text: We admired a stunning antique wooden chest.

options.label: D
options.text: We admired an antique stunning wooden chest.
options.rationale: Opinion adjectives like “stunning” usually come before age adjectives like “antique.”

items.stem: The committee needs ____ information before approving the project.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Information” is uncountable, and the comparing word “more” fits uncountable nouns correctly.
explanation.tip: Use more/less for uncountable nouns like information, and more/fewer for countable nouns.

options.label: A
options.text: more

options.label: B
options.text: less information’s
options.rationale: This adds an incorrect possessive ending to an uncountable noun.

options.label: C
options.text: much more many
options.rationale: This piles up comparing words incorrectly in one phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: fewer
options.rationale: “Information” is an uncountable noun, so “fewer” is incorrect.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a participial adjective to describe a feeling rather than a cause?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Fascinated” correctly describes the audience’s feeling, caused by the trick.
explanation.tip: -ed participial adjectives describe how someone feels; -ing ones describe what causes the feeling.

options.label: A
options.text: The audience was fascinate by the magician’s final trick.
options.rationale: “Fascinate” is a verb form, not the adjective needed here.

options.label: B
options.text: The audience were fascinated by the magician’s final trick, fascinatingly.
options.rationale: Adding “fascinatingly” creates an unnecessary and awkward repetition of the same idea.

options.label: C
options.text: The audience was fascinating by the magician’s final trick.
options.rationale: “Fascinating” describes something that causes fascination, not a group feeling it.

options.label: D
options.text: The audience was fascinated by the magician’s final trick.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly places a long string of coordinate adjectives with commas?

explanation.whyCorrect: Each coordinate adjective in the series is separated by a comma, and the final one sits right before the noun.
explanation.tip: Commas separate coordinate adjectives, but none comes right before the noun itself.

options.label: A
options.text: The museum displayed a rare, delicate, hand-painted vase.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum displayed, a rare, delicate, hand-painted, vase.
options.rationale: There should be no comma directly after the verb “displayed” or directly before the noun “vase.”

options.label: C
options.text: The museum displayed a rare, delicate hand painted, vase.
options.rationale: The comma placement is wrong, and “hand painted” needs a hyphen before the noun.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum displayed a rare delicate hand-painted vase.
options.rationale: Coordinate adjectives of equal weight in a series need commas separating them.

items.stem: Which sentence correctly compares using “farther” versus “further” (farther for physical distance, further for extent or degree)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Farther” is the traditional choice for physical distance, which fits the hikers walking a longer distance.
explanation.tip: Farther usually describes physical distance; further usually describes degree or extent.

options.label: A
options.text: The hikers walked far than the map had suggested.
options.rationale: “Far” needs the comparative ending to compare two distances: farther.

options.label: B
options.text: The hikers walked farther than the map had suggested.

options.label: C
options.text: The hikers walked farer than the map had suggested.
options.rationale: “Farer” is not a correct comparative form.

options.label: D
options.text: The hikers walked further than the map had suggested, in distance.
options.rationale: For physical distance, “farther” is the traditional choice, not “further.”

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Unique” is generally treated as an absolute adjective meaning one of a kind, so it is not usually compared with “more.”
explanation.tip: Treat unique like an absolute adjective; avoid “more unique” or “most unique.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a predicate adjective after a linking verb, rather than an adverb?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Seemed” links “decision” to a quality, so the predicate adjective “fair” is correct.
explanation.tip: After linking verbs like seem, appear, and become, choose an adjective, not an adverb.

options.label: A
options.text: The committee’s decision seem fair to everyone involved.
options.rationale: “Decision” is singular, so the verb must be “seemed.”

options.label: B
options.text: The committee’s decision seemed fair to everyone involving.
options.rationale: “Involving” does not fit here; “involved” correctly describes everyone affected.

options.label: C
options.text: The committee’s decision seemed fair to everyone involved.

options.label: D
options.text: The committee’s decision seemed fairly to everyone involved.
options.rationale: “Seemed” is a linking verb here, so it needs the adjective “fair,” not the adverb “fairly.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly orders a long string of adjectives across several categories (opinion, age, origin, material)?

explanation.whyCorrect: The conventional order places opinion first, then age, then origin, then material: beautiful, old, Japanese, porcelain.
explanation.tip: When several categories appear together, work through the order one category at a time.

options.label: A
options.text: She inherited an old, beautiful, Japanese, porcelain tea set.
options.rationale: Opinion adjectives like “beautiful” usually come before age adjectives like “old.”

options.label: B
options.text: She inherited a Japanese, old, beautiful, porcelain tea set.
options.rationale: Origin adjectives like “Japanese” come after opinion and age, not before them.

options.label: C
options.text: She inherited a porcelain, beautiful, old, Japanese tea set.
options.rationale: Material adjectives like “porcelain” usually come last, not first.

options.label: D
options.text: She inherited a beautiful, old, Japanese, porcelain tea set.

items.stem:
Read this poem.

“The desert wakes at break of day,
Soft golden light begins to play.

The camels rise with gentle sound,
Their shadows stretch across the ground.”

How many stanzas does this poem have?

explanation.whyCorrect: A blank line separates the poem into two groups of two lines each, so there are two stanzas.
explanation.tip: Count the groups of lines separated by blank lines.

options.label: A
options.text: two

options.label: B
options.text: four
options.rationale: Each stanza here has two lines, not one line each, so there are only two stanzas.

options.label: C
options.text: three
options.rationale: There are only two groups of lines, separated by one blank line.

options.label: D
options.text: one
options.rationale: The poem has a blank line in the middle, which separates it into two stanzas.

items.stem: Read these lines: “The river flows so calm and wide, / Fish dart and dive and glide and hide.” Which pair of words rhymes?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Wide” and “hide” end with the same sound.
explanation.tip: Rhyming words usually share the same ending sound.

options.label: A
options.text: flows, calm
options.rationale: These words do not sound alike at the end.

options.label: B
options.text: wide, hide

options.label: C
options.text: river, fish
options.rationale: These words do not sound alike at all.

options.label: D
options.text: dart, dive
options.rationale: These words do not sound alike at the end.

items.stem:
Read: “The kitten naps,
The kitten plays,
The kitten purrs
Through sleepy days.”
Which word is repeated at the start of several lines?

explanation.whyCorrect: “The kitten” begins three of the four lines, which is a repeated phrase.
explanation.tip: Repetition often appears at the start or end of several lines.

options.label: A
options.text: sleepy
options.rationale: This word only appears once, and not at the start of a line.

options.label: B
options.text: plays
options.rationale: This word only appears once.

options.label: C
options.text: The kitten

options.label: D
options.text: naps
options.rationale: This word only appears once.

items.stem:
Read: “The wind blows free,
Across the sea,
No set beat to its song,
It wanders right along.”
What is this poem’s rhyme pattern for the first two lines?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Free” and “sea” share the same ending sound, forming a rhyming pair.
explanation.tip: Check the very last sound of each line to find rhyming pairs.

options.label: A
options.text: Every line in the poem rhymes with every other line.
options.rationale: Only some lines share the same ending sound, not all four.

options.label: B
options.text: The lines rhyme in the middle, not at the end.
options.rationale: The rhyme occurs at the end of the lines, not in the middle.

options.label: C
options.text: They do not rhyme with any other line.
options.rationale: “Free” and “sea” share the same ending sound, so they do rhyme.

options.label: D
options.text: They rhyme with each other (free, sea).

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Stanza” needs the plural form “stanzas” to match the number “three.”
explanation.tip: Match singular and plural forms: one stanza, three stanzas.

items.stem: Read: “Stars appear one by one tonight, / Tiny sparks of silver light.” Which word best describes the overall mood created by these lines?

explanation.whyCorrect: The quiet image of stars gently appearing creates a calm, peaceful mood.
explanation.tip: Picture the scene the words describe, then name the feeling it gives you.

options.label: A
options.text: peaceful

options.label: B
options.text: frightening
options.rationale: The imagery of gentle, tiny sparks of light does not suggest fear.

options.label: C
options.text: angry
options.rationale: Nothing in the lines suggests anger or conflict.

options.label: D
options.text: chaotic
options.rationale: The slow, gentle appearance of stars suggests order, not chaos.

items.stem: A poem with lines that do not rhyme and have no regular rhythm, like a short descriptive paragraph broken into lines, is called what?

explanation.whyCorrect: Free verse poetry has no required rhyme or regular rhythm pattern.
explanation.tip: Free verse = free from strict rhyme and rhythm rules.

options.label: A
options.text: a limerick
options.rationale: A limerick follows a strict five-line pattern with a set rhyme scheme.

options.label: B
options.text: free verse

options.label: C
options.text: a rhyming couplet
options.rationale: A rhyming couplet is exactly two lines that rhyme, which is the opposite of free verse.

options.label: D
options.text: a haiku
options.rationale: A haiku has a strict structure of three lines with set syllable counts, unlike free verse.

items.stem:
Read: “The market hums with morning trade,
Fruit stacked high in sun and shade.

Voices call and coins exchange,
Colors bright and smells so strange.”
How do the two stanzas work together?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first stanza introduces the market, and the second stanza builds on it with more sensory details.
explanation.tip: Ask how each new stanza adds to or builds on the one before it.

options.label: A
options.text: The stanzas have no connection to each other.
options.rationale: Both stanzas build one connected picture of the market.

options.label: B
options.text: The two stanzas describe two completely different markets.
options.rationale: Both stanzas describe the same single market scene.

options.label: C
options.text: The first stanza sets the scene, and the second adds sounds and smells to it.

options.label: D
options.text: The second stanza contradicts everything in the first.
options.rationale: The second stanza adds more detail; it does not contradict the first.

items.stem: Read: “Tap, tap, tap, the rain falls down, / Drip, drip, drip, upon the town.” Which poetic element is created by repeating “tap” and “drip” three times each?

explanation.whyCorrect: Repeating “tap” and “drip” imitates the actual sound of rain falling.
explanation.tip: Repeated sound words often imitate the noise they describe.

options.label: A
options.text: the color of the rain
options.rationale: Repeating a sound word does not describe color.

options.label: B
options.text: the size of the town
options.rationale: The repeated words describe a sound, not the town’s size.

options.label: C
options.text: a rhyme with the word “down”
options.rationale: “Tap” and “drip” do not rhyme with “down”; the repetition imitates sound instead.

options.label: D
options.text: the sound of the falling rain

items.stem: A poem has three lines: the first and third rhyme, and the middle line does not rhyme with either. What is this rhyme pattern usually written as?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first and third lines share the same letter (A) because they rhyme, while the middle line gets a different letter (B).
explanation.tip: Label each line’s rhyme sound with a letter, starting from A.

options.label: A
options.text: ABA

options.label: B
options.text: AAA
options.rationale: AAA would mean all three lines rhyme with each other.

options.label: C
options.text: ABC
options.rationale: ABC would mean none of the lines rhyme with each other.

options.label: D
options.text: AAB
options.rationale: AAB would mean the first two lines rhyme and the third is different.

items.stem:
Read this poem.

“The harbor wakes before the sun,
Boats creak and sway, their long day begun.

Gulls circle low with hungry cries,
And nets are cast beneath gray skies.

By noon the catch is sorted fast,
And morning's rush has slipped into the past.”

How many stanzas does this poem have?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two blank lines divide the poem into three stanzas of two lines each.
explanation.tip: Count blank lines, then add one to find the number of stanzas.

options.label: A
options.text: two
options.rationale: There are two blank lines in the poem, which creates three stanzas, not two.

options.label: B
options.text: three

options.label: C
options.text: one
options.rationale: Two blank lines divide the poem into three separate groups of lines, not one.

options.label: D
options.text: six
options.rationale: There are six lines total, but they form only three stanzas of two lines each.

items.stem: Read: “The city hums with endless sound, / Lights and voices all around.” Which pair of words rhymes?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Sound” and “around” share the same ending sound.
explanation.tip: Focus only on the final sound of each line when checking for rhyme.

options.label: A
options.text: lights, voices
options.rationale: These words do not share the same ending sound.

options.label: B
options.text: endless, all
options.rationale: These words do not share the same ending sound.

options.label: C
options.text: sound, around

options.label: D
options.text: city, hums
options.rationale: These words do not share the same ending sound.

items.stem:
Read: “The orchard waits in silver frost,
Its summer fruit all long since lost.

Yet roots still hold their steady ground,
And spring will come, as spring is bound.”
How does the second stanza relate to the first?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first stanza focuses on what is lost, while the second stanza turns toward hope for spring’s return.
explanation.tip: Track how the poem’s feeling or focus shifts from one stanza to the next.

options.label: A
options.text: The first stanza is hopeful, and the second stanza is hopeless.
options.rationale: This reverses the actual mood; the first stanza describes loss, and the second brings hope.

options.label: B
options.text: The second stanza describes a completely unrelated season.
options.rationale: The second stanza still describes the same orchard, just later in its cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: The stanzas repeat the exact same idea twice.
options.rationale: The second stanza shifts the idea forward from loss toward renewal, not simple repetition.

options.label: D
options.text: The first stanza shows loss, and the second stanza offers hope for renewal.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is already written correctly; a rhyme pattern like ABAB uses capital letters with no spaces or punctuation between them.
explanation.tip: Rhyme-scheme labels are written as capital letters side by side, like ABAB or AABB.

segments: in every stanza except the last.

items.stem: A poem has four lines where the first rhymes with the second, and the third rhymes with the fourth. What is this rhyme pattern called?

explanation.whyCorrect: The first two lines share one rhyme (AA), and the last two lines share a different rhyme (BB).
explanation.tip: Label each line with a letter in order, repeating a letter only when the rhyme matches.

options.label: A
options.text: AABB

options.label: B
options.text: ABAB
options.rationale: ABAB would mean the first and third lines rhyme, and the second and fourth rhyme.

options.label: C
options.text: ABBA
options.rationale: ABBA would mean the first and fourth lines rhyme, and the second and third rhyme.

options.label: D
options.text: AAAA
options.rationale: AAAA would mean all four lines rhyme with each other.

items.stem: Which poetic form is traditionally written in three unrhymed lines with a 5-7-5 syllable pattern, often about nature?

explanation.whyCorrect: A haiku follows a strict three-line, 5-7-5 syllable structure, often focused on nature.
explanation.tip: Haiku: 3 lines, 5-7-5 syllables, usually about nature.

options.label: A
options.text: limerick
options.rationale: A limerick has five lines with a strict rhyme scheme, not three unrhymed lines.

options.label: B
options.text: haiku

options.label: C
options.text: sonnet
options.rationale: A sonnet traditionally has fourteen lines, not three.

options.label: D
options.text: free verse
options.rationale: Free verse has no required syllable pattern, unlike the strict 5-7-5 of a haiku.

items.stem: Read: “The train pulls slowly from the station, / Carrying hopes to each far-off destination.” What is the overall effect of the repeated long “o” and “a” vowel sounds across these lines?

explanation.whyCorrect: The repeated long vowel sounds slow the reading pace, mirroring the train’s slow departure.
explanation.tip: Notice how vowel sounds can speed up or slow down how a line feels when read aloud.

options.label: A
options.text: It has no effect on the poem's rhythm at all.
options.rationale: Repeated vowel sounds shape how smoothly or slowly a line is read.

options.label: B
options.text: It changes the meaning of the word “train” entirely.
options.rationale: Vowel sound repetition affects rhythm and mood, not a word's basic meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: It creates a slow, drawn-out rhythm that matches the train’s gradual movement.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes the lines sound fast and choppy.
options.rationale: Long vowel sounds tend to slow down a reader's pace, not speed it up.

items.stem: Read: “The lantern swings from the old ship's bow, / Guiding sailors home, as it always does, somehow.” When a sentence or idea continues from one line into the next without a pause, this is called what?

explanation.whyCorrect: When the sentence flows past the end of the line without stopping, it is called enjambment.
explanation.tip: Enjambment: a thought that runs on past the line break without a pause.

options.label: A
options.text: a refrain
options.rationale: A refrain is a line or phrase that repeats throughout a poem, which is different from a sentence running across lines.

options.label: B
options.text: a stanza break
options.rationale: A stanza break is a blank line separating groups of lines, not a sentence running across lines.

options.label: C
options.text: a rhyme scheme
options.rationale: A rhyme scheme describes the pattern of rhyming sounds, not how sentences flow across lines.

options.label: D
options.text: enjambment

items.stem: A short phrase or line that repeats at set points throughout a song or poem, such as after every stanza, is called what?

explanation.whyCorrect: A refrain is a phrase or line that repeats at regular points in a poem or song.
explanation.tip: Refrain = a line that returns again and again, like a chorus.

options.label: A
options.text: a refrain

options.label: B
options.text: an acrostic
options.rationale: An acrostic is a poem where the first letters of each line spell a word, not a repeated phrase.

options.label: C
options.text: an ode
options.rationale: An ode is a poem praising a person, object, or idea, not a repeated phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: an elegy
options.rationale: An elegy is a poem written to mourn someone, not a repeated phrase.

items.stem: In a poem about rebuilding after a storm, the final stanza suddenly shifts to describing a brand-new morning, using only short, simple sentences. What effect does this structural shift likely create?

explanation.whyCorrect: Shifting to short, simple sentences about a new morning reflects the community’s fresh, hopeful start.
explanation.tip: A sudden shift in sentence structure near the end often signals a shift in feeling or meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: It proves the poem has no connection between its stanzas.
options.rationale: A shift in tone or structure can still connect meaningfully to earlier stanzas.

options.label: B
options.text: It mirrors the fresh start the community feels after the storm has passed.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the storm has returned even stronger.
options.rationale: Describing a new morning signals calm and recovery, not a returning storm.

options.label: D
options.text: It means the poet made an error in the final stanza.
options.rationale: A deliberate shift in sentence length and tone is a structural choice, not a mistake.

items.stem:
Read this poem.

“The quarry sleeps beneath the dust,
Its ancient stone begins to rust.

Yet workers come with steady hands,
To shape new life from these old lands.”

How many stanzas does this poem have, and how many lines are in each?

explanation.whyCorrect: The blank line divides the poem into two stanzas, each containing two lines.
explanation.tip: Count the blank lines first, then count the lines within each resulting group.

options.label: A
options.text: two stanzas, with three lines each
options.rationale: Each stanza here contains exactly two lines, not three.

options.label: B
options.text: four stanzas, with one line each
options.rationale: The lines are grouped in pairs, not standing alone as separate stanzas.

options.label: C
options.text: two stanzas, with two lines each

options.label: D
options.text: one stanza, with four lines
options.rationale: A blank line divides the poem into two separate stanzas, not one.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: The verb needed here is “called,” the past participle form, not “call.”
explanation.tip: Check that participles like “called” or “named” are spelled correctly after a noun phrase.

items.stem: The regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of poetry is called what?

explanation.whyCorrect: Meter refers to the regular rhythm created by stressed and unstressed syllables.
explanation.tip: Meter is the “heartbeat” rhythm of a poem's syllables.

options.label: A
options.text: rhyme scheme
options.rationale: Rhyme scheme describes the pattern of rhyming sounds at line endings, not stress patterns.

options.label: B
options.text: stanza
options.rationale: A stanza is a group of lines, not a pattern of stressed syllables.

options.label: C
options.text: enjambment
options.rationale: Enjambment describes a sentence running past a line break, not a stress pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: meter

items.stem: A poem written in two rhyming lines that form a complete thought, often used to end a longer poem, is called what?

explanation.whyCorrect: A couplet is exactly two lines that rhyme and usually express one complete thought.
explanation.tip: Couplet = a pair (“couple”) of rhyming lines.

options.label: A
options.text: a couplet

options.label: B
options.text: a stanza break
options.rationale: A stanza break is simply a blank line between stanzas, not a specific two-line form.

options.label: C
options.text: a quatrain
options.rationale: A quatrain is a four-line stanza, not a pair of rhyming lines.

options.label: D
options.text: a refrain
options.rationale: A refrain is a repeated phrase, not a specific two-line rhyming unit.

items.stem: Read: “The factory hums both day and night; / Its tired workers long for light.” Which word choice most strongly contributes to the poem's weary, exhausted tone?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tired” directly names the workers' exhaustion, strongly shaping the poem's weary tone.
explanation.tip: Look for words that directly name an emotion or physical state to find what shapes a poem's tone.

options.label: A
options.text: hums
options.rationale: This word describes a steady sound, not weariness.

options.label: B
options.text: tired

options.label: C
options.text: factory
options.rationale: This word simply names the setting; it does not itself carry an emotional weight.

options.label: D
options.text: night
options.rationale: This word names a time of day; it does not by itself suggest exhaustion.

items.stem: A songwriter groups her verses into blocks of exactly four lines each. What is each of those blocks called?

explanation.whyCorrect: A poetry block made of exactly four lines has its own special name: a quatrain.
explanation.tip: Memorize the family of length names together so you can tell them apart quickly.

options.label: A
options.text: a sestet
options.rationale: That name is reserved for a block of six lines, not four.

options.label: B
options.text: a tercet
options.rationale: That name is reserved for a block of three lines, not four.

options.label: C
options.text: a quatrain

options.label: D
options.text: a couplet
options.rationale: That name is reserved for a block of just two lines, not four.

items.stem: Read: “The old clock ticks, its gears worn thin, / Marking time that none can win.” How does the structure of comparing a clock to an unwinnable race contribute to the poem's meaning?

explanation.whyCorrect: Comparing time to a race no one can win emphasizes that time's passage is unstoppable, which supports the poem's theme.
explanation.tip: When a poem compares an object to an abstract idea, ask what larger meaning that comparison supports.

options.label: A
options.text: It proves the poem has no central theme.
options.rationale: The comparison actually supports a clear theme about the passage of time.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that the poem is only about repairing clocks.
options.rationale: The clock serves as a symbol for time itself, not a literal instruction manual.

options.label: C
options.text: It suggests the clock will stop working very soon.
options.rationale: The comparison is about time's unstoppable nature, not predicting a mechanical failure.

options.label: D
options.text: It reinforces the idea that time moves forward no matter what anyone does.

items.stem: A poem shifts from long, flowing sentences in its first half to short, clipped sentences in its second half, right as the subject changes from a calm morning to a sudden storm. What is the most likely purpose of this structural shift?

explanation.whyCorrect: Shortening the sentences as the storm begins mirrors the sudden, sharp change in the weather.
explanation.tip: A shift in sentence length or rhythm often mirrors a shift in the action or mood being described.

options.label: A
options.text: To make the pace of the lines match the sudden change in the weather.

options.label: B
options.text: To prove that the storm was not actually dangerous.
options.rationale: Short, clipped sentences typically build tension, which would suggest more danger, not less.

options.label: C
options.text: To show that the poet ran out of ideas partway through.
options.rationale: A deliberate change in sentence length and rhythm is a stylistic choice, not a sign of running out of ideas.

options.label: D
options.text: To separate the poem into two unrelated topics.
options.rationale: Both halves describe the same day and setting, just before and during the storm.

items.stem: In a poem about an abandoned lighthouse, the final stanza repeats the exact first line of the poem, unchanged. What effect does this repetition most likely create?

explanation.whyCorrect: Returning to the exact opening line creates a circular, unchanging structure that reflects the lighthouse's unchanging state.
explanation.tip: A poem that ends by repeating its opening line often suggests something has come full circle.

options.label: A
options.text: It proves the lighthouse was recently rebuilt.
options.rationale: The repetition relates to the poem's structure and meaning, not a literal construction update.

options.label: B
options.text: It gives the poem a circular structure, suggesting the lighthouse's story continues unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: It means the second half of the poem should be ignored.
options.rationale: A repeated first line typically frames the whole poem, rather than canceling out what comes between.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that the poet forgot what was already written.
options.rationale: Repeating a line deliberately is a structural choice, not an accidental oversight.

items.stem: A six-line stanza is more specifically called what?

explanation.whyCorrect: A stanza made up of exactly six lines is called a sestet.
explanation.tip: Learn the stanza-length names: couplet (2), tercet (3), quatrain (4), sestet (6).

options.label: A
options.text: a quatrain
options.rationale: A quatrain refers to a four-line stanza, not six.

options.label: B
options.text: a couplet
options.rationale: A couplet refers to a two-line stanza, not six.

options.label: C
options.text: a sestet

options.label: D
options.text: a tercet
options.rationale: A tercet refers to a three-line stanza, not six.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “Please put the letter over ____.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “There” points to a location, which fits “over ____.”
explanation.tip: There = place, their = ownership, they're = they are.

options.label: A
options.text: their
options.rationale: “Their” shows ownership, like “their letter,” not location.

options.label: B
options.text: there

options.label: C
options.text: thare
options.rationale: This is a misspelling of “there.”

options.label: D
options.text: they're
options.rationale: “They’re” means “they are” and does not fit this sentence.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “Is ____ time to leave yet?”

explanation.whyCorrect: “It’s” is the contraction for “it is,” which fits this question.
explanation.tip: It's = it is; its = belonging to it.

options.label: A
options.text: it is'
options.rationale: This is not a correct way to write a contraction.

options.label: B
options.text: its
options.rationale: “Its” shows ownership and does not mean “it is.”

options.label: C
options.text: it's

options.label: D
options.text: its'
options.rationale: This is not a real word; “its” never takes an apostrophe for ownership.

items.stem: Which pair of words are homophones (same sound, different spelling and meaning)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Flower” and “flour” sound exactly the same but have completely different meanings and spellings.
explanation.tip: Homophones sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things.

options.label: A
options.text: run, running
options.rationale: These are two forms of the same word, not two different words that sound alike.

options.label: B
options.text: quick, fast
options.rationale: These words sound different but mean nearly the same thing; that makes them synonyms, not homophones.

options.label: C
options.text: happy, sad
options.rationale: These words have opposite meanings and do not sound alike.

options.label: D
options.text: flower, flour

items.stem: In which sentence does “bow” mean to bend forward out of respect?

explanation.whyCorrect: In this sentence, “bow” describes the dancers bending forward to show respect to the audience.
explanation.tip: Homographs are spelled the same but can be pronounced and mean differently — use context to decide.

options.label: A
options.text: The dancers took a graceful bow at the end of the show.

options.label: B
options.text: The ship's bow cut through the waves.
options.rationale: Here “bow” means the front part of a ship.

options.label: C
options.text: She tied a red bow on the gift box.
options.rationale: Here “bow” means a decorative knot, not a bending motion.

options.label: D
options.text: The archer carried his bow across the field.
options.rationale: Here “bow” means the weapon used to shoot arrows.

items.stem: Read: “The wind was too strong, so we had to wind the kite string back in.” How are the two words pronounced?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Wind” (moving air) and “wind” (to coil something) are spelled the same but pronounced differently.
explanation.tip: Some homographs change pronunciation depending on their meaning.

options.label: A
options.text: The sentence contains a spelling mistake.
options.rationale: There is no spelling mistake; the word “wind” simply has two different pronunciations and meanings.

options.label: B
options.text: They are pronounced differently, even though they are spelled the same.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the second “wind” is a real word.
options.rationale: Both uses of “wind” are real words with different meanings and pronunciations.

options.label: D
options.text: They are pronounced exactly the same way.
options.rationale: The first “wind” (moving air) and the second “wind” (to coil) are pronounced differently.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Through” means to move from one side of something to the other, while “threw” is the past tense of the verb “throw.”
explanation.tip: Through = passing across a space; threw = past tense of throw.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “My ____ is on the desk.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Stationery” refers to paper and writing supplies, which fits an item on a desk.
explanation.tip: Stationery (with an e) = paper supplies; stationary (with an a) = not moving.

options.label: A
options.text: stationary
options.rationale: “Stationary” means “not moving,” which does not fit an item sitting on a desk for writing.

options.label: B
options.text: stationarry
options.rationale: This is a misspelling of “stationary.”

options.label: C
options.text: stationeri
options.rationale: This is a misspelling of “stationery.”

options.label: D
options.text: stationery

items.stem: Which sentence uses “desert” to mean a dry, sandy region, not to abandon something?

explanation.whyCorrect: In this sentence, “desert” refers to the dry, sandy land the camel crosses.
explanation.tip: Note the stress: DES-ert (the place) vs. de-SERT (to abandon).

options.label: A
options.text: The soldiers were ordered not to desert their post.
options.rationale: Here “desert” means to abandon, not a dry region.

options.label: B
options.text: He feared the team would desert him before the game.
options.rationale: Here “desert” means to abandon, not a dry region.

options.label: C
options.text: The camel crossed the vast, sandy desert.

options.label: D
options.text: She would never desert her best friend.
options.rationale: Here “desert” means to abandon someone.

items.stem: Which pair of words are homographs (same spelling, different meaning)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Bat” is spelled the same in both cases but has two completely different meanings.
explanation.tip: Homographs look identical on the page but can mean very different things.

options.label: A
options.text: sun, son
options.rationale: These words sound alike but are spelled differently, making them homophones, not homographs.

options.label: B
options.text: cat, hat
options.rationale: These two words are spelled differently and are unrelated in meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: run, ran
options.rationale: These are two different tenses of the same verb, not two unrelated meanings of one spelling.

options.label: D
options.text: bat (the animal), bat (used in baseball)

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “It took almost an ____ for the bus to finally arrive.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hour” is the unit of time that fits after “an” in this sentence about waiting.
explanation.tip: Hour = unit of time; our = belonging to us.

options.label: A
options.text: hour

options.label: B
options.text: our
options.rationale: “Our” shows ownership, like “our bus stop,” not a measure of time.

options.label: C
options.text: are
options.rationale: “Are” is a verb and does not fit this blank.

options.label: D
options.text: hour's
options.rationale: An apostrophe here would incorrectly suggest ownership, which does not fit this sentence.

items.stem: In which sentence does “lead” rhyme with “bed” (meaning the heavy metal)?

explanation.whyCorrect: In this sentence, “lead” refers to the metal and is pronounced to rhyme with “bed.”
explanation.tip: Lead (the metal) rhymes with bed; lead (to guide) rhymes with bead.

options.label: A
options.text: The old pipes were made of lead.

options.label: B
options.text: She will lead the team to victory.
options.rationale: Here “lead” means to guide, and it rhymes with “bead,” not “bed.”

options.label: C
options.text: The coach will lead the warm-up exercises.
options.rationale: Here “lead” means to guide, rhyming with “bead,” not “bed.”

options.label: D
options.text: Who will lead the discussion tomorrow?
options.rationale: Here “lead” means to guide, rhyming with “bead,” not “bed.”

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The teacher gave us good ____ on the project.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Advice” is the noun form meaning guidance or suggestions, which fits after “good.”
explanation.tip: Advice is the noun (a piece of advice); advise is the verb (to advise someone).

options.label: A
options.text: advise
options.rationale: “Advise” is a verb meaning to give suggestions, not the noun for the suggestion itself.

options.label: B
options.text: advice

options.label: C
options.text: advisement
options.rationale: This word does not fit naturally in this common sentence pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: advize
options.rationale: This is a misspelling.

items.stem: Which sentence uses “object” to mean a physical thing, not to disagree?

explanation.whyCorrect: In this sentence, “object” is a noun meaning a physical thing found on the shore.
explanation.tip: Notice the stress: OB-ject (the thing) vs. ob-JECT (to disagree).

options.label: A
options.text: Did anyone object to the new schedule?
options.rationale: Here “object” means to disagree, not a physical thing.

options.label: B
options.text: A strange object appeared on the shore after the storm.

options.label: C
options.text: The lawyer stood up to object to the question.
options.rationale: Here “object” means to disagree or protest.

options.label: D
options.text: Several citizens plan to object at the town meeting.
options.rationale: Here “object” means to voice disagreement.

items.stem: Tap the part of the sentence that has an error.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Principal” refers to the head of a school, while “principle” means a basic rule or belief, so it cannot give instructions.
explanation.tip: Principal = a person (or main thing); principle = a rule.

items.stem: “The orchard hired extra workers to record record harvest numbers.” How do the two uses of “record” differ?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Record” shifts both meaning and stress depending on whether it is used as a verb or as a noun/adjective.
explanation.tip: Check the word's job in the sentence (verb, or noun/adjective) to find its correct pronunciation.

options.label: A
options.text: Both words mean exactly the same thing and are pronounced the same way.
options.rationale: The two uses have different meanings and different stress patterns, even though they are spelled the same.

options.label: B
options.text: The first “record” describes the harvest, and the second is the verb.
options.rationale: This reverses the correct order of the verb and the describing word in the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: The first “record” is a verb meaning to write down, and the second is an adjective describing the largest-ever harvest; they are stressed differently.

options.label: D
options.text: The sentence has a typo and should use two different words.
options.rationale: There is no typo; “record” can correctly serve as both a verb and a noun or adjective.

items.stem: Choose the correct word: “The patient waited with great ____ in the hospital.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Patience” means the ability to wait calmly, which fits this sentence.
explanation.tip: Patience = calm waiting; patients = people being treated by a doctor.

options.label: A
options.text: patients
options.rationale: “Patients” refers to people receiving medical care, not the quality of waiting calmly.

options.label: B
options.text: patients'
options.rationale: An apostrophe here incorrectly suggests possession, which does not fit this sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: patience

options.label: D
options.text: patiences
options.rationale: This is not a correct plural or standard form.

items.stem: Which sentence uses “content” to mean satisfied, not the information inside something?

explanation.whyCorrect: In this sentence, “content” describes the campers' feeling of satisfaction.
explanation.tip: Notice the stress: con-TENT (satisfied) vs. CON-tent (what's inside).

options.label: A
options.text: The teacher checked the content of each essay carefully.
options.rationale: Here “content” refers to the ideas and information in each essay.

options.label: B
options.text: The website's content was updated last week.
options.rationale: Here “content” refers to the information found on the website.

options.label: C
options.text: Please review the content of the report before the meeting.
options.rationale: Here “content” means the information inside the report.

options.label: D
options.text: After the long hike, the campers felt completely content.

items.stem: Which pair best shows a true set of homophones?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Peace” and “piece” sound exactly alike but have completely different spellings and meanings.
explanation.tip: True homophones must sound identical, even though their spelling and meaning differ.

options.label: A
options.text: peace, piece

options.label: B
options.text: quiet, calm
options.rationale: These words are similar in meaning but sound different, making them synonyms, not homophones.

options.label: C
options.text: large, larger
options.rationale: These are two forms of the same word, not two different words that sound alike.

options.label: D
options.text: bright, light
options.rationale: These words sound different from each other and are not homophones.

items.stem: Choose: “The new policy will ____ every department in the company.”

explanation.whyCorrect: “Affect” is the verb meaning to influence something, which fits this sentence about the policy's influence.
explanation.tip: Affect is usually the verb (to influence); effect is usually the noun (a result).

options.rationale: An apostrophe here does not fit; this word is a plain verb, not a possessive.

options.label: B
options.text: a-fect
options.rationale: This is not a correctly spelled word.

options.label: C
options.text: effect
options.rationale: “Effect” is usually a noun meaning a result, not a verb meaning to influence.

options.label: D

items.stem: In which sentence does “tear” rhyme with “bear,” meaning to rip?

explanation.whyCorrect: In this sentence, “tear” means to rip and is pronounced to rhyme with “bear.”
explanation.tip: Tear (rip) rhymes with bear; tear (crying) rhymes with ear.

items.stem: “Only a minute fraction of the seeds sprouted after the frost.” How is “minute” pronounced and what does it mean here?

options.label: B
options.text: It is pronounced my-NOOT and means sixty seconds.
options.rationale: The pronunciation my-NOOT goes with the meaning “extremely tiny,” not a unit of time.

options.label: C
options.text: It is pronounced my-NOOT and means extremely tiny.

options.label: D
options.text: It is pronounced MIN-it and means extremely tiny.
options.rationale: The meaning “extremely tiny” uses the pronunciation my-NOOT, not MIN-it.

explanation.tip: If something is being influenced, use affect as the verb; effect is usually the noun for the result.

items.stem: Which sentence uses “refuse” to mean garbage, not to decline?

explanation.whyCorrect: In this sentence, “refuse” is a noun meaning trash or garbage collected by the city.
explanation.tip: REF-use (noun, garbage) is stressed differently from re-FUSE (verb, to decline).

options.text: The city collects refuse from every street twice a week.

explanation.tip: Which = a question or relative word; witch = a person in folklore. Check the meaning needed.

segments: of the project's cost, witch seemed reasonable.

items.stem: Which pair of words best shows true homophones in formal, academic writing?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Capital” (a main city or wealth) and “capitol” (a government building) sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning.
explanation.tip: Capital = main city or money; capitol = the government building.

options.label: A
options.text: city, state
options.rationale: These words are unrelated in sound and meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: capital, capitol

options.label: C
options.text: large, huge
options.rationale: These words are similar in meaning but sound different, making them synonyms, not homophones.

options.label: D
options.text: govern, government
options.rationale: These are related word forms, not two unrelated words that happen to sound alike.

items.stem: Which line uses alliteration (repeated sounds at the START of words)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Big, brown, bears, bathed, barn” all start with the b sound.
explanation.tip: Alliteration repeats the first consonant sound in nearby words.

options.label: A
options.text: Big brown bears bathed by the barn.

options.label: B
options.text: The sun set behind the hill.
options.rationale: No repeated beginning sounds appear in this line.

options.label: C
options.text: A dog barked twice last night.
options.rationale: The words here do not start with the same sound.

items.stem: Which line uses alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Tiny, turtles, trotted, toward, tide” repeat the t sound at the start.
explanation.tip: Read the line aloud and listen for a sound that keeps coming back.

options.label: A
options.text: The moon rose slowly tonight.
options.rationale: No words here share the same beginning sound.

options.label: B
options.text: Tiny turtles trotted toward the tide.

options.label: C
options.text: Birds flew over the lake.
options.rationale: The beginning sounds of these words are all different.

items.stem: Which line uses assonance (a repeated VOWEL sound inside the words)?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Light, bright, kite, high, tonight” all share the long i sound.
explanation.tip: Assonance repeats a vowel sound; it does not have to be at the start of the word.

options.label: A
options.text: Birds sang sweetly in the trees.
options.rationale: No single vowel sound is repeated across these words.

options.label: B
options.text: The cat sat on the bench.
options.rationale: This repeats a consonant sound, which is consonance, not assonance.

options.label: C
options.text: The light, bright kite flies high tonight.

items.stem: Which line uses consonance (a repeated sound inside or at the end of words, not at the start)?

explanation.whyCorrect: The ck sound repeats inside “black, trucks, stacked, rocks.”
explanation.tip: Consonance can repeat a consonant sound anywhere in the word, not just the start.

options.label: A
options.text: The black trucks stacked rocks at dusk.

options.label: B
options.text: The cat sat on the mat.
options.rationale: This line has rhyme, which repeats whole ending sounds, not a scattered inside sound.

options.label: C
options.text: Birds chirped in the garden.
options.rationale: No repeated inside or ending sound stands out here.

items.stem: Which line uses alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Dusty, desert, camels, crossed, cracked, canyon” share the hard c/k sound at the start.
explanation.tip: Alliteration can repeat a sound spelled with different letters, like c and k.

options.label: A
options.text: The sun was hot and bright.
options.rationale: No repeated beginning sounds appear in this line.

options.label: B
options.text: Dusty desert camels crossed the cracked canyon.

options.label: C
options.text: The camel walked slowly across the sand.
options.rationale: Only one word begins with a matching sound here.

items.stem: Which line uses assonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Pale, gray, paint, faded, away” all share the long a sound.
explanation.tip: Say the line slowly and listen for one vowel sound echoing through it.

options.label: A
options.text: The train stopped at the station.
options.rationale: No single vowel sound repeats across several words here.

options.label: B
options.text: The driver waved at the crowd.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat one vowel sound.

options.label: C
options.text: The train's pale gray paint faded away.

items.stem: The repeated f sound in “Five fat frogs flopped into the pond” is called ____.

explanation.whyCorrect: The repeated beginning consonant sound is alliteration.
explanation.tip: Beginning sound repeated = alliteration.

options.label: A
options.text: alliteration

options.label: B
options.text: rhyme
options.rationale: Rhyme matches the ending sounds of words, not their beginning sounds.

options.label: C
options.text: assonance
options.rationale: Assonance repeats a vowel sound, not a beginning consonant sound.

items.stem: Which line uses alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Sly, sailors, sailed, silver, ship” repeat the s sound at the start.
explanation.tip: Underline the first letter of each word to spot the repeating sound.

options.label: A
options.text: Six sly sailors sailed past the silver ship.

options.label: B
options.text: The waves crashed onto the shore.
options.rationale: No repeated beginning sounds appear in this line.

options.label: C
options.text: The ship sailed across the ocean.
options.rationale: Only one pair of words shares the same beginning sound here.

items.stem: Which line uses assonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Bright, firefly, flies, high, sky” all share the long i sound.
explanation.tip: Assonance is easiest to hear if you say the line slowly, stretching the vowels.

options.label: A
options.text: A moth landed on the lamp.
options.rationale: No vowel sound repeats across these words.

options.label: B
options.text: The bright firefly flies high in the sky.

options.label: C
options.text: The firefly glowed in the dark yard.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat one vowel sound through several words.

items.stem: Which line uses consonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: The ck/k sound repeats inside “kicked, quick, slick, shots.”
explanation.tip: Listen for a consonant sound echoing in the middle or end of several words.

options.label: A
options.text: The ball rolled into the goal.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat a consonant sound inside the words.

options.label: B
options.text: The kids played soccer after school.
options.rationale: No inside or ending sound repeats across these words.

options.label: C
options.text: The kids kicked quick, slick shots at the net.

items.stem: Which line uses alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Six, sweet, scones, sat, shelf” repeat the s sound at the start.
explanation.tip: Alliteration often appears in groups of three or more words in a row.

options.label: A
options.text: Six sweet scones sat on the shelf.

options.label: B
options.text: The shelf held fresh bread.
options.rationale: Only one pair of words here shares a beginning sound.

options.label: C
options.text: The baker opened the shop early.
options.rationale: No repeated beginning sounds appear in this line.

items.stem: Which line uses assonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Green, bees, sleep, deep, leaves” all share the long e sound.
explanation.tip: Look for the same vowel spelled in different ways, like ee and ea.

options.label: A
options.text: The bees buzzed around the hive.
options.rationale: No single vowel sound repeats across several words here.

options.label: B
options.text: The green bees sleep deep in the leaves.

options.label: C
options.text: The garden was full of flowers.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat one vowel sound.

items.stem: In the line “The slimy snake slithered silently,” the repeated s sound at the start of each word is an example of alliteration.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Slimy, snake, slithered, silently” all begin with the s sound, which is alliteration.
explanation.tip: A repeated sound at the START of nearby words is alliteration.

items.stem: Which line uses consonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: The ck sound repeats inside “rocks, clicked, clacked.”
explanation.tip: Consonance can repeat a sound in the middle of a word, not only at the end.

options.label: A
options.text: The water was cold and clear.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat a consonant sound inside the words.

options.label: B
options.text: The river flowed past the village.
options.rationale: No inside or ending sound repeats across several words here.

options.label: C
options.text: The river rocks clicked and clacked below.

items.stem: Which line uses alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Hungry, hikers, hauled, heavy” repeat the h sound at the start.
explanation.tip: Four or more words sharing a beginning sound is a strong clue to alliteration.

options.label: A
options.text: Hungry hikers hauled heavy packs uphill.

options.label: B
options.text: The hikers reached the top at noon.
options.rationale: No repeated beginning sounds appear in this line.

options.label: C
options.text: The trail was steep and rocky.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat one beginning sound.

items.stem: Match each sound device with the line that shows it.

explanation.whyCorrect: Alliteration repeats a beginning sound, assonance repeats a vowel sound inside words, consonance repeats a consonant sound inside or at the end of words, and onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound.
explanation.tip: Ask: where in the words is the sound repeated — start, middle, or is it a sound-word itself?

pairs.right: Wild winds whipped the willow tree.
The deep green stream gleamed in the light.
The black truck backed into the dock.

items.stem: Which line uses BOTH alliteration and assonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: The s sound repeats at the start (alliteration) and the long i sound repeats inside the words (assonance).
explanation.tip: Check the start of the words first, then check the vowel sounds inside them.

options.label: A
options.text: Sly snakes crawled through the grass.
options.rationale: This line has alliteration but no repeated vowel sound running through it.

options.label: B
options.text: Sly snakes slide through slippery, shiny slime.

options.label: C
options.text: The grass was wet and green.
options.rationale: Neither a repeated beginning sound nor a repeated vowel sound appears here.

items.stem: Which line uses assonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Deep, stream, seemed, gleam” all share the long e sound.
explanation.tip: Try reading only the vowels aloud to notice which sound keeps repeating.

options.label: A
options.text: The water sparkled in the morning sun.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat a single vowel sound.

options.label: B
options.text: The stream flowed quietly through the valley.
options.rationale: No one vowel sound repeats through several words here.

options.label: C
options.text: The deep stream seemed to gleam at dawn.

items.stem: Which line uses consonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: The ck sound repeats inside “flashed, flickered, cracked.”
explanation.tip: Consonance is often easiest to hear near the ends of words.

options.label: A
options.text: The bright lights flashed, flickered, and cracked.

options.label: B
options.text: The crowd cheered loudly below.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat one consonant sound.

options.label: C
options.text: The fireworks lit up the night sky.
options.rationale: No inside or ending consonant sound repeats across several words here.

items.stem: Which line uses alliteration?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Quiet, quick, questions” repeat the qu sound at the start.
explanation.tip: Alliteration can repeat a sound spelled the same way, like qu.

options.label: A
options.text: The library was calm and still.
options.rationale: No repeated beginning sounds appear in this line.

options.label: B
options.text: Quiet, quick questions filled the library.

options.label: C
options.text: Students studied at the long tables.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat one beginning sound.

items.stem: Which line uses assonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: “Pale, whale, sailed, away, daybreak” all share the long a sound.
explanation.tip: Stretch out the vowels as you read the line to notice the repeated sound.

options.label: A
options.text: The ocean was calm that morning.
options.rationale: This line does not repeat one vowel sound.

options.label: B
options.text: The whale swam near the boat.
options.rationale: No single vowel sound repeats through several words here.

options.label: C
options.text: The pale whale sailed away at daybreak.

items.stem: Which line uses consonance?

explanation.whyCorrect: The r sound repeats inside “trucks, rolled, horns, blared, flared.”
explanation.tip: Consonance can repeat a sound in several different positions within words.

options.label: A
options.text: Trucks rolled past, horns blared and flared.

options.label: B
options.text: Trucks rolled slowly down the street.
options.rationale: No inside or ending consonant sound repeats across several words here.
